name: Mucopolysaccharidosis | type I-H/S
description: Attenuated mucopolysaccharidosis type I (Hurler Scheie) is a progressive multisystem lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha L iduronidase deficiency, leading to dermatan and heparan sulfate buildup and worsening joint restriction and skeletal disease, corneal clouding with vision loss risk, and cardiac valve thickening. Weekly lifelong intravenous laronidase can improve some non neurologic features but often does not halt progression in eyes, valves, joints, or spine and carries infusion burden and anaphylaxis risk, leaving a need for safer, more durable disease modifying therapies that reach hard to treat tissues.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent/reverse progressive arthropathy (large joints/hands) and spinal disease/cord compression not improved by IV laronidase ERT
- Improve/prevent corneal clouding–related vision loss and slow cardiac valvular disease progression not impacted by ERT
- Reduce weekly multi-hour IV infusion burden and infusion-related risks (venous access issues, hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis) versus chronic laronidase

name: Polycystic ovary syndrome
description: Polycystic ovary syndrome is a hormone imbalance disorder often involving insulin resistance, with ovulatory dysfunction and androgen excess causing irregular or absent periods, hirsutism, acne, weight gain, and infertility. There is no cure and care is largely symptom focused, while clinicians try to reduce long term risks such as type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and endometrial hyperplasia or cancer. Key unmet needs include disease modifying options and pregnancy compatible treatments, since common weight loss and antiandrogen drugs have pregnancy constraints and fertility induction can require intensive monitoring and carries multiple pregnancy risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pregnancy-safe anti-androgen therapy for hirsutism without mandatory effective contraception
- Fertility-compatible anti-obesity/metabolic therapy for higher-weight PCOS with better tolerability/durability and no contraception requirement
- Ovulation induction that lowers multiple pregnancy/OHSS risk and reduces intensity of ultrasound monitoring

name: Atopic dermatitis
description: Atopic dermatitis is a common, chronic immune driven eczema marked by skin barrier dysfunction and intense itch that can drive a scratch rash cycle and disrupt sleep. Care often requires frequent moisturizers and topical anti inflammatories, but adherence drops quickly, leaving many patients under controlled. When disease escalates, systemic options can improve control yet bring tradeoffs such as ocular side effects with dupilumab and serious safety warnings for Janus kinase inhibitors, sustaining demand for faster, more durable itch and sleep relief with simpler long term regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid, durable itch reduction with meaningful sleep restoration for AD patients with severe pruritus/sleep loss
- High-efficacy systemic therapy for refractory moderate–severe AD without dupilumab-linked ocular AEs or JAK inhibitor boxed-warning risks
- Simplified, low-burden regimens that replace multi-step daily topical routines to improve adherence

name: Subclavian steal syndrome
description: Subclavian steal syndrome is usually caused by proximal subclavian artery stenosis or occlusion, most often atherosclerosis, which reverses vertebral artery flow and can divert blood from the brain to the arm. Many patients are asymptomatic, but some develop exertional arm claudication with vertebrobasilar symptoms such as dizziness, vertigo, syncope, or blurred vision. Management relies on vascular risk reduction and antiplatelet based therapy, with revascularization for symptomatic disease, yet drug only options have limited evidence and stenting durability is constrained by 12 to 18.7% restenosis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drug therapy for symptomatic relief in medically refractory symptomatic subclavian artery stenosis/coronary subclavian steal (alternative to revascularization)
- Adjunct pharmacotherapy to prevent/mitigate in-stent restenosis and improve long-term durability after subclavian stenting
- Lower-bleeding-risk, better-tolerated antithrombotic strategies for chronic prevention and peri-/post-stent periods (vs aspirin/clopidogrel regimens)

name: Combined hyperlipidemia
description: Inherited dyslipidemia with fluctuating mixed hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia, often silent until adulthood, that drives premature coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction; key unmet needs are reducing triglyceride rich lipoprotein driven residual cardiovascular risk despite optimal low density lipoprotein lowering, and improving long term persistence given statin myalgias and high discontinuation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Outcomes-proven residual ASCVD risk reduction (MACE) for mixed dyslipidemia patients with elevated remnant cholesterol/TG-rich lipoproteins despite statin-based LDL-C control.
- Non-statin LDL‑C/apoB-lowering options for statin-intolerant/discontinuing patients that minimize muscle-symptom–driven discontinuation.
- Simplified or low-frequency dosing (e.g., fixed-dose combos or infrequent clinic-administered therapy) to improve ≥1-year adherence/persistence vs multi-drug oral regimens.

name: Non-small cell lung cancer | squamous
description: Smoking-associated central-airway non-small cell lung cancer causing cough, dyspnea, chest pain and hemoptysis; often presents late with few actionable mutations, and after first-line chemo-immunotherapy later-line options (eg docetaxel ± antiangiogenic therapy) have modest benefit and many patients deteriorate before further treatment.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Overall-survival–improving therapy for metastatic squamous NSCLC after progression on platinum chemotherapy + PD‑1/PD‑L1 inhibitors (vs docetaxel benchmark)
- Biomarker-selected targeted therapies for squamous-enriched oncogenic drivers where prior PI3K/cell-cycle/FGFR1 strategies have failed
- Better-tolerated, less burdensome regimens (fewer serious AEs and reduced infusion-visit burden) for the typical older, smoking-associated central-airway sqNSCLC population

name: Hyponatremia
description: Hyponatremia is low blood sodium, common in older hospitalized or medically complex patients, where water shifts into cells and can cause neurologic dysfunction from gait and memory problems to seizures and coma. Care is often driven by lab monitoring yet remains hard to manage because first line fluid restriction is frequently impractical or ineffective and sodium correction must be tightly controlled to avoid osmotic demyelination. Pharmacologic options are constrained, with tolvaptan requiring inpatient initiation and limited to 30 days, leaving a need for safer, predictable, outpatient friendly therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Outpatient oral therapy that maintains Na ≥130–135 mEq/L without strict fluid restriction/urea palatability issues and without vaptan limits (hospital initiation, <30-day use/liver-toxicity concern)
- Acute severe hyponatremia regimen with rapid-on/rapid-off titration (or an on-demand “brake”) to hit +4–6 mEq/L initially while capping total correction ≤8–10 mEq/L/24h to reduce overcorrection/ODS and intensive monitoring burden
- Therapies for older adults with mild chronic hyponatremia that improve functional endpoints (falls, gait stability, attention/cognition) beyond serum sodium normalization

name: Wart | Plantar
description: Plantar warts are contagious human papillomavirus lesions on the sole, common in children and young adults, that can be painful on weight bearing. They often persist for months to years, and current options such as topical salicylic acid and cryotherapy are slow, irritating or painful, and inconsistently effective, with low short term clearance and frequent recurrence because treatments remove infected skin rather than eradicate the virus.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, high-complete-clearance therapy for stubborn/recalcitrant plantar (incl. palmo-plantar) warts with low recurrence, including better efficacy in immunosuppressed patients
- Child-/adolescent-appropriate weight-bearing–site therapy minimizing pain/blistering and avoiding scarring/pigment change
- Shorter, simpler primarily at-home regimens (fewer steps/clinic visits) vs ≥12-week daily prep and repeated cryotherapy visits

name: Chlamydia trachomatis infection
description: Chlamydia trachomatis is a common sexually transmitted bacterial infection that is frequently asymptomatic and therefore detected mainly through screening. When untreated it can progress to pelvic inflammatory disease with lasting reproductive harm including infertility and ectopic pregnancy, and repeat infections further increase risk. Antibiotics clear infection but cannot reverse established tissue damage, and there is no licensed vaccine, leaving major unmet needs in scalable prevention and adherence friendly regimens that reliably eradicate rectal infection where single dose therapy can underperform.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable primary-prevention vaccine for adolescents/young adults to prevent primary genital chlamydia infection and reinfection.
- Female-controlled, non-condom prophylaxis (e.g., on-demand vaginal microbicide/gel) to prevent urogenital C. trachomatis (ideally also gonorrhea).
- Single-dose or ultra-short-course oral cure matching doxycycline-like microbiologic cure for rectal (ideally oropharyngeal) infection.

name: Onychomycosis
description: Chronic fungal nail infection, usually of the great toenail, causing thickened brittle nails with subungual debris, lifting and sometimes pain. It is common in older adults and higher risk in diabetes, yet eradication is slow and relapse is frequent. Topicals often require nearly a year and are limited by poor nail penetration and adherence, while more effective oral antifungals carry systemic adverse effects and drug interaction risk, leaving demand for safer high efficacy therapies with durable clearance.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Improve complete-cure rates (negative mycology + 100% clear nail) in hard-to-treat/large-area or matrix-involved disease by overcoming poor nail penetration.
- Provide oral-level efficacy with fewer systemic safety constraints/monitoring for patients with liver disease, CHF, or major drug–drug interaction burden.
- Shorten/simplify regimens versus 48-week topicals while improving durability (lower relapse) and reducing resistance-linked treatment failure.

name: Migraine | with aura
description: Migraine with aura features gradually developing, reversible visual or sensory symptoms lasting 5 to 60 minutes followed by headache with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound, disproportionately affecting women. Aura is thought to reflect cortical spreading depression. Key unmet needs include therapies proven to abort or shorten aura, nonvasoconstrictive acute options for patients with cardiovascular contraindications to triptans, and better tolerated, more reliably effective preventive treatments given discontinuations with topiramate and incomplete early response to calcitonin gene related peptide monoclonal antibodies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute therapy taken at aura onset to abort/reduce aura symptoms (including aura-without-headache) and prevent progression to headache.
- Non‑vasoconstrictive acute option with triptan‑like 2‑hour outcomes for patients with CV/CVA contraindications to triptans.
- Preventive with topiramate‑class efficacy but much better tolerability/persistence, and efficacy in the ~15–25% who don’t respond to anti‑CGRP mAbs.

name: Dry eye disease
description: Dry eye disease is a multifactorial ocular surface disorder caused by loss of tear film homeostasis, where tear film instability and hyperosmolarity drive a vicious cycle of inflammation, surface damage, and neurosensory dysfunction. Patients experience gritty burning discomfort, photophobia, blurred vision, and sometimes paradoxical tearing, often in older adults and post menopausal women. The condition spans aqueous deficient and evaporative forms, frequently linked to meibomian gland dysfunction, and some patients have neuropathic pain with few objective signs. Current management is largely chronic and symptomatic with limited high quality evidence, creating demand for therapies that restore meibomian lipid biology, improve pain control, and reduce daily treatment burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapies that restore meibomian gland/lipid-layer function for evaporative/MGD-driven DED.
- Treatments targeting neuropathic ocular pain (“symptoms ≫ signs”) phenotypes.
- Better-tolerated, lower-burden chronic therapy (less frequent dosing; fewer local AEs like burning/dysgeusia/sneezing) to reduce drop fatigue.

name: Hypertrophic scar
description: Hypertrophic scars are an excessive collagen response after acute skin injury that forms thick, firm, raised red scars confined to the original wound, often starting within weeks and causing itch, pain, and sometimes contractures with major quality of life impact. Current care is burdensome and inconsistent in the real world, relying on months of near continuous silicone or pressure therapy and often painful steroid injections with local side effects. Surgical or laser revision can recur, sometimes worse, creating unmet need for better prevention, more tolerable treatments, and durable post procedure recurrence control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- True prophylaxis in fresh high-risk wounds (burns/surgical incisions) to prevent hypertrophic scar formation without months-long wear-time regimens
- Post–scar-revision adjuvant therapy to prevent recurrence over ~6–12 months (e.g., improved POSAS/VSS outcomes) versus high regrowth after excision
- Non-steroid, low-pain therapies that reduce itch/pain and improve ROM (esp. scars over joints) while avoiding intralesional steroid injection pain and local AEs

name: Long COVID
description: Long COVID is a complex multisystem disorder after SARS-CoV-2 infection, with symptoms starting within 3 months and lasting at least 2 months, often dominated by fatigue, breathlessness, pain and cognitive dysfunction, and clusters like autonomic dysfunction and post-exertional malaise with delayed crashes. With no approved tests or specific treatments and limited evidence for disease-level pharmacologic options, care is largely symptom-based, leaving a major unmet need for mechanism-targeted, endotype-aware therapies that deliver sustained functional recovery rather than incremental symptom control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Biomarker-stratified disease-modifying therapy targeting root-cause endotypes (e.g., viral persistence) with sustained functional/QoL improvement.
- Targeted pharmacotherapy for the dysautonomia/POTS phenotype improving orthostatic intolerance symptom scores and stand/HR physiologic measures.
- PEM-focused therapy reducing delayed post-exertional symptom crashes (12–48h; days–weeks) while increasing safe functional capacity.

name: Arteriosclerosis obliterans
description: Arteriosclerosis obliterans is lower extremity peripheral artery disease where narrowed leg arteries reduce blood flow, typically in adults over 65, causing exertional leg pain that improves with rest and progressing in severe cases to rest pain, ulcers, gangrene, and amputation risk. Key unmet needs include therapies that meaningfully improve walking beyond modest cilostazol gains, bleeding sparing approaches to prevent ischemic events when intensifying antithrombotics, and true limb salvage options for the roughly 20% with critical limb ischemia who are not candidates for revascularization.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Claudication drug producing large, durable improvements in pain-free and maximal walking distance.
- Bleeding-sparing therapy to reduce MACE/MALE with efficacy comparable to rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BID + aspirin, enabling use in higher-bleeding-risk patients.
- Limb-salvage therapy for “no-option” chronic limb-threatening ischemia patients ineligible for revascularization, improving pain, wound healing, and amputation outcomes.

name: Vesicoureteral reflux
description: Vesicoureteral reflux is a pediatric urinary tract defect where urine flows backward from the bladder toward the ureters and kidneys, often found after a febrile urinary tract infection and risking recurrent infections and permanent renal scarring that can lead to later hypertension. Care relies on monitoring, long-term low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis and sometimes surgery, but prophylaxis can drive antibiotic resistance and reduces infection recurrence without clearly preventing new scarring, leaving a premium on non-antibiotic prevention, kidney-protective approaches, and lower-burden ways to track renal injury.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent recurrent febrile/symptomatic UTIs in pediatric post-UTI VUR while avoiding antibiotic-driven resistance
- Renal-protective adjuncts that prevent DMSA-defined new renal scarring (not just fewer UTIs)
- Therapies that drive durable reflux resolution or meaningfully reduce breakthrough febrile UTI in high-risk subgroups (grade III–V and/or BBD)

name: Nephropathy | diabetic
description: Diabetic nephropathy is progressive kidney injury from chronic hyperglycemia, where scarring of kidney filtering units causes albumin to leak into urine and a gradual decline in kidney function. It is often silent for years and detected through urine protein and blood kidney function tests, but later leads to fatigue, nausea, edema, shortness of breath, itching, and can progress to dialysis or transplant. Key unmet needs include better detection and treatment for the growing non-albuminuric phenotype and safer, easier-to-use therapies that avoid frequent potassium and kidney function monitoring and exclusion based on hyperkalemia risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Add-on renoprotective therapy that further reduces residual risk of kidney failure or sustained ≥40% eGFR decline despite optimized RASi + SGLT2i ± finerenone.
- Potassium-neutral antifibrotic/anti-inflammatory option usable in advanced DKD (including eGFR <20 mL/min/1.73m²) without hyperkalemia-driven exclusions/monitoring burden.
- Therapy proven to slow eGFR decline specifically in non-albuminuric DKD (eGFR decline without albuminuria), a phenotype underrepresented by albuminuria-gated trials.

name: Blepharoconjunctivitis
description: Blepharoconjunctivitis is chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins extending to the conjunctiva, causing burning or gritty foreign body sensation, tearing, itching, photophobia, and fluctuating vision, with lid erythema and debris plus conjunctival injection and superficial keratopathy. It is recurrent and can progress to corneal ulceration and scarring with visual impairment. Management relies on long term lid hygiene, while flares often require antibiotics or topical steroids that are limited by resistance, ocular surface toxicity, and risks like infection, cataract, and raised intraocular pressure, creating demand for safer steroid sparing and non antibiotic options including Demodex targeted approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable remission that reduces chronic long-term “maintenance” (hygiene/warm compress) burden
- Steroid-sparing control of eyelid + conjunctival inflammation avoiding IOP/glaucoma and cataract risks
- MGD/rosacea therapies that avoid systemic tetracycline tolerability issues and antibiotic-resistance pressure while improving objective signs/symptoms

name: Furunculosis
description: Recurrent furunculosis is a deep Staphylococcus aureus hair follicle infection that forms painful boils and abscesses on hair bearing skin, often in friction areas like armpits, buttocks, and thighs, and it persists through colonization and household spread despite treating flares. Prevention relies on burdensome multi step decolonization such as intranasal mupirocin, chlorhexidine washes, and laundering, with variable durability and concern for resistance, creating demand for simpler, longer lasting non mupirocin options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, household-level *S. aureus* carriage suppression/eradication that lowers boil/SSTI recurrence over months
- Non-mupirocin decolonization active vs mupirocin-resistant *S. aureus* to prevent recurrence without accelerating resistance
- Simpler, safer alternatives to today’s multi-step 5-day decolonization/decontamination regimen with comparable or better recurrence outcomes

name: Borderline personality disorder
description: Borderline personality disorder is a serious mental illness that typically begins in adolescence or early adulthood and is marked by severe emotion dysregulation, impulsivity, unstable self image, and chaotic relationships, often alongside depression, anxiety, post traumatic stress disorder, or substance use. Many patients cycle through crises with recurrent self harm and elevated suicide risk, frequently via medication overdose. Treatment relies on psychotherapy, yet no medicines are regulator approved for the disorder and guidelines discourage drug treatment for core symptoms, leaving a major unmet need for overdose safe, scalable options that reduce self injury and support durable functional recovery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Overdose-safe pharmacotherapy that reduces nonsuicidal self-injury and suicide attempts/overdose-driven crises
- Proven-efficacy medication for core BPD symptoms (beyond short-term adjunct use)
- Therapeutics that drive durable social/vocational functional recovery (not just symptom remission)

name: Myocardial infarction
description: Myocardial infarction is an acute blockage of coronary blood flow, often from plaque rupture and clot, causing oxygen deprivation and heart muscle death with chest discomfort, shortness of breath, and radiating upper body pain. Despite rapid reperfusion and secondary prevention, residual injury from coronary microvascular obstruction drives ongoing risk of adverse remodeling, heart failure, and mortality. Escalating antiplatelet intensity is constrained by bleeding, leaving a premium on therapies that protect microcirculation and myocardium while maintaining acceptable safety.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct peri-primary-PCI cardioprotection in STEMI to prevent microvascular obstruction/no‑reflow, differentiated on CMR infarct size/MVO/myocardial salvage endpoints.
- Post‑MI remodeling/heart-failure prevention in high-risk survivors (e.g., CKD/diabetes), differentiated by lowering incident HF and HF hospitalizations post-discharge.
- Bleeding-sparing antithrombotic regimens for elderly/high-bleeding-risk ACS/MI patients on prolonged DAPT ± anticoagulation, lowering major bleeding/hospitalizations without increasing ischemic events.

name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
description: Carpal tunnel syndrome is median nerve compression at the wrist causing numbness and tingling in the thumb to ring fingers that often wakes patients at night and can progress to hand weakness and permanent dysfunction. Current nonoperative care such as splinting and corticosteroid injections is common but typically temporary, with guideline evidence showing no long term benefit, and injections can transiently raise blood glucose in people with diabetes. Surgery helps many but symptoms can recur, often from scarring around the median nerve, leaving demand for more durable non surgical, nerve sparing options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable non-surgical therapy delivering ≥12-month sustained symptom + function improvement (e.g., BCTQ-based) for mild–moderate CTS patients avoiding surgery
- Non-steroid local injectate/topical providing steroid-like symptom relief without clinically meaningful post-injection hyperglycemia in diabetics
- Peri-/post-operative anti-fibrotic or anti-scar adjunct to reduce median-nerve scarring and recurrent symptoms/revision after carpal tunnel release

name: Peripheral artery disease
description: Atherosclerotic narrowing of arteries outside the heart that reduces limb blood flow, often in older smokers and patients with diabetes, hypertension, or hyperlipidemia. Many are asymptomatic or develop exertional leg pain that limits function, progressing in severe cases to rest pain, nonhealing ulcers, gangrene, and amputation. Key gaps include safer, bleeding sparing antithrombotic strategies after revascularization, symptom therapies for claudication that are usable in heart failure, and limb salvage options for no option critical limb ischemia when revascularization is not feasible.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- VOYAGER-PAD–level event reduction after LER without increased ISTH major bleeding (bleeding-sparing antithrombotic efficacy).
- Convenient claudication therapy that improves walking distance and is safe in any-severity heart failure (cilostazol-contraindicated) to reduce reliance on intensive SET.
- Limb-salvage pharmacotherapy for “no-option” CLTI (often diabetes/ESRD) that improves wound healing and 1-year amputation-free survival.

name: Thin basement membrane disease
description: Inherited type IV collagen glomerular disorder with uniformly thinned glomerular basement membrane causing persistent microscopic hematuria, often found incidentally with normal kidney function. Most cases are benign, but development of proteinuria can signal higher risk progression to chronic kidney disease. Care is surveillance and supportive renoprotection with no disease specific therapy, leaving unmet needs in risk stratification and disease modifying treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Add-on renoprotective therapies for higher-risk TBMD (proteinuria/HTN) to improve albuminuria (UACR) and preserve eGFR beyond ACEi/ARB
- Hematuria-directed drugs to reduce glomerular bleeding (micro-/macrohematuria episodes), beyond reassurance/monitoring
- Mutation-targeted disease modification for COL4/type-IV-collagen TBMD to restore GBM integrity and prevent progression to Alport-spectrum CKD/ESKD

name: Glaucoma | open-angle
description: Open-angle glaucoma is a progressive optic nerve disease that often has no early symptoms and is typically detected on routine eye exams after peripheral vision loss begins. Care centers on lowering intraocular pressure, usually with daily eye drops, but real-world adherence is poor at around 60 percent and preservatives such as benzalkonium chloride can drive ocular surface disease. Some patients still progress despite pressure control, including those with normal-tension glaucoma, creating demand for preservative-sparing, sustained-release drug delivery and neuroprotective, disease-modifying approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Sustained-release IOP-lowering delivery to replace multi-dose daily drops and improve adherence/self-administration.
- Preservative-free/BAK-free (ocular-surface–sparing) IOP-lowering options for patients with ocular surface disease/dry eye worsened by current drops.
- IOP-independent/adjunctive neuroprotective therapies to preserve retinal ganglion cells for patients who progress despite controlled IOP (e.g., normal-tension glaucoma).

name: Uterine cancer
description: Uterine cancer, usually endometrial cancer, typically affects postmenopausal women and presents with abnormal vaginal bleeding; while most cases are diagnosed localized, high risk or extrauterine disease often relapses despite adjuvant therapy, and advanced treatments can be toxic, while fertility sparing progesterone regimens have high recurrence (20–50%).
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Better-tolerated, high-efficacy systemic therapy for pMMR/MSS advanced/recurrent endometrial cancer to improve OS/PFS with less severe toxicity than lenvatinib+pembrolizumab
- Biomarker-driven therapies for high-risk uterine subtypes (uterine serous carcinoma/carcinosarcoma; HER2/TP53-altered) to reduce spread/recurrence and improve survival, with safer HER2-targeting than ILD-prone ADCs
- More durable fertility-sparing medical therapy for stage IA, grade 1 endometrioid endometrial cancer to increase complete-response rates and reduce recurrence vs current progestin/IUD approaches

name: Epiretinal membrane
description: Epiretinal membrane (macular pucker) is a fibrocellular layer on the inner retinal surface that wrinkles the macula, causing slowly progressive central vision distortion (wavy lines, reading difficulty) often in one eye of older adults. Most cases are monitored, but there is no vision restoring drug or laser therapy, leaving vitrectomy with membrane peeling as the main option with tradeoffs including incomplete visual recovery, frequent cataract acceleration, and some recurrence risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical, vision-improving therapy for symptomatic idiopathic ERM to reduce metamorphopsia and improve reading/detail vision.
- Anti-fibrotic prophylaxis to prevent secondary ERM after eye surgery/trauma/intraocular inflammation/diabetic retinopathy/retinal vein occlusion.
- Peri-/post-vitrectomy adjunct pharmacotherapy to reduce cataract acceleration, ERM recurrence, and other vitrectomy complications.

name: Otitis externa
description: Otitis externa, or swimmer’s ear, is acute inflammation or infection of the outer ear canal, typically in teens and young adults, causing intense itching and pain worsened by tragus or pinna movement plus drainage, fullness, and temporary hearing loss. Management relies on 10 to 14 days of topical antibiotic drops, but real world care is limited by poor drop delivery when the canal is swollen or obstructed, the need for cleaning or wicks, and safety constraints when the eardrum is perforated or tubes are present. Fungal cases can recur and become harder to eradicate, driving interest in simplified single dose otic therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non‑ototoxic, low‑sensitization ototopical anti‑infective for patients with non‑intact TM/tympanostomy tubes and/or neomycin sensitivity
- Long‑acting (single‑application) or low‑frequency otic formulation that maintains efficacy despite canal edema/debris to reduce need for aural toilet/wick and dosing errors
- Relapse‑resistant antifungal therapy/formulation for otomycosis with durable symptom and fungal clearance

name: Stuttering
description: Stuttering is a childhood-onset fluency disorder marked by repetitions, prolongations, and speech blocks, sometimes with visible struggle behaviors, that can drive anxiety, avoidance, and major quality-of-life impact into adulthood. Care is still dominated by speech-language therapy and coping strategies that can be costly and variably effective, while many children recover but a meaningful subset develops persistent, lifelong impairment. There is no cure and no Food and Drug Administration approved medication, with off-label drugs constrained by side effects, leaving a clear unmet need for safe, durable, disease-modifying and scalable interventions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- FDA-approved medication option for persistent developmental stuttering post–speech therapy, improving fluency and life-impact endpoints (SSI-4, OASES-A) and reducing anxiety/avoidance
- Better-tolerated long-term pharmacotherapy that avoids dopamine/antipsychotic adverse effects (EPS/tardive dyskinesia, akathisia, weight gain/metabolic burden)
- Pediatric-safe, home-administered adjunct drug options that reduce the time/logistics burden of parent/SLP-led behavioral therapy (weekly visits + daily practice)

name: Keloid scar
description: Keloids are aggressive fibroproliferative scars that grow beyond the original wound and persist, disproportionately affecting younger people and those with darker skin, often causing itching or pain and major cosmetic and psychosocial burden. Care depends on repeated office procedures such as serial injections, pressure devices, and excision, yet regrowth is common and recurrence after surgery is frequently very high, driving demand for durable, lower burden, steroid sparing treatments that better control symptoms and prevent recurrence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct/local therapy that delivers low 1-year keloid recurrence after excision/debulking.
- Non-steroid or steroid-sparing option effective in steroid-resistant/intolerant patients with meaningful POSAS/VSS + scar-height improvements and fewer local AEs (atrophy/telangiectasia/dyspigmentation).
- Self-administered or long-acting therapy that improves symptoms/QoL (DLQI) while reducing months of monthly injections and prolonged pressure-device wear.

name: Melanoma | cutaneous
description: Cutaneous melanoma is a malignancy of pigment producing melanocytes, often presenting in adults in their fifties to seventies as a new or changing mole. Most cases are caught early and cured with excision, but advanced disease remains hard to control. Many patients eventually develop resistance to programmed cell death 1 inhibitors and symptomatic brain metastases respond poorly. Even in the adjuvant setting, immune checkpoint therapy can cause serious immune related toxicity, creating a premium for more durable, brain active, and better tolerated treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Effective post–anti–PD‑1 progression therapies for metastatic/advanced cutaneous melanoma with substantially higher and more durable responses vs current options
- Systemic treatments that achieve meaningful intracranial responses in melanoma brain metastases, especially symptomatic/steroid‑requiring patients
- Better‑tolerated, less burdensome adjuvant options for resected Stage IIB/IIC melanoma (lower severe immune toxicity/discontinuation; reduced infusion burden)

name: Wart | Genital
description: Genital warts are common, benign, contagious anogenital growths usually caused by low risk human papillomavirus types 6 or 11, often painless but sometimes itchy or bleeding and frequently associated with psychosocial distress. Care focuses on clearing visible lesions with topical therapies or destructive in clinic procedures, but the virus persists so recurrences are common, especially early, and treatments can be painful and take weeks to months. The biggest gaps are faster, better tolerated, more durable clearance, particularly for immunosuppressed patients who respond less well and relapse more often.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, recurrence-suppressing therapy to reduce high short-term relapse, including improved efficacy in HIV/immunosuppressed patients with larger/more numerous lesions and poorer responses
- Non-caustic, low-pain therapy achieving clearance without ulceration/erosion/inflammatory reactions and minimizing collateral tissue injury
- Short-course or single-visit pharmacotherapy to replace prolonged/frequent topical regimens and reduce need for repeated follow-up/weekly clinic applications

name: Cholelithiasis
description: Cholelithiasis is gallstone formation in the gallbladder, often asymptomatic until episodic biliary colic causes hours long postprandial right upper quadrant or epigastric pain and can progress to cholecystitis, cholangitis, or pancreatitis. Management still relies on analgesics and laparoscopic cholecystectomy, with limited noninvasive options since oral dissolution is slow and recurrence is common, and rising rapid weight loss and bariatric surgery increase demand for practical prevention strategies such as ursodiol prophylaxis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical, durable gallstone clearance for symptomatic patients who are not surgical candidates (beyond the narrow current oral-dissolution-eligible subgroup).
- More adherence-friendly prophylaxis to prevent gallstones during rapid weight loss (e.g., bariatric/VLCD/GLP‑1RA weight-loss regimens) vs temporary UDCA.
- Safer “rescue” pharmacotherapy for biliary colic matching NSAID-level analgesia while avoiding NSAID CV/GI and opioid respiratory-depression risks.

name: Osteoarthritis
description: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease where cartilage and other joint tissues progressively break down, sometimes to bone on bone rubbing with bone spurs, causing pain, swelling, and loss of motion. It typically presents in adults aged 45 or older with activity related joint pain and brief morning stiffness. There is no cure, so care is largely symptomatic with analgesics limited by systemic safety risks and steroid injections that often provide only short lived relief.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-/structure-modifying therapy for progressive knee/hip OA that slows/stops/reverses joint damage and delays arthroplasty
- Non-NSAID (or systemic-sparing) chronic analgesics for older/comorbid OA patients that improve pain/function without GI/renal/liver/CV toxicity limits
- Longer-acting intra-articular therapies that deliver materially longer pain relief to reduce repeat injection burden vs short-lived IA corticosteroids

name: Chronic cough | refractory
description: Refractory chronic cough is a persistent, usually dry cough driven by cough hypersensitivity, with throat tickle and urge to cough triggered by irritants like perfume or cold air. It disproportionately affects women in their 50s to 60s and can cause exhaustion, sleep disruption, social embarrassment, difficulty speaking, and urinary incontinence. Despite thorough workup and guideline based care, patients often cycle through cough control therapy and off label neuromodulators or low dose opioids limited by side effects. Newer P2X3 antagonists can markedly reduce cough frequency but taste disturbance remains a key tolerability barrier.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-opioid antitussive with step-change improvement in 24‑h cough frequency and LCQ QoL vs current P2X3 standards
- Taste-sparing therapy minimizing dysgeusia/ageusia (key limitation of gefapixant)
- Non-sedating, low-burden option avoiding gabapentinoid CNS effects/opioid side effects and reducing titration/long follow-up needs

name: Photoallergic dermatitis
description: Photoallergic dermatitis is an eczema-like rash triggered when ultraviolet light converts a topical or systemic chemical exposure into a delayed immune reaction. It typically appears 24 to 72 hours after sun as an intensely itchy eruption on sun-exposed areas such as the face, neck, V of chest, and dorsal hands, and can become chronic and lichenified. Care relies on identifying and avoiding the culprit and strict photoprotection, with topical anti-inflammatories and occasional systemic steroids, but options are limited by steroid toxicity on thin facial skin and the practical challenge that common chemical sunscreen filters such as oxybenzone can themselves be photoallergens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Hypoallergenic, broad-spectrum photoprotection options for patients with sunscreen-filter PACD (esp. oxybenzone/benzophenone-3).
- Steroid-sparing topical therapies for thin, sun-exposed sites (face/eyelids/neck) with improved tolerability and no atrophy risk.
- Systemic steroid–sparing treatments for widespread/extensive photocontact dermatitis (>20% BSA) to avoid repeat oral corticosteroid courses.

name: Psoriasis | plaque
description: Chronic immune mediated inflammatory skin disease with thick scaly plaques often on elbows knees trunk and sometimes scalp palms soles genitals with common nail involvement. No cure and relapse is common without maintenance therapy so key unmet needs are durable deep clearance after stopping treatment and more reliable control of high impact sites especially nails that drive quality of life burden even with limited body surface area.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies achieving PASI90+ with durable treatment‑free remission after stopping therapy
- Reliable clearance of hard‑to‑treat sites (scalp, nails, palmoplantar, genital) even with low BSA involvement
- High‑clearance, non‑injectable, low‑monitoring long‑term options reducing injection anxiety/topical burden and serious infection risk

name: Molluscum contagiosum
description: Molluscum contagiosum is a common poxvirus skin infection in children ages 1 to 10 causing small, umbilicated pearly papules that are often painless but itchy. It spreads by contact and contaminated objects and can persist for months to years, staying contagious until all lesions clear, driving demand for faster clearance. Unmet needs include better tolerated, lower irritation treatments that can be used on sensitive sites and more effective options for immunosuppressed patients who may develop numerous larger, refractory lesions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Immune-safe therapy that reliably clears extensive/recalcitrant molluscum in immunocompromised patients (e.g., HIV/AIDS) who often fail standard approaches
- Faster, higher complete-clearance regimen (majority cleared by ~Week 4–6) to shorten the infectious/autoinoculation window vs ~12-week treatment horizons
- Non-vesicant, low-pain topical usable on periocular + genital/mucosal lesions with fewer local reactions vs current site-restricted, high-reaction options

name: Major depressive disorder
description: Major depressive disorder is a common, serious psychiatric illness marked by at least two weeks of depressed mood or loss of interest that disrupts daily functioning, sleep, appetite, and work, and in severe cases can lead to hospitalization or suicide. Treatment is constrained by slow onset of standard antidepressants, frequent tolerability issues such as sexual dysfunction, and limited access to truly rapid relief since fast acting options like esketamine are tied to supervised, in clinic dosing with post dose monitoring.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid-acting antidepressant for TRD/acute suicidality that can be self-administered at home/outpatient (avoiding clinic-based monitoring requirements).
- Therapies that achieve “clean” remission by eliminating residual symptoms and improving functional recovery beyond symptom-score remission.
- Maintenance antidepressants with substantially better tolerability/adherence—lower discontinuation and sexual-dysfunction burden than SSRIs.

name: Microvascular angina
description: Microvascular angina causes chronic chest pain from dysfunction and spasm in the heart’s smallest coronary vessels, often leaving patients symptomatic despite normal large artery imaging. It disproportionately affects women, especially around menopause, and is not benign with elevated risk of major adverse cardiovascular events and death. Care is hampered by limited high quality trial evidence and disappointing response and tolerability with nitrates, leaving persistent angina and poor quality of life. The field is moving toward endotype guided, mechanism based therapies such as targeting endothelin 1 signaling or alternative vasodilator pathways.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Biomarker-/endotype-selected endothelin-A antagonism (zibotentan-class) for endothelin-driven microvascular vasoconstriction/spasm, improving exercise time and angina/QoL.
- Non-nitrate vasodilator options for nitrate-nonresponsive microvascular angina (e.g., PDE-5 inhibition) to improve coronary flow reserve.
- Disease-modifying CMD therapies that reverse microvascular pathology and reduce hard outcomes (MACE), especially in severe mixed structural+functional endotypes.

name: Von Willebrand disease | type 1
description: Type 1 von Willebrand disease is the most common, mildest form of von Willebrand disease, caused by low or dysfunctional von Willebrand factor leading to mucocutaneous bleeding such as nosebleeds, easy bruising, heavy menstrual bleeding, and procedure related bleeding that may only emerge after hemostatic challenges. Current control relies on desmopressin and antifibrinolytics, but response is variable and limited by tachyphylaxis and hyponatremia related fluid restriction, while intravenous factor infusions are costly and inconvenient for patients needing more reliable coverage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Hyponatremia-free, repeat-dose–reliable on-demand “VWF-boosting” therapy for type 1 VWD that avoids desmopressin tachyphylaxis and lab/water-restriction burden
- Menstrual-bleed–focused therapies for women with VWD that materially improve function/QoL (reduce heavy menstrual bleeding limitations)
- Convenient non-IV prophylaxis for “frequent bleeders” (high annualized bleed rates) that reduces bleeding events without IV concentrate burden

name: Hydronephrosis
description: Hydronephrosis is kidney swelling from urine backing up behind an obstruction, often from benign prostatic hyperplasia or ureteral stones, and can be silent or cause flank pain, nausea and vomiting, urinary symptoms, and infection. Care hinges on urgent decompression with stents or percutaneous drainage to prevent permanent kidney damage, but gaps remain in evidence based adjunct medical therapy, fibrosis can persist after obstruction relief, stone passage options are limited beyond alpha blockers, and pain control is constrained by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug renal risk and opioid safety issues.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Renoprotective anti-fibrotic therapy to preserve renal recovery in prolonged/recurrent obstructive hydronephrosis despite delayed decompression
- Next-gen medical expulsive therapy that reliably increases ureteral stone expulsion (esp. distal stones >5 mm), shortens time-to-expulsion, and reduces need for invasive procedures vs alpha-blocker MET
- Outpatient renal-colic analgesia with NSAID-level efficacy but lower CV/GI risk than NSAIDs and lower addiction/respiratory-depression risk than opioids/tramadol

name: Peptic ulcer disease
description: Peptic ulcer disease is mucosal breakdown in the stomach or duodenum, usually due to Helicobacter pylori infection or long term nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, causing burning epigastric pain with nausea, bloating and early satiety and risking bleeding, perforation or obstruction; key unmet needs are simpler, more reliable Helicobacter pylori eradication as antimicrobial resistance rises and pill burden limits adherence, and better strategies to prevent recurrent bleeding in high risk patients who must continue aspirin or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Resistance-robust *H. pylori* eradication for patients with (known/likely) clarithromycin-resistant infection and/or prior macrolide exposure where standard regimens have low cure rates
- High-cure *H. pylori* regimens with lower pill burden/simpler dosing to improve adherence vs 14-day multi-times-daily bismuth quadruple therapy
- Improved ulcer/upper-GI bleeding prevention for patients who must continue NSAIDs/aspirin/antithrombotics, reducing recurrent bleeding despite PPI co-therapy and improving tolerability

name: Venous leg ulcer
description: Venous leg ulcers are chronic, often painful and exudative open sores on the lower leg caused by venous insufficiency and venous hypertension leading to skin breakdown and stalled healing. Standard care is compression plus wound care, but real world adherence is limited by pain, drainage, and application difficulty, so healing can take months and some ulcers never close. Even after closure, recurrence is a major unmet need, with 12 month recurrence reported at 26% to 69%, underscoring demand for more durable, easier to use disease modifying approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct topical/systemic pro-healing drug achieving confirmed complete venous leg ulcer closure by Week 12 for non-healing/recalcitrant ulcers
- Post-closure maintenance pharmacotherapy to prevent high venous leg ulcer recurrence (up to ~70% at 5 years)
- Pain/exudate-reducing, skin-tolerable adjunct drug that improves compression adherence/usability and reduces frequent dressing/bandage changes (1–3×/week)

name: Allergy | peanut
description: Peanut allergy is an immunoglobulin E mediated food allergy where reactions can occur within minutes to two hours of exposure and range from wheezing to severe vomiting or diarrhea, sometimes triggered by trace amounts, especially in high risk infants with severe eczema. Despite risk reducing options such as Palforzia and omalizumab, there is no cure, so patients must maintain strict avoidance and carry epinephrine for breakthrough anaphylaxis. The biggest gaps are safer lower burden treatments that provide durable protection or remission off treatment.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable remission/sustained unresponsiveness after stopping therapy (beyond on-treatment desensitization)
- Safer disease-modifying therapy than peanut OIT with far fewer serious treatment-triggered reactions and fewer exclusions (e.g., asthma/EoE risk)
- Lower-burden, scalable protection against accidental exposure with less clinic monitoring and less frequent dosing while maintaining meaningful food-challenge thresholds

name: Tenosynovitis
description: Tenosynovitis is inflammation of the tendon sheath, often in the wrist and hand, causing pain, swelling, and impaired movement. It can follow overuse or strain or be driven by inflammatory disease or infection, with infectious cases needing prompt treatment. Care relies on rest or splinting, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and corticosteroid injections, but symptoms often recur and may progress to surgery in stenosing forms like trigger finger. Splinting can fail due to high recurrence and low compliance, and steroid injections are less effective in diabetes and can temporarily raise blood sugar.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, recurrence-preventing local therapy (steroid-sparing and/or sustained-release) for stenosing tenosynovitis (trigger finger/de Quervain’s) to reduce repeat injections/surgery.
- Diabetes-tailored, steroid-sparing treatment for trigger finger to avoid steroid-induced hyperglycemia while maintaining symptom control.
- NSAID-sparing, convenient self-administered anti-inflammatory analgesia (e.g., superior topical/local delivery) to reduce systemic NSAID risk and prolonged splint burden.

name: Erythrasma
description: Erythrasma is a chronic superficial Corynebacterium minutissimum infection of moist skin folds and toe webs, causing sharply bordered reddish brown scaly patches with minimal itch and coral red Wood lamp fluorescence, often in overweight or diabetic adults. It is frequently mistaken for fungal intertrigo, delaying appropriate therapy. Current care relies on topical antibiotics and oral macrolides for extensive or recurrent disease, but recurrence is common when sweating and occlusion persist, and interdigital cases often have mixed fungal and gram negative co infection that can defeat single agent regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Relapse-prevention/maintenance therapy for recurrent intertriginous erythrasma in high-risk patients (e.g., obesity/diabetes/hyperhidrosis) when predisposing factors persist.
- Macrolide-sparing, US-available topical/oral options for erythromycin/clarithromycin non-responders that improve complete response and reduce systemic AEs.
- Combination regimens for toe-web/interdigital and tinea look-alike/mixed intertrigo presentations (antibacterial ± antifungal/anti-biofilm/keratolytic) to eradicate hidden reservoirs and avoid ineffective antifungal-only care.

name: Trichuriasis
description: Trichuriasis is a whipworm infection of the large intestine, concentrated in children living in tropical settings with poor sanitation. Many cases are asymptomatic, but heavy worm burdens can cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, bloody stools, rectal prolapse, iron deficiency anemia, and growth retardation. Treatment relies on benzimidazoles such as albendazole and mebendazole, yet cure rates with single dose regimens are often poor and highly variable, undermining mass drug administration. Better reliably curative short course regimens and deployable alternative or combination therapies remain the key unmet need.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- High-cure, short-course (ideally single-dose) oral therapy for moderate/heavy-intensity trichuriasis where benzimidazoles underperform.
- More effective MDA-suitable regimen (new MoA and/or combination) that reliably clears whipworm and reduces rapid post-treatment reinfection.
- Pediatric- and co-endemic–safe therapy/formulation deployable at scale (e.g., safe in children <15 kg and in Loa loa–endemic areas).

name: Rumination disorder
description: Rumination disorder is an under-recognized functional gastrointestinal condition marked by effortless regurgitation of recently eaten, undigested food for at least one month, driving avoidant eating, nutrition and quality-of-life impairment, and complications such as weight loss and dental enamel erosion. Treatment relies largely on intensive behavioral therapy such as diaphragmatic breathing and biofeedback, which is access and adherence dependent, with limited pharmacologic options like three-times-daily baclofen constrained by tolerability issues including dizziness and drowsiness.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, meal-independent pharmacotherapy for patients who fail or cannot access first-line diaphragmatic breathing/biofeedback
- Better-tolerated alternative to baclofen that reduces regurgitation without common CNS side effects (drowsiness/dizziness/headache)
- More convenient regimen than intensive meal-linked behavioral practice and TID baclofen (e.g., once-daily or pre-meal dosing)

name: Hypertensive crisis
description: Hypertensive crisis is severe blood pressure elevation above 180/120 mm Hg that splits into hypertensive urgency without acute target organ injury and hypertensive emergency with evolving organ damage, often triggered by antihypertensive nonadherence and presenting with headache, chest pain, dyspnea, neurologic changes, or vision symptoms. Care depends on rapid but carefully titrated intravenous blood pressure lowering under close monitoring, yet limited randomized outcomes evidence drives major practice variation and leaves unmet need for safer, easier-to-deliver, standardized acute therapies with proven outcome benefit.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid-onset acute BP lowering for hypertensive emergencies that achieves ~20–25% MAP reduction in 1–2 hours without continuous IV infusion/ICU-level monitoring.
- Acute antihypertensive with safer, more predictable titration that avoids major SoC safety/workflow liabilities (eg, labetalol postural hypotension, nicardipine phlebitis/line changes, nitroprusside precipitous hypotension/cyanide toxicity).
- RCT-proven agent + protocol that improves clinical outcomes (target-organ damage/mortality) and standardizes care vs current evidence gaps and practice variation.

name: Lipoma
description: Very common benign, slow growing subcutaneous fatty tumors presenting as soft, rubbery, mobile lumps in midlife. Most need no treatment, but bothersome or multiple lesions often require excision or liposuction, creating scar and repeat procedure burden and occasional recurrence with incomplete removal. Key unmet need is minimally invasive, cosmetically sparing options that reduce procedures, pain, bruising and visible scarring.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Scar-sparing intralesional lipolysis for cosmetically sensitive sites (e.g., face/neck) achieving near-complete clearance with low injection-site pain
- Capsule-eradicating injectable/enzymatic therapy to reduce recurrence versus approaches that leave capsule remnants
- Multi-lesion “field” therapy for multiple-lipoma phenotypes to avoid repeated excisions/scarring while maintaining good cosmetic outcomes

name: Post-cardiac arrest syndrome
description: Post-cardiac arrest syndrome is the abnormal physiology after return of spontaneous circulation following whole body ischemia, combining post-arrest brain injury, myocardial dysfunction, and systemic ischemia reperfusion response often with coma, seizures or myoclonus, and hypotension from myocardial stunning. Care is largely supportive intensive care with vasoactive support and targeted temperature management, while major unmet needs include therapies that prevent neurologic injury and improve reliable early prognostication.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early neuroprotection for comatose post-ROSC OHCA/IHCA patients to improve functional independence (e.g., 30-day mRS) beyond targeted temperature management (TTM)
- Post-ROSC shock therapies that stabilize hemodynamics and reduce vasopressor exposure/organ failure where no specific vasopressor is evidence-preferred
- Seizure/status-epilepticus control post-ROSC that minimizes sedative cardiopulmonary effects to enable earlier/cleaner neurologic assessment

name: Goiter | nodular
description: Nodular goiter is abnormal thyroid enlargement from one or more nodules, often with normal thyroid hormone levels, presenting as a neck lump that can progress to compressive breathing or swallowing symptoms. In autonomous nodules causing toxic multinodular goiter, drugs control hormone excess but are noncurative and carry rare severe toxicity, while definitive surgery or radioactive iodine can leave patients hypothyroid and dependent on lifelong replacement. Key unmet need is durable nodule shrinkage and symptom control that preserves thyroid function, with image guided ablation emerging as a minimally invasive option.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Thyroid-function–preserving medical therapy to shrink symptomatic benign euthyroid multinodular goiters/nodules (e.g., ≥28% volume reduction at 6 months with improved tracheal caliber/pressure symptoms), especially in low-RAI-uptake/large-goiter patients.
- Definitive pharmacologic control of toxic multinodular goiter/autonomously functioning nodules that restores euthyroidism while avoiding permanent post-RAI/surgery hypothyroidism.
- Safer long-term alternative to antithyroid drugs for patients needing medical therapy (avoid agranulocytosis and severe hepatotoxicity; reduce need for lifelong ATD exposure in TMNG).

name: Traveler’s diarrhea | enterotoxigenic E. coli
description: Travelers’ diarrhea is an abrupt-onset infectious gastroenteritis, often driven by enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli toxins, causing urgent watery stools with cramps and sometimes vomiting, fever, or bloody diarrhea. Most cases are self-limited, but moderate episodes can derail trips and prompt empiric antibiotic use. Management is constrained because travelers cannot reliably distinguish invasive from noninvasive disease in the field, creating demand for simpler, resistance-sparing self-treatment. Prevention is a major gap since no widely available vaccines cover common pathogens, and enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli vaccine development is challenged by antigenic diversity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-antibiotic (or resistance-sparing) oral therapy that delivers faster symptom relief / improved TLUS vs current antibiotics
- Single-dose empiric oral regimen safe/effective for invasive/dysenteric TD (no need to distinguish invasive vs noninvasive or carry backup antibiotics)
- Broadly protective ETEC immunoprophylaxis (vaccine or oral passive immunotherapy) covering multiple CFA antigens plus LT/ST toxins for high-risk travelers

name: Delayed puberty
description: Delayed puberty is late onset of sexual maturation, defined as no breast development by age 12 to 13 in girls or no testicular enlargement by age 13 to 14 in boys, often causing short stature and psychosocial distress. Many cases are constitutional, but chronic disease or hypogonadism can disrupt hypothalamus pituitary gonadal signaling. Care uses low dose sex steroids to trigger changes, yet testosterone induction in gonadotropin deficiency can virilize without testicular development or spermatogenesis, leaving a key unmet need for lower burden, fertility capable pubertal induction.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Fertility-capable pubertal induction for adolescent males with congenital/secondary hypogonadotropic hypogonadism using gonadotropins/HPG-axis agonists to drive testicular growth and spermatogenesis (vs testosterone-only virilization).
- More physiologic, ultra-low starting doses with fine-grained titration to mimic normal pubertal tempo and avoid growth/development harms from rapid hormone escalation.
- Lower-burden, pediatric-appropriate delivery that reduces painful frequent IM injections and patch-site irritation while preserving titratability (avoiding non-titratable long-acting depots).

name: Ocular hypertension
description: Ocular hypertension is elevated intraocular pressure above 21 mm Hg with no optic nerve damage or vision loss, usually asymptomatic and found on routine exams, but it raises glaucoma and irreversible vision loss risk. Management relies on pressure lowering eye drops and monitoring, yet real world control is limited by adherence problems, drop instillation burden, and preservative related ocular surface toxicity, while office hour testing can miss nocturnal pressure peaks. Key needs include better tolerated therapies, long acting drug delivery, and 24 hour pressure monitoring.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Repeatable multi‑month sustained‑release IOP lowering to replace daily drops and overcome poor adherence.
- BAK/BAC‑free chronic IOP‑lowering therapies to reduce preservative‑driven ocular surface disease/toxicity.
- Proven 24‑hour (especially nocturnal/supine) IOP control to prevent off‑hours pressure peaks missed in clinic.

name: Epicondylitis
description: Epicondylitis is an overuse elbow tendinopathy where repetitive forearm activity causes tendon microtears that fail to heal, leading to gradually worsening lateral or medial elbow pain, pain with gripping or twisting, and weak grip, sometimes with ulnar nerve tingling. Care is mainly rest, activity modification, bracing, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, but common injections can give short-term relief with high recurrence and poorer long-term outcomes, leaving a need for durable therapies that restore tendon healing and sustained function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable ≥12‑month pain + function improvement (e.g., PRTEE/QuickDASH) with materially lower recurrence than corticosteroid injection
- Tendon-healing/collagen-restoration therapies that improve objective tendon integrity on imaging alongside symptom scores
- Safer, non-invasive local analgesic/anti-inflammatory delivery avoiding systemic NSAID CV/GI risk and injection complications

name: Monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance
description: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance is an asymptomatic, premalignant plasma cell disorder marked by low monoclonal protein and no classic end organ damage, usually found incidentally in older adults. Care is mainly surveillance despite persistent progression risk and nonmalignant morbidity such as fractures, osteoporosis, renal disease, and infections. The key gap is distinguishing who will progress or suffer clone driven organ injury and enabling low toxicity, clone directed intervention for patients who cross into monoclonal gammopathy of clinical significance.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Low-toxicity “interception” therapy to prevent/delay progression in high-risk MGUS by eliminating abnormal plasma cells/M-protein.
- Clone-directed treatment for MGCS (e.g., MGRS) in patients without myeloma-defining criteria, including cases with hard-to-detect/track clones and inadequate response biomarkers.
- Bone-protective therapy tailored to MGUS-associated osteoporosis/vertebral fracture risk with long-term safety suitable for an otherwise asymptomatic population.

name: Cervical weakness
description: Cervical insufficiency is a pregnancy complication where the cervix painlessly dilates without contractions, often in the second trimester and sometimes only recognized after loss, leading to membrane exposure, miscarriage, or very early preterm birth. Care relies on surveillance, cerclage, and daily vaginal progesterone, but options are limited in twin pregnancies and rescue cerclage frequently fails when infection, inflammation, or preterm contractions intervene. This leaves a need for less burdensome, longer acting, biology targeted adjuncts that better prevent early delivery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct anti-infective/anti-inflammatory therapy around exam-indicated/rescue cerclage with exposed/prolapsed membranes to reduce intra-amniotic infection/inflammation and extend pregnancy latency.
- Pharmacologic prevention of spontaneous preterm birth in twin gestations with short cervix where current interventions remain “trial-only.”
- Long-acting/non-daily prophylaxis that maintains preterm-birth risk reduction while avoiding months of daily vaginal progesterone dosing.

name: Aneurysm | intracranial
description: Intracranial aneurysms are balloon-like outpouchings of brain arteries, often silent until rupture causes life threatening subarachnoid hemorrhage or stroke. Management hinges on surveillance imaging and invasive clipping or endovascular coiling, both with procedural risk and uncertain benefit for many unruptured aneurysms. A key unmet need is better prediction of which aneurysms will grow or rupture so patients can avoid overtreatment while high risk lesions are treated earlier, alongside safer preventive therapies and less morbid interventions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying pharmacotherapy to reduce growth/rupture risk in conservatively managed unruptured intracranial aneurysms not eligible for surgical/endovascular repair.
- More effective prevention of delayed cerebral ischemia after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage beyond nimodipine, improving functional outcomes.
- Safer, less variable antiplatelet regimens for stent-assisted coiling/flow diversion that preserve thromboembolic protection with lower hemorrhagic risk vs standard DAPT.

name: Staphyloenterotoxemia
description: Acute toxin mediated food poisoning from preformed Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin causing abrupt nausea vomiting cramps and diarrhea within 30 minutes to 8 hours and usually resolving within 24 hours. Management is mainly fluids and symptom control since antibiotics do not help and toxin can persist after cooking. Key unmet need is faster toxin neutralization and safer antiemetic and antidiarrheal options for patients at risk of dehydration electrolyte derangements and cardiac arrhythmias.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid-onset (ideally oral) enterotoxin-neutralizing/binding therapy early to abort vomiting/diarrhea and prevent dehydration-driven IV fluids, especially in infants and older adults.
- Antiemetic for acute toxin-mediated vomiting without QT-prolongation/Torsades risk, particularly in patients with electrolyte derangements.
- Safer antidiarrheal option avoiding loperamide-linked serious cardiac events and usable in young children where antidiarrheals are discouraged.

name: Hydrocele
description: Hydrocele is fluid buildup around a testicle that typically presents as painless, water balloon like scrotal swelling and may cause heaviness in adults. Many newborn cases reflect an unclosed channel from the abdomen and often resolve by age 1, while adult hydroceles usually persist. Care is largely procedural with hydrocelectomy for ongoing symptoms but surgery carries risks such as hematoma, infection, and recurrence. Aspiration is less invasive but commonly recurs, and aspiration plus sclerotherapy has higher recurrence than surgery, leaving a need for durable low recurrence outpatient options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Office-based aspiration + sclerotherapy with optimized sclerosant regimens to achieve durable low-recurrence resolution while avoiding hydrocelectomy complications/reoperations.
- Peri-hydrocelectomy local pharmacologic hemostasis/anti-infection adjuncts to reduce bleeding/hematoma reoperations and unplanned ER visits.
- Disease-modifying medical therapy for lymphatic-filariasis–associated hydrocele to reduce established scrotal swelling (not just parasite load) and lessen reliance on surgery.

name: Schistosomiasis
description: Schistosomiasis is an acute and chronic blood fluke infection acquired through freshwater exposure, often affecting school aged children, with symptoms driven by immune reactions to eggs ranging from abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea to haematuria and longer term anaemia, stunting, and impaired learning. Care relies on praziquantel, but reinfection is common, activity is weaker against juvenile parasites, and large bitter tablets limit paediatric dosing, creating demand for better single course therapies, child friendly formulations, and preventive approaches including vaccines in Phase 2.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Single-course therapy active vs juvenile/pre-patent schistosomes to avoid repeat praziquantel dosing and improve cure/egg-reduction.
- Palatable, low-pill-burden pediatric oral formulation (esp. preschool-age) to overcome large bitter tablets and improve adherence.
- Reinfection-preventing intervention (vaccine or long-acting prophylaxis) to complement MDA since praziquantel doesn’t prevent reinfection.

name: Atrial fibrillation
description: Atrial fibrillation is an irregular, often fast heart rhythm that can be silent or cause fatigue, palpitations, chest pain, and shortness of breath, and it raises stroke risk because blood can pool and clot. It primarily affects older adults, especially those with hypertension and obesity. Care still depends on oral anticoagulants that reduce stroke risk but carry bleeding risk and require consistent daily dosing, yet real world adherence is poor, leaving many patients intermittently unprotected.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Add-on/next-gen strategy to reduce residual ischemic stroke/systemic embolism in high-risk AF patients despite OAC (e.g., CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥4, nonparoxysmal AF, prior stroke, renal impairment)
- Anticoagulation that materially lowers major bleeding risk without loss of stroke-prevention efficacy
- Longer-acting/“forgiving” anticoagulation to improve real-world adherence and persistence

name: Paronychia | acute
description: Acute paronychia is a rapid, usually single digit nail fold infection after minor trauma such as nail biting or manicures, causing sudden pain, redness, swelling, and sometimes pus that can progress to an abscess. Management hinges on timely drainage when an abscess forms, while systemic antibiotics are often unnecessary after adequate drainage and complicated by resistant pathogens. Care remains inconsistently standardized, with limited trial grade evidence on optimal drainage techniques or topical add ons, leaving a need for better validated, topical first pathways that prevent progression and avoid procedures.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drainage-sparing local therapy that can clear fluctuant abscesses and avert incision & drainage.
- RCT-backed topical-first regimen that shortens pain/inflammation in non-abscess cases without escalation to oral antibiotics.
- High-risk (cellulitis/diabetes/immunosuppression/MRSA-risk) therapy providing staph/strep (incl. MRSA) coverage with minimal systemic exposure and simpler administration.

name: Strongyloidiasis
description: Strongyloidiasis is a soil transmitted roundworm infection that can persist for decades via autoinfection, often with minimal gastrointestinal or skin symptoms and eosinophilia until immunosuppression triggers lethal hyperinfection or dissemination. The biggest gaps are preventing missed cases before steroids or transplant, lack of an approved parenteral option when oral absorption fails in severe disease, safety constraints where Loa loa exposure makes ivermectin risky, and the absence of a reliable test of cure to confirm eradication.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Readily available human parenteral/subcutaneous anti-Strongyloides therapy for hyperinfection/disseminated disease in immunosuppressed patients (incl. ileus/malabsorption)
- Ivermectin-sparing strongyloidiasis treatment for patients with confirmed/suspected *Loa loa* coinfection to avoid encephalopathy risk
- More reliable eradication regimens for chronic intestinal strongyloidiasis (esp. pre-immunosuppression/transplant) despite lack of definitive test-of-cure

name: Neurotic excoriation
description: Excoriation (skin picking) disorder is a body focused repetitive behavior, typically beginning in adolescence and often seen in women seeking care, marked by recurrent picking of accessible skin that causes lesions, scabs, scars, and sometimes infection and disfigurement, and can consume hours a day. Treatment relies on habit reversal based behavioral therapy and off label options such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or N acetylcysteine, but evidence is limited, trials are short, side effects are common, and there are no Food and Drug Administration approved drugs, leaving a need for durable, well tolerated, disease modifying therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- FDA-approvable pharmacotherapy with higher responder rates and larger NE‑YBOCS reductions than current short/small RCT evidence to reduce tissue damage/infection morbidity
- Long-term maintenance therapy that prevents relapse beyond typical ~12‑week studies
- Better-tolerated, practical alternative to off-label SSRIs (e.g., fewer discontinuations/sexual dysfunction), usable when specialist CBT access is limited

name: Dermatographia
description: Common chronic inducible urticaria where minor scratching or pressure rapidly triggers linear wheals that fade within 30 to 60 minutes; often starts in young adults and can disrupt sleep and cause fatigue. Management relies on long term sometimes high dose non sedating antihistamines, but control is often incomplete and delayed dermographism can be treatment resistant, creating demand for longer acting mast cell directed therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Mechanism-based therapies for adults uncontrolled despite high-dose antihistamines, achieving complete provocation-test response plus meaningful itch improvement by Week 12
- Long-acting options that reduce continuous daily antihistamine prophylaxis and avoid sedating add-ons, improving symptom-free days and DLQI
- Biomarker-guided mast-cell–directed escalation for refractory patients (e.g., tryptase/SCF) to enable selection/monitoring beyond histamine blockade

name: Seasonal affective disorder
description: Seasonal affective disorder is recurrent major depression with a seasonal pattern, typically beginning in a person’s twenties or thirties with late fall or winter onset and spring or summer remission. Winter episodes often feature hypersomnia, low energy, carbohydrate cravings with weight gain, and sometimes suicidal thoughts. Treatment is constrained by the burden and safety limits of daily morning bright light therapy and by incomplete response, leaving a need for more convenient, broadly usable options that can reliably prevent seasonal episodes and sustain adherence across the full winter season.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable winter-to-winter relapse prevention with lower second-winter recurrence than standard acute light therapy
- Convenient non–light-box alternative that reduces daily 30–45 min light-therapy burden and works for patients with adherence/eligibility gaps (e.g., eye disease, photosensitizing meds)
- Better-tolerated fall-initiated pharmacologic prophylaxis matching/improving bupropion’s prevention efficacy while reducing AEs (e.g., insomnia, headache, nausea)

name: Campylobacteriosis
description: Campylobacteriosis is an acute bacterial gastroenteritis with onset typically 2 to 5 days after infection, causing often bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, and nausea or vomiting, usually resolving in 3 to 6 days with supportive rehydration. The key unmet needs are better options for severe disease in older adults, pregnancy, and immunocompromise amid common fluoroquinolone resistance, and prevention of post infectious sequelae such as reactive arthritis, Guillain Barré syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, and nerve damage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Microbiome-sparing oral therapy to prevent progression to severe disease in high-risk groups (≥65, pregnant, immunocompromised)
- Oral non-fluoroquinolone agents active vs fluoroquinolone-resistant Campylobacter (ideally macrolide-sparing)
- Adjunct/early therapies that reduce post-infectious sequelae risk (e.g., PI-IBS, reactive arthritis, GBS)

name: Dermatosis papulosa nigra
description: Dermatosis papulosa nigra is a benign seborrhoeic keratosis variant causing multiple small dark papules on the face and neck, most common from adolescence in people with darker skin (Fitzpatrick IV to VI) and more often in women. Lesions are usually symptomless but can be cosmetically and psychosocially distressing. Treatment is largely elective procedural destruction, yet in skin of colour it carries meaningful risk of post inflammatory pigment change, scarring, and keloids, and is often paid out of pocket. A key unmet need is scalable, non destructive, durable clearance with low recurrence and minimal pigment sequelae.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-destructive topical clearance for skin of color (Fitzpatrick IV–VI) without dyspigmentation/scarring/keloids
- Durable lesion removal with low recurrence/regrowth to avoid repeat procedures
- Scalable, low-visit, affordable therapy to treat dozens of facial/neck lesions and reduce self-pay burden

name: Ichthyosis vulgaris
description: Ichthyosis vulgaris is a common inherited disorder of skin cornification that typically appears in early childhood, causing chronic dry rough scaling on the lower legs and other extensor surfaces with sparing of skin folds. Filaggrin gene mutations weaken barrier function and hydration, so management is largely lifelong daily exfoliation and moisturising with keratolytic agents that can irritate, especially with coexisting atopic dermatitis. Key unmet needs are durable, low irritation infant safe topicals and disease modifying approaches that restore filaggrin and barrier function rather than repeatedly treating symptoms.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Topical filaggrin (FLG) replacement/restoration to correct the underlying barrier defect (vs chronic symptomatic exfoliation/moisturizing).
- Infant/toddler-safe, low-irritation descaling topical usable <2 years with less frequent dosing yet meaningful IGA/scale improvement.
- Retinoid-sparing systemic/targeted topical option for severe/refractory disease that avoids teratogenicity/pregnancy restrictions and other systemic burdens.

name: Tendinitis
description: Tendinitis is inflammation and swelling of a tendon, usually from injury or repetitive overuse, causing localized pain and tenderness near a joint that worsens with movement and can lead to recurrent symptoms and rupture. Care is largely supportive with rest, physical therapy, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and sometimes steroid injections, but chronic tendinopathy can be refractory in up to 40% and long term nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use is limited by cardiovascular and gastrointestinal bleeding risks, leaving a need for safer durable pain control and therapies that restore tendon function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- NSAID-sparing pain control suitable for sustained (weeks–months) symptom management without GI/CV/renal risk
- Disease-modifying/regenerative therapy for chronic tendinopathy (>3 months) with durable pain + function improvement
- Steroid-sparing local therapy with durable ≥1-year outcomes and low recurrence

name: Acute coronary syndrome
description: Acute coronary syndrome is a sudden, dangerous drop in blood flow to the heart muscle, encompassing heart attack and unstable angina, typically triggered by plaque rupture and clot and presenting with chest pressure and systemic symptoms requiring immediate care. Key unmet needs include bleeding risk on antithrombotics especially in older patients, persistent no reflow microvascular obstruction after percutaneous coronary intervention with suboptimal treatments, and low long term adherence around 40 to 75 percent to complex secondary prevention regimens, creating demand for bleeding sparing, microvascular protective, and simplified fixed dose combination strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Bleeding-sparing antithrombotic regimens for older/high-bleeding-risk ACS patients that maintain ischemic protection while enabling safer alternatives to default prolonged DAPT.
- Adjunct acute therapies to prevent/treat microvascular obstruction (no-reflow) and ischemia–reperfusion injury during/after primary PCI in STEMI to improve myocardial perfusion and reduce infarct size.
