- Adherence- and simplicity-improving secondary-prevention therapeutics (e.g., fixed-dose combinations/long-acting approaches) to reduce regimen complexity/polypharmacy post-ACS.

name: Necatoriasis
description: Necatoriasis is human hookworm disease caused by *Necator americanus*, acquired when larvae in faeces-contaminated soil penetrate skin, often after walking barefoot. Most infections are silent, but heavier burdens cause ground itch, abdominal pain or diarrhea, and chronic intestinal blood loss leading to iron-deficiency anaemia that harms child development and pregnancy outcomes. Control depends on benzimidazole mass drug administration, yet single-dose albendazole has limited cure rates, reinfection is rapid, and resistance is a concern, with infants and first-trimester pregnancy often excluded, driving demand for better single-dose regimens, new drug classes, and preventive vaccines.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- High single-dose parasitological cure/egg-reduction vs current single-dose albendazole/mebendazole in mass-treatment groups (esp. school-aged children)
- Non-benzimidazole (non–β-tubulin) anthelmintic/combination effective under repeated MDA drug-pressure and against resistance genotypes
- Pregnancy- and infant/toddler-safe regimen (incl. 1st-trimester label and strong evidence in children <2 years)

name: Adhesive capsulitis
description: Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) is an inflammation driven stiffening and fibrotic contracture of the shoulder capsule causing pain and marked loss of active and passive range of motion, often with night pain and difficulty reaching overhead or behind the back in midlife adults. Recovery can take 1 to 3 years and care is largely symptomatic with analgesics, steroid injections, and intensive daily physiotherapy, sometimes escalating to procedures, with uncertain optimal management. Key unmet needs are faster, durable restoration of motion and steroid sparing, disease modifying anti fibrotic approaches, especially for patients at risk of steroid induced hyperglycemia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early (≤3 months, pain‑predominant) disease‑modifying injectable to reduce pain/sleep disruption and prevent progression to stiffness/ROM loss
- Anti‑fibrotic therapy to reverse capsular scarring and deliver faster, clinically meaningful ROM restoration (esp. external rotation/abduction)
- Steroid‑sparing options for high‑risk/contraindicated patients (esp. diabetes) with durable pain/function and ROM gains without corticosteroid drawbacks

name: Artery stenosis | coronary
description: Coronary artery stenosis is atherosclerotic plaque narrowing of the coronary arteries that limits oxygen delivery to heart muscle, often presenting as exertional stable angina relieved by rest or medication and sometimes progressing to myocardial infarction when a clot abruptly blocks flow. Despite modern low density lipoprotein cholesterol lowering, many patients retain residual risk including genetically driven lipoprotein(a), while intensifying antithrombotic therapy is limited by bleeding and gastrointestinal injury. Key unmet needs include safer thrombosis prevention, targeted lipoprotein(a) lowering, and durable options for no option refractory angina.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Lp(a)-targeted therapies for established ASCVD/CVD patients with high Lp(a) (e.g., ≥70 mg/dL) that demonstrate expanded MACE reduction.
- Factor XI/FXIa antithrombotics for post-ACS/PCI or high-ischemic-risk CAD that reduce MACE with less bleeding than current intensification strategies.
- One-time regenerative/angiogenic therapies (e.g., gene therapy) for “no-option” refractory angina due to obstructive CAD that improve exercise tolerance, angina frequency, and objective ischemic burden/QoL.

name: Acne | conglobata
description: Acne conglobata is a rare, severe chronic nodulocystic acne marked by clustered comedones and deep inflammatory nodules that form interconnecting abscesses and sinus tracts with foul smelling purulent drainage, typically on the trunk and buttocks, and it inevitably scars and disfigures. Care relies on prolonged, often repeated oral isotretinoin with limited benefit from topicals and intermittent systemic antibiotics or corticosteroids, but relapse, antibiotic resistance constraints, and heavy psychological burden remain. The biggest unmet need is earlier, durable disease control that prevents tunneling disease and permanent scarring, supported by more robust evidence for targeted immunomodulatory approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prospective-trial–validated targeted immunomodulation (e.g., TNF/IL‑17) for isotretinoin-recalcitrant acne conglobata with reduced flares/recurrence.
- Pharmacologic prevention/resolution of sinus-tract (“tunneling”) disease and disfiguring scarring not responsive to isotretinoin.
- Antibiotic- and iPLEDGE-sparing systemic alternatives with isotretinoin-like efficacy to reduce resistance pressure and monthly monitoring burdens.

name: Spinal stenosis
description: Degenerative spinal canal or foraminal narrowing, most often in older adults, compresses neural tissue and causes posture dependent neurogenic claudication with leg or buttock pain and neurologic symptoms that worsen with standing or walking and improve with sitting or leaning forward, limiting walking. Management starts with physical therapy, analgesics and epidural steroid injections, but durable functional relief is uncommon, with long term outcomes often incomplete and many patients ultimately considering decompression surgery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Walking-capacity restoration by targeting nerve-root ischemia/venous-congestion biology and/or canal-narrowing drivers (e.g., ligamentum-flavum hypertrophy/fibrosis), with benefit measured on treadmill time/distance and ODI/ZCQ.
- Geriatric-safe oral symptom control that improves function without falls/orthostasis/anticholinergic burden seen with current SNRI/TCA options.
- Durable non-steroidal epidural/injectable therapies for stenosis-related radicular pain after PT/oral meds that avoid serial steroid injections and their questionable efficacy/safety risks.

name: Thrombophilia | activated protein C resistance
description: Inherited activated protein C resistance (Factor V Leiden) that increases risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, often presenting with leg pain and swelling or chest pain and shortness of breath. Management is largely anticoagulation, but bleeding risk limits use and pregnancy and breastfeeding constrain oral options, while post thrombotic syndrome can leave chronic leg pain and swelling. A key unmet need is safer, hemostasis sparing anticoagulants and better prevention of recurrent clots and long term complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer indefinite secondary VTE prevention in high-recurrence-risk Factor V Leiden/APC-resistance patients with materially lower major/clinically relevant bleeding vs current anticoagulants.
- Pregnancy/breastfeeding–compatible anticoagulation that avoids daily subcutaneous LMWH (ideally an oral option) for women with Factor V Leiden/prior VTE.
- Post-DVT adjunct therapy that prevents or meaningfully treats post-thrombotic syndrome (reduced PTS incidence/Villalta severity), beyond anticoagulation alone.

name: Cellulitis
description: Cellulitis is a rapidly spreading bacterial infection of the skin and deeper tissues, typically a unilateral hot swollen painful red lower leg that may come with fever or chills. Most cases respond to oral antibiotics, but severe or high risk patients often need intravenous therapy or admission, especially when coverage must span streptococci and methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Key unmet needs include preventing frequent recurrences when risk factors persist, and enabling reliable single visit outpatient treatment that avoids hospitalization.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Recurrence-prevention (prophylactic/maintenance) therapy for recurrent lower‑extremity cellulitis despite risk‑factor management (≥3–4 episodes/year)
- True single‑dose/ultra‑short outpatient regimens that avoid hospitalization and multi‑day IV dosing while meeting standard early response and cure endpoints
- MRSA+streptococci coverage for severe/nonpurulent cellulitis with MRSA risk factors that can replace vancomycin‑centric IV strategies and improve safety vs clindamycin/vancomycin

name: Hemangioma | infantile
description: Infantile hemangioma is a common benign vascular tumor of infancy that appears in the first weeks of life as bright red or bluish skin lesions, often on the head and neck, and grows fastest at 1 to 3 months. A short early treatment window means delayed referral can leave ulceration and permanent scarring. Oral propranolol is effective but burdensome and risky in infants due to feed timed dosing, required monitoring, hypoglycemia and bronchospasm, and 10 to 25 percent rebound after stopping, driving demand for safer systemic and more effective topical and maintenance options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer, non‑β‑blocker systemic option for high‑risk/contraindicated infants that avoids propranolol hypoglycemia/bradycardia/bronchospasm/PHACE stroke risk and eliminates feeding‑timed dosing + 2‑hour HR/BP monitoring burden
- Lesion‑penetrant localized (topical/transdermal) therapy effective for bulky/deep IH during the early 1–3 month rapid‑growth window to prevent permanent skin changes/disfigurement without systemic exposure
- Adjunct/maintenance strategy to reduce rebound regrowth after propranolol taper/stop (esp. deep/mixed IH or stopping before 9 months) enabling shorter/cleaner discontinuation and less retreatment

name: Gonorrhea
description: Gonorrhea is a common bacterial sexually transmitted infection of the genitals, rectum, or throat, often asymptomatic in women yet capable of causing pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and neonatal infection. Treatment is increasingly brittle, with US guidance relying on a single intramuscular ceftriaxone regimen, while pharyngeal disease is harder to eradicate and typically requires a test of cure visit. Rising antimicrobial resistance heightens the risk of treatment failure and makes simple, oral, partner deliverable cures and new resistance breaking options a high priority.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Single-dose (preferably oral) therapy that achieves high microbiologic cure for pharyngeal gonorrhea and eliminates the mandated 7–14 day test-of-cure return visit.
- Novel agents active against ceftriaxone-reduced-susceptibility/ceftriaxone-resistant gonorrhea to avoid dependence on the last remaining first-line IM ceftriaxone regimen.
- Partner-deliverable, single-dose oral therapy suitable for expedited partner therapy (EPT) (and for patients unable/unwilling to receive IM ceftriaxone) to improve partner treatment and reduce reinfection.

name: Heart failure | preserved ejection fraction
description: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (left ventricular ejection fraction ≥50%) accounts for ~half of heart failure, often in multimorbid patients (hypertension, diabetes, obesity, coronary artery disease, chronic kidney disease) and disproportionately affects women; patients have persistent exertional dyspnea and fatigue with severe exercise intolerance, poor quality of life, frequent hospitalizations, and high mortality, and treatments have historically offered little mortality or functional benefit, especially in kidney vulnerable patients.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- HFpEF therapy that reduces cardiovascular death (not just HF hospitalizations)
- Drugs that improve exercise tolerance/physical function and QoL (e.g., peak VO2, 6MWT, KCCQ physical limitation)
- Renal-/hyperkalemia-safer HFpEF options (esp. in CKD/diuretic-treated patients) enabling broader neurohormonal modulation

name: Oppositional defiant disorder
description: Oppositional defiant disorder is a childhood disruptive behavior condition marked by at least 6 months of persistent anger, hostility, and defiance toward authority figures that can seriously impair family and school functioning. Care is largely behavioral, relying on parent management training and other intensive psychosocial interventions, while medications mainly target comorbidities and options for severe aggression are constrained by adverse effects. A major unmet need is for easier to deliver, durable treatments that rapidly reduce irritability and oppositional behavior with low monitoring burden while families await or struggle to access comprehensive therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ODD-indicated, non-stimulant drug that directly reduces core irritability/anger and oppositionality (e.g., improves SNAP-IV oppositional subscale) in primary ODD (including without ADHD).
- Rapid anti-aggression/emotional-dysregulation therapy for severe cases that is metabolically neutral and prolactin-sparing vs antipsychotics.
- Easy-to-administer, low-monitoring “bridge/adjunct” pharmacotherapy to reduce caregiver/time burden while accessing intensive behavioral care (esp. <6y).

name: Seborrheic dermatitis
description: Seborrheic dermatitis is a common, chronic, relapsing inflammatory condition of oil rich skin that typically affects the scalp and central face with greasy scale, dandruff, and itch and can meaningfully impair quality of life. Disease is linked to inflammation driven by Malassezia yeast, so control often depends on ongoing antifungal shampoo routines with intermittent short courses of topical steroids. Key unmet needs are durable, steroid sparing therapies that reduce maintenance burden, work in azole resistant disease, and better control harder phenotypes including Parkinson’s disease or human immunodeficiency virus associated seborrheic dermatitis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Relapse-proof remission with ≤once-weekly (or truly discontinuable) dosing vs indefinite maintenance shampoos/leave-on routines
- Steroid-free long-term facial/scalp anti-inflammatory control avoiding topical steroid atrophy risks and calcineurin-inhibitor long-term-use limits/burning
- Efficacy in severe/refractory seborrheic dermatitis (e.g., HIV-, Parkinson’s-associated) including non-azole options active against azole-resistant *Malassezia*

name: Sarcopenia
description: Sarcopenia is an age linked progressive loss of skeletal muscle strength and function that drives slow gait, weakness, difficulty rising from a chair, falls, fractures, disability, and loss of independence in older adults. Care is still dominated by strength training and nutrition support, but these programs are often unattainable for frail, multi morbid patients, and there are no approved drugs. The unmet need is scalable, home usable therapies that deliver meaningful, durable real world functional gains, including in sarcopenic obesity where excess fat and impaired muscle function coexist.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral pharmacotherapy delivering meaningful mobility/functional gains beyond resistance training + protein (e.g., ≥0.1 m/s improvement in 400‑m walk gait speed)
- Safe, home-administered drug option for frail/comorbid non-responders or patients unable to adhere to/access exercise-nutrition programs
- Sarcopenic obesity/metabolic-syndrome–tailored therapy that improves function (chair-stand/SPPB/gait speed) while preserving or increasing lean mass by DXA

name: Fibromyalgia
description: Fibromyalgia is a chronic syndrome of widespread pain with fatigue plus sleep and cognitive or mood disruption, thought to reflect abnormal central pain processing and disproportionately affecting women. There is no cure and care is symptom focused, yet only about 1 in 10 patients get substantial pain relief from common medicines, and adverse effects drive poor adherence and discontinuation. The unmet need is durable, better tolerated, non-opioid therapies that meaningfully reduce pain while also improving sleep, fatigue, and cognition.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable ≥50% pain reduction with functional/work improvement in >~10% of moderate–severe patients, with efficacy maintained >6 months
- Clinically meaningful improvements beyond pain (fatigue, non-restorative sleep, cognitive symptoms)
- Better-tolerated, adherence-friendly non-opioid therapy (less dizziness/somnolence/weight gain/nausea) with long-term (>6 month) safety/efficacy data

name: Hepatitis B
description: Chronic hepatitis B is a long running hepatitis B virus infection that often stays silent for years yet can still progress to cirrhosis and primary liver cancer. Today most patients are managed with lifelong oral antivirals such as tenofovir or entecavir that suppress replication but rarely deliver a functional cure. Persistent hepatitis B surface antigen from covalently closed circular DNA and integrated viral DNA makes durable antigen clearance difficult, creating strong demand for finite, combination regimens that can achieve hepatitis B surface antigen loss and reduce long term cancer and liver failure risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Finite-duration, interferon-free regimens achieving functional cure (sustained HBsAg loss ≥24 weeks off-therapy with HBV DNA <LOQ).
- Therapies targeting the HBV antigen reservoir (cccDNA-driven transcription and integration-driven HBsAg production), especially for HBeAg-negative patients, to enable partial cure (HBsAg <100 IU/mL + HBV DNA <LOQ at 24 weeks off-therapy) or functional cure.
- Renal-/bone-sparing (and/or long-acting) long-term suppression options that reduce TDF renal/BMD toxicity and the adherence burden of prolonged nucleos(t)ide therapy.

name: Panic disorder
description: Panic disorder is an anxiety disorder marked by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks with intense physical symptoms that drive emergency-like care seeking and high medical use, plus ongoing anticipatory anxiety and avoidance between attacks. Current maintenance options such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors can take weeks to work, while fast-acting benzodiazepines are limited by sedation and dependence and are discouraged for routine use, leaving a need for rapid, non-sedating rescue therapies and more durable disease control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- On-demand, rapid-onset anti‑panic therapy that avoids benzodiazepine tolerance/dependence and sedation/cognitive impairment (esp. older adults).
- Maintenance therapy that increases sustained remission and prevents rapid relapse/recurrence (including panic with agoraphobia).
- Faster-onset, better-tolerated alternative to SSRIs/SNRIs that avoids early anxiety/panic worsening and discontinuation/withdrawal issues (reducing reliance on intensive CBT schedules).

name: Scabies
description: Scabies is a highly contagious skin infestation caused by Sarcoptes scabiei mites that burrow and lay eggs, triggering a delayed allergic reaction with intense nocturnal itch and burrows or papules and sometimes bacterial superinfection. Treatment is operationally hard because standard topical permethrin must be applied neck down for 8 to 14 hours and repeated since eggs survive, with whole households treated to stop transmission. Oral ivermectin often needs at least two doses but has safety and access constraints in pregnancy, small children, and some geographies, while rising permethrin resistance increases demand for new, broadly deployable, egg killing options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- True single-dose oral scabicide achieving complete cure by Day 28 to replace neck-down 8–14h topical permethrin regimens and ease contact/outbreak logistics
- New mechanism scabicide for treatment-failure/resistance-suspected scabies to reduce need for multi-dose ivermectin (3–7 doses)
- Systemic (oral) scabies therapy with established safety in children <15 kg, pregnant women, and Loa loa–endemic settings

name: Restless legs syndrome
description: Restless legs syndrome is a sleep related movement disorder marked by uncomfortable leg sensations and an urge to move that worsens at rest in the evening or night, fragments sleep, and drives daytime impairment. It is linked to low iron stores and dopamine pathway dysfunction, but current therapies are limited by dopamine agonist augmentation and impulse control harms, gabapentinoid sedation dizziness and respiratory depression risk, and a treatment ceiling that can push severe refractory patients toward low dose opioids. The unmet need is durable symptom and sleep control with better long term safety and tolerability.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Long-term RLS control on IRLS without dopamine-agonist augmentation/impulse-control disorders
- Symptom and sleep improvement without gabapentinoid sedation/dizziness or respiratory-depression risk in vulnerable patients
- Effective non-opioid option for refractory RLS to reduce reliance on opioid monotherapy (e.g., low-dose oxycodone)

name: Gout
description: Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by long term urate buildup that forms needle shaped crystals in and around joints, triggering sudden often nighttime flares that commonly start in the big toe or lower limb. It typically affects men in middle age and women after menopause, and can progress to tophi that damage joints and soft tissue. Despite treat to target urate lowering goals under 6 mg/dL, care is constrained by comorbid chronic kidney disease limiting nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and by safety limits for allopurinol ineligible patients given febuxostat boxed warning mortality risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CKD stage ≥3–safe acute-flare control and ULT‑initiation prophylaxis where NSAIDs/steroids are relatively contraindicated and colchicine evidence/dosing is limited.
- Urate-lowering option for allopurinol-ineligible patients (e.g., HLA‑B*58:01 hypersensitivity risk) without febuxostat-like CV mortality concerns.
- High-persistence, low-monitoring treat-to-target regimen that reliably maintains serum urate <6 mg/dL (and <5 mg/dL in severe/tophaceous disease).

name: Salmonellosis
description: Non typhoidal salmonellosis is a foodborne Salmonella gastroenteritis causing acute watery sometimes bloody diarrhea with fever and cramps that typically resolves in 4 to 7 days, but can cause life threatening dehydration in children and older adults and weeks of stool shedding. Care is largely supportive because antibiotics usually do not shorten illness and can prolong carriage and disrupt the microbiome, while the highest stakes are invasive infections in immunocompromised patients where rising antimicrobial resistance is eroding reliable treatment options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Microbiome-sparing therapy for acute nontyphoidal salmonellosis that shortens diarrhea/fever and reduces post-infection shedding/carriage.
- Oral (or single-dose long-acting) options active against fluoroquinolone-/ceftriaxone-/azithromycin-non-susceptible nontyphoidal Salmonella in severe/high-risk cases.
- Adjunctive/optimized regimens to reduce mortality and recurrence in invasive nontyphoidal Salmonella bacteremia, especially in HIV-infected adults and young children.

name: Rosacea
description: Rosacea is a chronic, relapsing central facial skin disorder (often starting ages 30 to 50) marked by persistent redness and flushing, visible blood vessels, inflammatory papules and pustules, and sometimes ocular involvement that can threaten vision. Persistent facial erythema is often the most disruptive symptom, yet current topical vasoconstrictors can wear off within hours and may cause rebound redness. Control of inflammatory and ocular disease still commonly relies on systemic tetracyclines such as doxycycline, highlighting demand for durable, antibiotic sparing long term therapies that prevent relapse.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Long-duration, non-rebound control of persistent facial erythema (± visible vessels) beyond current ≤12-hour alpha-agonist effects.
- Antibiotic-sparing, durable papulopustular rosacea control that prevents relapse after stopping systemic antibiotics.
- Ocular rosacea–specific therapy (topical/ophthalmic) that prevents corneal morbidity/vision loss while reducing reliance on systemic doxycycline.

name: Primary ovarian insufficiency
description: Primary ovarian insufficiency is early loss or dysfunction of ovarian follicles causing irregular menses or amenorrhea before age 40, infertility, and menopause like symptoms. Beyond fertility, patients face higher risks of bone loss and fractures and cardiovascular disease. Care is largely hormone replacement to control symptoms and reduce long term sequelae, but there is no proven way to restore normal ovarian function or reliably restore fertility, leaving many to pursue donor egg in vitro fertilization. Intermittent ovulation and a small chance of spontaneous pregnancy complicate contraception and family planning. Regenerative and immune based approaches are emerging but remain experimental.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Fertility-restoring therapy that reliably increases ovarian activity/ovulation to enable autologous pregnancy/live birth in non-surgical POI.
- Non-estrogen systemic alternatives that provide bone/CV protection and symptom control for POI patients who cannot use systemic hormone therapy (e.g., prior breast cancer).
- Combined physiologic hormone replacement plus reliable contraception for POI with intermittent ovarian function (to prevent unintended pregnancy while maintaining replacement benefits).

name: Diabetic retinopathy
description: Diabetic retinopathy is a diabetes driven microvascular retinal disease that is often silent early, then progresses to bleeding, scarring, and vision loss including diabetic macular edema with central blurring. Treatment is dominated by frequent intravitreal anti vascular endothelial growth factor injections, yet many patients still have persistent edema and vision impairment despite monthly dosing. Steroid implants can help but are limited by cataract and increased intraocular pressure risk, leaving a premium on longer lasting, more reliable control with fewer procedures.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ≥16‑week (or longer) dosing that maintains anti‑VEGF–level control of CI‑DME and improves DR severity, reducing injection/visit burden
- Therapies for incomplete anti‑VEGF responders (~40% with persistent central macular edema at 2 years) to deliver more reliable OCT drying + BCVA gains without more frequent injections
- Steroid-/procedure‑sparing options that avoid cataract/IOP elevation risks (esp. phakic or glaucoma‑risk patients) while minimizing intravitreal injection complications

name: Radiculopathy
description: Radiculopathy is a common syndrome where inflammation or pressure on a spinal nerve root, often from disc herniation or age related degenerative narrowing, causes electric burning radiating pain with numbness tingling and weakness. Many patients improve with conservative care, but current medical management relies on drugs with major tradeoffs including opioid dependence risk, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory gastrointestinal and renal toxicity, and limited evidence and sedation from gabapentinoids, creating demand for rapid non opioid functional relief and safer options for older comorbidity heavy patients.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid, non-opioid bridge therapy for acute radicular leg pain improving leg-pain (NRS/VAS) and disability/function (ODI) during the 8–16 week conservative window.
- Disease-targeted radicular/neuropathic pain drug that improves symptoms plus pain/function without gabapentinoid/opioid-like dependence risk.
- NSAID-sparing analgesic/anti-inflammatory options for older adults/comorbidity-heavy patients that maintain pain/function benefit with materially lower GI/CV/renal adverse-event risk.

name: Bronchoconstriction | exercise-induced
description: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction is transient airway narrowing triggered by physical activity, often worsened by cold or dry air, causing post-exercise cough, wheeze, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. Treatment still relies on short-acting inhaled beta-2 agonists taken before exercise that last only a few hours, can fail in some patients, and lose effect with frequent use. Anti-inflammatory options take weeks to fully help, and montelukast is constrained by a boxed warning for serious neuropsychiatric effects, leaving demand for longer-lasting, reliable, safer prevention.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Tolerance-free, long-duration EIB prophylaxis for high-frequency exercisers that avoids β2-agonist tachyphylaxis and sustains low max post-exercise % fall in FEV1.
- Rapid-onset non–β2-agonist rescue/pretreatment for SABA non-responders or intolerant patients, improving time to recovery of FEV1.
- Same-day anti-inflammatory prevention that avoids weeks-long ICS ramp and montelukast neuropsychiatric risk/usage restrictions while reducing max post-exercise % fall in FEV1/AUC0–20.

name: Endometrial hyperplasia
description: Endometrial hyperplasia is an overgrowth of the uterine lining driven by prolonged unopposed estrogen, often in perimenopausal or postmenopausal women with obesity or chronic anovulation, presenting with abnormal uterine bleeding. Atypical disease, also called endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia, is a precancerous lesion with endometrial cancer found in about 30 to 50 percent of hysterectomy specimens. Hysterectomy is definitive, but uterus sparing progestin therapy demands frequent surveillance biopsies every 3 to 6 months for up to 2 years and still has about 23 percent recurrence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable uterus-sparing therapy for EIN/AEH that reduces post-response recurrence (~23%, median time to recurrence 24 months).
- Effective options for obesity-associated relapse/progestin resistance (esp. BMI ≥35) and “progestin-insensitive” AEH achieving timely complete histologic response (≤28–32 weeks).
- Better-tolerated, lower-burden medical regimens that reduce the need for frequent invasive surveillance biopsies (q3–6 months up to 2 years) and improve bleeding/pain tolerability vs LNG-IUS.

name: Hyperkalemia
description: Hyperkalemia is an abnormally high blood potassium level, typically in chronic kidney disease or acute kidney injury and in patients on renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockers. It is often asymptomatic until it precipitates palpitations, weakness, or sudden cardiac arrest. Management swings between rapid but risky temporizing measures like insulin that can cause hypoglycemia and slower oral potassium binders whose delayed onset, edema risk, and medication separation rules limit usability. The practical unmet need is fast, predictable, durable potassium control that keeps patients safe and allows continued use of cardio-renal protective therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- RAASi-enabling chronic potassium control to prevent recurrent hyperkalemia in CKD/HF patients who otherwise need RAASi/MRA dose reduction or discontinuation.
- Rapid, predictable emergency potassium-lowering therapy for severe hyperkalemia that avoids insulin-associated hypoglycemia and delayed-onset binders.
- Better-tolerated, lower-burden outpatient maintenance options that minimize drug–drug interaction dose-separation requirements and reduce edema/GI safety risks.

name: Diverticulitis
description: Diverticulitis is inflammation or infection of colonic diverticula, usually in adults over 50, causing acute left lower abdominal pain with fever, nausea or vomiting, and bowel habit changes. Most cases are uncomplicated but some progress to abscess, peritonitis, obstruction, stricture, or fistula. The clinical burden comes from unpredictable recurrence and persistent post-episode gastrointestinal symptoms, creating demand for better prevention and symptom control while enabling safe antibiotic sparing outpatient management.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Recurrence prophylaxis for high-risk recurrent left/sigmoid diverticulitis (reduce 1-year recurrence/time-to-first recurrence).
- Therapies for post-diverticulitis IBS/functional bowel disease to reduce chronic abdominal pain and altered bowel habits.
- Antibiotic-sparing outpatient acute uncomplicated diverticulitis treatment with non-inferior 30-day abscess/perforation/surgery complications.

name: Post-traumatic stress disorder
description: Post traumatic stress disorder is a trauma triggered mental health condition diagnosed when symptoms persist beyond a month and cause clinically significant functional impairment. It features intrusive reliving such as nightmares and flashbacks, avoidance, negative shifts in mood and thinking, and hyperarousal with insomnia and irritability that can persist for years. Talk therapy and medications help but response is variable, leaving many patients with ongoing symptoms, especially sleep and nightmare burden, and access to trained trauma focused therapy remains a major bottleneck.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Better-tolerated, higher-response pharmacotherapy for SSRI/SNRI partial- or non-responders.
- Mechanism-driven drugs that meaningfully reduce PTSD nightmares/insomnia and improve sleep quality.
- Therapy-sparing, scalable medications that deliver symptom/functional gains when trauma-focused psychotherapy is unavailable, infeasible, or not preferred.

name: Peptic esophagitis
description: Peptic esophagitis is erosive esophageal injury from repeated gastroesophageal reflux, typically causing heartburn and regurgitation with possible cough or wheeze, hoarseness, and dysphagia, especially in older, obese, or pregnant patients. Proton pump inhibitors and lifestyle changes reduce acidity but do not prevent reflux events, require strict pre meal dosing, and leave about 30% symptomatic; relapse is common off therapy. Key unmet needs are durable control including nonacid reflux and effective long term maintenance with less chronic exposure.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non–acid-suppression therapies for the ~1/3 of GERD/erosive-esophagitis patients with persistent symptoms on standard-dose PPIs (e.g., weakly acidic/nonacid reflux).
- Timing-insensitive oral regimens that eliminate strict pre-meal dosing to reduce incorrect PPI use and deliver faster, durable heartburn control.
- Maintenance/recurrence-prevention options that reduce relapse after stopping PPIs while minimizing long-term PPI exposure risks.

name: Hyperparathyroidism | secondary
description: Secondary hyperparathyroidism in advanced chronic kidney disease is a sustained rise in parathyroid hormone driven by hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and low active vitamin D, often identified on routine labs and common in dialysis patients. It causes bone and joint pain, fractures, fatigue, and pruritus, and over time contributes to vascular calcification and cardiovascular risk. Current vitamin D and calcimimetic approaches can control labs but have limited evidence for improving hard outcomes and add safety and operational burdens including hypocalcemia risk and frequent calcium monitoring.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer/tolerable PTH lowering in hemodialysis sHPT with less hypocalcemia/QT risk and GI intolerance than current calcimimetics
- Demonstrated reduction in hard outcomes (death/major cardiovascular events) beyond iPTH control in moderate-to-severe dialysis sHPT
- Lower-burden PTH control for CKD G4–G5 patients not on hemodialysis/home modalities, avoiding vitamin D–related hypercalcemia and reducing monitoring burden

name: Bladder cancer | non-muscle invasive
description: Non muscle invasive bladder cancer is an early stage urothelial cancer confined to the bladder lining or just beneath it often presenting in older male smokers with painless hematuria and urinary irritative symptoms. Treatment typically requires transurethral resection followed by years of intravesical therapy and frequent often lifelong cystoscopic surveillance because recurrence is common. The biggest gaps are durable bladder sparing options after Bacillus Calmette Guérin failure and fragile access to Bacillus Calmette Guérin due to recurring supply shortages as well as safer biomarker guided surveillance that can reduce procedure burden without missing recurrences.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Bladder-sparing therapy for BCG-unresponsive high-risk NMIBC that delivers durable complete responses (≥12 months) and prolongs cystectomy-free outcomes vs current options.
- Adjuvant and/or biomarker-guided approaches that lower recurrence enough to safely de-intensify cystoscopy surveillance.
- BCG-independent intravesical therapy that reduces instillation/dwell-time burden and serious toxicity while avoiding vulnerability to BCG supply constraints.

name: Otitis media | suppurative
description: Suppurative otitis media is a pediatric middle ear infection often following a viral upper respiratory illness, peaking at 6 to 24 months, with ear pain, fever, irritability, sleep disruption, and sometimes ear drainage. When drainage persists through a perforated eardrum for weeks it becomes chronic suppurative otitis media, a major preventable cause of hearing loss. Care is constrained by biofilm driven pathogens such as Pseudomonas and only moderately effective antibiotics, plus the need to avoid ototoxic ear drops when the middle ear is open, creating demand for safe, effective non ototoxic antibiofilm topical therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-ototoxic ototopical anti-biofilm/anti-*Pseudomonas* therapy to eliminate persistent middle-ear discharge through tympanic perforation and prevent hearing loss.
- Microbiome-sparing, low-diarrhea short-course oral therapy for infants/toddlers with acute suppurative AOM/otorrhea that remains effective after ≥48h antibiotic failure.
- Non-antibiotic prophylaxis for recurrent AOM driven by viral URTIs (e.g., antiviral/immune-targeted prevention) to reduce repeat antibiotic exposure.

name: Osteomalacia
description: Osteomalacia is adult bone softening, usually from vitamin D deficiency, causing diffuse weight bearing bone pain, proximal weakness, gait difficulty, falls, and minimal trauma fractures. Even with vitamin D and calcium repletion, improvement can take months and is difficult in malabsorption or after bariatric surgery. Fibroblast growth factor 23 driven hypophosphatemic forms are often misdiagnosed and rely on burdensome multi dose daily phosphate and active vitamin D regimens with monitoring and tolerability limits, leaving a need for faster diagnosis and lower burden, durable phosphate normalization.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Faster bone remineralization/functional recovery in vitamin‑D–deficiency osteomalacia (earlier normalization of bone turnover/mineralization markers)
- Vitamin D + calcium repletion that works in malabsorption/bariatric patients without high-dose oral “mega-dose” regimens
- Low-burden, safer phosphate normalization for FGF23-mediated hypophosphatemic osteomalacia/TIO to replace frequent multi-dose phosphate + active vitamin D regimens

name: Prelabor rupture of membranes
description: Prelabor rupture of membranes is rupture of the fetal membranes before labor, typically presenting as watery vaginal fluid leakage without regular contractions. In preterm cases it creates a high stakes tradeoff between prolonging pregnancy for fetal maturity and rising risk of ascending infection and chorioamnionitis once the barrier is lost. Care is largely supportive with hospitalization, antibiotics, corticosteroids, and careful delivery timing, but there is no sensitive early test for chorioamnionitis and no proven way to reseal or repair membranes. At term it is common and often managed with induction, which can be challenging when the cervix is unfavorable.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Membrane-sealing/repair therapeutics for PPROM that restore fetal-membrane integrity and re-establish a barrier against ascending infection.
- Biomarker-guided, infection-modulating latency therapy (e.g., IL-6–guided antibiotics/steroids) to prolong pregnancy >7 days after PPROM while reducing antibiotic exposure and chorioamnionitis/funisitis.
- Lower-burden induction pharmacotherapy for term PROM that avoids continuous IV oxytocin/monitoring while maintaining timely delivery and reducing uterine overstimulation–related fetal heart-rate changes.

name: Heart block | sinoatrial
description: Sinoatrial block is a sinus node dysfunction, typically in adults over 50, where impaired pacemaker activity causes inappropriate bradycardia and sinus pauses leading to fatigue, dizziness, and syncope. Acute episodes are temporized with atropine, transcutaneous pacing, or catecholamine infusions, but most symptomatic patients ultimately need a permanent pacemaker. The unmet need is less about acute rescue and more about avoiding lifelong device burdens such as pocket infection and repeat generator replacements every 10 to 15 years, and enabling safer oral chronotropic therapies or biological pacing approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral, titratable chronotropic drug therapy to prevent long sinus pauses and reduce presyncope/syncope in intermittent SA exit block/SND patients who would otherwise require permanent pacing
- Gene- or cell-based “biological pacemaker” to replace electronic pacemakers and avoid battery/lead complications and infection risk
- Drug-based strategies to prevent peri-implant pacemaker infection and other procedure-related complications (e.g., anti-biofilm prophylaxis)

name: Generalized anxiety disorder
description: Generalized anxiety disorder is a chronic, disabling pattern of excessive, hard to control worry across everyday domains lasting at least six months, with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance that can significantly impair functioning. Care is constrained by first line antidepressants that take weeks to work and often need long continuation to prevent relapse, while benzodiazepines provide rapid relief but are limited to short term crisis use due to dependence and withdrawal risk. This leaves a need for fast acting, non dependent bridging options and more durable, remission grade therapies that are easier to discontinue.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid-onset, non-sedating, non-dependence-forming PRN/bridge anxiolytic to cover the early-treatment gap while SSRIs/SNRIs take weeks and benzodiazepines are crisis-only.
- Remission-grade efficacy for treatment-resistant/partial-response GAD after ≥1 adequate SSRI/SNRI trial.
- Durable long-term control with easier discontinuation (lower relapse risk and reduced withdrawal/AE-driven discontinuation).

name: Conduct disorder
description: Conduct disorder is a childhood and adolescent condition marked by persistent rule breaking and aggression, often with truancy, substance use, and major school impairment that can persist into adult functional problems. Treatment is largely intensive psychosocial care such as multisystemic therapy and frequent case management visits, while medication is generally not routine. Short term risperidone may be used only for severe aggression after psychosocial failure but is limited by metabolic and extrapyramidal risks, leaving demand for durable, better tolerated anti aggression options and approaches tailored to the more severe limited prosocial emotions subgroup.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Weight‑neutral, low‑EPS anti‑aggression alternative to short‑term risperidone for severely aggressive youth refractory to psychosocial interventions
- Pharmacotherapies specifically validated for the callous‑unemotional/limited‑prosocial‑emotions conduct‑disorder subgroup
- Durable medication effects that reduce reliance on high‑intensity, time‑burdensome psychosocial programs

name: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
description: Obsessive compulsive disorder is a chronic condition where intrusive obsessions drive repetitive compulsions that can consume more than an hour a day and impair daily function, usually beginning in late childhood or young adulthood. First line care combines exposure and response prevention therapy with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, yet benefits may take 8 to 12 weeks and 40 to 60 percent have only partial or no response, with long term use limited by adverse effects such as sexual dysfunction. This leaves a premium on better tolerated non serotonergic medicines and scalable neuromodulation options for treatment resistant disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Mechanistically novel drugs achieving response-level benefit (≥25–35% Y‑BOCS reduction) in the 30–50% of OCD patients who are SSRI/ERP/clomipramine nonresponders.
- Better-tolerated long-term pharmacotherapy (esp. markedly less sexual dysfunction and fewer discontinuations) vs SSRIs/clomipramine.
- Rapid-acting, self-administered treatments that reduce reliance on intensive ERP and shorten the 8–12 week SSRI time-to-effect.

name: Stroke | transient cerebral ischemia
description: Transient ischemic attack is a brief, stroke like episode of focal neurologic dysfunction from transient brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia without acute infarction, usually resolving within an hour and by 24 hours. It is a high risk warning event with the greatest stroke risk in the first 48 hours, yet prevention remains limited by variable antiplatelet response such as reduced clopidogrel effect in CYP2C19 poor metabolizers and by adherence and pill burden. Key frontiers include safer anticoagulation via factor XI inhibition and single pill combination prevention strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Bleeding-sparing antithrombotic add‑on (e.g., Factor XIa inhibition) for recent non‑cardioembolic stroke/high‑risk TIA to reduce recurrent ischemic stroke without increasing major bleeding.
- CYP2C19 genotype–aware (or genotype‑agnostic) antiplatelet strategy for clopidogrel low‑response (LOF allele) carriers to lower 90‑day stroke without more moderate/severe bleeding.
- Regimen simplification (e.g., fixed‑dose combination “polypill”) to improve 1‑year persistence/adherence to secondary‑prevention medications and reduce residual risk.

name: Anovulation
description: Anovulation is failure to ovulate, typically from hormonal imbalance, presenting with infertility and irregular or missed periods. Bleeding can be heavy and erratic enough to cause anemia. First line oral ovulation induction helps many, but nonresponders often require escalated, closely monitored therapy to avoid multiple pregnancy and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, creating demand for more reliable, safer, lower burden approaches that achieve single follicle ovulation and better pregnancy outcomes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral ovulation induction that improves live-birth rates in anovulatory infertility patients who fail first-line oral agents, avoiding escalation to injectable gonadotrophins
- Monofollicular ovulation induction that maintains pregnancy/live birth while reducing multiple gestation and OHSS risk vs clomiphene/gonadotropins
- Lower-burden (ideally non-injectable) ovulation induction that reduces need for intensive ultrasound/estradiol monitoring and repeated injections

name: Neuropathy | sensory peripheral
description: Sensory peripheral neuropathy involves peripheral nerve damage, often from diabetes, causing length dependent tingling, numbness and often nighttime pain in the feet and hands that can lead to unrecognized injuries and falls. Treatment is mostly symptomatic with agents such as duloxetine, gabapentin and pregabalin, yet pain control is often inadequate and limited by sedation and dizziness, leaving strong demand for better tolerated analgesia and disease modifying approaches that restore protective sensation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pain therapy with clinically meaningful relief in a majority of patients (vs ~1/3 responders on current first-line monotherapy).
- Drug that reverses underlying nerve damage to restore protective sensation/nerve function (not just analgesia).
- Better-tolerated, lower-burden treatment (minimize dizziness/somnolence; avoid TID dosing and HCP-administered topical procedures).

name: Postherpetic neuralgia
description: Postherpetic neuralgia is long lasting, often burning or touch sensitive neuropathic pain after shingles, mainly in adults over 60, driven by shingles related nerve damage that disrupts sleep and mood. Care relies on neuropathic pain medicines and topical lidocaine, but dosing often requires slow titration and pain is rarely fully relieved, leaving a need for better tolerated, more consistently effective options, even as shingles vaccination can prevent new cases.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Novel-mechanism analgesics achieving meaningful responder rates (≥50% pain reduction) and improving allodynia/hyperalgesia and sleep disruption in PHN inadequately controlled on current meds
- Geriatric-/comorbidity-friendly systemic options that avoid CNS/anticholinergic adverse effects (e.g., dizziness/somnolence, falls/cognitive issues, opioid-like sedation/constipation)
- More convenient regimens that reduce long titration and frequent dosing and avoid burdensome topical capsaicin workflows (including practical options for head/face PHN where patches are impractical)

name: Telogen effluvium
description: Telogen effluvium is a diffuse, non scarring hair shedding disorder where illness, childbirth, medications, or severe stress push follicles into the shedding phase, with sudden loss often appearing about three months after the trigger and sometimes coming out in handfuls. While many cases resolve over months, chronic or idiopathic shedding can persist beyond six months. Care is largely trigger management and reassurance, with no therapies proven to speed regrowth, and pregnancy or breastfeeding restricts minoxidil, leaving a need for fast, objectively proven shedding control and regrowth acceleration, especially postpartum.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Proven, rapid shedding control/regrowth acceleration in acute TE (objective shedding reduction + target-area hair count improvement within weeks)
- Mechanism-based therapy for chronic/idiopathic TE (>6 months or trigger-unclear) without systemic side effects (e.g., edema/hypertrichosis/dizziness)
- Pregnancy/postpartum-safe TE treatment usable during pregnancy/breastfeeding with objective shedding/regrowth improvement

name: Artery stenosis | renal
description: Renal artery stenosis is usually atherosclerotic narrowing of the renal arteries that reduces kidney perfusion, activates the renin angiotensin aldosterone system, and drives resistant hypertension, declining kidney function, and sometimes flash pulmonary edema. Despite stenting and revascularization, outcomes often do not improve because downstream microvascular loss and fibrosis can make renal damage irreversible, leaving a premium on disease modifying renoprotective therapies and better tools to identify the small high risk subgroup that truly benefits from intervention.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Reno-protective/ischemic-nephropathy–modifying therapy that prevents progression to occlusion and slows renal-function loss (e.g., improves eGFR slope, reduces RRT events) in atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis.
- Kidney-sparing BP-control option for ACEi/ARB-intolerant renovascular-HTN patients that avoids ACEi/ARB exposure/early creatinine monitoring and reduces polypharmacy.
- Medical prevention of recurrent flash pulmonary edema/HF hospitalization in bilateral or occlusive RAS (“high-risk” phenotype) underrepresented in revascularization RCTs.

name: Intermittent explosive disorder
description: Intermittent explosive disorder is a psychiatric condition marked by recurrent, impulsive anger or aggressive outbursts that are out of proportion to triggers, with otherwise normal behavior between episodes. Episodes come on rapidly and usually last under 30 minutes, yet can cause major social, work or school, and legal harm. Treatment relies on cognitive behavioral therapy and off label psychotropics with variable benefit, and there are no United States Food and Drug Administration approved drugs specifically for intermittent explosive disorder, creating demand for fast acting de escalation options and better tolerated, durable therapies proven to reduce aggression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid, on-demand “rescue” drug that can blunt an imminent outburst within hours.
- FDA-approvable maintenance therapy with robust, IED-specific efficacy on validated aggression endpoints (e.g., MOAS/OAS‑M responder-level improvement).
- Youth-safe long-term option with fewer SSRI suicidality concerns and reduced burdensome side effects (e.g., weight gain/insomnia) seen with current off-label meds.

name: Dengue fever
description: Mosquito-borne viral illness causing abrupt fever with severe headache and retro-orbital pain, myalgias and arthralgias, nausea and rash, plus leukopenia and thrombocytopenia; can rapidly worsen at defervescence as capillary leak and bleeding risk emerge. With no specific antiviral, care relies on close monitoring and carefully titrated fluids, leaving major unmet need for outpatient antivirals and agents that stabilize vascular leak and hemorrhage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early outpatient antiviral/neutralizing therapy for dengue without warning signs to reduce need for supportive-care–only management and daily follow-up/CBC monitoring
- Capillary-leak/vascular-permeability–stabilizing adjunct around critical phase/defervescence to prevent plasma leakage → shock/respiratory distress and reduce intensive IV-fluid titration burden
- Bleeding/thrombocytopenia-directed therapy to prevent clinically significant bleeding and reduce transfusion dependence without increasing fluid overload

name: Meibomian cyst
description: Chalazion is a firm, usually painless eyelid nodule caused by blockage of a meibomian oil gland, most often presenting in adults aged 30 to 50. Many lesions resolve over weeks to months with warm compresses and lid hygiene, but persistent or recurrent cases, particularly in people with blepharitis or acne rosacea, often need incision and curettage or intralesional steroid injection. Procedural care is inconvenient and steroids can cause skin depigmentation and rare serious ocular complications, creating demand for convenient steroid sparing treatments that clear established lesions, improve gland function, and reduce recurrence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-procedural “step-up” pharmacotherapy to clear chalazia persisting >~1 month despite conservative care, avoiding escalation to incision-and-curettage.
- Recurrence-prevention / meibomian-gland–dysfunction (MGD)–modifying therapy for intractable recurrent chalazion, including post-surgical recurrences.
- Steroid-sparing anti-inflammatory alternatives (or safer delivery) to intralesional triamcinolone that maintain efficacy while reducing risks (e.g., depigmentation, elevated IOP, globe perforation, retinal/choroidal vascular occlusion).

name: Raynaud disease
description: Raynaud disease is an episodic cold or stress triggered vasospasm that reduces blood flow to fingers and toes, causing painful color changes, numbness, and tingling on rewarming. It often begins in the teens and is more common in women. Most primary cases are mild, but secondary disease can progress to ischemic complications such as digital ulcers and even digit loss. Current care is largely behavioral plus vasodilators like calcium channel blockers that ease symptoms but do not cure the condition and are limited by side effects such as headache and edema.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Larger, patient-meaningful reductions in Raynaud attack frequency/duration and symptom severity vs first-line calcium-channel blockers
- Effective attack prevention for patients who can’t tolerate or safely uptitrate vasodilators due to edema/headache/lightheadedness/hypotension
- Outpatient therapies that prevent and rapidly heal systemic-sclerosis–associated digital ulcers/critical digital ischemia, reducing reliance on hospital-only IV prostacyclin/iloprost

name: Endometriosis
description: Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory disease where endometrium-like tissue grows outside the uterus, driving pelvic inflammation, scarring, severe period and chronic pelvic pain, heavy bleeding, and infertility, often affecting sex, bowel and bladder function, and mental health. Diagnosis is commonly delayed 4 to 12 years, and care is largely symptom control because there is no cure, symptoms often persist or recur, and hormonal suppression can be poorly tolerated, time limited, or incompatible with pregnancy. Many patients still have pain after surgery, highlighting the need for durable, fertility compatible, non-hormonal, mechanism-based pain relief.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Fertility-compatible (non-hormonal/ovulation-sparing) control of dysmenorrhea and non‑menstrual pelvic pain for patients actively trying to conceive.
- Long-term pain control that avoids GnRH-class hypoestrogenic toxicity, specifically preserving bone mineral density and minimizing menopausal symptoms.
- Mechanism-based therapy for refractory chronic pelvic pain driven by central sensitization/neuropathic mechanisms, including persistent pain after surgery and/or hormonal suppression.

name: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis
description: Metabolic dysfunction associated steatohepatitis is the progressive inflammatory form of metabolic dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease, typically in people with obesity or type 2 diabetes, often silent until fibrosis advances to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer. Key gaps include scalable noninvasive diagnosis since biopsy remains central, plus better tolerated, outcomes proven therapies beyond the first accelerated approval in F2 to F3 disease, with fewer gastrointestinal side effects and fewer drug interaction constraints in a polypharmacy population.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Approved therapy for compensated MASH cirrhosis (F4) that reduces decompensation/transplant/death.
- Outcomes-proven disease modification beyond biopsy surrogates (fewer major liver events and/or cirrhosis progression).
- Better tolerability/contraindication “escape hatch”: anti-fibrotic benefit with less GI burden and fewer GLP‑1 contraindications/management complexities (e.g., DDIs).

name: Baastrup syndrome
description: Degenerative lumbar “kissing spine” pain syndrome where adjacent spinous processes approximate and strain the interspinous ligament, often causing interspinous bursitis, typically L4 to L5 in adults over 70, with midline low back pain worse on extension and relieved by flexion. Care is largely symptomatic with analgesics, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, injections or surgery, but misdiagnosis, relapse when mechanics persist, inconsistent surgical benefit, and potential steroid related ligament weakening leave a need for durable targeted structure preserving therapies that reduce chronic pain medication use in older adults.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Long-acting, interspinous-bursa/ligament–targeted injectables delivering ≥6–12 months pain relief while avoiding repeat corticosteroid exposure/ligament weakening
- Geriatric-safe, NSAID-/opioid-sparing chronic axial pain pharmacotherapy for the typical >70-year-old population
- Structure-preserving therapies targeting interspinous-ligament degeneration/mechanical driver to reduce relapse/progression vs symptom-only approaches

name: Alzheimer’s disease
description: Alzheimer’s disease is a progressive dementia that typically begins in the mid 60s or later, with memory loss that disrupts daily life plus impaired judgment, repeating questions, getting lost, difficulty managing money, and mood or behavior changes. Pathology builds for years before symptoms, driven by amyloid plaques and tau tangles. Care remains largely supportive with no cure and only modest symptomatic benefit. Newer anti amyloid antibodies are limited to early symptomatic patients and carry a meaningful safety and operational burden from amyloid related imaging abnormalities requiring repeated magnetic resonance imaging. Agitation and psychosis are common yet hard to treat safely because antipsychotics increase mortality in dementia related psychosis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ARIA-free, low-monitoring early-AD disease modification that avoids baseline/serial MRI surveillance and ApoE ε4–linked risk-management burden
- Disease-modifying therapy effective in later symptomatic AD beyond the current mild cognitive impairment/mild dementia initiation window, preserving cognition + function
- Safer, targeted pharmacologic control of AD-related agitation/aggression/psychosis (rapid symptom reduction without antipsychotic-class mortality risk)

name: Bartholin gland cyst
description: Bartholin gland cysts are blocked-duct swellings near the vaginal opening, often in women aged 20 to 50, that may be painless until enlargement or infection triggers a rapidly developing, very painful abscess that disrupts walking, sitting, and sex. Care still relies on drainage and weeks with a catheter, typically requiring abstinence and imposing meaningful lifestyle burden, yet recurrence persists at roughly 7 to 9% after common procedures. Faster-healing, procedure-sparing approaches that prevent recurrence remain a key unmet need.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-procedural (local/topical/intralesional) anti-infective that reliably resolves symptomatic/persistent Bartholin abscesses without incision/drainage while rapidly relieving pain.
- Recurrence-prevention adjunct (e.g., post-drainage intracystic/ductal pharmacotherapy) that cuts long-term recurrence (~20%) to single-digit rates.
- Faster-healing/epithelialization therapy that eliminates 4–6 week indwelling Word catheter use and associated lifestyle restrictions (avoid sex/tampons/swimming).

name: Pulmonary heart disease | acute
description: Acute pulmonary heart disease is abrupt right ventricular failure from a sudden rise in pulmonary vascular pressure, most often triggered by massive pulmonary embolism. Patients can present like a heart attack with chest pain and severe shortness of breath and can rapidly deteriorate into obstructive shock and death. Treatment centers on anticoagulation and urgent reperfusion, but the core constraint is balancing rapid clot removal against major bleeding risk, especially intracranial hemorrhage with systemic thrombolysis. The near term frontier is faster right ventricle rescue with lower bleeding using catheter based reperfusion and thrombectomy approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Ultra–low-bleeding reperfusion for high‑risk/massive PE with acute RV failure (thrombolysis-like hemodynamic benefit with materially lower major bleeding/ICH).
- Rapid RV-rescue pharmacotherapy (selective pulmonary vasodilation and/or RV inotropy without systemic hypotension) to prevent early circulatory collapse in shock-presenting PE.
- Simplified early anticoagulation that is predictable and rapidly reversible without continuous IV UFH titration and frequent aPTT monitoring.

name: Graves' disease
description: Graves’ disease is an autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism where antibodies overstimulate the thyroid, driving heat intolerance, palpitations, anxiety, weight loss and diarrhea and sometimes thyroid eye disease with bulging eyes and vision risk. Antithyroid drugs can control symptoms but relapse after stopping therapy is common, making durable off drug remission elusive. Treatment in pregnancy is constrained by fetal risk with methimazole early and rare but severe propylthiouracil hepatotoxicity. For eye disease, targeted biologics add significant infusion burden and safety tradeoffs such as hyperglycemia and hearing impairment.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that achieve durable off-drug remission/euthyroidism in Graves’ patients with persistently elevated TRAb who commonly relapse after standard ATD courses.
- Pregnancy-compatible antithyroid treatment that avoids both methimazole teratogenic risk in 1st trimester and PTU severe hepatotoxicity, eliminating the PTU→MMI switch.
- Thyroid eye disease treatments with clinically meaningful proptosis reduction delivered with lower treatment burden (non-IV/shorter course) and improved safety vs teprotumumab (less hyperglycemia/hearing impairment).

name: Allergy | pollen-food
description: Pollen food allergy syndrome, also called oral allergy syndrome, is a pollen driven cross reaction where raw fruits, vegetables, or some tree nuts trigger rapid itching or swelling in the mouth and throat in people with hay fever, often teens and young adults. Most reactions stay localized and many patients tolerate cooked foods, but a small subset can have systemic reactions including anaphylaxis. Management is mainly avoidance and antihistamines, with epinephrine for higher risk patients, leaving unmet need for disease modifying options such as allergen immunotherapy and more convenient non injectable epinephrine delivery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying immunotherapy that enables safe reintroduction of key raw trigger foods by increasing oral food-challenge tolerance thresholds.
- Therapies that prevent systemic reactions/anaphylaxis in higher-risk PFAS patients (e.g., heat-stable LTP phenotypes with cooked-food reactivity and cofactor-amplified severity).
- Needle-free, rapidly acting epinephrine rescue alternatives to autoinjectors to reduce real-world administration burden.

name: Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy
description: Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy is a progressive loss of corneal endothelial pump cells, leading to fluid buildup, corneal swelling, and morning worse blurry or hazy vision in typically women over 50. Care is largely symptomatic with hypertonic saline, with vision limiting disease treated by donor endothelial keratoplasty, but nothing reverses the condition. The biggest gaps are disease modifying and donor independent regenerative options that reduce reliance on complex surgery and scarce tissue, including tissue sparing procedures supported by Rho associated kinase inhibitors and cultured endothelial cell injection approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Topical oxidative-stress–targeted cytoprotective therapy to slow early FECD progression (improve/maintain endothelial cell metrics and central corneal thickness).
- Drug adjunct to DSO/DWEK (e.g., ROCK-inhibitor–like) to increase corneal clearing rates and speed visual recovery, reducing “non-clearers” in ECC≥1,000 cells/mm² candidates.
- Single-procedure regenerative endothelial replacement (e.g., intracameral cell therapy) to deliver meaningful BCVA gains and edema/CCT reduction in advanced disease, avoiding keratoplasty.

name: Gilbert syndrome
description: Gilbert syndrome is a common, usually benign inherited reduction in UGT1A1 activity that causes intermittent unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and mild jaundice, often first noted in adolescence and triggered by fasting, illness, dehydration, exercise, or menstruation. Most patients need reassurance rather than treatment, but low UGT1A1 can complicate medication use, raising toxicity risk or forcing dose and regimen changes with drugs such as irinotecan and some HIV protease inhibitors.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-sedating, on-demand bilirubin–lowering therapy for Gilbert syndrome patients with intermittent jaundice that meaningfully impairs quality of life.
- Adjunct to prevent/treat atazanavir/indinavir-associated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia/jaundice in UGT1A1*28 (Gilbert) carriers to avoid drug discontinuation/switching.
- Supportive therapy to reduce irinotecan toxicity (and dose reductions) in Gilbert syndrome/UGT1A1*28 patients (e.g., genotype-guided regimens plus pharmacologic detoxification/UGT1A1-augmentation concepts).

name: Arteriosclerosis | Mönckeberg
description: Mönckeberg arteriosclerosis is progressive calcium phosphate calcification of the arterial media, often in older patients with diabetes or chronic kidney disease, that can stay clinically silent for decades and cause stiff noncompressible arteries and misleadingly high ankle brachial index readings. Despite minimal stenosis, it worsens limb hemodynamics and is linked to below the knee disease, foot ulcers, chronic limb threatening ischemia, and higher amputation risk. No pharmacotherapy or causal disease modifying treatment exists, leaving major unmet needs in early detection, risk stratification, and therapies that prevent calcification and limb complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy to halt/reverse medial arterial calcification (CaP deposition) and reduce arterial stiffness/CLTI progression in diabetes/CKD-associated MAC.
- Limb-salvage therapies for T2DM/CKD patients with infrapopliteal/foot MAC to improve nonhealing ulcer outcomes and reduce amputation risk.
- Bleeding-sparing cardiovascular event prevention for advanced CKD/dialysis patients with MAC (safer antiplatelet/antithrombotic strategies with dedicated evidence).

name: Peyronie’s disease
description: Peyronie’s disease is a chronic fibrotic scarring disorder of the penile tunica that causes penile curvature, pain, deformity, and often erectile dysfunction, impairing sexual function and psychosocial wellbeing. Typically presenting in the mid 50s, curvature can worsen during the active phase and spontaneous improvement is uncommon. Nonsurgical options are limited mainly to injection intensive intralesional collagenase in selected stable cases, with serious injury risk and restricted access, leaving a need for convenient disease modifying therapies that halt fibrosis and address complex deformities earlier.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Active-phase (pain-defined) therapy that prevents penile curvature progression/worsening
- Non-injection (or far fewer-visit) regimen achieving Xiaflex-like curvature benefit with lower local AEs/penile-injury risk (ideally without REMS restrictions)
- Efficacy in currently under-served subgroups (ventral plaques/curvature, hourglass/hinge defects, severe curvature >90°, calcified plaques, and/or significant erectile dysfunction)

name: Trichomoniasis | Trichomonas tenax
description: Trichomoniasis is a highly prevalent sexually transmitted protozoal infection of the urogenital tract that is often asymptomatic but can cause malodorous vaginal discharge, irritation, and inflammation, and is associated with higher risk of human immunodeficiency virus acquisition and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Care is hampered by reliance on a single effective drug class, nitroimidazoles, with metronidazole resistance, limited options for true allergy, and high recurrence largely driven by reinfection, making adherence friendly regimens and effective partner co-treatment key needs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non‑5‑nitroimidazole systemic option for metronidazole‑resistant trichomoniasis and for patients with true 5‑nitroimidazole hypersensitivity.
- True single‑dose (or ultra‑short) regimen achieving microbiologic cure comparable to 7‑day metronidazole.
- Reinfection‑resistant strategy (e.g., index+partner co‑treatment/EPT‑aligned pack) to reduce recurrence from untreated partners.

name: Urticaria | chronic spontaneous
description: Chronic spontaneous urticaria is recurrent, unpredictable itchy wheals and sometimes angioedema lasting over six weeks, driven by skin mast cell activation. It most often affects women aged 30 to 50 and can drag on for years before diagnosis, disrupting sleep, work, and quality of life. Standard step therapy leaves many patients inadequately controlled, with a severe type IIb autoimmune subgroup responding poorly to antihistamines and anti-immunoglobulin E. Key gaps include practical biomarkers to guide endotyping, plus treatments that are both convenient and safe given injection monitoring burdens and potential bleeding or liver constraints with newer oral options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Reliable complete control (UAS7=0 and AAS7=0) in patients refractory to up-dosed antihistamines and omalizumab.
- Biomarker/endotype-guided treatment specifically for Type IIb (IgG-mediated) autoimmune CSU where omalizumab response is poor/late and routine detection is difficult.
- Lower-burden long-term options avoiding Xolair clinic initiation/observation and avoiding BTK-inhibitor safety constraints (e.g., bleeding risk; hepatic-impairment restrictions).

name: Plica syndrome
description: Plica syndrome is an overuse knee condition where an inflamed synovial fold causes anterior or anteromedial pain, swelling, and clicking, often in runners and cyclists. It is frequently missed and can become fibrotic and irritate adjacent cartilage. Treatment is typically stepwise and slow, starting with rest, physical therapy, and anti inflammatory drugs, then injections or arthroscopic resection. Key unmet needs include faster, durable local symptom relief and steroid and nonsteroidal anti inflammatory drug sparing options that reduce bleeding, joint damage, and infection risks.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid-acting (ideally local) anti-inflammatory/analgesic to speed return to pain-free activity and avoid prolonged conservative care or arthroscopic resection recovery.
- Steroid- and NSAID-sparing symptom control (e.g., non-steroidal intra-articular/topical) that preserves pain/swelling relief while avoiding NSAID GI risks and cortisone-shot cartilage/infection risks.
- Targeted anti-fibrotic/chondroprotective therapy for impinging type C/D plicae with suspected cartilage damage to prevent progression and reduce need for arthroscopy.

name: Malaria | Plasmodium malariae
description: Quartan malaria from Plasmodium malariae often presents as a mild flu-like illness with low parasitemia, weakness, splenomegaly, and mild anemia and thrombocytopenia, and can be missed because of longer incubation. The core unmet need is sterilizing, kidney-compatible treatment since the parasite can persist at very low densities for decades or life, driving chronic infection and nephrotic syndrome risk, and standard short artemether lumefantrine courses may be suboptimal for its 72-hour replication cycle.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Ultra-short (ideally single-dose) sterilizing regimen to eradicate chronic/asymptomatic *P. malariae* carriage.
- Regimens validated to prevent late persistence/recrudescence (e.g., longer exposure than 3-day ACT) and overcome chloroquine resistance.
- Renal-/cardiac-safer oral therapy for patients with nephrotic syndrome/severe renal impairment and/or QT-risk (avoiding chloroquine QT/hypoglycemia constraints).

name: Asthma | type 2-high
description: Type 2-high asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease marked by episodic wheeze and breathlessness, often triggered by viral infections, exercise, or cold air, and associated with biomarkers such as elevated blood eosinophils and exhaled nitric oxide. A subset remains uncontrolled despite optimized inhaled therapy, leading to reliance on oral corticosteroids with serious adverse effects or on injectable or infusion biologics. Even then, only a minority achieve clinical remission, leaving a premium on durable, steroid sparing control with lower treatment burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- True clinical remission for most biologic-treated patients (ACQ‑5 <1.5, no OCS, and FEV1 above LLN/within 100 mL of baseline)
- Steroid-free control for patients uncontrolled on maximal optimized high-dose ICS‑LABA, avoiding long-term systemic corticosteroid toxicity
- Lower administration/safety burden vs injectable biologics via oral/inhaled or ultra–long-acting dosing with fewer injections and reduced anaphylaxis risk

name: Wernicke encephalopathy
description: Wernicke encephalopathy is an acute neurologic emergency caused by thiamine deficiency, most often in undernourished people with alcohol use disorder or malabsorption, presenting with confusion, gait ataxia, and eye movement abnormalities. It is frequently missed because the classic triad is uncommon and there is no rapid confirmatory test, so treatment is delayed until irreversible cognitive injury occurs. Even with thiamine, many patients are left with persistent memory and learning deficits or Korsakoff syndrome, creating a premium on earlier recognition, better diagnostics, and more effective prevention of long term neurologic disability.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct neuro-restorative add-on to thiamine that reduces persistent neurologic sequelae (esp. memory/learning impairment) and improves standardized cognitive outcomes.
- CNS-penetrant thiamine formulation/analog enabling once-daily or single-dose dosing to replace burdensome multi-dose parenteral regimens.
- Prevention/prophylaxis therapy for high-risk chronic alcohol users with malnutrition/poor absorption where oral thiamine is unreliable, using parenteral or absorption-enhanced delivery (± magnesium co-repletion).

name: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
description: Wernicke Korsakoff syndrome is thiamine deficiency driven brain injury often in chronic alcohol use or malnutrition, presenting with acute confusion, ataxia, and eye movement abnormalities and sometimes progressing to largely irreversible Korsakoff amnesia with confabulation. The main unmet need is faster, more reliable recognition since the classic triad is often absent and many cases are missed, delaying parenteral thiamine with magnesium and leaving preventable, persistent cognitive disability once Korsakoff syndrome is established.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neurorestorative/pro‑cognitive add‑on therapies to improve persistent memory/learning impairment after acute treatment
- Rapid-start, low-threshold ED/prehospital-ready regimens effective despite missed/atypical presentation to prevent delayed treatment and progression to Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome
- Cofactor-optimized thiamine platforms (e.g., fixed thiamine+magnesium) to overcome hypomagnesemia-related impaired thiamine utilization/treatment failure

name: West Nile fever
description: West Nile fever is a seasonal mosquito borne West Nile virus infection that usually causes a self limited flu like illness but can leave weeks to months of fatigue. Rarely it progresses to neuroinvasive meningitis or encephalitis, especially in older or immunocompromised patients, with meaningful mortality and frequent long term neurologic sequelae. Care is supportive with no proven antivirals or licensed human vaccine, creating unmet need for early outpatient therapies that prevent progression and for inpatient disease modifying treatments that improve neurologic outcomes and shorten prolonged post infection weakness.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early outpatient antiviral/immunotherapy to prevent progression to neuroinvasive disease in high‑risk patients (≥65 or immunocompromised)
- Disease-modifying therapy for hospitalized neuroinvasive West Nile (encephalitis/meningitis/AFM) to reduce mortality and permanent neurologic sequelae
- Therapy to shorten prolonged post–West Nile fatigue/weakness and restore function/work capacity

name: Accommodative esotropia
description: Common pediatric strabismus where hyperopic accommodative effort drives inward eye crossing, often presenting at 18 to 36 months, risking amblyopia and lost depth perception. Care relies on full time glasses often bifocals plus patching or atropine, with surgery for residual deviation, leaving a need to reduce years of optical and penalization burden while preserving stereopsis and avoiding surgery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-bifocal pharmacologic control of accommodative convergence for high AC/A accommodative esotropia to improve stereopsis and reduce progression to strabismus surgery.
- Safer, more effective topical therapy to reduce accommodative effort/convergence and lessen full-time spectacle dependence (especially poor-adherence children).
- Lower-burden drug (or drug-device) adjunct to prevent/treat amblyopia while reducing patching irritation/distress and atropine side effects/monitoring.

name: Adjustment disorder
description: Adjustment disorder is a maladaptive, time-limited reaction to an identifiable stressor that begins within about 3 months and can cause anxiety, low mood, and physical symptoms that impair functioning, usually resolving within 6 months after the stressor ends.
