- Disease-modifying therapy for primary/degenerative (myxomatous) MR that halts leaflet/ECM degeneration (e.g., TGF‑β–linked VIC/ECM remodeling)
- LV-remodeling/contractility-restoring pharmacology for ventricular functional (secondary) MR that produces clinically meaningful MR-severity reduction (e.g., EROA/regurgitant-volume reductions) beyond standard HF drugs
- Atrial/annular anti-remodeling therapy for atrial functional MR (AF/HFpEF-driven) that reverses atrial/annular dilatation and reduces MR burden while supporting durable rhythm control

name: Dissociative identity disorder
description: Chronic trauma related disorder with alternating identity states and amnestic gaps that impair functioning and is often misdiagnosed; high burden from comorbid depression, anxiety, substance use, self injury and suicidality. Care relies on long term psychotherapy and symptomatic medications, with no drugs that directly treat dissociation and frequent crises driving high acuity needs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- DID-targeted pharmacotherapy that reduces dissociation/identity alteration itself (not just comorbid depression/anxiety)
- Drug intervention specifically reducing self-harm and suicide-attempt burden in DID
- Safe adjunct/maintenance medication that reduces years-long high-frequency psychotherapy and crisis hospitalization needs (avoiding dependence/abuse liabilities)

name: Muscle dysmorphic disorder
description: Muscle dysmorphic disorder is a body dysmorphic disorder subtype, usually starting in late teens to early adulthood (mainly in males), marked by a persistent belief that one is too small or not muscular enough despite being normal or very muscular, driving compulsive training and diet rituals and sometimes anabolic steroid misuse. It carries high burden through impaired quality of life and elevated suicidality and substance use. Treatment relies on cognitive behavioral therapy and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, but there are no United States Food and Drug Administration approved medicines and relapse is common after stopping medication.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid-acting, non-SRI pharmacotherapy for adolescent/young-adult males achieving meaningful MDDI/BDD-YBOCS improvement within ~4–6 weeks
- Durable maintenance/relapse-prevention (or taper-support adjunct) to sustain response when SSRIs are reduced/stopped
- Pharmacotherapy tailored to male muscle-dysmorphia patients with anabolic-androgenic steroid/PED misuse to reduce MD severity and steroid reliance while managing addiction/withdrawal sequelae

name: Narcissistic personality disorder
description: Narcissistic personality disorder is a chronic condition marked by grandiosity, need for admiration, and lack of empathy, with hypersensitivity to criticism that can trigger shame or rage and damage work and relationships. Burden is compounded by common comorbid mood and anxiety disorders, substance use, and suicide risk. Care relies largely on psychotherapy despite no randomized trial evidence and no Food and Drug Administration approved medications, and engagement is a key bottleneck with psychotherapy dropout reported around 63 to 64 percent, leaving a need for better supported, scalable approaches that improve social cognition and stabilize shame driven affect.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacologic adjunct that measurably improves empathic processing/social-cognitive functioning to drive durable interpersonal functioning gains
- Medication that reduces shame/humiliation-driven affect storms to prevent alliance ruptures and cut the ~63–64% psychotherapy drop-out rate
- Well-tolerated, non-dependence-forming pharmacotherapy for high-comorbidity (mood/anxiety, substance use) and suicide-risk patients, optimized to avoid sexual/cognitive adverse effects that depress adherence

name: Pancreatic cancer | adenocarcinoma
description: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is an aggressive, often asymptomatic cancer that is frequently diagnosed after regional spread or metastasis, causing weight loss, abdominal pain, jaundice, and new onset diabetes. Standard first line metastatic chemotherapy extends survival by months but is highly toxic, while dense desmoplastic stroma and the dominance of KRAS driven biology limit drug delivery and broad targeted options. With few actionable subtypes such as rare microsatellite instability, the central unmet need is earlier detection and better tolerated disease modifying therapies that meaningfully improve survival in advanced disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Improve 1L metastatic PDAC survival beyond current chemo benchmarks (median OS 11.1 mo with FOLFIRINOX; 8.5 mo with nab‑paclitaxel+gemcitabine)
- Less toxic, less logistically burdensome systemic regimens suitable for less‑fit patients (vs ECOG 0–1–limited, infusion-intensive, high grade ≥3 toxicity regimens)
- Precision therapies for the majority of PDAC by targeting dominant drivers (esp KRAS non‑G12C variants), beyond rare MSI‑H/dMMR subsets

name: Paranoid personality disorder
description: Paranoid personality disorder is a chronic pattern of pervasive distrust and suspicion, often starting in late teens or early adulthood, that leads patients to interpret others’ motives as malicious and restrict relationships and functioning. Many lack insight and are highly wary of clinicians, making engagement and rapport difficult. Care is largely ad hoc, with no proven effective treatments, no Food and Drug Administration approved medications, and no disorder specific clinical trials, leaving a major unmet need for evidence based, scalable interventions that patients will accept and that meaningfully improve social and occupational functioning.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- PPD-specific, RCT-validated pharmacotherapy that reduces paranoia/suspiciousness and improves social/occupational functioning.
- Medications that meaningfully reduce hostile/aggressive behavior in PPD with clearer efficacy than off-label antipsychotics.
- Low-burden, well-tolerated anxiolytic/anti-paranoia option that rapidly reduces arousal to enable psychotherapy engagement (reduce dropout/strengthen alliance).

name: Goiter | non-toxic
description: Nontoxic (simple) goiter is a usually benign enlargement of the thyroid with normal hormone levels, often presenting as painless neck swelling but sometimes causing compressive symptoms such as hoarseness, cough, dysphagia, or dyspnea when large. Management ranges from observation for small goiters to radioactive iodine or surgery for volume reduction, yet both can be unsuitable or undesirable due to pregnancy and breastfeeding contraindications and frequent iatrogenic permanent hypothyroidism requiring lifelong thyroid hormone replacement, creating demand for predictable thyroid sparing outpatient shrinkage options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Predictable, non-surgical goiter shrinkage (≥45–65% volume reduction) in symptomatic euthyroid multinodular goiter, including very large (>100 mL) or low-radioiodine-uptake glands.
- Thyroid-sparing volume reduction that matches radioiodine efficacy while minimizing hypothyroidism, radiation thyroiditis, and transient post-treatment thyroid swelling.
- Non-radioactive, outpatient self-administered therapy usable when radioiodine is contraindicated/impractical (e.g., pregnancy/breastfeeding) and avoiding low-response/riskier long-term TSH-suppressive levothyroxine.

name: Thrombophilia | prothrombin G20210A
description: Inherited prothrombin (F2 G20210A) thrombophilia that elevates risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, particularly with pregnancy or estrogen exposure; current care relies on anticoagulation with persistent bleeding tradeoffs and chronic post thrombotic morbidity, creating demand for safer long term and pregnancy compatible options such as factor XI inhibition.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Bleeding-sparing long-term secondary VTE prevention for prothrombin G20210A carriers needing indefinite anticoagulation after unprovoked VTE.
- Pregnancy-/breastfeeding-compatible anticoagulation that avoids daily LMWH injections for ante/postpartum prophylaxis/therapy.
- Adjunct therapy to prevent or reduce post-thrombotic syndrome after proximal DVT (leg pain/edema/skin changes/ulceration risk) despite anticoagulation.

name: Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
description: Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is a chronic, early-adulthood-onset pattern of maladaptive perfectionism, orderliness, and need for control that slows task completion, drives real-world impairment like missed deadlines, and strains relationships. Symptoms are often ego-syntonic, making engagement and change difficult. Care is psychotherapy-forward, but there is no definitive empirically supported treatment and no Food and Drug Administration approved medication, creating a major unmet need for scalable, evidence-based interventions that measurably improve functioning.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacotherapy that reduces core maladaptive perfectionism/rigidity to improve objective real-world functioning (e.g., task completion/deadlines; occupational/interpersonal functioning).
- An adjunct drug that increases insight/readiness-for-change and reduces controlling rigidity to improve engagement with psychotherapy in ego-syntonic/low-insight patients.
- Non-SSRI or SSRI-sparing options with improved tolerability vs off-label SSRIs/SRIs (e.g., less QTc monitoring/dose-limiting risk and fewer sexual side effects/discontinuations).

name: Oligohydramnios
description: Oligohydramnios is too little amniotic fluid in pregnancy, typically detected on ultrasound, often tied to membrane rupture, placental insufficiency, or reduced fetal urine output but sometimes unexplained. It raises risks of cord compression and fetal distress, operative delivery, neonatal morbidity, and with prolonged early cases, underdeveloped lungs. Management is largely close surveillance and decisions about timing delivery, leaving a need for outpatient, disease modifying approaches that reliably restore fluid and address placental dysfunction or membrane leaks.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Outpatient maternal therapy that reliably normalizes AFI/DVP in isolated/idiopathic oligohydramnios to avoid guideline-driven early delivery and reduce induction/continuous fetal monitoring.
- Pharmacologic membrane leak–reduction/sealing therapy for PPROM-related oligohydramnios to maintain amniotic fluid and reduce repeated testing/induction.
- Placental perfusion/function–targeted therapy for FGR/placental-insufficiency–associated oligohydramnios to reduce fetal compromise/stillbirth risk and lessen frequent antenatal surveillance.

name: Leukoplakia
description: Oral leukoplakia is a persistent, often painless, non-scrapable white or gray oral patch typically in adults over 40 with chronic irritation from tobacco and sometimes heavy alcohol use. Because it can be premalignant, management relies on biopsy, risk factor removal, and selective excision, yet recurrence is common and no drug has proven benefit in preventing oral cancer, driving unmet need for durable low-toxicity local chemoprevention and reduced lifetime surveillance burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Proven chemoprevention for high-risk oral leukoplakia (e.g., dysplasia/non-homogeneous or large tongue–floor-of-mouth lesions) that reduces malignant transformation over multi-year follow-up.
- Durable lesion control to prevent post-procedure recurrence/new lesions (field cancerization) and reduce lifetime surveillance/biopsy burden.
- Long-residence topical/local drug delivery (e.g., mucoadhesive formulations/patches) suitable for chronic use with minimal systemic toxicity.

name: Periodic limb movement disorder
description: Periodic limb movement disorder causes repetitive leg or arm jerks during sleep that fragment sleep and lead to insomnia, nonrestorative sleep, and next day fatigue, often recognized by a bed partner and more common in middle and older age. It is a sleep study confirmed diagnosis of exclusion, since periodic movements can be incidental and symptoms may reflect restless legs syndrome or untreated obstructive sleep apnea. The field is constrained by disputed adult causality, thin modern treatment evidence, and tolerability tradeoffs, creating demand for better phenotyping and therapies that reliably improve daytime function without impairing side effects.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- PLMD-specific therapy with modern RCT evidence that lowering frequent PLMS (≥15/h) causally improves sleep disturbance and daytime dysfunction
- Non-sedating/low-dizziness PLMD therapy that preserves next-day functioning
- Treatment targeted to rigorously phenotyped “true PLMD” (diagnosis-of-exclusion) supported by standardized diagnostic workflow/biomarkers

name: Hypertension | secondary
description: Secondary hypertension is high blood pressure driven by an identifiable cause such as kidney, vascular, endocrine, sleep related, or medication factors, and is often silent until it presents as abrupt, very high, or resistant disease with major cardiovascular and renal risk. The key unmet need is reliably finding and treating reversible biology, especially under-screened primary aldosteronism that often lacks low potassium and may explain about one fifth of resistant cases. Progress hinges on better diagnostic pathways and targeted add-on options for true resistant patients, including endothelin pathway blockade and longer acting gene silencing approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Aldosterone-pathway precision therapy for the large (often missed) primary-aldosteronism/low-renin resistant-HTN subgroup, with BP lowering while reducing MRA safety/monitoring friction (e.g., hyperkalemia monitoring, gynecomastia).
- Long-acting antihypertensives that “design out” adherence/pill-burden via infrequent dosing (e.g., quarterly/biannual SC angiotensinogen-siRNA) while maintaining sustained 24‑h BP control.
- Non-RAAS add-on mechanisms for “true” resistant hypertension uncontrolled on standardized triple therapy—specifically endothelin receptor antagonism.

name: Selective IgE deficiency disease
description: Selective immunoglobulin E deficiency is an isolated finding of very low serum immunoglobulin E, typically below 2.5 international units per milliliter, with otherwise normal immunoglobulins. Many patients are asymptomatic, but a clinically important subset develops recurrent upper respiratory infections with high antibiotic burden, chronic sinusitis, and asthma, plus a possible increased malignancy risk that appears higher in nonatopic patients. Care is largely reactive and symptom driven, leaving unmet needs for better risk stratification, antibiotic sparing infection prevention, steroid sparing airway control, and clearer long term monitoring guidance.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Antibiotic-sparing prevention of recurrent sinopulmonary infections in selective IgE deficiency (IgE <2.5 IU/mL; normal IgA/G/M).
- Steroid-sparing control of asthma/rhinosinusitis in IgE-deficient patients via non–IgE-dependent anti-inflammatory mechanisms that don’t worsen infection risk.
- Malignancy-risk–reducing therapy for the highest-risk subgroup with absent serum and cell-bound IgE (negative type I skin tests).

name: Pica disease
description: Pica is a feeding and eating disorder marked by persistent ingestion of nonfood substances for at least one month in people older than age 2, most often seen in young children and during pregnancy. Care centers on behavioral and environmental interventions and correcting nutrient deficiencies, yet serious complications like gastrointestinal obstruction and lead poisoning remain. With no pica specific medications and imperfect adherence to iron or other supplementation due to gastrointestinal side effects, there is a major unmet need for safe, reliable therapies that reduce episodes and prevent high consequence harms.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Behavior-targeted pharmacotherapy that safely/reproducibly reduces pica episodes/compulsive ingestion (e.g., in ASD/IDD)
- Better-tolerated iron (± zinc) repletion that corrects deficiency without GI side effects driving nonadherence
- Overdose-resistant iron therapy/dispensing (formulation + packaging + controlled access) to reduce fatal pediatric ingestion risk

name: Pigment dispersion syndrome
description: Pigment dispersion syndrome is a bilateral anterior segment disorder, classically in myopic young men, where mechanical rubbing sheds iris pigment that clogs the drainage angle and drives intermittent intraocular pressure spikes that can progress to pigmentary glaucoma. Patients are often asymptomatic or notice halos and blurry vision after exercise or in the dark. Care largely relies on chronic pressure lowering drops and laser, but current drugs do not stop pigment release and long term preserved drops can worsen ocular surface disease and adherence, creating demand for drop sparing, preservative sparing, longer acting pressure control and disease modifying approaches that blunt trigger driven pigment shedding.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non‑miotic pharmacotherapy to reduce/stop iris pigment liberation (iris–zonule chafing) in young/high‑myope PDS patients
- Therapies to blunt dilation‑ or vigorous‑exercise–triggered transient IOP spikes and reduce IOP variability in pigmentary glaucoma
- Long‑acting, preservative‑sparing IOP lowering to improve adherence and avoid ocular‑surface toxicity from chronic topical drops

name: Plantar fasciitis
description: Plantar fasciitis is a common cause of heel pain, typically in adults aged 40 to 60 and in athletes, overweight patients, or people who stand for long periods. Pain is worst with the first steps in the morning and the condition often reflects chronic tissue degeneration that can take 6 to 18 months to resolve. Treatment is high burden and largely supportive, while steroid injections are constrained by the risk of weakening the fascia and causing rupture, leaving a need for safer, faster healing and more durable pain relief.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Longer-lasting, non-steroidal local therapy for chronic/recalcitrant plantar fasciitis to replace short-duration steroid injections.
- Degeneration-targeted (non-inflammatory) therapy that shortens the typical 6–18 month course, especially for athletes/standing-job patients unable to fully rest.
- Low-burden, safer symptomatic-control option that reduces frequent self-care (e.g., multiple daily icing) and avoids prolonged NSAID exposure.

name: Separation anxiety disorder
description: Separation anxiety disorder is a developmentally inappropriate, persistent fear of being apart from a primary caregiver that can drive school refusal, distress at separation, and somatic complaints. Care is anchored in cognitive behavioral therapy with exposure, but access and the months long time commitment are major barriers for families. When symptoms are severe or therapy is insufficient, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors may be used, yet they take weeks to work and require close monitoring in youth due to early treatment suicidality risk. The field needs faster acting, safer, durable options that fit acute separation crises without prolonged therapy or long medication courses.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Fast-acting (days-not-weeks) pediatric anxiolytic usable short-course/PRN around separations (e.g., school drop-off)
- Pediatric SAD pharmacotherapy with materially lower suicidality/behavioral-risk monitoring burden than SSRIs/SNRIs
- More durable, relapse-resistant treatment that increases stable remission and reduces relapse, including for CBT nonresponders

name: Staphyloma
description: Pathologic myopia is driven by axial elongation that stretches the posterior globe, producing posterior staphyloma with progressive thinning of retina and choroid and macular degeneration including schisis, chorioretinal atrophy, and choroidal neovascularization. Patients are often working age adults who develop central blurring, distortion, or scotomas and can lose vision irreversibly. Anti vascular endothelial growth factor injections treat neovascular episodes, but nothing reliably slows the underlying structural progression or addresses posterior staphyloma and atrophy, leaving a premium on disease modifying and tissue preserving approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drug therapy to stabilize posterior staphyloma/scleral ectasia in pathologic myopia to prevent downstream maculopathy
- Treatments to slow/stop myopic macular/chorioretinal atrophy progression (reduce atrophic-area enlargement; preserve BCVA/ETDRS letters)
- More durable/lower-burden myopic CNV control beyond intravitreal anti-VEGF (fewer retreatments/monitoring; sustain long-term vision; prevent CNV→atrophy transition)

name: Adenoma | thyroid, non-toxic
description: Benign, nonfunctioning thyroid adenoma typically presents as a painless thyroid nodule, often incidentally found in older women, and is usually asymptomatic unless it causes neck compression. Management centers on ruling out cancer while avoiding unnecessary surgery that can lead to lifelong hypothyroidism, and there is no safe, effective medical therapy to reliably shrink or stabilize nodules since thyroid stimulating hormone suppression offers only modest benefit with potential harms. Recurrent cystic nodules often require repeat procedures, with surgery or percutaneous ethanol injection still common, driving demand for more durable, minimally invasive ablation approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Progression-stopping therapy for the “growing benign nodule” subset to prevent significant growth and avoid escalation to thyroidectomy.
- Non-hormonal (non–TSH-suppressive) oral therapy that delivers meaningful nodule shrinkage in euthyroid patients without iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis risk.
- Improved intranodular therapy for recurrent benign cystic nodules to prevent high post-aspiration re-accumulation and reduce ethanol-injection burden/tolerability issues.

name: Pulmonary emphysema
description: Pulmonary emphysema is a chronic obstructive lung disease where destruction of alveolar walls leaves fewer, larger air sacs and impaired gas exchange, causing progressive breathlessness and chronic cough, typically emerging after age 40 in long term smokers. It remains incurable so care is largely symptomatic, and key gaps are limited disease modification and burdensome trade offs such as pneumonia risk with inhaled corticosteroids, poor tolerability of oral anti inflammatories like roflumilast, and widespread inhaler technique errors that blunt real world benefit, sustaining demand for safer anti inflammatory control and therapies that slow structural tissue loss.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy that slows structural emphysema progression (e.g., improved CT densitometry/PD15), not just symptom control.
- Exacerbation-prevention anti-inflammatory therapy matching/outsourcing ICS triple-therapy efficacy with lower pneumonia risk and better tolerability than roflumilast.
- Less technique-dependent (“error-proof”) delivery options to improve real-world effectiveness in patients prone to inhaler misuse/nonadherence.

name: Trombiculiasis
description: Trombiculiasis is an outdoor acquired dermatitis from larval chigger bites causing intense itching and clustered red papules or hives, often at the waistline, ankles, and skin folds. Symptoms can begin within hours and persist up to two weeks, with lesions typically resolving in 1 to 2 weeks. Care is largely symptomatic with antihistamines and topical corticosteroids, and scratching can trigger secondary bacterial infection such as impetigo or cellulitis. Key unmet needs are faster, longer lasting itch control and lower burden prevention beyond repeated use of DEET repellents and permethrin treated clothing.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid-onset, steroid-sparing antipruritic control that sustains relief across the full itch window (up to ~2 weeks) without sedating antihistamines
- Fast interruption of the itch–scratch cycle to prevent secondary bacterial skin complications (e.g., impetigo/cellulitis) and avoid antibiotic escalation
- More convenient, long-duration prophylaxis for outdoor re-exposure (e.g., skin-safe or longer-lasting repellents/acaricides) vs permethrin clothing limitations

name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
description: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is an age related enlargement of the prostate that compresses the urethra, causing lower urinary tract symptoms such as weak stream, urgency, frequency, nocturia, and sometimes urinary retention. Current drugs trade symptom relief against dizziness or sexual side effects and prostate shrinking agents can take up to six months, while procedures help but leave demand for faster, safer, nocturia focused control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Nocturia-focused therapy that meaningfully reduces night-time voids and patient-reported nocturia bother
- Symptom relief (IPSS/Qmax) without orthostatic hypotension/syncope (reduced fall risk) in older/medically complicated men
- Faster-acting progression-modifying therapy that lowers acute urinary retention/surgery risk without 5‑ARI sexual dysfunction

name: Alzheimer’s disease | mild cognitive impairment
description: Alzheimer’s disease is an irreversible, progressive neurodegenerative brain disorder marked by amyloid beta plaques and tau tangles that slowly destroys memory, thinking, and daily function, typically starting after age 65. Early patients may remain largely independent, but decline is relentless and no therapy stops or reverses lost cognition. New anti amyloid antibodies modestly slow progression but require amyloid confirmation, frequent intravenous infusions, and magnetic resonance imaging monitoring, with boxed warning risks of amyloid related imaging abnormalities and rare intracerebral hemorrhage, limiting scalability and leaving major need for safer, easier, truly disease modifying options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ARIA/ICH‑safer disease modification for early AD (MCI/mild dementia), especially usable in ApoE ε4 homozygotes and patients on anticoagulants/thrombolytics
- Therapies delivering stabilization or improvement (not just modest slowing) on cognition/function endpoints (CDR‑SB, iADRS, ADL/iADL)
- Lower‑burden, more scalable treatment with minimal monitoring (avoid frequent IV infusions, serial MRIs, and amyloid confirmation/PET‑guided stopping)

name: Age-related macular degeneration | wet
description: Wet age-related macular degeneration is a late-stage retinal disease driven by abnormal fragile blood vessel growth under the retina that leaks and scars the macula, causing central vision loss with preserved side vision. Patients often notice wavy or distorted lines and a blurry central spot that can undermine reading and driving. Anti vascular endothelial growth factor injections can stabilize vision but create heavy visit burden with many needing monthly or bimonthly injections, while 40 to 50 percent still have retinal fluid at 12 months and rare injection related complications persist, motivating longer lasting therapies and gene based approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durability that reduces injection/visit burden for “injection‑intensive” patients while maintaining vision with far fewer than monthly intravitreal injections.
- Improved efficacy for the ~25–35% with suboptimal/late anti‑VEGF response, achieving sustained drying (no intraretinal fluid) and ideally adding antifibrotic benefit.
- Safer therapies (and/or less invasive delivery) that lower serious injection/drug risks (e.g., endophthalmitis, intraocular inflammation/vasculitis/occlusion) and minimize systemic VEGF‑inhibitor exposure.

name: Amoebiasis
description: Amoebiasis is a fecal orally transmitted Entamoeba histolytica infection that is often asymptomatic but can cause diarrhea and abdominal pain, progress to bloody dysentery with fever, or rarely spread to the liver causing abscesses with fever and right upper quadrant pain. Care still relies on nitroimidazoles that have tolerability and alcohol interaction issues and do not clear luminal cysts, forcing a second luminal agent step with uneven access, leaving demand for a simple single course oral cure that reliably eradicates both invasive disease and carriage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Single-course oral cure that clears both invasive trophozoites and luminal cyst carriage (stool eradication), eliminating the mandatory nitroimidazole → luminal 2-step regimen.
- Tissue-active alternative to metronidazole/tinidazole that avoids key nitroimidazole safety/adherence liabilities (e.g., alcohol disulfiram-like reaction, neurologic toxicity).
- Salvage options for metronidazole-refractory/partially resistant amebic colitis with dependable cyst clearance and less reliance on problematic luminal agents (limited diloxanide access; iodoquinol neuro-ophthalmic risk).

name: Coxsackie B virus infection
description: Coxsackievirus B is an enterovirus infection usually starting with a flu like prodrome and sometimes epidemic pleurodynia with severe pleuritic chest or abdominal pain, but with a dangerous tail of myocarditis, aseptic meningitis, and in neonates potentially fatal multiorgan disease. Management is largely symptomatic and supportive with no specific antiviral treatment or prophylaxis, creating a premium on therapies that can rapidly curb viral replication early and on peripartum prevention strategies to protect high risk newborns.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early antiviral (oral/IV) to prevent/attenuate viral myocarditis/myopericarditis and fulminant HF/arrhythmias in neonates & young children
- Peripartum/neonatal prophylaxis (vaccine or passive neutralizing antibody around delivery) to prevent severe neonatal Coxsackie infection within 2 weeks after birth
- CNS-penetrant antiviral/immunotherapy to reduce severity of enteroviral meningitis/encephalitis and related hospitalization in infants/children

name: Streptococcal infection | group A
description: Group A Streptococcus infection most often presents as strep throat in school age children with sudden sore throat, fever, painful swallowing, inflamed tonsils and anterior neck lymph nodes, but can rarely progress to life threatening invasive disease such as pneumonia, necrotizing fasciitis or streptococcal toxic shock syndrome. Care still depends on accurate testing and a 10 day penicillin or amoxicillin course to prevent acute rheumatic fever, creating demand for shorter regimens and reliably effective options for penicillin allergy amid substantial macrolide and clindamycin resistance. Adjunctive treatments for toxin mediated severe disease remain uncertain.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course, narrow-spectrum antibiotic regimen for confirmed GAS pharyngitis that matches 10-day penicillin/amoxicillin on cure/eradication while still preventing acute rheumatic fever in children
- Penicillin-allergy-safe oral option with reliable activity despite macrolide/clindamycin resistance (reducing need for susceptibility testing)
- Adjunct anti-toxin/immune-modulating therapy for invasive GAS (STSS/necrotizing fasciitis) that reduces mortality beyond current adjuncts

name: Hookworm infection
description: Soil transmitted intestinal helminth acquired via larvae penetrating skin from feces contaminated soil, often from barefoot exposure. Light infections may be asymptomatic, but heavy burdens cause diarrhea and abdominal pain, malnutrition, and chronic blood loss leading to iron deficiency anemia, with disproportionate harm in children and women of reproductive age including pregnancy risks. Control still depends on repeated mass deworming plus sanitation and behavior changes to prevent reinfection, with limited durable protection and a practical treatment gap in first trimester pregnancy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Single-dose, field-deployable oral therapy with higher hookworm cure/egg-reduction than current MDA benzimidazoles
- Durable post-treatment protection that reduces reinfection and the need for repeated MDA rounds
- Anthelmintic with safety sufficient for use in the 1st trimester of pregnancy

name: Mycoplasma genitalium infection
description: Mycoplasma genitalium is a sexually transmitted infection causing urethritis and cervicitis and linked to pelvic inflammatory disease, often presenting with non purulent urethral discharge or post coital bleeding. Treatment is constrained by intrinsic beta lactam ineffectiveness and high macrolide resistance, forcing multi step resistance guided regimens that are limited by access to resistance testing and by fluoroquinolone safety risks, creating demand for simpler, safer oral options for resistant infections.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral, high microbiologic-cure therapy for macrolide-resistant and dual-resistant *M. genitalium* (incl. moxifloxacin failures).
- Non-fluoroquinolone second-line option avoiding moxifloxacin boxed-warning toxicities/QT risk.
- Short-course, single-regimen treatment replacing two-stage/sequential therapy and reducing need for test-of-cure at ≥3 weeks.

name: Pediculosis pubis
description: Pediculosis pubis is a sexually transmitted infestation with pubic lice (Phthirus pubis) causing intense genital itching and visible lice or nits. Current care is effective but operationally burdensome, often requiring repeat applications, treatment of recent sexual partners, and decontamination of bedding and clothing, with retreatment or agent switching when eggs persist. Management is particularly awkward when eyelashes are involved because standard regimens should not be used around the eyes, creating a need for safer, simpler, one and done options that reliably clear lice and eggs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Single-application, ovicidal pubic-lice therapy that kills eggs to avoid nit removal and repeat treatment.
- Resistance-breaking (non‑pyrethroid) option for permethrin/pyrethrin failures without malathion/ivermectin tradeoffs.
- Ophthalmic-safe pediculicide for eyelash involvement to replace multi-day occlusive ointment regimens.

name: Tinea versicolor
description: Common benign superficial fungal skin infection from overgrowth of normal Malassezia yeast causing finely scaly hypo or hyperpigmented patches on the trunk and neck, often in teens and young adults; antifungals clear infection but discoloration can linger for weeks to months and relapse is frequent, driving long term maintenance or monthly whole body prophylaxis, while oral azoles for refractory cases add liver test and drug interaction risks.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Long-acting relapse-prevention therapy for patients with frequent recurrent tinea versicolor to eliminate ongoing monthly full-body prophylaxis.
- Adjunct treatment that speeds repigmentation/skin-tone normalization after antifungal cure (dyspigmentation can persist weeks–months).
- Short-course whole-body therapy for widespread or topical-refractory disease that avoids systemic azole safety/drug–drug interaction liabilities.

name: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection
description: Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus is an antibiotic resistant staph infection that often presents as a painful pus draining skin boil or abscess but can progress to pneumonia, bloodstream infection, sepsis, and death. Key unmet needs include faster clearance of prolonged bacteremia, effective options for biofilm and device associated infections where removal may be the only cure, and safer less burdensome therapy that avoids intensive monitoring and toxicities such as vancomycin related kidney injury and linezolid related blood count suppression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies/adjuncts that kill persister/tolerant MRSA to clear persistent MRSA bacteremia (≥3–7 days positive blood cultures) after vancomycin/daptomycin failure.
- Biofilm-active MRSA drugs to eradicate device/foreign-body and deep-seated infections (catheters/CIEDs/prostheses/osteomyelitis/endocarditis) without prolonged courses and removal surgery.
- Monitoring-/toxicity-sparing serious-MRSA regimens (e.g., simplified IV-to-oral or long-acting options) that avoid vancomycin nephrotoxicity/AUC monitoring and linezolid weekly CBC monitoring.

name: Hypertension | gestational
description: Gestational hypertension is new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks in a previously normotensive pregnancy, often asymptomatic but carrying substantial risk of progression to preeclampsia and placental mediated maternal and fetal harm including placental abruption, fetal growth restriction, and stillbirth. Management is surveillance heavy with frequent blood pressure, lab, and fetal monitoring and often timed delivery, while antihypertensive treatment for nonsevere disease has limited impact on outcomes, leaving unmet needs for better risk stratification, safer and more effective medications, and tools to prevent progression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Progression-modifying therapy (beyond BP lowering) for nonsevere gestational HTN that improves maternal–fetal outcomes and reduces intensive weekly monitoring
- Fetal-safe, better-tolerated oral maintenance antihypertensive achieving ≤135/85 for women unsuitable/contraindicated for labetalol (and avoiding tachycardia/sedation)
- Rapid-onset, non-IV “rescue” agent for severe-range gestational HTN (≥160/110) with faster time to non-severe BP and fewer maternal/fetal/neonatal adverse effects

name: Preeclampsia
description: Preeclampsia is a hypertensive pregnancy syndrome arising after 20 weeks, diagnosed on prenatal screening via new hypertension with proteinuria or organ injury, and can rapidly endanger mother and fetus through seizures, stroke, fetal growth restriction, and preterm birth. Management is intensive monitoring with antihypertensives and magnesium sulfate, but definitive cure remains delivery, making early onset disease especially hard to treat without precipitating prematurity. Key unmet needs include disease modifying therapies that safely prolong gestation, better prevention beyond low dose aspirin, and improved biomarker guided triage to reduce monitoring burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy for preterm/early-onset preeclampsia that safely prolongs gestation (time to delivery) and improves neonatal outcomes (e.g., birthweight, neonatal length of stay) in ~<32–34 week cases.
- More effective prevention of preterm preeclampsia in high-risk pregnancies than aspirin prophylaxis.
- Lower-burden outpatient maternal stabilization that reduces intensive twice-weekly surveillance/labs and avoids prolonged IV magnesium sulfate infusions/monitoring toxicity risk.

name: Renal cyst
description: Simple renal cysts are common, usually benign fluid filled kidney sacs that increase with age and are often found incidentally, especially in older men. Most need no treatment, but enlarging, infected, or ruptured cysts can cause pain, fever, hematuria, or obstruction. Care for symptomatic disease is largely procedural with percutaneous drainage plus alcohol sclerotherapy or laparoscopic deroofing, and the main gap is durability since recurrence after sclerotherapy is frequent and comparative trial evidence is limited.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical pharmacologic cyst shrinkage for symptomatic/complicated large simple renal cysts (e.g., ≥9 cm with mass-effect/obstruction/hypertension).
- Single-session outpatient intracystic therapy that prevents re-accumulation/recurrence after drainage.
- Better-tolerated sclerosants/adjuncts vs ethanol that maintain efficacy while reducing pain/fever/systemic reactions.

name: Hyperaldosteronism
description: Hyperaldosteronism is excess adrenal aldosterone, typically presenting as midlife hypertension that may be resistant to standard drugs and can cause weakness, cramps and arrhythmias when potassium is low. Treatment relies on chronic mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists with frequent electrolyte and kidney monitoring, but side effects such as gynecomastia and sexual dysfunction and the fact these drugs do not lower aldosterone itself leave a gap for better tolerated, disease targeted therapies. The near term frontier is directly suppressing aldosterone production with aldosterone synthase inhibitors.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Once-daily CYP11B2 (aldosterone synthase) inhibition to directly suppress aldosterone and improve outcomes vs MRAs
- MR antagonism that maintains BP control while eliminating spironolactone’s androgen/progesterone-mediated tolerability limits (e.g., gynecomastia)
- Effective primary aldosteronism therapy with materially less hyperkalemia risk and reduced potassium/renal-function lab-monitoring burden vs current options

name: Hypermagnesemia
description: Hypermagnesemia is excess blood magnesium, usually in patients with acute or chronic kidney disease who receive an added magnesium load from antacids or laxatives or iatrogenic magnesium sulfate. Mild cases may be asymptomatic or cause weakness, nausea, dizziness, and confusion, while severe toxicity can lead to hypotension, respiratory depression, and cardiac arrest. Management is largely reactive using intravenous calcium, diuresis when possible, and dialysis, creating unmet need for better prevention in high risk renal patients and faster renal independent reversal.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-absorbed oral magnesium binder to prevent recurrent hypermagnesemia in advanced CKD/ESRD patients exposed to Mg-containing antacids/laxatives, with low hypomagnesemia risk.
- Rapid renal-independent IV magnesium-sequestration therapy for severe symptomatic hypermagnesemia in AKI/ESRD to reduce reliance on dialysis/large-volume fluids/loop diuresis.
- L&D-ready, non-vesicant fast antidote for iatrogenic MgSO₄ toxicity in preeclampsia/eclampsia as a safer alternative to IV calcium gluconate.

name: Hypernatremia
description: Hypernatremia is a water deficit relative to salt, most often affecting older or nursing home patients with impaired thirst or limited access to fluids, causing dehydration and nonspecific neurologic decline that can progress to delirium, seizures, coma, and death. Treatment is still careful free water replacement, often intravenous, but is operationally difficult because sodium must be corrected slowly with frequent lab monitoring to avoid iatrogenic cerebral edema and permanent brain injury, leaving a need for safer, more error tolerant correction and better prevention of recurrence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer, more error-tolerant sodium-lowering therapy that reduces q2–4h sodium monitoring and lowers iatrogenic cerebral edema risk.
- Low-burden non-IV correction/prevention for frail/delirious patients unable to drink, reducing multi-day inpatient IV hydration.
- Mechanism-based pharmacotherapy for DI-driven/recurrent hypernatremia (esp. nephrogenic DI) plus central-DI options with lower desmopressin-associated hyponatremia risk.

name: Hypomagnesemia
description: Hypomagnesemia is low serum magnesium that may be silent until it causes weakness, cramps, seizures, or dangerous ventricular arrhythmias. Management is constrained by poorly absorbed, diarrhea limited oral magnesium and the need for hospital based intravenous magnesium in severe cases. Many patients have persistent drivers such as renal magnesium wasting or long term proton pump inhibitor use, where supplementation alone can fail unless the cause is addressed, creating demand for durable outpatient correction.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Outpatient magnesium repletion that sustains normal serum Mg without diarrhea-limited oral dosing or hospital-only IV administration
- Adjunct magnesium-sparing therapy for renal magnesium-wasting hypomagnesemia (e.g., diuretic- or cisplatin-associated)
- Mechanism-based treatment for PPI-induced hypomagnesemia that corrects Mg without stopping PPIs

name: Nephrolithiasis
description: Nephrolithiasis is kidney stone disease where crystal deposits form in the kidney and can obstruct the urinary tract, causing severe flank or back pain, hematuria, and vomiting. Most stones are calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate and cannot be reliably dissolved, so care often defaults to symptom control, medical expulsive therapy, and procedures. Recurrence prevention is weak and can carry metabolic side effects, highlighted by hydrochlorothiazide failing to meaningfully reduce recurrence in NOSTONE, leaving a premium on true stone dissolution and safer, durable prevention.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- True medical dissolution therapy for calcium oxalate/phosphate stones (majority of kidney stones).
- More effective, safer recurrence-prevention for recurrent calcium-stone formers vs thiazides (durable reduction in symptomatic/radiologic recurrence).
- On-label, reliable outpatient stone-passage + pain pharmacotherapy beyond distal ureteral stones >5 mm, including options safer than NSAIDs for patients with impaired renal function.

name: Hypotension | orthostatic
description: Orthostatic hypotension is a positional drop in blood pressure of at least 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing, most common in older adults and often worsened by polypharmacy. Patients experience dizziness or lightheadedness on standing, blurred vision, weakness, confusion, and syncope, driving falls and cardiovascular risk. Current pressor therapies can improve standing pressure but are limited by supine hypertension and bothersome side effects such as urinary retention, and evidence often relies on short term symptom endpoints. Durable, upright selective symptom control that reduces falls with better long term tolerability remains the key unmet need.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Upright-selective BP support that improves orthostatic symptoms/standing BP with minimal impact on supine BP (avoiding/worsening supine hypertension), especially in patients with comorbid/uncontrolled hypertension.
- Durable efficacy with sustained improvement on validated symptom/function PROs (e.g., OHQ/OHSA/OHDAS) and reduction in clinically meaningful outcomes like falls/syncope beyond short-term (days–2 weeks) effects.
- Lower-burden, better-tolerated regimens that reduce TID dosing/bedtime cutoffs and avoid volume/electrolyte toxicities (e.g., hypokalemia, CHF/CKD worsening) and discontinuation drivers like urinary retention/supine hypertension.

name: Nephropathy | reflux
description: Reflux nephropathy is kidney damage from backward urine flow, usually due to vesicoureteral reflux, often first detected after pediatric urinary tract infections or hydronephrosis. Recurrent infections can lead to permanent renal scarring, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease. Management relies on monitoring, blood pressure control, and daily antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent urinary tract infections, but evidence suggests it does not reduce scarring and increases antimicrobial resistance, leaving a need for antibiotic sparing strategies that prevent infection and protect long term kidney function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent new DMSA-defined renal scarring (~2 years) in high-risk pediatric VUR after febrile/symptomatic UTI.
- Non-antibiotic/antibiotic-sparing prophylaxis to prevent recurrent febrile/symptomatic UTI without selecting for antimicrobial resistance.
- Therapies for established reflux nephropathy that reduce proteinuria and slow eGFR decline/CKD progression beyond BP/RAS blockade.

name: Allergy | tree nut
description: Childhood-onset, often lifelong immunoglobulin E mediated tree nut allergy with unpredictable reactions and anaphylaxis risk from trace exposures. Management is still strict avoidance plus epinephrine readiness, with cross contact and labeling making avoidance fragile. Immunotherapy and newly approved omalizumab can raise reaction thresholds and reduce accidental exposure risk but require ongoing dosing and avoidance and do not replace emergency treatment, leaving a gap for durable, low burden multi nut protection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable multi–tree-nut tolerance achieving high oral-food-challenge thresholds (~2 g protein/nut) with sustained unresponsiveness.
- Pharmacologic prophylaxis that reliably prevents moderate-to-severe reactions/anaphylaxis from trace accidental exposures (including high-potency nuts like cashew).
- Lower-burden, safer long-term maintenance options that reduce OIT reactogenicity/discontinuation and avoid frequent q2–4 week injections/clinic-dependent escalation.

name: Paronychia | chronic
description: Chronic paronychia is persistent inflammation of the nail folds lasting over 6 weeks, most often in wet work and irritant exposed patients (frequently women). Cuticle breakdown allows irritants and microbes to enter, driving recurrent flares that can scar the nail folds and reduce drug penetration. Care depends on irritant avoidance and repeated topical anti inflammatories, but adherence is hard and long term steroids risk skin thinning while calcineurin inhibitors carry cancer warnings, creating demand for wash resistant barrier restoring steroid sparing treatments that prevent recurrence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Wash-resistant, long-acting topical anti-inflammatory + barrier-forming therapy for wet-work patients unable to keep hands dry
- Steroid-sparing topical anti-inflammatory avoiding long-term potent steroid atrophy and tacrolimus malignancy-risk concerns
- Pro-regenerative/anti-fibrotic therapy for recalcitrant fibrosed nail folds with poor drug penetration, accelerating cuticle/barrier re-formation to prevent recurrence

name: Alport syndrome
description: Alport syndrome is a rare inherited type IV collagen basement membrane disorder that often starts in childhood with microscopic hematuria, progresses to proteinuria and chronic kidney disease, and is frequently accompanied by hearing loss and occasional eye findings. Current care mainly relies on supportive kidney protection such as renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockade, which can delay kidney failure but does not correct the underlying defect, and there are no disease specific approved therapies or treatments to prevent Alport related hearing loss.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Mutation-targeted collagen-IV restoration for COL4A3/4/5 nonsense-mutation patients to improve structural kidney biomarkers and proteinuria beyond ACEi/ARB
- Add-on kidney-protective therapy to reduce residual proteinuria and preserve eGFR despite optimized RAAS blockade
- Drug therapy to prevent/slow Alport-associated sensorineural hearing loss (esp. XLAS males) with audiometry-threshold preservation

name: Toxic shock syndrome
description: Toxic shock syndrome is a rare, toxin driven emergency from staphylococcal or streptococcal infection that can strike otherwise healthy people after tampon or menstrual cup use or an infected wound, rapidly progressing from fever and rash to hypotension, shock, and multi organ failure driven by superantigen induced cytokine storm and capillary leak. Outcomes hinge on early recognition, standardized protocols, and rapid intensive care support plus antibiotics that suppress toxin production. Key gaps are faster diagnosis and more targeted prevention or toxin neutralization, with vaccines and immunomodulatory approaches still emerging.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early standardized anti-superantigen/toxin-neutralizing adjunct (e.g., high-titer Ig or mAb cocktail) to blunt cytokine overactivation/capillary leak.
- Non-steroidal host-directed immunomodulator to rapidly improve vasopressor-refractory shock/organ dysfunction (e.g., SOFA/vasopressor days).
- TSST-1–targeted prevention (vaccine or long-acting passive prophylaxis) for menstrual/high-risk populations.

name: Postcholecystectomy syndrome
description: Postcholecystectomy syndrome is persistent or recurrent biliary type right upper quadrant pain after gallbladder removal, often with fatty food intolerance, nausea, diarrhea and occasional jaundice. Causes are heterogeneous and hard to localize, commonly bile acid diarrhea from excess colonic bile acids or sphincter of Oddi disorders, making diagnosis and durable symptom control difficult. Current bile acid sequestrants are often poorly tolerated and only partly effective, while suspected sphincter pathology can push patients toward invasive endoscopy and sphincterotomy, leaving a need for better diagnostics and targeted, tolerable medical therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Better-tolerated, durable therapy for post‑cholecystectomy bile acid diarrhea improving stool frequency and stool form.
- Non-invasive pharmacologic control of post‑cholecystectomy biliary-type pain from sphincter of Oddi dysfunction to reduce reliance on ERCP/sphincterotomy.
- Targeted pharmacotherapy for bile‑reflux gastropathy/gastritis after cholecystectomy where current agents lack sufficient evidence and no bile-reduction–specific drug exists.

name: Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy
description: Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy is an exudative macular disorder from abnormal polypoidal choroidal vessels that typically presents in adults aged 60 to 72 with central vision loss or distortion such as metamorphopsia and central scotoma. Care relies on repeated intravitreal anti vascular endothelial growth factor injections and sometimes verteporfin photodynamic therapy, yet fluid control does not consistently close polyps, leaving ongoing activity and hemorrhage risk. High, often monthly injection burden and inflammation associated safety risks constrain durable, disease modifying treatment.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable therapy enabling much longer dosing intervals to reduce intravitreal injection/clinic-visit burden.
- Monotherapy (or new MOA combos) achieving high complete polyp regression/polyp+AVN closure without ICGA-guided verteporfin PDT “rescue.”
- Comparable efficacy/durability with improved ocular safety vs agents associated with intraocular inflammation, retinal vasculitis and/or retinal vascular occlusion.

name: Multiple system atrophy
description: Multiple system atrophy is a rare, rapidly progressive synucleinopathy starting in the 50s to 60s that causes autonomic failure with parkinsonism or cerebellar ataxia, leading to severe blood pressure, bladder, gait, balance, speech, and swallowing problems. Care is symptomatic only, with no cure and no proven disease slowing therapy, and Parkinson disease drugs often provide limited sustained benefit. A key unmet need is safer control of orthostatic hypotension without worsening supine hypertension, alongside treatments that meaningfully slow functional decline and extend survival.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy for early MSA (≤5 years from motor symptom onset) that slows mortality-adjusted progression on UMSARS/mUMSARS and time-to-death over ~72 weeks
- Orthostatic hypotension treatment that increases upright BP without worsening supine hypertension (reducing falls/syncope without pressor trade-offs)
- Therapy that meaningfully improves gait/ataxia/parkinsonism (or slows motor decline) in MSA-P/MSA-C despite poor/absent levodopa response

name: Marginal zone lymphoma | extranodal
description: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa associated lymphoid tissue is a rare, usually localized, indolent B cell lymphoma often arising in the stomach of older adults, causing site specific symptoms such as dyspepsia, reflux or occult bleeding. First line care is typically Helicobacter pylori eradication, but responses can take months to over a year and require repeated endoscopy and biopsies. The biggest gaps are Helicobacter pylori negative or antibiotic refractory disease and biomarker defined poor responders, where faster, less burdensome, chemo sparing disease control is needed.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Biomarker-guided systemic (non-radiotherapy) therapy for antibiotic-refractory gastric MALT (H. pylori–negative and/or API2/MALT1-positive).
- Chemo-free regimens for advanced/R/R extranodal MZL with deeper, more durable remissions than BTK-inhibitor monotherapy.
- Therapies that shorten time-to-(clinical/endoscopic/histologic) remission and reduce repeat endoscopy/biopsy burden in gastric MALT.

name: Bullous pemphigoid
description: Autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease of older adults causing weeks of intense itch followed by large tense blisters and erosions, typically on flexor limbs and trunk. Care relies on potent topical steroids and, when extensive, oral prednisone, but frail patients often cannot tolerate prolonged immunosuppression and its serious sometimes fatal adverse effects. With many cases resolving within 1 to 5 years, the key need is rapid itch relief and durable steroid sparing disease control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-free durable remission off oral corticosteroids in very elderly/frail BP patients
- Rapid, clinically meaningful pruritus relief (e.g., ≥4-point improvement in peak pruritus NRS), not just blister control
- Reduced treatment/caregiver burden vs whole-body super-potent topical steroid regimens (e.g., high-volume clobetasol applications)

name: Hairy cell leukemia | classic
description: Classic hairy cell leukemia is a rare, indolent B cell malignancy of the bone marrow and spleen, often found incidentally or with fatigue, infections, and splenomegaly in men in their 50s to 60s. Purine analog therapy is effective but can cause months of immunosuppression in an already infection prone population where infection drives morbidity and mortality. Relapse remains a concern, especially with measurable residual disease, creating demand for deeper remissions and less burdensome time limited outpatient regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Infection-safe (non–purine-analog) disease control for patients with active infection and/or older/frail, infection-prone patients
- MRD-negative complete remission and longer MRD-free survival to reduce relapse/retreatment
- More convenient/time-limited outpatient regimens reducing visit burden vs multi-day cladribine infusions (± weekly rituximab) and months-long q2w IV pentostatin

name: Yellow fever
description: Yellow fever is a mosquito-borne viral infection endemic in South America and sub-Saharan Africa that often starts as an abrupt flu-like febrile illness but can progress after a brief remission to a toxic phase with jaundice, bleeding, shock, and multi-organ failure with high short-term mortality. Prevention is vaccine-led, yet the live attenuated vaccine can be contraindicated in key risk groups and shortages can limit outbreak control. Once infected, care is largely supportive with no proven antivirals, creating demand for fast-acting therapeutics, passive protection for vaccine-ineligible people, and intensive-care rescue approaches that prevent liver and kidney failure and hemorrhage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-phase direct-acting antiviral to prevent progression to severe hemorrhagic/toxic disease and reduce mortality vs supportive-only care.
- Rapid-onset non-live prophylaxis/passive immunization (e.g., mAb) providing immediate protection for vaccine-ineligible people and during outbreaks with vaccine shortages.
- Adjunctive rescue therapy in toxic-phase/ICU patients to reduce liver/kidney failure, bleeding/shock, and improve 7–10 day survival beyond supportive management.

name: Vitamin D-dependent rickets
description: Rare inherited failure of vitamin D signaling causing infant-onset hypocalcemia and defective bone mineralization, leading to hypotonia, poor growth, seizures and later painful deforming rickets. Care relies on daily active vitamin D plus calcium, but dosing can be high and prolonged in resistant forms and carries risks of hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis, driving frequent monitoring. Major unmet need is safer, less burdensome, more reliably effective disease control that prevents skeletal deformity while sparing kidneys and reducing intensive supplementation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Renal-sparing active vitamin D replacement that heals rickets while avoiding hypercalciuria/nephrocalcinosis/hypercalcemia and reducing monitoring burden.
- Longer-acting/less-frequent oral therapy to replace lifelong multi-dose (often BID) calcitriol regimens and improve adherence.
- Effective VDDR2A/HVDRR treatment that avoids prolonged IV calcium dependence in severe vitamin-D–resistant patients with limited oral calcium tolerance.

name: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
description: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is an Epstein Barr virus linked head and neck cancer of the nasopharynx that often presents late with nasal obstruction or bleeding, hearing loss, and neck nodes. Many patients have locoregionally advanced disease and are treated with platinum based chemoradiotherapy, but 20 to 30 percent still recur and the curative backbone can leave durable kidney, hearing, swallowing, and dry mouth toxicities, creating demand for more effective and less toxic, biomarker guided treatment strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Cisplatin-sparing (or cisplatin-free) radiosensitizing/immuno-radiotherapy regimens for locoregionally advanced NPC that maintain cure rates while reducing severe acute toxicity and irreversible kidney/hearing damage.
- EBV-DNA–guided adjuvant/maintenance therapies for patients who remain plasma EBV-DNA–positive after standard concurrent chemoradiation to improve long-term PFS/OS.
- Post-platinum (and post–checkpoint inhibitor) therapies for recurrent/metastatic NPC with materially higher ORR and longer PFS/OS (better durability) than current salvage benchmarks.

name: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
description: Acute respiratory distress syndrome is a life threatening acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, typically after pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration, trauma, or pancreatitis, driven by fluid filled alveoli that stiffen the lungs and rapidly impair gas exchange. Treatment is still largely supportive ventilation and intensive care, with few drugs effective across heterogeneous patient phenotypes. Mortality remains high at about one third overall and up to 45 percent in severe disease, and many survivors face long term cognitive impairment and muscle weakness, underscoring the need for disease modifying and phenotype targeted therapies that improve Day 28 mortality and ventilator free days.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute disease-modifying therapy that lowers 28‑day all-cause mortality and increases ventilator‑free days in mechanically ventilated moderate-to-severe ARDS
- Phenotype-targeted immunomodulator for the ~30–40% hyperinflammatory ARDS subphenotype to improve mortality/ventilator‑free days vs one-size-fits-all care
- Adjunct acute/early-recovery drug that prevents ICU-acquired weakness and improves long-term functional outcomes in ARDS survivors

name: Primary biliary cholangitis
description: Primary biliary cholangitis is a chronic autoimmune disease where progressive destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts causes cholestasis, fibrosis, and eventual cirrhosis or liver failure. It mainly affects middle aged women and is often diagnosed incidentally, yet fatigue and pruritus can be debilitating and frequently persist despite therapy. Ursodeoxycholic acid improves outcomes, but up to 40% have an inadequate biochemical response and face higher risk of transplant or death, leaving unmet need for deeper disease control and better treatments for itch and especially fatigue.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer, more potent 2nd-line/add-on therapy achieving complete biochemical response (ALP + bilirubin normalization) in UDCA inadequate responders/intolerant patients
- Fatigue-targeted therapy delivering clinically meaningful improvements on validated PROs (e.g., PBC-40, Fatigue Severity Scale, PROMIS Fatigue)
- Anti-pruritic that meaningfully reduces itch and sleep interference with fewer drug–drug interactions/monitoring burdens and improved tolerability vs current options

name: Cystic fibrosis
description: Cystic fibrosis is an inherited disease where thick, sticky mucus clogs the airways causing recurrent bacterial infections and progressive lung damage, often alongside pancreatic dysfunction with malnutrition and poor growth and sometimes neonatal bowel obstruction. Newborn screening can identify risk early, but patients still face a heavy daily treatment burden. Despite major advances, care is constrained by mutation limited CFTR modulators that do not help people who make little or no CFTR protein, and by persistent, increasingly drug resistant pathogens including Pseudomonas and nontuberculous mycobacteria.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-agnostic CFTR restoration for the ~7% of people with CF who don’t respond to CFTR modulators (incl. ~3% with nonsense mutations).
- Anti-infectives that suppress/eradicate chronic CF airway pathogens (esp. *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* and hard-to-treat NTM) to reduce lung-function decline and pulmonary exacerbations.
- Therapies that materially cut daily treatment burden (airway-clearance + inhaled regimens) and reduce safety monitoring requirements while preserving ppFEV1 and exacerbation control.

name: Systemic mastocytosis | indolent
description: Indolent systemic mastocytosis is a chronic, usually benign mast cell neoplasm with abnormal mast cell accumulation mainly in bone marrow and often skin, causing urticaria pigmentosa and mediator driven symptoms such as pruritus, flushing, syncope, headache, and gastrointestinal pain or diarrhea. Patients remain at risk of severe anaphylaxis and sometimes osteoporosis or fractures. Nonspecific symptoms and reliance on invasive biopsy contribute to long diagnostic delays, and treatment is largely symptomatic with antihistamines and rescue epinephrine, leaving unmet need for earlier diagnosis and more durable multi domain control that reduces polypharmacy and prevents anaphylaxis and bone complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Clinically meaningful, durable multi-domain symptom control (skin/GI/neurocognitive/musculoskeletal) in moderate-to-severe ISM inadequately controlled on BSC polypharmacy, enabling de-escalation of high-burden regimens.
- Prophylaxis that reduces severe anaphylaxis events and decreases reliance on rescue epinephrine/clinic-based monitoring requirements.
- Disease-modifying therapy that prevents/reverses ISM-associated osteopenia/osteoporosis and lowers fragility-fracture risk, including bisphosphonate-unresponsive patients.

name: Dystonia | cervical
description: Cervical dystonia is a rare, often midlife onset movement disorder where involuntary neck muscle contractions twist the head and cause disabling pain and headaches. Botulinum toxin injections can help but benefits often wear off before the next 12 to 16 week dosing window, with many patients reporting symptom return around 10.5 weeks. Dysphagia and other swallowing or breathing risks, plus secondary loss of response that leads 30% to 40% to discontinue, leave a premium on longer lasting, end of cycle stable relief and better options for poor responders.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Longer-lasting, end-of-cycle–stable symptom + pain control to reduce “wearing off” across the ~12-week injection cycle
- Lower dysphagia/respiratory-compromise risk while preserving efficacy
- Non–botulinum-toxin (or rescue) options effective in poor responders/secondary non-responders to reduce discontinuation

name: Laryngeal cancer | squamous cell carcinoma
description: Laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma is a predominantly tobacco and alcohol associated cancer of the voice box, typically diagnosed around age 66 and more common in men, where early hoarseness can herald a disease that threatens speech, swallowing, and breathing. Standard care for locally advanced tumors often requires intensive chemoradiation or total laryngectomy, which can leave patients with a permanent stoma and loss of natural voice. The central unmet need is durable control with organ preservation and less toxicity, driving interest in immunotherapy, targeted approaches, and radiosensitizers.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Response-guided larynx-preservation regimens that improve functional organ preservation (e.g., LEDFS: disease-free with functioning larynx, no tracheotomy/feeding tube).
- Cisplatin-sparing/cisplatin-free concurrent therapy options for cisplatin-unfit locally advanced disease that maintain control while reducing severe mucosal toxicity.
- Effective post–anti-PD-(L)1 progression treatments for recurrent/metastatic disease that improve durability/OS vs limited-benefit salvage chemotherapy.

name: Graft-versus-host disease
description: Graft versus host disease is a potentially life threatening complication of allogeneic stem cell or bone marrow transplant in which donor immune cells attack the recipient, causing early skin rash, gastrointestinal diarrhea, and liver injury. High dose steroids remain first line but only about half respond and immunosuppression drives serious infections. Many patients with chronic disease require prolonged multi line therapy, often becoming steroid resistant or dependent, while a subset develops progressive fibrosis such as sclerodermatous skin disease and bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome with lung outcomes that have not improved in decades.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, infection-sparing control for steroid-refractory grade II–IV acute GVHD, improving on ruxolitinib durability benchmarks
- Steroid-sparing options for moderate-to-severe chronic GVHD that enable successful taper to steroid-free control with symptom/QoL improvement
- Organ-restorative/anti-fibrotic therapies for fibrotic cGVHD (e.g., pulmonary BOS, deep cutaneous sclerosis) that deliver measurable organ-function gains (e.g., FEV1 improvement)

name: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia | mixed-phenotype
description: Mixed-phenotype acute leukemia is a rare, clinically aggressive acute leukemia where blasts show both lymphoid and myeloid identity, typically presenting with marrow failure and severe cytopenias. Treatment is largely empirical, often using acute lymphoblastic leukemia type induction followed by allogeneic stem cell transplant when feasible, leaving major unmet needs for standardized, less toxic options for older or unfit patients and for durable relapse prevention given resistance mechanisms like post immunotherapy lineage switch.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Chemo-sparing, largely outpatient induction for newly diagnosed CD19+ MPAL patients ≥75/unfit, achieving MRD-negative CR with substantially lower severe toxicity vs ALL-like multi-agent induction
- Post-remission therapies that reduce relapse and nonrelapse mortality after/without allo-HSCT, lowering dependence on transplant-intensive care
- Strategies that prevent lineage plasticity/antigen-escape relapse after targeted immunotherapies (e.g., CAR-T/blinatumomab), particularly in KMT2A-rearranged MPAL

name: Tropical spastic paraparesis
description: HTLV-1 associated myelopathy tropical spastic paraparesis is a rare chronic immune mediated inflammatory spinal cord disease, usually adult onset and more common in women, causing slowly progressive spastic leg weakness with early gait impairment plus bladder and bowel dysfunction and sensory symptoms, concentrated in HTLV-1 endemic regions. Care is largely supportive and corticosteroid based, with no proven therapy that modifies long term disability, creating a major unmet need for steroid sparing disease modifying treatments that reduce proviral load and immune driven injury and preserve mobility and bladder function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- HTLV‑1–targeted therapy that lowers proviral load (blood/CSF) and immune activation to modify disease activity.
- Steroid‑sparing disease‑modifying treatment with durable improvement in progressive motor disability (e.g., EDSS/timed-walk) and delayed wheelchair dependence.
- Bladder/OAB-focused drugs for early urinary dysfunction (possible/probable HAM/TSP) to improve QoL and reduce UTI/kidney-injury risk.

name: Sarcoidosis | cutaneous
description: Cutaneous sarcoidosis is a rare skin manifestation of sarcoidosis, often the first sign that prompts workup for systemic disease, presenting as papules or plaques, scar or tattoo infiltration, or disfiguring facial lupus pernio that can scar. Treatment is stepwise with topical or intralesional corticosteroids followed by systemic immunosuppression, but chronic lesions are difficult to control and relapse is common with glucocorticoid tapering, while prolonged steroid use carries substantial toxicity. Key unmet needs are durable steroid sparing disease control and validated outcomes for trials such as the Sarcoidosis Activity and Severity Index and Cutaneous Sarcoidosis Activity and Morphology Instrument.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing systemic therapy providing durable, clinically meaningful improvement on validated cutaneous endpoints (CSAMI-A/SASI) in moderate–severe cutaneous sarcoidosis.
- Reliable clearance of chronic facial/lupus pernio lesions to prevent scarring and permanent disfigurement.
- Convenient localized/topical options for skin-limited disease that avoid local steroid AEs (atrophy/hypopigmentation) and reduce frequent intralesional injection visits.

name: Paraganglioma
description: Paraganglioma is a rare neuroendocrine tumor of paraganglia along the sympathetic chain or in the head and neck, often causing episodic catecholamine symptoms such as headache, palpitations, sweating, and hypertension or local effects such as hearing loss and pulsatile tinnitus. Surgery can be curative when localized, but unresectable or metastatic disease is still treated largely palliatively, with most systemic options achieving disease stabilization rather than durable remissions. Radioligand strategies are constrained by variable tumor uptake and hematologic toxicity, creating demand for safer, genotype guided therapies that deliver lasting tumor control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemic therapy with meaningful tumor shrinkage for unresectable/metastatic paraganglioma patients who are MIBG-scan–negative and/or low-SSTR-uptake (radionuclide-ineligible).
- Non-myelosuppressive alternatives that avoid long-latency therapy-related MDS/acute leukemia and other serious toxicities seen with radiopharmaceuticals/alkylators.
- Genotype-informed regimens that achieve durable remissions (not just disease stabilization) in aggressive metastatic SDHB/SDHx (cluster 1) disease.

name: Restenosis
description: Coronary in stent restenosis is re narrowing of a treated artery after angioplasty, typically over 50% within or adjacent to a prior stent, driven by neointimal tissue overgrowth and later neoatherosclerosis. Patients can re present within months with recurrent angina or acute coronary syndromes and often need repeat revascularization. Key unmet needs are more durable prevention and therapies that reduce repeat procedures, especially in higher risk groups such as people with diabetes, while limiting bleeding risk from prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy. Emerging work is probing inflammation targeted adjuncts for recurrent restenosis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Reduce recurrent coronary in-stent restenosis events by lowering repeat revascularisation/target-vessel revascularisation after ISR PCI.
- Provide ISR prophylaxis with superior efficacy in high-risk diabetics who have persistently higher ISR rates despite DES.
- Enable bleeding-sparing ISR management that avoids prolonged/lifelong antiplatelet therapy needs (e.g., after vascular brachytherapy in refractory/multilayer ISR).

name: Craniopharyngioma
description: Craniopharyngioma is a rare benign tumor near the pituitary and hypothalamus, often presenting in children and again in older adults. Its location means both tumor growth and treatment can damage optic pathways and endocrine control, causing headaches from hydrocephalus, visual field loss, and lifelong pituitary hormone deficiencies. Standard surgery and radiotherapy can control disease but frequently leave severe survivorship morbidity, especially hypothalamic injury leading to difficult-to-treat obesity affecting about half of survivors. Biology guided approaches, including BRAF targeted therapy in papillary tumors and anti inflammatory interleukin-6 pathway blockade for cystic disease, aim to reduce reliance on morbid local therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neoadjuvant/adjuvant oral BRAF+MEK targeted therapy for BRAF V600E papillary craniopharyngioma to achieve major MRI tumor-volume debulking pre-local therapy and reduce long-term morbidity.
- Systemic and/or intracystic anti-inflammatory therapy for adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma (e.g., IL‑6/IL‑6R blockade) to control cystic growth/recurrence where effective medical options are lacking.
- Outpatient pharmacotherapy for post-treatment hypothalamic syndrome/obesity in craniopharyngioma survivors with clinically meaningful weight loss and better tolerability than current approaches.

name: Neuromyelitis optica
description: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder is a relapse driven autoimmune attack on the optic nerves and spinal cord, causing painful vision loss, limb weakness or paralysis, and bladder or bowel dysfunction, typically in women with onset around the 40s. Even when attacks remit, cumulative damage often leaves permanent disability, so patients need better neuroprotection and functional repair after relapses. Treatment gaps include effective options for aquaporin 4 antibody negative and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein associated disease, and safer, easier long term therapy given infusion burden and meningococcal infection risk with some complement inhibitors.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Post-attack neuroprotection/repair to improve recovery (vision + spinal cord function) beyond IV steroids ± plasma exchange.
- Relapse-prevention therapies for AQP4-IgG–seronegative (“double-negative”) NMOSD and MOGAD.
- Safer, less burdensome long-term maintenance that reduces serious infection/REMS burden and IV/SC administration logistics.

name: Nontuberculous Mycobacterial Pulmonary Infection
description: Environmental nontuberculous mycobacteria can cause a chronic lung infection that often presents as slowly progressive nodular bronchiectasis in postmenopausal nonsmoking women, with cough, fatigue, and weight loss. Care requires prolonged macrolide based multidrug therapy for 12 to 18 months and may escalate to parenteral amikacin, where ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity limit use. Outcomes remain poor in macrolide resistant Mycobacterium avium complex and in Mycobacterium abscessus because effective oral options are scarce, leaving a premium on better tolerated and more reliably curative regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- High-conversion regimens for cavitary/advanced or macrolide‑resistant MAC‑PD that improve sputum culture conversion and reduce reliance on IV aminoglycosides.
- Proven-efficacy regimens for *Mycobacterium abscessus* complex pulmonary disease that avoid prolonged IV multidrug therapy and toxicity-driven regimen changes.
- Shorter, better-tolerated first-line MAC/NTM‑PD regimens (esp. nodular/bronchiectatic disease) that achieve durable culture negativity with substantially less duration and AE burden.

name: Angiofibroma
description: Tuberous sclerosis complex associated facial angiofibromas are childhood onset reddish pink papules on the cheeks and nose that can bleed and cause psychosocial distress. Care relies on laser or electrosurgery and topical suppression, but topical sirolimus gel requires twice daily chronic use with relapse after stopping and is only approved for ages 6 and up, leaving unmet need for more durable clearance and pediatric options for children under 6.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Higher facial angiofibroma clearance/near-clearance rates vs current topical sirolimus (reduce need for ablative lasers)
- Durable lesion control that persists off-treatment / prevents relapse after stopping topical sirolimus
- Pediatric- and caregiver-friendly therapy (safe/effective <6 years; less burdensome than twice-daily refrigerated gel; better local tolerability)

name: Amebic liver abscess
description: Amebic liver abscess is an invasive Entamoeba histolytica infection that forms a pus filled liver cavity after fecal oral exposure, typically in men under 50 with endemic travel or immigration, causing fever and right upper quadrant pain often without diarrhea.
