- Endotype/biomarker-guided therapies tailored to CholU heterogeneity (e.g., MGL_1304 sweat-allergy vs CHRM3-low anhidrosis/hypohidrosis subtypes).
- Rapid, on-demand prophylaxis/rescue dosing before predictable triggers to avoid continuous daily/up-dosed antihistamines and reduce need for injectable biologics.

name: Tuberous sclerosis
description: Tuberous sclerosis complex is a genetic, multisystem tumor syndrome (TSC1 or TSC2 variants) that often presents in infancy with seizures, infantile spasms, developmental delay, and neuropsychiatric problems. Management is chronic and symptomatic, with no cure, and treatment is constrained by safety and access tradeoffs, including vigabatrin’s permanent vision loss risk and restricted distribution and systemic mTOR inhibition that can cause immunosuppression and pneumonitis. A key unmet need is safer, earlier disease modifying approaches that prevent epilepsy related neurodevelopmental injury and better address TSC associated neuropsychiatric disorders.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pre-symptomatic anti-epileptogenic therapy in EEG-biomarker–positive infants with TSC to prevent progression to drug-resistant epilepsy and improve neurodevelopment, without vigabatrin’s irreversible vision toxicity/REMS burden.
- Non-immunosuppressive alternative to chronic systemic mTOR inhibition for renal AML/SEGA (and other systemic manifestations) that preserves lesion control while avoiding serious/fatal infection and pneumonitis risks.
- TSC-specific pharmacologic treatments for TAND symptom clusters (autism/ADHD/anxiety/executive & scholastic deficits) that meaningfully reduce neuropsychiatric burden and close the evaluation/treatment gap.

name: Anal fistula
description: Anal fistula is a chronic tunnel between the anal canal and perianal skin, usually following an infected anal gland abscess, causing persistent painful drainage and recurrent flares. It rarely heals spontaneously and lacks a medical cure, so treatment is largely surgical, but clinicians must balance closure against sphincter injury, incontinence risk, and recurrences that can reach ~50% in complex cases. The key unmet need is durable, continence preserving, minimally invasive therapies, with growing interest in local regenerative or cellular approaches layered onto limited debridement.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Sphincter-preserving local drug/biologic that cures cryptoglandular anal fistula without surgery (complete healing/closure with no drainage)
- Continence-sparing therapy for complex/high fistulas that avoids sphincter division while improving durable healing (lower Wexner/incontinence impairment; lower recurrence)
- Post-op adjunct to accelerate epithelialization and reduce dressing-change pain to reduce daily wound-care burden

name: Hemorrhagic cystitis
description: Hemorrhagic cystitis is an acute, sometimes life threatening bladder lining injury with bleeding, most often after cyclophosphamide or ifosfamide chemotherapy, pelvic radiation, or BK polyomavirus in immunosuppressed stem cell transplant patients. It can progress from painful urinary frequency and gross hematuria to clot obstruction requiring catheterization, irrigation, transfusions, and surgery. Care is heterogeneous with no standardized, durable sequence, leaving a premium on reliable outpatient hemostatic therapies, better prophylaxis beyond mesna, and validated antiviral or immune strategies for BK virus associated disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Outpatient, rapidly acting, durable hemostatic therapy for radiation‑induced hemorrhagic cystitis with persistent/recurrent gross hematuria.
- More reliable prophylaxis for cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide chemical hemorrhagic cystitis beyond mesna to prevent severe (grade III–IV) clot/hematuria.
- Evidence-based antiviral/immune therapy for BK polyomavirus hemorrhagic cystitis after allogeneic HSCT to reduce prolonged hospitalization and reliance on irrigation/transfusions.

name: Polycythemia vera
description: Polycythemia vera is a chronic myeloproliferative blood cancer, typically in older adults, where the marrow overproduces red blood cells, thickening blood and driving clots plus microvascular symptoms and pruritus. Care relies on ongoing phlebotomy and low dose aspirin to control counts and reduce thrombosis, yet many patients still carry residual clot risk, burdensome symptoms, and a long term chance of progression to myelofibrosis or acute myeloid leukemia, creating demand for therapies that more durably prevent thrombosis, relieve symptoms, and modify the underlying mutant stem cell disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Hard-outcome reduction of arterial/venous thrombosis despite “optimal” phlebotomy + low-dose aspirin
- Therapies that reduce phlebotomy frequency and/or persistent non-thrombotic symptom burden (QoL) even when blood counts are controlled
- Disease-modifying therapy to prevent/delay premature death and transformation to AML or post-PV myelofibrosis

name: Pulmonary hypertension | group 1
description: Pulmonary arterial hypertension is a progressive small pulmonary arteriole remodeling disease that raises pulmonary pressures, drives worsening dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, syncope, and edema, and can end in right heart failure and death. Current therapies can slow progression but are not curative, and major gaps remain for true disease modification, pregnancy safe options given teratogenic risk with endothelin receptor antagonists, and prostacyclin level efficacy without burdensome central line pumps, infection risk, or severe subcutaneous infusion site pain.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying efficacy for intermediate/high-risk PAH via RV reverse remodeling (larger PVR reductions; lower 3-year mortality)
- Non-teratogenic PAH therapies suitable for women of childbearing potential, avoiding ERA pregnancy contraindication/mandatory monthly testing programs
- Parenteral-prostacyclin–level efficacy without pumps/central lines or severe SC infusion-site pain

name: Hypothyroidism | congenital
description: Congenital hypothyroidism is thyroid hormone deficiency from birth, often clinically silent until newborn screening, that can rapidly cause irreversible neurocognitive and growth impairment if treatment is delayed. Levothyroxine is effective but care is constrained by a narrow early window to normalize thyroid levels, infant-unfriendly dosing and formulations, absorption interference from diet and supplements, and intensive early-life monitoring to keep thyroid stimulating hormone and thyroxine in range.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Replacement approaches that reliably normalize thyroid function within ~2 weeks in severe congenital hypothyroidism to minimize residual neurocognitive deficits
- Precision/forgiving dosing to reduce early-life over- and under-treatment cycles (esp. preterm/LBW and central CH)
- Infant-ready, absorption-robust formulations that avoid crushing/mixing errors and reduce interference from soy/iron/calcium and brand/formulation switching

name: Neurofibroma | dermal
description: Dermal or cutaneous neurofibromas are benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors in neurofibromatosis type 1 caused by NF1 mutations that disable the tumor suppressor neurofibromin. Lesions often begin at puberty and accumulate over decades into hundreds or thousands of visible rubbery skin bumps that can itch or hurt, driving disfigurement and quality of life impairment. Management is largely physical removal, limited by scarring, regrowth, cost, and lack of prevention of new lesions, creating demand for scalable topical or systemic therapies that shrink and prevent tumors and improve patient reported itch and pain.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Noninvasive at-home topical drug that shrinks multiple cNFs (incl. facial lesions) with objective lesion-response benchmarks (e.g., ≥50% volume/height reduction in ≥50% of treated lesions at ~6 months), avoiding procedural wound morbidity/scarring
- Systemic (oral) therapy that reduces whole-body cNF burden (count + 3D volume/area) and prevents new-lesion emergence during high-growth windows (puberty/aging/pregnancy)
- Symptom/QoL-targeted therapy (topical or systemic) that measurably improves pruritus/pain/dysesthesia and validated dermatology QoL metrics (e.g., Skindex)

name: Embolism | peripheral arterial
description: Peripheral arterial embolism (acute limb ischemia) is a sudden limb artery blockage, often embolic from atrial fibrillation, causing abrupt loss of perfusion with a cold painful pulseless limb and high risk of tissue necrosis, amputation, and death or disability. Treatment is urgently time sensitive and typically requires thrombectomy or thrombolysis, but many patients are poor candidates due to bleeding risk and contraindications, and even successful revascularization can trigger reperfusion injury and compartment syndrome, creating demand for faster safer reperfusion and tissue protection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Ultra-rapid, safer pharmacologic reperfusion to replace/shorten catheter-directed thrombolysis and reduce major bleeding/stroke risk.
- Effective reperfusion drug option for thrombolysis-ineligible ALI patients with high bleeding risk/lysis contraindications.
- Adjunct drug therapy around revascularization to prevent/treat lower-limb ischemia–reperfusion injury and reduce downstream organ/limb damage.

name: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy
description: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy is a genetic, typically adolescent onset condition marked by progressive, often asymmetric weakness and atrophy of facial, shoulder girdle and upper arm muscles, later causing foot drop, falls and wheelchair use in some patients. Disease is linked to toxic DUX4 activity that damages muscle cells. Care today is mainly supportive with physical therapy, orthoses and pain management, leaving a major unmet need for disease modifying therapies that suppress the DUX4 pathway and better address debilitating pain and fatigue.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemically deliverable DUX4-pathway suppression/neutralization (root-cause) for genetically confirmed FSHD
- Clinically meaningful gains in upper-limb/shoulder function (e.g., Reachable Workspace) and slowed progression to wheelchair dependence
- Better-tolerated long-term pharmacologic reduction of debilitating pain and fatigue

name: Scleroderma | limited
description: Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST) is an autoimmune small vessel and collagen driven fibrotic disease, typically in midlife women, marked by Raynaud phenomenon, distal skin tightening, calcinosis, telangiectasia, and esophageal dysmotility. Care is largely organ based and symptomatic because there is no proven disease modifying therapy. Key unmet needs include preventing and healing ischemic digital ulcers, addressing painful calcinosis without an effective medical option, and improving gastrointestinal motility beyond reflux focused supportive care.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Reduce new ischemic digital ulcers and speed healing (with pain/hand-function benefit) in lcSSc patients with Raynaud’s inadequately controlled on first-line dihydropyridine CCBs.
- Improve esophageal motility and dysphagia (not just reflux) in SSc patients requiring escalated/long-term PPIs.
- Medical (non-surgical) therapy to reduce calcinosis cutis burden and related pain/ulceration/hand dysfunction in CREST/lcSSc.

name: Myelofibrosis
description: Myelofibrosis is a rare bone marrow blood cancer where fibrosis scars the marrow, causing cytopenias with anemia driven fatigue and dyspnea, infection and bleeding risk, and extramedullary hematopoiesis with splenomegaly leading to abdominal pain and early satiety, often with fevers and night sweats. Patients are typically diagnosed at ages 50 to 80 and may be asymptomatic for years, but treatment is largely symptom focused. Curative transplant is high risk and not feasible for many, leaving major unmet need for disease modifying options that improve cytopenias and reduce transfusion dependence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Achieve RBC transfusion independence (≥12 weeks) / meaningful hemoglobin rise for transfusion-dependent myelofibrosis anemia on background JAK-inhibitor therapy
- Deliver clinically meaningful spleen volume reduction and symptom improvement in myelofibrosis patients with severe thrombocytopenia (platelets ≤50×10^9/L) without worsening cytopenias
- Provide CALR-mutation–targeted, disease-modifying therapy with measurable molecular response (driver allele-burden reduction/clone eradication)

name: Mast cell activation syndrome
description: Mast cell activation syndrome is a chronic multisystem disorder marked by recurrent anaphylaxis like flares with hives and swelling, hypotension or syncope, breathing difficulty, and severe gastrointestinal symptoms. Patients are often adult women. Diagnosis is difficult because there are no routine clinical biomarkers and confirmation depends on catching mediator rises during attacks plus treatment response. Management is symptomatic and burdensome with multi drug stacking and inconvenient dosing. With no Food and Drug Administration approved therapies and no treatment that reduces tissue mast cell burden, major unmet needs are durable, disease modifying control and more convenient, safer long term options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Effective oral, mast-cell–directed option for “severe MCAS with handicap unresponsive to optimal symptomatic treatment,” achieving ≥50% improvement in key handicaps (e.g., pruritus, flushes, depression) over ~24 weeks
- Chronic mediator-control alternative to montelukast/leukotriene blockade that avoids serious neuropsychiatric risk (boxed warning)
- Lower-burden maintenance therapy reducing reliance on high-friction cromolyn QID dosing and/or biologics needing supervised initiation for anaphylaxis risk (e.g., omalizumab)

name: Butyrylcholinesterase Deficiency
description: Rare, usually silent butyrylcholinesterase enzyme deficiency that presents during anesthesia when succinylcholine or mivacurium causes prolonged paralysis and apnea, sometimes for hours, requiring ventilation and sedation; often recognized only after delayed recovery. Care is largely supportive with no causal therapy, creating demand for rapid, safe reversal options including for higher risk patients where current agents have bradycardia and renal limitations.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid antidote to terminate unexpected succinylcholine/mivacurium paralysis in BChE deficiency, reducing prolonged ventilation/sedation.
- BChE-independent rapid-sequence paralytic option (e.g., ultrashort nondepolarizer with predictable rapid reversal) for known/suspected BChE-deficient patients.
- Safer/renal-compatible rocuronium reversal alternative to sugammadex that avoids bradycardia/cardiac-arrest risk and is usable in severe renal impairment.

name: Epilepsy | juvenile myoclonic
description: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy starts in adolescence and persists into adulthood, with morning myoclonic jerks often causing dropping objects and frequent generalized tonic clonic seizures; sleep loss and alcohol are common triggers. Many patients need long term antiseizure therapy because stopping medication relapses seizures in up to 90%, and a substantial minority are drug resistant. Valproate is highly effective but limited by pregnancy risks, creating demand for safer options that deliver durable seizure control and enable withdrawal without relapse.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pregnancy-compatible, valproate-level control of myoclonic jerks + GTCS for adolescent girls/women with JME
- Durable remission enabling safe ASM withdrawal (materially lower relapse risk)
- Effective therapy for drug-resistant JME (~1/3) without paradoxical worsening of myoclonus

name: Gestational trophoblastic disease
description: Rare pregnancy related spectrum of placental tissue overgrowth in the uterus, typically presenting with abnormal vaginal bleeding, enlarged uterus and very high human chorionic gonadotropin. Most are cured with surgery and chemotherapy but care is burdensome with weeks of testing and months of surveillance, and chemo resistant placental site and epithelioid trophoblastic tumors remain the key unmet need, driving interest in programmed cell death 1 and PD L1 checkpoint immunotherapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- PD‑1/PD‑L1 regimens achieving rapid β‑hCG normalization and durable treatment‑free remission in chemo‑refractory/multidrug‑resistant GTN.
- Systemic (non‑surgical) therapies providing durable control/biomarker response for chemotherapy‑resistant PSTT/ETT, including metastatic/unresectable disease.
- Peri‑evacuation/neoadjuvant drug strategies that prevent persistence/progression and shorten the current prolonged weekly→monthly β‑hCG surveillance period.

name: Hepatocellular carcinoma
description: Hepatocellular carcinoma is an aggressive primary liver cancer that typically arises on a background of cirrhosis, often in older men, and is frequently detected late because early tumors are asymptomatic. Treating it is uniquely hard because patients have portal hypertension and impaired liver function, limiting tolerability and making anti vascular endothelial growth factor regimens risky for hemorrhage, with endoscopic variceal assessment required in some cases. Major evidence gaps persist for patients with poorer hepatic reserve such as Child Turcotte Pugh B, and there is little high quality guidance on optimal sequencing after first line immunotherapy plus antiangiogenic therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- 1L systemic option for unresectable HCC that is safe/usable in portal-hypertension/high-bleeding-risk patients (no mandatory recent endoscopy/variceal clearance; no anti‑VEGF hemorrhage constraints), including those on full‑dose anticoagulants/antiplatelets
- Systemic therapy with proven safety/efficacy in Child‑Pugh B liver dysfunction (moderate hepatic impairment)
- Post–atezolizumab+bevacizumab 2L option with prospective evidence (OS and/or high ORR) specifically in PD-(L)1+anti‑VEGF–exposed disease

name: Eclampsia
description: Life threatening escalation of hypertensive disease in pregnancy marked by new onset seizures or coma in a patient with preeclampsia, typically after 20 weeks gestation and often within 48 hours postpartum; care relies on magnesium sulfate, blood pressure control, and often delivery, leaving gaps in magnesium sparing seizure prevention, neuroprotection for posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, and disease modifying options that safely prolong severe preterm disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non‑magnesium anticonvulsant prophylaxis/treatment matching MgSO4 seizure prevention (incl. postpartum) but avoiding toxicity/monitoring and usable in contraindicated patients (e.g., renal failure, myasthenia gravis)
- Adjunct neuroprotective/CNS recovery therapy for eclampsia‑associated PRES to reduce neurologic sequelae beyond seizure suppression and BP control
- Disease‑modifying therapy for severe preterm preeclampsia to halt/reverse progression and safely prolong gestation, reducing need for early delivery to prevent eclampsia

name: Short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks
description: SUNCT and SUNA are rare trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias that typically start around midlife and cause seconds long, stabbing unilateral orbital or temporal pain with ipsilateral tearing and conjunctival injection that can recur up to hundreds of times per day. The burden is amplified by frequent misdiagnosis and years long diagnostic delay, and by the lack of practical outpatient abortive therapy for ultra brief attacks, with intravenous lidocaine reserved for monitored inpatient use. Preventives such as lamotrigine help some, but there is no cure and many patients remain symptomatic for years.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Outpatient, rapid-acting rescue for severe exacerbations/status to replace monitoring-intensive IV lidocaine infusions
- Higher-efficacy, durable preventive therapy for lamotrigine non-responders and multi-drug–refractory patients (e.g., more selective sodium-channel modulation)
- Better-tolerated long-term chronic management options (improved cognitive/psychiatric safety and overall tolerability)
medlineUrl: No specific MedlinePlus URL for SUNCT/SUNA

name: Scurvy
description: Scurvy is severe vitamin C deficiency that can develop within 4 to 12 weeks of inadequate intake, causing fatigue, anemia, bleeding spongy gums with loose teeth, skin hemorrhages, and poor wound healing from impaired collagen synthesis. It is readily reversible with vitamin C, but often missed because early symptoms are vague and patients may have restricted diets or malabsorption. Key needs are earlier recognition and reliable non oral repletion options, plus safer repletion strategies for patients with kidney disease or iron overload.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Parenteral (IV/IM/SC) vitamin C repletion for scurvy when oral therapy is not feasible/insufficient/contraindicated (e.g., severe vomiting, critical illness, suspected malabsorption).
- Absorption-optimized oral vitamin C (e.g., high-bioavailability/liposomal formulations) for malabsorptive or post-bariatric patients where standard tablets may be unreliable.
- Safer vitamin C replacement that corrects scurvy while minimizing oxalate nephropathy/nephrolithiasis risk in CKD/stone-prone patients and avoiding iron-overload exacerbation in hemochromatosis.

name: Transplant rejection | lung
description: Immune mediated lung graft injury after transplant that can be silent early yet progresses to chronic lung allograft dysfunction marked by sustained forced expiratory volume in 1 second decline, with major unmet needs in reliable detection and disease modifying therapies. Care relies on tacrolimus based triple immunosuppression requiring close monitoring and carrying substantial infection and malignancy risk, while antibody mediated rejection lacks randomized evidence and chronic lung allograft dysfunction still has no effective pharmacologic treatment.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying CLAD/BOS therapy that halts or reverses the persistent ≥20% FEV1 decline defining CLAD in lung-transplant recipients.
- AMR/DSA-directed therapy that reliably clears donor-specific antibodies and restores graft function to prevent graft failure/death and downstream CLAD.
- CNI-sparing or lung-targeted maintenance immunosuppression that maintains rejection control while reducing serious infections/malignancy, nephrotoxicity, and trough-level monitoring burden.

name: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
description: Inherited vascular malformation disorder causing fragile arteriovenous malformations and mucocutaneous telangiectasias, dominated by recurrent childhood-onset nosebleeds and gastrointestinal bleeding leading to iron deficiency anemia and sometimes transfusion dependence. Multi-organ shunting can involve the lungs, brain, liver, and gut, driving complications like stroke, seizures, and high-output cardiac failure. Care is largely supportive, with escalation to burdensome intravenous anti-angiogenic therapy or even transplantation, leaving a major unmet need for durable, self-administered disease-modifying treatments that reduce bleeding and iron infusion burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable epistaxis control that lowers ESS/bleed duration and normalizes hemoglobin while reducing IV iron/RBC transfusions in patients failing topical therapy and oral tranexamic acid.
- Oral/self-administered systemic anti-angiogenic therapy that reduces transfusion/IV-iron dependence in moderate–severe HHT-related GI bleeding.
- Medical therapy that improves hepatic-VM–driven high-output cardiac failure/pulmonary hypertension as an alternative to IV bevacizumab and liver transplant.

name: Status epilepticus
description: Status epilepticus is a neurologic emergency defined by seizures lasting more than 5 minutes or recurring without recovery that can cause permanent brain damage or death, often triggered in adults by stroke or missed or withdrawn antiseizure medicines. Care depends on rapid benzodiazepine rescue but real world under dosing due to respiratory depression concerns and frequent progression to refractory cases requiring intensive care, intubation, coma level suppression, and continuous electroencephalography, creating unmet need for faster, safer prehospital options and more reliably effective escalation therapies that avoid prolonged critical care.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prehospital, non‑IV rescue therapy that terminates convulsive status epilepticus before ED arrival while reducing respiratory/airway complications vs benzodiazepines.
- Higher‑efficacy second‑line option for benzodiazepine‑refractory SE achieving >~70% seizure cessation with improved consciousness within 60 minutes.
- Anesthetic‑sparing therapy for refractory/super‑refractory SE that avoids prolonged ICU IV anesthesia/continuous EEG and lowers intubation/hypotension burden.

name: Copper deficiency
description: Acquired copper deficiency is a typically delayed, often post bariatric surgery or zinc excess micronutrient disorder that causes cytopenias and a B12 like myeloneuropathy with gait disturbance and paresthesias. Copper replacement can quickly correct blood counts but neurologic injury often only partially improves and may become irreversible, making earlier detection and lower burden, absorption independent repletion key unmet needs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Meaningful reversal (not just stabilization) of established copper-deficiency myelopathy neurologic deficits (spastic gait/ataxia ± neuropathy)
- Absorption-independent copper repletion for post–upper-GI/bariatric surgery, malabsorption, or zinc-overload patients with impaired upper-GI copper absorption
- Lower-burden maintenance/repletion (e.g., long-acting/less-frequent dosing) to reduce daily therapy/IV courses plus ongoing monitoring

name: Hypochondroplasia
description: Hypochondroplasia is a rare fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 driven skeletal dysplasia where impaired cartilage to bone conversion causes disproportionate short stature with short limbs, broad hands and feet, macrocephaly, and lumbar lordosis, typically presenting in early childhood as growth velocity drops. The burden extends beyond height to craniocervical and spinal stenosis that can require orthopedic or neurosurgical intervention, plus increased risk of seizures and learning differences. Care remains largely supportive, with no licensed disease modifying therapy and growth promoting approaches still in clinical trials.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-invasive, approved drug that increases linear growth and improves body proportionality in FGFR3-confirmed pediatric hypochondroplasia.
- Disease-modifying therapy to prevent/mitigate craniocervical compression and lumbar spinal stenosis and reduce need for decompression/laminectomy.
- Therapies targeting neurodevelopmental comorbidities (e.g., temporal lobe epilepsy/seizures, cognitive/learning difficulties) beyond symptomatic management.

name: T-cell lymphoma | Mycosis fungoides
description: Mycosis fungoides is the most common primary cutaneous T cell lymphoma, typically presenting in older adults as chronic patch and plaque lesions on sun-protected skin that are often misdiagnosed as eczema or psoriasis. It usually follows an indolent, relapsing course but can progress to tumors and, in a minority, systemic spread. The disease is hard to cure and treatment is largely palliative, leaving a premium on more durable disease control and reliable, evidence-based relief of severe pruritus that disrupts sleep and quality of life.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pruritus-targeted therapy providing meaningful, sustained itch relief (with downstream sleep/QoL improvement) for MF/CTCL patients.
- Better-tolerated, more convenient skin-directed therapy for Stage IA–IB MF that avoids high dermatitis/discontinuation risk and removes cold-chain/PPE handling burden.
- More durable systemic disease control for advanced/refractory MF that materially outlasts chemotherapy and reduces infusion toxicity/visit burden vs current IV options.

name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
description: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor is a rare cancer of the stomach or small intestine arising from interstitial cells of Cajal, typically presenting in adults 40 to 70 with bleeding driven anemia and fatigue. Most tumors are driven by KIT or platelet derived growth factor receptor alpha mutations, making therapy highly genotype dependent, but secondary KIT mutations commonly emerge and drive resistance. Harder subsets such as succinate dehydrogenase deficient or other wild type disease are often broadly tyrosine kinase inhibitor resistant, and long duration adjuvant treatment can be difficult to sustain due to tolerability and discontinuation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Mutation-guided 2L therapy with durable PFS for imatinib-resistant KIT exon 11 GIST with secondary KIT exon 17/18 activation-loop resistance
- Effective systemic options for SDH-deficient and other KIT/PDGFRA–wild-type biomarker-defined GIST (e.g., BRAF/NF1/NTRK/FGFR)
- Safer, lower-burden long-term (or fixed-duration adjuvant) regimens to reduce indefinite TKI exposure and frequent dose interruptions/reductions

name: Optic neuropathy | non-arteritic anterior ischemic
description: Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is an acute ischemic injury of the optic nerve head in adults over 50 that causes sudden painless one-eye vision loss, often on awakening, with visual field defects and optic disc edema. There is no proven acute treatment, and secondary prevention is limited to risk-factor control with uncertain benefit, leaving a need for rapidly deployable vision-restoring therapy and evidence-based strategies to prevent fellow-eye events over time.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute, rapidly deployable therapy started ≤14 days from symptom onset that delivers clinically meaningful central-vision recovery (e.g., ≥15‑ETDRS‑letter BCVA gain by Week 24)
- Therapy that produces objective recovery of persistent visual-field loss (e.g., improved visual-field mean sensitivity/mean deviation by Week 24 and/or preservation of retinal ganglion cell structure)
- Proven secondary-prevention drug that reduces fellow-eye NAION over 5 years (baseline ~15%) with a safer long-term profile than daily aspirin

name: Pulmonary hypertension | group 3
description: Pulmonary hypertension group 3 arises from chronic lung disease and hypoxia, most often chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or interstitial lung disease, and presents as worsening exertional breathlessness with fatigue, chest pressure, dizziness, palpitations, and edema. Care largely optimizes the underlying lung disease with oxygen, ventilatory support when needed, and pulmonary rehabilitation, but disease specific options are limited because pulmonary arterial hypertension drugs have mixed evidence and can worsen gas exchange, creating demand for lung selective therapies that improve outcomes with lower treatment burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- PH-COPD: Improve exercise capacity/hemodynamics (e.g., 6MWD/PVR) without worsening gas exchange or increasing serious AEs/mortality.
- Severe PH-ILD/RV dysfunction: RCT-proven (ideally oral) therapies with durable impact on clinical worsening/hospitalizations/survival beyond short-term 6MWD.
- Lung-selective, oxygenation-preserving treatments with lower burden/better tolerability than QID inhaled prostacyclins.

name: Retinopathy of prematurity
description: Retinopathy of prematurity is abnormal retinal blood vessel development in very premature or very low birth weight infants, often silent until detected on scheduled dilated exams at about 4 to 9 weeks of life. Fragile vessels can leak, scar, and progress to retinal detachment and permanent vision loss, forcing urgent invasive treatment with laser or intravitreal anti vascular endothelial growth factor injections. Key unmet needs include safer therapies that limit systemic vascular endothelial growth factor suppression in developing organs, more durable disease control to prevent late reactivation, and reduced monitoring and procedural burden from frequent exams that can extend to ~70 weeks postmenstrual age.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemically safer anti‑angiogenic therapy for Type 1 ROP that minimizes systemic VEGF suppression/exposure vs intravitreal anti‑VEGF
- More durable disease control that prevents late reactivation/recurrence and shortens mandated surveillance
- Less invasive/non‑intravitreal pharmacotherapy (treatment or prophylaxis) to reduce procedural and monitoring burden

name: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis
description: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is a recurrent, often seasonal allergic inflammation of the ocular surface that mainly affects young boys, causing intense itching, photophobia, and ropy mucus that can disrupt daily life. The clinical priority is preventing vision threatening corneal complications such as shield ulcers while reducing reliance on topical corticosteroids that carry cataract and glaucoma risk and require ongoing intraocular pressure monitoring. Durable steroid sparing maintenance therapies and more child friendly dosing remain key unmet needs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing rapid flare control for moderate-to-severe pediatric VKC with keratitis/corneal-ulcer risk, avoiding glaucoma/cataract/IOP-monitoring burden.
- Long-acting (≤QD) maintenance therapy to replace multi-agent, 4–6×/day drop regimens and simplify drop-spacing logistics.
- Better-tolerated steroid-sparing immunomodulators/formulations that avoid instillation pain/burning/pruritus to support consistent pediatric use.

name: Antiphospholipid syndrome
description: Antiphospholipid syndrome is an autoimmune disease in which antiphospholipid antibodies trigger dangerous venous and arterial clots and pregnancy morbidity, often first recognized after an unexpected thrombosis or recurrent miscarriage in women in their 30s to 40s. Care is dominated by long term anticoagulation, where warfarin brings bleeding risk and frequent international normalized ratio monitoring, yet some patients still have breakthrough events. Pregnancy focused regimens such as heparin plus aspirin are widely used but supported by low certainty evidence, leaving a major unmet need for safer, monitoring light anticoagulation and immune targeted approaches that better prevent thrombosis and improve live birth outcomes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Monitoring-free anticoagulation for high-risk (triple-positive/arterial) APS with warfarin-like efficacy but lower bleeding/drug–food interaction burden
- Non-anticoagulant add-on (e.g., immune/complement pathway–directed) to prevent breakthrough thrombosis in anticoagulant-refractory APS
- Obstetric APS therapies to improve live-birth/successful pregnancy outcomes and prevent placental-mediated complications in women failing aspirin + heparin/LMWH

name: Duodenal cancer
description: Duodenal adenocarcinoma is a rare small bowel cancer, typically diagnosed in older adults, with vague early symptoms that delay diagnosis until anemia, obstruction, or jaundice signal advanced disease. Many patients are unresectable at presentation, and care relies on surgery when feasible plus colorectal cancer derived chemotherapy backbones such as fluoropyrimidine with oxaliplatin. Biomarker guided options are limited, with checkpoint inhibitors mainly for microsatellite instability high or mismatch repair deficient tumors and only a small subset harboring targetable human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 alterations, leaving a major unmet need for earlier detection and disease modifying systemic therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Immunotherapy effective in MSS/pMMR advanced duodenal adenocarcinoma (beyond MSI‑H/dMMR-only benefit).
- Clinically validated HER2/ERBB2-targeted regimens for ERBB2-altered duodenal adenocarcinoma (~13–16% of duodenal primaries).
- Better-tolerated, lower-burden alternatives to FOLFOX/CAPOX that maintain 1L efficacy and improve outcomes after oxaliplatin failure (scarce 2L options).

name: Polymyositis
description: Polymyositis is an uncommon autoimmune inflammatory myopathy causing slowly progressive symmetric proximal muscle weakness, often in women aged 45 to 60. Dysphagia and respiratory muscle involvement can be life threatening through aspiration pneumonia and respiratory failure. Treatment still hinges on prolonged high dose corticosteroids with slow tapers and escalation such as intravenous immunoglobulin for refractory disease, creating a need for safer steroid sparing options that deliver durable strength recovery and better control of bulbar and respiratory complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing control with durable strength/function gains that enables faster prednisone taper than ~9–12 months with less monitoring burden
- Targeted prevention/treatment of bulbar and respiratory muscle involvement (dysphagia/aspiration risk; respiratory failure risk)
- Convenient non-IV alternatives for refractory/steroid-resistant patients currently escalated to repeated monthly multi-day IVIG courses

name: Interstitial cystitis
description: Interstitial cystitis or bladder pain syndrome is a chronic, heterogeneous condition marked by bladder pain that worsens with filling and improves after urination, often with urinary urgency and frequency, and is far more common in women. Diagnosis is largely by exclusion with persistent symptoms and negative urine cultures, and there is no cure. Care is trial and error across phenotypes such as Hunner lesions, with inconsistent relief and meaningful safety constraints. A key unmet need is safer, more reliable disease modifying therapies, especially given pentosan polysulfate’s warning for potentially irreversible retinal pigmentary changes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- PPS/Elmiron replacement that preserves symptom relief while eliminating macular-toxicity risk and reducing TID/meal-timing dosing burden
- Non-sedating, better-tolerated oral therapy achieving meaningful symptom response (e.g., ≥30% O’Leary‑Sant ICSI reduction) without amitriptyline-like AE/withdrawal rates
- Hunner-lesion–targeted therapy providing durable lesion/symptom control with safer immunomodulation than systemic cyclosporine

name: Uterine cancer | carcinosarcoma
description: Uterine carcinosarcoma is a rare, high grade endometrial cancer with mixed carcinoma and sarcoma elements, typically affecting postmenopausal women (mean diagnosis age about 67) and often presenting with abnormal vaginal bleeding. It is aggressive, with extrauterine spread in up to 45 percent at presentation and about 35 percent five year survival. Standard first line paclitaxel plus carboplatin is highly myelosuppressive, and there is no established standard for recurrent disease, leaving a major need for better tolerated and more effective systemic, biology guided therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Survival-improving systemic therapy for advanced uterine carcinosarcoma that meaningfully extends OS beyond ~10 months in stage IV (and ~21 months in stage III)
- Less myelosuppressive/neurotoxic alternatives to paclitaxel+carboplatin that avoid very high grade 3–5 hematologic toxicity (~82%) and treatment-related QOL decline
- Carcinosarcoma-specific, evidence-based post‑platinum regimens (prospective trials) rather than extrapolation from endometrial cancer studies that exclude carcinosarcoma, ideally with reduced infusion/visit burden vs q3‑week IV chemo

name: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
description: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is a childhood autoimmune arthritis causing chronic joint pain, swelling, stiffness and limping, often starting before age 16 with a common toddler onset affecting knees and ankles. Beyond joint damage, silent uveitis is a major risk and can progress to vision loss without long term screening. Treatment escalates from nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to disease modifying immunosuppression, but long term corticosteroids are poorly suited in children due to bone and growth toxicity, leaving unmet need for steroid sparing control of arthritis and uveitis and more durable remission.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing prevention/control of chronic anterior uveitis in high-risk (ANA+, early-onset) JIA
- More durable inactive-disease/remission therapies to reduce flares and prevent joint damage + growth abnormalities in persistent JIA
- Better-tolerated, lower-risk systemic options (ideally oral/low-burden) to replace/augment MTX and reduce reliance on TNF-blockers in children unable to tolerate or safely remain on them

name: Dermatitis | herpetiformis
description: Chronic, intensely itchy blistering rash caused by gluten sensitive autoimmunity, typically associated with celiac disease, with symmetric papules and vesicles on extensor surfaces. A strict gluten free diet is disease modifying but can take 6 months to 2 years to clear lesions, so patients often need dapsone for rapid relief despite serious hematologic toxicities and monitoring burden, especially in glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Dapsone-sparing rapid flare control with dapsone-like speed but fewer hematologic toxicities/monitoring needs (incl. options usable in G6PD deficiency)
- Diet-independent (or gluten-exposure–protective) disease control to reduce reliance on strict lifelong gluten-free diet
- Validated therapy for refractory/recalcitrant dermatitis herpetiformis not controlled by GFD plus sulfonamides

name: Medulloblastoma
description: Grade 4 malignant cerebellar brain tumor of childhood (often ages 5–9) causing headaches, vomiting, lethargy, and ataxia; ~30% present with cerebrospinal fluid spread. Standard surgery plus craniospinal radiation and chemotherapy can cure but leaves major late toxicities (hearing loss, endocrine injury, progressive cognitive decline). The hardest unmet need is effective relapse therapy, with <10% 5-year survival after recurrence, alongside safer, risk-adapted treatment that reduces long-term harm.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable control/survival benefit in post‑irradiation relapsed medulloblastoma where current salvage is largely transient/palliative (esp. Group 3 relapse)
- Cisplatin‑sparing or otoprotective approaches that reduce severe treatment‑related hearing loss while preserving cure rates
- Drug strategies enabling de‑escalation and/or neuroprotection to cut long‑term neurocognitive impairment and improve adult functional independence (e.g., in good‑prognosis WNT subgroup)

name: Essential thrombocythemia
description: Essential thrombocythemia is a myeloproliferative blood cancer marked by chronic platelet overproduction, often found on routine labs in women over 50. Many patients are initially well, but elevated platelets drive serious clotting risk and can also cause abnormal bleeding, alongside fatigue and cognitive complaints. Care relies on low dose aspirin and platelet lowering drugs such as hydroxyurea, interferon alpha, or anagrelide to prevent complications rather than cure, leaving unmet need for safer long term control, better options after hydroxyurea, symptom relief, and therapies that reduce progression or rare transformation to myelofibrosis or acute leukemia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying ET therapy that measurably reduces progression to myelofibrosis/AML.
- Better-tolerated 2nd-line cytoreduction for high-risk ET patients who are hydroxyurea intolerant/resistant.
- Symptom-first therapy that delivers large MPN-SAF TSS improvements (e.g., ≥50% reduction) for persistent ET symptom burden.

name: Adrenal insufficiency | primary
description: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease) is usually an autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex that causes chronic cortisol and often aldosterone deficiency, with months of nonspecific fatigue, weight loss, gastrointestinal symptoms, hyperpigmentation, salt craving, and orthostatic hypotension until stress or poor absorption triggers a potentially fatal adrenal crisis requiring urgent injectable hydrocortisone. Lifelong steroid replacement is lifesaving but imperfect because standard oral dosing creates nonphysiologic peaks and troughs, driving persistent symptoms, adherence burden, and ongoing crisis risk, leaving demand for circadian-mimicking regimens, easier rescue delivery, and earlier immune or regenerative approaches to preserve adrenal function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Circadian-mimicking glucocorticoid replacement to improve early-morning cortisol exposure and reduce morning fatigue/QoL impairment without over/under-replacement
- Easy, fast “can’t-keep-pills-down” rescue/parenteral hydrocortisone to lower the ~6%–8%/year adrenal-crisis rate
- Disease-modifying autoimmune Addison’s therapies for patients with residual adrenal function to reduce lifelong steroid dependence

name: Epilepsy | juvenile absence
description: Idiopathic generalized epilepsy starting in adolescence with frequent absence seizures causing brief staring and impaired responsiveness, often alongside generalized tonic clonic seizures. Even when seizures respond to medication, many patients have attention and memory problems that impair school performance, and long term therapy is often needed. Current options have gaps, including drugs that do not cover tonic clonic seizures and valproate limits in women of childbearing potential due to teratogenicity and cognitive side effects, leaving a need for durable, well tolerated control into adulthood.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Valproate-sparing broad-spectrum control of absence + generalized tonic–clonic seizures in adolescents with JAE.
- Attention-/mood-sparing seizure control (ideally with cognitive benefit) vs current ASMs’ attention/behavior side effects.
- Durable remission enabling safe AED withdrawal (≥2-year seizure freedom off medication) with low relapse risk.

name: Choline deficiency disease
description: Clinically significant choline deficiency is most often seen in intestinal failure patients on long term parenteral nutrition, where depletion impairs very low density lipoprotein synthesis and drives fatty liver with elevated liver enzymes and sometimes subclinical muscle injury. Care is largely supportive, and although guidelines recommend routine choline addition, there is still no widely available, stable parenteral choline product, making adequate dosing hard in practice. The frontier is developing injectable choline formulations that can be reliably compounded and delivered to prevent or reverse parenteral nutrition associated liver disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Commercially available PN-compatible parenteral choline product that can be routinely added to adult/pediatric PN.
- Demonstrated prevention/treatment of PN-associated liver injury with improvements in steatosis/fibrosis and liver enzymes (not just biochemical repletion).
- Longer-acting/intermittent parenteral choline dosing/formulation to avoid continuous infusion burden.

name: Common variable immunodeficiency
description: Common variable immune deficiency is a heterogeneous primary antibody failure typically diagnosed in the 20s to 30s, marked by recurrent sinopulmonary infections and pneumonia that can drive chronic lung disease and irreversible bronchiectasis. Lifelong immunoglobulin replacement reduces infections but does not reliably prevent progressive airway damage or inflammatory lung disease, and many patients develop immune dysregulation such as autoimmunity and gastrointestinal inflammation with diarrhea and weight loss. Key unmet needs include lung protective, steroid sparing targeted immunomodulation and less burdensome, more effective antibody replacement strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing targeted immunomodulators for the high-risk immune-dysregulation CVID phenotype (e.g., GLILD/progressive lung disease, autoimmunity, GI inflammatory disease) inadequately controlled by Ig replacement.
- Add-on therapies that prevent progression of bronchiectasis/chronic airway damage (HRCT + spirometry/diffusion endpoints) despite adequate Ig replacement.
- More convenient, safer antibody-replacement approaches that reduce lifelong infusion burden while maintaining protective IgG troughs.

name: Macular dystrophy | vitelliform
description: Genetic macular dystrophy (often childhood onset) with lipofuscin buildup under the macula causing progressive central vision blurring and distortion. Patients may have years of near normal acuity before the egg yolk lesion ruptures and macular atrophy and vision loss accelerates, sometimes with choroidal neovascularization requiring anti vascular endothelial growth factor injections. Management is largely supportive and complication focused with no curative or disease modifying therapy, driving unmet need for treatments that preserve central vision and prevent structural degeneration, with gene and stem cell approaches emerging.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- BEST1-targeted disease modification in early-stage pediatric BVMD to prevent lipofuscin-driven photoreceptor injury and preserve central vision/BCVA
- Regenerative/repair therapy for late-stage BVMD with central RPE/retinal atrophy (Stage V) to recover/maintain reading vision
- Safer/more durable CNV control for the ~20% who develop CNV (Stage VI) to prevent severe vision loss while reducing intravitreal anti-VEGF injection burden/complications

name: Bronchiolitis obliterans
description: Bronchiolitis obliterans is a rare small airway disease where inflammatory scarring progressively narrows and can obliterate bronchioles, causing fixed, nonreversible obstruction and air trapping with persistent, worsening dyspnea and cough. It is a major driver of chronic lung allograft dysfunction after transplant and limits long term survival. Care often starts late once forced expiratory volume in 1 second has already declined and fibrosis is largely irreversible, and current immunosuppression based regimens show limited, inconsistent benefit. The priority unmet needs are earlier biomarker or imaging based detection and truly disease modifying therapies that stabilize or improve lung function without high burden immunosuppression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable stabilization or improvement of FEV₁ in established BOS/CLAD (beyond modest slowing of decline on SOC).
- Biomarker-driven, phenotype-tailored treatments to identify and effectively treat rapid decliners/non-responders.
- Early interception therapies (pre-/early BOS) that prevent progression while sparing steroids/CNIs and avoiding augmented immunosuppression.

name: Pseudomyxoma peritonei
description: Pseudomyxoma peritonei is a rare, usually appendix derived malignancy where a ruptured mucinous appendiceal tumor seeds the peritoneum, producing mucinous ascites that gradually distends the abdomen and impairs bowel function, often with late, nonspecific presentation around the early 50s. Cytoreductive surgery with heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy is standard, but recurrence and extensive spread frequently make complete resection difficult or impossible, leaving a substantial unresectable group and ongoing risks of obstruction, malnutrition, and decline. Key needs include effective non surgical, disease modifying local and systemic options, including mucin debulking and mucolytic strategies plus biomarker guided therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical, locally delivered mucin-liquefying/debulking therapy for unresectable or recurrent PMP to enable drainage/extraction and relieve obstruction/mass-effect symptoms.
- Biomarker-guided systemic targeted/immune therapy for CRS-HIPEC–noncured PMP, prioritizing actionable subgroups (e.g., KRAS/BRAF alterations, GNAS-mutant vaccine/PD-1 strategies).
- Neoadjuvant/downstaging drug regimens for “huge”/high-PCI PMP to increase subsequent CC-0/CC-1 complete cytoreduction rates at CRS+HIPEC.

name: Psoriasis | pustular
description: Generalized pustular psoriasis is a rare, high-acuity inflammatory psoriasis with recurrent, unpredictable flares of painful widespread erythema and sterile pustules often accompanied by fever and systemic inflammation that can be life-threatening. Episodes are triggered by infection or medication changes and in some patients are linked to interleukin-36 pathway mutations. Care today often requires rapid escalation and hospitalization, yet prevention remains difficult, and legacy systemic drugs can be poorly tolerated or contraindicated in pregnancy, creating demand for fast flare control outside the hospital and safer, durable disease suppression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Outpatient/self-administered flare aborters that reliably clear pustules within 1 week
- Durable, low-burden maintenance therapies that prevent recurrent/unpredictable flares
- Pregnancy- and pediatric-friendly targeted options (avoiding teratogenic/monitoring-heavy legacy agents)

name: PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome
description: PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome is a rare inherited PTEN tumor suppressor disorder causing multisystem hamartomas, gastrointestinal polyps, and high lifetime risks of breast, thyroid, kidney, and endometrial cancers, often presenting by the late 20s with macrocephaly and mucocutaneous lesions. Care is dominated by intensive lifelong cancer surveillance and endoscopic polyp management, with little proven chemoprevention, leaving a premium on disease modifying strategies that reduce tumor and polyp burden. Neurodevelopmental disorders including autism spectrum disorder are common and effective treatments for neurobehavioral symptoms remain a major gap.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Cancer chemoprevention that measurably lowers incident breast/endometrial/thyroid/renal cancers in germline PTEN carriers.
- Non-immunosuppressive medical therapy that reduces PHTS GI polyp burden with endpoints like decreased polyp number/stage.
- Targeted therapy that improves PTEN-related neurodevelopmental/social impairment using validated measures (e.g., SRS total score).

name: Prolactinoma
description: Prolactinoma is a benign prolactin secreting pituitary tumor that commonly causes menstrual disruption, galactorrhea, and infertility in women. Dopamine agonists usually normalize prolactin and shrink tumors, but a meaningful minority are cabergoline resistant, many require long term therapy with relapse risk off treatment, and side effects including psychiatric and impulse control problems can limit use. Pregnancy adds complexity because therapy is typically stopped while larger tumors may enlarge, leaving a need for better tolerated, durable, disease modifying control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Normoprolactinemia plus meaningful tumor shrinkage in dopamine-agonist–resistant (~10% cabergoline; ~5% micro vs ~20% macro) or intolerant (~3–12%) prolactinoma.
- Chronic control that avoids/meaningfully reduces valvopathy/valvular-fibrosis monitoring and psychiatric/behavioral toxicities (e.g., impulse-control disorders) that drive DA discontinuation.
- Higher, more durable off-therapy remission (vs ~30–40% after DA withdrawal) including pregnancy-compatible tumor control when DAs are typically stopped and macroprolactinomas risk growth.

name: Scarlet fever
description: Scarlet fever is a contagious childhood illness caused by toxin producing group A Streptococcus, typically presenting in ages 5 to 15 with fever and sore throat followed within 12 to 48 hours by a sandpaper like rash and sometimes strawberry tongue. It is usually curable with penicillin or amoxicillin, but care still depends on 10 day oral courses or an injection, making adherence and rapid symptom control a practical challenge. Backup options for penicillin allergy are pressured by macrolide and clindamycin resistance, and delayed or inadequate treatment risks immune mediated complications such as acute rheumatic fever and post streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Single-dose or ≤3–5‑day oral/long-acting anti‑GAS regimen that matches penicillin cure/eradication vs adherence-limited 10‑day multidose courses in children
- Penicillin-allergy backup antibiotic that stays reliably active despite macrolide/clindamycin resistance and avoids clindamycin-associated colitis risk
- Adjunctive anti-toxin/anti-superantigen therapy to more rapidly control toxin-driven rash/systemic inflammation and reduce progression to serious complications (e.g., invasive GAS)

name: Hepatitis | autoimmune
description: Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic immune mediated liver inflammation, often in women, with insidious or asymptomatic onset that delays diagnosis and leaves about one third cirrhotic at presentation. Treatment still hinges on prednisone plus azathioprine, but long term steroid toxicity and high relapse after stopping therapy create demand for safer steroid sparing, durable disease control and earlier detection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing/steroid-free regimens that maintain remission while avoiding long-term predniso(lo)ne toxicities (fractures, cataracts, diabetes), including options suitable for cirrhosis/portal-hypertension patients where budesonide is not preferred.
- Better-tolerated, more effective alternatives to azathioprine for patients who are intolerant or fail to achieve complete biochemical remission (normal transaminases + IgG within 6 months).
- Therapies enabling durable drug-free remission or reliable withdrawal without relapse (50–90% relapse after stopping immunosuppression, often within 12 months).

name: Mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis
description: Mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis is a kidney biopsy pattern seen across multiple immune complex diseases, marked by mesangial hypercellularity with possible immune complex deposition and often presenting in young adults with nephrotic syndrome or hematuria. The pressing unmet need is durable proteinuria control and preservation of kidney function before progression to chronic kidney failure, ideally with steroid sparing given infection and metabolic toxicity, and with lower access and monitoring burdens than chronic therapies that require restricted distribution and frequent lab monitoring.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable renal protection in proteinuric patients (≥0.5 g/day) achieving sustained proteinuria <0.3–0.5 g/day and lifetime eGFR slope <1 mL/min/year.
- Steroid-sparing disease control for high-risk patients with persistent proteinuria >1 g/day despite 3–6 months of maximal supportive care.
- Chronic antiproteinuric therapy that avoids sparsentan-like REMS restrictions and routine q3-month liver enzyme monitoring for hepatotoxicity.

name: Chromoblastomycosis
description: Chromoblastomycosis is a chronic implantation fungal infection of skin and subcutaneous tissue, usually acquired when soil or plant fungi enter through skin breaks in tropical and subtropical settings, often in rural outdoor workers. Slow growing warty plaques on limbs can persist for years, causing scarring, swelling, fibrosis and disability with difficulty walking and occasional skin cancer. Care is hindered by prolonged oral antifungal courses that may still not cure severe disease and relapse after stopping, plus limited access and affordability of itraconazole in endemic regions, leaving a need for durable, practical curative oral regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course (≈3–6 month) oral therapy that reliably cures moderate–severe/extensive limb disease (vs months–years today)
- Single-regimen option effective in severe/refractory/relapsing cases to avoid multi-drug combinations and reduce relapse
- Affordable, reliably supplied, better-tolerated oral antifungals for endemic resource-limited settings to enable completion and avoid toxic ketoconazole fallback

name: Biliary dyskinesia
description: Functional gallbladder motility disorder causing recurrent biliary type epigastric or right upper quadrant pain with nausea or vomiting despite normal imaging and labs, typically supported by low gallbladder ejection fraction on cholecystokinin HIDA. Management largely defaults to cholecystectomy because effective medical therapy is not established, yet symptom relief is variable and often not durable, especially in pediatrics, creating unmet need for non-surgical motility treatments and better tools to predict surgical responders.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral non-surgical therapy delivering clinically meaningful biliary pain relief (e.g., ≥30–50% VAS reduction within ~4 weeks) for adults with biliary dyskinesia currently routed to cholecystectomy.
- Pharmacologic options to reduce persistent biliary pain and improve QoL in the ~30% who remain symptomatic after cholecystectomy (including post-cholecystectomy/SOD-type pain).
- Mechanism-targeted motility modulation (e.g., CCK/CCK-A pathway) to provide validated medical therapy—especially for pediatric and hyperkinetic gallbladder populations with limited evidence for surgery.

name: Psoriasis | erythrodermic
description: Erythrodermic psoriasis is a rare, life threatening psoriasis subtype with near total body erythema and scaling causing skin failure, fluid and temperature instability, and systemic complications including infection and heart failure. Patients often need hospitalization and rapid acting systemic therapy, but care is hampered by limited high quality evidence and no dedicated randomized trials, leaving unmet need for ultra rapid stabilization, safer options for medically fragile patients, and relapse resistant maintenance supported by prospective comparative data.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Ultra–rapid-acting EP flare therapy that stabilizes fluid/temperature balance and achieves skin clearance on a ~1–2 week emergency timeline
- Rapid systemic option with lower immunosuppression suitable for infection-prone/medically fragile EP patients
- EP-specific, relapse-resistant maintenance strategy to prevent rebound flares, supported by prospective comparative evidence

name: Sarcosinemia
description: Sarcosinemia is a rare autosomal recessive sarcosine dehydrogenase deficiency that causes persistently elevated sarcosine in blood and urine and is usually benign, often detected on newborn screening. The key unmet need is identifying and treating the small, uncertain subgroup with possible neurologic impairment where causality is debated and supportive options are limited, with mechanism based central nervous system approaches so far showing no clear clinical benefit.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Sarcosine-lowering therapy for the rare symptomatic subgroup with neurodevelopmental disability, with differentiation via improved neurologic function plus normalization of plasma/urine sarcosine.
- CNS-targeted neuroprotective therapy for newborn-screen–detected infants/children with hypersarcosinemia to mitigate potential NMDA-mediated excitotoxicity risk beyond reassurance-only care.
- Effective CNS-directed treatment that measurably improves neurologic signs in symptomatic sarcosinemia where memantine has shown no clinical benefit.

name: Alpha thalassemia | transfusion independent
description: Transfusion independent alpha thalassemia commonly presents as hemoglobin H disease with early childhood onset chronic mild to moderate anemia, jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly causing fatigue and episodic worsening. Despite limited transfusions, ineffective erythropoiesis drives low hepcidin and increased iron absorption so many accumulate iron overload by adulthood, with longer term risks including splenomegaly related complications, thrombosis, and pulmonary hypertension. Care is largely supportive with folate, selective transfusion, and chelation, leaving strong demand for disease modifying therapies that sustainably raise hemoglobin and normalize iron homeostasis to reduce lifelong organ damage risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Sustained anemia improvement (≥1.0 g/dL Hb) with meaningful fatigue relief (e.g., FACT‑An), especially in higher-burden non‑deletional HbH patients
- Prevent iron overload in transfusion‑independent HbH via non‑chelator iron/hepcidin-pathway modulation to avoid hepatic organ damage
- Reduce extramedullary hematopoiesis/splenomegaly to lower thrombosis and pulmonary hypertension risk and reduce reliance on splenectomy/supportive care

name: Neurofibroma | plexiform
description: NF1 associated plexiform neurofibromas are congenital, diffuse benign nerve sheath tumors that enlarge through childhood and can cause pain, disfigurement, and compressive dysfunction. Surgery is often incomplete and tumors can regrow. Selumetinib is approved for symptomatic inoperable disease but requires ongoing monitoring and dose interruptions due to cardiac and ocular toxicity risk, leaving demand for safer, fixed duration treatments that deliver durable control or eradication.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- True complete responses/tumor eradication (not just partial volumetric shrinkage) to better resolve disfigurement/functional morbidity
- Comparable efficacy with markedly lower cardiotoxicity/ocular toxicity and fewer dose interruptions/reductions (reduced monitoring/adherence burden)
- Durable control with fixed-duration or intermittent therapy to prevent regrowth during treatment holds and reduce lifelong dosing

name: Progressive supranuclear palsy
description: Progressive supranuclear palsy is a rare 4R tau neurodegenerative disorder starting in the mid to late 60s, causing progressive balance and gait impairment with backward falls, vertical gaze palsy, dysarthria and dysphagia, and complications such as choking, pneumonia and head injury. Diagnosis is often delayed 3 to 4 years and symptomatic drugs like levodopa offer minimal short lived benefit. No therapy meaningfully slows progression, leaving a premium on earlier diagnosis, safer symptom control, and disease modifying approaches targeting tau pathology.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- 4R‑tau–directed disease‑modifying therapy for early PSP that slows disability progression on PSPRS-family scales over ~52–72 weeks
- Symptomatic therapy for ambulatory PSP that reduces backward falls/postural instability and improves gait/postural PSPRS domains beyond minimal/short-lived levodopa benefit
- Therapy to preserve swallowing/bulbar function in PSP patients with dysphagia to prevent aspiration pneumonia and delay feeding-tube dependence

name: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
description: Rare inherited arrhythmia from disordered cardiac calcium handling in otherwise structurally normal hearts, where exercise or emotional stress can trigger ventricular tachycardia leading to syncope, cardiac arrest, or sudden death, often starting in childhood. Diagnosis is difficult because resting electrocardiogram is often normal. Beta blockers with or without flecainide reduce events but require careful titration, can be poorly tolerated, and force major lifestyle restrictions, leaving a need for more durable, disease modifying options such as calcium channel repair and gene therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-targeted calcium-handling correction for CPVT1 (RYR2 “leaky channel”) patients with persistent exercise-test ventricular ectopy despite beta-blocker ± flecainide.
- Therapies that fully normalize exercise stress testing (no exercise-induced ectopy/arrhythmias) to enable safe strenuous/competitive activity and relax current sports restrictions.
- Better-tolerated, adherence-friendly chronic prophylaxis for pediatric/young CPVT to reduce side-effect–driven nonadherence/discontinuation and breakthrough events.

name: Dementia | frontotemporal
description: Frontotemporal dementia is a midlife-onset neurodegenerative disease caused by neuron loss in the frontal and temporal lobes, often presenting as behavioral variant disease with progressive personality, judgment, and social behavior changes while memory is relatively spared early. Care remains largely symptomatic, using drugs such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and sometimes low-dose antipsychotics, because there is no cure and no proven way to slow or prevent progression. The biggest unmet need is disease-modifying therapy, with momentum around genetically defined biology such as progranulin deficiency and C9orf72 repeat expansion and biomarker tools to track target engagement.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Progranulin-restoration disease modification for bvFTD due to heterozygous GRN loss-of-function (slow decline on CDR® plus NACC FTLD-SB).
- C9orf72 repeat-expansion–lowering therapies for C9orf72-associated FTD/FTD-ALS, with CSF poly(GP) reduction as a target-engagement biomarker.
- Safer, non-antipsychotic pharmacologic control of severe bvFTD behavioral symptoms (agitation/aggression/compulsions) to reduce reliance on black-box antipsychotics, measured by NPI agitation/aggression improvement.

name: Hypereosinophilic syndrome
description: Hypereosinophilic syndrome is a rare, heterogeneous disorder marked by persistent high eosinophil counts that drive inflammatory organ damage, most often affecting skin and lungs and sometimes the heart and nervous system, typically in adults aged 20 to 50. Patients can cycle through rashes, cough, shortness of breath, fatigue and fever while silent cardiac injury accumulates and can become fatal. Care still leans on systemic glucocorticoids, but long term toxicity and imperfect protection from organ damage create demand for durable steroid sparing control. Targeted biologics, especially those blocking interleukin 5, are the main frontier.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing, flare-preventing therapies for recurrent-flare/persistent HES that reduce cumulative systemic corticosteroid morbidity and help prevent irreversible organ damage (esp. cardiac).
- Add-on treatments for biologic-treated HES patients with controlled AEC (<0.5×10^9/L) but persistent moderate symptoms (asthma/AD/CRSwNP/EoE), improving HES-MBS/HES-SI.
- Lower-burden maintenance biologics (fewer injections/less-frequent dosing than mepolizumab’s 3 injections every 4 weeks) while maintaining flare reduction in uncontrolled HES.

name: Myasthenia gravis | generalized
description: Generalized myasthenia gravis is a chronic autoimmune disorder of neuromuscular transmission causing fluctuating, activity worsened muscle weakness that can progress from ocular symptoms to bulbar and respiratory failure with life threatening myasthenic crisis. Treatment often escalates to long term corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants, creating a tradeoff between symptom control and cumulative side effects and infection risk, while acute relapses still rely on hospital based intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange. Heterogeneous antibody subtypes such as acetylcholine receptor and muscle specific kinase drive variable responses, keeping demand high for rapid, durable, steroid sparing control across subgroups.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing long-term gMG control that reduces chronic steroid side effects/infection risk and avoids daily oral immunosuppressants plus regular blood-test monitoring.
- Rapid rescue for acute worsening (days–~1 week) that prevents progression to myasthenic crisis without requiring hospital-based IVIG or plasma exchange.
- Demonstrated efficacy in non-AChR+ gMG (MuSK+ and seronegative) and refractory patients beyond AChR-focused trial/label populations.

name: Glycogen storage disease | type 2
description: Pompe disease is an inherited acid alpha glucosidase deficiency that causes toxic lysosomal glycogen buildup, progressively damaging skeletal and respiratory muscle. Late onset disease often appears in adolescence or adulthood with slowly worsening limb and trunk weakness and declining breathing capacity that can progress to wheelchair use, respiratory failure, or ventilator dependence. Treatment is dominated by lifelong intravenous enzyme replacement every two weeks with multi hour infusions, risk of serious hypersensitivity, and highly variable functional benefit, leaving a premium on more muscle penetrant and immune tolerant options that improve walking endurance and preserve lung function while reducing infusion burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Skeletal-muscle–penetrant correction that meaningfully improves ambulatory + respiratory endpoints (6MWD + sitting FVC % predicted), especially in ERT non-improvers
- Lower-immunogenicity/immune-tolerant therapy reducing infusion hypersensitivity/IARs and eliminating anaphylaxis risk
- Simplified administration that avoids lifelong q2w multi-hour infusions and infusion-visit fasting/timing requirements

name: Thygeson's superficial punctate keratopathy
description: Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis is an uncommon, non-contagious corneal surface inflammation of unknown cause that typically starts in the 20s to 30s and relapses and remits for years. Central punctate epithelial lesions drive photophobia with tearing, foreign body sensation, and mild visual blur. Low-dose topical steroids can rapidly suppress flares but often lead to prolonged, monitored use due to cataract and intraocular pressure risk. Steroid-sparing agents such as cyclosporine or tacrolimus are slower and still chronic, with tolerability, cost, and adherence friction, leaving demand for faster, durable nonsteroidal control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-steroidal therapy with steroid-equivalent rapid flare control (≈1–3 days) without IOP/glaucoma/cataract/infection risks or monitoring burden.
- Durable steroid-sparing maintenance that prevents recurrences over years/decades and enables discontinuation of steroids/cyclosporine.
- Better-tolerated, adherence-friendly immunomodulators (low-sting, less frequent dosing) with controlled-trial evidence in TSPK.

name: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
description: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is an acquired disorder where autoantibodies destroy red blood cells, causing anemia and hemolysis symptoms such as fatigue, dyspnea, jaundice, dark urine, and splenomegaly, typically in middle aged to older adults. Flares can be fulminant and life threatening. First line steroids often induce initial responses but relapse and taper dependence are common, leaving a major need for rapid steroid sparing control, durable remissions, and safer management given frequent venous thromboembolism risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing, low-toxicity, easy-to-administer therapy for steroid-resistant/steroid-dependent wAIHA with durable hemoglobin response.
- Durable relapse prevention/long-term remission maintenance after steroid taper/discontinuation to avoid repeated immunosuppression.
- Rapid-acting control of acute, life-threatening hemolysis with a differentiated thrombosis-risk profile and lower infusion/treatment burden.

name: Fabry disease
description: Fabry disease is an inherited lysosomal storage disorder in which globotriaosylceramide accumulates, causing childhood onset neuropathic pain, hypohidrosis, skin and eye findings, and gastrointestinal symptoms that often go unrecognized until adulthood. Progressive kidney and cardiac injury then drives renal failure, cardiomyopathy, and stroke. Current options rely on lifelong biweekly intravenous enzyme replacement or variant limited oral chaperone therapy, with high treatment burden, antibody mediated loss of effect, and limited ability to reverse established fibrosis and end organ damage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Reverse/slow myocardial fibrosis and LVH progression in advanced Fabry cardiomyopathy patients who respond poorly to ERT.
- Prevent progressive eGFR decline and control proteinuria in Fabry patients with significant baseline proteinuria/established CKD despite ERT.
- Mutation-agnostic, non-IV (or infrequent-dose) durable disease control to replace biweekly ERT and reduce infusion reactions, including for non-amenable GLA variants.

name: Complex regional pain syndrome | type 1
description: Complex regional pain syndrome type 1 is a chronic, post injury one limb pain disorder without confirmed nerve injury, often emerging weeks after trauma or surgery with disproportionate burning pain, allodynia, swelling, and autonomic skin changes that can drive years of disability. Care is largely symptomatic with no cure and no single proven, trial validated standard, and long term opioid use creates additional problems. The central unmet need is durable, evidence backed treatments that restore function and reduce chronic pain without prolonged opioid dependence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CRPS-specific, trial-validated therapy for early “warm” CRPS-1 (≤6 months) delivering rapid, durable pain reduction (≥50% NRS) plus objective functional restoration by ~12 weeks.
- Maintenance/relapse (“top-up”) pharmacotherapy for chronic/refractory CRPS with ongoing pain and reduced QoL after standard physical/behavioral/pain treatments.
- Opioid-sparing neuropathic-pain agent with materially better tolerability (less dizziness/somnolence discontinuation) and safer use in COPD/elderly/opioid co-use vs gabapentinoids.

name: Cystinuria
description: Cystinuria is a rare inherited kidney tubule transport disorder where cystine is not reabsorbed, accumulates in urine, and crystallizes into recurrent stones that cause obstruction, severe flank pain, hematuria, and infections, often starting in adolescence or young adulthood. Management is dominated by demanding lifelong prevention with very high fluid intake including at night and urine alkalinization. Thiol drugs can help but are frequently limited by toxicity and discontinuation, and no current therapy corrects the underlying transport defect, leaving a major need for safer, durable disease modifying prevention.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent symptomatic and silent stone recurrence in patients with frequent stones despite hydration/diet/urine alkalinization
- Safer long-term cystine-solubilizing therapy avoiding thiol toxicities (e.g., proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome; neutropenia/thrombocytopenia) and monitoring-driven discontinuation
- Reduce regimen burden driving nonadherence (around-the-clock/overnight hydration, frequent alkalinizer dosing, frequent urine pH self-checks, high pill burden)

name: Wilms tumor | favorable
description: Favorable histology Wilms tumor is an early childhood kidney cancer that often presents as a palpable abdominal mass, sometimes with hematuria or hypertension. Standard care uses nephrectomy plus chemotherapy, with radiation for higher risk disease, and cures exceed 90 percent, but relapse remains a key challenge for tumors with adverse biomarkers such as chromosome 1q gain or loss of heterozygosity on 1p and 16q. With many long term survivors, reducing late effects like chronic heart or kidney disease, infertility, and second cancers drives biomarker guided risk stratification and dose sparing approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Biomarker-driven relapse prevention and improved salvage for high-risk FHWT (e.g., 1q gain and/or LOH 1p/16q).
- Late-effect–sparing alternatives or dose-reduction strategies to replace anthracycline/radiation intensification while maintaining cure rates.
- Biology-guided chemo-sparing de-escalation for very-low/standard-risk Stage I–II FHWT (expand nephrectomy-only/observation eligibility and reduce treatment visits).

name: Primary sclerosing cholangitis
description: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is a rare chronic fibroinflammatory bile duct disease, often diagnosed in men in their 30s to 40s with ulcerative colitis, where progressive duct scarring and obstruction causes cholestasis, pruritus, fatigue, jaundice, recurrent cholangitis, and eventual cirrhosis or liver failure. Care is largely symptomatic and complication focused because no therapy has been shown to prevent or reverse progression, leaving patients facing transplant risk and a 10 to 20% lifetime risk of cholangiocarcinoma. The commercial and clinical prize is a disease modifying drug that slows progression, improves itch and fatigue, and reduces cancer risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying PSC therapy that prevents progression to liver transplantation, with durable improvement in progression markers (e.g., ALP, liver stiffness/VCTE, bilirubin).
