- Chemoprevention/anti-neoplastic therapy to reduce cholangiocarcinoma risk in PSC, especially early after diagnosis and in higher-risk patients (e.g., dominant stricture).
- Safer, more effective antipruritic therapy for moderate–severe cholestatic pruritus (and fatigue/sleep/QoL impacts) that avoids current safety limits (e.g., rifampicin hepatotoxicity) and improves PRO endpoints.

name: Fragile X syndrome
description: Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited developmental disability caused by an X linked FMR1 CGG repeat expansion that silences fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein production, leading to early language delay and cognitive and behavioral symptoms including anxiety, hyperactivity, and autism spectrum features. Care is largely symptomatic, leaving a premium on earlier disease modifying approaches that improve language and adaptive functioning and reduce sensory driven social impairment, while avoiding long term antipsychotic toxicities such as weight gain, insulin resistance, and rare tardive dyskinesia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Preschool (ages ~2–6) therapy that delivers clinically meaningful gains in expressive language/communication and adaptive function (e.g., Mullen expressive language; Vineland ABC), not just ADHD/anxiety symptom control.
- Non-sedating anxiolytic/anti-hyperarousal that reduces sensory-driven hyperarousal and social approach–avoidance (gaze avoidance) with objective social-participation improvement (e.g., eye-tracking social gaze; SPM-P).
- Anti-irritability/anti-aggression options for adolescents that maintain efficacy while avoiding antipsychotic-associated rapid weight gain/insulin-resistance and long-term movement-disorder (tardive dyskinesia) risk.

name: Neuroendocrine tumor | pulmonary
description: Pulmonary carcinoids are slow growing but malignant lung neuroendocrine tumors that are often found incidentally or after vague airway symptoms such as cough, wheeze, hemoptysis, dyspnea, or recurrent pneumonia from obstruction. Surgery is frequently curative when localized, but atypical tumors more often present with nodal spread. In advanced disease, systemic options are limited and often deliver disease stability rather than tumor shrinkage, with some therapies constrained by somatostatin receptor expression and little evidence to guide optimal adjuvant treatment post resection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemic therapies that achieve meaningful tumor shrinkage/RECIST responses (vs largely stable disease with current options).
- SSTR-independent treatments for SSTR-low/negative lung carcinoids not eligible for SSA/PRRT.
- Adjuvant systemic therapy to reduce post-resection recurrence in higher-risk atypical carcinoid (e.g., node-positive/high-risk locoregional disease).

name: Tuberculosis | multidrug-resistant
description: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis is TB resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampin, typically causing prolonged cough with systemic symptoms and sometimes hemoptysis. Care is hampered by lengthy regimens that can run 18 to 20 months, heavy clinic visit burdens, and frequent toxicities from key drugs like linezolid including peripheral neuropathy and myelosuppression. The biggest gaps are shorter, simpler, better tolerated regimens that maintain cure and more effective options for highly resistant disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Linezolid-sparing/replacement MDR‑TB regimens that maintain BPaL/BPaLM-level cure while reducing peripheral neuropathy and myelosuppression.
- Effective options for pre‑XDR/XDR or bedaquiline‑resistant MDR‑TB without stacking QT‑prolonging agents.
- Ultra‑short and/or long‑acting regimens that reduce adherence burden and need for dose‑by‑dose DOT, especially when ≥9–18 month fallback regimens are required.

name: Autosomal dominant hypocalcemia
description: Autosomal dominant hypocalcemia is a rare inherited calcium sensing disorder marked by low blood calcium with inappropriately low or normal parathyroid hormone and ongoing urinary calcium loss. Many patients are asymptomatic or have cramps and tingling, while severe cases can present with seizures in infancy or childhood. Standard calcium and active vitamin D can relieve symptoms but often worsen hypercalciuria, raising risks of kidney stones, nephrocalcinosis, and renal impairment and increasing monitoring burden. Kidney sparing, more physiologic control remains the key need, with parathyroid hormone analogues and calcium sensing receptor targeted therapies emerging.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Renal-sparing calcium control (normalize serum Ca while reducing urinary Ca to prevent nephrocalcinosis/nephrolithiasis/renal decline)
- Pediatric seizure prevention without worsening hypercalciuria/renal calcifications
- Lower pill burden with more stable Ca/PO4/Mg biochemical control (avoid wide serum-Ca fluctuations; address hyperphosphatemia/hypomagnesemia)

name: GRIN1-related neurodevelopmental disorder
description: Rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorder caused by GRIN1 variants that disrupt N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor signaling, leading from infancy to developmental delay or intellectual disability with often refractory epilepsy plus hypotonia, movement and feeding problems. Care is symptomatic with no approved disease-modifying therapies, and functional heterogeneity across gain-of-function versus loss-of-function variants makes one-size-fits-all treatment hard, driving demand for genotype-guided receptor modulation and better seizure and feeding support.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-stratified NMDA-receptor negative modulation for GRIN1/GRIN2 gain-of-function patients with refractory motor seizures, targeting ≥50% seizure reduction plus functional/behavioral improvement.
- Variant-directed NMDA-receptor potentiation for GRIN1 loss-of-function patients with severe neurodevelopmental impairment (e.g., nonverbal phenotype) to improve communication/adaptive function beyond symptom management.
- Drug control of hyperkinetic/dystonic movement disorder and dysphagia/feeding dysfunction (reducing G-tube dependence) to improve mobility and safe oral feeding.

name: Achromatopsia
description: Rare inherited cone dysfunction present at birth causing early nystagmus, severe photophobia and markedly reduced visual acuity with little to no color discrimination; care is symptomatic with filters and low-vision aids and no cure, leaving major unmet need for disease-modifying therapies that restore cone function, broaden genotype coverage beyond CNGA3/CNGB3, and reduce reliance on invasive subretinal surgery for gene delivery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Cone-function restoration in CNGA3/CNGB3 achromatopsia with measurable gains in BCVA/contrast sensitivity/color vision and reduced photophobia
- Genotype-expanding/agnostic therapies for the ~20% non-CNGA3/CNGB3 or unknown-cause patients (e.g., other genes/ATF6)
- Less invasive (non-subretinal/vitrectomy) delivery enabling broader eligibility (earlier pediatrics and patients with stricter BCVA/retinal thickness limits)

name: Antisynthetase syndrome
description: Antisynthetase syndrome is a rare, female-predominant chronic autoimmune disease driven by autoantibodies to aminoacyl transfer RNA synthetases, causing multisystem inflammation with myositis, inflammatory arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, cracked thickened hands, and often severe, rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease that may be the first or only presentation with exertional shortness of breath and dry cough. Treatment relies on early high-dose prednisone plus additional immunosuppression, but relapse and flares are common during steroid tapering, leaving a major unmet need for durable steroid-sparing control that preserves lung function while controlling muscle and joint disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent/slow ASyS‑ILD progression to progressive pulmonary fibrosis and oxygen dependence (e.g., improved FVC/DLCO, HRCT outcomes)
- Single agent that effectively treats ILD + myositis + polyarthritis (multi‑manifestation disease control)
- Durable steroid‑sparing disease control enabling safe tapering (e.g., prednisone ≤7.5 mg/day) with fewer flares/relapses

name: Optic neuritis
description: Inflammatory optic nerve injury, usually unilateral, causing painful eye movement, acute vision loss and color desaturation with risk of permanent disability; affects mainly women aged 20 to 40 and may signal multiple sclerosis. Steroids speed recovery but do not improve final vision and oral steroids can raise recurrence risk, leaving unmet need for therapies that improve durable visual outcomes and prevent relapsing damage, especially in neuromyelitis optica and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disorder.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute neuroprotective/remyelinating therapy that improves *final* visual outcomes (OCT RNFL/GCIPL preservation + low-contrast acuity at ~6 months), not just faster recovery
- Targeted acute + relapse-preventing immunotherapy for recurrent/antibody-mediated ON (AQP4-NMOSD, MOGAD/CRION) to prevent attack-driven permanent vision loss and steroid-withdrawal relapses
- Steroid-sparing, convenient outpatient/self-administered acute options that reduce IV infusion logistics and systemic steroid side effects while preserving early recovery

name: Retinitis pigmentosa
description: Retinitis pigmentosa is an inherited retinal degeneration in which photoreceptors progressively fail, typically starting with night blindness and peripheral field loss in childhood or adolescence and advancing to tunnel vision and later central vision loss. Care is largely supportive, with limited symptomatic options such as carbonic anhydrase inhibitors for cystoid macular edema, and there is no broadly applicable disease modifying therapy. Gene therapy exists only for a small RPE65 subset, leaving most patients needing treatments that slow progression and, in advanced disease, restore useful vision.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Mutation-/gene-agnostic disease modification to preserve rod/cone function (night vision + peripheral field) beyond Luxturna’s biallelic RPE65 subset
- Vision restoration for advanced RP (very poor BCVA) via intravitreal optogenetics targeting inner retinal neurons
- Improved RP-associated cystoid macular edema therapy to boost central vision (BCVA) with fewer CAI side effects/monitoring and less frequent dosing

name: Congenital chylothorax
description: Rare, potentially life threatening neonatal pleural effusion where chyle accumulates in the pleural space, causing early respiratory distress plus major nutritional and immune losses; often detected prenatally with fetal lung compression or hydrops. Care is largely supportive with drainage and prolonged nutrition strategies, with inconsistent drug efficacy, frequent long hospitalizations, and escalation to surgery, leaving need for safe prenatal and rapid, reliable leak closure therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prenatal/early neonatal therapy that prevents or reverses hydrops fetalis in congenital chylothorax
- Rapid “leak-closure” pharmacotherapy to reduce chest-tube dependence and prolonged fasting/TPN (shorten NICU stay/resource use)
- Safer, trial-validated alternative to off-label octreotide that avoids hemodynamic/GI toxicity

name: Ileus
description: Ileus is a functional shutdown of bowel motility without mechanical obstruction, most often after abdominal or retroperitoneal surgery, typically appearing on postoperative days 3 to 5 with distension, nausea or vomiting, and failure to pass gas or tolerate oral intake. Care is largely supportive, and current drug options are operationally constrained, with alvimopan limited to short term inpatient use at registered hospitals and neostigmine requiring continuous monitoring for cardiopulmonary risk, leaving a need for broadly usable therapies that reliably speed gastrointestinal recovery and shorten length of stay.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non‑restricted (non‑REMS), opioid‑tolerant–compatible perioperative agent that accelerates GI recovery across broader abdominal surgeries beyond alvimopan’s hospital‑only narrow label.
- Colonic ileus/ACPO prokinetic or decompression therapy with neostigmine‑like efficacy but without continuous BP/ECG monitoring requirements (safer/easier in higher‑risk patients).
- Convenient post‑diagnosis treatment for established postoperative ileus that reduces supportive‑care needs (NPO/IV fluids/NG) and shortens time‑to‑bowel‑function/discharge endpoints.

name: Lymphogranuloma venereum
description: Lymphogranuloma venereum is an invasive sexually transmitted infection caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis* (L1 to L3) that often presents as proctocolitis with rectal discharge and bleeding, anal pain, constipation, fever, and tenesmus and can progress to chronic fistulas, strictures, and rectal scarring. Care relies on a 21 day doxycycline course, but evidence gaps around optimal duration, limited pregnancy data, and tolerability issues with erythromycin leave a premium on shorter, durable regimens and better options for pregnancy and severe disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ≤14-day (or single-dose long-acting) regimen matching 21-day BID doxycycline cure rates to reduce adherence burden in rectal LGV (common in MSM)
- Pregnancy-optimized, evidence-based regimen with defined azithromycin dose/duration and outcomes to avoid doxycycline fetal-tooth risk and erythromycin GI intolerance
- Proven therapy for complicated/severe LGV (buboes, fistulas/strictures) that rapidly sterilizes infection to prevent tissue damage/scarring and avoid prolonged courses

name: Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia | myelodysplastic
description: Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia is a clonal bone marrow cancer with overlapping myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative features, marked by sustained monocytosis, cytopenia or proliferative symptoms such as splenomegaly and weight loss, and a meaningful risk of progression to acute myeloid leukemia. Most patients are older men with frailty and comorbidities. Current drug options such as hydroxyurea and hypomethylating agents are not disease modifying, complete remissions are uncommon, and the only curative approach, allogeneic stem cell transplantation, is feasible for a small minority. Outcomes after hypomethylating agent failure can be measured in months.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Outpatient-friendly, disease-modifying therapy for HMA‑naïve CMML delivering deeper remissions (↑CR) vs current hydroxyurea/HMA.
- Effective post‑HMA‑failure salvage that meaningfully extends OS and reduces/halts AML transformation.
- Durable anemia therapy achieving long-lasting transfusion independence in lower‑risk/dysplastic CMML beyond ESA durability.

name: Melioidosis
description: Melioidosis is a soil and freshwater acquired Burkholderia pseudomallei infection that often presents as severe pneumonia and can rapidly progress to septicemia with disseminated abscesses, especially in adults with diabetes or renal disease. It is frequently misdiagnosed, and mortality remains ~10 to 50 percent even with antibiotics. Care requires weeks of intravenous therapy followed by 3 to 6 months of oral eradication therapy, yet recurrence occurs in ~13 to 23 percent, creating demand for faster diagnostics and shorter, safer, more sterilizing regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- TMP‑SMX–sparing oral eradication regimens that prevent relapse while avoiding high discontinuation/toxicity (AKI/SCAR), especially in older patients and those with renal disease.
- Simplified, less resource‑intensive intensive‑phase options (e.g., once‑daily/long‑acting IV or oral) to replace weeks of q6–8h ceftazidime or q8h meropenem.
- More sterilizing therapies that penetrate intracellular/sequestered foci (granuloma/abscess/multifocal disease) to reduce 13–23% recurrence and shorten prolonged multi‑phase antibiotic courses, especially in diabetes/immunodeficiency.

name: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
description: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome is a potentially serious iatrogenic complication of in vitro fertilisation where overstimulated ovaries swell and vascular leak causes fluid to shift into the abdomen or chest, typically presenting soon after the trigger injection with abdominal distension and pain and, rarely, thrombosis or breathing difficulty. Management is largely supportive with no therapy that reverses the syndrome, sometimes requiring paracentesis and prolonged anticoagulant injections, while prevention can force disruptive cycle changes such as freezing embryos and delaying transfer.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent pregnancy-driven late-onset OHSS in high-risk IVF stimulators (e.g., PCOS/high follicle count/high estradiol) to avoid freeze-only cycle segmentation while maintaining near-zero moderate–severe OHSS risk.
- Acute pharmacologic OHSS treatment that reverses vascular leak (ascites/effusions, hemoconcentration) to reduce admissions/procedures and organ complications.
- Pregnancy-safe, non-injectable thrombosis-prevention (or vascular-stabilizing) strategy that avoids prolonged heparin injections through ~12 weeks’ gestation.

name: Necrobiosis lipoidica
description: Necrobiosis lipoidica is a rare granulomatous skin disease linked to diabetes, typically affecting young to middle-aged women with shin lesions that progress from red papules to yellow-brown atrophic plaques. About a third develop ulceration after minor trauma, with ulcers often painful, infection-prone, slow to heal, and recurrent. No therapy is definitively effective, leaving a major unmet need for steroid-sparing, disease-modifying treatments that reliably heal ulcers and provide durable control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Ulcer-focused therapy that prevents and/or rapidly heals ulcers (complete closure within ~6 months) in ulcerated NL.
- Steroid-sparing (preferably topical) anti-inflammatory therapy improving validated NL Lesion Score by ~Week 12 without worsening glycemic control in diabetics.
- Durable, convenient long-term control that reduces relapse and minimizes administration burden (avoid painful intralesional injections and frequent twice-daily topicals) while improving pain/DLQI.

name: IgG4-related disease
description: Immunoglobulin G4 related disease is a rare chronic immune mediated fibroinflammatory syndrome that causes tumor like inflammatory masses and progressive fibrosis, often across multiple organs such as the pancreas, kidneys, salivary glands, and retroperitoneum. It commonly mimics other conditions, delaying diagnosis until organ injury is established. Glucocorticoids can induce rapid improvement, but relapse during tapering is frequent and long term steroid toxicity is a major burden. Because established fibrotic damage can be irreversible, there is strong unmet need for earlier recognition, safer steroid sparing maintenance, and therapies that prevent progression and preserve organ function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing maintenance that prevents relapse/flares during and after taper (improve Week-52 time-to-first treated/adjudicated flare; flare-free, treatment-free complete remission)
- Anti-fibrotic/organ-protective control to halt progression to irreversible fibrosis and organ failure
- Non-steroidal, safer long-term therapies with easier chronic administration vs glucocorticoids and B-cell depletion (lower toxicity/infection risk; enable at-home/SC dosing vs IV)

name: Aphasia | progressive non-fluent
description: Nonfluent/agrammatic primary progressive aphasia is a frontotemporal dementia syndrome typically beginning in the 60s, marked by progressively effortful, halting speech and loss of grammar with relative early sparing of single word meaning. Over time patients may lose speech, develop unsafe swallowing and parkinsonian features overlapping progressive supranuclear palsy or corticobasal syndrome, raising aspiration pneumonia risk and caregiver burden. Care is largely supportive with speech language therapy and assistive communication, but there are no disease specific medicines or proven ways to slow progression, leaving a premium on tau aligned disease modification and scalable home communication and swallowing support.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Biomarker-confirmed FTLD‑tau nfvPPA (often 4R‑tau PSP/CBD biology) disease-modifying therapy to slow loss of motor speech/grammar.
- Home-administered symptomatic therapy that improves speech production/fluency and functional communication beyond speech-language therapy (measured by objective speech capture + validated language scales).
- Therapies that delay/mitigate later-stage dysphagia and parkinsonian/motor progression (PSP/CBS-overlap) to maintain safe oral intake/mobility and reduce pneumonia/infection morbidity.

name: Phenylketonuria
description: Phenylketonuria is a rare inherited amino acid metabolism disorder where phenylalanine cannot be properly processed, and elevated levels can cause irreversible brain injury. Most patients are diagnosed as asymptomatic newborns via screening, then face lifelong low protein diet and medical foods with adherence often deteriorating in adolescence and adulthood. Only a minority respond to cofactor therapy, while enzyme substitution can reduce dietary burden but is limited by hypersensitivity risk and access controls. Women of childbearing age have a particularly high unmet need because phenylalanine targets must be tightly controlled before conception and throughout pregnancy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Diet-liberating, adherence-proof phenylalanine control (including in non–BH4/sapropterin responders) to keep blood Phe in target long-term.
- Pegvaliase-like Phe lowering without hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis/REMS burdens (no mandatory epinephrine, supervised first dose/observation).
- Pregnancy-compatible control maintaining maternal blood Phe 120–360 µmol/L for ≥3 months preconception and throughout pregnancy (including unplanned pregnancies).

name: Leishmaniasis | cutaneous
description: Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a sandfly transmitted parasitic skin infection causing weeks to months delayed, often painless ulcers on exposed skin that can take months to years to heal and leave disfiguring lifelong scars and stigma, increasingly seen in travelers and migrants. Treatment is difficult to standardize because efficacy depends on parasite species and geography and current systemic therapies can be toxic, prolonged, and limited in pregnancy, driving need for rapid species guided or broadly effective short course regimens and lesion directed options that speed healing, prevent relapse, and reduce scarring.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pregnancy-/lactation-compatible short-course systemic therapy (≤14 days) achieving CL clinical cure (e.g., Day-90 100% re-epithelialization) in *Viannia* CL
- Species/region-robust regimen (or rapid species-ID + tailored regimen) delivering durable cure with low relapse (e.g., no Day-180 reopening) across Old- and New-World CL
- Lesion-directed therapy that accelerates healing and reduces long-term scarring (e.g., improved 12-month tissue scarring), especially for exposed/cosmetically sensitive sites

name: Short bowel syndrome
description: Short bowel syndrome is acquired intestinal failure after loss or surgical resection of small intestine, causing malabsorption that can spiral into dehydration and malnutrition. Many patients require long term intravenous parenteral nutrition, bringing catheter related complications and intestinal failure associated liver disease. Jejunostomy patients are especially vulnerable to high output stoma losses and rapid dehydration. The unmet need is for safer, more durable reduction in parenteral support dependence and better control of fluid and electrolyte losses with less treatment and monitoring burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable reduction of parenteral support (PN/IV fluids) volume/days to achieve enteral autonomy and eliminate central-line dependence.
- Targeted therapy for end-jejunostomy/high-output stoma (“no colon”) patients to reduce stoma output and improve fluid/electrolyte absorption.
- Teduglutide-like parenteral support–reduction efficacy with less frequent dosing and reduced colonoscopy/neoplasia-monitoring burden.

name: Hereditary spastic paraplegia
description: Hereditary spastic paraplegia is a rare inherited neurodegenerative disorder caused by selective degeneration of long corticospinal axons, leading to slowly progressive lower limb spasticity, weakness, and worsening gait, often with urinary urgency. Treatment is symptomatic only, focused on spasticity control and mobility support, and no therapies prevent, slow, or reverse progression. Key unmet needs are better tolerated spasticity management that preserves ambulation and disease modifying, genotype guided approaches such as gene targeted strategies for common subtypes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy for SPG4 (SPAST-HSP) that prevents/slows/reverses progression and preserves ambulatory function (e.g., Timed 25‑foot walk).
- Genotype-specific CNS gene therapies for severe childhood-onset complex HSP (e.g., SPG47/SPG50) that improve long-horizon motor-development milestones (e.g., GMFM‑88).
- Better-tolerated, more effective spasticity control improving gait/spasticity metrics (e.g., Modified Ashworth Scale) without systemic adverse effects or invasive escalation (intrathecal baclofen pump/botulinum).

name: Biliary atresia
description: Infant-onset bile duct obstruction causing cholestasis and progressive liver injury to cirrhosis, presenting at 2 to 8 weeks with persistent jaundice, pale stools, and dark urine; Kasai surgery is non-curative and many children progress to liver transplant, with major unmet needs in durable bile drainage and reducing recurrent cholangitis and portal hypertension.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Post‑Kasai adjuvant therapy to increase bile drainage/jaundice clearance and improve 2‑year transplant‑free survival
- Therapies that prevent/reduce early post‑Kasai cholangitis to cut hospitalization/IV‑antibiotic use and delay transplant
- Anti‑fibrotic / portal‑hypertension–modifying therapy for long‑term native‑liver survivors post‑Kasai to avoid late transplant and improve QoL

name: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
description: Chronic lung disease of very premature or ventilated newborns caused by arrested lung development and treatment related injury, diagnosed when breathing support is still needed at 28 days or near due date. High burden from prolonged oxygen needs, long term lung damage, and complications such as pulmonary hypertension. Care is largely supportive, with a major need for steroid sparing approaches due to serious adverse effects and for targeted therapies for bronchopulmonary dysplasia associated pulmonary hypertension.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pro‑lung‑development therapy reversing alveolar simplification/microvascular injury to achieve room‑air/no positive‑pressure support by 36 weeks corrected age.
- Steroid‑sparing strategy enabling extubation/CLD prevention without dexamethasone toxicities (e.g., hyperglycemia, hypertension, GI perforation) and cerebral palsy signal.
- Pulmonary‑hypertension–targeted therapy for PH‑BPD to reduce progression to right‑heart failure/mortality with improved hemodynamic tolerability (less hypotension).

name: Nephrotic syndrome
description: Pediatric nephrotic syndrome is a glomerular filter disorder, typically in boys aged 2 to 7, causing heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia, often presenting as morning periorbital swelling with foamy urine and fatigue. Care is dominated by prednisone despite few approved alternatives, but repeated courses drive growth and metabolic toxicity. Steroid resistant disease is harder to control and more likely to progress to end stage kidney disease, while steroid sparing options like calcineurin inhibitors often require prolonged use, relapse when stopped and can be nephrotoxic, leaving a need for safer durable relapse prevention and kidney protection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing relapse prevention achieving durable (≥1-year) relapse-free remission in pediatric SSNS/FRNS/SDNS.
- Sustained proteinuria remission and kidney-failure prevention in SRNS/secondary SRNS (incl. genetically guided therapy).
- Non-nephrotoxic, low-monitoring alternative to long-term calcineurin inhibitors that maintains remission and reduces high withdrawal-relapse.

name: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
description: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a severe inherited muscle-wasting disease caused by loss of dystrophin, with onset before age 6, loss of walking around age 12, and later cardiopulmonary decline. Care is dominated by long term steroids that slow weakness but cause significant toxicity including weight gain and bone fragility, while mutation specific exon skipping helps only subsets. The premium unmet need is genotype agnostic dystrophin restoration with durable benefit, alongside better therapies to prevent or treat cardiomyopathy and respiratory failure.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-agnostic dystrophin restoration for DMD patients not covered by current mutation-specific exon-skipping therapies
- Cardiomyopathy/heart-failure modifying therapies improving cardiac function (e.g., cardiac MRI strain/LVEF) in later-stage/non-ambulatory DMD
- Steroid-sparing therapies for non-ambulatory DMD that preserve upper-limb and respiratory function (PUL 2.0; % predicted FVC) while reducing glucocorticoid toxicities (weight gain/Cushingoid changes, fracture risk)

name: Traumatic hemorrhagic shock
description: Traumatic hemorrhagic shock is life threatening circulatory collapse from major bleeding, marked by tachycardia, altered mental status, falling urine output, and cold poorly perfused extremities that can rapidly progress to organ failure. Despite damage control resuscitation, outcomes are limited by early fibrinogen depletion that destabilizes clots and citrate driven hypocalcemia during transfusion. Key needs are faster, more deployable hemostatic resuscitation, including prehospital blood products with built in calcium support, to control bleeding and prevent coagulopathy, acidosis, and hypothermia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Ultra-early, goal-directed fibrinogen repletion (fibrinogen concentrate/cryoprecipitate) for massively bleeding trauma patients with hypofibrinogenemia (Clauss ≤1.5 g/L or viscoelastic deficit) to reduce exsanguination/transfusion needs vs plasma-heavy resuscitation.
- Logistically deployable prehospital hemostatic resuscitation (e.g., shelf-stable plasma/blood products) during transport for patients at risk of hemorrhagic shock to improve coagulation and reduce 30-day mortality.
- Built-in mitigation of transfusion-associated hypocalcemia/citrate toxicity (e.g., co-packaged calcium strategy or citrate-sparing products) to maintain ionized Ca ≥1.0 mmol/L and reduce mortality/massive transfusion risk.

name: Spinocerebellar ataxia
description: Autosomal dominant, progressive cerebellar neurodegeneration starting in early mid life that steadily worsens gait and limb coordination, speech and eye movements, often progressing to dysphagia and aspiration risk. No United States Food and Drug Administration approved symptomatic or disease slowing therapies, so care is largely rehabilitation and complication management, with major unmet need for disease modifying treatments and safer ways to preserve mobility and swallowing as gene therapy and antisense oligonucleotides move into early clinical testing.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy that slows functional progression (e.g., ≥50% reduction in 1‑year SARA progression / improved modified f‑SARA at ~48 weeks).
- Therapeutics that improve bulbar dysfunction (dysphagia/dysarthria) and reduce aspiration/aspiration-pneumonia risk.
- Non-sedating symptomatic control of spasticity/rigidity/tremor that does not worsen posture/balance or increase falls risk.

name: Germ cell tumor | brain
description: Rare midline brain tumors (pineal or suprasellar) in adolescents, often male, causing diabetes insipidus and progressive endocrine and visual deficits or hydrocephalus with Parinaud syndrome, headaches, nausea and vomiting. Cure rates are high, but long term burden is driven by permanent endocrinopathies and radiation late effects like cognitive decline, stroke, and psychiatric sequelae, while relapsed non germinomatous disease remains hard to salvage with guarded prognosis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- RT-sparing (or further dose/field-reduced) regimens for localized CNS germinoma to preserve ≥90% 5-year OS while lowering late neuroendocrine/cognitive and cerebrovascular toxicity.
- Relapse-preventing and relapse-salvage-active systemic therapies for malignant NGGCT (esp. metastatic/high-risk) to improve outcomes where post-treatment relapse is often fatal.
- Less myelotoxic/organ-sparing systemic regimens (and/or myeloprotective combinations) to reduce very high acute platinum/etoposide/ifosfamide-era toxicity and chemotherapy delays while maintaining disease control.

name: Thyroid cancer | medullary
description: Medullary thyroid cancer is a metastatic-prone neuroendocrine tumor arising from thyroid parafollicular C cells that often presents as a thyroid nodule with neck lymphadenopathy and can cause secretory diarrhea. Treatment remains constrained by resistance to selective RET inhibitors including RET G810 solvent front mutations, a sizable RET wild type subset with RAS mutations that falls outside RET targeted options, and a major quality of life burden from diarrhea that can be tumor driven and therapy worsened.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Next‑gen RET inhibitors active against acquired RET solvent‑front (esp. G810) ± gatekeeper mutations after selpercatinib/pralsetinib progression
- Precision therapies for RET‑wild‑type, RAS‑driven (esp. HRAS‑mutant) sporadic MTC to replace non‑selective MKIs
- Agents that control tumor‑secretory diarrhea while avoiding/worsening TKI/MKI diarrhea to improve QoL and tolerability

name: Scleroderma | systemic
description: Systemic sclerosis is an autoimmune disease marked by progressive collagen driven fibrosis that scars skin and internal organs, often starting with Raynaud phenomenon and puffy fingers that progress to skin thickening, alongside frequent reflux and dysphagia and sometimes silent but deadly lung involvement. Care is still largely organ by organ because no therapy reliably modifies the underlying disease course, and key complications such as interstitial lung disease and ischemic digital ulcers remain major drivers of morbidity and disability. Current antifibrotic options can be limited by tolerability, keeping demand high for safer, truly disease modifying approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Predictable, disease-modifying anti-fibrotic therapy for early diffuse cutaneous SSc with consistent clinically meaningful mRSS improvement beyond variable immunosuppressant response
- Better-tolerated SSc-ILD therapy that halts/meaningfully further slows FVC decline while avoiding nintedanib-like GI toxicity to support long-term use
- Vasculopathy-targeted therapy that prevents new and accelerates healing of ischemic digital ulcers, especially in severe digital fibrosis with poor healing

name: Sideroblastic anemia
description: Sideroblastic anemias are inherited or acquired bone marrow disorders marked by ring sideroblasts from iron loaded mitochondria, causing ineffective red cell production and progressive anemia. In myelodysplastic syndrome with ring sideroblasts this often worsens into transfusion dependence, with fatigue and iron overload that can lead to organ damage. Current care is largely supportive with repeated transfusions plus iron chelation that carries renal and hepatic toxicity monitoring burdens. Even newer erythroid maturation therapy achieves durable transfusion independence in only a minority, leaving a premium on safer, more durable disease modifying control of anemia and iron overload.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Higher-rate and more durable anemia control (sustained RBC transfusion independence) in MDS with ring sideroblasts patients with inadequate ESA benefit and incomplete luspatercept response.
- Iron-overload reduction that avoids chelator toxicity and intensive monitoring burden.
- Safer, lower-burden anemia therapies (preferably oral or longer-interval) that avoid ESA-class cardiovascular/thrombotic risks and frequent injections.

name: Esophageal varices
description: Esophageal varices are dilated submucosal veins in the distal esophagus caused by portal hypertension, usually from cirrhosis, often silent until a sudden bleed that can be fatal. Care centers on preventing rupture with nonselective beta blockers or repeated endoscopic band ligation and treating bleeds with vasoactive drugs, antibiotics, and endoscopic therapy. Major gaps persist because 6 week mortality after bleeding is still about 10 to 20 percent, many patients cannot take beta blockers or do not achieve adequate portal pressure reduction, banding is burdensome, and some vasoactive options carry serious toxicity risks such as respiratory failure.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-NSBB portal-pressure–lowering therapy for NSBB-contraindicated/intolerant patients that achieves bleeding-protective HVPG response (≤12 mmHg or ≥20% reduction).
- Safer, more effective acute variceal-bleed pharmacotherapy that reduces ~10–15% 6-week mortality without terlipressin-like respiratory toxicity.
- Durable outpatient secondary-prophylaxis drug that reduces urgent endoscopy and frequent repeat band ligation (q2–4 weeks) during the high-risk first 6 weeks post-bleed.

name: Pneumocystosis
description: Rare, life threatening opportunistic fungal pneumonia in immunocompromised adults, often advanced human immunodeficiency virus with CD4 counts below 200, causing subacute progressive dyspnea, fever, and nonproductive cough with ground glass changes on computed tomography. Care relies on a 21 day trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole course that drives treatment limiting toxicity in up to one third and can require intravenous delivery, while mortality can be high in non human immunodeficiency virus immunosuppressed patients, creating demand for safer, lower burden, more effective regimens and better adjunct steroid strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- TMP‑SMX–sparing curative regimen for patients with treatment‑limiting TMP‑SMX toxicity/intolerance (incl. SJS/TEN risk)
- Mortality‑reducing therapy/adjunct for severe non‑HIV immunocompromised PJP (reduce 28‑day death and invasive respiratory support)
- Lower‑burden outpatient‑feasible regimen (avoid q6–8h IV dosing; shorten ~21‑day course and/or reduce steroid exposure/complications)

name: Spinal muscular atrophy | type 2
description: Spinal muscular atrophy type 2 is an inherited SMN1 related motor neuron disease causing survival motor neuron protein deficiency, progressive muscle weakness and wasting, and the classic sitter phenotype with onset at 6 to 18 months. Children can sit but typically cannot stand or walk, and many develop recurrent respiratory infections, breathing problems, scoliosis, and contractures. Disease modifying therapies improve survival and function but are not curative and come with meaningful delivery and safety burdens, including repeated lumbar punctures, lifelong daily oral dosing, or one time gene therapy with liver injury risk. Key unmet needs include durable benefit across the body and safer, simpler long term options, including survival motor neuron independent add ons.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Achieve new motor milestones (standing/walking independently) in later-onset “sitter/never-walker” SMA2 patients via SMN-independent and/or muscle-targeted add-ons.
- Improve bulbar/respiratory outcomes (e.g., FVC; reduced feeding/ventilatory support) to match motor gains.
- Provide a safer, simpler, broadly accessible systemic therapy avoiding intrathecal delivery/monitoring burdens and AAV gene-therapy liver-toxicity and redosing/eligibility constraints.

name: Polycystic kidney disease | autosomal dominant
description: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is an inherited disorder where kidney cysts enlarge the kidneys, disrupt filtration, and can progress to kidney failure, with complications such as hypertension, flank or back pain, hematuria, and recurrent urinary tract infections. Diagnosis often occurs in midlife despite preserved function for decades. The only disease modifying option, tolvaptan, is constrained by aquaretic side effects, serious liver injury risk, and intensive monitoring, leaving a need for safer therapies that prevent kidney failure and reduce cyst driven pain and infections.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying ADPKD therapy proven to delay kidney failure/KRT (hard outcomes), not just slow eGFR/TKV.
- Non-aquaretic, liver-safe alternative to tolvaptan that avoids hepatotoxicity/REMS and intensive LFT monitoring while maintaining renal benefit.
- Cyst-burden–targeting therapies that reduce chronic flank/abdominal pain and hard-to-treat (antibiotic-refractory) cyst/urinary infections.

name: Acromegaly
description: Acromegaly is a rare adult endocrine disorder usually caused by a benign pituitary adenoma that chronically overproduces growth hormone, driving excess insulin-like growth factor 1 and slow, progressive tissue overgrowth. Patients often present late, frequently with macroadenomas, headaches or impaired vision, and established comorbidities such as type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Surgery and injectable medical therapy leave many patients uncontrolled, with long-acting somatostatin receptor ligands achieving biochemical control in only about half, and some drugs limited by hyperglycemia, sustaining demand for more effective, better tolerated, less burdensome treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable composite biochemical control (GH suppression + age/sex-adjusted IGF‑1 normalization) in treatment‑naïve/post‑surgery patients inadequately controlled on first‑generation long‑acting somatostatin analogs
- Biochemical control without worsening glycemia/diabetes in patients with baseline metabolic risk
- Lower-burden, non-injectable or much less frequent dosing that replaces chronic injection regimens while maintaining biochemical targets

name: Bartonellosis
description: Bartonellosis is a zoonotic bacterial infection most commonly seen as cat scratch disease after a cat scratch or bite, causing a papule followed by painful regional lymphadenopathy with fever, headache, and fatigue. Most cases are self limited, and antibiotics such as azithromycin offer modest benefit. The high stakes are in immunocompromised patients, where disease can become disseminated with vascular proliferative lesions or endocarditis requiring prolonged therapy that is hard to deliver because of drug interactions and toxicity, particularly rifamycin interactions with antiretrovirals and gentamicin associated nephrotoxicity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course oral therapy for uncomplicated cat-scratch disease that improves clinically meaningful outcomes (e.g., time-to-resolution of lymphadenopathy/systemic symptoms), not just lymph-node volume.
- Relapse-preventing, shorter-duration regimen for disseminated bartonellosis/bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients that avoids prolonged (≥3-month) courses and rifamycin–ARV interactions.
- Gentamicin-sparing (preferably fully oral) curative regimen for Bartonella endocarditis that maintains high success while avoiding IV aminoglycoside renal-toxicity risk.

name: Transverse myelitis
description: Rare inflammatory spinal cord syndrome where inflammation damages myelin and abruptly disrupts motor, sensory, and autonomic pathways, causing severe back pain, band-like truncal tightness, sensory loss, rapidly worsening weakness up to paralysis, and bowel or bladder dysfunction. Care is time critical with acute immunosuppression and escalation beyond intravenous steroids for nonresponders, yet incomplete recovery and lasting disability are common, creating unmet need for better steroid-refractory rescue and true repair therapies that remyelinate and restore function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-refractory acute rescue that prevents irreversible paralysis/autonomic injury while avoiding escalation to PLEX/IVIG/cyclophosphamide
- Neurorepair/remyelination to restore walking and bladder/bowel function after the acute attack
- Biomarker-guided relapse-prevention maintenance therapy (e.g., AQP4/MOG/underlying-disease subgroup) to reduce repeat attacks and cumulative disability

name: Malaria | Plasmodium ovale infection
description: Plasmodium ovale malaria is a flu like febrile illness after travel or residence in endemic areas, sometimes with 48 hour fever cycles, and is often missed due to low parasite density and nonspecific symptoms. The major unmet need is a relapse proof cure since dormant liver hypnozoites can trigger recurrence weeks to years later. Anti relapse therapy still relies on a 14 day primaquine course requiring glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase testing and is contraindicated in pregnancy, limiting real world use and adherence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Hypnozoitocidal (anti-relapse) radical-cure therapy that is safe/usable without quantitative G6PD screening and is safe in pregnancy and in children <16.
- Single-encounter or ≤3-day anti-relapse regimen that avoids 14-day primaquine adherence issues and tafenoquine’s chloroquine-only constraint.
- Relapse-prevention agent with efficacy robust to CYP2D6 impairment and high body weight (no ≥70 kg dose adjustment/extended dosing needed).

name: 7q11.23 duplication syndrome
description: Rare autosomal-dominant 7q11.23 duplication causing early speech and motor delay with prominent motor speech and anxiety phenotypes, plus high risk of progressive aortic dilatation. Care is largely supportive and therapy intensive, with major unmet need for disease-modifying neurodevelopmental treatment and prevention of life-threatening aortopathy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying neurodevelopmental therapy that measurably improves core speech/language and motor‑speech planning deficits (esp. childhood apraxia of speech/dysarthria).
- Targeted, pediatric-safe therapy for the high-frequency behavioral phenotype (social anxiety disorder + selective mutism ± ASD/ADHD/oppositional aggression) with more consistent efficacy than nonspecific psychotropics.
- Aortopathy-focused therapy that prevents progression of aortic dilatation in the ~half of patients affected, reducing dissection/rupture risk.

name: Aarskog syndrome
description: Rare genetic developmental syndrome, mainly in boys, marked by childhood short stature plus characteristic facial, hand and foot, and genitourinary anomalies such as shawl scrotum and sometimes heart defects; neurodevelopment is variable with some learning and behavioral challenges. Care is largely supportive and multidisciplinary, often involving surgeries for congenital anomalies, and growth hormone is sometimes tried but response is unpredictable and treatment is burdensome due to frequent injections, leaving a need for more reliable disease modifying options and less burdensome interventions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Clinically meaningful, predictable height/final-height gains for children with Aarskog vs variable/limited benefit from current GH use
- Lower-burden growth therapy that reduces/avoids frequent subcutaneous injections and at-home prep (e.g., longer-acting dosing)
- Pharmacologic improvement in learning/behavior outcomes (esp. ADHD symptoms) for the neurodevelopmentally affected subset

name: African tick-bite fever
description: Travel associated spotted fever rickettsiosis caused by Rickettsia africae, typically presenting 5 to 10 days after a tick bite with fever, headache, myalgias, one or more eschars and regional lymphadenopathy, with rash often absent. Most cases are self limited and respond to a 5 to 7 day doxycycline course, but care is constrained by limited validated alternatives for pregnancy or tetracycline intolerance and by occasional severe or prolonged complications such as neuropathy, myocarditis, reactive arthritis, or persistent fever.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pregnancy- and tetracycline-intolerance–compatible oral therapy with proven efficacy vs *R. africae*
- Ultra-short-course regimen (single-dose to ≤3 days) matching doxycycline outcomes to reduce adherence burden in travelers
- Therapy/adjunct to reduce prolonged recovery and rare severe complications (e.g., neuropathy, myocarditis, reactive arthritis, prolonged fever), especially in older patients

name: Acinetobacter infection
description: Acinetobacter baumannii is a healthcare associated, often multidrug resistant ICU pathogen that causes ventilator associated pneumonia, bloodstream, urinary tract, and wound infections. Mortality is highest in hospital pneumonia and bacteremia, yet care still relies on limited, toxic salvage antibiotics such as polymyxins with frequent kidney injury and occasional severe neurotoxicity. The key unmet need is reliable, safer, simpler regimens that overcome resistance and improve survival, alongside emerging non antibiotic approaches such as bacteriophage therapies now entering clinical testing.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Mortality-reducing CRAB therapy for ICU HABP/VABP ± bacteremia that improves day‑28 survival and enables earlier de-escalation from ≥2-drug regimens
- Renal-/neuro-sparing alternative to polymyxin-based salvage for severe MDR *Acinetobacter* (avoid nephrotoxicity/respiratory paralysis and mortality-signal fallback agents)
- Lower administration burden/simpler dosing vs prolonged high-frequency IV infusions (fewer/shorter infusions and ideally a step-down option)

name: Histoplasmosis
description: Histoplasmosis is a fungal lung infection acquired by inhaling Histoplasma spores from soil contaminated with bird or bat droppings, often causing fever, cough, and fatigue within 3 to 17 days. Most cases are mild, but immunocompromised patients can develop severe disseminated or central nervous system disease. Treatment still depends on intravenous amphotericin B with intensive toxicity monitoring, then prolonged itraconazole with drug level and interaction management, leaving a need for safer IV sparing induction and more predictable oral therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- IV-sparing induction for severe disseminated histoplasmosis (esp. advanced HIV) that matches amphotericin-B efficacy while reducing nephrotoxicity/monitoring burden
- Predictable, interaction-sparing oral maintenance/suppressive therapy for ≥12 months that avoids itraconazole’s erratic absorption, CYP3A4 interactions, and drug-level monitoring
- CNS histoplasmosis regimens with better CNS sterilization and shorter total therapy to reduce 4–6 weeks IV amphotericin induction plus ≥12 months azole maintenance and relapse risk

name: Angelman syndrome
description: Genetic neurodevelopmental disorder caused by loss of maternal UBE3A expression in neurons, presenting in infancy with severe developmental delay, minimal speech, ataxia, epilepsy, sleep disturbance, and behavioral excitability. Care is largely symptomatic, with no approved therapies for core symptoms; major unmet needs are disease modifying treatments that restore UBE3A biology and improve hard to control seizures and fragmented sleep while reducing treatment burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-invasive UBE3A-restoration therapies (avoiding repeated intrathecal/lumbar puncture dosing), especially for severe maternal 15q11.2–q13 deletion subtype
- Better-tolerated, more effective control of epilepsy/NCSE in deletion-genotype children with early high seizure risk and multiple seizure phenotypes
- More reliable sleep-initiation/maintenance pharmacology than melatonin for frequent awakenings and irregular sleep–wake cycles

name: Barmah Forest virus disease
description: Mosquito-borne Barmah Forest virus causes fever and rash with painful swollen joints and marked fatigue often with morning stiffness. Most recover within weeks but a minority have debilitating arthralgia and fatigue for months to a year impacting work and quality of life. With no specific treatment or vaccine and only supportive analgesia, the key unmet need is disease modifying therapy or prevention that shortens the long tail of post-viral symptoms.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early BFV-specific antiviral therapy initiated in acute infection to prevent prolonged/severe joint pain and fatigue
- Targeted treatment for post-acute/chronic BFV syndrome (arthralgia/swelling + fatigue) in patients with symptoms persisting ≥6 months
- Short-course anti-inflammatory/analgesic that restores function, reducing work restrictions and improving QoL/ability-to-work outcomes

name: Becker muscular dystrophy
description: Becker muscular dystrophy is an X linked DMD gene disorder where partially functional dystrophin drives slowly progressive pelvic and leg weakness and gradual loss of skeletal and cardiac muscle. Boys typically present in childhood or adolescence and may stay ambulatory for years, but cardiac fibrosis can accelerate into heart failure. Care is largely surveillance and supportive management including early angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors or beta blockers and sometimes steroids, leaving a major unmet need for true disease modifying therapies that preserve heart function and stabilize muscle while reducing long term steroid burden. Gene replacement and gene modification are key frontiers.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Cardiac anti‑fibrotic/anti‑remodeling drugs initiated at CMR‑detected subclinical myocardial fibrosis to prevent progression to DCM/HF beyond ACEi/β‑blockers
- Oral skeletal‑muscle stabilizers that reduce ongoing muscle injury biomarkers (e.g., CK/fast skeletal troponin I) and preserve ambulatory function (NSAA/6MWD) in adult BMD
- Steroid‑sparing chronic anti‑inflammatory therapy with improved long‑term metabolic/bone/adrenal safety while maintaining mobility outcomes (NSAA/timed run‑walk)

name: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
description: Congenital overgrowth syndrome recognized at birth with macroglossia, abdominal wall defects, and neonatal hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia that can require intensive glucose support. Key unmet needs are safer, lower-burden control of hypoglycemia and reducing the heavy early-childhood cancer surveillance burden driven by ~10% childhood tumor risk (notably Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma).
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer, lower-burden medical therapy for persistent BWS hyperinsulinism that maintains euglycemia while avoiding continuous IV dextrose and/or partial pancreatectomy (incl. improved safety vs diazoxide pulmonary hypertension risk).
- Tumor-risk–reducing pharmacologic strategy to de-intensify high-frequency hepatoblastoma/Wilms surveillance (q3-month ultrasound/AFP).
- Non-surgical medical approach for neonatal macroglossia/upper-airway obstruction to reduce need for intubation/tracheostomy and tongue-reduction surgery.

name: Blount disease
description: Blount disease is a pediatric disorder of the proximal tibial growth plate where the medial side slows or stops relative to the lateral side, causing progressive tibia vara with a bowlegged gait. It often presents in early walking, overweight toddlers and may be minimally painful early but can progress to severe deformity, leg length discrepancy, and disability. Care relies on bracing and often repeated orthopedic procedures, with key unmet needs in durable weight management support, earlier growth plate level disease modification, and preventing post correction recurrence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacologic weight/BMI reduction in obese early-onset Blount patients (BMI >90th percentile) to improve bracing success and prevent progression.
- Growth-plate–targeted therapy to reliably reverse early-stage (reversible) medial proximal tibial physeal disease.
- Adjunct pharmacotherapy to reduce post-surgical recurrence/reoperation (e.g., after osteotomy or guided growth).

name: Borrelia miyamotoi disease
description: Borrelia miyamotoi disease is an emerging Ixodes tick transmitted spirochetal infection that typically presents in middle aged adults as an acute nonspecific febrile illness, often without rash and with thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and mild transaminitis. It is frequently misdiagnosed as Lyme disease or ehrlichiosis, and confirmation often requires acute pretreatment polymerase chain reaction testing rather than standard Lyme serology. Treatment is largely borrowed from Lyme disease antibiotics, with limited prospective evidence and occasional severe neuroinvasive cases requiring intravenous therapy, creating unmet needs for better front line diagnostics and simpler validated outpatient regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Validated shorter-course (≤5–7 days) or single-administration oral regimen maintaining rapid 24–72h symptom response while reducing empiric ~2-week antibiotic exposure
- Pregnancy- and <8-year-old–friendly non-tetracycline oral option with doxycycline-like effectiveness (avoiding tetracycline-class fetal/child tooth-discoloration risk)
- Outpatient (oral or long-acting) CNS-penetrant regimen for neuroinvasive/chronic meningitis—especially in immunocompromised patients—to avoid hospitalization/IV ceftriaxone

name: Palmoplantar keratoderma
description: Palmoplantar keratoderma causes abnormal thickening of the skin on the palms and soles, often starting in early childhood in hereditary forms and progressing to symmetric yellow hyperkeratosis with sweating, infection, malodor, fissures, and sometimes severe pain that limits walking and work. Treatment is largely symptomatic with emollients, keratolytics, debridement, and retinoids, but benefits are temporary, no curative or disease modifying therapy exists for most hereditary disease, and systemic retinoids are limited by tolerability and strict pregnancy avoidance. Unmet need centers on durable, pregnancy compatible, mutation informed options that reduce thickening, sweating, infections, and pain.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-directed therapies for hereditary PPK (e.g., gene editing/siRNA/protein replacement/read-through) to address mutation-specific disease drivers beyond symptomatic care.
- Pregnancy-compatible, non-retinoid treatments that achieve durable clear/almost-clear skin with functional benefit (pain reduction and improved walking).
- Therapies that reduce hyperhidrosis and prevent/treat recurrent fungal superinfection to reduce flares and daily care burden.

name: Brugada syndrome
description: Brugada syndrome is an inherited cardiac ion channel disorder that disrupts ventricular rhythm and can cause syncope, seizures, or sudden cardiac arrest, often at rest or during sleep, typically in middle age and disproportionately in men. Care largely relies on implantable cardioverter defibrillators that terminate ventricular fibrillation but do not prevent recurrences, while drug options are limited and imperfect. Key unmet needs include better risk stratification for asymptomatic or intermediate risk patients, safer long term oral prevention, and faster, more practical acute rescue than intravenous isoproterenol.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Better-tolerated chronic antiarrhythmic to reduce ventricular arrhythmias/ICD shocks vs quinidine-class limits
- Non-device oral preventive therapy for asymptomatic or ICD-ineligible/refusing patients with validated ECG/EP and clinical outcome benefit
- Non-IV, rapidly acting rescue therapy for VF/electrical storm to reduce inpatient infusion dependence

name: Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy
description: CADASIL is an inherited small vessel cerebral arteriopathy caused by NOTCH3 mutations that typically presents in midlife with migraine with aura and recurrent subcortical strokes, progressing to white matter disease, cognitive decline, and mood or personality changes. Management is largely supportive, with no proven disease modifying therapy and commonly used antiplatelets lacking clear efficacy, while more intensive antithrombotic strategies are constrained by intracranial bleeding risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- NOTCH3/CADASIL-targeted disease-modifying therapy that slows progression (fewer ischemic events) and preserves cognition/MRI lesion burden
- Secondary stroke-prevention approach that reduces recurrent lacunar stroke/TIA without increasing cerebral microbleeds or intracerebral hemorrhage
- CADASIL-appropriate, non‑vasoconstrictive migraine (with aura) therapy that reduces disability (e.g., MIDAS/HIT‑6) with stronger evidence base

name: Cri du chat syndrome
description: Cri-du-chat syndrome is a rare chromosome 5p deletion disorder usually recognized at birth by a cat-like cry, low birth weight, microcephaly, and hypotonia, often followed by severe intellectual disability, communication impairment, feeding problems, and behavioral morbidity such as aggression or self-injury, sometimes with congenital heart defects. Care is largely supportive with early rehabilitation and no specific treatment, leaving a premium on disease-modifying approaches that address the consequences of 5p gene loss and reduce lifelong developmental, feeding, and behavioral burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-life disease-modifying therapy that improves expressive language/functional communication (e.g., via 5p haploinsufficiency targets such as CTNND2).
- Drug therapy to reduce infant hypotonia-related feeding/swallowing dysfunction (poor sucking/dysphagia/GERD) to prevent failure-to-thrive.
- Safe, non-sedating medication to reduce hyperactivity and self-injurious/repetitive behaviors beyond behavioral modification alone.

name: CHARGE syndrome
description: Rare CHD7-related multisystem congenital disorder with life-threatening infant morbidity; early disease burden dominated by feeding, swallowing, and airway dysfunction often causing aspiration and tube feeding, sometimes compounded by immunodeficiency and recurrent infections; care is largely surgical and supportive with no disease-modifying or effective medical therapy for swallowing disorders, leaving major unmet need to reduce aspiration, feeding-tube dependence, and infection risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Thymus/T-cell–restorative therapy for CHARGE patients with thymic aplasia/hypoplasia and T‑cell lymphopenia to prevent severe/recurrent infections
- Aerodigestive/cranial-nerve–targeted pharmacotherapy to reduce dysphagia/aspiration and enable safe oral feeding (reduce NG/G-tube dependence)
- Early (prenatal/neonatal) CHD7-pathway restoration (e.g., gene replacement/editing or CHD7 upregulation) to reduce severity of complex congenital heart defects and airway/feeding drivers of early mortality

name: Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency
description: Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency (cytochrome c oxidase deficiency) is a rare inherited mitochondrial energy disorder that typically presents before age 2 with multisystem disease and progressive neurologic decline, often with Leigh syndrome and life threatening lactic acidosis crises. Treatment is largely supportive with no curative therapy and inconsistent benefit from supplement based mitochondrial cocktails, and severe pediatric cohorts have high early mortality. The biggest gaps are genotype directed disease modification, better prevention and management of metabolic decompensation, and therapies that improve neurodevelopmental and seizure outcomes to reduce hospitalizations and extend survival.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-targeted disease modification to prevent early respiratory-failure death in COX-deficient Leigh syndrome (e.g., SURF1)
- Acute metabolic-crisis control (lactate/acidosis) to reduce ICU/hospital days
- Pediatric therapies that improve neurofunction (e.g., gross motor) while reducing refractory seizures and disease-related hospitalization burden

name: Edwards syndrome
description: Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) is a chromosomal disorder causing severe multi organ congenital anomalies, typically diagnosed in utero or at birth and marked by very high early mortality. Care is largely supportive with no definitive treatment, and families and clinicians struggle most with preventing cardiorespiratory failure from congenital heart disease and central apnea, alongside feeding dysfunction with reflux and aspiration that makes nutrition and infection prevention difficult.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neonatal-safe pharmacotherapy that reduces cardiorespiratory failure/mortality driven by congenital heart defects and pulmonary disease (e.g., pulmonary hypertension/hypoplasia).
- Targeted therapy to reduce central/obstructive apnea and hypoventilation to prevent respiratory decompensation and need for intensive ventilatory support.
- Therapies that improve feeding/swallow coordination and/or control GERD to reduce aspiration pneumonia and dependence on NG/G-tube feeding.

name: Cauda equina syndrome
description: Cauda equina syndrome is a rare, time critical spinal emergency caused by lumbar cauda equina nerve root compression that can rapidly progress from severe back or sciatic pain to saddle sensory loss and new bladder or bowel dysfunction. Outcomes depend on immediate recognition and urgent decompression, yet even prompt surgery can leave persistent bladder, bowel, sexual dysfunction and chronic pain. Key unmet needs center on preventing delays and developing neuroprotective and restorative therapies to preserve nerve root function before surgery and improve recovery after decompression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Immediate-on-suspicion adjunct neuroprotective drug (ED/ambulance) to preserve nerve-root function and improve urinary/rectal outcomes
- Post-decompression nerve repair/regeneration therapy to reduce long-term neurogenic bladder/bowel and sexual dysfunction
- Non-opioid/opioid-sparing analgesics that avoid constipation/urinary-retention while controlling severe radicular pain

name: Christianson syndrome
description: X linked neurodevelopmental disorder affecting mainly boys, with infant onset severe developmental delay and minimal speech, early epilepsy, ataxia, feeding and growth problems, and later regression with loss of walking and independent feeding. Care is largely supportive with no specific treatment, leaving a major need for durable seizure control and disease modifying therapies, with gene replacement for SLC9A6 an emerging direction.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-targeted SLC9A6/NHE6 restoration (e.g., gene replacement/ASO) to prevent/attenuate regression (loss of ambulation and independent feeding)
- Seizure-focused therapy for very-early-onset mixed-seizure epilepsy aiming for seizure freedom/marked reduction in difficult-to-control cases
- Therapeutics improving oropharyngeal dysphagia/feeding dysfunction and motor/ataxia deficits to drive gains in nutrition/growth and sustained mobility

name: Fanconi syndrome
description: Fanconi syndrome is a rare proximal renal tubule reabsorption failure causing multi solute urinary wasting of glucose, phosphate, bicarbonate, amino acids and electrolytes, leading to polyuria, dehydration, metabolic acidosis and bone disease such as rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults. Treatment is mainly supportive replacement and removal of an offending cause when possible, but there is no curative therapy to reverse the tubular defect, leaving high treatment burden and ongoing risk of complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Proximal-tubule function–restoring therapies that reverse renal Fanconi syndrome (vs indefinite supportive electrolyte replacement)
- Bone/mineral regimens that correct hypophosphatemia/vitamin D deficiency while reducing nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis risk
- Lower-burden replacement strategies that cut 3–4×/day alkali/electrolyte dosing and GI side effects to improve adherence (esp. children)

name: GNE myopathy
description: GNE myopathy is a rare inherited skeletal muscle disease caused by reduced GNE enzyme activity and impaired sialic acid biosynthesis, typically starting in young adulthood with foot drop and gait instability with relative quadriceps sparing and progressing to widespread weakness and frequent wheelchair dependence within 10 to 20 years. Care is symptomatic only, creating a major unmet need for disease modifying therapies that durably preserve ambulation and upper limb independence, ideally supported by biomarkers showing restored muscle sialylation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Reduce early bilateral foot-drop–driven gait instability/falls by improving ankle dorsiflexion strength (LEC/6MWT benefit)
- Slow mid/late-stage upper-extremity functional decline to preserve independence (UEC, GNEM-FAS UE domain)
- Restore muscle sialylation with clear target-engagement biomarker gains that translate to functional stabilization

name: Currarino syndrome
description: Rare congenital spectrum disorder with anorectal malformations, sacral anomalies and a presacral mass, often presenting in infancy with refractory constipation or bowel obstruction plus urinary retention, incontinence and infections. Care is largely supportive and procedure heavy, so durable nonprocedural bowel and continence control and better management of neurogenic bladder remain major gaps, alongside improved tools to stratify presacral mass malignancy risk given limited biomarkers.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-procedural constipation control achieving regular spontaneous stools and preventing fecal impaction/obstruction with fewer diarrhea/cramps and lower infant dehydration/electrolyte risk (vs laxatives/enemas).
- Pharmacotherapy to reduce persistent fecal incontinence/soiling post-surgery and avoid escalation to ACE/antegrade enemas.
- Therapies to improve neurogenic bladder function and reduce recurrent UTIs to lower need for clean intermittent catheterization.

name: Dandy-Walker syndrome
description: Dandy-Walker malformation is a rare congenital posterior fossa brain malformation with abnormal cerebellar development, absent or small vermis, and enlarged fourth ventricle, often presenting in early infancy with hydrocephalus and macrocephaly causing motor delay and risk of seizures and intellectual disability. Care is largely surgical management of hydrocephalus and cysts, not disease correction, leaving major unmet need for durable, surgery sparing options given high shunt failure and revision rates.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Shunt/ETV-sparing pharmacotherapy for infants with Dandy‑Walker–associated hydrocephalus to avoid CSF-diversion surgery and reduce ~50% early failure/revision burden
- Adjunct anti-obstruction/anti-infective drug strategies to prevent shunt failure drivers (obstruction/infection) and reduce repeat neurosurgeries/hospitalizations
- Neurodevelopmental therapeutics beyond hydrocephalus control to improve cognition/motor coordination and better manage seizures in the 15–30% subgroup

name: DiGeorge syndrome
description: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion syndrome) is a congenital multisystem disorder typically presenting in infancy with congenital heart defects, recurrent infections from T cell immunodeficiency due to thymic hypoplasia, and hypocalcemia from parathyroid hypoplasia. Care is largely supportive and organ specific, with no cure, leaving major unmet needs for disease modifying approaches that prevent life threatening infections and metabolic crises and address long term neurodevelopmental and psychiatric morbidity including elevated schizophrenia risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable immune reconstitution for congenital athymia/complete DiGeorge to normalize naïve functional T cells and reduce serious infections vs chronic IVIG/antibiotic prophylaxis.
- Physiology-based hypoparathyroidism control that maintains stable serum calcium while reducing hypercalciuria/nephrocalcinosis/kidney stones vs calcium+calcitriol.
- 22q11.2DS-specific neuropsychiatric therapeutics that improve cognition/psychiatric outcomes using validated syndrome-specific endpoints vs off-label extrapolation.

name: Dressler's syndrome
description: Dressler syndrome is a rare, immune mediated late pericarditis occurring weeks after myocardial infarction or other cardiac injury, causing pleuritic chest pain, fever, dyspnea, and sometimes pericardial or pleural effusions that can mimic recurrent ischemia. Despite anti inflammatory therapy with aspirin, other nonsteroidal anti inflammatory drugs, and colchicine, management is constrained by recurrence risk and post infarct antithrombotic regimens, while corticosteroids are a last resort due to side effects and potential interference with cardiac healing, creating demand for safer steroid sparing, recurrence preventing immunomodulation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid/NSAID alternatives for post-PCI coronary-stented Dressler’s syndrome patients where high-dose aspirin poses bleeding/thrombotic concerns
- Steroid-sparing options for patients who cannot take aspirin/NSAIDs (e.g., GI bleed risk or on anticoagulants) to avoid corticosteroid-driven recurrence/chronicity
- Longer-acting recurrence-prevention beyond colchicine (e.g., IL-1–pathway agents) with less frequent dosing and longer disease-free intervals

name: Duane retraction syndrome
description: Duane retraction syndrome is a rare congenital, nonprogressive eye movement disorder caused by abnormal cranial nerve innervation, leading to limited horizontal eye movement, strabismus, compensatory head turns, and globe retraction with eyelid fissure narrowing on adduction. Management uses amblyopia treatment, prisms, and selective strabismus surgery to reduce misalignment and abnormal head posture, but current interventions cannot restore normal motility or fix the underlying innervation defect, leaving a major unmet need for durable neuromodulatory and developmental or genetic approaches that address miswiring and secondary muscle contracture biology.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Long-acting, titratable extraocular-muscle chemodenervation to improve primary-position deviation/abnormal head turn and reduce upshoot/downshoot without surgical diplopia risk.
- Disease-modifying neurodevelopmental/gene-targeted therapy (e.g., CHN1/MAFB-defined isolated DRS) to restore ocular motility across gaze positions by addressing the innervation defect.
- Local anti-fibrotic/contracture-modulating therapy for restrictive co-contraction (“leash phenomenon”) to reduce globe retraction and mechanical upshoot/downshoot.

name: Ehlers–Danlos syndrome
description: Ehlers Danlos syndromes are inherited connective tissue disorders causing joint hypermobility and instability with chronic pain, fatigue, dysautonomia and gastrointestinal dysfunction. Care is largely symptomatic with no cure or disease specific treatments, leaving major unmet needs for disease modifying therapies that improve stability and reduce pain and fatigue, better biology based diagnostics for hypermobile Ehlers Danlos syndrome, and proven prevention of catastrophic arterial events in vascular Ehlers Danlos syndrome.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Evidence-backed non-opioid therapies for hEDS/HSD that meaningfully reduce chronic pain and severe fatigue (vs reliance on OTC NSAIDs/analgesics).
- Disease-targeted treatments for hEDS that reduce atraumatic recurrent joint dislocations/subluxations and improve joint stability.
- Event-prevention pharmacotherapy for genetically confirmed vEDS that lowers risk of arterial rupture/dissection and other catastrophic vEDS-related events.

name: Lassa fever
description: Lassa fever is a rodent borne viral haemorrhagic fever endemic to West Africa that often begins as a non specific febrile illness but can rapidly progress to shock, multi organ failure, and death, with many survivors left with permanent hearing loss. Care is largely supportive with no approved antiviral and ribavirin limited by uncertain efficacy, time sensitive administration, toxicity, and pregnancy contraindications, leaving a major need for safe, easy to deploy oral treatments that reduce mortality and prevent long term sequelae.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pregnancy-safe antiviral for 3rd-trimester Lassa fever (where ribavirin is contraindicated).
- Oral, lower-toxicity antiviral that can replace inpatient IV ribavirin and improve hard outcomes (e.g., mortality).
- Therapy to prevent permanent post-acute hearing loss after Lassa infection.

name: Frey syndrome
description: Frey syndrome is a delayed post parotidectomy or parotid region trauma complication where misdirected auriculotemporal nerve regrowth triggers meal induced unilateral facial warmth, flushing, and sweating. Care is symptomatic with topical antiperspirants or anticholinergics and botulinum toxin injections, but effects often wear off with recurrence reported up to 27 percent at 1 year and 92 percent at 3 years, creating a high retreatment burden. Key needs include longer lasting lower burden treatments and better perioperative prevention for high risk surgical patients.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- More durable symptom control than botulinum toxin (target ≥18–24 months) to reduce repeat intradermal injections.
- Noninvasive topical/transdermal therapy with Botox-like efficacy but low application burden and minimal anticholinergic side effects/tolerance.
- Peri-operative pharmacologic prevention post-parotidectomy for high-risk patients to prevent Frey syndrome onset.

name: Friedreich ataxia
description: Friedreich ataxia is a childhood onset inherited neurodegenerative disorder caused by FXN GAA repeat expansions that reduce frataxin, leading to progressive ataxia, loss of mobility and frequent wheelchair dependence within about 10 years, alongside life limiting cardiomyopathy. Omaveloxolone can slow progression but does not stop disease and is not established for children under 16, leaving major unmet need for earlier disease modifying therapy and stronger cardiac protection to reduce heart failure and arrhythmia driven mortality.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy for symptomatic Friedreich ataxia patients <16 years (esp. ages 2–15) improving balance/upright stability over ~1 year
- Cardiomyopathy-targeted therapy reducing arrhythmia/heart-failure mortality and preserving/improving ejection fraction (incl. high-risk EF-decline subgroup)
- Neurofunctional therapy with larger/broader mFARS benefit than omaveloxolone, effective in lower-mobility/reduced-cardiac-function patients, with less dosing/monitoring burden

name: Gerstmann syndrome
description: Rare focal cognitive syndrome, often post stroke or parietal injury, causing agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and left right disorientation; care is etiology directed plus rehabilitation and compensatory tools, with no curative symptom targeted therapy and a need for neuroprotective and neurorestorative approaches to speed recovery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct neurorestorative drug to accelerate recovery of acalculia/agraphia during rehabilitation (reduce delayed acalculia recovery).
- Symptom-targeted pharmacotherapy that improves the Gerstmann tetrad directly, beyond treating the underlying lesion/etiology.
- Acute neuroprotective/lesion-repair therapy to limit parietal white-matter injury and prevent progression to a full disabling tetrad.
medlineUrl: No MedlinePlus health topic URL; redirects to https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/gerstmanns-syndrome

name: Gitelman syndrome
description: Gitelman syndrome is an inherited renal salt wasting tubulopathy caused by SLC12A3 defects in the thiazide sensitive sodium chloride cotransporter, leading to chronic potassium and magnesium loss with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, low blood pressure, and fatigue, cramps, weakness, and paresthesias. Management is largely lifelong salt plus oral potassium and magnesium, but gastrointestinal intolerance, pill burden, and hypotension risk from potassium sparing add ons limit adherence and symptom control, leaving a need for better tolerated electrolyte replacement and therapies that reduce ongoing salt wasting and arrhythmia and chondrocalcinosis risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
