- GI-tolerable, lower-pill-burden K/Mg replacement that reliably achieves target K ~3.0 mmol/L and Mg ~0.6 mmol/L without dose-limiting diarrhea/abdominal pain or gastric irritation/ulcers
- Add-on salt-wasting–reducing therapy for persistent symptomatic hypokalemia when supplements fail/intolerable, with durable K/Mg improvement and better long-term safety than K-sparing diuretics/RAS blockade/NSAIDs
- Treatments that improve patient-reported symptoms/QoL and prevent severe complications (e.g., ventricular arrhythmia/tetany, chronic chondrocalcinosis), given symptom burden may not track electrolyte levels and can worsen with age

name: Meckel's diverticulitis
description: Meckel’s diverticulitis is infection driven inflammation of a congenital ileal diverticulum that often mimics appendicitis with acute abdominal pain, vomiting, fever and sometimes peritonitis. Diagnosis is frequently missed until surgery, and treatment typically requires resection plus broad spectrum antibiotics in complicated cases. Key unmet needs include faster, more accurate diagnostics to avoid unnecessary operations, more selective surgery sparing approaches where safe, and perioperative and antimicrobial strategies that reduce wound infection, postoperative ileus, and antibiotic associated Clostridioides difficile risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Surgery-sparing medical therapy (bowel rest + antibiotics) for selected Meckel’s diverticulitis/microperforation patients
- Perioperative adjunct drugs to reduce post-resection complications (surgical site infection, postoperative ileus, anastomotic leak)
- Microbiome-sparing antibiotic regimens that maintain intra-abdominal coverage while minimizing C. difficile risk

name: Goldenhar syndrome
description: Goldenhar syndrome, or oculo auriculo vertebral spectrum, is a rare congenital disorder with abnormal development of the eye, ear, and spine, often causing hemifacial microsomia with facial asymmetry, microtia, ocular dermoids, and vertebral anomalies. Severe cases can impair feeding and breathing. Care is largely staged reconstructive surgery across childhood, with multiple operations under anesthesia and donor site morbidity such as rib cartilage harvest. A key unmet need is less invasive, durable reconstruction, with tissue engineered grafts and 3D printed scaffolds emerging to reduce reoperations.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Mandibular growth–restoring regenerative therapy for severe jaw hypoplasia/airway-risk patients to reduce OSA/airway interventions and avoid repeat jaw operations
- Single-stage, low-morbidity auricular reconstruction biologic/implant to avoid rib-cartilage harvest and reduce multi-stage microtia surgeries
- Durable injectable soft-tissue regenerative therapy to correct facial asymmetry/volume deficits with fewer repeat grafting procedures

name: HELLP syndrome
description: HELLP syndrome is a rapidly progressive, life threatening pregnancy complication and severe preeclampsia variant defined by hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets, often presenting in late pregnancy or shortly postpartum with right upper quadrant pain, malaise, and nausea or vomiting. Care is largely supportive, and delivery is the only definitive treatment, forcing high stakes maternal fetal tradeoffs in early preterm disease. The major unmet need is pregnancy safe, disease modifying therapy that can stabilize labs, prevent sudden deterioration, and safely prolong gestation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pregnancy-safe disease-modifying therapy for early preterm HELLP (≈23–30 weeks) that halts progression and meaningfully prolongs latency-to-delivery.
- Angiogenic-axis (sFlt-1/PlGF) targeting drugs (e.g., anti-sFlt-1/siRNA/small molecules) to stabilize very-preterm severe disease and extend gestation.
- Fast-acting therapy that reverses HELLP labs (platelets >100k; AST/ALT/LDH normalization) to reduce transfusions and shorten hospitalization.

name: Hartnup disease
description: Rare inherited amino acid transport disorder causing poor absorption of neutral amino acids and aminoaciduria with episodic childhood neurocutaneous attacks such as photosensitive rash, ataxia, and psychiatric symptoms, often triggered by illness, stress, fever, or poor diet; care is largely nutritional and supportive, leaving a need for more reliable prevention of trigger driven episodes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- SLC6A19/B0AT1 functional restoration in intestinal epithelium and proximal renal tubules to prevent pellagra-like photosensitivity, intermittent cerebellar ataxia, and psychiatric symptoms.
- Transporter-bypassing tryptophan repletion (e.g., tryptophan ethyl ester / peptide-based delivery leveraging intact di-/tripeptide absorption) to restore systemic/CSF tryptophan and reduce neuropsychiatric episodes.
- More convenient, better-tolerated prophylaxis to prevent trigger-driven attacks lasting 1–4 weeks (improving adherence vs twice-daily niacin/niacinamide; favor non-flushing options).

name: Helsmoortel-Van der Aa syndrome
description: Helsmoortel-Van der Aa syndrome, or ADNP syndrome, is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder usually caused by a de novo autosomal dominant ADNP variant, marked by infant hypotonia and early developmental delay that progresses to intellectual disability with severe speech and motor impairment including oral apraxia, plus behavioral dysregulation, sleep disturbance, and feeding and gastrointestinal problems. Treatment is supportive with no disease specific therapy, leaving major unmet need for ADNP targeted disease modification and therapies that measurably improve language, behavior, and sleep.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying ADNP restoration (e.g., ASO upregulation of ADNP protein from the healthy allele) to address haploinsufficiency vs symptomatic care only.
- Pharmacotherapy that reliably improves severely delayed/absent speech including oral apraxia, with standardized receptive/expressive language gains.
- Treatments that reduce ASD-related behavioral dysregulation and stabilize sleep, with measurable improvements on validated behavior and sleep scales.

name: Hirschsprung disease
description: Hirschsprung disease is a congenital absence of enteric nerves in the distal bowel causing neonatal functional obstruction with delayed meconium, abdominal distension, and bilious vomiting, with risk of life threatening Hirschsprung associated enterocolitis. Standard pull through surgery is not reliably curative, and many patients have persistent dysmotility, bowel dysfunction, and recurrent enterocolitis requiring irrigations and broad spectrum antibiotics. A key frontier is regenerative restoration of the enteric nervous system using cell based approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-antibiotic prophylaxis/early-intervention to prevent Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (HAEC) and reduce hospitalizations/need for frequent irrigations + IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
- Mechanism-based therapy for post–pull-through dysmotility to improve constipation/fecal incontinence and reduce reliance on enemas/irrigation
- Regenerative enteric nervous system (ENS) replacement (cell therapy or glia→neuron transdifferentiation) to restore enteric neurons and potentially avoid pull-through surgery

name: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
description: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is a rare inherited STK11 driven disorder with childhood onset mucocutaneous pigmentation and hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps that cause bleeding anemia abdominal pain and recurrent obstruction or intussusception often requiring repeated endoscopy or surgery. Patients also face markedly elevated lifetime cancer risk. Management is surveillance and procedures rather than disease modification, leaving unmet need for safe chronic therapies that prevent small bowel polyp regrowth reduce cancer risk and cut the burden of frequent endoscopy and bowel resection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical suppression of small-bowel hamartomatous polyp growth to prevent childhood obstruction/intussusception and reduce repeated laparotomy/bowel resection.
- Chemoprevention that materially lowers PJS lifetime cancer risk to reduce cancer morbidity/mortality and the intensity of lifelong multi-organ surveillance.
- Safe chronic (ideally oral) therapy that reduces overall GI polyp burden enough to extend/simplify frequent invasive surveillance and avoid high-burden enteroscopy/surgery.

name: IgA vasculitis
description: IgA vasculitis is an immune mediated small vessel vasculitis, usually in children after an upper respiratory infection, causing palpable purpura with joint and abdominal pain and sometimes kidney inflammation with hematuria or proteinuria. Most cases self resolve, but nephritis is the long term threat and current management leans on corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants with meaningful side effects. The clinical premium is steroid sparing, mechanism based therapy that reduces proteinuria and preserves kidney function, including kidney directed anti inflammatory approaches and targeting complement and B cell pathways.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Terminal-complement (C5) blockade for IgA vasculitis nephritis (IgAVN) to reduce proteinuria/UPCR and preserve eGFR vs broad immunosuppression.
- Once-daily oral, steroid-sparing renoprotection to achieve durable proteinuria remission in pediatric IgAV with proteinuric glomerular disease.
- Disease-modifying therapy that reduces pathogenic IgA immune-complex formation in IgAVN (e.g., BLyS/APRIL pathway inhibition) with renal proteinuria endpoints.

name: Japanese encephalitis
description: Japanese encephalitis is a mosquito-borne viral brain infection in Asia and the western Pacific, mainly affecting children in rural agricultural areas. Once encephalitis develops, patients can deteriorate quickly with seizures, with 20 to 30 percent mortality and 30 to 50 percent of survivors left with serious long-term neurologic or psychiatric disability. Treatment remains supportive with no specific antiviral, creating a premium for post-onset antivirals and neuroprotective approaches. Prevention exists but is hard to deploy at scale because the inactivated vaccine requires two doses (day 0 and day 28) and refrigerated storage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Post-onset acute JE therapy (direct-acting antiviral/neutralizing biologic with CNS penetration) to cut ~30% encephalitis case-fatality beyond supportive care
- Adjunct neuroprotective/anti-inflammatory treatment to reduce long-term neurologic/cognitive/behavioral sequelae in survivors
- Single-visit/rapid-immunity, temperature-stable JE prophylaxis to replace the 2-dose/28-day series and refrigerated cold-chain constraints

name: Kallmann syndrome
description: Rare developmental genetic disorder causing congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia or hyposmia, leading to absent or delayed puberty and often infertility; managed with sex steroid replacement, but fertility typically requires complex, costly gonadotropin or pulsatile gonadotropin-releasing hormone regimens with adherence challenges, and there is no treatment for anosmia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-specific olfactory restoration for congenital anosmia/hyposmia in Kallmann syndrome
- Lower-burden, lower-cost fertility induction (esp. male spermatogenesis) that avoids prolonged, high-cost hCG+FSH/hMG regimens
- HPG-axis restoring therapy that reduces/eliminates lifelong sex-steroid replacement and avoids the “virilization vs fertility” tradeoff (without a lifestyle-interfering GnRH pump)

name: Kartagener syndrome
description: Kartagener syndrome is primary ciliary dyskinesia with situs inversus, where dysfunctional motile cilia impair mucus clearance causing neonatal respiratory distress and lifelong chronic wet cough, nasal and sinus disease, recurrent infections and bronchiectasis, plus frequent male infertility. Care is supportive and burdensome with airway clearance, repeated antibiotics, and vaccinations, and diagnosis is often delayed. The central unmet need is disease modifying therapy that restores ciliary function to prevent progressive lung damage and reduce infection and treatment burden, with early approaches such as inhaled messenger ribonucleic acid aiming to rescue ciliary activity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying ciliary rescue for genetically defined Kartagener/PCD subgroups (e.g., DNAI1 LoF) via inhaled gene/mRNA replacement to restore mucociliary clearance.
- Well-tolerated mucociliary-clearance/lung-function pharmacotherapy (e.g., ENaC modulation) to reduce reliance on daily airway clearance and irritant hypertonic-saline nebulization.
- Exacerbation-prevention comparable to azithromycin but with improved tolerability (less GI AEs) and reduced chronic antibiotic exposure.

name: Kawasaki disease
description: Kawasaki disease is an acute inflammatory vasculitis in infants and young children, presenting with at least 5 days of high fever and mucocutaneous signs. The main clinical urgency is preventing coronary artery inflammation and aneurysms, which can create lifelong cardiovascular risk. Standard first line intravenous immunoglobulin plus aspirin reduces but does not eliminate coronary complications, and 10 to 20 percent of children are refractory, often requiring repeat intravenous immunoglobulin with safety and logistical burdens including dose dependent hemolytic anemia. Key unmet needs include better early risk stratification and faster, more targeted rescue therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Upfront IVIG + adjunct anti-inflammatory therapy for children identified at diagnosis as high risk for coronary artery aneurysm (CAA), to further reduce CAA vs IVIG alone.
- Rapid “rescue” therapy for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease (~10–20% with persistent/recrudescent fever after IVIG) to stop fever quickly and lower subsequent CAA risk.
- Second-line alternative to repeat IVIG that lowers hemolysis risk and care burden (e.g., less hemolytic anemia, shorter infusion/hospital stay).

name: Klippel-Feil syndrome
description: Klippel-Feil syndrome is a rare congenital disorder marked by fusion of two or more cervical vertebrae, often presenting with a short neck, low posterior hairline, and restricted neck motion plus associated skeletal and sensory anomalies. Patients can develop chronic headaches and neck muscle pain, and cervical instability can increase spinal cord injury risk. Treatment is supportive, centered on physical therapy and symptomatic pain management, with surgery for selected complications, but there is no cure. Key unmet needs include durable non-opioid pain control, better prevention of neurologic injury, and genotype-informed approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, non-opioid control of chronic KFS neck pain/headaches and muscle spasm (incl. degenerative disk/pinched-nerve pain)
- Neuroprotective/anti-myelopathy therapy for KFS patients with cervical instability/stenosis at high spinal-cord injury risk
- Genotype-directed disease-modifying therapy targeting implicated developmental pathways (e.g., GDF6) for early-identified familial cases

name: Optic neuropathy | Leber hereditary
description: Rare inherited mitochondrial optic neuropathy causing rapid sequential bilateral central vision loss, often in teens or 20s and more common in males, frequently leading to legal blindness; there is no therapy that reliably halts or reverses vision loss (idebenone helps only some), creating a short window to protect the fellow eye and a major need for disease-modifying and vision-restoring treatments such as gene therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute-stage neuroprotection to prevent rapid fellow-eye conversion and preserve central visual acuity
- Vision-restoring therapy for established/chronic LHON (esp. MT‑ND4 G11778A cases with very low spontaneous recovery)
- More convenient/better-tolerated alternative to idebenone with less burdensome dosing/food requirements/monitoring and greater vision improvement

name: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease
description: Legg Calvé Perthes disease is a rare childhood hip disorder in which temporary loss of blood supply to the femoral head causes avascular necrosis and a multi year course where the weakened bone can collapse and heal misshapen, leading to limping, activity related groin or thigh or knee pain and limited hip motion. Care is largely symptomatic and biomechanical with activity restriction, physical therapy and sometimes casting or osteotomy, but there is no proven disease modifying therapy to prevent collapse or speed healing, leaving many at risk of adult hip arthritis and eventual hip replacement.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent femoral-head collapse/deformity during fragmentation in high-risk children (e.g., >50% head involvement/older age), improving sphericity (Stulberg I–II).
- Disease-modifying anti-inflammatory therapy beyond NSAIDs (e.g., IL‑1β/TNF‑α pathways) to improve pain, function and activity.
- Therapies that accelerate revascularization/healing to shorten the multi-year disease course and reduce later arthritis/hip-replacement risk.

name: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome
description: Severe childhood-onset epilepsy (usually before age 4) marked by tonic and atonic drop seizures with high injury risk plus progressive cognitive, developmental, and behavioral impairment; seizures are often drug-resistant despite polytherapy, making seizure freedom rare and driving need for safer, simpler regimens that reliably prevent drop attacks without worsening neurodevelopment.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Seizure-freedom–level control, especially elimination of drop attacks, in treatment‑resistant pediatric LGS
- Cognitive/developmental and behavioral improvement (or seizure control without cognitive/behavioral worsening)
- Safer, simpler regimens that reduce polytherapy burden and drop‑seizure injury risk

name: Leigh syndrome
description: Rare infant-onset mitochondrial neurometabolic disease causing rapid progressive neurodegeneration, feeding and swallowing impairment, and high risk of aspiration and respiratory failure with death often within 2 to 3 years; no definitive disease-modifying treatment beyond supportive vitamins, nutrition, and respiratory care, creating a major need for therapies that preserve function and prevent respiratory and feeding crises, with genotype-targeted gene therapy an emerging frontier.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy showing clinically meaningful stabilization/improvement on validated severity + function scales (e.g., NPMDS Sections 1–3; GMFM) in pediatric mtDNA-Leigh patients with measurable motor impairment.
- Therapy that reduces respiratory morbidity/mortality (improves oxygenation; prevents escalation to tracheostomy/ventilatory support; reduces ventilator/ICU days and pneumonia events) in high-risk children.
- Pediatric-friendly chronic drug that lowers real-world care burden (fewer devices/appointments/supportive add-ons) and is usable in dysphagia/feeding-tube patients, with better acceptability/palatability and caregiver-burden outcomes.

name: Loeffler syndrome
description: Rare, self limited eosinophilic lung reaction with mild or absent symptoms such as dry cough, wheeze, shortness of breath and fever plus migratory lung opacities and blood eosinophilia that typically resolves within a month. Management is largely supportive and trigger focused with antiparasitics and sometimes systemic steroids, but care is constrained by the need for steroid sparing options when Strongyloides is possible and by gaps in safe, effective deworming for pregnancy and small children.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing rapid control of severe respiratory symptoms to reduce systemic glucocorticoid exposure (esp. where occult Strongyloides risk exists)
- Pregnancy- and <15 kg pediatric-safe oral Strongyloides-active therapy/formulation as an alternative to ivermectin limitations
- Higher-efficacy short-course broad-spectrum deworming regimens that reliably clear hookworm + Strongyloides (incl. overcoming low single-dose benzimidazole efficacy/resistance)

name: MELAS syndrome
description: MELAS syndrome is a progressive multisystem mitochondrial disease, usually starting in childhood after normal development, that primarily affects the brain and muscles with headaches, vomiting, seizures, and stroke-like episodes causing focal deficits and visual changes. Most cases stem from mitochondrial DNA variants such as MT-TL1 that impair cellular energy production. Care is largely supportive with no cure or proven disease modifying therapy, and even commonly used supplements and arginine strategies lack randomized trial validation, leaving major unmet need for evidence based treatments that prevent or blunt neurologic crises and slow progression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- RCT-proven acute + preventive therapy for MELAS stroke-like episodes that reduces severity/neurologic sequelae and recurrence beyond low-evidence IV/oral L-arginine regimens.
- Therapy that meaningfully improves disabling fatigue and functional mobility/strength in adult m.3243A>G MELAS (e.g., Neuro‑QoL Fatigue and 5x sit‑to‑stand).
- Mitochondria-safe seizure control for drug-resistant MELAS epilepsy/SLE-associated seizures that avoids valproate toxicity while reducing seizure frequency/status epilepticus risk.

name: Spinocerebellar ataxia | type 3
description: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (Machado Joseph disease) is a rare, dominantly inherited neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG repeat expansion in ATXN3 that typically begins in mid adulthood with progressive gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria and eye movement problems, later complicated by dysphagia with aspiration risk and frequent eventual wheelchair dependence. Care is largely symptomatic, with no therapies proven to slow progression, and common antispasticity drugs can worsen sedation or swallowing, leaving a premium on disease modifying approaches such as safely lowering mutant ATXN3 while preserving function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying ATXN3-expansion–targeting therapy to slow/halt progression in genetically confirmed SCA3, ideally with lower procedure burden than lumbar intrathecal bolus dosing.
- Oral symptomatic therapy that improves/stabilizes core ataxia disability (gait/stance/speech) on validated scales (SARA/f‑SARA) in ambulatory SCA3.
- Dysphagia/aspiration-focused therapeutics that reduce aspiration pneumonia risk without adding swallow/breathing risk or sedation/dizziness that worsens falls.

name: Marfan syndrome
description: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder with skeletal and ocular features, but the major clinical risk is progressive aortic aneurysm and dissection. Care relies on serial imaging, beta blockers, and prophylactic aortic root surgery, yet substantial residual cardiovascular risk persists and options narrow in pregnancy because angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated. Other burdens such as dural ectasia related pain are largely managed symptomatically, underscoring the need for safer disease modifying aortic protection and better treatments for chronic complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Whole-aorta disease control beyond beta‑blocker/ARB therapy (meaningfully reduce annual aortic-root enlargement trajectory to defer prophylactic intervention and lessen high-intensity surveillance)
- Pregnancy-compatible aortic protection that avoids teratogenic ACEi/ARB risk and beta‑blocker fetal-growth concerns while controlling pregnancy/postpartum aortic dilation/dissection risk
- Disease-targeted therapy for symptomatic dural ectasia (pain and postural headaches) beyond symptomatic analgesics

name: Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome
description: Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome is a congenital absence or underdevelopment of the uterus and upper vagina, typically diagnosed in adolescence when normal puberty is followed by primary amenorrhea and infertility. Management is largely procedural, with first line daily vaginal dilation that can be painful and distressing, and surgery still requiring ongoing dilation to prevent neovaginal stenosis. Family building relies on gestational surrogacy, while uterus transplantation remains constrained by the risks and burden of immunosuppression, creating demand for more tolerable, durable anatomic and reproductive solutions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Immunosuppression-sparing/tolerance-inducing adjunct therapeutics for uterus transplantation to enable livebirth while reducing calcineurin/antimetabolite exposure.
- Local/topical pharmacologic adjuncts to first-line vaginal dilation that reduce urinary symptoms/bleeding/pain and shorten the daily time burden.
- Local anti-stenosis/anti-fibrotic therapies to prevent neovaginal stenosis/contracture after vaginoplasty and reduce postoperative dilation dependence.

name: Schwannoma | vestibular
description: Vestibular schwannoma is a benign, usually slow growing tumor on the hearing and balance nerves that causes one sided hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance and is often missed for years. Management is observation, radiation, or surgery, but treating the tumor can injure hearing or facial nerves and worsen function. A key unmet need is a hearing preserving drug that durably controls tumor growth with less burden and toxicity than intravenous bevacizumab.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Tumor-growth–slowing drug for refractory/high-risk vestibular schwannoma where surgery/radiosurgery is high-risk or insufficient (differentiate on objective tumor-control endpoints).
- Hearing/cranial-nerve–preserving medical therapy for small sporadic tumors with serviceable hearing (differentiate on maintaining useful hearing and minimizing facial-nerve morbidity).
- Durable, safer, lower-burden alternative to IV bevacizumab for progressive NF2-associated vestibular schwannoma to sustain hearing response and achieve ≥20% volumetric shrinkage with less toxicity and less frequent dosing.

name: Von Willebrand disease | acquired
description: Acquired von Willebrand syndrome is a rare adult onset bleeding disorder that mimics inherited von Willebrand disease but arises secondary to underlying conditions such as lymphoproliferative or myeloproliferative disorders and high shear cardiovascular states like aortic stenosis and left ventricular assist devices. Patients develop new mucocutaneous and often angiodysplasia associated gastrointestinal bleeding with disproportionate procedure related bleeding. Standard therapies such as desmopressin, von Willebrand factor concentrates, and intravenous immunoglobulin can be short lived or ineffective in some subtypes, making durable hemostasis difficult unless the underlying driver can be removed.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable (multi-day) hemostasis for MGUS-associated AVWS (esp. IgG-MGUS) despite rapid post-treatment VWF loss
- An IgM-MGUS–effective alternative to IVIG for AVWS (when IVIG fails)
- Sustained prevention of recurrent angiodysplasia/GI bleeding in high-shear AVWS (Heyde syndrome/LVAD) with lower thromboembolic risk and reduced infusion burden

name: Muenke syndrome
description: Muenke syndrome is an autosomal dominant FGFR3 driven craniosynostosis, usually premature coronal suture fusion that distorts infant head and face shape and can cause strabismus and sensorineural hearing loss. Care is largely symptom focused and still primarily surgical in early infancy, sometimes with helmet therapy, with risks like increased intracranial pressure, re-synostosis, and repeat operations plus ongoing burden from ear infections and hearing aid dependence. A key unmet need is early biology based therapy to prevent fusion and re-synostosis and protect hearing.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-life, mutation-targeted therapy to normalize FGFR3 overactivity and prevent/delay coronal suture fusion, reducing/avoiding cranial surgery and prolonged helmeting.
- Adjunct peri-/post-operative medical therapy to reduce postoperative ICP/hydrocephalus risk and re-synostosis/recurrent deformity after craniosynostosis repair.
- Disease-targeted otologic therapy to prevent/reverse sensorineural hearing loss and reduce recurrent ear infections/need for myringotomy tubes.

name: Acute myeloid leukemia | myelomonocytic
description: Acute myelomonocytic leukemia is an aggressive, rapidly progressive subtype of acute myeloid leukemia that mainly affects older adults and presents over weeks with marrow failure causing fatigue, infections, and bleeding. It often spreads outside the marrow, with frequent gum and skin infiltration. Frontline lower intensity therapy for unfit patients, such as venetoclax plus azacitidine, is less effective in monocytic biology, and relapse can be quickly fatal. The largest gap is effective treatment after venetoclax based regimen failure, where median survival is about 2.3 months.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Post–VEN+HMA failure rescue for monocytic AML by targeting venetoclax resistance (BCL2↓/MCL1↑ survival shift)
- Therapies with proven clearance/control of extramedullary disease sites common in M4/M5 (e.g., gingiva/oral soft tissue, skin/leukemia cutis)
- Outpatient-feasible regimens with materially better safety/tolerability vs intensive chemo and VEN+AZA (reduce prolonged hospitalization, febrile neutropenia/serious AEs)

name: Acute proliferative glomerulonephritis
description: Immune complex mediated kidney inflammation typically occurring 1 to 2 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis or 3 to 4 weeks after skin infection, presenting in children with dark cola colored urine, periorbital edema, proteinuria, and new hypertension. Management is largely supportive with no disease specific therapy, and rare severe cases require short term dialysis. Key unmet needs are disease modifying immunomodulation guided by complement biology and durable renoprotection, especially for higher risk adults and high burden Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course terminal complement inhibition (e.g., anti‑C5) for severe crescentic/oliguric PSGN to avoid dialysis and improve full renal recovery.
- Non‑steroid targeted immunomodulators to shorten persistent microscopic hematuria/proteinuria and speed weaning off antihypertensives.
- Long-term renoprotective therapy to prevent CKD/hypertension after PSGN in high‑risk groups (adults; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients).

name: Mycobacterium avium complex disease
description: Pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex disease is a slow growing chronic lung infection, often presenting as nodular bronchiectasis in thin older nonsmoking women or fibrocavitary disease in patients with underlying lung damage, causing persistent cough, dyspnea, fatigue, and weight loss. Diagnosis is often delayed and treatment requires months to years of multidrug therapy with substantial toxicity and drug interactions, typically continuing for 12 months after sputum culture conversion. Even after apparent success, recurrence is common at roughly 10 to 48 percent, driving demand for shorter, better tolerated regimens and strategies to prevent relapse.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Higher durable sputum-culture conversion for treatment‑refractory and macrolide‑resistant pulmonary MAC vs current salvage options
- Maintenance/prophylactic (recurrence-prevention) therapy for nodular‑bronchiectatic MAC-PD post successful treatment
- Safer, lower-burden regimen (ideally all‑oral, shorter-course) reducing toxicity/monitoring and avoiding device-dependent inhaled salvage

name: NARP syndrome
description: NARP syndrome is a maternally inherited mitochondrial DNA disorder, often due to MT-ATP6 Complex V point mutations (eg 8993 variants), that starts in childhood or early adulthood and progressively causes sensory neuropathy with weakness, ataxia, and retinal degeneration leading to vision loss and disability. Care is largely symptomatic with no proven disease modifying therapy, leaving major unmet needs for genotype targeted restoration of mitochondrial bioenergetics, retina directed vision preservation, and better tolerated control of dystonia and neuropathic pain.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-targeted mitochondrial bioenergetic restoration for MT-ATP6 m.8993T>G severe-phenotype NARP to improve functional outcomes (e.g., NMDAS) and prevent progression to wheelchair dependence.
- Retina-directed therapy to slow pigmentary retinopathy/retinitis pigmentosa and preserve vision (prevent blindness).
- Better-tolerated dystonia/spasticity/neuropathic-symptom control that reduces CNS/anticholinergic adverse effects and AE-driven discontinuation vs trihexyphenidyl/baclofen/gabapentin.

name: O’nyong-nyong fever
description: O’nyong-nyong fever is an Anopheles mosquito transmitted alphavirus infection endemic to sub-Saharan Africa that causes abrupt high fever with often crippling joint pain, rash, lymphadenopathy and conjunctivitis, sometimes leaving prolonged post acute arthralgia. It is usually self limiting but can briefly immobilize patients and strains outpatient care during outbreaks. With no effective vaccines or antivirals and management largely supportive, key unmet needs are rapid diagnosis, early outpatient therapeutics to shorten illness and prevent lingering joint disability, and scalable prevention through vaccination or passive immunization.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early outpatient antiviral to suppress ONNV replication and shorten acute febrile illness/“crippling” arthralgia
- Recovery-phase therapy for patients with persistent post-acute arthralgia to improve pain and function over weeks–months
- Single-dose (or infrequent) neutralizing mAb for post-exposure prophylaxis/very-early treatment to prevent joint/muscle dissemination and reduce disease

name: Oropouche fever
description: Emerging arboviral febrile illness in the Americas spread mainly by biting midges, causing abrupt fever with severe headache and myalgias and arthralgias and frequent relapse. Management is supportive only with no specific antivirals or vaccines, leaving major unmet needs for early outpatient antivirals and effective, pregnancy safe prevention amid concerns about neuroinvasive disease and adverse fetal outcomes including miscarriage and microcephaly.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early outpatient antiviral to shorten acute illness and prevent relapse/recurrence
- Pregnancy-safe treatment/prophylaxis to prevent vertical transmission and adverse fetal outcomes
- Vaccine or long-acting passive immunization to prevent severe complications (incl. CNS disease)

name: PFAPA syndrome
description: PFAPA is a pediatric periodic fever syndrome starting around ages 2 to 5 with sudden high fevers lasting 3 to 7 days every 3 to 6 weeks plus sore throat, mouth ulcers, and cervical lymphadenitis, with normal health and growth between flares. Care is episodic and inconsistent. Steroids can abort attacks but may shorten intervals and carry side effects, preventive drugs help only a minority, and tonsillectomy is effective for many but timing is unclear, leaving a need for predictable steroid sparing durable medical remission.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing flare-abort therapy that rapidly controls symptoms without shortening fever-free intervals/increasing attack frequency.
- High-response prophylaxis that prevents recurrent episodes in most children (beyond low/inconsistent cimetidine/colchicine benefit) with a defined treatment duration.
- Convenient, durable control/remission for frequent-flare children (e.g., >4 flares/2 months) achieving ≥50% flare reduction or zero attacks with minimal treatment burden/avoiding tonsillectomy.

name: Pelger-Huet anomaly
description: Pelger Huët anomaly is a benign, usually asymptomatic inherited neutrophil nuclear segmentation variant, often found incidentally on blood smear. The main unmet need is diagnostic clarity because similar hyposegmented neutrophils can be acquired in myelodysplastic syndromes, infections, or drug exposure, and misinterpretation can trigger unnecessary invasive workups including bone marrow procedures.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Pendred syndrome
description: Pendred syndrome is an inherited disorder causing early childhood, often fluctuating, progressive sensorineural hearing loss with enlarged vestibular aqueduct and possible vestibular delay, plus goiter developing from late childhood to early adulthood. Care is largely supportive with hearing aids, cochlear implantation, thyroid hormone as needed, and trigger avoidance, with no disease modifying therapy to prevent sudden drops or preserve inner ear function. A key frontier is biologic restoration of pendrin in the inner ear, supported by preclinical gene delivery studies showing hearing rescue in animal models.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable inner-ear pendrin (SLC26A4) restoration (e.g., early gene therapy) to prevent progressive/fluctuating hearing loss in infants/young children with early severe–profound SNHL
- On-demand/prophylactic therapy to reduce acute “attack” episodes of fluctuating hearing loss (lower attack frequency / preserve hearing), including after head injury/barotrauma triggers
- Thyroid-directed therapy to prevent/reduce enlarging euthyroid goiter burden arising in late childhood/early adulthood

name: Phelan-McDermid syndrome
description: Phelan McDermid syndrome (22q13.3 deletion, often SHANK3 loss) is a rare early onset neurodevelopmental disorder marked by neonatal hypotonia, global developmental delay, moderate to profound intellectual disability, and absent or severely delayed speech, often with autism related social communication impairment plus epilepsy and sleep disturbance. Care is largely symptomatic with no disease modifying therapy, leaving a premium on durable, measurable gains in functional communication, social engagement, and adaptive functioning while reducing seizure burden and medication complexity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Receptive/functional communication gains (e.g., Vineland-3 receptive communication raw-score improvement) in 3–12-year-old SHANK3-confirmed PMS patients.
- Treatments that reduce ASD-linked social withdrawal (ABC–Social Withdrawal) with fewer tolerability/monitoring burdens than current polypharmacy.
- Safer, PMS-relevant seizure control strategies for the >60% with epilepsy, reducing antiseizure-medication burden.

name: Poland syndrome
description: Poland syndrome is a rare congenital disorder with unilateral underdevelopment or absence of chest muscles, often the pectoralis major, with variable chest wall and limb anomalies. Mild cases may not be noticed until puberty when asymmetry becomes apparent. While many patients have limited functional impairment, the cosmetic and psychosocial burden is substantial. Management is largely individualized and surgery-focused rather than disease modifying, and reconstructive choices are difficult to standardize due to highly variable anatomy and limited evidence, driving interest in more tailored approaches such as custom-made implants.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Legionellosis | Pontiac fever
description: Pontiac fever is a mild, nonpneumonic form of legionellosis acquired by inhaling aerosolized water contaminated with Legionella, causing a brief influenza-like illness with fever, headache, and myalgias that starts within hours to 3 days and typically resolves in 2 to 5 days without specific therapy. The key unmet needs are practical rather than therapeutic, namely rapid outbreak detection and prevention through robust building and water system controls and monitoring.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid symptom-abortive therapy that shortens time-to-fever/myalgia/headache resolution vs the usual 2–5 days (<1 week)
- Post-exposure prophylaxis in outbreak settings to prevent symptom onset within hours–3 days after exposure
- Targeted therapy for rare higher-risk/atypical presentations (e.g., immunocompromised) to reduce complications beyond supportive care

name: Potocki-Lupski syndrome
description: Potocki Lupski syndrome is a rare chromosome 17p11.2 duplication disorder driven largely by RAI1 gene dosage, typically recognized in infancy with hypotonia and dysphagia causing feeding problems and failure to thrive, sometimes alongside congenital heart disease. As children grow, many develop developmental delay with moderate intellectual disability and significant neurobehavioral burden including attention and anxiety symptoms or autism spectrum disorder. Care today is multidisciplinary supportive management, so families and clinicians lack therapies that meaningfully improve feeding, sleep, and long term neurodevelopment by addressing the underlying gene dosage biology.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- RAI1-dosage–normalizing therapy for genetically confirmed 17p11.2 duplications to improve cognitive/language deficits and moderate intellectual disability.
- Pharmacotherapy for infant hypotonia-associated oropharyngeal dysphagia to prevent failure to thrive and reduce tube-feeding dependence.
- Targeted medications for PTLS neuropsychiatric morbidity (anxiety/ADHD/ASD behaviors) to improve functioning beyond screening/referral.

name: Prader-Willi syndrome
description: Rare genetic multisystem neuroendocrine disorder that shifts from infant hypotonia and feeding difficulty to childhood-onset hyperphagia causing chronic overeating, obesity, and complications; families often need constant food security and supervision, while care remains largely symptom-directed with major unmet need for durable treatments that meaningfully reduce hyperphagia, neurobehavioral symptoms, and excessive daytime sleepiness.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacologic suppression of hyperphagia/food-seeking that reduces reliance on locked food environments/constant supervision and improves HQ-CT plus food-security measures and weight/body-fat outcomes.
- Treatments that reduce core neurobehavioral symptoms (anxiety, temper outbursts/rigidity, obsessive-compulsive behaviors) with measurable improvements on standardized behavior scales.
- Therapies for excessive daytime sleepiness (± cataplexy-related burden) with improvement on sleepiness/functional impairment endpoints (e.g., PROMIS-SRI, ESS-CHAD).

name: Variant angina
description: Variant (vasospastic) angina is recurrent ischemic chest pain caused by transient coronary artery spasm, often in patients with normal-appearing coronary arteries between episodes. Attacks typically occur at rest overnight or early morning, last 5 to 30 minutes, show transient ST-segment changes, and respond to nitroglycerin. Calcium channel blockers are first line, but 10 to 15 percent remain refractory and chronic nitrate use is limited by tolerance, uncertain long-term outcomes, and poor efficacy in microvascular disease, leaving ongoing risk of myocardial infarction and fatal arrhythmias.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral chronic therapy for the ~10% refractory vasospastic/variant angina patients symptomatic despite CCB + nitrate, reducing attack frequency/nitroglycerin use and avoiding recurrent IV nitroglycerin hospital admissions
- Therapies specifically developed/tested for the microvascular-spasm endotype where nitrates are less effective and no therapies have been evaluated
- Nitrate-sparing long-term prophylaxis that improves hard outcomes (cardiac death/ACS/arrhythmias), not just symptom control, given nitrate tolerance and unclear prognostic benefit

name: Ramsay Hunt syndrome
description: Ramsay Hunt syndrome, or herpes zoster oticus, is a shingles complication where varicella zoster virus inflames the facial nerve near the ear, causing severe ear pain, vesicular rash, and sudden one sided facial paralysis often with vertigo or hearing changes. Outcomes depend on diagnosis and antivirals within about 72 hours, yet even prompt treatment can leave lasting synkinesis, postherpetic neuralgia, facial dysfunction, and permanent hearing loss, highlighting the need for faster recognition and therapies that truly rescue facial nerve function and protect hearing and balance.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Facial-nerve rescue to improve complete recovery and reduce synkinesis/permanent paralysis in patients presenting >72 hours after symptom onset.
- Cochleovestibular protection/restoration to prevent persistent hearing loss/tinnitus/vertigo (± hyperacusis).
- Prevention (not just symptomatic control) of postherpetic neuralgia/persistent neuropathic pain.

name: Rett syndrome
description: Rett syndrome is a rare neurodevelopmental brain disorder affecting almost exclusively girls, usually caused by MECP2 mutations. After 6 to 18 months of typical early development, children regress with loss of language and purposeful hand use, stereotyped hand movements, and major functional impairment often compounded by seizures and irregular breathing. Care remains largely symptomatic and the only approved therapy, trofinetide, adds dosing burden and frequent gastrointestinal side effects and weight loss, leaving a premium on better tolerated symptom control, treatments that normalize breathing, and carefully dose controlled MECP2 restoring approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Better-tolerated, lower-burden global-symptom therapy than trofinetide (less GI toxicity/discontinuation; simpler than weight-based BID liquid dosing).
- Drugs that specifically reduce Rett breathing dysautonomia (apneas/hyperventilation–hypoventilation cycling) with validated breathing endpoints.
- MECP2-directed disease-modifying gene/RNA therapies with tight dosage control to avoid MECP2 overexpression toxicity.

name: Rh isoimmunization
description: Rh isoimmunization is a maternal fetal blood group incompatibility where maternal antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal red cells, causing hemolytic disease with fetal anemia, hydrops, and neonatal jaundice with kernicterus risk. Despite routine prenatal screening, prevention still relies on donor plasma anti D immune globulin with supply constraints, and severe cases often require invasive intrauterine transfusions with procedural risk. After birth, some infants still need exchange transfusions and the role of intravenous immune globulin remains uncertain, leaving demand for safer, scalable prophylaxis and noninvasive therapies that prevent fetal anemia and reduce intensive neonatal interventions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Maternal therapy for high-risk pregnancies that prevents fetal anemia and avoids invasive rescue (no fetal loss/IUT/hydrops/neonatal death)
- Non–human-plasma-derived anti‑D prophylaxis (recombinant/monoclonal) to ensure reliable 28‑week + postpartum protection during RhIg shortages with low alloimmunization rates
- Neonatal therapy that reduces need for exchange transfusion (esp. severe hemolysis/rapidly rising bilirubin) given ET risks and lack of support for routine IVIG

name: SAPHO syndrome
description: SAPHO syndrome is a rare inflammatory disorder linking painful sterile bone and joint inflammation with skin disease, typically anterior chest wall and sternoclavicular arthritis alongside palmoplantar pustulosis or severe acne. It is often misdiagnosed as infection, driving delayed, burdensome workups. With no randomized trials and no agreed standard of care, patients cycle through off label anti inflammatories, immunomodulators, bisphosphonates, and biologics with variable benefit, and treatments that relieve bone pain can worsen skin disease, leaving a major need for reliable diagnosis and disease modifying, dual skin and bone control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- RCT-validated therapy for refractory osteoarticular SAPHO achieving ≥50% improvement in pain/global VAS in patients symptomatic despite NSAIDs/csDMARDs
- Single agent that concurrently controls bone and skin disease (PPP/acne) without paradoxical cutaneous reactions
- Safer, monitoring-light outpatient alternative to off-label regimens relying on chronic NSAIDs plus IV bisphosphonates and immunosuppressive DMARDs/biologics

name: SATB2-associated syndrome
description: SATB2-associated syndrome is a rare early onset genetic neurodevelopmental disorder caused by reduced SATB2 function, leading to moderate to profound developmental delay or intellectual disability with delayed or absent speech, plus palatal and dental anomalies, hypotonia and feeding difficulties, and behavioral dysregulation including aggression, autistic tendencies, and sleep problems. Care is supportive and multidisciplinary with early intensive speech and feeding therapy and augmentative and alternative communication, sometimes requiring gastrostomy tubes, leaving major unmet need for pediatric safe disease modifying treatments that improve communication and feeding and reduce irritability and sleep disruption.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early (infancy/early-childhood) disease-modifying SATB2 restoration/activation to drive meaningful expressive-communication gains (spoken words and/or independent AAC)
- Pediatric-safe pharmacotherapy that reduces irritability/aggression/self-injury and improves sleep maintenance
- Therapies improving hypotonia-related oral-motor control/dysphagia to normalize feeding/weight gain and reduce need for G-tube

name: Saethre-Chotzen syndrome
description: Saethre Chotzen syndrome is a TWIST1 related craniosynostosis where early coronal suture fusion reshapes the skull and face, often with ptosis, small ears, and mild limb anomalies. Treatment is largely early craniofacial surgery with long follow up to prevent complications such as raised intracranial pressure and papilledema. A major unmet need is a disease modifying alternative to repeated, higher risk surgeries that can reduce blood loss and procedural burden, with mutation targeted RNA based approaches beginning to enter clinical study.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying (non-surgical) suture-biology therapy for Saethre–Chotzen infants to replace early cranial vault surgery/helmeting.
- Perioperative blood-loss/transfusion–sparing pharmacologic adjuncts for craniosynostosis repair.
- Medical prevention/control of elevated intracranial pressure and optic-nerve injury to reduce ongoing surveillance/interventions.

name: Age-related choroidal atrophy
description: Late-life degenerative thinning of the choroid with loss of choroidal vessels causing tessellated fundus and macular pigment changes, often mimicking early age-related macular degeneration. Patients are typically in their 80s and may have symptoms despite only modest Snellen loss. There are no disease-modifying options beyond monitoring and managing complications, and a subset develops vision-threatening choroidal neovascularization while structural changes can mimic glaucoma, complicating diagnosis and follow-up.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Choroid-restorative/perfusion-targeted DMT for ARCA eyes with very thin choroid (<125 µm), to stabilize/increase SFCT/CVI and preserve VA
- Functional-vision therapy targeting reading and low-light difficulties, using endpoints beyond Snellen VA (e.g., low-luminance VA, contrast sensitivity, dark adaptation)
- Lower-burden anti-angiogenic therapy for CNV-complicated ARCA to maintain an exudation-free macula with fewer/non-injectable treatments

name: Sertoli cell-only syndrome
description: Sertoli cell-only syndrome is a form of nonobstructive azoospermia where testis biopsy shows seminiferous tubules lined only by Sertoli cells with absent or near absent spermatogenesis, often presenting as otherwise healthy men found to have azoospermia with high follicle stimulating hormone and normal testosterone. There is no disease modifying therapy, so care is largely surgical sperm retrieval that fails in many patients, can risk testicular damage, and is essentially futile in some genetic subtypes, leaving a premium on safer, more reliable fertility restoration approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drug therapy to induce sperm in ejaculate and/or avoid repeat micro-TESE in NOA/SCOS.
- Fertility restoration options for men with complete AZFa/AZFb microdeletions where TESE yield is 0% (non-TESE approaches).
- Adjunct therapeutics to improve micro-TESE sperm retrieval beyond ~44.5% in pure SCOS and/or mitigate TESE-induced transient hypogonadism.

name: Sheehan syndrome
description: Sheehan syndrome is postpartum hypopituitarism caused by severe obstetric hemorrhage or shock leading to pituitary necrosis, often recognized late after lactation failure, amenorrhea, fatigue, and hypotension. Care is lifelong multi hormone replacement rather than repair of pituitary damage, leaving patients with polypharmacy and persistent quality of life gaps. Key needs include more physiologic cortisol replacement to avoid low early morning levels, lower burden alternatives to daily growth hormone injections, and a solution for alactogenesis since prolactin is not commercially replaceable.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Physiologic/circadian cortisol replacement restoring the pre‑waking cortisol rise (e.g., 07:00 cortisol) to improve morning fatigue/QoL vs 2–3×/day immediate‑release hydrocortisone.
- Once‑weekly growth hormone replacement to reduce daily subcutaneous rhGH injection burden and improve adherence.
- Prolactin replacement to restore postpartum lactation (increase milk volume) in Sheehan syndrome–related agalactorrhea/alactogenesis.

name: Sjögren syndrome
description: Sjögren’s is a chronic autoimmune disease, most often diagnosed in women ages 40 to 50, in which immune attack damages the tear and salivary glands causing dry eyes and dry mouth, often alongside profound fatigue and musculoskeletal pain. It can mimic other conditions and be overlooked, while some patients develop systemic complications including neuropathy, major organ involvement, and increased lymphoma risk. Care remains largely symptomatic with no cure and patients report persistent gaps in disease control, with 77.2% dissatisfied with prescription therapy in a 2023 to 2024 multinational survey.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing systemic immunotherapies that meaningfully improve active systemic disease in moderate–severe patients (e.g., ESSDAI ≥5).
- Therapies that reliably reduce high symptom burden (ESSPRI), especially fatigue and pain, even when systemic activity is controlled.
- More convenient, better-tolerated sicca treatments vs current secretagogues/ocular drops (avoid QID/TID dosing, sweating-driven discontinuation, ocular burning).

name: Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome
description: Smith Lemli Opitz syndrome is a rare prenatal onset disorder of cholesterol biosynthesis caused by DHCR7 deficiency leading to low cholesterol and toxic sterol buildup, with growth restriction, microcephaly, feeding problems, congenital anomalies, and moderate to severe intellectual disability. Care is largely supportive and cholesterol supplementation does not correct central nervous system sterol deficiency, leaving neurologic and developmental outcomes hard to modify and no cure today.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-targeted sterol correction (brain-penetrant cholesterol delivery or DHCR7-restoring therapy) to improve neurodevelopment/behavior where dietary cholesterol does not raise CSF cholesterol
- Disease-modifying suppression/neutralization of toxic 7‑DHC–derived oxysterols (biomarker-driven endpoints)
- Lower-burden, more reliable systemic sterol repletion (ready-to-use pharmaceutical-grade cholesterol formulations and/or bile-acid strategies) to reduce dosing variability and caregiver burden

name: Smith-Magenis syndrome
description: Smith-Magenis syndrome is a genetic neurodevelopmental disorder, often driven by loss of RAI1 function, marked by developmental delay, speech impairment, mild to moderate intellectual disability, and severe behavioral dysregulation with self injury. Disrupted circadian biology causes fragmented sleep with nighttime waking and daytime sleepiness, and many patients develop hyperphagia and childhood onset obesity that can dominate family life. There is no cure and care is largely supportive, leaving a need for disease modifying therapies that durably reduce self injury, normalize sleep and appetite, and improve neurodevelopmental outcomes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacotherapies that reduce severe self-injury and behavioral dysregulation (tantrums/outbursts, aggression, impulsivity/inattention), including high-risk stereotypies (polyembolokoilamania/onychotillomania), beyond current sleep-focused care.
- Appetite/satiety-targeted drugs for the SMS hyperphagia/food-seeking phenotype (impaired satiety + maladaptive eating behaviors) to prevent/treat obesity.
- Mechanism-based therapies that improve neurodevelopmental outcomes (cognition and speech/language delays) beyond symptomatic circadian/sleep treatments.

name: Sotos syndrome
description: Rare genetic overgrowth syndrome (usually NSD1-related) presenting in infancy with rapid growth, macrocephaly and characteristic facies; long-term burden is developmental delay and learning disability with autism/attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, plus seizures and scoliosis. Care is supportive and multidisciplinary with no cure, leaving a major unmet need for disease-modifying therapies that improve neurodevelopment and reduce neurologic and orthopedic complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- NSD1-pathway restoration (gene/epigenetic therapies) to measurably improve cognition/learning, speech-language, and neurobehavioral comorbidities (ASD/ADHD/anxiety/impulsivity) in genetically confirmed Sotos syndrome
- Disorder-specific therapies to prevent or substantially reduce seizure burden (incl. febrile seizures) and EEG abnormalities in Sotos patients with epilepsy
- Disease-modifying control of overgrowth/skeletal maturation to slow advanced bone age and reduce scoliosis/orthopedic morbidity progression

name: Macular dystrophy | Stargardt
description: Stargardt disease is a rare inherited macular degeneration where toxic lipofuscin builds up in and under the macula, progressively destroying cells needed for sharp central vision. It often begins in childhood or young adulthood with blurred or distorted central vision and central blind spots, while peripheral vision is usually spared, undermining reading, driving, and face recognition. Care today is largely supportive with vision aids and rehabilitation, leaving a premium on disease modifying therapies and gene delivery approaches that can overcome vector packaging limits, plus regenerative options such as retinal cell therapy once damage is advanced.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ABCA4-mutation–correcting gene/RNA therapy that can deliver the oversized ABCA4 payload (beyond standard AAV capacity) to halt disease and preserve BCVA/microperimetry.
- Convenient oral disease-modifying small molecule to reduce toxic bisretinoids (lipofuscin/A2E) and slow OCT/FAF structural degeneration in early–mid-stage disease.
- Regenerative therapy for advanced Stargardt to restore central visual function with meaningful gains in BCVA/contrast sensitivity/microperimetry.

name: Stickler syndrome
description: Stickler syndrome is a congenital collagen connective tissue disorder causing early craniofacial airway and feeding problems plus childhood high myopia with risk of retinal detachment and blindness, progressive hearing loss, and early degenerative joint disease. Management is surveillance and symptomatic or procedural care such as prophylactic retinal laser, hearing aids, and pain control, with no cure and no proven prophylactic therapy to prevent joint damage or preserve vision and hearing. The key unmet need is disease modifying treatment, with early gene and protein targeted approaches beginning to emerge.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical prevention of retinal detachment (esp. high-risk COL2A1/Type 1 Stickler pediatric–young adult patients) via intravitreal gene/antisense/protein-replacement approaches.
- Disease-modifying joint-protective therapy that prevents early arthropathy progression/joint damage and delays/avoids joint replacement in young adults.
- Hearing-preservation therapy that prevents progression of sensorineural hearing loss (stabilizes thresholds/speech understanding) beyond hearing aids.

name: Sturge-Weber syndrome
description: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a rare congenital neurocutaneous disorder caused by a somatic GNAQ variant that drives abnormal capillaries, classically a facial port wine birthmark with brain and eye involvement. Infants often develop seizures around 6 months that can become medication refractory, alongside stroke like episodes, hemiparesis, cognitive disability, and glaucoma managed with drops or surgery. Care remains largely symptomatic with no curative therapy, leaving major unmet need for disease modifying approaches that prevent early epilepsy and stroke like episodes and better protect vision and neurodevelopment.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Presymptomatic anti-epileptogenic therapy in infants with brain involvement to delay/prevent seizure onset and preserve cognition.
- Alternatives to chronic low-dose aspirin to prevent venous-stasis–related stroke-like episodes/hemiparesis and progressive neurologic injury.
- Durable, surgery-sparing medical therapy for SWS secondary glaucoma (incl. elevated EVP forms) to maintain long-term IOP control in infants/children.

name: Takayasu arteritis
description: Autoimmune large vessel vasculitis causing inflammation of the aorta and major branches, typically in young women, progressing from nonspecific symptoms to limb claudication, dizziness, blood pressure differences and weak pulses as ischemia and fixed stenosis develop. Care relies on high dose prednisone plus immunosuppression, yet relapses are common and vascular damage can be permanent. Key unmet needs are durable steroid sparing remission, reliable imaging based monitoring because blood markers can be normal despite active disease, and pregnancy compatible options that minimize glucocorticoid exposure and avoid teratogens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Glucocorticoid-free durable remission in refractory/relapsing Takayasu arteritis (including patients unable to taper below ~10 mg/day), targeting NIH inactive disease (≤1) with steroid discontinuation by ~6 months.
- Prevent “silent” vascular progression despite clinical/biochemical quiescence, with no new/progressive arterial lesions on CTA/MRA/Doppler and reduced FDG-PET vascular hypermetabolism.
- Pregnancy- and lactation-compatible steroid-sparing therapy for young female TAK patients that avoids teratogens (e.g., methotrexate/leflunomide/cyclophosphamide) while maintaining remission and minimizing high-dose prednisone exposure.

name: Tietze's syndrome
description: Tietze syndrome is a rare, benign, self limiting inflammatory condition of the costal cartilage that causes acute, well localized anterior chest pain with palpable nonsuppurative swelling, usually unilateral at the second or third costochondral joint and most often in people under 40. It can mimic serious cardiopulmonary disease so diagnosis is typically by exclusion. Care is symptomatic with rest and short courses of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, but pain can persist for months up to a year and recur, sometimes requiring targeted local anesthetic and corticosteroid injection. Evidence for optimal treatment is thin with few trials.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Course-modifying anti-inflammatory therapy that shortens prolonged cases (months to ~1 year) to typical 1–2 week resolution and reduces recurrence
- NSAID-sparing, longer-duration outpatient anti-inflammatory analgesia for patients needing NSAIDs beyond ~10 days
- High-efficacy treatment for medically refractory disease (no improvement after ≥3 weeks) to avoid escalation to local anesthetic/steroid injections

name: Usher syndrome | type 2
description: Usher syndrome type 2 is an inherited deaf blindness disorder with congenital moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss and later onset retinitis pigmentosa causing night blindness and progressive tunnel vision, usually with normal balance. Care is largely supportive, using hearing aids or cochlear implants and standard management of retinal complications like cystoid macular edema, but no disease modifying therapy exists. A key unmet need is a convenient mutation agnostic retinal treatment since the common USH2A gene is too large for standard single adeno associated virus gene replacement and many emerging RNA approaches are mutation specific.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying retinal therapy that slows progression of night blindness → peripheral field loss/tunnel vision (e.g., preserves mean sensitivity and ellipsoid-zone metrics over ~12 months in early–moderate disease).
- Mutation-agnostic (or multi-mutation) USH2A therapy beyond exon-13–specific approaches, overcoming USH2A size constraints that limit single-AAV gene augmentation.
- More convenient and better-tolerated pharmacologic control of RP/Usher cystoid macular edema than frequent topical/systemic carbonic-anhydrase-inhibitor regimens (e.g., avoid TID eye-drop dosing/systemic risks).

name: VACTERL association
description: Rare congenital multisystem malformation pattern requiring at least three defects across vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, and limb systems, often presenting with neonatal feeding and breathing instability needing early surgery. Despite repair, many patients have chronic gastroesophageal reflux, dysmotility, recurrent respiratory infections and anastomotic strictures requiring repeat dilatations or reoperation, plus persistent constipation and fecal incontinence after anorectal repair that can last into adulthood. Care is fragmented and lifelong, with high family burden and a need for durable therapies that reduce postoperative scarring and long term gastrointestinal and respiratory morbidity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Anti‑fibrotic/anti‑scarring drugs to prevent post‑EA/TEF repair anastomotic strictures and reduce repeat dilatations
- Motility + anti‑reflux/anti‑aspiration therapies that reduce dysmotility‑driven GERD/aspiration respiratory morbidity beyond acid suppression
- Long‑term bowel‑function therapeutics post‑ARM/anal atresia repair to reduce chronic constipation and improve fecal continence

name: Waardenburg syndrome | type 1
description: Waardenburg syndrome type 1 is a congenital genetic auditory pigmentary disorder marked by sensorineural hearing loss with distinctive hair skin and eye pigmentation changes and dystopia canthorum. Care is largely supportive including hearing aids or cochlear implantation with no curative or disease modifying therapy, leaving a major unmet need for durable hearing restoration by correcting the underlying cochlear biology linked to melanocyte loss in the stria vascularis and impaired endocochlear potential.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neonatal (or earlier) inner-ear gene therapy correcting PAX3-driven cochlear melanocyte deficits to restore endocochlear potential and hearing in WS1 newborns
- Postnatal local regenerative (cell/biologic) therapy replacing/restoring stria vascularis intermediate cells (melanocytes) to re-establish endolymph electrochemistry and enable hearing restoration
- Ion-channel/transport–targeted therapeutics that partially rescue endocochlear potential via strial K+ handling pathways to improve speech-sound audibility and reduce reliance on early cochlear implantation

name: West syndrome
description: West syndrome is an infantile epileptic spasms syndrome starting around 4 to 8 months, marked by clustered spasms, hypsarrhythmia on electroencephalogram, and developmental plateauing or regression. It is etiologically diverse, and outcomes depend on rapid electroclinical remission, yet current first line therapies are urgent but burdensome, toxic, and not reliably durable, with risks such as hypertension and infections with adrenocorticotropic hormone and permanent peripheral vision loss with vigabatrin.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid, durable electroclinical remission (spasm cessation by day 7–14 plus hypsarrhythmia resolution on EEG within 2–4 weeks) for first-line nonresponders/relapsers.
- Therapies that improve long-term neurodevelopment/functional independence and reduce persistent/uncontrolled epilepsy beyond short-term spasm control.
- Safer, lower-burden first-line alternatives avoiding vigabatrin vision-loss/REMS monitoring and ACTH infection/hypertension risks plus twice-daily IM injections (ideally simple outpatient oral dosing).

name: Williams-Beuren syndrome
description: Williams Beuren syndrome is a rare 7q11.23 microdeletion disorder that disrupts elastin and drives multisystem disease, most notably progressive arterial stenoses such as supravalvular aortic stenosis, alongside early feeding and growth problems, endocrine issues like hypercalcemia, and lifelong neurodevelopmental and behavioral challenges including anxiety and phobias. Care is largely symptomatic with frequent procedures and lifelong cardiovascular monitoring, leaving a major need for disease modifying therapies for vasculopathy and hypertension and for treatments that meaningfully improve cognition, social functioning, and anxiety.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying medical therapy for elastin-related vasculopathy (SVAS/hypertension/arterial stenoses) to reduce reliance on surgery (e.g., improve IMT/arterial stiffness/stenosis gradients)
- Neurodevelopmental therapy improving core cognitive, motor, and social impairments beyond supportive care (e.g., Wechsler/NIH Toolbox; DTI myelin/white-matter metrics)
- Evidence-based pharmacotherapy for high-burden anxiety/phobias in Williams syndrome with meaningful improvement on validated scales (e.g., PARS; CGI-I response)

name: Wilson disease
description: Rare inherited copper overload disorder causing progressive liver disease and later neurologic and psychiatric impairment, often presenting from childhood through the teens. Untreated copper accumulation can be fatal, yet care requires lifelong copper lowering with tolerability and adherence challenges, including early chelation related neurologic worsening and rapid relapse if therapy is missed. Key unmet needs are safer, easier to sustain copper control and durable disease modifying approaches such as neurologically safer binders and one time gene targeted therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Better-tolerated copper-lowering therapy that reduces treatment-limiting adverse reactions vs chelators/zinc while maintaining effective decoppering.
- Neurologic-presentation–optimized therapy that prevents early paradoxical neurologic worsening and improves validated neurologic outcomes (e.g., UWDRS).
- One-time/infrequent disease-targeted modality (e.g., ATP7B gene therapy) that normalizes copper handling and enables tapering/discontinuation of chronic multi-dose chelators/zinc.

name: X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita
description: X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita is a rare NR0B1-linked congenital adrenal development disorder, typically presenting in infant boys around 3 weeks with life-threatening salt-wasting adrenal crises. Management is lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement, but day-to-day care is constrained by the narrow dosing window needed to support normal growth while preventing crises and by real-world access to rapid, injectable stress-dose hydrocortisone. Survivors often face hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with delayed puberty and infertility, leaving a persistent need for safer, more physiologic disease control and better reproductive management.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Precision/physiologic pediatric glucocorticoid replacement (incl. infant micro-dosing) that preserves normal linear growth without increasing adrenal-crisis risk
- Ready-to-use, field-usable stress-dose hydrocortisone rescue (IM/IV) with reliable pre-hospital/EMS availability to prevent adrenal-crisis deaths
- Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism/infertility-directed regimens that reliably achieve spermatogenesis/fertility beyond puberty induction

name: X-linked hereditary ataxia
description: Fragile X associated tremor ataxia syndrome is an X linked dominant late onset neurodegenerative disorder in FMR1 premutation carriers, typically affecting men after age 50, marked by progressive action tremor, cerebellar gait ataxia, falls, and cognitive decline from cerebellar and white matter injury. Current care is largely symptomatic with no controlled trial proven disease modifying therapy, leaving a premium on treatments that slow progression and preserve gait, independence, and cognition.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy targeting CGG-repeat–driven FXTAS mechanisms (e.g., toxic FMR1 mRNA/RAN-translation products like FMRpolyG) to slow white-matter neurodegeneration and delay cane/walker/wheelchair dependence.
- Pharmacologic motor therapy with proven benefit on gait ataxia/falls (not just tremor), improving FXTAS Rating Scale and deferring walking-aid milestones.
- CNS therapy to prevent or reverse executive dysfunction → dementia and associated psychiatric morbidity beyond supportive care, ideally in early-to-middle motor stages.

name: X-linked hypophosphatemia
description: X linked hypophosphatemia is a rare inherited disorder where PHEX mutations drive excess fibroblast growth factor 23, causing lifelong renal phosphate wasting and low vitamin D that weakens bone. Children develop rickets with short stature, bowed legs, craniosynostosis, and recurrent dental abscesses. Adults accumulate chronic pain, enthesopathy, osteoarthritis, and sometimes spinal stenosis. Standard phosphate plus active vitamin D is burdensome with multiple daily doses and risks kidney calcification and hyperparathyroidism and it does not prevent many long term skeletal and dental complications, leaving a need for safer disease modifying control of the pathway.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that prevent/reverse adult enthesopathy and osteoarthritis progression (incl. spine disease/spinal stenosis) not addressed by current medical therapy.
- Therapies that prevent/treat recurrent dental abscesses by correcting intrinsic dentin/cementum defects despite phosphate correction.
- Lower-burden, safer phosphate homeostasis restoration (less frequent/self-administered) without renal/parathyroid toxicity (e.g., nephrocalcinosis, hyperparathyroidism) or frequent injections.

name: X-linked ichthyosis
description: X linked ichthyosis is a rare male predominant genetic skin disorder that begins in infancy with generalized dark adherent scaling on the trunk and limbs and a typical dirty neck appearance with palms and soles usually spared. Steroid sulfatase deficiency leads to cholesterol sulfate buildup, impaired shedding and a disrupted skin barrier. Management is largely symptomatic with emollients and keratolytics that can irritate young children and require lifelong, high burden use, and evidence for definitive benefit is limited. Disease modifying therapies that correct the underlying defect and improve tolerability remain a key unmet need.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Root-cause STS restoration / cholesterol-sulfate reduction (gene/enzyme/substrate-reduction) for males with STS deletions
- Anti-scaling therapy that clearly beats vehicle/emollient on validated endpoints (e.g., ≥2-point IGA scaling+fissuring improvement at Week 12)
- Pediatric-safe, low-irritation, lower-frequency topical regimen to reduce frequent daily emollient use and avoid age/tolerability limits (e.g., AHA stinging, salicylic-acid restrictions, retinoid irritation)

name: Zika fever
description: Zika fever is a mosquito borne viral illness that is often asymptomatic or mild in adults but can spread sexually and from mother to fetus, causing congenital Zika syndrome including microcephaly and other malformations, and is associated with Guillain-Barré syndrome. Management is supportive only with no vaccine or antiviral, leaving major unmet needs for pregnancy compatible prevention and interventions that rapidly clear virus after exposure.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pregnancy-safe prophylaxis (vaccine or long-acting mAb) for women of reproductive age/pregnant to prevent congenital Zika syndrome and pregnancy loss
- Early-start, pregnancy-compatible antiviral to reduce viral replication and lower risk of neurologic complications (e.g., GBS/neuropathy/myelitis)
- Post-exposure/clearance therapy that rapidly eliminates genital-tract infectiousness (esp. semen) to shorten safer-sex window and prevent sexual transmission

name: Esophageal achalasia
description: Esophageal achalasia is a rare motility disorder caused by degeneration of esophageal nerves, leading to failed lower esophageal sphincter relaxation and loss of peristalsis, with progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids, regurgitation, weight loss, and aspiration risk. Care is largely palliative and procedural, with limited drug tolerability and a tradeoff of post intervention reflux, and no current way to restore peristalsis, creating demand for durable nonprocedural symptom control, better reflux prevention, and therapies that improve esophageal clearance.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Long-acting, non-procedural LES-relaxing drug therapy for patients unfit for definitive achalasia procedures, achieving durable Eckardt score control (≤3) without multi-daily dosing/BP–edema side effects.
- Adjunct anti-reflux pharmacotherapy post-definitive therapy (esp. post‑POEM) to reduce reflux esophagitis/GERD.
- Peristalsis/esophageal-clearance restoring therapy to reduce nocturnal regurgitation and aspiration-related morbidity.

name: Achondroplasia
description: Achondroplasia is the most common short limbed dwarfism, caused by FGFR3 variants that impair conversion of cartilage to bone, leading to disproportionate limb shortening and characteristic craniofacial and hand features. Clinical risk is driven less by height than by complications such as infant foramen magnum stenosis with brainstem compression causing sleep apnea or hydrocephalus, and later spinal stenosis that can limit walking and often requires surgery. Current pharmacotherapy mainly targets linear growth and adds daily injection and reconstitution burden, leaving a premium on safer, less invasive, complication focused disease modification.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Low-burden administration (ideally oral; no reconstitution/cold-chain) achieving current linear-growth benefit while avoiding injection logistics/AEs.
- Pharmacotherapy to prevent/reverse craniocervical junction constriction/foramen magnum stenosis in infants/children to reduce central apnea and avoid decompression.
- Adult-focused treatment for symptomatic lumbar spinal stenosis that reduces pain/claudication/neurologic impairment and lowers need for laminectomy/spine surgery.

name: Acneiform dermatitis
description: Drug induced acne like papulopustular eruption on the face scalp and upper chest and back, often emerging in the first weeks of epidermal growth factor receptor targeted cancer therapy. Up to 75% of patients are affected and flares can be itchy or tender and force dose reductions delays or discontinuation. Care relies on topical corticosteroids and antibiotics plus oral tetracyclines, leaving demand for steroid and antibiotic sparing prevention, better control of grade 2 to 3 disease, and culture guided approaches when superinfection is suspected.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid/antibiotic-sparing pre-emptive prophylaxis started at EGFR-inhibitor initiation to prevent CTCAE grade ≥2 acneiform/papulopustular rash.
- Rapid symptom/QoL control for grade 2–3 eruptions to minimize EGFRi dose modification/discontinuation (improve itch/pain and EGFRi-specific PROs).
- Culture-guided, resistance-aware anti-infective options for late/superinfected eruptions to reduce prolonged antibiotic exposure and resistant secondary infections.

name: Acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans
description: Late-stage Lyme borreliosis skin manifestation, often in middle-aged/older women, with unilateral bluish-red distal limb swelling that can progress to thin, wrinkled atrophic “cigarette paper” skin; antibiotics clear infection but established atrophy and painful polyneuropathy may persist, driving need for earlier recognition and adjunct skin-repair and neuropathy treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
