- Adjunct therapies that reverse late-stage ACA atrophic/sclerotic skin damage and restore dermal integrity.
- Neuropathy-directed treatments that improve ACA-associated sensory polyneuropathy (pain/paresthesia) beyond what antibiotics resolve.
- Shorter-course, relapse-resistant (ideally all-oral) antimicrobial regimens that reduce prolonged/repeated antibiotic exposure and speed resolution.

name: Acute intermittent porphyria
description: Acute intermittent porphyria is a rare inherited hepatic heme synthesis disorder caused by hydroxymethylbilane synthase deficiency, with drugs, fasting, alcohol, infection, or hormonal shifts triggering acute neurovisceral attacks often in young women. Episodes feature severe abdominal pain with gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, and neuropsychiatric symptoms and often require hospitalization for dextrose and sometimes intravenous hemin. Monthly givosiran can reduce recurrences but requires liver and kidney monitoring, and patients remain at risk for progressive organ damage including chronic kidney disease and hepatocellular carcinoma, creating demand for safer preventive options and home startable abortive care.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Home-startable, non‑IV acute-attack abortive therapy that reduces hospitalization/urgent-care/IV rescue use vs multi-day IV hemin
- Safer recurrent-attack prophylaxis that avoids givosiran hepatotoxicity/monitoring burden and chronic hemin line complications/iron monitoring
- Disease-modifying therapy that prevents long-term organ complications (CKD, hypertension, hepatocellular carcinoma) beyond reducing acute attack rate

name: Acute interstitial pneumonia
description: Acute interstitial pneumonia is a rare, fulminant idiopathic interstitial lung disease that often affects previously healthy adults and rapidly progresses over 1 to 3 weeks from fever, cough, and dyspnea to severe hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. Diagnosis is often late and may require high resolution computed tomography and lung biopsy. Care is largely supportive with empiric immunosuppression, yet mortality remains high above 50 percent, creating urgent unmet need for earlier, less invasive diagnosis and proven therapies that reduce early deaths and limit chronic lung damage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Proven acute-phase therapy to reduce early mortality and prevent progression to ventilator-dependent respiratory failure
- Earlier non-invasive diagnosis plus predictive/prognostic biomarkers for patient stratification and timely trial enrollment
- Evidence-based, steroid-sparing treatment standards (better-tolerated agents for critically ill patients)

name: Intestinal ischemia | acute
description: Acute mesenteric ischemia is a sudden loss of intestinal blood supply, typically in older adults, that presents with severe abdominal pain and can rapidly progress to bowel necrosis, sepsis, and death with 60% to 80% mortality. The core gaps are earlier diagnosis and adjunct treatments to limit reperfusion injury and capillary leak, plus safer and more consistently used catheter directed mesenteric vasodilator strategies for non occlusive disease in critically ill intensive care patients.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacologic adjunct post-revascularization/bowel resection to reduce reperfusion-injury capillary leak and inflammatory/toxic cascade driving multiorgan failure.
- Evidence-backed, catheter-directed mesenteric vasodilator strategy/agent for NOMI in shock/vasopressor ICU patients that improves outcomes without systemic hypotension/sudden death.
- Early gut-directed medical therapy to prevent progression to transmural necrosis and 30-day necrosis/death by preserving mucosal barrier and reducing bacterial translocation/sepsis.

name: Adenoid cystic carcinoma
description: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is a rare malignancy of secretory glands, usually arising in head and neck salivary tissue, that often presents as a slow growing painless mass but can invade nerves and cause pain or numbness. Local control with surgery and radiation is common, yet many patients relapse years later with lung metastases and require lifelong monitoring. The central unmet need is effective systemic therapy for recurrent or metastatic disease since no approved drugs exist, alongside adjuvant options to prevent late distant relapse and targeted approaches for tumors with MYB or MYBL1 rearrangements or Notch pathway alterations such as NOTCH1.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjuvant systemic therapy post-surgery/RT to prevent late distant metastasis/relapse (especially lung metastases).
- MYB/MYBL1 fusion–pathway targeted agents that produce meaningful objective responses in MYB/MYBL1-rearranged ACC.
- NOTCH-pathway therapy to improve relapse-free/overall survival in high-risk NOTCH1-mutant (solid-subtype) ACC.

name: Adenomatoid tumor
description: Benign mesothelial neoplasm usually presenting as a painless, well circumscribed epididymal or paratesticular mass in men aged 30 to 50. The key unmet need is diagnostic certainty because ultrasound often cannot distinguish it from malignancy, leading to potentially unnecessary orchiectomy even though local surgical excision is curative.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Asherman's syndrome
description: Asherman syndrome is a rare acquired disorder in which intrauterine scar tissue, often after dilation and curettage following miscarriage or delivery, leads to menstrual abnormalities, pelvic pain, infertility and recurrent miscarriage. Standard hysteroscopic adhesiolysis can restore uterine anatomy, but re-adhesion is common, leaving patients facing repeat procedures and uncertain chances of pregnancy or live birth. The key unmet needs are durable prevention of scar recurrence and reliable restoration of a healthy endometrial lining with disease modifying regeneration rather than purely mechanical removal.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Local intrauterine anti‑fibrotic adjunct after hysteroscopic adhesiolysis to reduce re‑adhesion/recurrence and repeat procedures
- Regenerative biologics for moderate–severe IUA to restore thin endometrium (endometrial thickness) and improve pregnancy/live‑birth outcomes
- Short‑course local prophylaxis post pregnancy‑related D&C (esp. repeated D&Cs or 2–4 weeks postpartum) to prevent adhesion formation

name: Adiposis dolorosa
description: Adiposis dolorosa (Dercum disease) is a rare disorder, typically in overweight women aged 35 to 50, marked by multiple benign subcutaneous lipomas that cause severe, sometimes disabling chronic pain with fatigue and cognitive or mood symptoms. The biology is poorly understood and diagnosis and management are inconsistent, so care is largely symptomatic and relief from procedures is often temporary. The key unmet need is durable, disease modifying therapy that reduces lipoma burden and provides long lasting pain control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, non-surgical reduction/clearance of multiple painful lipomas (ultrasound-measured volume/dimensions) with improved lipoma pain, overcoming temporary/recurrence-prone excision or liposuction effects
- Long-lasting control of chronic, disabling adipose-tissue pain resistant to traditional analgesics (beyond short-term symptomatic relief)
- Therapies that improve the systemic symptom cluster (fatigue, cognitive impairment/“brain fog,” mood disturbance, sleep issues) alongside pain using validated PRO/QoL measures

name: Adrenocorticotropic hormone deficiency
description: Central (pituitary) adrenal insufficiency from low adrenocorticotropic hormone causing low cortisol with typically preserved mineralocorticoids. Patients often have insidious fatigue, anorexia or weight loss, nausea or vomiting, sometimes hypoglycemia or hyponatremia, and lack hyperpigmentation until stress precipitates adrenal crisis requiring urgent hydrocortisone. Standard hydrocortisone replacement improves outcomes but poorly matches circadian cortisol, dosing is hard to individualize without objective biomarkers, and preventable crises persist, creating demand for more physiologic delivery and better monitoring and rescue readiness.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Circadian‑mimicking cortisol replacement (e.g., modified-/dual‑release hydrocortisone) to reduce persistent diurnal fatigue and impaired HR‑QoL despite standard regimens.
- Ready‑to‑use out‑of‑hospital adrenal‑crisis rescue (IM/SC hydrocortisone, ideally autoinjector) for high‑risk patients to reduce crisis incidence/mortality.
- Precision glucocorticoid replacement that minimizes chronic under/over‑replacement toxicity via more consistent exposure and simpler titration despite lack of reliable tissue cortisol biomarkers.

name: Adrenoleukodystrophy
description: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy is an ABCD1 disorder where very long-chain fatty acids accumulate, damaging myelin and the adrenal cortex and causing progressive neurologic decline and adrenal insufficiency. Adult adrenomyeloneuropathy typically begins in the late twenties with slowly worsening spastic paraparesis, gait impairment, and bladder and sexual dysfunction that can lead to major disability. Care is largely symptomatic with no cure, while cerebral disease requires time sensitive high risk transplant or gene therapy with serious safety tradeoffs, creating strong demand for safer disease modifying therapies that preserve ambulation and function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy for adult AMN myeloneuropathy that preserves/improves walking disability (e.g., 2‑Minute Walk Test/EDSS) rather than symptomatic-only spasticity/pain control.
- Non-transplant (adult-inclusive) therapy for early active cerebral ALD that stabilizes MRI lesion activity (gadolinium enhancement/Loes score) without HSCT eligibility constraints and without Skysona-like hematologic malignancy risk.
- Safe chronic VLCFA-targeting therapy for presymptomatic males (including newborn-screen–identified) to prevent conversion to cerebral ALD and/or slow AMN progression suitable for long-term use.

name: Androgen insensitivity syndrome
description: Androgen insensitivity syndrome is a rare 46,XY difference of sex development caused by androgen resistance, spanning complete to mild forms and often presenting in adolescence with primary amenorrhea, absent uterus, and undescended testes. Care is largely supportive, with major unmet needs in partial disease where virilization outcomes are hard to predict, and in complete disease where timing of gonad removal and hormone replacement are not standardized, complicating long term bone health. Sexual function support often relies on vaginal dilation, highlighting demand for less burdensome options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Predictable AR-pathway functional rescue for PAIS/MAIS (46,XY; male-reared infants) to achieve reliable virilization beyond trial-and-error androgen use
- Evidence-based, bone-protective post-gonadectomy hormone regimens in CAIS that maintain/improve DXA bone mineral density (optimized HRT type/dose/duration)
- Drug adjuncts to reduce dyspareunia and reliance on mechanical vaginal dilation in CAIS (e.g., local mucosal therapies)

name: Anemia of prematurity
description: Anemia of prematurity is a common NICU complication in infants born before 32 weeks, emerging 4 to 12 weeks after birth when low erythropoietin signaling, rapid growth, short red cell lifespan, and phlebotomy losses outstrip production. It can worsen feeding and cardio respiratory stability with tachycardia, apnea, and bradycardia. Management still relies heavily on repeated red blood cell transfusions plus iron, but transfusion exposure is linked to complications such as retinopathy of prematurity and necrotizing enterocolitis, and erythropoietin strategies have not shown durable neurodevelopment benefit.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Transfusion-sparing erythropoiesis for ELBW/VLBW NICU infants to avoid repeated allogeneic PRBC transfusions and donor exposures.
- Gut-safe, oxidation-limited iron repletion that achieves iron sufficiency without intestinal inflammation/dysbiosis or oxidative injury (e.g., NEC/ROP risk).
- Anemia-directed therapy with proven improvement in 22–26 month corrected-age neurodevelopment outcomes (Bayley/NDI), beyond reducing transfusion metrics.

name: Anorectal stricture
description: Anorectal stricture or anal stenosis is a rare scar driven narrowing of the anal canal, often after hemorrhoid surgery or with inflammatory bowel disease, causing constipation, pencil thin stools, painful defecation, bleeding, and incomplete evacuation. Care is largely mechanical with stool softeners or fiber, dilation, and sometimes reconstructive surgery, but fibrosis drives recurrence and there are no specific anti fibrotic therapies, creating demand for local anti scarring and anti restenosis approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Local anti-fibrotic/anti-scarring therapy to prevent post-hemorrhoidectomy scar-driven anal stenosis.
- Adjuvant anti-restenosis drug (e.g., intralesional anti-fibrotic injection) to prolong dilation-free intervals and reduce repeat balloon dilations.
- Improved medical therapy for IBD-associated anorectal/rectal strictures to achieve higher healing/lumen restoration than current biologics.

name: Antithrombin III deficiency
description: Hereditary antithrombin III deficiency is an inherited clotting disorder where low functional antithrombin drives recurrent venous thrombosis risk including deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, often triggered by surgery, immobility, or pregnancy. Management hinges on individualized anticoagulation, but sparse evidence leaves uncertainty around prophylaxis and antithrombin replacement, especially in pregnancy. Low antithrombin can also cause heparin resistance in hospital settings, creating demand for simpler, more durable prevention and clearer guidance.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pregnancy/peri-partum prophylaxis that maintains antithrombin activity at 80–120% without IV loading + continuous infusion and frequent lab-driven dose adjustments
- Rapid, durable correction of antithrombin-dependent heparin resistance in CPB/cardiac surgery to achieve target ACT without repeated UFH escalation
- Long-acting strategy to reduce VTE recurrence in congenital antithrombin deficiency and meaningfully reduce/avoid lifelong anticoagulation (and associated heparin/anti-Xa management challenges)

name: Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia
description: Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia is a rare CSF1R mutation driven neurodegenerative white matter disease that typically begins in the forties with personality and executive dysfunction, then rapidly progresses to dementia, gait failure and parkinsonism, often leaving patients unable to walk, speak or self care and leading to death within a few years. Management is largely supportive and even symptomatic neuropsychiatric drugs can worsen falls. The premium is on scalable disease modifying approaches that restore microglial function and on objective biomarkers such as magnetic resonance imaging and blood neurofilament light chain to detect early disease and track progression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying CSF1R-pathway therapy for genetically confirmed CSF1R-ALSP that slows progression on cognition/function and objective biomarkers (MRI volume loss, blood NfL).
- Safer, scalable drug/biologic alternative to HSCT that restores microglial function without transplant morbidity (e.g., GVHD).
- Non-sedating, better-tolerated symptomatic therapies for combined neuropsychiatric and motor impairment that avoid worsening falls risk.

name: Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita
description: Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita is a rare umbrella of congenital disorders marked by fixed joint contractures in two or more body regions, often driven by reduced fetal movement and underdeveloped muscle, leading to lifelong mobility and functional impairment. Treatment is largely supportive with early physical therapy, serial casting, and repeated orthopedic procedures, rather than addressing root cause. Major unmet needs are disease modifying prenatal and postnatal approaches that prevent contracture formation, improve muscle driven function, and reduce the need for ongoing interventions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prenatal (in‑utero) therapy to restore fetal movement early in gestation to prevent development of contractures
- Postnatal systemic therapy to improve muscle weakness/fibrosis and increase active range of motion and functional autonomy beyond PT/casting
- Anti‑fibrotic/tissue‑remodeling therapy (local or systemic) to reduce joint-capsule/connective-tissue fixation and lessen serial casting and repeat orthopedic surgeries

name: Cerebral palsy | ataxic
description: Ataxic cerebral palsy is a rare, nonprogressive cerebral palsy subtype caused by early brain injury, marked by impaired balance, coordination, tremor, and a wide based unsteady gait that can limit walking and hand control. Care is supportive with no cure, and commonly used symptomatic drugs can add sedation, constipation, and safety risks. The key unmet need is disease modifying or restorative approaches that directly improve balance and fine motor function with better tolerability, rather than simply managing complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Ataxia-targeted therapy that measurably improves balance/coordination and gait (beyond tone-only muscle relaxants).
- Non-sedating treatment to reduce tremor/overshoot and improve upper-limb fine-motor function (avoid CNS drowsiness/weakness).
- Safer, lower-burden pharmacologic management of swallowing/drooling symptoms that avoids anticholinergic constipation and botulinum-toxin systemic spread risk.

name: Atheroembolic renal disease
description: Atheroembolic renal disease is subacute kidney injury from cholesterol crystal debris showering from atherosclerotic plaque into renal arterioles, often after angiography, catheterization, or vascular surgery in older, high risk patients, sometimes with livedo reticularis or blue toes. Care is largely supportive and focused on avoiding further embolization and managing renal failure, yet prognosis is poor and many progress to dialysis, creating a need for better peri procedural prevention and kidney rescue therapies that improve dialysis free recovery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Peri-procedural prophylaxis to prevent cholesterol-crystal showering/renal injury after catheterization or vascular surgery in high-risk atherosclerotic patients
- Kidney-directed therapy that treats established renal cholesterol microemboli to improve renal recovery/dialysis-free survival
- Steroid-sparing anti-inflammatory therapy that improves 1-year survival and 1-year renal survival / prevents progression to ESRD in severe systemic cholesterol crystal embolism

name: Alexia
description: Alexia is an acquired loss of reading ability despite preserved writing and spelling, most often after a dominant posterior cerebral artery stroke affecting the occipital cortex and callosal splenium, frequently with a right visual field defect and slow letter by letter reading. Management is largely rehabilitation based using strategies like oral rereading and tactile kinesthetic techniques, but no therapy reliably restores normal reading, creating unmet need for scalable adjuncts that improve real world reading fluency with less practice and clinic burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacologic adjunct to SLT that restores near-normal reading fluency (higher words-per-minute on untrained everyday text) in chronic post-stroke pure alexia
- Drug improving letter identification accuracy/visual-orthographic processing in severe alexia to reduce reliance on letter-by-letter compensatory strategies
- Low-monitoring oral therapy that reduces rehab/home-practice time and visit burden while preserving gains in reading speed/comprehension

name: Allergic cutaneous vasculitis
description: Allergic cutaneous vasculitis is a usually skin-limited inflammation of small vessels, often triggered by a new medication or infection, presenting with lower leg palpable purpura that can ulcerate. While many cases resolve, a relapsing chronic subset develops painful ulcers with infection and scarring risk. Treatment relies on immunosuppression with limited randomized-trial evidence and meaningful toxicity, leaving unmet need for steroid-sparing, oral options that control flares and speed ulcer healing.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing, non-toxic long-term control for the ~10% with persistent/recurrent cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis
- Ulcer-focused therapy that rapidly heals ulcers and reduces ulcer-associated pain while preventing infection/cellulitis, chronic leg ulcers, and scarring
- Oral targeted therapy for refractory disease after failure of conventional agents (e.g., prednisone, methotrexate, colchicine, azathioprine), avoiding escalation to rituximab/IVIG

name: Alopecia universalis
description: Alopecia universalis is a rare, severe autoimmune form of alopecia areata in which immune attack on hair follicles causes sudden, often relapsing and unpredictable near total loss of scalp and body hair including eyebrows and eyelashes, with major emotional and functional burden. Recently approved oral Janus kinase inhibitors have expanded options for severe disease but require ongoing infection screening and lab monitoring and carry boxed safety warnings, limiting long term use. No approved therapies exist for children under 12, and patients still need safer, more convenient, durable disease control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Treatment-free durability (maintain SALT ≤20 ≥1 year after stopping therapy) to avoid chronic dosing in alopecia universalis
- Long-term therapy with lower systemic risk/monitoring burden than oral JAK inhibitors (avoid boxed-warning risks; minimal TB/CBC monitoring)
- On-label option for severe alopecia totalis/universalis in children <12 years with acceptable long-duration safety

name: Epilepsy | autoimmune
description: Immune driven seizure disorder resembling limbic encephalitis with rapid cognitive and psychiatric decline and high frequency focal seizures that are often drug resistant and can progress to new onset refractory status epilepticus; diagnosis is time critical even with negative antibodies, treatment is consensus based with limited definitive trials, and relapse rates reach up to 35%.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Empiric, diagnosis-agnostic “start-now” immunotherapy that can be initiated within days (not weeks/months) without waiting for antibody confirmation and delivers larger functional improvement (CASE-score reduction).
- NORSE/fulminant autoimmune-epilepsy rescue that achieves rapid seizure control (days) and improves long-term neurocognitive outcomes (not just seizure cessation).
- Steroid/IVIG/rituximab-sparing maintenance therapy (ideally outpatient/self-administered) that prevents relapse while reducing serious immunotherapy risks.

name: Pancreatitis | autoimmune
description: Autoimmune pancreatitis is a rare chronic inflammatory pancreatitis, often in older men, that commonly presents with painless obstructive jaundice and can mimic pancreatic cancer. Corticosteroids induce remission in most patients, but up to one third relapse or become steroid dependent, with cumulative risk of biliary strictures and exocrine or endocrine pancreatic insufficiency. A key unmet need is durable steroid sparing maintenance therapy that prevents recurrence and preserves long term pancreatic and biliary function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Relapse-proof maintenance for high-relapse-risk type 1 AIP to prevent frequent post-steroid relapse and enable steroid discontinuation.
- Steroid-sparing maintenance that avoids multi-year low-dose prednisone toxicity with simpler dosing/less monitoring.
- Long-term organ-preserving control that prevents endocrine/exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and biliary-stricture complications while maintaining remission.

name: Alpha thalassemia | transfusion dependent
description: Transfusion dependent alpha thalassemia is a severe inherited hemoglobin production disorder that can present before birth as hydrops fetalis and, in survivors, causes lifelong severe anemia requiring intrauterine and then chronic blood transfusions. Care is dominated by transfusion and iron chelation, with iron overload an unavoidable, burdensome complication. The unmet need is durable transfusion reduction or independence and disease modifying, potentially prenatal definitive approaches such as in utero stem cell transplantation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that deliver ≥50% transfusion-burden reduction (≥2-unit RBC reduction over 12 weeks) and/or ≥8-week transfusion independence in transfusion-dependent α-thalassemia.
- In utero definitive therapy for α-thalassemia major to prevent fetal/neonatal death and reduce the need for serial intrauterine transfusions.
- Iron-overload treatments with improved safety and substantially reduced monitoring/administration burden versus current chelators (deferasirox/deferiprone/deferoxamine).

name: Urethral calculus
description: Urethral calculus is a rare, male skewed urinary tract stone impacted in the urethra, often linked to strictures or diverticula and presenting with painful obstructive voiding symptoms, a palpable mass, and acute urinary retention. Management is usually procedural, with retrograde manipulation, endoscopic lithotripsy, or open urethrolithotomy, and delayed diagnosis can cause serious morbidity. Key unmet needs include faster emergency stone clearance with fewer procedures, potential nonprocedural options for select radiolucent or uric acid stones, and better recurrence prevention in infection and urinary stasis phenotypes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-invasive chemolysis for radiolucent/uric-acid urethral stones to achieve stone clearance without procedural intervention
- ED-ready urethral “expulsion enablement” pharmacotherapy (smooth-muscle relaxation + local anesthesia/lubrication) to shorten time-to-catheter-free voiding in acute urinary retention/pain presentations
- Recurrence-prevention pharmacotherapy for urethral-stasis subtypes (e.g., anti-biofilm/anti-infective and/or anti-fibrotic approaches) in patients with diverticulum/stricture

name: Rheumatoid arthritis interstitial lung disease
description: Rheumatoid arthritis associated interstitial lung disease is a severe extraarticular complication where inflammation and fibrosis scar the lungs, most often in usual interstitial pneumonia or nonspecific interstitial pneumonia patterns. It often emerges within about five years of rheumatoid arthritis diagnosis and can be missed until dry cough and exertional breathlessness progress to crackles and physiologic decline. Outcomes are poor with median survival around three years after diagnosis, especially in the fibrotic usual interstitial pneumonia phenotype. Care is largely empiric with limited guideline level evidence and few randomized trials, creating demand for better tolerated disease modifying options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that prevent/slow RA‑ILD progression and reduce high mortality (e.g., avoid ≥10% FVC decline or death)
- Better‑tolerated antifibrotics/immunomodulator regimens that improve persistence (fewer GI AEs/infusion reactions and withdrawals)
- RA‑ILD therapies targeted to high‑risk UIP phenotype with clearer patient selection and optimized first‑line use

name: Rhinoscleroma
description: Rhinoscleroma is a rare, slowly progressive chronic granulomatous infection of the nose and upper airway caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis, progressing from foul crusting discharge to deforming obstructive masses and then fibrotic scarring that can block the airway. Treatment remains long, burdensome courses of antibiotics often with surgery, with major unmet needs in preventing recurrence and limiting or reversing scarring and airway compromise.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable regimens that eradicate intracellular *K. rhinoscleromatis* and reduce relapse/recurrence vs prolonged antibiotics.
- Non–fluoroquinolone/rifampin alternatives for patients with contraindications that still achieve histopathologic resolution.
- Adjunct anti-fibrotic/anti-stenotic therapy to prevent/reverse airway stenosis and procedure-induced fibrosis, reducing repeat interventions/tracheostomy risk.

name: Right atrial isomerism
description: Right atrial isomerism is the asplenia form of heterotaxy, with abnormal organ arrangement and typically severe congenital heart defects that present in the first days of life with cyanosis plus breathing and feeding difficulty. Management is surgery intensive and complicated by immune vulnerability from absent or dysfunctional spleen, often requiring daily antibiotic prophylaxis. Many infants also need ductal patency support with alprostadil, which can trigger apnea and increase the mechanical ventilation burden, underscoring the need for safer cardiopulmonary stabilization and more durable disease modifying options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non–ICU-dependent ductal-patency therapy for duct-dependent neonates that avoids alprostadil-related apnea/ventilation burden
- Pediatric-friendly Fontan/single-ventricle thromboprophylaxis that lowers thromboembolism without warfarin/heparin bleeding + monitoring burden (and beyond limited DOAC evidence)
- Long-acting, resistance-sparing infection prophylaxis for congenital asplenia to prevent encapsulated-bacteria sepsis without lifelong daily penicillin

name: Scleredema adultorum
description: Rare diabetic-associated connective tissue disorder causing persistent woody, nonpitting thickening of neck and upper back skin that can restrict movement and breathing; pathogenesis is poorly understood and there is no specific, consistently effective therapy beyond symptomatic measures such as phototherapy and occasional intravenous immunoglobulin, with sparse clinical development.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- More consistently effective systemic therapy for diabetic/type 3 scleroedema when methotrexate fails, with objective lesion-volume reduction endpoints.
- Home-administered (oral/topical) option to replace high-burden phototherapy requiring many treatment sessions.
- Non-IVIG, non-cytotoxic escalation option for severe/extensive disease to avoid IVIG-associated thrombosis and renal risk (notably in diabetics).

name: Septo-optic dysplasia
description: Septo optic dysplasia is a rare congenital disorder of early brain development, typically involving optic nerve hypoplasia with nystagmus, strabismus and vision loss alongside midline brain malformations and pituitary hypoplasia causing evolving hormone deficiencies. Newborns may present with hypoglycemia, jaundice and genital anomalies. Care is symptomatic with lifelong multidisciplinary monitoring and hormone replacement, but there is no cure and core visual deficits are largely untreatable, creating demand for vision restorative therapies and more durable approaches to endocrine instability and obesity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Vision-restorative/neuroregenerative therapy that measurably improves visual function in congenital optic nerve hypoplasia (SOD/ONH spectrum)
- Anti-hyperphagia/anti-obesity pharmacotherapy for the hypothalamic dysfunction subgroup to deliver meaningful BMI and hunger reductions
- Long-acting/physiologic multi-hormone replacement (adrenal/thyroid/GH) that reduces monitoring burden and prevents decompensation as pituitary deficits evolve over childhood

name: Short chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency
description: Short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency is an inherited ACADS-related fatty acid oxidation disorder that impairs energy generation from fats, usually detected on newborn screening with most infants asymptomatic. A minority develop fasting or illness triggered episodes such as hypoglycemia, lethargy, seizures, developmental issues, or later muscle weakness. Care is largely preventive and burdensome with fasting avoidance and sick day plans, but clinicians cannot reliably predict who will become symptomatic and there is no proven disease modifying therapy, leaving persistent ambiguity about long term risk and the need for chronic intervention.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- At-home sick-day/fasting crisis-prevention or rapid-rescue therapy to reduce illness/fasting-triggered metabolic decompensation.
- ACADS-targeted disease-modifying therapy for symptomatic SCADD to prevent/improve seizures, developmental delay, and progressive myopathy.
- Evidence-based chronic metabolic support that meaningfully reduces restrictive diet + fasting avoidance burden and enables more normal feeding/fasting routines.

name: Solar retinopathy
description: Rare photochemical injury to the fovea after unprotected sun or eclipse viewing causing acute central vision loss and scotoma; often improves over 3–6 months but can leave permanent deficits, and there is no proven post-exposure therapy beyond prevention and monitoring, creating need for neuroprotective and retinal repair treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute post-exposure retinal neuroprotection (hours–1–2 days after sun‑gazing/eclipse exposure) to prevent permanent central/paracentral scotoma and preserve ellipsoid-zone integrity on OCT
- RCT-proven anti-inflammatory treatment that improves final visual function vs observation, replacing inconsistent systemic steroid use while avoiding steroid risks (CSC/cataract/IOP)
- Therapy for chronic/incomplete recovery (persistent distortion/scotoma beyond ~3–6 months) targeting repair/regeneration of chronic outer-retinal loss

name: Oropharyngeal cancer | HPV-positive
description: HPV mediated oropharyngeal squamous cell cancer arises in the back of the throat including tonsils and base of tongue, increasingly affecting midlife patients who often become long term survivors. Presentation commonly includes a neck mass with dysphagia and referred ear pain. Treatment is highly curative but still relies on cisplatin based chemoradiation that can leave unpredictable late toxicity, especially swallowing injury, creating pressure to preserve cure while reducing treatment harm. For the minority who recur or metastasize, checkpoint inhibitors benefit only a subset, leaving a need for more durable systemic options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Cisplatin-sparing curative-intent concurrent therapy that maintains definitive RT+cisplatin survival while materially reducing severe systemic/acute toxicity.
- Radioprotective/mucosal-protective drugs or de-intensification–enabling systemic agents that reduce dysphagia and feeding-tube dependence during/after definitive (chemo)RT without compromising cure.
- Higher-depth, more durable systemic options for recurrent/metastatic post-platinum (and post–PD-1) disease beyond current immunotherapy response/survival benchmarks.

name: Parkinsonism | vascular
description: Stroke related parkinsonism with leg predominant gait and balance impairment, often with cognitive and urinary symptoms and minimal tremor; poor levodopa response leaves largely supportive care plus stroke prevention, creating unmet need for therapies that improve gait and reduce falls while slowing motor and cognitive decline.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drug control of shuffling/freezing gait and fall risk in lower-body vascular parkinsonism with poor dopaminergic/levodopa responsiveness.
- Cerebrovascular-targeted disease modification beyond vascular risk-factor control to slow VP progression (mobility/cognition decline).
- Therapies that improve cognitive/behavioral and urinary symptoms without worsening confusion/agitation or postural instability in fall-prone VP patients.

name: Piedra | white
description: White piedra is a superficial Trichosporon hair shaft infection causing soft white to light brown nodules encasing terminal hairs, often asymptomatic or mildly pruritic, typically on pubic, axillary, or facial hair. It is common in young people, especially women, with long hair and humid exposure. The key bottleneck is that shaving or hair removal is most reliably curative but often socially or culturally unacceptable, while topical antifungals are variably effective without shaving and pubic disease frequently recurs, driving need for fast, low burden, non shaving clearance and recurrence prevention.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacologic regimen achieving reliable clinical/mycologic clearance without shaving/cutting hair
- Durable anti-recurrence therapy for pubic/genital white piedra (e.g., post-clearance prophylaxis/regimen preventing reinfection)
- Rapid, low-burden topical that clears in ~1–2 weeks (avoiding prolonged/high-frequency regimens)

name: Spina bifida
description: Spina bifida is a neural tube defect from incomplete spinal closure early in pregnancy that causes irreversible spinal cord and nerve damage, often presenting with an open back lesion, leg weakness or paralysis, hydrocephalus, and lifelong bowel and bladder dysfunction. There is no cure, so care is chronic and high burden, built around continence and kidney protection with clean intermittent catheterization, bowel programs, and poorly tolerated oral anticholinergics that can drive escalation to botulinum toxin injections and surgery, leaving a premium on better tolerated, noninvasive bladder therapies and earlier interventions that reduce lifelong disability.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Well-tolerated (non-anticholinergic) pediatric therapies for spina-bifida neurogenic detrusor overactivity that improve urodynamics/continence while reducing clean intermittent catheterization burden and delaying escalation to botulinum toxin/invasive interventions.
- Drug options for neurogenic bowel that reliably reduce both constipation and fecal incontinence with sustained QoL benefit, avoiding multi-component trial-and-error bowel regimens.
- Early-life neuroprotective/regenerative therapeutics for myelomeningocele that measurably improve lower-extremity motor function/ambulation by reducing permanent nerve damage.

name: Spondylocostal dysostosis
description: Congenital vertebral segmentation and rib malformation disorder causing short-trunk scoliosis; severe cases develop thoracic insufficiency with life-threatening neonatal breathing problems, poor lung growth, recurrent infections and pulmonary hypertension. Care is largely supportive (eg, surgery such as vertical expandable prosthetic titanium ribs) with no disease-modifying therapy, leaving unmet need for early interventions that expand thoracic capacity, preserve cardiopulmonary function, and ultimately address disrupted Notch-pathway somitogenesis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prenatal Notch/somite-segmentation rescue for genetically diagnosed pregnancies to prevent vertebral/rib malformations driving neonatal small-thorax morbidity
- Early pulmonary-hypertension prevention/treatment in the severe restrictive-thorax subset to avoid progression to cardiac failure
- Thoracic-insufficiency pharmacotherapy that increases lung capacity (and reduces recurrent infections) to reduce reliance on supportive care and serial VEPTR expansion surgeries

name: Stomach diverticulosis
description: Stomach diverticulosis usually refers to rare gastric diverticula, often incidental in adults (typically 50 to 70), but sometimes causing chronic dyspepsia and epigastric pain, nausea, early satiety, belching and halitosis from food retention. Care is mostly observation or acid suppression with often temporary relief, while larger lesions over 4 cm carry higher complication risk and respond poorly to medical therapy, leaving surgery as the only reliably effective option for refractory symptoms and prevention of serious events like bleeding or perforation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable non-procedural symptom control for symptomatic gastric diverticulum refractory to PPI/H2/antacids (esp. large >4 cm diverticula).
- Therapies targeting food retention/bacterial overgrowth symptoms (e.g., belching and socially disabling halitosis) beyond acid suppression.
- Medical prevention of major complications in large (>4 cm) diverticula (ulceration, bleeding/hemorrhage, perforation).
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus page (no specific URL)

name: Stress polycythemia / Gaisböck syndrome
description: Stress polycythemia (Gaisböck syndrome) is a relative erythrocytosis from plasma volume contraction, classically in hypertensive overweight male smokers, causing headaches and facial rubor. Care is mainly risk factor control and avoiding diuretics, but thrombotic risk prevention and use of aspirin or venesection are inconsistently applied due to limited syndrome specific evidence and guidance often extrapolated from polycythemia vera.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Plasma-volume–restoring therapy targeting the low plasma volume/hemoconcentration phenotype in apparent erythrocytosis (Gaisböck syndrome)
- Evidence-based thrombosis-prevention/viscosity-reduction strategy for patients at thrombotic risk (currently case-by-case venesection decisions)
- Hypertension regimens that avoid diuretic-associated volume contraction/hemoconcentration while maintaining tight BP control
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus URL for stress polycythemia (Gaisböck syndrome)

name: Syringomyelia
description: Syringomyelia is a rare, often Chiari I associated disorder where disrupted cerebrospinal fluid flow creates a fluid filled cyst within the spinal cord that can enlarge over years, causing chronic pain, headaches, progressive weakness, and loss of pain and temperature sensation plus balance or bowel and bladder dysfunction. Management is largely monitoring and surgery to restore flow or drain the syrinx with pain control and rehabilitation, but recurrence is common and permanent cord injury can leave persistent deficits, driving unmet need for durable, disease modifying and neurorepair approaches beyond iterative neurosurgery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical/post-surgical adjunct drug for refractory syringomyelia achieving objective MRI syrinx shrinkage plus functional improvement (e.g., ASIA motor/sensory gains).
- Neuroregenerative/neuroprotective therapy to reverse persistent neurologic deficits (sensory loss, dysesthesias, weakness) that remain after decompression.
- Better-tolerated, opioid-sparing neuropathic pain therapy for chronic pain/numbness that often persists despite surgery.

name: Tarsal tunnel syndrome
description: Tarsal tunnel syndrome is tibial nerve compression at the ankle causing burning, tingling plantar foot pain that often worsens with standing, walking, and at night. Typical patients have overuse or biomechanical risk such as very flat feet. Management is largely symptomatic with rest, activity modification, orthotics, medications, injections, and sometimes surgery, but diagnosis and predicting responders are uncertain and surgical outcomes are variable, leaving a need for more reliable, function preserving relief.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-sedating, peripherally targeted neuropathic-pain control that preserves walking/standing function (vs CNS AEs/discontinuation with gabapentin/pregabalin and GI harm with NSAIDs)
- Longer-acting local anti-inflammatory/anti-edema therapy (vs short-acting steroid injections), prioritized for patients with slow tibial-nerve conduction predictive of conservative failure
- Adjunct anti-fibrotic/neuroprotective pharmacotherapy for refractory disease to improve outcomes where surgical benefit is variable/uncertain

name: Tetralogy of Fallot
description: Tetralogy of Fallot is a cyanotic congenital heart defect causing low blood oxygen and newborn cyanosis with episodic desaturation spells, often requiring prostaglandin ductal support before surgical repair. While repair improves survival, many patients develop chronic pulmonary valve regurgitation with right heart enlargement, reduced exercise capacity, and ongoing arrhythmia and occasional sudden death risk, driving demand for durable, lower burden approaches that preserve right sided function and prevent late rhythm events.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying drug therapy for repaired TOF with chronic pulmonary regurgitation/RVOT dysfunction that prevents RV dilatation/systolic dysfunction and improves cardiopulmonary performance (e.g., RVEF/RV volumes, VO2max).
- Therapies that reduce ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death risk in repaired TOF (e.g., lowering sustained VT/ICD therapies).
- Safer, lower-burden ductus-patency maintenance for ductal-dependent TOF neonates vs continuous IV alprostadil (reduced apnea/need for ventilation-ready ICU infusion).

name: Thoracic outlet syndrome
description: Thoracic outlet syndrome is a rare compression disorder at the neck to upper chest where nerves or blood vessels are squeezed, causing unilateral neck shoulder and arm pain with tingling numbness weakness and sometimes swelling or cool discolored skin. It often affects otherwise healthy young active adults, especially women with neurogenic disease, and the broad symptom spectrum drives frequent diagnostic delay. Care is largely physical therapy and pain control, with thrombolysis and anticoagulation for clotting forms, leaving unmet needs for earlier cleaner diagnosis, durable non surgical symptom relief, and simpler safer clot prevention.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct pharmacotherapy for PT-refractory neurogenic TOS to improve pain/paresthesias and arm function (VAS, DASH/SF‑36) with fewer CNS (somnolence/dizziness) and NSAID GI/CV toxicities.
- Longer-acting, mechanism-targeted injectable alternative to Botox/nerve blocks that delivers symptom relief well beyond ~2–3 months.
- Safer, easier-to-administer thrombolytic→anticoagulant strategy for venous/arterial TOS thrombosis to dissolve clots and prevent recurrence (reducing reliance on invasive pathways).

name: Thromboangiitis obliterans
description: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) is a rare, progressive, nonatherosclerotic inflammatory occlusion of small and medium vessels in the hands and feet, typically in young to middle aged smokers, causing distal ischemia, Raynaud phenomenon, rest pain, ulcers and sometimes superficial thrombophlebitis with risk of amputation. Management depends on complete tobacco cessation, yet even minimal nicotine exposure can sustain disease, and distal diffuse anatomy often precludes bypass or endovascular revascularization, leaving limited limb salvage options beyond symptom control and infusion therapies such as intravenous iloprost.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non‑nicotine, higher‑efficacy smoking‑cessation pharmacotherapy for TAO/Buerger patients who continue to use tobacco.
- Non‑IV/outpatient limb‑salvage perfusion therapy (e.g., oral/SC prostacyclin‑pathway) matching iloprost‑benchmarked healing/amputation outcomes.
- Drug therapy for distal critical ischemia not amenable to revascularization, improving rest pain, ulcer healing, and major amputation‑free survival.

name: Thrombophlebitis migrans
description: Thrombophlebitis migrans is a recurrent, “moving” superficial vein thrombosis where one inflamed vein segment resolves as new painful, cordlike nodules arise elsewhere. It can involve multiple sites and occasionally deep veins, with risk of serious thromboembolism such as pulmonary embolism. Management is complicated by the need to detect occult malignancy that may emerge months to years later and by uncertain, sometimes anticoagulation refractory disease in cancer associated cases, creating demand for durable recurrence prevention with lower bleeding risk and less burdensome long term therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent recurrent migratory SVT/PE in cancer-associated (Trousseau) thrombophlebitis migrans, including anticoagulation-refractory cases
- Define evidence-based, low-bleeding anticoagulation strategies for highest-risk SVT patients (e.g., thrombus near saphenofemoral junction, active cancer, bleeding-risk conditions) excluded from key trials
- Develop less burdensome regimens than prolonged daily injections (e.g., 45-day fondaparinux), including oral options to avoid injection burden

name: Thyroid hormone resistance syndrome
description: Thyroid hormone resistance syndrome is a rare inherited disorder, usually driven by thyroid hormone receptor beta gene variants, where tissues under respond to thyroid hormone so free thyroid hormones are high while thyroid stimulating hormone is not suppressed and many patients appear clinically near euthyroid but present in childhood or adolescence with goiter and a mix of cardiovascular and neurobehavioral symptoms. Care is symptom driven and highly individualized since goiter can be refractory or recurrent and misdiagnosis can lead to unnecessary invasive treatment, leaving unmet need for clearer diagnosis and monitoring and receptor targeted therapies that normalize feedback without worsening tachycardia or cognitive burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- TRβ mutation-/isoform-selective thyroid-hormone analogs that restore pituitary feedback (TSH suppression/normalize FT4–FT3) without TRα-mediated tachycardia
- Drug therapy to shrink and prevent recurrence of refractory goiter (thyroid-volume endpoint)
- Accessible regimens that improve neurobehavioral/learning symptoms (e.g., ADHD/hyperactivity) beyond current limited-access, 2–3×/day TRIAC

name: Urticaria pigmentosa
description: Urticaria pigmentosa (maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis) is a mast cell driven skin disease often beginning in infancy with brown patches that itch, hive, or blister when rubbed, sometimes with systemic mediator episodes including flushing, gastrointestinal symptoms, hypotension, or anaphylaxis. Many children improve by puberty, but adult onset tends to persist, leaving patients reliant on symptomatic care and high burden options like frequent phototherapy that often relapses within 6 to 12 months, underscoring the need for more durable disease control and better protection from severe reactions such as sting triggered anaphylaxis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable lesion/pruritus clearance for adult-onset/persistent urticaria pigmentosa that avoids high-burden repeated phototherapy and rapid relapse
- Whole-body mast-cell mediator symptom control beyond antihistamines and gut-limited cromoglycate to reduce systemic episodes (e.g., flushing, hypotension/anaphylaxis, diarrhea/GI bleeding)
- Anaphylaxis-risk reduction to decrease reliance on rescue epinephrine (incl. sting-triggered reactions)

name: Vulvar cancer | adenocarcinoma
description: Vulvar cancer is a rare, largely postmenopausal malignancy often preceded by years of vulvar itching before a lesion, bleeding, or pain prompts diagnosis. Care is dominated by surgery, but groin node procedures can cause major morbidity such as chronic lymphedema, making organ and function sparing approaches a priority. Outcomes in advanced or recurrent disease are limited by the lack of a standard, proven systemic regimen, driving unmet need for durable systemic control and biomarker guided options, including HER2 targeted strategies in Paget spectrum tumors and neoadjuvant approaches that reduce vulvar and groin morbidity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable systemic disease control for recurrent/metastatic vulvar adenocarcinoma (esp. post‑platinum/not amenable to curative local therapy)
- HER2‑targeted therapy for the HER2‑overexpressing subset of vulvar adenocarcinoma‑spectrum tumors (notably vulvar extramammary Paget disease)
- Neoadjuvant/organ‑sparing drug regimens to reduce need/extent of morbid groin/vulvar surgery ± adjuvant RT while maintaining local control

name: Xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis
description: Xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis is an uncommon, destructive chronic gallbladder inflammation often associated with gallstones, where bile leaks into the gallbladder wall and drives foamy macrophage rich granulomatous inflammation and dense fibrosis. It presents like acute cholecystitis in older adults with right upper quadrant pain and sometimes jaundice, but can mimic gallbladder cancer on imaging and at surgery. Definitive treatment is cholecystectomy, yet hostile anatomy leads to frequent conversion to open surgery and higher risk of bile duct injury, creating a need for better preoperative diagnosis and safer operative pathways, including drainage plus antibiotics when septic.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Preoperative anti‑fibrotic/anti‑inflammatory therapy for severe XGC wall thickening/fibrosis to reduce laparoscopic→open conversion and bile‑duct injury risk.
- Optimized non‑operative “bridge” regimen (antimicrobial + anti‑inflammatory) for acute/septic XGC to stabilize patients with drainage/antibiotics and avoid emergent high‑risk surgery.
- Upstream gallstone/bile‑driven inflammation intervention in high‑risk chronic cholecystitis to prevent progression to XGC and reduce need for open surgery.

name: Angioleiomyoma
description: Angioleiomyoma is a rare benign vascular smooth muscle tumor, usually presenting in midlife as a solitary slow growing painful subcutaneous nodule often on the lower leg with stimulus triggered paroxysmal pain. Diagnosis is frequently uncertain until excision and pathology. Surgery is typically curative with low recurrence, but patients still face unmet needs around durable pain control and nonsurgical options for lesions in cosmetically or functionally sensitive sites where conservative measures may ease pain without stopping growth.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable non-opioid pain control for painful angioleiomyoma (oral or local) to eliminate paroxysmal pain/tenderness without excision
- Topical/intralesional therapy that halts growth and shrinks lesions in cosmetically/functional critical sites where current nonsurgical options don’t slow growth
- Image-guided intralesional “drug ablation” for deep/intra-articular angioleiomyoma to avoid invasive excision/arthroscopy

name: Anterior spinal artery syndrome
description: Rare acute ischemic spinal cord infarction from anterior spinal artery occlusion, often peri aortic surgery or atherosclerosis, causing sudden back pain, paralysis with loss of pain and temperature and neurogenic bowel or bladder while position and vibration are spared; no evidence based acute therapy reliably reverses established injury so prevention and true disease modifying treatment remain key unmet needs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Evidence-based acute reperfusion (e.g., IV thrombolysis) within ≤4.5–6 hours for suspected embolic/atherosclerotic ASA infarction to improve functional outcomes (mRS/ambulation)
- Rapid neuroprotective pharmacotherapy in the hours after onset to reduce permanent motor paralysis and autonomic dysfunction (bladder/bowel)
- Drug-based peri-aortic-surgery spinal-cord-ischemia prophylaxis/rescue to prevent/reverse delayed paraplegia in high-risk TEVAR/TAAA patients

name: Aortic atresia
description: Aortic atresia is most often part of hypoplastic left heart syndrome where an underdeveloped left ventricle and aorta cannot sustain systemic circulation, so newborns can crash into cardiogenic shock as the ductus arteriosus closes in the first 24 to 48 hours. Survival depends on prostaglandin infusion to keep the ductus open, but apnea and the need for ventilation complicate stabilization and transport. Even after multistage palliation that converts the right ventricle into the systemic pump, the first year remains the highest risk and many survivors face neurodevelopmental injury from hypoperfusion or thromboemboli. Hybrid stent based palliation is an emerging direction.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer, less resource-intensive ductal-patency bridge than continuous alprostadil/PGE1 infusion (reduce apnea/need for ventilatory support)
- Interstage therapy that improves systemic RV function and reduces major complications (mortality/thrombosis)
- Neuroprotective therapy to reduce perioperative hypoxic-ischemic brain injury and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment

name: Basal laminar drusen
description: Basal laminar (cuticular) drusen are small yellow deposits beneath the retinal pigment epithelium on Bruch’s membrane, often seen in younger, female patients. Vision is usually preserved until the fovea is involved, but some progress to geographic atrophy or choroidal neovascularization with vision loss. Management is largely surveillance since there is no indicated therapy for isolated disease and geographic atrophy vision loss is not treatable, leaving a major unmet need for disease modifying approaches that prevent progression and preserve central vision.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prophylactic therapy for isolated basal laminar/cuticular drusen (currently observation-only) to prevent progression to geographic atrophy/choroidal neovascularization and vision loss.
- CFH/complement-pathway targeted therapy for genetically associated, early-adulthood–onset basal laminar drusen to prevent downstream GA/CNV.
- Less-burdensome (non-injection or extended-interval) therapies for BLD patients who develop CNV, including options effective for BLD-associated vitelliform macular detachment where anti-VEGF may not work.

name: Epilepsy | Rolandic
description: Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes, or Rolandic epilepsy, is a childhood focal epilepsy starting in otherwise typical early school age children, often sleep activated and usually remitting by puberty. Seizures are typically brief facial or oral events that can impair speech and cause drooling. The key unmet need is identifying and treating the minority with meaningful neurodevelopmental burden, as language and executive function problems can emerge or worsen and some children progress along an epilepsy aphasia spectrum into spike wave activation in sleep syndromes with skill regression and potential permanent intellectual disability.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Night-only/PRN seizure prevention for infrequent nocturnal seizures with near-zero cognitive/behavioral adverse effects
- Treatments that improve learning/language/attention/behavior during the active phase (not just seizure counts), ideally by reducing sleep-activated epileptiform discharges
- Disease-modifying therapy for atypical evolution to CSWS/Landau-Kleffner achieving complete remission and neurodevelopmental recovery

name: Epilepsy | benign familial infantile
description: Rare inherited epilepsy in otherwise healthy infants, with afebrile seizures starting around 3 to 12 months that often cluster but occur alongside normal development and typically remit by about age 2. The key unmet need is safer infant friendly rescue and short course maintenance options that avoid unnecessary exposure to anti seizure drug risks such as hyponatremia with oxcarbazepine and rare severe skin reactions with carbamazepine while genetic testing guides diagnosis and prognosis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Infant-appropriate (<12y), caregiver-administered rescue therapy for seizure clusters to reduce reliance on benzodiazepines
- Safer first-line maintenance alternative to sodium-channel blockers avoiding hyponatremia (oxcarbazepine) and severe cutaneous reactions (carbamazepine)
- Lower-burden infant formulation/strategy (fewer steps + fewer daily doses) aligned to short, self-limited disease course and enabling earlier weaning

name: Mastocytoma
description: Mastocytoma is an infant-onset cutaneous mast cell lesion, usually a solitary indurated hyperpigmented plaque or nodule that itches and can urticate or blister with rubbing due to mediator release. Most cases regress spontaneously through childhood, so care centers on trigger avoidance and symptomatic relief with antihistamines and short-term topical steroids. Key gaps are infant-safe, lesion-directed options that better control pruritus and degranulation without prolonged systemic therapy, and improved prevention and preparedness for the uncommon but serious risk of anaphylaxis in higher-risk patients.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Infant-safe, lesion-directed topical therapy to prevent rubbing/pressure–triggered degranulation (Darier-sign urtication ± blistering) and rapidly control pruritus without systemic antihistamine reliance
- Pharmacologic anaphylaxis prophylaxis for higher-risk pediatric subsets (e.g., blistering/extensive disease/elevated tryptase/prior anaphylaxis), beyond epinephrine rescue
- Localized mast-cell cytoreduction (e.g., KIT-pathway–directed, topical/low-systemic exposure) for rare high–mediator-release solitary mastocytoma to avoid radical excision and persistent post-excision urtication

name: Blind loop syndrome
description: Blind loop syndrome is a rare post surgical complication where altered intestinal anatomy causes stasis and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, leading to malabsorption with bloating, diarrhea or steatorrhea, weight loss, and nutrient deficiencies such as vitamin B12 deficiency and anemia. Care relies on short courses of broad oral antibiotics and nutritional repletion, but relapse is common because antibiotics do not correct the underlying anatomy, leaving a need for durable microbiome sparing therapies that prevent recurrence and restore absorption without repeated antibiotic cycling or further surgery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable (months-long) recurrence prevention in blind-loop/SIBO patients with predisposing structural problems to avoid repeated 10–14 day/cyclic antibiotic courses.
- Targeted correction of steatorrhea/fat malabsorption and nutritional deficits by preventing bacterial bile-salt disruption and vitamin B12 depletion.
- Microbiome-sparing long-term control that reduces antibiotic-associated complications (e.g., C. difficile) while maintaining symptom control and absorption.

name: Leprosy | borderline
description: Borderline spectrum leprosy is Hansen disease affecting skin and peripheral nerves, causing hypopigmented or red patches with sensory loss and nerve thickening. Borderline forms are prone to type 1 reversal reactions with acute inflammation, pain, and rapid nerve damage. Standard therapy is 12 months of rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine, often alongside prolonged corticosteroids for neuritis. Key unmet needs are earlier diagnosis to prevent disability, steroid sparing options that protect nerve function, and shorter better tolerated regimens without increasing relapse risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing control of Type 1 (reversal) reactions/acute neuritis in borderline leprosy to prevent irreversible nerve-function impairment
- ≤6-month, better-tolerated multidrug therapy for multibacillary/borderline disease without increased relapse (improving adherence vs dapsone/clofazimine toxicity)
- Post-cure therapies for chronic leprosy neuropathy/neuropathic pain that improve nerve recovery and achieve meaningful pain reduction

name: Boutonneuse fever
description: Boutonneuse fever (Mediterranean spotted fever) is a tick borne Rickettsia conorii infection that presents abruptly about a week after a bite with high fever, severe headache, myalgias, a black eschar at the bite site, and a maculopapular rash often involving palms and soles and sparing the face. Early symptoms are nonspecific, diagnosis is easy to miss, and delays in antibiotics can be life threatening, especially in older or immunocompromised patients. Empiric doxycycline works quickly but requires multi day courses, creating unmet need for doxycycline sparing options, scalable regimens for severe disease, and validated ultra short course treatment.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pregnancy- and doxycycline-contraindication–compatible empiric oral anti-rickettsial therapy with doxycycline-like outcomes
- IV/adjunct regimens for severe/complicated cases (e.g., vomiting/obtunded) that reduce hospitalization intensity and prolonged-course needs
- Validated ultra-short oral regimens (single-day or 1–2 day) to replace conventional 5–14 day courses and improve tolerability/adherence

name: Calcific band keratopathy
description: Calcific band keratopathy is a slowly progressive corneal degeneration where calcium deposits form a horizontal band in the superficial cornea, often starting asymptomatically but eventually causing irritation, photophobia, pain, foreign body sensation, and reduced visual acuity. Care is still largely procedural with epithelial debridement and ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid chelation, which can be surface toxic, and recurrence is common when underlying drivers are not controlled, leaving a need for non-surgical calcium clearing and more durable prevention.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical, epithelium-sparing calcium-clearing eye drops that improve Snellen visual acuity and pain while avoiding scraping/EDTA toxicity
- Recurrence-prevention/durable control therapy for patients with persistent underlying drivers to reduce repeat chelation
- Post-procedure healing/tolerability adjuncts to shorten bandage-lens/topical-drop use and reduce complications (pain, infection, scarring/edema, irregular astigmatism)

name: Renal agenesis | bilateral
description: Bilateral renal agenesis is a rare fetal malformation in which both kidneys and often the ureters fail to form, eliminating fetal urine and rapidly causing anhydramnios that leads to lethal pulmonary hypoplasia. Diagnosis is typically prenatal on ultrasound, and without intervention most infants die shortly after birth. Serial amnioinfusions can sometimes rescue lung development long enough to reach dialysis access, but survivors face immediate end stage kidney failure, high neonatal morbidity, and prolonged dialysis while awaiting transplant. The key unmet need is durable fetal or neonatal kidney replacement, regeneration, or other disease modifying options beyond supportive fetal therapy and organ replacement.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prenatal pulmonary-rescue therapy for early-pregnancy renal anhydramnios/bilateral renal agenesis to prevent pulmonary hypoplasia and improve neonatal survival to dialysis access ≥14 days.
- Renal replacement/regeneration (cell/gene/tissue therapy) to provide sustained kidney function so survivors are not dialysis-dependent from birth.
- Genotype-directed early-gestation molecular rescue (e.g., GREB1L-variant fetuses) to restore metanephros/ureteric-bud development before irreversible non-formation.

name: Bile duct cancer | adenocarcinoma
description: Cholangiocarcinoma is a rare bile duct adenocarcinoma that is usually silent until it presents late with biliary obstruction, causing jaundice, itching, dark urine, pale stools, abdominal pain, and weight loss, typically in older adults. First line care for unresectable or metastatic disease relies on gemcitabine plus cisplatin with an added checkpoint inhibitor, but real world patients with persistent jaundice and elevated bilirubin are often hard to treat and underrepresented in pivotal trials. After progression, evidence to guide second line therapy is limited and benefits are modest, leaving a need for more effective, broadly tolerable systemic options and earlier detection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Larger and more durable 1L OS benefit beyond durvalumab+GemCis (TOPAZ‑1) while reducing severe toxicity
- Cisplatin-optional regimens effective in jaundiced/biliary-obstructed patients with impaired liver tests/high bilirubin who are often trial-ineligible
- More effective and more convenient post-progression therapy than 2L FOLFOX for the biomarker-negative majority

name: Brachial plexus neuritis
description: Brachial plexus neuritis (Parsonage Turner syndrome, neuralgic amyotrophy) is an acute inflammatory neuropathy causing sudden, severe shoulder and upper arm pain often worse at night, followed by weakness, with recovery that can take months to years and sometimes leaves residual pain and functional loss. Care is largely supportive because no randomized trials support any therapy, creating unmet needs for early attack aborting immunomodulation, durable non opioid pain control, and recurrence prevention especially in hereditary, trigger prone disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute disease‑modifying immunomodulation within ~1 month of onset to shorten severe pain and accelerate motor/strength recovery vs supportive care.
- Recurrence‑prevention therapy (especially for hereditary neuralgic amyotrophy) to reduce attack rate/extend attack‑free intervals and prevent cumulative disability.
- More effective, preferably non‑opioid analgesia for acute attacks (weeks to ~1 month) with durability to treat persistent post‑acute pain/fatigue.

name: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency
description: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency is an inherited fatty acid oxidation disorder that leaves patients unable to reliably use long chain fats for energy, especially during fasting or exertion. The common myopathic form often begins in childhood or adolescence with trigger driven attacks of severe muscle pain and weakness, rhabdomyolysis, and dark urine from myoglobin, which can escalate into kidney threatening crises requiring intensive supportive care. Management focuses on strict avoidance of triggers and metabolic support such as frequent dosing triheptanoin, but adherence is difficult and gastrointestinal side effects are common, leaving a need for more dependable attack prevention and faster rescue therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Attack-prevention that enables normal daily activity by preventing exercise/fasting/cold/stress-triggered myalgia/rhabdomyolysis (including patients symptomatic with moderate exertion)
- Rapid “attack-abortive”/renal-protective pharmacotherapy to reduce rhabdomyolysis-related kidney injury and avoid escalation to IV hydration/dialysis during myoglobinuria crises
- Lower-burden metabolic therapy/formulation with fewer GI adverse effects and reduced dosing frequency vs triheptanoin (≥4x/day)

name: Artery dissection | carotid
description: Extracranial carotid artery dissection is a rare tear in the carotid artery wall, often in otherwise healthy adults around age 45, presenting with headache or facial and neck pain sometimes with partial Horner syndrome and carrying an early stroke risk highest in the first 2 to 4 weeks. Care relies on antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy, but choices are individualized due to uncertain comparative benefit and bleeding tradeoffs, with limited evidence for direct oral anticoagulants. Key unmet needs are faster, more reliable diagnosis and risk stratification, safer standardized antithrombotic regimens, and therapies that promote vessel healing and prevent persistent aneurysm.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early, risk-stratified stroke-prevention therapy that lowers ischemic events in the first 2–4 weeks post-diagnosis while minimizing intracranial hemorrhage risk in high-bleed-risk patients
- Fixed-dose oral anticoagulation with a better bleeding/monitoring profile than heparin/VKA pathways (reduced lab monitoring burden)
- Adjunct vessel-healing/remodeling therapy to accelerate recanalization and reduce dissecting-aneurysm/pseudoaneurysm persistence or evolution beyond what antithrombotics achieve

name: Sarcoidosis | cardiac
description: Cardiac sarcoidosis is an inflammatory granulomatous infiltration of the myocardium that can scar over time, presenting with atrioventricular conduction block, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy and heart failure, with risk of sudden cardiac death. Treatment is typically corticosteroid led immunosuppression, but diagnosis often cannot be biopsy confirmed and relies on imaging and probability. Relapse is common during steroid tapering, creating demand for steroid sparing regimens, and the field lacks convincing randomized trials tied to hard clinical outcomes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing control achieving FDG‑PET remission while reducing prednisone exposure and glucocorticoid-toxicity/QoL burden.
- Therapies that cut sustained VT/appropriate ICD therapies and improve LVEF (hard outcomes) in patients with recurrent VT despite current antiarrhythmic + immunosuppressive therapy.
- HF-safe, non–TNF‑α immunomodulators for refractory/persistent inflammation with simpler (ideally oral/subcutaneous) administration vs infusion-center biologics.

name: Cardiac tamponade
description: Cardiac tamponade is a time critical emergency where pericardial fluid or blood compresses the heart, impairing filling and rapidly causing shock or death. Patients typically present with dyspnea and obstructive shock signs including hypotension, jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus. Treatment is urgent pericardial drainage, but high recurrence after pericardiocentesis in malignant effusions and safer, more predictable bleeding management in anticoagulated patients remain key unmet needs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Anti-recurrence intrapericardial therapy for malignant effusion–driven tamponade to prevent post-drainage recurrence and repeat procedures
- Safer heparin-reversal/hemostasis drugs for iatrogenic/anticoagulated hemopericardium to reduce protamine-associated cardiopulmonary collapse/anaphylaxis risk
- Rapid pericardial-fluid–reducing pharmacotherapy to bridge/avoid invasive pericardiocentesis and its complications in selected patients

name: Cartilage-hair hypoplasia
description: Inherited skeletal dysplasia causing congenital short-limbed short stature and sparse hair with variable immunodeficiency leading to recurrent infections and risks of severe varicella, Hirschsprung disease, bone marrow failure, and lymphoma/leukemia; management is largely supportive with immunoglobulin replacement and infection precautions, and while hematopoietic stem cell transplant can correct severe immune defects it does not improve growth or skeletal features, leaving a need for non-transplant disease-modifying options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Immune reconstitution to prevent severe/recurrent infections (incl. dangerous varicella) and reduce reliance on chronic prophylactic antibiotics + IVIG
- Cancer/lymphoma risk–reducing or early-intercept therapy to address markedly elevated lymphoma/BCC burden and late-stage presentation
- Non-transplant drug therapy to restore erythropoiesis/reduce transfusion dependence and control immune dysregulation in severe CHH hematologic phenotypes

name: Prostate cancer | castration-resistant
description: Castration-resistant prostate cancer is prostate cancer that keeps growing despite ongoing androgen deprivation and castrate testosterone levels, sometimes first signaled only by a rising prostate-specific antigen. As it becomes metastatic it is frequently dominated by bone metastases, driving pain, fractures, and other skeletal-related events. Treatment is constrained by cross-resistance between sequential androgen receptor targeted agents and by regimen burden and toxicity, such as strict fasting plus chronic steroid use with abiraterone. The premium is for disease-modifying options beyond the androgen axis that better prevent skeletal morbidity and are easier to sustain long term.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Bone-metastasis–directed therapies that prevent/delay symptomatic skeletal events and reduce SRE-driven pain/functional impairment
- Non–AR-axis, non-taxane options for progressive mCRPC after prior NAAD + ≥1 taxane (incl. PSMA-independent activity) with improved OS/rPFS and less marrow toxicity
- Safer long-duration nmCRPC regimens for high-risk patients (PSA doubling time ≤10 months) that extend metastasis-free survival with fewer CNS/fall/fracture effects and simpler administration (no fasting + chronic steroids)

name: Cat-scratch disease
description: Cat-scratch disease is a Bartonella henselae infection typically acquired from a kitten scratch, disproportionately affecting children under 15, causing an inoculation papule or pustule followed by tender regional lymphadenopathy with fatigue and sometimes fever that can linger for 2 to 4 months. Most cases are self-limited, and short-course azithromycin has limited evidence for improving overall outcomes, leaving a gap in reliably shortening symptoms or preventing suppuration that may require drainage. The highest-stakes unmet need is in disseminated or immunocompromised cases, where prolonged multi-antibiotic regimens are needed and complications drive burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapy proven to shorten overall duration of uncomplicated CSD lymphadenopathy (e.g., time-to-resolution/≥80% node resolution by day 30)
- Drug regimen for suppurated CSD lymphadenitis that avoids repeat aspirations/incision/excision by day 28 while reducing node volume/pain
- Safer, more reliable regimens for immunocompromised and disseminated/atypical CSD that avoid weeks–months multi-antibiotic/IV aminoglycoside therapy and reduce relapse

name: Complex regional pain syndrome | type 2
description: Complex regional pain syndrome type 2 is a post injury limb pain disorder triggered by a defined peripheral nerve injury, where pain becomes disproportionate and disabling with burning pain, extreme touch sensitivity, swelling, autonomic skin changes, and loss of movement. There is no cure and symptoms can worsen or spread, leaving patients reliant on imperfect symptom control. Outcomes are highly time sensitive since early treatment offers the best chance of improvement or remission. Key unmet needs include earlier recognition and effective disease modifying therapy, and targeted options for an immune defined subgroup with β2 adrenergic and muscarinic 2 receptor autoantibodies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early post–nerve-injury “warm/acute” CRPS-2 intercept therapy to prevent progression to chronic/cold disease and long-term disability.
- Biomarker-guided immunomodulation for an autoantibody-positive CRPS subgroup (e.g., β2-adrenergic/M2-muscarinic receptor autoantibodies) to better control pain + edema.
- Non-sedating, simplified-dosing analgesics that deliver meaningful improvement on pain NRS + allodynia + CRPS Severity Score versus multi-dose gabapentinoids with dizziness/somnolence.

name: Malaria | cerebral
description: Most severe neurologic complication of Plasmodium falciparum malaria causing coma and seizures, largely in young children in sub-Saharan Africa; despite artesunate, mortality remains ~15–25% and survivors often have lasting cognitive and neurologic disability. Key unmet needs are resource-light adjunctive therapies to prevent brain swelling and intracranial pressure related death and to reduce long-term neurocognitive sequelae where intensive support like mechanical ventilation is limited.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunctive anti–brain-swelling/ICP-lowering therapy with artesunate to reduce persistent ~17% case-fatality in high–brain-edema risk children
- Neuroprotective + seizure-modulating adjunct to prevent long-term neurocognitive/neurologic sequelae in survivors (esp. <5 years)
- Simplified, field-deployable severe-malaria regimen that reduces IV/ICU infrastructure needs, timed dosing, and post-treatment monitoring burden

name: Choledochal cyst
description: Congenital dilation of the bile ducts that obstructs bile flow, usually presenting in infancy or childhood with jaundice, right upper abdominal pain or palpable mass, pale stools, and episodes of cholangitis or pancreatitis. Definitive care is cyst excision with biliary reconstruction, but patients still face late anastomotic strictures, recurrent cholangitis, antibiotic resistance from prolonged prophylaxis, and a lifelong elevated risk of biliary malignancy, creating unmet need for better long term prevention, surveillance, and risk reduction.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Chemoprevention to reduce lifelong post-resection cholangiocarcinoma risk (esp. resected Todani type I/IV patients).
- Anti-fibrotic/anti-stricture adjunct to hepaticoenterostomy/hepaticojejunostomy to prevent bile-stasis complications (stones, recurrent cholangitis/pancreatitis) and reduce re-interventions.
- Long-term, resistance-sparing prophylaxis to prevent recurrent ascending cholangitis in patients with biliary-enteric diversion, reducing reliance on chronic broad-spectrum antibiotics.

name: Cholesteryl ester transfer protein deficiency
