description: Pituitary apoplexy is a time critical hemorrhage or infarction of the pituitary, usually within a pituitary adenoma, causing sudden severe headache, cranial nerve palsies and vision loss and sometimes adrenal crisis with hypotension and altered consciousness. Treatment hinges on rapid hydrocortisone and selective urgent decompressive surgery when vision is threatened. Long term, hypopituitarism is common with about 80 percent requiring hormone replacement and complete recovery in only 5 to 37 percent, leaving persistent endocrine morbidity and, in those presenting with blindness, limited visual recovery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute pituitary cytoprotective/regenerative therapy to raise complete pituitary-function recovery above 5–37% and reduce chronic hormone replacement need (~80%).
- Adjunct anti-edema/neuroprotective therapy to improve visual-field/acuity recovery in patients presenting with unilateral/bilateral vision loss.
- Longer-acting, field/ED-deployable glucocorticoid regimen that avoids continuous IV infusion and reduces need for neurosurgical HDU transfer/monitoring.

name: Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia
description: Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia is a rare interstitial lung disease pattern with relatively uniform alveolar inflammation and fibrosis, often in non smoking middle aged women with progressive breathlessness and cough over weeks to months and lower lobe ground glass changes on high resolution computed tomography. Care is largely empiric immunosuppression with little NSIP specific trial or guideline support, and antifibrotics are not well studied, creating a need for better tolerated steroid sparing and disease modifying options that prevent progressive fibrosing decline.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Better-tolerated antifibrotic for progressive-fibrosing NSIP that preserves/improves FVC benefit while reducing nintedanib GI AEs and discontinuations.
- Targeted steroid-sparing immunomodulator that stabilizes moderate–severe NSIP without broad immunosuppression boxed-warning risks and intensive monitoring.
- Relapse-preventing/remission-inducing therapy with durable steroid-free stability, reducing progression to refractory rescue regimens and backed by NSIP-specific evidence.

name: Nonsyndromic aplasia cutis congenita
description: Nonsyndromic aplasia cutis congenita is a rare birth defect in which a newborn has a localized area of missing skin, usually a single scalp vertex lesion resembling an ulcer or open wound. Small defects are managed with cleansing and topical antibacterial ointment and often heal over weeks to months but leave an atrophic, hairless scar. More severe cases can involve underdeveloped skull and exposed dura, raising high stakes risks of infection and life threatening hemorrhage and sometimes requiring surgical repair, underscoring the need for neonate safe, scar sparing closure and hair bearing skin regeneration.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Hair-follicle–preserving (scar-minimizing) regeneration for small vertex-scalp lesions that otherwise heal into an atrophic, hairless scar/alopecia.
- Neonate-safe, low-sensitization topical antimicrobial/barrier for prolonged daily wound care (avoiding bacitracin allergy/anaphylaxis and silver sulfadiazine restrictions in newborns).
- Fast-acting pro-healing topical/biologic for large/deep scalp defects with skull/dura involvement to shorten exposure time and reduce hemorrhage/infection risk.

name: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
description: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a potentially treatable older adult syndrome where excess cerebrospinal fluid enlarges the ventricles and causes a gait-first triad of walking impairment, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence that develops over months. Care remains largely procedural, with shunt surgery the only proven therapy, yet many patients present atypically or are hard to distinguish from other neurodegenerative conditions, making diagnosis and response prediction unreliable. Shunt complications and failures including obstruction, infection, and overdrainage drive revisions, and cognitive and urinary benefits are less consistent than gait improvement.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical, disease-directed drug therapy that produces clinically meaningful gait/balance improvement (e.g., 10‑meter walk + TUG composite) to reduce reliance on shunt surgery
- Therapies that improve less shunt-responsive symptoms—cognition and urinary urgency/incontinence—especially in biomarker-defined patients with comorbid Alzheimer pathology and diminished post-shunt gains
- Adjunct/local pharmacologic approaches that reduce shunt complications and revision drivers (infection, obstruction, overdrainage → subdural collections/hematoma)

name: Placental insufficiency
description: Placental insufficiency is a pregnancy complication in which abnormal placentation and impaired uteroplacental perfusion limit oxygen and nutrient transfer to the fetus, driving fetal stress and growth restriction with downstream neurodevelopmental risk. Diagnosis often follows lagging uterine growth and ultrasound findings, with umbilical artery Doppler used to stratify severity and trigger high intensity, sometimes inpatient, surveillance. With no disease modifying therapy, care centers on monitoring and timing delivery, leaving major unmet needs for treatments that restore placental function, reduce the surveillance burden, and safely prolong gestation while protecting fetal development.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pregnancy-safe prophylaxis to prevent placental-insufficiency–driven FGR in high‑risk pregnancies.
- Disease-modifying placental therapy to safely prolong gestation in severe early-onset placental insufficiency/FGR and reduce need for inpatient/twice‑weekly surveillance.
- Fetal-protective adjunct to improve fetal wellbeing and reduce hypoxic brain injury in early-onset severe FGR (neurodevelopmental outcomes).

name: Postgastrectomy syndrome
description: Postgastrectomy syndrome is a cluster of meal triggered problems after partial or total gastrectomy driven by rapid gastric emptying and disrupted gut hormone control, causing early gastrointestinal and vasomotor symptoms and later reactive hypoglycemia. Symptoms often lead to food avoidance, weight loss, and nutritional deficiencies including common vitamin B12 and iron deficiency anemia. Management relies on dietary changes plus agents like acarbose and injectable somatostatin analogs, but gastrointestinal side effects and injection burden limit adherence, leaving demand for better tolerated oral options that stabilize postprandial glucose and protect nutrition.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- GLP‑1/insulin‑axis modulation to prevent late dumping/post‑bariatric hypoglycemia (reduce Level 2/3 hypoglycemic events) with better tolerability than acarbose.
- Non‑injectable therapy for early dumping (≤1 hour post‑meal vasomotor/GI attacks) with somatostatin‑analog–like efficacy without daily injections.
- Drug therapy that reduces symptom‑driven food avoidance/lifestyle constraints and prevents rapid weight loss, nutritional deficiencies, and dehydration in severe cases.

name: Proximal renal tubular acidosis
description: Proximal renal tubular acidosis (type 2 RTA) is a proximal tubule bicarbonate reabsorption defect causing urinary bicarbonate wasting and hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, often presenting in infancy with dehydration, weakness, rickets or osteomalacia, and growth impairment. Treatment is largely supportive with very high dose alkali replacement often plus thiazides, but it adds substantial daily pill and electrolyte burden, can worsen hypokalemia, and does not modify the underlying disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying restoration of proximal bicarbonate transport in genetic pRTA (e.g., SLC4A4/NBCe1-linked AR proximal RTA with ocular abnormalities)
- High-capacity, palatable, low-frequency oral alkalinization that meets very high alkali needs without QID dosing (esp. infants/children)
- Potassium-sparing acid–base correction that avoids alkali-induced kaliuresis/hypokalemia and reduces monitoring burden

name: Pulmonary stenosis
description: Pulmonary valve stenosis is usually a congenital narrowing of the pulmonary valve that restricts blood flow to the lungs, often detected by an infant heart murmur; severe cases cause exertional dyspnea and fatigue or neonatal cyanosis with right sided heart failure. Key unmet needs include safer alternatives to prolonged alprostadil bridging given apnea risk, reducing post repair pulmonary regurgitation, and improving durability of pulmonary artery stents to avoid restenosis and repeat interventions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ICU-sparing ductal-patency drug for ductal-dependent critical neonatal pulmonary stenosis that avoids continuous PGE1/alprostadil infusion and reduces apnea/ventilatory-support risk
- Adjunct therapy to prevent/mitigate late pulmonary regurgitation → RV dilation after balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty (esp. severe/early-infancy cases) to reduce pulmonary valve replacement need
- Anti-proliferative therapy to prevent tissue-ingrowth in-stent restenosis after pulmonary-artery stenting for peripheral pulmonary stenosis (improve durability vs repeat interventions)

name: Oesophagostomiasis
description: Focal West African intestinal helminth infection where Oesophagostomum bifurcum forms inflammatory colonic nodules, often presenting as appendicitis like acute abdomen or a painful periumbilical mass in school aged children. Albendazole can shrink nodules but does not stop rainy season reinfection, leaving a need for durable prevention, better diagnostics, and surgery sparing rapid cures.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Surgery-sparing oral therapy that rapidly clears intestinal-wall nodules/Dapaong tumour (esp. pediatric cases)
- Transmission-blocking/long-acting (seasonally targeted) regimen to prevent rainy-season reinfection and target stages surviving in intestinal-wall nodules
- Single-dose broad-spectrum empiric deworming that reliably cures both O. bifurcum and hookworm in mixed infections

name: Olivopontocerebellar atrophy
description: Olivopontocerebellar atrophy, often referring clinically to the cerebellar subtype of multiple system atrophy, is a rare progressive neurodegenerative disorder that typically starts in the mid 50s with worsening gait and limb ataxia and slurred speech, followed early by autonomic failure such as orthostatic symptoms and urinary dysfunction that drives disability and complications. Management is largely symptomatic because there is no cure, creating a major need for disease slowing therapies and better tolerated treatments for autonomic dysfunction that preserve function and quality of life.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy that slows mortality-adjusted clinical progression (UMSARS/mUMSARS + survival) over ~72 weeks.
- Durable neurogenic orthostatic hypotension/autonomic-failure therapy with proven functional benefit (not just BP) and reduced supine-HTN risk/monitoring + less burdensome dosing.
- Symptom-targeted treatment that meaningfully improves MSA-C cerebellar motor deficits (gait/limb ataxia/speech), beyond today’s partial symptomatic ceiling.

name: Pyeloureteritis cystica
description: Pyeloureteritis cystica (ureteritis cystica) is a rare, benign upper urinary tract condition with multiple small submucosal ureteral cysts driven by chronic irritation from stones or recurrent infection, often in older diabetic women. It is frequently an incidental imaging finding but can present with hematuria or flank pain. The core unmet need is reliable, noninvasive differentiation from upper tract urothelial cancer to avoid unnecessary invasive workups, since there is no lesion specific therapy beyond treating underlying causes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Lesion-targeted anti-inflammatory/anti-fibrotic therapy to prevent cyst/scar-related ureteral obstruction and pain in symptomatic patients.
- Anti-infective strategies that eradicate persistent/recurrent upper-tract infection to reduce hematuria/uroinfections when short-course antibiotics fail.
- Non-antibiotic (or immune-based) prophylaxis to prevent recurrent UTIs in older/diabetic patients while avoiding long-term antibiotic prophylaxis harms/resistance.

name: Radial nerve lesion
description: Radial nerve injury or compression causing wrist drop with loss of wrist, finger, and thumb extension, often with dorsal hand sensory loss and pain. Care is largely splinting and rehabilitation with surgery for persistent deficits, and recovery can take months up to a year. Key unmet needs include faster nerve repair and better tolerated pain control since neuropathic analgesics often cause CNS side effects and topical capsaicin can be irritating.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute pro-regeneration therapy to restore wrist/finger/thumb extension and functional grip within ~6–8 weeks in traumatic/compressive radial nerve palsy
- Adjunct neurorepair therapy for patients without signs of reinnervation by 3–4 months to improve completeness of reinnervation and reduce persistent deficits
- Better-tolerated (ideally local/targeted and/or long-acting) neuropathic-pain control with fewer CNS side effects/discontinuations vs systemic agents

name: Reactive arthritis
description: Infection triggered inflammatory arthritis emerging 1 to 6 weeks after a gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection, typically affecting knees and ankles with possible sacroiliac, eye, and urinary inflammation. Many cases resolve in weeks to months, but a subset becomes chronic or recurrent, especially in HLA-B27 carriers. Current care is largely symptomatic and step up, and antibiotics do not improve outcomes once arthritis is established, leaving a need for therapies that shorten disease course and prevent chronicity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent chronic/recurrent reactive arthritis in high-risk patients (HLA‑B27+ and/or Chlamydia-triggered), including control of chronic axial/sacroiliac disease.
- Develop curative anti-infective “anti-persistence” therapies for chronic Chlamydia-induced reactive arthritis (>6 months) where antibiotics don’t reliably clear arthritis.
- Provide better-tolerated, evidence-backed options for NSAID failures to reduce reliance on immunosuppressive DMARD/TNF step-up therapy with unclear indications.

name: Ossifying fibroma
description: Rare benign fibro-osseous jaw tumor that replaces normal bone with fibrous tissue, often asymptomatic until it causes jaw expansion, facial swelling, asymmetry, and tooth shifting. Treatment is surgery, but recurrence can be substantial, especially in children, and syndromic cases may be multifocal, driving a need for therapies that reduce recurrence, downstage surgery, and prevent new lesions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Post-op adjuvant therapy to cut recurrence in juvenile/high-risk ossifying fibroma and reduce repeat jaw surgeries/long surveillance.
- Neoadjuvant/downstaging medical therapy to preserve jaw bone and avoid extensive resection and reconstructive bone grafting.
- Systemic prevention/maintenance therapy for CDC73 (HPT‑JT) patients to prevent new lesions/control multifocal locally aggressive jaw tumors (incl. unresectable disease).

name: Osteitis fibrosa
description: Osteitis fibrosa cystica is a rare late stage bone disorder from prolonged excess parathyroid hormone activity, often in severe uncontrolled hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease. Excess osteoclast activity drives bone pain, deformity, fractures, and brown tumor lesions, with high disability risk. While parathyroid surgery can reverse many skeletal changes, medical control in dialysis is constrained by calcimimetic related hypocalcemia and gastrointestinal intolerance plus a heavy phosphate binder pill burden and low adherence, leaving demand for simpler mineral control and faster bone rebuilding.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid bone-structure rescue (pain, fracture prevention/repair, brown-tumor lesion resolution) in late-stage/severe hyperparathyroidism/CKD patients beyond PTH lowering
- Better-tolerated PTH suppression in dialysis patients with less hypocalcemia and GI intolerance than cinacalcet-like calcimimetics
- Simplified CKD-MBD regimens to reduce meal-timed TID phosphate binders and frequent Ca/P lab monitoring without sacrificing phosphate/PTH control

name: Osteochondritis dissecans
description: Osteochondritis dissecans is a joint disorder in which subchondral bone under the cartilage loses blood supply and can die, letting bone and cartilage fragments loosen and cause pain and impaired joint motion, often in highly active adolescents. Patients may have months of vague activity related knee pain that can progress to locking or catching. Management is prolonged and uncertain, with conservative care taking about 6 months and healing rates only 50 to 75 percent in juveniles and 50 percent or less in adults, who often require surgery, leaving a need for faster, more reliable healing and durable cartilage restoration.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Intra-articular therapy to boost and accelerate healing of stable juvenile knee OCD lesions beyond current ~50–75% conservative healing and shorten the ~6-month recovery pathway.
- Non-surgical pharmacologic/biologic option for skeletally mature/adult knee OCD to improve ≤50% nonoperative healing and avoid surgery after 3–6 months conservative failure.
- Adjunct joint-preservation therapy to prevent cartilage degeneration/osteoarthritis and improve long-term durability beyond fibrocartilage-type repair, especially in higher-risk patients (deeper lesions, older age, higher BMI).

name: Adenoma | sebaceous
description: Sebaceous adenoma is a benign, usually solitary oil gland tumor presenting as a slow growing painless yellowish papule or nodule on the face or scalp in older adults, typically managed with simple excision. The main unmet need is when it signals Muir Torre syndrome, where patients face heightened internal cancer risk, need biopsy plus genetics and lifelong surveillance, and often develop multiple lesions with cumulative procedural and disfigurement burden. Chemoprevention and disease modifying options remain limited, with retinoids supported mainly by case experience and tolerability constraints.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical topical/lesion-directed therapy that reliably clears solitary sebaceous adenomas (vs excision/shave biopsy)
- Better-tolerated long-term chemoprevention to reduce new sebaceous adenomas in Muir–Torre syndrome (improving on isotretinoin-based regimens)
- Systemic cancer-preventive regimens for Muir–Torre/Lynch that reduce both cutaneous sebaceous tumors and visceral malignancies beyond retinoid-based case experience

name: Osteopoikilosis
description: Osteopoikilosis is a rare, usually incidental sclerosing bone dysplasia marked by small round sclerotic bone spots on x ray near joints. Most patients are asymptomatic, but about 15 to 20 percent have joint pain and effusions that can be persistent. The biggest practical gap is diagnostic, since the imaging pattern can mimic osteoblastic metastases and trigger unnecessary cancer workups. For symptomatic patients, care is largely supportive with no standardized regimen and no proven disease modifying therapy, with lesion targeted options such as bisphosphonates used inconsistently and with controversial benefit.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, non-opioid pain control that restores/maintains daily functioning for the symptomatic subset with persistent pain.
- Anti-inflammatory therapy that reduces recurrent joint swelling/effusion (beyond episodic analgesia) in patients with joint pain/swelling/effusion.
- Disease-modifying option for rare high-symptom “active lesion” cases where current pharmacologic approaches are non-standardized/controversial.

name: Palindromic rheumatism
description: Relapsing inflammatory arthritis with sudden, severe, unpredictable flares of painful swollen joints that resolve to normal between attacks without lasting damage; key unmet needs are evidence based disease modifying therapy to control attacks and prevent progression to rheumatoid arthritis, plus clearer diagnostic criteria and better understanding of underlying biology.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent progression to persistent rheumatoid arthritis in biomarker-high-risk palindromic rheumatism (RF+/anti-CCP+).
- Rapid, reliable flare-abortive therapy for unpredictable, debilitating PR attacks with variable NSAID response.
- Safer long-term flare prevention that reduces NSAID boxed-warning CV/GI risks and avoids hydroxychloroquine/DMARD monitoring burdens.

name: Papillary hidradenoma
description: Rare benign tumor of anogenital mammary like apocrine glands, usually a small solitary vulvar or perianal nodule in midlife women, often asymptomatic but can itch, ulcerate, bleed, or discharge. The main unmet need is earlier accurate diagnosis since it mimics common lesions and is often confirmed only after excision. Complete local excision is typically curative, with recurrence mainly after incomplete removal and malignant transformation very rare.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Paranasal sinus cancer | squamous cell carcinoma
description: Rare sinonasal mucosal squamous cell carcinoma arising in the paranasal sinuses or nasal cavity, often mistaken for sinus disease until unilateral blockage or bloody discharge appears; silent early growth leads to late, locally advanced presentation near the eyes and brain, making curative treatment difficult and surgery and chemoradiation highly morbid, driving need for earlier detection, organ preserving downstaging, and biomarker guided systemic and neoadjuvant approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neoadjuvant/induction drug regimens to downstage locally advanced paranasal/sinonasal SCC and enable orbit/skull-base preservation without sacrificing curative local control.
- Systemic or combined-modality drug strategies to improve 1-year local control/3-year failure-free survival in unresectable or excessively morbid T4 disease (e.g., carotid/cavernous sinus/brain/orbital apex involvement).
- Biomarker-guided systemic therapy (e.g., PD‑L1–stratified immunotherapy combinations) to increase ORR and durable benefit in recurrent/metastatic or post–platinum/RT-failure sinonasal SCC.

name: Macular dystrophy | patterned
description: Inherited macular retinal pigment epithelium disorder marked by patterned pigment deposition and lipofuscin accumulation, often linked to PRPH2 variants; typically silent until the 40s to 50s then causes gradual central visual distortion and loss. Progression is usually slow but some patients develop geographic atrophy after 60 or choroidal neovascularization requiring anti vascular endothelial growth factor injections. There is no evidence based therapy to clear the underlying pigment and lipofuscin, so care is monitoring, low vision support, and complication management.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy that halts/reverses RPE lipofuscin/pigment accumulation to prevent progressive central vision loss.
- Therapy to prevent geographic atrophy/retinal cell loss (noted esp. in patients >60) and preserve central vision.
- Lower-burden, safer CNV treatment for the ~15% with wet-AMD–like neovascularization, reducing frequent intravitreal injections and procedure/agent-related ocular risks.

name: Periventricular nodular heterotopia
description: Periventricular nodular heterotopia is a fetal neuronal migration disorder where neurons form nodules lining the ventricles, creating a structural driver of epilepsy that often presents in adolescence with otherwise preserved cognition. Many cases are X linked due to FLNA variants and affect mostly females, making long term seizure control especially challenging given pregnancy safety and tolerability constraints. Seizures are frequently medication resistant, leaving a need for more durable seizure freedom with fewer drugs and better targeting, with focal ablation or epilepsy surgery used when anatomically feasible.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Seizure-freedom/durable control for PVNH patients with drug‑resistant focal epilepsy after failing ≥2 antiseizure medications
- Mechanism-/genotype-directed (e.g., FLNA-pathway) therapies to replace empiric ASM polypharmacy and prevent progression to intractable seizures
- Female-/pregnancy-optimized long-term seizure control minimizing teratogenic risk while maintaining efficacy

name: Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy | secondary
description: Secondary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is a paraneoplastic or systemic syndrome, often linked to advanced lung cancer in male heavy smokers, causing digital clubbing, periostosis, synovial effusions, and severe disabling arthralgia with excruciating long bone pain that may respond poorly to opioids. Management focuses on treating the underlying trigger, but there is no definitive symptomatic therapy, leaving a need for faster, safer outpatient pain control and pathway targeted options when the cause is not quickly reversible.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- VEGF-pathway inhibition to suppress the final common pathway and relieve periostitis/pain in patients whose underlying cause cannot be rapidly cured.
- Rapid, non-opioid pain control for severe-symptom secondary HPOA where NSAIDs have minimal benefit and opioids may be ineffective (e.g., PGE2-pathway approaches beyond conventional NSAIDs).
- Safer, lower-burden outpatient symptomatic therapy that avoids NSAID CV/GI risks, IV bisphosphonate infusion/renal/ONJ risks, and octreotide biliary/pancreatic toxicity.

name: Syphilis | secondary
description: Systemic Treponema pallidum sexually transmitted infection emerging weeks after the primary chancre, causing non itchy rash on palms and soles, mucous patches, condyloma lata, and lymphadenopathy; treatment relies on single dose intramuscular benzathine penicillin G, with longer less certain nonpenicillin alternatives and no documented pregnancy alternative, and may trigger an unpreventable Jarisch Herxheimer reaction that can destabilize pregnancy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course oral (ideally single-visit) alternative matching single-dose IM benzathine penicillin efficacy, reducing reliance on 14-day doxycycline or daily IM/IV ceftriaxone courses
- Penicillin-free regimen with documented pregnancy efficacy/safety (including penicillin-allergic patients) to avoid desensitization
- Adjunct/modified therapy that prevents or materially reduces Jarisch–Herxheimer reactions (especially in pregnancy/early high-bacterial-load disease)

name: Selective IgG deficiency disease
description: Selective IgG subclass deficiency is an antibody disorder with persistently low one or two IgG subclasses despite normal total IgG, leading to recurrent ear and sinus infections and sometimes bronchitis or pneumonia from encapsulated bacteria. Diagnosis hinges on documenting recurrent infections and poor vaccine antibody responses. Management relies on antibiotics, pneumococcal vaccination, and in selected patients intravenous or subcutaneous immunoglobulin replacement, yet infections can persist, vaccines may not protect, and repeated bronchitis can cause permanent lung damage, driving need for more durable prevention with less antibiotic and infusion burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent recurrent encapsulated-bacteria respiratory infections in vaccine–poor-responders (e.g., *S. pneumoniae*, *H. influenzae*) using infection-burden/functional endpoints.
- Non-antibiotic alternatives that reduce/eliminate chronic prophylactic or continuous antibiotics while maintaining infection control.
- Lower-burden, safer immune-replacement options vs frequent supervised IVIG infusions and high-frequency SCIG dosing.

name: Dementia | semantic
description: Semantic dementia (semantic variant primary progressive aphasia) is a rare frontotemporal degeneration, usually starting before age 65, marked by fluent speech but progressive loss of word meaning with anomia and impaired single word comprehension while episodic memory is relatively preserved early; later, disinhibition and rigid food preferences can develop. Most cases are linked to TDP 43 pathology and there is no cure or proven way to slow progression, leaving a premium on disease modifying therapies plus safer options for behavioral symptom control given antipsychotic risk in dementia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying FTLD‑TDP/TDP‑43‑C therapy that slows svPPA progression with benefit on language endpoints (e.g., Boston Naming Test/semantic fluency) and reduced temporal-lobe atrophy on MRI.
- Symptomatic pharmacologic therapy that improves/stabilizes anomia and single-word comprehension (word-meaning loss).
- Better-tolerated behavioral-symptom control (e.g., disinhibition/rigid food preferences/agitation) that avoids antipsychotic-associated dementia mortality risk.

name: Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous
description: Persistent fetal vasculature (persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous) is a congenital failure of regression of fetal eye vessels, usually unilateral in an otherwise healthy full term infant, presenting with leukocoria, microphthalmia, cataract, and a fibrovascular stalk. Treatment is early surgery plus optical correction and patching, followed by lifelong surveillance, yet many children still develop amblyopia and complications such as secondary glaucoma, hemorrhage, retinal detachment, and phthisis with persistently poor vision. A key gap is safer, more effective adjuncts to reduce intraoperative bleeding and postoperative recurrence and improve long term visual outcomes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Posterior/combined PFV drugs that reduce persistent-fetal-vasculature traction to prevent progression to retinal detachment/phthisis.
- Glaucoma-preventive / IOP-lowering pharmacotherapy for severe PFV eyes at risk of angle-closure/secondary glaucoma.
- Adjunct intraocular anti-angiogenic therapy (e.g., anti-VEGF) for anterior PFV to reduce intraoperative bleeding and postoperative recurrence.

name: Piebaldism
description: Piebaldism is a rare congenital, usually nonprogressive inherited pigment disorder caused by failure of melanocyte migration, producing sharply demarcated depigmented skin patches and often a white forelock. Patients are otherwise healthy but face lifelong cosmetic and psychosocial burden plus increased sunburn and skin cancer risk in unpigmented areas, making daily photoprotection essential. Current repigmentation is largely limited to camouflage or invasive grafting and cell based procedures, leaving unmet need for durable non surgical melanocyte restoration and longer acting protection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical melanocyte restoration to durably repigment congenital stable depigmented patches (replacing grafting/cell-transplant procedures).
- Durable (non–hair-dye) treatment for white forelock/poliosis.
- Long-acting photoprotective therapies for melanocyte-lacking patches to reduce sunburn/skin-cancer risk and the daily sunscreen/avoidance burden.

name: Pilomatrixoma
description: Pilomatrixoma is a benign hair follicle matrix tumor that typically presents in children and adolescents as a small, hard subcutaneous lump, most often on the head or neck. Management is surgical excision, but cosmetically sensitive locations make scarring and incomplete resection meaningful, with 2% to 6% recurrence. Most cases are driven by somatic CTNNB1 activation that keeps beta catenin signaling on, suggesting room for future scar sparing local approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Office-based intralesional/topical β‑catenin/Wnt (CTNNB1)-targeted therapy to clear pediatric face/neck lesions and avoid excision/scars/general anesthesia.
- Post-excision topical/intralesional adjuvant to eradicate residual tumor after margin-limited resections and reduce ~2–6% recurrence.
- Systemic or field-directed chemoprevention for patients with multiple/syndromic pilomatrixomas to reduce repeated excisions.

name: Polyarteritis nodosa
description: Polyarteritis nodosa is a very rare necrotizing vasculitis of small and medium arteries that causes aneurysms and occlusions, leading to subacute multi organ ischemic injury affecting kidneys, gut, skin, and nerves with systemic symptoms like fever, weight loss, abdominal pain, neuropathy, and hypertension. Care relies on prolonged high dose corticosteroids and in severe disease cyclophosphamide, but toxicity, intensive monitoring, and frequent relapse drive demand for safer steroid sparing, more durable treatments and better subtype targeted approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer, non-cytotoxic induction for newly diagnosed active severe systemic PAN to replace cyclophosphamide + high-dose glucocorticoids while reducing malignancy/infection risk.
- Relapse-preventing maintenance that delivers durable multi-year remission (not only short-term control).
- Lower-burden (home/outpatient-friendly) induction regimens that avoid frequent IV pulses and intensive lab monitoring.

name: Sickle cell anemia
description: Inherited hemoglobin disorder detected via newborn screening where sickled red cells block blood flow, causing early infant anemia, jaundice, painful swelling, recurrent vaso occlusive pain crises and chronic pain, with progressive organ damage including chronic kidney disease; key unmet needs are more effective fetal hemoglobin induction, kidney protective therapies, and opioid sparing long term pain control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safe, specific *in vivo* HbF inducer achieving “transformative” HbF levels for the majority of SCD patients.
- Targeted therapy for sickle cell nephropathy that slows CKD progression (e.g., reduces albuminuria and preserves eGFR).
- Non-opioid (or opioid-sparing) analgesics that reliably control severe acute VOC pain and chronic sickle pain.

name: Melanoma | cutaneous amelanotic
description: Cutaneous amelanotic melanoma is a rare, nonpigmented melanoma (about 5% of cases) that often mimics benign lesions and is diagnosed later; advanced disease is treated like other melanomas but major unmet needs include effective options after PD-1 failure, reducing severe immune-related toxicity, and improving convenience beyond clinic-based intravenous immunotherapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Higher-ORR, durable salvage therapies for unresectable/metastatic patients progressing after anti–PD-1 treatment
- Lower-toxicity systemic regimens suitable for very elderly patients and avoiding severe immune-mediated AEs seen with current IO escalation
- More convenient non-IV and/or less clinic-dependent systemic options vs routine IV infusion-based anti–PD-1 dosing

name: Polycystic liver disease
description: Polycystic liver disease is a rare inherited disorder marked by progressive growth of multiple liver cysts, often alongside autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. Most patients are diagnosed incidentally and retain normal liver function, but a symptomatic minority develop massive hepatomegaly causing pain, early satiety, reflux, dyspnea, malnutrition, and major quality of life loss. Current drug therapy with injectable somatostatin analogs offers only modest, burdensome volume reduction with tolerability issues, leaving a need for durable, convenient control of liver volume and symptoms that can delay invasive procedures and transplantation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Trajectory-changing hepatomegaly control in diffuse symptomatic PLD with clinically meaningful symptom/PRO improvement beyond SSA’s typical 2–8% TLV reduction.
- SSA-sparing chronic therapy with improved tolerability (less early GI toxicity and fewer metabolic/biliary AEs such as glucose intolerance and cholelithiasis).
- More convenient and durable treatment than repeated long-acting injections (oral/ultra-long-acting/self-administered) with reduced rebound/relapse after stopping.

name: Polymicrogyria
description: Polymicrogyria is a congenital brain malformation where the cortex forms too many small folds, with severity driven by how much and which regions are affected. Most patients develop childhood onset seizures alongside developmental delay and speech, swallowing, and motor impairment. The central challenge is that the malformation is irreversible and epilepsy can be medication refractory, leaving care largely symptomatic and families cycling through anti seizure drugs with limited durability and tolerability. A key frontier is mechanism based therapy in molecularly defined subtypes such as PIK3CA related syndromes now in Phase 2 testing.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Seizure-freedom (or major seizure-frequency reduction) for drug-resistant polymicrogyria epilepsy, especially severe bilateral/generalized disease
- Genotype/pathway-targeted therapy for PIK3CA-mutant polymicrogyria (e.g., MCAP/PROS) that improves adaptive neurodevelopmental function and reduces seizures
- Pediatric-optimized anti-seizure therapies with fewer serious adverse events to enable durable monotherapy and reduce polytherapy burden

name: Small intestine cancer | adenocarcinoma
description: Small bowel adenocarcinoma is a rare gastrointestinal cancer that is often diagnosed late after months of vague symptoms or in emergencies like obstruction or bleeding. Treatment in advanced disease is largely borrowed from colorectal cancer, with no clear metastatic standard beyond first line fluoropyrimidine oxaliplatin regimens that can be burdensome to administer and limited by cumulative neuropathy. Only a minority of tumors are mismatch repair deficient or microsatellite instability high, and other precision options such as HER2 targeting remain based on sporadic experience.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- First-line systemic therapy that improves survival in metastatic pMMR/MSS small bowel adenocarcinoma (beyond CRC-extrapolated chemo).
- SBA-specific HER2/ERBB2-targeted therapies (including activity against ERBB2 point mutations, not just amplifications).
- Pump-free, neurotoxicity-sparing alternatives to FOLFOX/CAPOX that avoid 46-hour 5-FU infusion and oxaliplatin-induced cumulative neuropathy while maintaining efficacy.

name: Porencephaly
description: Porencephaly is a rare cerebral malformation in which a fluid-filled brain cyst forms after early injury such as hemorrhage or ischemia, leading to seizures, spastic weakness, and global developmental delay. Care is symptomatic and supportive because the structural lesion cannot be reversed, leaving unmet need for durable seizure control, improved spasticity management, and in COL4A1-related disease, prevention of hemorrhagic stroke that drives cyst formation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-specific anti-seizure/anti-epileptogenic therapy achieving durable seizure freedom in porencephaly-associated epilepsy, including medically intractable/startle epilepsy
- Better-tolerated, more effective spasticity pharmacotherapy for infants/children with porencephaly-associated spastic hemiparesis/quadriparesis
- Mechanism-targeted vascular stabilization/hemorrhage-prevention therapy for the COL4A1-related familial porencephaly subgroup to prevent bleeding-driven cyst formation

name: Porokeratosis
description: Porokeratosis, including disseminated superficial actinic porokeratosis, is a keratinisation disorder causing chronic annular lesions with a raised rim on sun exposed skin, often emerging in the 30s to 40s and sometimes itching or stinging. Management relies on often irritating topicals and procedures with no cure and no durable long term control, leaving persistent field disease and the need for standardized effective therapies. Ongoing surveillance is driven by malignant transformation risk, particularly squamous cell carcinoma, and current promising approaches remain variable compounded off label statin plus cholesterol formulations.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, field-directed DSAP treatment that maintains lesion clearance/DSAP-GASI improvement beyond short (12-week) topical courses and reduces relapse after stopping therapy
- Standardized, FDA-approved GMP-quality topical mevalonate-pathway therapy (e.g., statin ± cholesterol) to replace variable compounded products and improve access/tolerability
- Chemopreventive/anti-malignancy drug approach to reduce SCC risk in porokeratosis, especially higher-risk linear/giant subtypes
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus page for porokeratosis (as of Apr 2026)

name: Porphyria | cutanea tarda
description: Porphyria cutanea tarda is an acquired liver disorder caused by low uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity, leading to porphyrin buildup and adult onset photosensitive, fragile skin with blistering and hypertrichosis, sometimes with dark urine. Standard care uses phlebotomy or low dose hydroxychloroquine but symptom control can take 6 to 9 months and relapse can occur. Key gaps are faster, more durable control and workable options for patients with anemia or end stage renal disease where hydroxychloroquine is contraindicated and frequent phlebotomy is poorly tolerated.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Maintenance/relapse-prevention therapy to sustain biochemical remission and reduce PCT recurrence
- Renal-/anemia-compatible porphyrin & iron-lowering therapy for advanced renal disease/dialysis patients where phlebotomy is contraindicated and antimalarials are ineffective
- Faster fixed-duration, non-procedural regimen that clears porphyrins/skin disease with less monitoring vs serial phlebotomy and months-long low-dose antimalarials

name: Steatocystoma multiplex
description: Rare pilosebaceous skin disorder causing multiple benign sebum filled cysts, typically starting in adolescence on the torso and nearby areas. Treatment is largely procedural and burdensome with no gold standard, frequent recurrence, and retinoids that are only temporarily helpful, leaving patients with ongoing cosmetic and quality of life impact plus inflammation and scarring.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable disease-modifying control of cyst formation (vs isotretinoin’s temporary, non-curative shrinkage with flare/recurrence), especially in familial/KRT17-associated disease
- Targeted anti-inflammatory therapy for steatocystoma multiplex suppurativa to prevent rupture/drainage, pain and scarring where antibiotics are poorly effective and isotretinoin can flare
- Scalable, cosmetically sparing “field therapy” for many lesions that reduces reliance on repeated procedures and avoids systemic isotretinoin pregnancy-risk restrictions (iPLEDGE)

name: Primary ciliary dyskinesia
description: Primary ciliary dyskinesia is a rare inherited disorder of motile cilia that impairs mucociliary clearance, causing neonatal respiratory distress followed by lifelong wet cough, chronic rhinitis, sinus and ear infections, and progressive bronchiectasis. Diagnosis is often delayed due to complex testing, so preventable lung damage may already be present. Care is supportive with daily airway clearance and repeated antibiotics, with no cure or disease modifying therapy, leaving major unmet needs for lower burden flare prevention and treatments that restore ciliary function such as genotype targeted inhaled nucleic acid approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-targeted ciliary-rescue therapies (e.g., inhaled gene/mRNA) to restore mucociliary clearance beyond infection management.
- Exacerbation-prevention therapies that reduce acute respiratory infections/exacerbations to prevent irreversible lung-function decline/bronchiectasis, including options for patients where macrolides aren’t usable (e.g., NTM present).
- Lower-burden airway-hydration/mucolytic drugs that meaningfully reduce the need for daily airway-clearance physiotherapy/devices.

name: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
description: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is a fulminant nephritic syndrome with rapid loss of kidney function, hematuria and proteinuria often with oliguria, usually showing crescentic glomerulonephritis on biopsy. It can be driven by pauci immune vasculitis, anti glomerular basement membrane antibodies, or immune complex disease and may progress to renal failure within days to weeks, sometimes with lung involvement. The central unmet need is speed and safety, since delayed diagnosis and toxic, often slow acting immunosuppression and antibody removal can still come too late to prevent irreversible kidney failure and dialysis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing (ideally steroid-replacing) induction for ANCA-associated RPGN to maintain remission while reducing high-dose glucocorticoid toxicity
- Renal recovery/dialysis-avoidance therapies for severe renal AAV-RPGN (e.g., eGFR <30 at presentation) to increase kidney-function recovery and prevent ESKD
- Rapid pathogenic IgG/autoantibody elimination in severe anti-GBM RPGN (especially dialysis-start/high-crescent cases) to improve kidney salvage beyond current plasma exchange timelines

name: Subacute thyroiditis
description: Subacute thyroiditis (de Quervain) is an acute, likely post viral inflammatory thyroid disease causing anterior neck pain, tenderness, and fever with a typical triphasic course from transient hyperthyroidism to hypothyroidism and recovery. Treatment is largely symptomatic with nonsteroidal anti inflammatory drugs, glucocorticoids, and beta blockers, but relapses can prolong steroid exposure and there is no definitive protocol. Key unmet needs are better relapse control and steroid sparing options, and preventing the minority who develop persistent hypothyroidism requiring thyroid hormone replacement.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing relapse prevention in moderate–severe subacute thyroiditis during prednisone taper
- Reduce risk of permanent hypothyroidism post-SAT to avoid lifelong levothyroxine
- Faster, simpler pain/inflammation control with less NSAID/steroid exposure and monitoring burden

name: Ependymoma | supratentorial
description: Supratentorial ependymoma is a rare pediatric brain tumor of the cerebral hemispheres, often presenting with headaches, seizures, or focal deficits, and frequently driven by aggressive ZFTA fusions. Treatment relies on maximal surgery and postoperative focal radiation, yet local recurrence is common and conventional chemotherapy offers only modest benefit. Key unmet needs include brain penetrant systemic therapies and radiation sparing approaches, particularly for very young children who often need daily anesthesia and face long term toxicity risks.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- BBB-penetrant fusion-targeted systemic therapy for supratentorial ZFTA-fusion ependymoma (e.g., targeting MERTK dependency) to improve poor long-term disease control.
- Radiotherapy-sparing/de-intensifying systemic therapy for very young children to delay, reduce, or replace prolonged focal RT courses requiring repeated anesthesia/immobilization.
- BBB-penetrant salvage/maintenance systemic or locoregional therapy to improve local control/PFS in residual or recurrent disease when repeat gross-total resection is not feasible.

name: Supravalvular aortic stenosis
description: Congenital narrowing of the aorta just above the aortic valve, often detected as an infant heart murmur and progressing to dyspnea, chest pain, and heart failure. Many cases involve ELN variants and occur in Williams syndrome with added coronary stenosis and anesthesia risk. Treatment is primarily surgical, yet durability is limited with substantial lifetime reintervention and lifelong surveillance needs. The frontier is disease modifying approaches that restore elastin rather than only relieving downstream obstruction.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-life elastin-restoration therapy for ELN-haploinsufficiency SVAS/Williams to prevent progression and avoid catheter/surgical repair
- Coronary-stenosis/ischemia–preventive pharmacotherapy (esp. syndromic SVAS/Williams) to reduce sudden-death/peri-anesthesia risk
- Anti-restenosis/repair-durability adjunct (peri-/post-op or non-surgical) to reduce recurrent SVAS and long-term reinterventions

name: Aphasia | primary progressive
description: Primary progressive aphasia is a neurodegenerative syndrome, typically starting age 50 to 70, in which language progressively deteriorates and can be the only major deficit for the first 2 to 3 years. Biology is heterogeneous across subtypes, complicating diagnosis and therapeutic targeting. There is no cure and no approved medicines, so care relies on speech language therapy and practical communication adaptations that help function but do not slow progression, leaving a major unmet need for disease modifying, mechanism matched treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Alzheimer’s-pathology–targeted disease‑modifying therapy for biomarker-confirmed lvPPA to slow naming/word-finding decline (e.g., Boston Naming Test)
- TDP‑43–directed therapy for svPPA to preserve confrontation naming and single‑word comprehension
- Safe, scalable outpatient symptomatic drug that measurably improves validated language/communication scales (e.g., WAB‑R AQ, PASS, verbal fluency) to reduce reliance on recurring speech‑language‑therapy logistics

name: Progressive muscular atrophy
description: Rare late adult onset lower motor neuron disease, often starting in the limbs, causing progressive flaccid weakness, muscle wasting, fasciculations, cramps, and loss of reflexes. Some patients later develop upper motor neuron signs, and outcomes are largely driven by respiratory muscle failure. Treatment is mainly supportive with equipment and therapies to maintain function, leaving a major unmet need for disease modifying options that slow decline and preserve breathing capacity and independence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Respiratory-function preservation therapies (VC/FVC-focused) to delay respiratory insufficiency and extend ventilation-free survival in late-adult PMA.
- Motor-neuron–protective/regenerative treatments to slow spread beyond initial limb onset, preserve function (e.g., ALSFRS-R), and prevent progression to UMN involvement.
- Better-tolerated, lower-burden symptomatic drugs for cramps/spasticity to reduce reliance on sedating/hepatotoxic/anticholinergic, frequent-dose regimens.

name: Tibial muscular dystrophy
description: Tibial muscular dystrophy (Udd distal myopathy) is a rare TTN gene disorder with adult onset distal weakness of the anterior lower leg, causing loss of ankle dorsiflexion with difficulty heel walking and, over 10 to 20 years, progressive foot drop, clumsiness, and falls risk while lifespan is typically preserved. Care is largely supportive with orthoses and occasional tendon transfer surgery, leaving a central unmet need for disease modifying TTN targeted therapies that preserve dorsiflexion and prevent progression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- TTN-variant–targeted therapy to halt tibialis-anterior fatty degeneration and preserve ankle dorsiflexion/heel-walking
- Pharmacotherapy to reduce foot-drop severity and falls/tripping (vs braces/orthoses)
- Progression-slowing therapy to delay 10–20-year spread to long-toe extensors/foot drop and postpone need for tendon-transfer surgery/cane dependence

name: Aspergilloma
description: Pulmonary aspergilloma is a fungal ball that colonizes a preexisting lung cavity, often in non-immunocompromised people with prior structural lung disease such as post-tuberculosis cavities. Many are asymptomatic until hemoptysis emerges as the defining threat. Surgery can be curative but is frequently not feasible in patients with limited lung reserve or comorbidities, and bronchial artery embolization often provides only temporary control with rebleeding. Systemic azole therapy is burdensome due to drug interactions, toxicity, and required monitoring, creating demand for safer chronic suppression and better local antifungal delivery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, non-surgical prevention of recurrent hemoptysis (incl. post-BAE rebleeding) for inoperable/poor surgical-candidate patients
- Local (intrabronchial/intracavitary/inhaled) antifungals that achieve therapeutic cavity exposure to shrink/eradicate aspergilloma
- Chronic suppressive therapy with far fewer drug–drug interactions and reduced monitoring burden (TDM/LFT/ECG), especially in patients on anticoagulants/corticosteroids/statins

name: Artery stenosis | pulmonary
description: Pulmonary artery stenosis is a congenital narrowing of the pulmonary valve or main and branch pulmonary arteries that restricts blood flow from the right ventricle to the lungs, often first detected as an infant heart murmur. Severe or diffuse disease can cause cyanosis, shortness of breath, heart failure, and pulmonary hypertension. Treatment is largely procedural with balloon angioplasty and stenting, but restenosis and frequent reinterventions are common. Ductal dependent newborns may require continuous alprostadil infusion with meaningful apnea risk, underscoring the need for more durable, lower burden therapies including antiproliferative strategies to prevent in stent restenosis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Anti-restenosis therapy (systemic or local drug-delivery such as drug-eluting balloons/stents) to reduce repeat narrowing/reinterventions after branch/peripheral PA angioplasty/stenting.
- A non–ICU-tethering ductal-patency strategy for ductal-dependent severe neonatal pulmonary stenosis that avoids continuous IV infusion and reduces alprostadil-associated apnea risk.
- A systemic anti-remodeling/anti-proliferative therapy for diffuse/syndromic peripheral PA stenosis (e.g., Alagille) to prevent/treat pulmonary artery hypertension when disease is distal/multifocal and not fully addressable procedurally.

name: Pyomyositis
description: Pyomyositis is a rare bacterial infection of skeletal muscle that forms a deep intramuscular abscess, usually in the thigh or pelvis, causing pain, fever, swelling and sometimes a limp despite often normal overlying skin. Most cases are due to Staphylococcus aureus with rising methicillin-resistant strains, and diagnosis commonly occurs only after weeks when an abscess has formed. Treatment typically requires prolonged antibiotics and frequent drainage procedures, leaving a premium on earlier detection and shorter, safer outpatient regimens that reliably cover resistant organisms and avoid invasive interventions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Antibiotic regimens that sterilize stage‑2 intramuscular abscess pyomyositis without requiring drainage/surgery.
- Short-course, outpatient-friendly (high-bioavailability oral or long-acting parenteral) regimens to replace IV-first, multi-week therapy.
- Safer empiric MRSA-active (± gram-negative) options for high-risk/culture-negative cases with lower nephrotoxicity/GI toxicity vs vancomycin/clindamycin-based care.
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus pyomyositis page; https://medlineplus.gov/myositis.html

name: Severe combined immunodeficiency | RAG2 deficiency
description: RAG2 deficiency causes a T− B− NK+ severe combined immunodeficiency in infants, leading to life threatening recurrent or opportunistic infections plus persistent thrush, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive and sometimes Omenn syndrome. Care relies on isolation, immunoglobulin, and antimicrobial prophylaxis while pursuing hematopoietic stem cell transplant or gene therapy, but outcomes are limited by graft rejection risk in this subtype and by graft versus host disease and the toxicity of chemotherapy conditioning, especially when infants are already infected. Demand is high for safer, more reliable immune reconstitution and non genotoxic conditioning approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non‑genotoxic (mAb/ADC; e.g., anti‑CD117/c‑Kit) conditioning to enable engraftment while avoiding chemo-related organ toxicity/TRM
- Donor‑independent curative gene correction for infants without matched donors, avoiding allogeneic GVHD risk
- Therapies that control infections/immune dysregulation (Omenn/hypomorphic RAG2) pre‑HSCT to prevent organ damage that worsens survival and immune recovery

name: Renal glycosuria
description: Renal glycosuria is usually a familial proximal tubule glucose reabsorption defect, most often from SLC5A2 variants, causing glucose in urine despite normal blood sugar and typically found incidentally on urinalysis. Most cases are benign and need no treatment, but a symptomatic minority with very high urinary glucose losses can develop polyuria or enuresis, recurrent urinary tract infections, and dehydration or ketosis during pregnancy or starvation. Care is largely reassurance, leaving unmet need in identifying and supporting higher risk patients and preventing complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- SGLT2 (SLC5A2) functional rescue to reduce massive urinary glucose loss in symptomatic severe patients (polyuria/dehydration)
- Non-antibiotic prevention of recurrent urinary/genital infections in severe familial renal glucosuria
- Stress-period (pregnancy/starvation) prophylaxis to prevent dehydration and ketosis episodes

name: Tracheal stenosis
description: Progressive fibrotic narrowing of the trachea (often post intubation, inflammatory or autoimmune, or idiopathic) causing dyspnea and stridor and frequently misdiagnosed as asthma, with care dominated by repeat dilations and other procedures due to high restenosis and limited durable steroid sparing disease control or local drug delivery to extend time between interventions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing anti-fibrotic/immune-targeted therapy for iSGS that prolongs recurrence-free interval (weeks between operative interventions) vs dilation-based care.
- Local, durable drug delivery at the stenosis site (e.g., drug-coated balloon/drug-eluting airway device) to improve freedom-from and time-to reintervention after dilation.
- Biomarker-guided systemic immunomodulation for GPA-associated SGS to reduce procedure frequency/tracheostomy reliance while minimizing glucocorticoid exposure/toxicity.

name: Tracheomalacia
description: Tracheomalacia is a structural weakness of the tracheal cartilage causing excessive, often ≥50% expiratory airway collapse, leading to noisy breathing, barky cough, feeding related respiratory distress, recurrent lower respiratory infections, and cyanotic spells. Many children improve by 18 to 24 months, but severe disease can drive ongoing infections and hypoxic events. Management remains largely supportive, with limited evidence for commonly used medications and a lack of randomized trial data, creating unmet need for disease modifying approaches that reduce collapsibility and prevent infections.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Airway-stabilizing, disease-modifying drug therapy for severe congenital/pediatric tracheomalacia to prevent life-threatening hypoxic events and reduce reliance on CPAP/surgical rescue.
- Safer, evidence-backed prevention of recurrent respiratory infections/exacerbations to reduce antibiotic-requiring episodes, hospitalizations, and QoL impairment.
- Proven mucoactive/mucokinetic regimens that improve mucus clearance and reduce daily-care burden while avoiding ineffective or harmful prior approaches.

name: Transient global amnesia
description: Transient global amnesia is a sudden, self limited episode of profound anterograde and retrograde memory loss lasting up to 24 hours, usually in adults aged 50 to 70, with preserved identity but time disorientation, anxiety, and repetitive questioning. It often mimics stroke or seizure and is frequently missed initially, driving extensive emergency workups. With no specific treatment or evidence based prophylaxis, care is largely supportive, leaving unmet need for faster diagnosis, episode shortening, and recurrence prevention, aided by diffusion weighted magnetic resonance imaging showing punctate hippocampal CA1 lesions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Abortive/rapid-reversal therapy to shorten acute TGA episodes and reduce need for hospital observation.
- Recurrence-prevention prophylaxis for higher-risk patients (e.g., migraine history) to reduce repeat episodes.
- Mechanism-/biomarker-guided (hippocampal CA1 DWI lesion) neuroprotective pathway modulation to prevent/reverse CA1 dysfunction and reduce acute anxiety/distress.

name: Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy
description: Developmental delay in an infant’s own immunoglobulin G production after maternal antibodies wane, causing a prolonged low immunoglobulin G window beyond about 6 months and recurrent ear and respiratory infections despite normal growth. Care is mainly infection prevention and antibiotics, with rare immunoglobulin replacement for severe cases, and a major unmet need is early tools to distinguish self resolving cases from evolving primary immunodeficiency since diagnosis is only confirmed retrospectively when immunoglobulin G normalizes, often by ages 2 to 5.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Antibiotic-sparing infection prevention for symptomatic THI infants (5–24 months) with very frequent URT infections who cycle through repeated antibiotic courses/prophylaxis
- Lower-reactogenic, lower-burden passive IgG option (IVIG-sparing or home-compatible) for the small subgroup with severe/recurrent respiratory infections despite antibiotics
- Therapy that accelerates time-to-IgG normalization to shorten the vulnerability/monitoring window (months–years)
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus page; see https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001307.htm and https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003545.htm

name: Myeloproliferative syndrome | transient
description: Neonatal preleukemic myeloproliferation in babies with Down syndrome caused by trisomy 21 plus acquired GATA1 mutations, presenting in the first week with circulating blasts, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia and hepatomegaly with jaundice. Most remit by 3 months, but severe cases can cause cholestatic liver failure and multiorgan dysfunction, and 20 to 30 percent later develop myeloid leukemia of Down syndrome. Care is mainly supportive with low dose cytarabine for life threatening cytoreduction, leaving unmet needs for safer cytoreduction and liver and leukemia prevention.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Targeted eradication of preleukemic clones after TAM/TMD to prevent progression to ML‑DS.
- Drugs that prevent/stop TAM-associated progressive cholestatic hepatopathy and fulminant hepatic fibrosis leading to early death.
- Ultra–low-toxicity, rapid cytoreduction for infants with life‑threatening TAM (infiltration/hyperleukocytosis) to reduce severe toxicity and enable timely treatment.

name: Tricuspid atresia
description: Tricuspid atresia is a critical congenital heart defect where the tricuspid valve fails to form, causing low oxygen circulation and cyanosis from birth and requiring staged single ventricle surgeries that are not curative. Long term morbidity is dominated by Fontan circulation complications including protein losing enteropathy and plastic bronchitis, progressive Fontan associated liver fibrosis and cirrhosis, and ongoing thromboembolism risk. Care is largely surgical and supportive, leaving major unmet need for durable disease modifying therapies and simpler anticoagulation that reduces monitoring and treatment burden in children.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Medical therapy to prevent/resolve post-Fontan lymphatic failure complications (protein-losing enteropathy/plastic bronchitis) with improvements in serum albumin/edema/effusions/ascites.
- Disease-modifying antifibrotic therapy to slow/reverse Fontan-associated liver disease progression (congestion → fibrosis/cirrhosis) using liver stiffness/biomarker/biopsy endpoints.
- Fixed-dose, low-monitoring anticoagulation that reduces post-Fontan thromboembolism vs aspirin while avoiding warfarin’s monitoring burden (with acceptable bleeding risk).

name: Valve disease | tricuspid stenosis
description: Rheumatic scarring narrows the tricuspid valve, obstructing flow from right atrium to right ventricle and driving right sided congestion in young adults with fatigue, dyspnea, edema, hepatomegaly, and ascites. Care is mostly symptomatic with salt restriction, diuretics, and aldosterone antagonists plus selective valve intervention, with little evidence to guide management and no disease modifying cure for the underlying rheumatic heart disease. Patients often face persistent decongestion needs and, when atrial fibrillation coexists, burdensome warfarin style anticoagulation and monitoring.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non–INR-monitored anticoagulation with lower major/fatal bleeding risk for AF in rheumatic valve disease where warfarin remains first-line.
- Right-sided decongestive therapy improving venous-congestion control beyond diuretics while reducing electrolyte depletion and monitoring burden.
- Disease-modifying anti-inflammatory/anti-fibrotic therapy to slow rheumatic TS progression and delay/avoid valve intervention.

name: Tropical sprue
description: Rare acquired small intestinal malabsorption syndrome after prolonged tropical exposure, causing chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, and progressive folate and vitamin B12 deficiency leading to anemia. Care relies on months long antibiotics plus micronutrient repletion, so major unmet needs are shorter, better tolerated oral regimens and more durable remission, especially for patients in endemic or relapsing settings.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course, low-burden oral regimen that resolves malabsorption without 6–12 months of QID/empty-stomach + no-dairy tetracycline and B12 injections
- Relapse-prevention/durable-remission therapy for patients who remain in or return to endemic areas
- Safer, equally effective non-tetracycline option for poor responders/contraindications (e.g., southern India nonresponse; children/pregnancy) with improved tolerability vs tetracyclines/sulfonamides

name: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
description: Twin to twin transfusion syndrome is a complication of monochorionic twin pregnancy where shared placental vessels shunt blood from a donor fetus to a recipient, producing oligohydramnios in the donor and polyhydramnios with progressive cardiomyopathy and heart failure risk in the recipient. Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation at roughly 16 to 26 weeks is standard, but outcomes are still dominated by prematurity, especially iatrogenic preterm premature rupture of membranes with no proven prevention. A key frontier is safer, less invasive transplacental approaches that stabilize recipient cardiovascular disease while reducing procedure related preterm birth.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical transplacental therapy for Quintero stage II–IV TTTS (16–26 weeks) to reduce fetal loss vs laser-era residual “no survivors” cases
- Adjunct drug to prevent PPROM/prematurity after fetoscopic laser and improve downstream neurodevelopmental outcomes
- Recipient-cardiomyopathy–targeted transplacental cardiovascular therapy (e.g., nifedipine) to improve recipient survival in mild–moderate TTTS cardiomyopathy

name: Distichiasis
description: Distichiasis is an eyelid margin disorder where an extra row of eyelashes grows from meibomian gland openings and rubs the ocular surface, causing tearing, foreign body sensation and photophobia that can progress to corneal erosion, ulceration and scarring. It may be congenital such as with FOXC2 related lymphedema distichiasis syndrome or acquired in scarring ocular surface disease. Care is largely lubrication plus repeated lash removal or ablation, but lashes regrow within weeks and outcomes are limited in cicatrizing disease, creating demand for longer lasting, eyelid safe ways to prevent recurrence and protect the cornea.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Long-acting, non-procedural eyelid-margin therapy to suppress aberrant lash regrowth for months (vs epilation regrowth in weeks).
- Ocular-surface-safe follicle-targeted therapy for acquired distichiasis in cicatrizing ocular surface disease with higher success and less inflammation/xerosis.
- Adjunct corneal-protective/epithelial-healing pharmacotherapy to prevent abrasion/ulceration/scarring and photophobia in patients with keratopathy.

name: Cardiomyopathy | Takotsubo
description: Stress triggered, usually reversible cardiomyopathy that mimics acute myocardial infarction but typically lacks obstructive coronary artery disease, causing transient left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Most often affects postmenopausal women after emotional or physical stress and can progress to acute heart failure or cardiogenic shock in about 10%. Treatment is largely empirical due to limited prospective randomized evidence, with key gaps in early myocardial protection, shock management tailored to left ventricular outflow obstruction, and secondary prevention for thromboembolism and recurrence (around 4%).
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute early-start (≤24h) cardioprotective therapy reducing myocardial injury (hs‑troponin AUC) and accelerating LV recovery (LVEF at 24–48h)
- Shock/LVOTO-tailored hemodynamic therapy improving cardiogenic shock outcomes without catecholamine inotrope dependence
- Evidence-based secondary prevention (beyond beta-blockers) to prevent recurrence and reduce MACE/stroke (incl. anticoagulation strategies in severe LV dysfunction)

name: Sarcoidosis | Löfgren syndrome
description: Sarcoidosis is an immune mediated granulomatous disease that most often hits the lungs and chest lymph nodes, with risk of permanent scarring. Löfgren syndrome is an acute form marked by fever, erythema nodosum, and painful ankle arthritis with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy that usually resolves within two years, but some patients need immunosuppression and about 10 percent develop chronic disease. Care still leans heavily on corticosteroids, and toxicity plus poor tools to predict who will progress or need early treatment leaves demand for safer steroid sparing control and better prognostic markers.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course therapy that reliably resolves the acute Löfgren symptom cluster faster than the typical 6‑months–2‑years course
- Better-tolerated/easier-to-administer steroid-sparing option for refractory/persistent disease failing NSAIDs (avoiding glucocorticoids/MTX/infliximab)
- Early intervention to prevent progression to chronic disease in the ~10% who persist >2 years, paired with predictors to target treatment and reduce follow-up burden

name: Giant cell arteritis
description: Giant cell arteritis is an immune driven vasculitis of medium and large arteries in adults over 50 that causes new headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication and can rapidly lead to blindness or stroke. Care still relies on immediate, prolonged high dose glucocorticoids often for 1 to 2 years with major toxicity and infection risk in the elderly and frequent relapse despite treatment. Steroid sparing control remains the core need, with biologics such as tocilizumab reducing but not eliminating steroid exposure and durable maintenance strategies still emerging.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing (ideally steroid-minimising) regimens that maintain remission while materially reducing glucocorticoid toxicity.
- Durable maintenance therapies that prevent relapse after stopping IL‑6R blockade (avoiding re-escalation to ~20 mg/day prednisolone), especially in patients with prior relapse on tocilizumab or large‑vessel involvement.
- Rapid-acting therapies that prevent cranial ischaemic events (vision loss/stroke) during high-risk presentations/relapses while avoiding infection-risk tradeoffs of intensive IV steroid strategies in elderly patients.

name: Myelodysplastic syndrome | lower-risk
description: Lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes are bone marrow failure cancers, typically diagnosed in older adults in their 70s, where defective stem-cell maturation causes chronic cytopenias, most often anemia with fatigue and shortness of breath, plus infection and bleeding risk. Care is largely supportive, and many patients cycle through short-lived transfusions with cumulative iron overload while remaining vulnerable to complications and a meaningful risk of progression to acute myeloid leukemia. The premium is for durable, low-toxicity therapies that restore blood production across lineages and reduce transfusion dependence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, high-rate RBC transfusion independence (≥12 weeks) with meaningful Hb rise from low-toxicity (ideally oral) therapy in transfusion-dependent lower-risk MDS anemia
- EPO-/phenotype-agnostic anemia efficacy for “hard-to-treat” patients (e.g., high endogenous EPO/high transfusion burden; non–ring sideroblast, non–del(5q))
- Therapies that also correct neutropenia/thrombocytopenia to reduce serious infections and bleeding risk

name: ATTR amyloidosis | wild-type
description: Wild type transthyretin amyloidosis is an age related protein misfolding disease where normal transthyretin forms amyloid deposits, typically in the heart, causing stiffening, arrhythmias, and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. It is often missed in older men, with carpal tunnel syndrome or lumbar spinal stenosis as early clues and multi year diagnostic delays. Current transthyretin stabilizers and gene silencers mainly slow new amyloid formation, leaving a major need for safe therapies that clear existing cardiac deposits and help patients who present late with advanced heart failure.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Amyloid-fibril “depleter” drugs that clear existing cardiac TTR deposits, with objective amyloid-burden reduction plus 6MWT/KCCQ improvement.
- Therapies proven effective in advanced ATTRwt-CM (NYHA IV and high-risk NYHA III) populations largely excluded from pivotal trials.
- Lower-burden options for elderly/comorbid patients (self/less-frequent administration and fewer monitoring liabilities vs HCP-only injections, vitamin A management, and early renal-lab changes).

name: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
description: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a rare autoimmune small vessel vasculitis that often begins in adults with asthma or allergies and eosinophilia, then progresses to multisystem, organ damaging inflammation affecting lungs and sinuses as well as nerves, heart, and kidneys. Care still relies heavily on systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppression, yet relapses are common and cumulative steroid toxicity is a major burden. Key unmet needs are durable steroid sparing remission and proven options for severe organ threatening disease that is often underrepresented or excluded in clinical trials.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, steroid-minimizing remission in relapsing/refractory EGPA (BVAS=0 with prednisone/prednisolone ≤4 mg/day, ideally steroid-free) and fewer relapses during/after taper.
- Proven therapies for organ-/life-threatening EGPA manifestations (e.g., neuropathy, cardiomyopathy, glomerulonephritis/alveolar hemorrhage) where evidence is scarce/excluded from IL-5 trials.
- Lower treatment burden vs current biologics (e.g., fewer injections/longer dosing intervals than mepolizumab’s 3 injections every 4 weeks).

name: Idiopathic neonatal atrial flutter
description: Rare sustained neonatal atrial tachyarrhythmia presenting mostly within 48 hours of birth that can range from asymptomatic tachycardia to heart failure or hydrops. Acute care prioritizes rapid, predictable rhythm conversion via transoesophageal overdrive pacing or synchronized cardioversion since drug conversion is variable. Pharmacologic options like sotalol add friction due to required inpatient electrocardiographic monitoring and torsade de pointes risk, creating demand for safer, faster, less resource intensive cardioversion pathways.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- QT/TdP-sparing single-dose chemical cardioversion option to replace sotalol while avoiding ≥3-day ECG-monitored initiation
- Non-sedating/non-shock drug-based acute conversion to reduce reliance on transoesophageal overdrive pacing or synchronized DC cardioversion
- High-efficacy rhythm-control regimen for fetal-onset/hydrops-risk or hemodynamically compromised cases

name: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy
description: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy is a usually adult-onset inherited heart muscle disease caused by desmosomal gene defects, where the right ventricular myocardium is progressively replaced by fat and scar, destabilizing electrical signaling and triggering ventricular tachycardia, syncope, and sudden death, often during exercise. Typical patients are diagnosed in their 20s to 40s after exertional palpitations or fainting. Current care centers on exercise restriction, antiarrhythmic drugs, ablation, and implantable defibrillators that reduce risk but do not address the genetic root cause or halt remodeling, creating demand for safer chronic suppression and disease-modifying anti-remodeling and gene-replacement approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- PKP2 genotype–targeted gene therapy to restore/boost myocardial PKP2 and reduce PVC/NSVT burden and ICD therapies in PKP2-ACM/ARVC.
- Anti-fibrotic/RV-remodeling therapies that prevent RV functional deterioration (e.g., RV strain/diameter) while reducing ventricular ectopy/VT.
- Safer chronic arrhythmia suppression that reduces VT/ICD therapies without sotalol’s monitored initiation requirement or amiodarone’s multi-organ toxicity/monitoring burden.

name: Desminopathy
description: Desminopathy is an inherited myofibrillar myopathy driven by abnormal desmin protein aggregates that disrupt muscle fibers, causing progressive distal to proximal weakness that can progress to tetraparesis and wheelchair dependence. Many patients develop cardiac conduction disease and malignant arrhythmias needing pacemakers or defibrillators, plus nocturnal hypoventilation that can evolve into respiratory failure. Care is largely supportive and complication focused, with no disease specific therapy, leaving a major unmet need for treatments that slow muscle degeneration and protect cardiac and respiratory function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that prevent/clear toxic desmin-positive protein aggregates (e.g., anti-aggregation, autophagy/proteasome modulation) to slow progressive skeletal myopathy and loss of ambulation.
- Cardiac-directed treatments that reduce severe arrhythmias/conduction block progression to prevent sudden cardiac death and delay/avoid pacemaker dependence.
- Respiratory-muscle–preserving therapies that prevent nocturnal hypoventilation progressing to daytime respiratory failure (e.g., stabilize vital capacity decline/diaphragm involvement).

name: Hypereosinophilic syndrome | primary
description: Rare, heterogeneous eosinophil driven disorder with sustained high eosinophils causing multi-organ damage (skin, lungs, gut, heart, nervous system); care still relies on systemic corticosteroids with variable second-line efficacy, leaving major unmet need for steroid-sparing, durable control that prevents irreversible cardiac fibrosis and thrombosis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Flare-free disease control in primary HES without rescue oral corticosteroid escalation/therapy escalation.
- Rapid, durable oral precision therapy for clonal HES beyond FIP1L1–PDGFRA (F/P)-positive disease.
- Disease-modifying prevention/reversal of eosinophil-driven cardiac fibrosis and thrombosis (cardioprotection).

name: Romano-Ward syndrome
description: Autosomal dominant congenital long QT syndrome with prolonged QT interval and risk of torsades de pointes causing syncope or sudden cardiac arrest, often triggered by exercise or stress and sometimes masked by reduced penetrance. Care centers on avoiding QT prolonging drugs and beta blockers, but breakthrough events and intolerance can necessitate left cardiac sympathetic denervation or an implantable cardioverter defibrillator. QT shortening drugs like mexiletine exist, yet there are no proven gene specific therapies that reduce mortality.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Add-on/alternative therapies that prevent breakthrough syncope/TdP/cardiac arrest and reduce QTc in LQT2 patients inadequately protected on beta-blockers.
- Beta-blocker–sparing anti-arrhythmic prophylaxis for patients with intolerance/contraindications (e.g., bradycardia/fatigue/bronchospasm) to avoid escalation to LCSD/ICD.
- Genotype-driven mechanism-corrective drugs (e.g., KCNH2 trafficking-rescue in LQT2 and better-tolerated late sodium current blockers for LQT3 vs mexiletine GI/CNS AEs).

name: Myotonic dystrophy
