description: Inherited repeat expansion disorder where toxic RNA clumps disrupt protein splicing, causing progressive myotonia and distal muscle weakness with multisystem complications including cataracts, excessive daytime sleepiness, and life threatening cardiac conduction disease. Onset is often in the 20s to 30s and disability accumulates as weakness and fatigue worsen. Care is largely symptomatic because no therapies slow progression, leaving high unmet need for disease modifying RNA or splicing targeted treatments, better tolerated anti myotonia options, and interventions that reduce cardiac morbidity and sudden death.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy that corrects DMPK RNA/splicing pathology and yields clinically meaningful functional gains in progressive weakness
- Therapy that prevents/reverses cardiac conduction disease/arrhythmias to reduce sudden death/early mortality and delay/avoid pacemaker dependence
- Better-tolerated, simpler anti-myotonia therapy vs mexiletine (fewer GI/CNS AEs, less monitoring, less frequent dosing, usable in AV-block patients)

name: Triglyceride deposit cardiomyovasculopathy
description: Rare adult-onset disorder where impaired intracellular long-chain triglyceride breakdown causes lipid buildup in heart and coronary vessel cells, driving severe cardiomyopathy, diffuse coronary disease, arrhythmias, and transplant-level heart failure. Symptoms include dyspnea, fatigue, angina, and palpitations with risk of sudden cardiac death. Standard lipid lowering and revascularization are often ineffective, leaving a major unmet need for disease-modifying therapies that restore myocardial lipid handling and halt progression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Restore impaired intracellular long-chain TG lipolysis (ATGL/PNPLA2 axis) to reduce myocardial/coronary TG deposition (esp. primary TGCV with normal plasma TG)
- Reverse diffuse TG-deposit coronary disease/angina that is resistant to lipid-lowering therapy and PCI/revascularization
- Reduce HF/ventricular arrhythmia major events (SCD/cardiopulmonary arrest, HF hospitalizations, stroke, device procedures) to improve poor 5-year outcomes

name: AL amyloidosis
description: Immunoglobulin light chain amyloidosis is a plasma cell disorder in which misfolded light chains form amyloid deposits, most often damaging the heart and kidneys and driving progressive organ failure. Symptoms are nonspecific, so patients are frequently misdiagnosed and treatment is delayed. Current therapy can suppress the plasma cell clone, but established organ injury is hard to reverse, leaving major unmet need for earlier diagnosis and for treatments that rapidly improve organ function, especially in advanced cardiac disease where standard regimens are not recommended outside trials.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safe/effective “cardiac rescue” regimens for Mayo Stage IIIB / NYHA IIIB–IV patients excluded/not recommended for current daratumumab-based SoC.
- Amyloid-fibril clearance/organ-remodeling add-ons that accelerate cardiac recovery (e.g., earlier NT-proBNP organ response) and improve mortality/CV hospitalization endpoints.
- More convenient, better-tolerated post–D-VCd/post-daratumumab options (incl. oral/biomarker-selected) for ≥VGPR non-responders and daratumumab-refractory relapse, usable in frail high-risk cardiac patients.

name: Ocular histoplasmosis syndrome
description: Presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome is an inflammatory chorioretinal disorder, typically in White adults aged 20 to 50 from histoplasmosis endemic regions, that is often silent until choroidal neovascularization causes painless central blur, distortion, and scotoma with risk of irreversible central vision loss from disciform scarring. Management is largely reactive and injection heavy, relying on frequent intravitreal anti vascular endothelial growth factor therapy once neovascularization appears, leaving unmet needs for more durable treatment, preventing first events in high risk eyes, and reducing recurrence and scarring.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, less-than-monthly control of POHS-related CNV (e.g., sustained-delivery anti‑VEGF/alternative pathway) to reduce injection/procedure burden and risks
- Pharmacologic prevention of CNV in high-risk but asymptomatic POHS (e.g., macular histo spots or peripapillary atrophy) vs watchful waiting
- Anti-scarring/anti-recurrence adjuncts for foveal/subfoveal POHS CNV to prevent disciform scar–driven central vision loss

name: Behçet's Disease
description: Behçet’s disease is a rare, poorly understood inflammatory vasculitis, typically starting in adults in their 20s to 30s, marked by relapsing flares of painful oral and genital ulcers with eye and skin involvement. The central challenge is preventing irreversible organ damage such as vision loss from ocular inflammation and serious vascular events including thrombosis and aneurysms. With no cure, current immunosuppression and steroid based approaches often provide inconsistent control, can be disappointing for mucosal ulcers, and may not reliably protect against sight threatening disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Self-administered (ideally topical/local) therapy for recurrent Behçet genital ulcers that rapidly achieves complete ulcer closure (“ulcer area of zero”) with meaningful pain reduction.
- Steroid-sparing regimen for posterior-segment Behçet uveitis/retinal vasculitis that induces and maintains clinical + angiographic remission to prevent vision loss with less need for combination immunosuppression/anti‑TNF escalation.
- Safer, relapse-preventing therapy for vascular Behçet (pulmonary/peripheral artery aneurysms, major venous thrombosis) achieving durable clinical/radiologic remission with reduced reliance on high-dose steroids and cyclophosphamide/anti‑TNF–intensive approaches.

name: Alice in Wonderland Syndrome
description: Episodic perceptual disorder causing transient distortions of vision, body schema, and time, often in children and linked to infections such as Epstein Barr virus encephalitis or to migraine aura and epilepsy. Episodes last minutes to hours and can be frightening but are not psychosis. Care is mostly reassurance and treating the underlying trigger, with few syndrome specific options and limited evidence for aborting attacks or preventing recurrence in chronic migraine or seizure related cases.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid-onset, as-needed symptomatic therapy to abort disabling AIWS perceptual-distortion episodes.
- Prophylaxis specifically validated to reduce recurrence in migraine-/epilepsy-associated AIWS.
- Etiology-tailored anti-infective/immune-directed therapies for pediatric encephalitis-associated (especially EBV-linked) AIWS.

name: Brown syndrome
description: Brown syndrome is a restrictive vertical strabismus caused by impaired superior oblique tendon movement through the trochlea, leading to limited elevation in adduction, diplopia, and compensatory head posture. Many congenital cases improve spontaneously, so observation is common, but persistent misalignment can require surgery with risk of overcorrection and iatrogenic superior oblique palsy. Acquired inflammatory or scarring cases may relapse and need repeated anti inflammatory or steroid based interventions, leaving unmet need for durable, nonsurgical, steroid sparing options that reliably restore alignment and binocular vision.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical therapy for symptomatic congenital Brown syndrome (peds) to restore elevation-in-adduction and resolve primary-position hypotropia/head-tilt/diplopia while avoiding post-op iatrogenic superior oblique palsy/secondary surgery.
- Steroid-sparing, durable local anti-inflammatory treatment for acquired inflammatory Brown syndrome/trochleitis to achieve rapid remission (no primary-gaze diplopia) with fewer repeat injections/treatment failures.
- Anti-fibrotic/adhesion-modifying therapy to prevent or reverse peritrochlear scarring/stenosing tenosynovitis–driven mechanical restriction in acquired (post-trauma/iatrogenic) cases.

name: Eales disease
description: Eales disease is a rare, typically bilateral retinal vasculitis in young men that progresses from venous inflammation to occlusion and ischemia driven neovascularization, with recurrent vitreous hemorrhage causing painless floaters and episodic vision loss. Care is stage based and procedure heavy using corticosteroids, laser photocoagulation, frequent intravitreal anti vascular endothelial growth factor injections, and sometimes vitrectomy. Key unmet needs are durable neovascular and inflammation control with fewer interventions, steroid sparing options that avoid glaucoma and cataract risk, and clearer evidence for when antitubercular therapy is beneficial and safe.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable control of proliferative-stage retinal neovascularization to prevent recurrent vitreous hemorrhage/tractional RD while reducing q4w anti‑VEGF, laser and vitrectomy burden
- Steroid-sparing therapy for inflammatory/periphlebitis stage (incl. macular edema) that avoids steroid-induced cataract and IOP elevation
- Shorter, better-tolerated systemic regimens for TB-associated occlusive retinal vasculitis/Eales-like disease that still prevent ischemia-driven NV and recurrent hemorrhage
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus URL for Eales disease

name: Bacillus cereus infection
description: Bacillus cereus causes rapid-onset, toxin-mediated food poisoning with vomiting and diarrhea, typically after improperly stored starchy foods, and is usually self-limited with supportive hydration. The key unmet needs are preventing severe outcomes from heat-stable cereulide toxin with potential multi-organ dysfunction, and improving management of invasive infections in high-risk patients such as neonates and immunocompromised hosts where biofilm on catheters and beta-lactam resistance make eradication difficult and often necessitate device removal.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Cereulide-focused antitoxin/toxin-binding therapy for emetic *B. cereus* food intoxication (toxin-driven illness where antibiotics are ineffective).
- Biofilm-penetrant therapy (e.g., catheter-lock or systemic) to eradicate *Bacillus* catheter-related bloodstream infection with catheter salvage and lower recurrence.
- Neonatal-/immunocompromised-optimized, rapidly bactericidal regimens for invasive *B. cereus* with predictable activity despite uncertain/variable resistance.

name: Enterococcus infection
description: Enterococcus infections are opportunistic, healthcare associated infections from normal gut flora that disproportionately affect frail, catheterized patients and often present as complicated urinary tract infection with fever, flank pain or delirium. Treatment is difficult because biofilms on indwelling devices and intrinsic multidrug resistance including vancomycin resistance drive persistence and recurrence, often necessitating 10 to 14 days of therapy with intravenous agents and lab monitoring. Key unmet needs include easier oral or long acting options, less monitoring intensive regimens, and anti biofilm or device focused approaches to prevent and clear infection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral or long-acting outpatient options for upper-tract and/or bacteremic VRE (E. faecium) UTI to complete 10–14-day courses without IV dependence.
- Lower-toxicity, lower-monitoring VRE/Enterococcus-active regimens for frail/comorbid (esp. renal-risk) patients vs linezolid/daptomycin/vancomycin monitoring burdens.
- Anti-biofilm/catheter-targeted therapeutics to eradicate device-associated enterococcal colonization and prevent progression to bacteremia without requiring device removal.

name: Isosporiasis
description: Cystoisosporiasis is an intestinal infection caused by Cystoisospora belli, typically acquired from fecally contaminated food or water, and marked by weeks of profuse watery non-bloody diarrhea with dehydration, weight loss, and malabsorption. In people with uncontrolled human immunodeficiency virus it can become chronic and debilitating with frequent relapses. Care still relies on trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole, with some patients needing long term secondary prophylaxis, and the main unmet need is effective, well supported alternatives for patients who cannot take sulfonamides since second line options are less effective and backed by limited data.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- TMP‑SMX–sparing, non‑sulfonamide therapy with TMP‑SMX-like efficacy for sulfa‑intolerant HIV patients
- Relapse‑proof regimen that avoids chronic secondary prophylaxis in advanced HIV (CD4 <200 cells/mm³)
- Absorption‑independent (e.g., parenteral/long‑acting) option for severe diarrhea with malabsorption/inability to take oral meds

name: Kingella kingae infection
description: Kingella kingae is a throat carried Gram negative bacterium that spreads in daycare aged toddlers and commonly causes subtle osteoarticular infections such as septic arthritis and osteomyelitis. Many children are afebrile and routine cultures are often negative, so diagnosis increasingly depends on polymerase chain reaction testing of joint fluid. Care is still built around empiric inpatient intravenous beta lactams followed by weeks of oral antibiotics, creating avoidable hospitalization and uncertainty, especially with beta lactamase mediated aminopenicillin resistance. Outbreak control is also difficult since chemoprophylaxis only partially clears carriage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Outpatient-first, short-course therapy for 6–48‑month-olds with suspected/confirmed *K. kingae* osteoarticular infection that avoids routine OR drainage and shortens/avoids inpatient IV antibiotics
- Beta-lactamase–robust, pediatric-friendly definitive option usable in severe penicillin/cephalosporin allergy to replace fallback co-trimoxazole/ciprofloxacin pathways
- More effective, better-tolerated daycare cluster chemoprophylaxis/decolonization that reliably and durably eradicates *K. kingae* carriage

name: Noma
description: Noma (cancrum oris) is a rapidly progressive gangrenous infection of the mouth and face, mainly in malnourished children aged 2 to 6 in extreme poverty. It can evolve from gum sores to massive soft tissue and bone loss within days, causing fever, pain, foul odor, and hypersalivation, and leaving survivors with severe disfigurement and impaired speech and eating. The biggest gap is ultra early recognition and access to basic hygiene, antibiotics, and nutrition, since there is no point of care diagnostic test and delayed care shifts to complex, scarce reconstructive surgery and rehabilitation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course, field-deployable broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy to halt early-stage noma (acute necrotizing gingivitis) in malnourished children
- Adjunct progression-blocking therapy in oedema/acute-phase noma to prevent tissue necrosis and gangrenous progression
- Regenerative/wound-healing therapeutics post-gangrene to reduce scarring/trismus and feeding/speech disability (reducing need for multiple reconstructive surgeries)

name: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
description: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a rare, rapidly progressive motor neuron disease in which upper and lower motor neurons degenerate, causing limb or bulbar weakness that advances to paralysis and loss of breathing control. Diagnosis is most often between ages 55 and 75, and survival is typically 2 to 5 years, with death commonly from respiratory failure. There is no cure and no therapy proven to halt or reverse progression, while existing disease modifying options have only modest benefit and the most targeted approach applies only to small genetic subgroups, leaving a premium on broadly effective disease modification and reliable biomarkers to guide development.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Broadly applicable disease-modifying therapy that meaningfully extends survival and delays respiratory failure beyond current modest survival benefit.
- Scalable precision/genetic therapies beyond SOD1-ALS (esp. C9orf72-ALS) with biomarker-tracked target engagement (e.g., CSF poly(GP)).
- Treatments proven effective in later-stage/advanced ALS populations typically excluded from pivotal trials, with clinically meaningful endpoints (delay NIV/tracheostomy or tube feeding).

name: Multiple sclerosis | primary progressive
description: Primary progressive multiple sclerosis is a neurodegenerative form of multiple sclerosis with gradual, relentless disability accumulation and rare relapses, typically presenting in the 40s to 50s with worsening gait and leg stiffness or weakness, often alongside balance problems, fatigue, and bladder or bowel dysfunction. Disease biology is driven by compartmentalized chronic inflammation with smouldering lesions, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and remyelination failure, making progression hard to modify. Treatment options are narrow, largely limited to ocrelizumab for selected patients with active early disease, and its intravenous anti-CD20 risks infections and infusion reactions, leaving unmet need for broader, safer therapies that slow disability and support remyelination and neuroprotection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Greater slowing of disability progression (12-/24-week CDP) in broader PPMS populations (e.g., age >55 and/or EDSS 7–8), beyond “early/MRI-active” disease.
- CNS-penetrant neuroprotective/remyelination therapies targeting “smouldering” progression (e.g., chronic active/slowly expanding paramagnetic rim lesions).
- Lower-burden, safer long-term alternatives to IV anti-CD20 (fewer URTIs/infusion reactions; reduced hypogammaglobulinemia/serious infection risk; less infusion/observation time).

name: Pediculosis corporis
description: Body lice infestation with insects living and laying eggs in clothing seams, causing intense itching, sores and secondary bacterial infection, and chronic skin thickening and darkening. It disproportionately affects people in crowded low hygiene settings such as homelessness and refugee shelters, where control hinges on access to bathing, laundering, and clean clothes. Current pediculicides have limited real world durability and can drive resistance, leaving a need for long lasting, resistance robust, shelter deployable delousing strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Long-acting (ideally systemic/endectocidal) delousing that maintains lice-free status through ≥Day 45 in unhoused/shelter populations
- Non-pyrethroid pediculicide with high barrier to resistance where permethrin-resistant haplotypes are prevalent
- Safer, simpler shelter-deployable topical ovicide/adulticide that avoids malathion hazards and reduces reliance on hot-laundry/clean-clothes measures

name: Pneumocystis pneumonia
description: Pneumocystis pneumonia is a rare, serious fungal lung infection in immunocompromised patients, often progressing over days to weeks with worsening shortness of breath, fever, and dry cough and risking hypoxemic respiratory failure. Treatment still relies on ~21 days of trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, but high toxicity and frequent intolerance force regimen changes, and outcomes are especially poor in non-HIV immunosuppressed patients with reported 35–50% mortality, driving demand for safer, simpler, more effective therapies that prevent ventilation and death.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- TMP‑SMX–sparing (non‑sulfonamide) regimens for patients unable to tolerate first‑line therapy due to severe toxicity (esp. transplant/hematologic malignancy patients with renal/bone‑marrow vulnerability).
- Shorter/less burdensome regimens than standard 21‑day, q6–8h divided TMP‑SMX dosing, reducing need for toxic rescue therapy and intensive lab monitoring.
- Therapies for severe non‑HIV immunocompromised PCP that reduce progression to invasive ventilation/ARDS and early (e.g., 30‑day) mortality.

name: Bladder sphincter dyssynergia
description: Detrusor sphincter dyssynergia is a neurogenic miswiring, often after spinal cord injury or in multiple sclerosis, where the bladder contracts to void while the urethral sphincter paradoxically tightens, causing obstructed emptying, incontinence and chronic retention. The high pressure bladder that results can drive reflux, stones, recurrent urinary tract infections, autonomic dysreflexia, and progressive upper tract and kidney damage, especially when pressures exceed about 40 cm water. Current care is burdensome and invasive, relying on frequent intermittent catheterization and escalating to medications, botulinum toxin, sphincterotomy, permanent catheterization, or diversion, leaving a premium on durable pressure control with fewer procedures.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drug-driven control of DSD/DSD-related bladder pressures to achieve DLPP <40 cm H2O (upper-tract protection) in high-risk suprasacral SCI/MS patients.
- Therapy that reduces every-4–6-hour intermittent catheterization by enabling predictable low-residual emptying while keeping bladder volumes <500 mL and preventing AD/AKI.
- Chronic NLUTD option with materially better tolerability than antimuscarinics/α-blockers (e.g., less dry mouth/constipation/somnolence and less orthostasis/syncope).

name: BRASH Syndrome
description: BRASH syndrome is a life threatening self perpetuating loop where atrioventricular nodal blockers plus acute kidney injury, often triggered by dehydration in older patients, drive hyperkalemia and profound bradycardia that can rapidly progress to hypotension and shock. Care is high stakes and resource heavy, requiring simultaneous potassium shifting, perfusion support, and chronotropic rescue, since atropine often fails and escalation to pacing or dialysis may be needed. Key unmet needs include faster potassium removal and more targeted, reliable reversal of bradycardia to prevent invasive escalation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Hypoglycemia-sparing rapid hyperkalemia control (K+ <6.0 mmol/L within ~2 hours) for BRASH patients with AKI/CKD to avoid insulin–dextrose monitoring burden
- Targeted pharmacologic reversal of profound, non‑vagal BRASH bradycardia when atropine is ineffective to reduce need for pressors/pacing
- Emergency-use potassium elimination that rapidly removes K+ (not just shifts it) to prevent rebound and reduce dialysis reliance vs delayed-onset oral binders

name: High altitude renal syndrome
description: High altitude renal syndrome is a hypoxia driven cardiorenal cluster in long term high altitude residents marked by excessive erythrocytosis, hyperuricemia, systemic hypertension, and early microalbuminuria or proteinuria despite relatively preserved glomerular filtration rate. Care is largely limited to descent or supplemental oxygen, with little clinical evidence that kidney targeted drugs modify renal pathology, leaving a major unmet need for therapies that prevent hypoxia linked glomerular and podocyte injury and improve renal outcomes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Renal-outcome–proven therapy that durably reduces albuminuria/proteinuria and preserves eGFR in high-altitude residents with HARS.
- Better-tolerated, adherence-friendly oral therapy to lower hematocrit/hemoglobin and improve oxygenation without acetazolamide-like CNS adverse effects.
- Upstream disease-driver drugs (e.g., hypoxia/HIF-2α-pathway or endothelin-axis modulation) to treat hypoxia-driven HAPC and prevent downstream hyperuricemia/HTN/proteinuria when descent/oxygen aren’t feasible.
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus URL for HARS

name: Nephropathy | IgA
description: Immunoglobulin A nephropathy is an autoimmune kidney disease where IgA antibody clumps deposit in the kidneys, driving inflammation and kidney damage that often shows up as blood and protein in the urine and can progress to kidney failure. Patients are commonly diagnosed in adolescence to midlife, sometimes after a respiratory infection or incidentally on urinalysis. Care is constrained by steroid toxicity and a need for durable, steroid sparing therapies that reliably preserve kidney function beyond proteinuria based surrogate endpoints.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Kidney-function–preserving therapies (eGFR slope/CKD progression) proven beyond proteinuria-only surrogates for the broader “at-risk” IgAN population (proteinuria ≥0.5 g/day)
- Steroid-sparing regimens that avoid corticosteroid toxicities/immunosuppression burden and reduce access/monitoring friction (e.g., FILSPARI REMS, liver labs, embryo‑fetal risk constraints)
- Effective options for advanced/aggressive IgAN populations under-served by pivotal evidence (e.g., lower eGFR, crescentic/rapidly progressive disease currently defaulting to cyclophosphamide + systemic glucocorticoids)

name: Loin pain hematuria syndrome
description: Loin pain hematuria syndrome is an ultra rare renal pain disorder marked by severe unilateral or bilateral flank pain with microscopic or gross hematuria, often in young women, with largely preserved kidney function despite high disability. Diagnosis is prolonged and exclusionary, and care is mostly symptomatic, frequently escalating to high dose opioids and even last resort procedures. The central unmet need is durable opioid sparing pain control and reliable flare prevention, ideally via better targeted approaches including renal hemodynamic modulation in suspected thin glomerular basement membrane subgroups.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Opioid-sparing chronic analgesia providing durable flank-pain reduction for patients currently requiring high-dose opioids/NSAIDs
- Hematuria-and-pain flare prevention with renal hemodynamic modulators (ACEi/ARB-class or novel) in the suspected glomerular/“thin GBM” subgroup
- Non-invasive neuromodulatory pharmacotherapy (systemic or targeted renal delivery) with sustained benefit for refractory pain vs short-lived/intolerable local-drug approaches

name: Medullary sponge kidney
description: Congenital kidney collecting duct malformation with cystic dilatation of the medulla that typically presents in teens to 20s with recurrent calcium kidney stones and urinary tract infections driven by distal tubular dysfunction such as hypercalciuria and hypocitraturia. Management is preventive and symptomatic with hydration, potassium citrate, thiazides, and sometimes antibiotics, but there is no way to reverse the underlying condition, leaving persistent recurrence risk and, in a subset, disabling chronic pain despite an often benign long term prognosis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-targeted prevention of urinary stones/nephrocalcinosis beyond potassium citrate + thiazides by correcting distal RTA/hypocitraturia/hypercalciuria drivers
- Non-antibiotic prophylaxis to reduce recurrent UTIs/pyelonephritis and avoid chronic low-dose antibiotic suppression
- Therapies for the chronic severe pain/high-stone-burden phenotype to reduce pain crises and pain-related hospitalizations

name: Nutcracker syndrome
description: Nutcracker syndrome is left renal vein compression, usually between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery, causing renal venous hypertension with hematuria, flank pain, and proteinuria, often in thin teens and young adults with pelvic congestion or varicocele. Diagnosis is inconsistent and many patients cycle through conservative measures such as weight gain before facing invasive procedures, where durability issues like stent migration and restenosis keep reintervention risk high.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-procedural therapy to reduce recurrent gross hematuria (incl transfusion-requiring episodes) and anemia
- Non-opioid therapy to improve severe flank/abdominal/pelvic pain and pelvic congestion to avoid narcotic-requiring/hospitalization cases
- Adjunct pharmacotherapy to reduce restenosis/recurrence and re-intervention after renal vein decompression/transposition/stenting

name: Renal infarction
description: Renal infarction is a rare, abrupt arterial occlusion that causes renal ischemia and tissue necrosis, typically in older adults and people with atrial fibrillation, presenting with sudden flank or abdominal pain and hematuria. Because it mimics kidney stones or pyelonephritis, diagnosis is often delayed and the window for reperfusion can be missed, leaving anticoagulation and selective thrombolysis or endovascular therapy as imperfect options. Many patients still progress to acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, or hypertension, driving unmet need for faster recognition and kidney protective therapies when reperfusion is no longer effective.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute reno-cytoprotective/ischemia–reperfusion injury modulator to preserve renal parenchyma in late-diagnosed renal infarction where reperfusion is ineffective.
- Post-infarct anti-fibrotic/anti-remodeling adjunct to reduce CKD and refractory hypertension after renal infarction.
- Bleeding-sparing, low-monitoring antithrombotic option for secondary prevention (esp. cardioembolic/AF-related) vs heparin→warfarin/INR monitoring.

name: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
description: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a rare, chronic relapsing vasculitis that primarily affects the sinuses and airways, lungs, and kidneys, often starting with persistent cold-like symptoms but risking progressive organ damage including life-threatening renal failure. Care relies on immunosuppression such as corticosteroids, yet treatment toxicity and recurrent flares remain common, creating a premium on steroid-sparing disease control, durable relapse prevention, and kidney-protective approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing remission induction that maintains efficacy while enabling rapid taper/off glucocorticoids in organ-threatening GPA.
- More durable relapse prevention for high-relapse-risk PR3-ANCA/ENT–lung GPA, reducing repeated infusion-based maintenance over long treatment horizons.
- Kidney-protective therapies for GPA glomerulonephritis that improve eGFR recovery and reduce progression to ESRD, especially in low-baseline-GFR patients.

name: Nephropathy | CFHR5
description: Inherited complement driven C3 glomerulopathy (endemic in Cypriots) causing persistent microscopic hematuria and infection triggered flares with visible hematuria and stepwise renal decline; over 80% of men progress to end stage kidney failure in adulthood, and there is no proven effective therapy with nonspecific immunosuppression inconsistent and sometimes harmful.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Infection-episode prophylaxis/on-demand therapy to prevent synpharyngitic macroscopic hematuria flares and associated acute renal-function deterioration
- Male-focused renal-survival/eGFR-preserving therapy to prevent stepwise decline to ESKD (vs proteinuria-centric benefit)
- CFHR5-genotype–specific complement-regulation correction to avoid inconsistent/potentially injurious immunosuppression and reduce systemic complement-inhibitor serious-infection/REMS burden

name: Nephropathy | DHA crystalline
description: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency causes excess 2,8-dihydroxyadenine that crystallizes into radiolucent urinary stones and crystal nephropathy, triggering recurrent acute kidney injury and progressive chronic kidney disease that can reach kidney failure. Many patients present in adulthood and are diagnosed late, sometimes only after kidney transplant dysfunction. Lifelong suppression with allopurinol or febuxostat can help, but serious allopurinol hypersensitivity and febuxostat’s cardiovascular death boxed warning leave a major need for safer long term crystal prevention that preserves native and transplanted kidney function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Renal-outcome–proven control that durably eliminates urinary 2,8‑DHA/crystalluria and slows CKD→ESRD progression in late-diagnosed adults.
- Chronic prophylaxis option that maintains high-potency DHA suppression while avoiding allopurinol hypersensitivity/SJS-TEN risk and febuxostat boxed-warning mortality concerns.
- Transplant-optimized prevention that reliably prevents post-transplant DHA crystal recurrence/graft loss with less reliance on very high-dose, months-long pre-transplant allopurinol.

name: Hyperoxaluria
description: Primary hyperoxaluria is a rare inherited liver metabolism disorder that overproduces oxalate, driving recurrent calcium oxalate kidney stones and nephrocalcinosis from childhood or adolescence and progressing to kidney failure with systemic oxalosis. Care is still largely supportive with high fluid intake and citrate, with pyridoxine helping only select genotypes, leaving a major need for durable oxalate lowering therapies that prevent renal decline and avoid the heavy dialysis burden in advanced disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapies effective in PH2/PH3 that address extrahepatic/alternative oxalate sources and reduce stone burden
- Treatments for advanced CKD/ESKD/systemic oxalosis that lower plasma oxalate and reduce dialysis/transplant burden
- More convenient regimens that reduce daily hyperhydration requirements and enable at-home/self-administered dosing (vs clinic-administered injections)

name: Microscopic polyangiitis
description: Microscopic polyangiitis is a rare antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody associated, pauci immune necrotizing small vessel vasculitis that can present as aggressive kidney and lung disease and rapidly progress to organ failure. Care for organ threatening disease still relies on high dose glucocorticoids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide, creating a difficult balance between controlling inflammation and serious treatment toxicity, especially infection risk. Even with therapy it behaves as a chronic relapsing condition and severe cases can end in kidney failure requiring dialysis or transplant, sustaining demand for safer, steroid sparing and more durable disease control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-/infection-sparing induction for organ-/life-threatening MPA (severe renal involvement and/or pulmonary hemorrhage) while preserving death/ESKD efficacy.
- Kidney-outcome–improving therapies for MPA with rapidly progressive GN/low eGFR to reduce death/ESKD and accelerate eGFR recovery.
- More durable, lower-toxicity maintenance for relapse-prone MPA to reduce relapses and enable immunosuppressive withdrawal.

name: Milk-alkali syndrome
description: Milk-alkali syndrome is a preventable calcium carbonate and absorbable alkali toxicity causing hypercalcemia, metabolic alkalosis, and acute kidney injury, seen mainly in older adults such as postmenopausal patients using over the counter calcium for osteoporosis and people with chronic kidney disease. Symptoms can be subtle or include confusion, nausea, constipation, and polyuria. Severe cases often require inpatient intravenous saline and diuresis, and current calcium lowering options have tradeoffs, creating need for outpatient feasible, kidney safe therapies that avoid calcitonin tachyphylaxis and prolonged bisphosphonate induced hypocalcemia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Outpatient/ED-observation–feasible therapy that rapidly normalizes calcium without requiring hospital admission and large-volume IV isotonic saline (“saline diuresis”).
- Renal-safe, titratable calcium-lowering agent that outlasts calcitonin’s ~48-hour tachyphylaxis but avoids delayed/prolonged bisphosphonate effects and treatment-induced hypocalcemia.
- Kidney-protective adjuncts that improve completeness of renal recovery after acute episodes (reduce risk of permanent renal impairment).

name: Minimal change disease
description: Minimal change disease is a common childhood cause of nephrotic syndrome, typically presenting at ages 2 to 9 with abrupt edema, foamy urine, and heavy protein loss, and diagnosed by electron microscopy. Most children remit quickly on prednisone, but 50 to 75 percent relapse, forcing repeated steroid courses with cumulative toxicity and frequent escalation to calcineurin inhibitors that add nephrotoxicity risk and intensive drug level monitoring. The clinical and commercial gap is durable relapse prevention with steroid sparing, kidney safe long term control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing induction for new-onset pediatric SSNS/MCD that preserves rapid remission while reducing early prednisolone toxicity.
- Durable relapse prevention for frequently relapsing/steroid-dependent pediatric MCD (reduce relapse frequency and prolong time-to-first-relapse to cut cumulative steroid exposure).
- CNI-free long-term control for FR/SD and/or treatment-resistant MCD that avoids monthly trough monitoring and chronic CNI nephrotoxicity while minimizing caregiver monitoring burden.

name: Multicystic dysplastic kidney
description: Congenital fetal kidney malformation where the affected kidney is nonfunctional, often detected prenatally and managed with postnatal surveillance. Most children live with one working kidney, but outcomes hinge on protecting the solitary functioning kidney since contralateral reflux or obstruction is relatively common and can drive albuminuria, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease risk over decades. The severe end is bilateral disease with renal anhydramnios, where absent fetal urine leads to pulmonary hypoplasia and near universal neonatal fatality, motivating fetal fluid restoration approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prenatal kidney-function rescue for fetuses with bilateral MCDK/renal anhydramnios to prevent oligohydramnios → pulmonary hypoplasia → neonatal death.
- Long-term renoprotection for unilateral MCDK patients with a solitary functioning kidney to prevent hyperfiltration-driven hypertension and albuminuria/proteinuria (CKD risk).
- Medical prevention of injury to the working kidney in MCDK with contralateral CAKUT by reducing UTI burden and reflux/obstruction-related damage (e.g., VUR or UPJ obstruction/hydronephrosis).

name: Nephropathy | sickle cell
description: Sickle cell nephropathy is progressive kidney injury in sickle cell disease that often starts silently in childhood with tubular concentrating defects and glomerular hyperfiltration, later developing albuminuria or proteinuria and sometimes hematuria, and can progress to chronic kidney disease and kidney failure. The renal medulla’s hypoxic, acidic, hypertonic environment drives ongoing sickling and ischemic damage. Current care relies on renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system inhibitors and hydroxyurea, but evidence for long term disease modification is limited, leaving a premium on therapies that deliver hard outcome renoprotection and restore tubular concentrating function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Hard-outcomes renoprotection for adults with KDIGO-confirmed kidney dysfunction to prevent CKD progression (e.g., 40% eGFR decline/ESKD), beyond albuminuria lowering
- Early-intervention therapies for adolescents/young adults with microalbuminuria delivering clinically meaningful ACR/UACR responses (e.g., ≥30% reduction) without ACEi/ARB safety-monitoring constraints
- Tubular-function restoration to improve hyposthenuria-related polyuria/nocturia and dehydration/enuresis by targeting renal hypoxia/ischemia/hemolysis biology beyond hydroxyurea

name: Limb–girdle muscular dystrophy
description: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy is a group of inherited disorders causing progressive weakness and wasting of proximal shoulder and hip muscles, often starting with waddling gait and difficulty rising from chairs or climbing stairs, sometimes with cardiomyopathy or respiratory compromise. Care remains largely supportive since no treatment reverses weakness, leaving a major unmet need for durable, genotype-targeted disease-modifying therapies that preserve ambulation and cardiopulmonary function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy that durably improves/stabilizes motor function (NSAD/timed tests) and delays loss of ambulation in ambulatory LGMD.
- Genotype-targeted therapy for FKRP-related LGMD2I/R9 that improves long-horizon function (NSAD/10m walk) with biomarker response (glycosylated α-dystroglycan).
- Options safe/effective for patients excluded from systemic AAV gene therapy (e.g., high anti-AAVrh74 titers and/or advanced cardiopulmonary impairment).

name: Chondrosarcoma
description: Rare cartilage derived bone cancer in adults often pelvis or proximal long bones causing progressive deep pain with swelling or a mass. Care is largely surgical because conventional tumors are chemo and radiation resistant, leaving few options for unresectable or metastatic disease and a premium on effective systemic tumor shrinking and durable control. Biomarker guided strategies including isocitrate dehydrogenase mutant targeting are an emerging direction.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neoadjuvant tumor-shrinking therapy (RECIST PR) for large pelvic/hip primary tumors to reduce need for highly morbid surgery
- Durable systemic disease control/OS benefit in unresectable or metastatic chondrosarcoma (incl. biomarker-stratified approaches such as IDH1/2)
- Much higher objective response rates and survival-improving regimens for dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma vs current low-response chemotherapy

name: Familial chylomicronemia syndrome
description: Familial chylomicronemia syndrome is an ultra rare inherited defect in fat metabolism where absent or impaired lipoprotein lipase activity causes chylomicron buildup and extreme triglycerides, leading to recurrent abdominal pain and pancreatitis that can become chronic and rarely life threatening, sometimes with eruptive xanthomas and lipemia retinalis. Care is dominated by a very low fat diet, yet many patients cannot reliably reach triglyceride levels associated with lower pancreatitis risk, and available drug therapy carries thrombocytopenia risk and frequent platelet monitoring, leaving a premium on safer durable triglyceride control and disease modifying approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pancreatitis-proof control despite diet lapses (maintain fasting TG <500 mg/dL; drive adjudicated acute pancreatitis events toward ~0)
- Platelet-safe triglyceride lowering that avoids thrombocytopenia and frequent platelet monitoring
- Reduce lifelong very-low-fat diet burden with pediatric-appropriate pharmacotherapy

name: Ependymoma | subependymoma (WHO Grade 1)
description: Subependymoma is a rare, usually slow growing World Health Organization grade 1 tumor that arises in the brain’s ventricular system and is often found incidentally in middle aged adults. When it causes problems, obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid leads to hydrocephalus with headaches, nausea or vomiting, and gait or balance changes. Management is typically magnetic resonance imaging surveillance or neurosurgical resection, leaving few options for patients who are not surgical candidates or have unresectable or residual disease. Better molecular stratification may help identify higher risk subtypes and guide future therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- BBB-penetrant medical therapy to control symptomatic subependymoma that is not fully resectable due to location, reducing need for surgery/radiation.
- Post-op adjuvant/maintenance systemic or locoregional therapy for residual disease and/or mixed subependymoma–ependymoma to improve radiographic control/recurrence-free survival while sparing radiation.
- Molecularly stratified targeted therapy for higher-risk posterior fossa subependymomas with TERT promoter mutation and/or chromosome 6 loss.

name: Hereditary angioedema
description: Hereditary angioedema is a rare inherited C1 inhibitor disorder causing excess bradykinin and unpredictable, non itchy swelling attacks of skin, gut, and sometimes the airway with asphyxiation risk. Despite better options, patients still face high treatment burden since prevention and rescue often require frequent injections, and some have incomplete control. A major gap remains for hereditary angioedema with normal C1 inhibitor, where diagnosis is difficult and no Food and Drug Administration approved therapy exists.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral, self-administered on-demand HAE attack treatment with rapid symptom relief (hours), including for laryngeal attacks, avoiding injection-site tolerability burden.
- Ultra-long-acting prophylaxis that achieves complete/attack-free control with lower dosing and rescue-medication burden vs q2–4 week injections or daily oral prophylaxis.
- Targeted therapies (with validated biomarkers) for HAE with normal C1-inhibitor (HAE-nC1-INH) to address diagnostic uncertainty and lack of approved treatments/mechanism clarity.

name: Thymic carcinoma
description: Thymic carcinoma is a rare anterior mediastinal cancer of thymic epithelial tissue, often incidentally found until local mass effects cause cough, dyspnea, chest pain, hoarseness, or superior vena cava syndrome. It can metastasize, and advanced unresectable disease has few good systemic options because platinum chemotherapy has limited efficacy and immune checkpoint inhibitors may cause severe immune toxicities including myocarditis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- More effective, durable systemic therapy for advanced/unresectable thymic carcinoma that meaningfully improves on platinum–taxane outcomes
- Checkpoint-immunotherapy with substantially lower severe autoimmune toxicity (especially myocarditis) while preserving efficacy
- Biomarker-driven precision therapies (ideally oral) for molecularly defined subsets (e.g., KIT/ERBB2/KRAS/TP53-altered) to reduce reliance on repetitive IV chemo/IO

name: Generalized lymphatic anomaly
description: Generalized lymphatic anomaly is an ultra-rare, multisystem developmental lymphatic disorder usually presenting in infancy or childhood, with abnormal dilated lymphatic vessels across organs. It can cause life-threatening thoracic lymphatic leak with chylothorax and frequent lytic bone disease leading to pain and fractures. Management is largely supportive and noncurative. Pathway inhibitors such as phosphoinositide 3-kinase and mammalian target of rapamycin blockade may reduce symptoms but often fail to durably regress established disease and can have serious side effects, driving demand for durable, genotype-guided therapies in PIK3CA-driven disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable pharmacologic control of life‑threatening thoracic lymphatic leak (esp. chylous pleural effusions) in pediatric multisystem GLA
- Disease modification with lesion regression/complete radiologic response plus stabilization/healing of vertebra/rib lytic bone disease
- Genotype‑directed systemic therapy for GLA (e.g., PI3Kα or MEK inhibitors) with improved long‑term tolerability vs sirolimus and reduced monitoring burden

name: Melanoma | mucosal
description: Rare, aggressive melanoma of mucous membranes (head and neck, anorectal, vulvovaginal) typically in older adults; hidden sites and nonspecific bleeding symptoms drive late metastatic diagnosis and poor survival. Low tumor mutational burden and often low programmed death ligand 1 expression limit checkpoint inhibitor benefit, while KIT targeted therapy helps a subset but responses are rarely durable, leaving a need for earlier detection and more effective, better tolerated systemic and immune sensitizing treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Immune-sensitizing systemic regimens that improve ORR/OS beyond anti–PD‑1 monotherapy in advanced/metastatic mucosal melanoma, including efficacy in typically PD‑L1–negative/low‑TMB patients.
- Durable, mutation-selected targeted therapy for KIT-mutant mucosal melanoma that extends disease control beyond short-lived single-agent imatinib responses.
- Checkpoint strategies with substantially lower grade 3/4 toxicity and discontinuation than nivolumab+ipilimumab and reduced infusion burden vs frequent IV PD‑1 dosing.

name: Fusariosis
description: Fusariosis is a rare, invasive mold infection in profoundly immunocompromised patients such as those on acute leukemia induction chemotherapy or after allogeneic stem cell transplant, often presenting as disseminated disease with persistent fever, positive blood cultures, painful metastatic skin lesions, and pneumonia. Mortality is driven by failure of neutrophil recovery and can approach 100% with ongoing neutropenia. Treatment relies on voriconazole and amphotericin B despite low susceptibility and intrinsic echinocandin resistance, leaving major gaps in rapid diagnosis and reliably active, better tolerated systemic agents.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Improve clinical success and short-term survival in disseminated invasive fusariosis in neutropenic hematologic malignancy/HSCT patients.
- Provide consistent efficacy against resistant/high-MIC Fusarium across species complexes (including intrinsic echinocandin non-susceptibility).
- Reduce toxicity, therapeutic drug monitoring needs, and prolonged IV burden (enable safer oral/IV step-down options).

name: Schwannomatosis
description: Schwannomatosis is a rare disorder marked by multiple benign schwannomas on peripheral and spinal nerves, typically presenting in adulthood with chronic localized or diffuse pain that can occur even without an identifiable tumor, plus numbness, tingling, weakness, and headaches. Care is largely symptomatic since there is no cure or proven drug to treat the tumors, leaving repeat surgeries that carry nerve injury and regrowth risk and often fail to provide durable pain relief. A key need is disease modifying therapies that reduce tumor burden and deliver sustained, protocolized pain control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Mechanism-based non-surgical analgesia delivering durable, clinically meaningful worst-pain (NRS-11) reduction in moderate-to-severe refractory schwannomatosis pain (including pain without identifiable tumors)
- Systemic medical therapy that shrinks or stabilizes schwannomas (tumor size/growth), especially for multiple rapidly enlarging and/or inoperable painful tumors
- Function-preserving drug alternatives to repeated tumor resections that reduce nerve-injury risk and regrowth-driven symptom recurrence

name: Amyloidosis | familial visceral
description: Rare inherited amyloidosis with liver produced mutant fibrinogen depositing in kidney glomeruli, causing proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome and hypertension with rapid progression to end stage kidney disease. Care is largely supportive and transplant based but deposits cannot be cleared and isolated kidney grafts often fail from recurrence. High value needs are therapies that suppress hepatic precursor production, remove renal amyloid and prevent post transplant recurrence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Liver-targeted suppression/editing of the amyloidogenic FGA variant to halt new glomerular deposition and delay/avoid rapid proteinuria→ESRD progression
- Amyloid-depleting renal therapy that goes beyond symptomatic proteinuria reduction to preserve/improve kidney function
- Post–kidney-transplant anti-recurrence therapy to extend graft durability after isolated renal transplant

name: Early myoclonic encephalopathy
description: Rare neonatal developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with fragmentary myoclonus and erratic focal seizures starting within hours to days of birth, suppression burst electroencephalography, hypotonia and feeding difficulties, and typically profound developmental impairment. Care is largely supportive because seizures are frequent and drug resistant, and rapid deterioration can include apnea and respiratory failure. The biggest unmet needs are neonatal safe rapid seizure control and fast workup to identify treatable metabolic causes such as pyridoxine or pyridoxal 5 phosphate disorders and nonketotic hyperglycinemia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid, neonatal-appropriate anti-seizure therapy with sustained EEG-confirmed seizure cessation and lower cardiorespiratory toxicity/ICU-escalation than phenobarbital-class regimens.
- Etiology-specific metabolic therapy for the nonketotic hyperglycinemia (NKH)–driven early myoclonic encephalopathy subgroup that improves apnea/hypotonia and long-term outcomes.
- Precision vitamin-responsive DEE (pyridoxine/P5P-responsive) rapid rescue/maintenance to promptly terminate seizures and prevent irreversible neurodevelopmental injury.

name: Metachromatic leukodystrophy
description: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is an ultra rare inherited lysosomal disorder caused by arylsulfatase A deficiency that leads to sulfatide buildup, progressive demyelination, and rapid loss of motor and cognitive function often beginning in the second year of life. Many children are diagnosed after symptoms emerge, when disease is already too advanced for current disease modifying approaches. Even when eligible, gene therapy requires intensive chemotherapy conditioning and long term malignancy surveillance. The major unmet need is safer, scalable treatments that work after symptom onset, including for late juvenile and adult disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy for late-infantile MLD after symptom onset that preserves motor function/locomotion
- Disease-modifying approach that avoids myeloablative/high-dose chemotherapy conditioning and reduces associated toxicities/long-term genotoxicity monitoring burden
- Disease-modifying therapy with proven efficacy/safety in late-juvenile MLD

name: Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis
description: Rare inherited skeletal muscle channelopathy causing brief, triggerable episodes of flaccid weakness or paralysis (often starting in infancy or early childhood) with hyperkalemia and myotonia; strength returns between attacks but repeated episodes can lead to permanent weakness. Management relies on trigger avoidance and empiric drugs with limited effectiveness, leaving unmet need for reliable, better tolerated prevention and muscle preserving therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Potassium-trigger–resilient, SCN4A/Na\_v1.4–targeted prophylaxis that delivers consistent, statistically robust reductions in weekly attack rate with better tolerability and less monitoring than carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.
- Therapies that prevent/slow chronic progressive myopathy and permanent fixed weakness, with demonstrated improvements in objective strength/muscle measures (not just attack suppression).
- Pediatric-ready prophylaxis and rescue options with established safety/efficacy for childhood-onset HyperPP.

name: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva
description: Ultra rare genetic disorder where children are born with malformed big toes and later develop trauma or illness triggered painful flare ups that cause heterotopic ossification, progressive stiffness, and permanent immobility; treatment is largely supportive with non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs and short steroid courses, with no cure and a major need for therapies that prevent flare ups and halt soft tissue turning into bone.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer disease-modifying option for currently underserved youngest patients (females <8y/males <10y) and pregnancy-capable patients, avoiding teratogenicity and premature epiphyseal closure
- Flare-up preventive/abortive therapy that stops painful inflammatory flare-ups from converting into mature heterotopic bone (beyond steroids/NSAIDs symptom control)
- Pharmacologic reduction of established heterotopic bone/ankylosis to restore function without triggering new heterotopic ossification

name: Angiosarcoma
description: Angiosarcoma is a very rare, aggressive cancer arising from blood or lymphatic vessels, often presenting in older adults as a bruise-like purplish lesion on the scalp or head and neck that enlarges, bleeds, and ulcerates, delaying diagnosis. Even with surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy, relapse and metastasis are common and systemic therapy rarely delivers durable control, leaving a premium on better tolerated, relapse preventing options and more reliable biomarker guided immunotherapy for responsive subsets.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Effective (neo)adjuvant systemic therapy to prevent relapse after curative-intent local treatment in cutaneous angiosarcoma (reduce high 5-year local recurrence/metastasis).
- Biomarker-directed immunotherapy (e.g., UV/TMB/PD-L1–selected) for head/neck cutaneous angiosarcoma to improve response durability vs chemotherapy.
- Lower-toxicity, lower-visit-burden systemic options to replace/augment weekly IV taxanes and reduce dependence on daily external-beam RT schedules, especially for older patients.

name: Epidermolysis bullosa | junctional
description: Junctional epidermolysis bullosa is a rare inherited skin anchoring disorder with blistering and erosions from birth that can progress to bleeding granulation tissue, airway involvement, severe infections, fluid and protein loss, and early infant death in the most severe forms. Care is largely supportive and highly burdensome, with chronic wounds often colonized by resistant bacteria, leaving major unmet need for disease modifying approaches that restore stable skin adhesion biology such as laminin 332 and for better pain control and anti infective wound care.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable skin-anchoring restoration to prevent life‑threatening erosions/sepsis and reduce early mortality in generalized severe (Herlitz) JEB
- Mutation-defined therapy for the high-prevalence LAMB3 nonsense subset to restore laminin‑332/hemidesmosomes and reduce blistering/improve wound closure
- Topical anti-infective wound therapy active on MRSA/*Pseudomonas* colonized/infected wounds that also reduces dressing-change procedural pain/pruritus

name: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency | familial
description: Familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency is a rare inherited loss of lipoprotein lipase activity causing chylomicronemia and extreme hypertriglyceridemia from childhood, with abdominal pain and recurrent acute pancreatitis plus xanthomas and organ enlargement. Care still depends on an ultra low fat diet around 10 to 20 g per day that dominates daily life yet may not prevent dangerous triglyceride spikes or pancreatitis. Antisense therapy requires chronic injections and intensive platelet monitoring, and lacks pediatric data, leaving a clear need for safer, easier, disease modifying options that reliably prevent pancreatitis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pediatric-label therapy (≤17y) that reduces adjudicated acute pancreatitis event rate in familial LPL deficiency
- Diet-liberalizing therapy that maintains fasting TG below pancreatitis-risk thresholds (≤1000 mg/dL; ideally ≤500 mg/dL) to prevent recurrent pancreatitis
- Triglyceride-lowering option that avoids thrombocytopenia and frequent platelet monitoring vs APOC3 antisense (and ideally reduces injection burden)

name: Chordoma | classic
description: Chordoma is an ultra-rare, slow-growing bone tumor from embryonic notochord remnants, usually in the sacrum or skull base, typically diagnosed in adults 40 to 70 with pain and neurologic compromise including bowel or bladder dysfunction, headaches, and double vision. Care centers on surgery plus radiation, but durable local control is hard near vital structures and recurrence is common. There is no approved systemic therapy and drugs mostly stabilize disease, creating a premium for disease-modifying, biomarker-guided approaches such as targeting TBXT brachyury biology and CDK4/6 pathway vulnerability in p16 CDKN2A–loss tumors.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjuvant systemic therapy to prevent local relapse after surgery/radiation (improve local-recurrence–free survival).
- TBXT (brachyury) driver-targeted therapy for the near-universal TBXT-positive chordoma population.
- Biomarker-selected CDK4/6-pathway inhibition for p16/CDKN2A-inactivated tumors with improved benefit–risk vs current TKIs.

name: Ornithosis
description: Ornithosis (psittacosis) is an uncommon bird-borne infection caused by Chlamydia psittaci, typically acquired by inhaling aerosolized material from infected birds and presenting after about 5 to 14 days with abrupt flu-like illness and a dry cough that can progress to pneumonia. Care relies on tetracyclines, but diagnosis is often difficult, relapse can drive prolonged courses, and tetracyclines are problematic in pregnancy and young children. Severe cases may require hospitalization for complications, and adjunctive immunomodulatory approaches are being studied for severe pneumonia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pregnancy- and pediatric-safe (<9 years) first-line psittacosis regimen with proven efficacy when tetracyclines are contraindicated
- Adjunctive/optimized therapy for severe/ICU psittacosis pneumonia to prevent ARDS/multi-organ dysfunction and reduce 28-day mortality
- Shorter, lower pill-burden curative regimen that maintains rapid symptom control while reducing relapse vs prolonged treatment (≥10–14 days after fever abates)

name: Pancreatic cancer | acinar cell carcinoma
description: Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma is a rare pancreatic cancer, typically in older men, that often presents late with bulky tumors causing weight loss and abdominal or back pain. Treatment for unresectable disease lacks a standard and commonly relies on gemcitabine or fluorouracil based chemotherapy with limited evidence. Major unmet needs are earlier detection and disease modifying, molecularly matched therapies, given sizable actionable subsets with DNA repair alterations, RAF rearrangements, and a small microsatellite instability high group potentially responsive to immunotherapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- MAPK-pathway targeted therapy (BRAF/MEK or MEK inhibition) for the ~23% of PACC with BRAF/RAF1 rearrangements to achieve deep remissions vs limited-efficacy cytotoxic chemo.
- Oral PARP-inhibitor therapy (e.g., olaparib) for the ~22% of PACC with BRCA1/2 deficiency to drive objective responses with less burden than infusional multi-agent chemo.
- PD-1 checkpoint blockade for MSI-H/dMMR PACC (2.1%–14%) to achieve pCR and potentially convert unresectable disease to resectable after chemo failure.

name: Congenital myasthenic syndrome
description: Congenital myasthenic syndromes are inherited neuromuscular junction disorders causing early onset fatigable weakness, often involving ocular, bulbar, and limb muscles with feeding and swallowing difficulty, delayed motor milestones, and infection or fever triggered apnea or respiratory crises. Care is symptomatic and highly genotype dependent. Standard acetylcholinesterase inhibitor therapy can be ineffective or worsen key subtypes such as COLQ and DOK7, leaving a major unmet need for disease modifying, subtype targeted treatments that stabilize neuromuscular transmission and prevent respiratory decompensation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- NMJ-structure–restoring (non-AChEI) therapies for AChR-clustering–pathway CMS (e.g., DOK7/LRP4/MUSK, COLQ) where AChEIs are ineffective or can worsen symptoms
- Respiratory-crisis prevention therapies for presynaptic CMS with fever/infection-triggered apneic attacks (notably CHAT/RAPSN)
- Clinically validated, simplified-dosing therapies for ultra-rare CMS genotypes with no established treatment playbook (e.g., SLC5A7/SNAP25/SYT2/SCN4A/SLC25A1)

name: Ebola virus disease
description: Ebola virus disease is a severe viral hemorrhagic illness that starts suddenly with fever and fatigue, then can progress to vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain and kidney or liver impairment, with bleeding less common and typically later. Approved therapies are limited to Zaire ebolavirus, leaving Sudan and Bundibugyo outbreaks without proven treatments and creating a premium on pan ebolavirus options that can be deployed rapidly early in infection. Current monoclonal antibodies require intravenous infusion, a major operational bottleneck during epidemics, driving unmet need for easier delivery such as intramuscular dosing outside high resource settings.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pan-orthoebolavirus therapeutics (e.g., Sudan & Bundibugyo) where no approved treatments exist beyond Zaire ebolavirus
- Field-deployable non-IV options (oral or IM/SC) usable early outside ETUs to reduce reliance on intensive IV supportive care
- Rescue regimens that materially reduce mortality in high-viral-load/late-presenting patients where current mAbs still have very high 28-day mortality

name: Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm
description: Rare, aggressive blood cancer of plasmacytoid dendritic cells, typically in older adults, often starting with bruise like violaceous skin plaques or nodules and progressing to bone marrow, blood, lymph nodes and sometimes the central nervous system with cytopenias. Current intensive regimens can induce responses but remissions are short and relapse is common including central nervous system sanctuary relapse. Key needs are safer more durable outpatient therapies, better routine central nervous system screening and prophylaxis, and transplant independent long term disease control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer outpatient CD123-targeted therapy that avoids tagraxofusp/ELZONRIS capillary leak syndrome and reduces inpatient Cycle 1 requirement (incl broader eligibility beyond albumin-gated patients)
- Durable, transplant-independent remissions in relapsed/refractory BPDCN to improve short post-relapse survival
- CNS-penetrant systemic therapy plus routine CNS screening and prophylaxis/therapy to prevent occult CNS-driven relapse

name: Imerslund-Gräsbeck syndrome
description: Imerslund Gräsbeck syndrome is a rare inherited intestinal vitamin B12 malabsorption disorder caused by AMN or CUBN variants disrupting the cubam receptor, typically presenting in early childhood with megaloblastic anemia, failure to thrive, and often proteinuria with preserved kidney function. Lifelong vitamin B12 injections keep most patients well, but delayed diagnosis can leave irreversible neurologic injury and the chronic injection burden plus persistent proteinuria highlight the need for earlier recognition, needle free replacement, and disease correcting approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Needle-free high-dose oral/transmucosal vitamin B12 replacement achieving IM-equivalent hematologic recovery
- Disease-correcting restoration of the CUBN/AMN “cubam” pathway (e.g., gene/mRNA therapy) to re-enable dietary B12 absorption (and potentially renal manifestations)
- Adjunct neuroprotective/neurorecovery therapies for patients with neurologic involvement/severe neurocognitive manifestations

name: Castleman disease | multicentric
description: Idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease is a rare, life threatening lymphoproliferative disorder driven by a hyperinflammatory state often involving interleukin 6, causing systemic inflammatory symptoms and generalized lymphadenopathy with fevers, weight loss, anemia, hypoalbuminemia, anasarca, renal dysfunction and organ failure in aggressive subtypes. Anti interleukin 6 antibodies are first line, but about half of patients do not respond and therapy can require ongoing intravenous infusions every 3 weeks, creating a major need for rapid disease control options beyond interleukin 6 and lower burden maintenance, including for human herpesvirus 8 associated disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid, non–IL‑6–pathway therapies for iMCD (incl. severe/TAFRO) to achieve durable tumor + symptomatic responses in anti‑IL‑6 nonresponders
- Lower-burden maintenance vs indefinite q3‑week IV siltuximab (e.g., SC/oral or longer-acting regimens with less monitoring)
- HHV‑8–associated (often HIV+) MCD therapies that are Kaposi-sarcoma–safe and HHV‑8–relevant (alternatives to rituximab/IL‑6 mAbs)

name: Marginal zone lymphoma | nodal
description: Rare, slow growing B cell non Hodgkin lymphoma arising in lymph nodes, usually diagnosed after age 50 and often already stage 3 or 4 with bone marrow involvement. Treatment can work initially but relapse is common, some cases transform to aggressive disease, and care is largely extrapolated from other indolent lymphomas. The biggest unmet need is durable, evidence based disease control, especially for patients who progress early within 24 months who have markedly worse survival.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies for POD24/high-risk NMZL (relapse/progression within 24 months) to improve OS and reduce histologic transformation.
- Chemo-free or less myelosuppressive regimens to lower neutropenia-driven serious infection risk versus bendamustine+rituximab.
- More convenient, better-tolerated outpatient/oral, ideally fixed-duration options that reduce infusion burden and avoid BTKi off-target AEs (e.g., bleeding/AF/HTN/diarrhea).

name: T-cell lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma
description: Aggressive malignancy of immature T cells, often in adolescent and young adult males, frequently presenting with an anterior mediastinal mass causing respiratory distress. Treatment requires intensive multiagent chemotherapy for 2 to 3 years plus central nervous system prophylaxis with intrathecal therapy, creating major toxicity and burden. The core unmet need is effective, less toxic disease control in relapse where salvage outcomes remain poor with under 25 percent survival, along with therapies that eradicate minimal residual disease and better bridge patients to transplant.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- MRD-negative salvage therapy for relapsed/refractory T‑ALL/T‑LBL that reliably induces MRD-negativity to enable curative HSCT
- Toxicity-sparing regimens that preserve ALL-like efficacy while reducing severe chemo-backbone AEs (e.g., pegaspargase grade ≥3 toxicities, vincristine neuropathy, AYA osteonecrosis)
- Shorter, outpatient-friendly treatment that reduces the 2–3 year, intrathecal procedure-heavy therapy burden

name: Gangliocytoma
description: Rare, usually low grade neuronal or mixed neuronal glial brain tumor, often in the temporal lobe, typically presenting in children and young adults with focal seizures that are frequently drug refractory and can be accompanied by mass effect symptoms. Surgery is the main curative option but complete resection is not always feasible and seizure freedom without ongoing antiseizure medication is not universal, leaving a need for effective brain penetrant, molecularly matched systemic therapies for unresectable or recurrent disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drug therapies achieving Engel class I seizure freedom (ideally ASM discontinuation) for patients with persistent post-resection seizures and drug-resistant epilepsy.
- Brain-penetrant, lower-toxicity systemic options for symptomatic unresectable/progressive or relapsed disease to avoid multi-regimen chemotherapy backbones.
- Molecularly matched targeted therapies beyond BRAF V600E (including strategies for non–BRAF V600E alterations/fusions such as KRAS/FGFR/RAF1/NTRK/NF1 and resistance-ready approaches).

name: Factor XI deficiency
description: Rare inherited bleeding disorder from low or dysfunctional factor XI, often silent until delayed, prolonged bleeding after surgery, dental work, or trauma, especially at mucosal sites; women may have heavy menses or postpartum bleeding. Bleeding risk is hard to predict and does not track well with factor levels, complicating peri procedural management. Current prophylaxis leans on high volume fresh frozen plasma and, in some markets, limited access to factor XI concentrates, creating demand for safer, more predictable, widely available options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Low-thrombosis, low-volume peri‑procedural hemostatic replacement (surgery/trauma/childbirth) to avoid FXI concentrate thrombosis and FFP volume/transfusion risks
- Standardized, predictable perioperative prophylaxis (drug + dosing algorithm) despite poor correlation of bleeding risk with FXI level/genotype and limited assay predictiveness
- Women-focused bleeding control for abnormal uterine bleeding/menorrhagia and postpartum hemorrhage with safer, more accessible options (incl. where FXI concentrates are hard to obtain)

name: Biphenotypic acute leukaemia
description: Mixed phenotype acute leukemia is a rare, aggressive acute leukemia where blasts co express myeloid and lymphoid markers, making lineage assignment and treatment selection difficult. Patients often present abruptly with marrow failure causing infections, bleeding and profound fatigue. Standard care borrows acute lymphoblastic leukemia type induction and, if remission is achieved, allogeneic stem cell transplant, but outcomes are limited by therapeutic resistance, high risk biology and a lack of prospective controlled trials. Key needs include safer induction options for older or unfit patients and deeper measurable residual disease clearance before transplant.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Chemo-light/outpatient induction options for newly diagnosed older (≥75) or medically unfit CD19+ MPAL patients to reduce induction toxicity/early mortality vs intensive ALL-like regimens.
- MRD-eradication bridge therapy for MRD-positive MPAL in morphologic remission to achieve deep MRD-negativity prior to allo-HSCT.
- Post–allo-HSCT maintenance to prevent relapse without increasing transplant-related mortality or chronic GVHD.

name: Cryoglobulinemia
description: Cryoglobulinemia is an immune complex small vessel vasculitis in which cold precipitating antibodies clump and inflame or obstruct vessels, often in midlife women and commonly linked to chronic hepatitis C infection. Patients can develop purpura, arthralgias, neuropathy, skin ulcers, and glomerulonephritis that can progress to kidney failure. Treating hepatitis C helps but cryoglobulins clear in only about half of patients within 12 months, leaving persistent or relapsing disease that threatens kidneys and nerves. Current organ threatening care still relies on glucocorticoids and anti CD20 therapy, sometimes with plasmapheresis, creating demand for safer durable disease control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Relapse-prevention/maintenance after DAA SVR, especially protecting renal and peripheral neuropathy outcomes
- Steroid-sparing, infection-safer remission induction achieving complete response with corticosteroid withdrawal by ~6 months
- More durable control in rituximab-refractory/relapse-prone patients with fewer clinic visits than IV anti‑CD20 induction

name: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding
description: Preventable bleeding disorder of newborns and young infants caused by insufficient vitamin K, leading to impaired clotting and sometimes catastrophic hidden bleeding such as intracranial hemorrhage (often 2–8 weeks in exclusively breastfed infants who missed the vitamin K shot); oral prophylaxis is less effective than injection and severe bleeds may require plasma or blood transfusions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-injectable newborn prophylaxis acceptable to IM-refusers/missed IM that achieves IM-like prevention of late VKDB.
- Bile-independent prophylaxis effective in breastfed infants with occult cholestasis/malabsorption where oral vitamin K fails.
- Safer, rapid acute rescue for severe VKDB that avoids higher-risk injectable vitamin K formulations/preservatives and reduces need for high-volume blood products (e.g., FFP).

name: Paget disease of the breast
description: Mammary Paget disease is a rare nipple and areola cancer, usually in postmenopausal women, that presents as a unilateral red scaly crusted rash with itching or burning and is often mistaken for eczema, delaying biopsy and diagnosis. In most patients it coexists with underlying ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive breast cancer and is frequently human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 driven, making biomarker guided systemic therapy important. Local control still commonly means excision of the nipple areola complex with mastectomy or breast conserving surgery plus whole breast radiotherapy, creating unmet need for earlier recognition and effective nipple sparing approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Nipple/areola-sparing local therapy for “pure” mammary Paget disease or Paget+DCIS (often HER2+) to clear epidermal/underlying in-situ disease and avoid nipple–areola excision + post-BCS radiotherapy
- Cardio-safer, less clinic-intensive HER2-directed regimens for HER2+ invasive/high-risk patients (lower CHF/cardiomyopathy risk; rapid SC and/or shorter total duration)
- Better-tolerated endocrine strategies for the ER+ subset to reduce AE-driven discontinuation while preserving recurrence prevention

name: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency
description: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 is a rare, life threatening primary immunodeficiency where leukocytes cannot migrate to infection sites, causing severe bacterial and fungal infections from birth with delayed umbilical cord separation, absent pus, poor wound healing, and later destructive periodontal disease. Management relies on aggressive or prophylactic antibiotics, but this is not disease modifying. The only corrective option is allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which carries major toxicity from chemotherapy and radiation conditioning and is not accessible or safe for all patients, leaving a need for safer curative and inflammation targeted therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Conditioning-sparing curative therapy for severe pediatric LAD‑I achieving ≥10% CD18+ neutrophils and reducing infection-related hospitalizations
- Neonatal/early-infant (<3 months) bridge infection-prevention regimen from diagnosis until eligibility for definitive gene therapy
- Targeted treatment of LAD‑I inflammatory pathology (esp. periodontal disease/tooth loss) with objective oral-inflammation improvement

name: Fallopian tube cancer | serous
description: Rare serous epithelial gynecologic cancer managed like ovarian and primary peritoneal cancer, often diagnosed at advanced stage after spread in older postmenopausal women with vague abdominal or pelvic symptoms. Biggest unmet need is durable control after relapse, especially platinum resistant disease where single agent chemotherapy responses are about 10 to 15 percent and benefit from poly ADP ribose polymerase inhibitor maintenance is limited in homologous recombination proficient tumors, with added hematologic toxicity and monitoring burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that materially improve outcomes in platinum-resistant/refractory relapse vs the ~10–15% ORR of single-agent non‑platinum chemotherapy
- Maintenance/combination strategies that substantially extend PFS in HRD‑negative/HRp tumors where PARP benefit is modest
- Lower-toxicity, lower-monitoring maintenance options that reduce hematologic toxicity and dose interruption/discontinuation burden

name: Rabies
description: Rabies is a viral zoonotic infection that causes progressive, fatal inflammation of the brain and spinal cord, usually after a dog bite or scratch and often in children. It presents as furious encephalitis with hydrophobia or paralytic disease with paralysis and coma. The biggest unmet needs are simpler, more accessible post exposure prophylaxis including standardized passive immunization and lower cost vaccine delivery, and an effective treatment once symptoms begin when death is otherwise expected.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Post-symptom therapeutic that improves survival in confirmed clinical rabies.
- Single-administration standardized passive immunization (multi-mAb cocktail) to replace HRIG/ERIG for WHO Category III exposures with day-0 wound infiltration.
- Simplified PEP regimens that cut vaccine visits/technique-dependent RIG while maintaining protective RVNA (≥0.5 IU/mL).

name: Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency
description: Ultra rare inherited mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation disorders causing early infantile multisystem energy failure with progressive encephalopathy, hypotonia, lactic acidosis and rapid liver failure, often fatal in early childhood. Care is largely supportive with vitamins and cofactors and symptom control, and patients can decompensate during infections or other stress. Major unmet needs are disease modifying genetically targeted therapies and better prevention of metabolic crises to preserve brain and liver function and improve survival.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Gene-corrective therapy for GFM1/COXPD1 to prevent neonatal-onset rapidly progressive encephalopathy (often with liver failure) and premature death.
- Crisis-prevention therapy to stop febrile illness/seizure-triggered neurologic regression and acute metabolic decompensation/encephalomyopathy leading to multiorgan failure.
- Mitochondria-compatible seizure control to reduce refractory seizures/status epilepticus and the need for anti-seizure polytherapy/empiric vitamin–cofactor regimens.

name: Leukoencephalopathy with vanishing white matter
