description: Rare genetic leukodystrophy with typically normal early development followed by progressive childhood-onset motor decline (ataxia, spasticity) and episodic “crashes” triggered by fever, infection, minor head trauma, or fright; cognitive decline often later. Care is largely preventive and supportive, with no curative or disease-modifying therapy, creating a major need for treatments that protect white matter from stress-triggered deterioration and address ovarian failure in affected females.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying CNS therapy that slows/halts white-matter degeneration (MRI rarefaction/cystic decay) and preserves motor + adaptive function in early-onset (<4y) VWM.
- Stressor-episode prophylaxis/acute rescue to prevent rapid neurologic deterioration triggered by fever/febrile infection, minor head trauma, or anesthesia.
- Female-specific ovarian function/fertility preservation therapy to address common ovarian insufficiency/dysgenesis and downstream estrogen-deficiency consequences in VWM.

name: Pineocytoma
description: Pineocytoma is a rare, typically slow growing World Health Organization grade 1 tumor of the pineal gland that often becomes urgent when it obstructs cerebrospinal fluid flow, causing hydrocephalus with headaches, nausea and vomiting, gait and balance problems, and eye movement deficits including Parinaud syndrome, usually starting in adulthood. Treatment centers on maximal safe surgery, but the location makes resection technically difficult, and evidence for benefit of adjuvant radiation after subtotal resection is uncertain. Few proven systemic options exist, a particular gap for rare cases with malignant transformation or leptomeningeal spread.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-penetrant, outpatient tumor-directed drug option for patients unable to safely undergo complete resection (durable ORR/PFS).
- Evidence-backed adjuvant therapy for post–subtotal resection patients to improve long-term OS/PFS where radiotherapy benefit is uncertain.
- Neuraxis/CSF-active therapy for rare leptomeningeal dissemination/malignant transformation to reduce reliance on craniospinal radiation and extend control.
medlineUrl: No specific MedlinePlus URL for Pineocytoma

name: Familial partial lipodystrophy
description: Familial partial lipodystrophy is an ultra rare inherited disorder marked by loss of limb and hip subcutaneous fat with compensatory fat gain in the face, neck, and abdomen, driving severe insulin resistance, diabetes, hypertriglyceridemia with pancreatitis risk, and fatty liver disease. Care is largely metabolic complication management, with no therapy that reverses the underlying fat loss, leaving major unmet need for disease modifying approaches that improve insulin sparing glycemic control, sustainably lower triglycerides, and prevent or reverse hepatic steatosis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Insulin-sparing glycemic-control therapy for severe insulin-resistant FPLD diabetes that reduces reliance on high-burden insulin delivery and avoids daily leptin injections/boxed-warning risks.
- Pancreatitis-preventing triglyceride-lowering therapy for patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia (e.g., TG ≥500 mg/dL), including prevention of flare-ups triggered by diet/estrogens/pregnancy.
- Liver-directed therapy that reduces hepatic steatosis and prevents progression to fibrosis/cirrhosis, measurable by MRI hepatic fat fraction.

name: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
description: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis is a rare hyperinflammatory immune failure driven by overactivated T cells and macrophages that infiltrate organs, causing prolonged high fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly and sometimes central nervous system injury, and can rapidly progress to fatal multiorgan failure. The biggest bottleneck is speed since diagnosis is difficult and often delayed while patients deteriorate in intensive care. First line etoposide based regimens are toxic and still fail to induce durable remission in many patients, and evidence is especially thin in malignancy associated HLH where prognosis is poor and there is no standard therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Etoposide-sparing first-line induction for treatment‑naïve primary/pediatric HLH that still reliably bridges to HSCT while reducing chemo-driven cytopenias/infections
- Prospectively validated, cytopenia-compatible regimen for malignancy-associated HLH that rapidly controls hyperinflammation without forcing case-by-case sequencing vs cancer therapy
- CNS-penetrant systemic therapy for CNS-HLH that improves neurologic outcomes and reduces reliance on repeated intrathecal methotrexate+dexamethasone

name: Chronic granulomatous disease
description: Chronic granulomatous disease is a rare inherited immunodeficiency caused by defective phagocyte killing, leading to early life recurrent, sometimes life threatening bacterial and fungal infections, deep abscesses, and obstructive granulomas, often with Crohn like colitis causing diarrhea and bleeding. Management depends on lifelong antibacterial and antifungal prophylaxis plus interferon gamma and steroids for granulomas, with ongoing breakthrough infection risk and drug toxicity monitoring. Stem cell transplant is the only established cure, but safer, disease modifying approaches that control inflammation without raising infection risk remain a major unmet need.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Curative NADPH-oxidase restoration for CGD patients (esp. X‑linked/CYBB) to replace lifelong prophylaxis and prevent residual infections
- Steroid-sparing therapy for CGD colitis/granulomatous inflammation that avoids high infection risk seen with anti‑TNF
- More effective, better-tolerated prevention/therapy for invasive mold infections (e.g., Aspergillus) to reduce mortality and avoid chronic azole toxicity/monitoring

name: Endodermal sinus tumor
description: Endodermal sinus tumor, also called yolk sac tumor, is a malignant primitive germ cell tumor that in children often presents as a painless testicular mass with elevated alpha fetoprotein. Most cases are stage I and outcomes are generally excellent with surgery plus surveillance or platinum chemotherapy, but major unmet needs are reducing cisplatin linked permanent hearing loss and bleomycin pulmonary toxicity while improving salvage for the minority who relapse, typically within the first year.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non‑platinum, higher‑cure salvage options for relapsed/platinum‑refractory yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumors where current salvage is rarely curative.
- First‑line de‑escalation/substitution vs BEP/PEb in pediatric/AYA patients to preserve cure while reducing late toxicities (e.g., cisplatin ototoxicity, bleomycin pulmonary risk).
- Risk‑adapted adjuvant/maintenance for “high‑risk” stage I pediatric testicular yolk sac tumors to reduce >50% surveillance relapse and lessen monitoring/imaging burden.

name: Hypotrichosis
description: Hypotrichosis is an early onset genetic hair growth disorder marked by sparse, fragile scalp hair from infancy that may also affect eyebrows and eyelashes and can progress to alopecia. Autosomal recessive forms are driven by mutations such as LIPH, LPAR6, or DSG4 that leave hair follicles structurally abnormal and underdeveloped, making true regrowth difficult. Care is largely cosmetic and often unsatisfactory, with options like nightly bimatoprost for eyelashes carrying ongoing burden and risks including periocular pigmentation and unintended hair growth, leaving a clear need for safe, durable, disease modifying follicle restoring therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable scalp-hair regrowth for pediatric hereditary hypotrichosis simplex (clinically meaningful ↑ scalp-hair density/coverage)
- Follicle-development “rescue” for autosomal recessive hypotrichosis (e.g., LIPH/LPAR6/DSG4) to ↑ hair length and ↓ breakage/fragility
- Safer, less burdensome alternative to nightly bimatoprost for eyelash hypotrichosis that avoids pigmentation and off-target hair growth

name: Intestinal pseudo-obstruction
description: Rare gastrointestinal motility disorder where impaired peristalsis causes obstruction-like episodes without a mechanical blockage, leading to distention, pain, nausea and vomiting, constipation or diarrhea, poor nutrient absorption, and progressive malnutrition. Often severe from birth in children. Care is largely supportive with prokinetics and long-term parenteral nutrition, which brings major risks such as liver disease, line thrombosis and sepsis. Intestinal transplantation is the only definitive option but is limited and morbid, creating demand for safer motility-restoring and gene-informed therapies (eg ACTG2 or FLNA).
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that restore enough motility in severe pediatric PIPO/CIPO to achieve enteral autonomy and avoid/wean TPN (reducing central-line infection and liver-failure risk).
- New prokinetics with meaningfully better safety/efficacy than current off-label options, delivering clinically significant reductions in global GI symptom burden.
- Genotype-/mechanism-targeted treatments for primary CIPO (e.g., ACTG2/FLNA variants) that restore smooth-muscle contractility/peristalsis beyond symptomatic “prokinetic push.”

name: Listeriosis
description: Listeriosis is a foodborne infection caused by Listeria monocytogenes that can grow at refrigerator temperatures, disproportionately harming older adults, immunocompromised people, and pregnant patients with invasive sepsis and central nervous system disease that usually requires hospitalization. Despite antibiotics such as ampicillin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, mortality remains high at around 20% and pregnancy associated disease often results in fetal or newborn loss. Gentamicin based combinations are limited by kidney and hearing toxicity, leaving a premium on safer bactericidal regimens, better central nervous system penetration, and earlier, practical treatment strategies for high risk exposures.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Gentamicin-sparing bactericidal regimens that match IV ampicillin+gentamicin outcomes while avoiding aminoglycoside nephro/ototoxicity.
- CNS-optimized neurolisteriosis therapies (better brain/CSF penetration and/or neuroprotective adjuncts) to reduce high mortality and neurologic sequelae.
- Evidence-backed oral early/post-exposure treatment for high-risk exposed patients with mild/afebrile symptoms to prevent progression (incl. pregnancy-associated fetal loss).

name: Familial adenomatous polyposis
description: Familial adenomatous polyposis is an inherited cancer predisposition syndrome with hundreds to thousands of colorectal adenomas starting in adolescence, making colorectal cancer essentially inevitable without colectomy and intensive lifelong surveillance. Major unmet needs are disease modifying chemoprevention that demonstrably lowers cancer risk and reduces reliance on surgery, plus better medical control of extracolonic disease including upper gastrointestinal polyposis and recurrent, morbid desmoid tumors.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- FDA-meaningful colorectal chemoprevention that reduces CRC risk and/or delays/avoids colectomy (not just adenoma shrinkage) with long-term safety avoiding NSAID CV/GI risks
- Durable medical regression of high-risk duodenal/periampullary polyposis (e.g., improved Spigelman stage) to prevent duodenal cancer and reduce endoscopic/surgical escalation
- Desmoid-tumor prevention/treatment that lowers post-surgical intra-abdominal desmoid morbidity/mortality with safer chronic systemic options than cytotoxic regimens

name: Neuroblastoma
description: Neuroblastoma is an early childhood cancer of immature nerve cells, often presenting before age 5 with an abdominal mass and frequently metastatic disease causing bone pain or eye findings. High risk disease is treated with intensive multimodal therapy including anti-GD2 immunotherapy, but relapse is common and recurrence carries a very poor prognosis. Current standards are also hard on patients and families, with GD2 targeting associated with severe neuropathic pain requiring intravenous opioids. A key unmet need is safer, more durable disease control, including better targeted options for subsets such as anaplastic lymphoma kinase mutated tumors.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that materially improve EFS/OS in relapsed/refractory high-risk neuroblastoma (raise post-relapse 2-year EFS above ~10%).
- More effective ALK-directed (and/or combination) regimens for ALK-altered high-risk neuroblastoma (~14% of patients) to close the OS gap vs ALK–WT.
- GD2-directed treatments with less neuropathic pain and lower infusion/opioid burden than current anti-GD2 antibodies while maintaining efficacy.

name: Primary hyperoxaluria | type 1
description: Inherited hepatic alanine glyoxylate aminotransferase deficiency causing oxalate overproduction, recurrent childhood kidney stones and nephrocalcinosis that can progress to systemic oxalosis and multi organ injury; care is burdensome with extreme fluid intake, dialysis often inadequate, and late disease may require transplant, highlighting need for kidney protective and liver correcting disease modifying therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drug approaches that prevent CaOx crystallization at physiologic urine volumes to reduce/replace 2–3 L/m²/day hyperhydration (and gastrostomy/NG-tube dependence) in pediatrics.
- Therapies that lower plasma oxalate and treat/prevent systemic oxalosis in advanced CKD/ESKD to reduce reliance on very frequent dialysis and/or combined liver–kidney transplantation.
- Durable liver-directed causal correction (ideally one-time) to avoid lifelong monthly/quarterly RNAi injections and address incomplete oxalate normalization/variable response.

name: Astrocytoma | anaplastic
description: Anaplastic astrocytoma is a diffusely infiltrating malignant astrocytic primary brain tumor traditionally classed as World Health Organization grade III, often diagnosed in midlife and presenting with headaches, seizures, personality changes, and focal neurologic deficits. Maximal safe resection plus radiotherapy and temozolomide can control disease but rarely cures because infiltrative cells extend into normal brain, and recurrence is common with possible progression to higher grade tumors. After progression there is no standard therapy and options are limited, leaving a premium on treatments that reliably extend survival with less cumulative toxicity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Overall-survival–extending systemic therapy for IDH-wildtype anaplastic astrocytoma/anaplastic glioma that beats RT±temozolomide.
- Post-progression treatments that improve overall survival (not just PFS/radiographic or steroid-sparing effects) beyond bevacizumab/lomustine regimens.
- Less toxic, less burdensome alternatives to surgery → ~6 weeks RT + prolonged adjuvant temozolomide (avoiding PCP prophylaxis/monitoring and severe cytopenias/myelosuppression).

name: Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma | nasal type
description: Aggressive Epstein Barr virus associated lymphoma usually arising in the nasopharynx, often presenting early with nasal obstruction or epistaxis and locally destructive growth. Treatment relies on intensive radiotherapy of at least 50 to 56 Gy plus non anthracycline chemotherapy, but toxicity can be severe with neutropenia and sepsis deaths. When disease relapses, outcomes are poor with median overall survival around 6.4 months, creating high unmet need for safer, more durable salvage options and biomarker guided response monitoring using plasma Epstein Barr virus DNA.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- MDR-bypassing salvage therapy that meaningfully extends survival for relapsed/progressive ENKTL beyond ~6.4-month median post-relapse OS.
- Lower-toxicity, asparaginase-sparing (or safer-asparaginase) regimens that maintain efficacy while reducing severe neutropenia/TRM and thrombosis/pancreatitis/hepatotoxicity risks.
- Response-adapted localized-disease strategies that de-escalate/replace ~5-week RT (50 Gy/25 fractions) using plasma EBV-DNA–guided escalation/de-escalation.

name: Immune-complex glomerulonephritis
description: Immune complex mediated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is a rare, biopsy-defined kidney disease where immunoglobulin immune complexes and complement deposit in glomeruli, causing hematuria, proteinuria, edema, hypertension, and declining renal function that can progress to kidney failure and recur after transplant. Care is largely a search for an underlying trigger plus broad immunosuppression with inconsistent, non-durable responses. A major gap is mechanism-based, immunosuppression-sparing options for idiopathic disease, with complement pathway inhibition and strategies to prevent post-transplant recurrence emerging as key frontiers.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Immunosuppression-sparing, disease-targeted therapy for idiopathic IC-MPGN achieving durable ≥50% UPCR reduction with eGFR stabilization.
- Therapies to prevent/treat post-kidney-transplant recurrence of IC-MPGN to preserve graft function.
- Lower-burden long-term regimens that maintain proteinuria/eGFR benefit while reducing dosing frequency and infection/REMS monitoring burden.

name: Renal cell carcinoma | papillary
description: Papillary renal cell carcinoma is a non clear cell kidney cancer usually diagnosed around age 64, more common in men, and often found incidentally while still localized. It spans distinct biology including MET driven type 1 disease and aggressive fumarate hydratase deficient tumors that can metastasize early. Treatment options in advanced disease deliver limited durability, with cabozantinib achieving about 9 months median progression free survival, and MET only inhibitors not outperforming sunitinib, underscoring the need for biomarker selected therapies with deeper, longer control. After nephrectomy, there is little evidence to guide adjuvant therapy in non clear cell disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Biomarker-selected MET-pathway therapy for MET-driven advanced/metastatic PRCC that delivers an overall-survival benefit beyond cabozantinib.
- Durable systemic therapies for aggressive FH-deficient/HLRCC-associated papillary RCC where ICIs show limited activity.
- Risk-directed adjuvant drug therapy post-nephrectomy for high-risk non-metastatic PRCC to reduce recurrence.

name: Astrocytoma | pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma
description: Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma is a very rare, usually superficial temporal lobe astrocytoma that often presents with seizures in children and adolescents. Tumors are typically World Health Organization grade 2 or 3 and about 70% harbor BRAF V600E, yet care still relies on surgery. Recurrence remains a major pain point because there is no standard treatment if the tumor returns and traditional systemic therapies have limited benefit, particularly for BRAF wild type disease where effective brain active options and seizure relevant outcomes are most needed.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjuvant systemic therapy that improves durability for high-risk PXA (WHO grade 3 and/or infiltrative margins) vs surgery/RT alone
- Brain-penetrant targeted therapies for the ~30% BRAF V600E–negative PXA population that avoid alkylator-like hematologic toxicity/monitoring burden
- Tumor-directed therapies differentiated by seizure control (e.g., seizure freedom and enabling ASM withdrawal)

name: Mucormycosis
description: Mucormycosis is a rare, life threatening invasive mold infection of immunocompromised patients, often involving the sinuses or lungs and capable of rapid spread to the brain. Management is an emergency requiring weeks of antifungals and often urgent surgical debridement, yet mortality remains very high. Care is constrained by the kidney toxicity and electrolyte effects of amphotericin based first line therapy and by imperfect oral azole step down options with variable activity and drug interaction burdens, leaving a premium on renal sparing regimens and more reliable, well tolerated oral therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Fungicidal regimen that improves survival in disseminated mucormycosis vs today’s high mortality outcomes.
- Renal-sparing first-line alternative achieving liposomal amphotericin B–level efficacy without nephrotoxicity-driven dose reductions.
- Predictable-exposure oral/outpatient step-down for weeks-to-months therapy with fewer CYP3A4 drug–drug interactions than current triazoles.

name: Cutis laxa
description: Cutis laxa is a rare inherited or acquired connective tissue disorder marked by loose, inelastic, prematurely aged skin and, in severe recessive subtypes, early emphysema, arterial aneurysms, and neurodevelopmental complications. Care is largely symptomatic and surgical, and laxity often recurs after cosmetic repair. With no effective medical therapies for severe inherited type 1 or acquired disease, the key unmet need is disease modifying treatment that preserves lung and vascular integrity and prevents respiratory failure, aneurysm related events, and developmental decline.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pulmonary disease–modifying therapy to halt early-onset emphysema progression and prevent cardio‑respiratory failure in severe ARCL1 (e.g., FBLN5-related).
- Arterial-stabilizing therapy to prevent/slow aortic & systemic aneurysms/tortuosity/stenosis and reduce the need for frequent MRA surveillance/surgery (e.g., EFEMP2-related ARCL1B).
- Neurodevelopmental/seizure-modifying therapy to prevent neurologic regression and reduce seizures/developmental disability in ATP6V0A2-related ARCL2A.

name: Atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumor
description: Atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumor is a very rare, fast growing brain or spinal cord cancer that mainly affects children under 3, often presenting over days to weeks with hydrocephalus symptoms. It is typically driven by SMARCB1 loss and frequently disseminates through cerebrospinal fluid at diagnosis. Care requires intensive multimodality therapy but radiotherapy is constrained in infants and can cause major neurodevelopmental toxicity. Relapsed disease has no standard of care and outcomes remain poor, creating demand for safer, durable control including for disseminated and recurrent tumors.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Radiation-sparing frontline regimens for infants/young children (<12–36 months) that improve survival without neurodevelopmental harm.
- CNS-penetrant systemic ± intrathecal therapies to eradicate neuraxis/leptomeningeal dissemination present at diagnosis.
- Lower-toxicity, durable-response options for recurrent/progressive AT/RT where no standard exists and outcomes are poor.

name: Bone cancer | giant cell tumor
description: Giant cell tumor of bone is a rare, locally aggressive benign bone tumor, usually in young adults around the knee, causing pain, swelling, and loss of joint motion and sometimes destroying bone or rarely spreading to the lungs. Treatment is mainly surgical curettage or resection, but recurrence is common and wide surgery can be morbid. Denosumab can shrink or control tumors when surgery is difficult, yet control is often not durable after stopping and long use raises safety concerns such as osteonecrosis of the jaw and rebound hypercalcemia, leaving a need for finite, durable, denosumab sparing options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drug (systemic or local adjuvant) that meaningfully reduces local recurrence after intralesional curettage
- Finite-duration therapy providing durable/definitive control in unresectable or high-morbidity GCTB, with biomarker-guided stopping/retreatment
- Denosumab-sparing alternative with fewer long-term toxicities (e.g., ONJ, rebound hypercalcemia) and reduced clinic/injection burden

name: Babesiosis
description: Babesiosis is a tick borne malaria like infection that invades and destroys red blood cells, causing fever, chills, profound fatigue and hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia and sometimes jaundice. Most cases respond to atovaquone plus azithromycin, but the highest burden is in asplenic or immunosuppressed patients who relapse, need prolonged treatment of six weeks or more, and can develop resistance. Salvage options such as quinine based regimens are limited by toxicity including tinnitus and hearing loss, leaving a need for better tolerated, relapse proof therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, relapse-proof anti-*Babesia* regimens for highly immunocompromised/asplenic (incl. rituximab-exposed) patients that cure without prolonged multi-week therapy.
- New MoA/optimized combinations effective after atovaquone/azithromycin treatment failure (incl. mutation-linked resistance) with an evidence-based salvage option.
- Better-tolerated severe-babesiosis regimens that rapidly control high parasitemia while avoiding quinine-associated toxicity (e.g., ototoxicity).

name: Diphtheria
description: Diphtheria is a toxin mediated infection that disproportionately affects unimmunized children, typically starting with sore throat and mild fever that can rapidly progress to an adherent gray pseudomembrane causing airway compromise. Systemic toxin effects can trigger myocarditis and neuropathy, driving much of the mortality. Care depends on immediate antitoxin plus antibiotics, often before confirmation, but the standard equine antitoxin is globally scarce, carries anaphylaxis risk, and only neutralizes circulating toxin, leaving patients vulnerable once toxin has bound tissues and organ injury has begun.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Human/recombinant anti–diphtheria-toxin antibodies to replace equine DAT and reduce hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis risk.
- Stockpile-ready, scalable antitoxin/mAb with rapid distribution to enable dosing in the first 1–2 days of illness.
- Adjunct therapies that remain effective after toxin is tissue-bound/internalized (e.g., preventing/mitigating toxin-mediated myocarditis).

name: Epidermolysis bullosa | dystrophic
description: Severe recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa is an inherited type VII collagen disorder where absent anchoring fibrils make skin and mucosa so fragile that minor friction causes widespread blistering, wounds, and scarring from birth, with feeding and swallowing problems that can drive malnutrition and disability. Care is largely symptomatic and dominated by painful, time consuming wound and dressing changes, with no cure or reliable way to prevent new injury. A major life limiting unmet need is preventing and effectively treating the early, aggressive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma that often emerges in young adulthood and is a leading cause of death.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Whole‑body (incl. mucosa) COL7A1/C7 restoration to prevent new blistering/scarring beyond wound‑only therapies
- Effective prevention and/or systemic treatment of RDEB‑associated aggressive cutaneous SCC (reduce recurrence/metastasis)
- Therapies that reduce daily care burden by cutting dressing‑change time/frequency and providing durable pain/itch control

name: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children
description: Rare, severe postCOVIDinfection hyperinflammatory syndrome in children that emerges 2 to 6 weeks after SARSCoV2 and can cause persistent fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, Kawasakilike mucocutaneous findings, cardiac dysfunction, shock, and multiorgan failure requiring hospitalization or intensive care. Treatment is empiric inpatient immunomodulation with intravenous immunoglobulin plus glucocorticoids, escalating to targeted cytokine blockade in refractory disease, but randomized evidence is limited and current regimens are burdensome and constrained by intravenous immunoglobulin access, motivating earlier and steroid sparing strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral/SC early-intervention therapy for SARS‑CoV‑2–exposed children with early MIS‑C features to prevent progression to hospitalized/ICU disease.
- Rapid, targeted cytokine-pathway immunomodulation for refractory MIS‑C (persistent fever and/or significant end-organ involvement after first-line therapy) to avoid rescue escalation and organ-support needs.
- IVIG-sparing (and steroid-minimizing) regimens that preserve cardiac protection while reducing IVIG access constraints and treatment burden.

name: Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma
description: Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma is a usually benign brain tumor in tuberous sclerosis complex that often arises near the foramen of Monro and can obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow, causing headaches, nausea or vomiting, blurred vision, and worsening seizures, with risk of acute hydrocephalus. Care is split between surgical resection in acute obstruction, which can carry substantial morbidity, and long term everolimus for unresectable disease, which requires therapeutic drug monitoring, is limited by stomatitis and infections, and may need indefinite treatment due to tumor regrowth after discontinuation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid SEGA tumor debulking/CSF-flow relief for acutely symptomatic (e.g., obstructive hydrocephalus) patients fast enough to avoid urgent surgery/shunting
- Durable SEGA control after a finite course (no regrowth after stopping therapy)
- Improved tolerability and reduced monitoring burden vs everolimus (less stomatitis/infection immunosuppression; less TDM/frequent MRI)

name: Propionic acidemia
description: Propionic acidemia is a rare inherited organic aciduria from propionyl Coenzyme A carboxylase deficiency, usually presenting in the first days of life with poor feeding, encephalopathy, metabolic acidosis, and hyperammonemia that can rapidly progress to seizures, coma, or death. Survivors face recurrent metabolic decompensations and chronic complications such as intellectual disability and serious cardiac disease including cardiomyopathy and long QT syndrome. Care is high burden and largely preventive with strict protein restriction and emergency anti-catabolic crisis protocols plus ammonia rescue, leaving a major unmet need for durable disease modifying therapies that reduce crises and protect neurologic and cardiac function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Reduce acute metabolic decompensation events (metabolic acidosis/hyperammonemia) and related hospitalizations in high-burden young children (0–6 years).
- Enable safe protein liberalization while reducing reliance on specialized medical foods and G-tube–facilitated feeding/medication delivery.
- Prevent/treat PA-associated cardiomyopathy and electrical instability (long QT/arrhythmias) using hard cardiac endpoints (e.g., LVEF, QTc, arrhythmia events).

name: Lymphoma | primary cutaneous follicle center
description: Primary cutaneous follicle centre lymphoma is a low grade germinal centre B cell lymphoma confined to the skin at diagnosis, typically presenting in men in their 50s to 60s with smooth pink to violaceous plaques or nodules on the scalp, head and neck, or trunk. Outcomes are generally favorable but 30 to 40 percent recur, creating a long tail of repeat local treatments, clinic visits, and cosmetic tradeoffs for visible lesions, while systemic therapy is usually reserved for more extensive or symptomatic disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Reduce post-clearance skin relapse/recurrence to avoid repeat local treatments
- Cosmesis-sparing control (non-scarring/alopecia-sparing) for head/neck and extensive lesions
- More convenient “treat-as-needed” options with less infusion/clinic burden and less immune compromise (e.g., preserve vaccine responses vs anti-CD20)

name: Pineal gland cancer
description: Ultra rare pineal region tumors, often in children, present with obstructive hydrocephalus causing headache vomiting and sometimes Parinaud syndrome. Pineoblastoma is the most malignant subtype, frequently disseminated at diagnosis, so treatment relies on aggressive craniospinal irradiation plus multi agent chemotherapy. Outcomes are constrained by relapse with no standard salvage therapy and by long term neurotoxicities, driving demand for better central nervous system penetrant therapies and locoregional targeted or immune approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- More effective CNS-penetrant systemic therapy for disseminated (M+) pineoblastoma at diagnosis to improve 5-year OS beyond ~10–30%
- A validated standard salvage regimen for relapsed/refractory pineoblastoma (currently no standard options)
- Curative-intent regimens that maintain tumor control while reducing severe acute toxicity and treatment burden (intensive chemo/RT, frequent delays, daily RT/CSI)

name: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis
description: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis is a rare inherited disorder of impaired bile secretion starting in infancy, causing bile acid buildup that drives severe pruritus, jaundice, poor growth, malabsorption and vitamin deficiencies, and progression to cirrhosis, portal hypertension and liver failure. Care remains largely symptomatic, with many children still needing surgery or liver transplant; newer ileal bile acid transporter inhibitors can be limited by diarrhea and dehydration and may not work in some progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 2 genotypes, leaving a premium on durable, well tolerated, disease modifying options such as liver targeted gene therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies effective in PFIC2 with ABCB11 variants causing non-functional/absent BSEP (BSEP-null), where IBAT inhibitors may be ineffective/not recommended.
- Disease-modifying treatments that delay/avoid portal hypertension and progression to liver failure (and ideally reduce HCC risk) beyond itch/sBA control.
- Better-tolerated, simpler regimens with lower diarrhea/dehydration risk and reduced dosing/timing burdens (e.g., avoid BID before meals and ≥4h separation from bile-acid resins).

name: Epilepsy | pyridoxine-dependent
description: Rare ALDH7A1 related neurometabolic epilepsy with prenatal or neonatal onset, causing prolonged seizures often refractory to standard antiseizure drugs and risking encephalopathy if missed. High dose vitamin B6 can control seizures, but most patients still develop developmental delay or intellectual disability because toxic lysine metabolites remain elevated. Care is lifelong and burdensome, relying on vitamin B6 plus dietary lysine reduction strategies such as lysine restriction and L-arginine, with a premium on early at birth initiation and better metabolite lowering approaches to protect cognition.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Metabolite-lowering therapies (reduce α‑AASA/Δ¹‑P6C/pipecolic acid) to prevent residual neurodevelopmental disability despite seizure control.
- Enable pre-symptomatic initiation (at birth/prenatal) to minimize intellectual-disability risk from diagnostic/treatment delays.
- Lower-burden, safer lifelong regimens vs high-dose/IV pyridoxine and restrictive lysine-reduction diets (reduce neuropathy/monitoring needs; improve tolerability).

name: Inclusion body myositis
description: Inclusion body myositis is an acquired, slowly progressive inflammatory myopathy of later adulthood, classically causing asymmetric quadriceps and deep finger flexor weakness that leads to falls and loss of grip, often with dysphagia and choking risk. Despite immune mediated pathology, it responds poorly to corticosteroids and immunosuppressants, leaving largely symptomatic management and a major need for disease modifying therapies that preserve mobility, hand function, and swallowing.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy that stabilizes or improves leg/hand function (e.g., IBMFRS, 6MWT, hand-grip strength) to prevent progressive disability and falls.
- Treatment that meaningfully improves dysphagia to reduce aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, and dehydration.
- Long-term, well-tolerated, convenient chronic pharmacologic option suitable for older adults vs limited-efficacy/burdensome immunosuppression and IVIG.

name: Glutaric acidemia | type 1
description: Glutaric acidemia type I is a rare inherited organic acid disorder caused by glutaryl CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, leading to toxic metabolite buildup that can injure the basal ganglia and cause irreversible dystonia after early childhood crises triggered by catabolic stress. Many infants are found on newborn screening while appearing well, often with macrocephaly, but prevention hinges on strict low lysine diet, carnitine, and rapid emergency protocols during illness. The biggest gaps are adherence sensitive residual risk of striatal injury and the heavy lifelong treatment burden, driving demand for disease modifying approaches such as gene replacement now entering Phase 1 testing.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent early-childhood striatal injury and subsequent dystonia despite newborn-screening-era metabolic standard of care.
- Reduce/eliminate reliance on strict low-lysine diet/medical formula, carnitine supplementation, and emergency illness protocols to improve long-term adherence.
- Provide predictable symptomatic benefit for established neurologic disease (e.g., secondary dystonia) in late-diagnosed or post-injury patients where metabolic therapy cannot reverse damage.

name: Multiple endocrine neoplasia | type 1
description: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 is a rare inherited syndrome in which tumors and hormone overproduction arise across endocrine glands, classically the parathyroid, pituitary, and pancreatic or gastroenteropancreatic tract. Patients often present in young adulthood with primary hyperparathyroidism causing hypercalcemia, kidney stones, and bone loss, alongside peptic ulcer disease and diarrhea from gastrinomas or sexual dysfunction from prolactinomas. Care is lifelong and surgical driven because the condition is incurable and tumors recur, and some pancreatic tumors can become malignant or metastatic. Key unmet needs include better systemic options to prevent progression and more durable medical control of calcium and hypoglycemia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying systemic therapy to prevent/slow MEN1 non-functioning pancreatic NET growth/new lesions/metastasis and avoid watchful-waiting vs pancreatectomy extremes.
- Durable medical control of MEN1 primary hyperparathyroidism achieving long-term normocalcemia while reducing recurrence/reoperation and post-op hypoparathyroidism risk.
- Safer pharmacologic control of MEN1 insulinoma hypoglycemia (bridge/alternative to surgery) that avoids diazoxide-associated fluid retention/CHF and severe dysglycemia emergencies.

name: Multiple sclerosis | progressive-relapsing
description: Progressive relapsing multiple sclerosis is a rare form of multiple sclerosis where immune mediated damage to central nervous system myelin drives steady disability worsening from onset with superimposed relapses, causing progressive gait and balance problems, weakness and spasticity, sensory and visual symptoms, and bladder dysfunction. There is no cure, and therapies that control relapses often have limited benefit once progression dominates, leaving a major unmet need for disease modifying treatments that slow neurodegeneration, protect neurons, and restore myelin through remyelination.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapies that halt (not just slow) disability accumulation and preserve ambulation in nonactive progressive MS (PPMS/nonactive SPMS)
- Remyelination/neuroregeneration drugs that repair existing CNS damage and restore function beyond relapse suppression
- Safer, lower-monitoring alternatives to current immunosuppressive SoC that reduce infection risk and lab/eye-exam monitoring burden

name: Erythromelalgia
description: Erythromelalgia is a rare disorder of episodic, heat or exercise triggered burning pain, redness, and swelling in the hands and feet that can start in childhood and become disabling. Primary inherited forms often involve SCN9A NaV1.7 sodium channel gain of function in pain sensing neurons, while secondary cases can be linked to myeloproliferative disease where aspirin may help. Care is largely symptomatic and many patients rely on extreme cooling that can damage skin and lead to ulcers and infection, leaving a major unmet need for durable, targeted analgesia and safer attack control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-targeted therapy for inherited/SCN9A (NaV1.7) erythromelalgia to durably reduce pain intensity and attack frequency.
- Non-cooling-dependent control of heat-/exercise-triggered attacks to reduce reliance on ice-water immersion and prevent skin injury (ulceration/necrosis/infection/gangrene).
- Lower-burden, better-tolerated symptom control (esp. topical/local) to avoid high-frequency oral polypharmacy while reducing pain-attack intensity and interference.

name: Solitary fibrous tumor
description: Solitary fibrous tumor is a rare, usually slow growing connective tissue tumor often arising in the pleura and diagnosed in older adults. It can be silent until large, then cause cough or shortness of breath. Surgery is the mainstay, but behavior is unpredictable with very late recurrences and 10 to 15 percent metastasizing, where effective therapies are lacking. Advanced disease relies on antiangiogenic regimens with limited durability, and a small subset develop Big insulin like growth factor II driven hypoglycemia that is hard to control without resection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable systemic control for unresectable/metastatic (esp. malignant/dedifferentiated) SFT with PFS meaningfully beyond current anti‑angiogenic benchmarks (~4.7–5.6 months) and higher objective response.
- Non-surgical therapy to control Doege–Potter syndrome (Big‑IGF‑II–driven hypoglycemia) in recurrent/unresectable SFT, preventing recurrent severe hypoglycemic episodes without indefinite supportive measures.
- Adjuvant/maintenance therapy post-resection in high-risk SFT to reduce very late relapse risk and enable de-escalation of long-term intensive surveillance.

name: Thyroid cancer | anaplastic
description: Anaplastic thyroid cancer is a rare, undifferentiated thyroid malignancy that progresses with extreme speed and lethality, typically affecting patients in their 60s to 70s who present with a rapidly enlarging neck mass causing airway and swallowing compromise. It is stage IV by definition and often metastatic at diagnosis, leaving little time for workup or treatment. Outcomes remain poor with months level survival and limited benefit from cytotoxic therapy. Targeted therapy helps the subset with BRAF V600E, but most patients still need fast acting, tolerable systemic options with more durable responses and less resistance.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Targeted systemic therapy for the majority (~75%) of ATC patients who are BRAF–wild-type, achieving rapid high ORR and meaningful durability vs low-evidence chemotherapy/clinical-trial-only guidance.
- Strategies (combinations/next-line agents) that prevent or overcome BRAF/MEK resistance in BRAF V600E ATC to extend duration of response and overall survival.
- Rapid-acting, tolerable regimens usable in very ill/dysphagic patients who can’t swallow pills or don’t meet ECOG 0–1/0–2 criteria for oral targeted therapies.

name: Cystinosis
description: Cystinosis is a rare inherited lysosomal storage disorder where cystine accumulates and crystallizes, typically presenting in late infancy with renal Fanconi syndrome, dehydration, acidosis, and poor growth, and progressing to childhood kidney failure plus painful corneal crystals and photophobia. Disease control depends on lifelong cysteamine, but systemic therapy is limited by foul taste and odor and gastrointestinal side effects, while ocular disease often requires hourly drops with difficult storage and handling. The premium is for durable disease modifying options that protect kidneys and eyes and reduce treatment burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Renal-protective therapy that prevents/delays progression to ESRD/dialysis/transplant despite early cysteamine (e.g., slowing eGFR decline/time-to-transplant).
- Better-tolerated systemic cystine-depletion that reduces odor/halitosis and GI intolerance and relaxes tight dosing schedules to improve adherence (especially in adolescents) while maintaining WBC cystine control.
- Sustained ocular corneal-crystal control with far fewer daily administrations and better tolerability/handling than topical cysteamine (burning + cold-chain/frozen storage + very frequent dosing), improving CCCS/photophobia/visual outcomes.

name: Aplastic anemia
description: Aplastic anemia is a rare immune mediated bone marrow failure disorder that destroys hematopoietic stem cells, causing pancytopenia with fatigue, infections, and easy bruising or bleeding, often in younger adults or the elderly. Care relies on hematopoietic stem cell transplant when feasible or immunosuppression when it is not, but many patients face inadequate durability, relapse, and clonal evolution to myeloid malignancy. The key unmet need is durable, safer nontransplant restoration of blood counts through more effective immune resetting and stem cell recovery while preventing malignant evolution.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable non-transplant salvage that restores trilineage hematopoiesis in refractory (no response at 3–6 months) or relapsed severe aplastic anemia patients when allo-HSCT isn’t feasible
- Maintenance/“immune-reset” approaches that prevent relapse and clonal evolution (incl. reducing secondary MDS/AML risk over ~4–6 years) after response to hATG + eltrombopag IST
- Safer, lower-burden alternatives to ATG/cyclosporine-based IST that reduce infusion anaphylaxis risk/monitoring and chronic calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity monitoring (e.g., nephrotoxicity, hypertension, infections)

name: Poliomyelitis
description: Poliomyelitis is a fecal oral viral infection that multiplies in the intestine and can invade the nervous system, mainly affecting children under five, with a febrile prodrome that can progress to rapid asymmetric flaccid paralysis and sometimes fatal bulbar respiratory failure. There is no cure and care is supportive. Key unmet needs include vaccines that better block intestinal shedding and transmission, antivirals to clear chronic excretion, and genetically stabilized oral vaccines that are less likely to revert and cause paralysis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral poliovirus antivirals to stop chronic iVDPV shedding in primary/B‑cell immunodeficiency long‑term excretors (no licensed treatment today).
- Vaccine/adjuvant approaches that reduce intestinal infection and fecal shedding in IPV‑vaccinated populations (IPV doesn’t prevent GI infection/shedding).
- Genetically stabilized oral outbreak vaccines that preserve OPV-like transmission control while minimizing reversion/VDPV emergence risk.

name: Lymphoma | anaplastic large cell
description: Systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma is a rare CD30 positive peripheral T cell non Hodgkin lymphoma, often presenting at advanced stage with B symptoms, lymphadenopathy, and frequent extranodal and bone marrow involvement. Despite brentuximab vedotin based frontline chemo, outcomes are limited by relapse especially in ALK negative disease and by pediatric treatment failure of about 25 to 30 percent. Current regimens are also constrained by toxicity such as febrile neutropenia and peripheral neuropathy that can drive dose delays, reductions, or discontinuation, sustaining demand for more durable and better tolerated disease control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Relapse-preventing frontline therapy for pediatric systemic ALCL to cut ~25–30% treatment failure and improve long-term cure, especially in high-risk patients.
- Durable, non–transplant-dependent options for relapse-prone ALK-negative systemic ALCL to improve survival beyond current frontline A+CHP outcomes.
- Chemo-sparing/lower-burden regimens that reduce key SoC toxicities (notably peripheral neuropathy and serious febrile neutropenia) while maintaining PFS.

name: Methemoglobinemia
description: Acquired methemoglobinemia is an acute oxidant injury that converts hemoglobin iron to the ferric state, blocking oxygen delivery and presenting with cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen, pulse oximetry around 85 percent, and chocolate colored blood, sometimes progressing to seizures, arrhythmias, or coma. Methylene blue is the standard antidote, but real world use is limited by serious serotonergic drug interactions and contraindication in glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, while slower alternatives like vitamin C and invasive workarounds leave a need for fast, broadly safe reversal options including for methylene blue nonresponders such as hemoglobin M.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid-acting acute antidote for acquired methemoglobinemia that is safe/effective in G6PD deficiency (methylene blue contraindicated/ineffective).
- Non-MAOI/non-serotonergic acute reversal usable with SSRIs/SNRIs/MAOIs/opioids to avoid methylene blue–associated serotonin syndrome.
- Pharmacologic option for methylene-blue–unresponsive etiologies (e.g., HbM) and/or better-tolerated chronic oral reducer vs burdensome high-dose vitamin C.

name: Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder
description: Post transplant lymphoproliferative disorder is a transplant associated spectrum from benign lymphoid proliferation to aggressive lymphoma, usually driven by Epstein Barr virus reactivation under pharmacologic immunosuppression. Patients may present within the first year or years later with fever, fatigue, lymphadenopathy, and frequent extranodal disease such as gastrointestinal involvement. First line management often starts with reducing immunosuppression and adding CD20 targeted antibodies with or without chemotherapy, but control is constrained by high relapse risk and the tradeoff with graft rejection and treatment toxicity. Chemo sparing regimens and immune based and Epstein Barr virus directed cellular therapies are emerging.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Chemo-sparing frontline regimens for treatment-naïve CD20+ PTLD that maintain high PET/CT CMR/ORR while avoiding CHOP/R-CHOP toxicity (TRM, severe cytopenias/infections).
- Graft-preserving PTLD control options for patients in whom immunosuppression reduction is unsafe/not feasible due to rejection risk.
- More durable therapies for relapsed/refractory PTLD after rituximab ± chemotherapy (including EBV+ PTLD).

name: Blastomycosis
description: Rare endemic fungal infection acquired by inhaling Blastomyces that usually presents as pneumonia but can disseminate to skin, bone, and central nervous system; major unmet needs are earlier diagnosis and shorter, easier-to-manage therapy since it is often misdiagnosed and treatment typically requires 6–12 months of antifungals with monitoring, with limited options in pregnancy and severe disease requiring amphotericin.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Amphotericin-sparing, CNS-penetrant therapy for severe/CNS blastomycosis that avoids prolonged IV induction and nephrotoxicity/monitoring burden
- Shorter, predictable outpatient oral regimen (vs 6–12 months) that avoids therapeutic drug monitoring and minimizes absorption/DDI constraints
- Pregnancy-compatible (non-teratogenic) antifungal alternative to azoles that reduces reliance on IV amphotericin

name: Primary effusion lymphoma
description: Rare, aggressive human herpesvirus 8 driven large B cell lymphoma presenting as malignant pleural, pericardial, or peritoneal effusions without a tumor mass, typically in profoundly immunosuppressed patients such as those with human immunodeficiency virus. Care relies on non specific multiagent anthracycline chemotherapy with no standard regimen, high infectious risk, and poor survival around 30 percent at one year, leaving a need for durable, less immunosuppressive and virus directed therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Frontline therapy that improves on CHOP/EPOCH outcomes (CR >55%–57% and median OS >18 months) with more durable remissions in HIV–PEL
- KSHV/HHV‑8–directed therapeutics leveraging PEL’s universal viral driver vs non-specific cytotoxic chemotherapy
- Chemo-/infection-sparing regimens for profoundly immunosuppressed patients that also reduce central-line, multi-day continuous-infusion (EPOCH) treatment burden

name: Mucopolysaccharidosis | type II
description: Hunter syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type II) is an X linked lysosomal storage disorder, mainly in boys, driven by glycosaminoglycan buildup that causes progressive multisystem disease starting in early childhood with airway obstruction, recurrent infections and sleep apnea, skeletal and joint disease, organ enlargement, and heart valve damage. In the neuronopathic form, children often regress around ages 6 to 8 and die young because standard weekly intravenous idursulfase reduces some somatic burden but does not cross the blood brain barrier and carries infusion and immunogenicity risks. The premium is on brain penetrant, lower burden disease modifying therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS disease modification for neuronopathic MPS II after neurocognitive decline is established, with benefit shown on clinical neurodevelopment/adaptive-behavior endpoints (not biomarker-only).
- Improved efficacy in hard-to-treat somatic disease (especially skeletal and cardiac valve pathology) where IV ERT has limited impact, on objective structural/functional measures.
- Infusion-sparing, safer, less immunogenic chronic therapy that reduces weekly supervised IV burden and lowers infusion reactions/anaphylaxis and anti-drug antibodies.

name: Histiocytoma | angiomatoid fibrous
description: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma is a rare, borderline malignant soft tissue tumor that usually arises in children and young adults as a slow growing, painless superficial limb nodule and is often misdiagnosed as a hematoma or vascular lesion. Surgery is standard, but local recurrence occurs in up to 15 percent and rare metastases can be life threatening, with generally fatal outcomes when unresectable. The core unmet need is earlier accurate diagnosis and effective systemic, biomarker led options for unresectable or metastatic disease, including approaches targeting cytokine driven inflammation such as interleukin 6 signaling in EWSR1 CREB1 fusion tumors.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemic therapy that improves response and survival in unresectable/metastatic AFH
- Non-cytotoxic targeted or immunotherapy (e.g., PD-1/PD-L1) options to replace limited-evidence chemo/RT in advanced AFH
- Biomarker-guided IL-6/IL-6R inhibition (tocilizumab-class) for EWSR1-CREB1, IL-6–secreting chemo-refractory metastatic AFH

name: Glycogen storage disease | type 3
description: Glycogen storage disease type III (Cori or Forbes disease) is an inherited disorder where abnormal glycogen accumulates in cells, impairing liver and often muscle and heart. It typically presents in infancy with fasting hypoglycemia, hyperlipidemia, elevated liver enzymes, and hepatomegaly, and management is dominated by frequent high protein feeding and early cornstarch. Even with diet, many patients develop progressive multi organ complications including myopathy and cardiomyopathy and later cirrhosis, liver failure, and hepatocellular carcinoma risk, leaving a major need for diet sparing metabolic control and true disease modifying therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Diet-sparing hypoglycemia prevention enabling safe overnight fasting without around-the-clock feeding/monitoring.
- Disease modification for GSD‑IIIa myopathy/cardiomyopathy (improve exercise capacity/cardiac function despite diet).
- Prevention of hepatic fibrosis/cirrhosis/HCC to reduce transplant need and malignancy risk.

name: Hepatocellular carcinoma | fibrolamellar
description: Rare primary liver cancer of adolescents and young adults without underlying liver disease, often asymptomatic until advanced or metastatic with vague abdominal symptoms and weight loss. Surgery is the only potentially curative option but relapse is common and lymph node spread frequent, and there are no clearly effective systemic therapies. The defining DNAJB1 PRKACA fusion creates a clear biologic target, but disease modifying treatments remain an urgent unmet need.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- More effective systemic therapy for unresectable/metastatic fibrolamellar HCC that materially improves on current first-line activity (~13% ORR; no complete responses).
- Adjuvant/maintenance therapy after curative-intent resection to extend recurrence-free survival given high early intrahepatic recurrence.
- DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion–directed precision therapy (inhibition/degradation or fusion-neoantigen immunotherapy) for the molecularly defined population.

name: Multifocal motor neuropathy
description: Multifocal motor neuropathy is a rare immune mediated motor neuropathy causing slowly progressive, asymmetric weakness with minimal sensory loss, usually affecting the upper limbs and eroding hand function for daily tasks. Care is dominated by intravenous immunoglobulin, the only established therapy, but benefits often fade and many patients require infusions every two to eight weeks. Despite maintenance dosing, axonal damage can drive continued progression, while long term immunoglobulin exposure carries risks such as thrombosis and renal dysfunction, sustaining demand for more durable disease control and immunoglobulin sparing options including home subcutaneous delivery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- IVIg-sparing maintenance therapy that sustains motor function and extends time-to-retreatment (reducing chronic infusion dependence)
- Disease-modifying therapy that prevents secondary axonal damage/axon loss driving slow progression despite regular IVIg
- Safer long-term alternative to immunoglobulin that reduces IVIg class risks (esp. thrombosis and renal injury) while maintaining efficacy

name: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor
description: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor is an ultra-rare, usually benign myofibroblastic spindle-cell tumor affecting mainly children and young adults, most often in the lung or abdominal soft tissues. Patients present with a mass and location-driven symptoms such as abdominal pain or cough, with some developing systemic inflammatory features like fever and weight loss. Surgery is first-line, but complete resection can be difficult and recurrence is common, while metastasis is uncommon. Kinase fusions such as anaplastic lymphoma kinase create targets, yet fusion-negative disease, acquired resistance, and the lack of standardized pediatric treatment leave a premium on durable, molecularly guided options for unresectable or recurrent disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Effective systemic therapies for ALK‑negative/non‑ALK‑rearranged IMT (incl. ROS1/RET fusion subgroups).
- Next‑generation ALK strategies that overcome acquired resistance and extend response durability beyond crizotinib.
- Better‑tolerated long‑term pediatric ALK+ IMT therapy that reduces dose interruptions/reductions/discontinuations while maintaining response.

name: Primary central nervous system vasculitis
description: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system is a rare, midlife-onset inflammatory vasculitis confined to the brain and spinal cord that typically evolves over weeks with headaches, cognitive decline, focal deficits, and sometimes stroke or seizures. It is hard to diagnose because it mimics many other neurologic conditions and often requires advanced imaging and sometimes brain biopsy rather than a single definitive test. Treatment relies on high-intensity immunosuppression despite no randomized trial evidence, and relapses are common at roughly 25 to 30 percent and reported as high as 55 percent, creating strong demand for safer, more targeted, disease-modifying approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent early new ischemic strokes after immunosuppression initiation (high-risk window ~10–20 days)
- Reduce high relapse burden with more effective relapse-preventing maintenance therapy
- Steroid/cyclophosphamide-sparing regimens with markedly improved safety and lower monitoring burden

name: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
description: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is a heterogeneous biopsy pattern, often driven by complement activation or immune complex deposition, that mainly affects children and young adults and presents with hematuria and proteinuria, frequently with hypertension and renal dysfunction. Many progress to chronic kidney failure within a decade and recurrence after kidney transplant is common. Current management is largely supportive and relies on broad immunosuppression with uncertain benefit, leaving a premium on durable, kidney sparing complement targeted approaches that reduce proteinuria and slow progression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Complement-pathway (C3/alternative-pathway) targeted therapy for C3G/primary IC‑MPGN that delivers durable proteinuria (UPCR/uPCR) reduction plus eGFR stabilization.
- Steroid-/broad immunosuppression–sparing options for idiopathic/immune-complex MPGN with nephritic sediment and/or nephrotic-range proteinuria where current regimens have limited efficacy and high toxicity.
- Therapies to prevent/maintain against post–kidney-transplant recurrence in C3G/primary IC‑MPGN (high recurrence and graft-failure risk).

name: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis
description: Rare hereditary immunodeficiency causing persistent or recurrent Candida infections of the mouth, skin, and nails, often starting with neonatal thrush and progressing to chronic nail and skin disease. Defects in interleukin 17 and T helper 17 immunity mean antifungals suppress rather than cure, so patients often need lifelong azoles with frequent relapse on stopping and substantial resistance over time. The premium is on durable, lower burden prophylaxis and disease modifying immune restoring approaches that reduce dependence on chronic antifungals.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Th17/IL-17 pathway immune restoration (e.g., JAK/STAT-axis modulation) in genetically defined CMC (STAT1‑GOF; APECED) to achieve durable mucocutaneous-candidiasis remission without continuous antifungal prophylaxis.
- Resistance-breaking non-azole antifungal options for azole‑refractory CMC (including STAT1‑GOF), targeting the ~39% of long‑term–treated patients with clinical antifungal resistance.
- Lower-burden pediatric maintenance/prophylaxis (e.g., once-weekly or otherwise long-acting regimens) to reduce daily dosing/monitoring burden while maintaining mucosal/skin/nail clearance.

name: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
description: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is an acquired complement mediated blood cell disorder, typically diagnosed in young adulthood, causing episodic hemolysis with dark urine, debilitating anemia and cytopenias, and life threatening thrombosis. Despite anti complement therapy, many patients have residual C3 driven extravascular hemolysis with persistent anemia, while infusion based care and serious infection risk requiring Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy programs create ongoing treatment burden, driving demand for more complete upstream complement control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Hemoglobin and fatigue normalization for PNH patients with residual anemia on anti‑C5 by preventing C3‑mediated extravascular hemolysis.
- Prevent clinical breakthrough hemolysis during complement‑amplifying stressors (e.g., infection, operative stress, pregnancy) via more complete/continuous complement control.
- Achieve PNH control without the serious encapsulated‑bacterial infection risk and REMS/vaccination access burden required for current complement inhibitors.

name: Xeroderma pigmentosum
description: Xeroderma pigmentosum is a rare autosomal recessive DNA repair disorder causing extreme ultraviolet sensitivity from infancy, with minutes to severe sunburn, early freckling, eye photophobia, and a dramatically elevated early skin cancer risk. Management depends on near total ultraviolet avoidance, frequent surveillance, and repeated lesion treatment, creating a heavy lifelong burden. Key gaps are durable, practical daily photoprotection that reduces DNA damage and new cancers, and disease modifying options for the roughly one quarter of patients who develop progressive neurodegeneration such as hearing loss.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable photoprotection to increase UV tolerance (MED) and reduce UV‑induced DNA damage in XP‑C/XP‑V, lowering daily sun-avoidance/sunscreen burden
- Safer non‑retinoid skin‑cancer chemoprevention to reduce new actinic keratoses/non‑melanoma skin cancers without systemic retinoid toxicities
- CNS‑penetrant therapy to prevent/slow progressive neurodegeneration in the ~25% of XP patients with neurologic involvement

name: Endometrial cancer | clear cell
description: Rare high grade endometrial cancer in older postmenopausal women, typically presenting with postmenopausal bleeding. Often uterus confined at diagnosis but has higher recurrence risk than typical early stage endometrioid tumors, driving use of adjuvant chemotherapy and leaving need for more effective disease control. In recurrence, pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib is active but frequently causes grade 3 or higher toxicities and dose reductions, underscoring demand for better tolerated, molecularly guided options such as approaches for ARID1A altered disease including EZH2 inhibition.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjuvant systemic therapy that prevents occult extrauterine disease and distant relapse in clinical stage I uterine clear cell carcinoma (UCCC).
- Molecularly targeted options for ARID1A-deficient UCCC (e.g., synthetic-lethal epigenetic strategies such as EZH2 inhibition) vs empiric carboplatin/paclitaxel.
- Better-tolerated, more durable systemic regimens for recurrent/advanced pMMR/MSS disease, improving efficacy while reducing discontinuations vs lenvatinib+pembrolizumab and severe chemo toxicity.

name: Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis
description: Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis is a rare autosomal recessive CYP27A1 bile acid synthesis and lipid storage disorder that drives lifelong, multisystem disease from infantile diarrhea and childhood cataracts to tendon xanthomas and progressive adult neurodegeneration. The biggest issue is that diagnosis is commonly missed for 20 to 25 years, so patients start chenodeoxycholic acid only after irreversible neurologic injury. While bile acid replacement can normalize cholestanol and halt progression, it does not readily reverse established deficits and adds monitoring and tolerability burden, making earlier detection and disease correcting approaches such as gene therapy a key frontier.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neuro-restorative benefit (ambulation/ataxia, cognition) for late-diagnosed/late-treated adults with established neurologic deficits beyond biomarker improvements
- CNS-inclusive disease-correcting therapy restoring CYP27A1/sterol 27-hydroxylase function to prevent/clear cholestanol accumulation
- Reduced treatment burden vs chenodiol (e.g., once-daily/long-acting), with fewer GI AEs and less liver monitoring

name: Hemosiderosis
description: Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis is a rare, mainly pediatric disorder marked by recurrent diffuse bleeding into the alveoli, leaving iron deposits that drive cough, dyspnea, intermittent hemoptysis, and iron deficiency anemia with poor growth. Flares can be life threatening and repeated injury can progress to interstitial and pulmonary fibrosis. Management still relies largely on systemic corticosteroids with limited evidence for steroid sparing immunosuppressants, creating unmet needs for safer relapse prevention, rapid hemorrhage control, and lung protective disease modifying approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing maintenance therapy that prevents pulmonary hemorrhage relapse during steroid taper (esp. refractory pediatric IPH).
- Anti-fibrotic/lung-protective therapy to prevent hemorrhage-driven scarring/pulmonary fibrosis and progression to end-stage lung disease.
- Rapid-acting rescue therapy to rapidly halt massive pulmonary hemorrhage and reduce ICU/ventilation/ECMO need during acute flares.
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus page for “Hemosiderosis”/“Idiopathic Pulmonary Hemosiderosis”; closest: https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/hereditary-hemochromatosis/

name: Hyperimmunoglobulinemia D periodic fever syndrome
description: Rare inherited autoinflammatory disease in the mevalonate kinase deficiency spectrum, usually beginning in infancy with recurrent 3 to 7 day high fever flares every few weeks plus lymphadenopathy, abdominal pain with vomiting or diarrhea, rash and arthralgia, with wellness between attacks. Key unmet needs are durable flare prevention and organ protection, since AA amyloidosis can occur and kidney involvement can progress to failure, while current interleukin 1 blockade often requires frequent injections and still yields incomplete remission with injection site pain and infections.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Flare-free remission for IL‑1–inhibitor inadequate responders, eliminating CRP-defined flares and reducing flare-severity scores without dose escalation/switching.
- Biomarker-deep control that normalizes SAA (not just CRP) to reduce long-term AA amyloidosis risk in patients with chronic inflammation.
- Lower treatment burden and better tolerability than injectable biologics (avoid daily painful injections/injection-site reactions and reduce infection complications).

name: Lymphoma | hepatosplenic T-cell
description: Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma is a rare, rapidly progressive gamma delta T-cell cancer that typically affects adolescent and young adult males, often after chronic immunosuppression for inflammatory bowel disease. It infiltrates the liver, spleen, and bone marrow, driving marked hepatosplenomegaly, systemic symptoms, and profound cytopenias with little lymphadenopathy. Conventional chemotherapy is frequently ineffective and hard to deliver safely in cytopenic patients, and outcomes remain poor even with intensive regimens and stem cell transplantation, creating a major unmet need for mechanism based therapies that can produce durable remissions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Mechanism-based therapies that overcome primary chemoresistance and achieve durable CRs in relapsed/refractory HSTCL.
- Regimens that are safe/effective despite baseline cytopenias, frequent bone-marrow involvement, and underlying immunosuppression (e.g., IBD on thiopurines/TNFα blockers).
- Outpatient-friendly, transplant-sparing options that reduce reliance on intensive induction chemo + SCT while matching/beat current response benchmarks.

name: Transplant rejection | kidney
description: Kidney transplant rejection is immune mediated injury to the transplanted kidney, often detected first by rising serum creatinine with few or nonspecific symptoms. Chronic rejection, including chronic active antibody-mediated rejection, is a leading cause of late graft failure, yet there are no approved treatments for acute or chronic antibody-mediated rejection. Current care relies on burdensome, variably effective measures like plasmapheresis or high dose intravenous immunoglobulin plus steroids, while long term calcineurin inhibitor use is constrained by nephrotoxicity, leaving a premium on safer, disease modifying approaches that preserve graft function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Effective therapy for late/chronic active antibody‑mediated rejection (DSA+; microvascular inflammation) that stabilizes graft function (e.g., eGFR slope) and reduces DSA burden.
- CNI‑sparing maintenance immunosuppression that prevents rejection while reducing calcineurin‑inhibitor nephrotoxicity/chronic allograft injury.
- Lower-burden, outpatient-manageable alternatives to PLEX + IVIG + high-dose steroids for active AMR/acute rejection that reduce hospitalization and infection risk.

name: Neurocytoma
description: Neurocytoma is an ultra-rare intraventricular brain tumor in young adults, typically arising in the lateral ventricles and causing symptoms of raised intracranial pressure such as headache, nausea and vomiting, drowsiness, vision problems, and cognitive or mental changes. Surgery aims for gross total resection, but residual disease frequently necessitates radiotherapy and there is no universally accepted post-operative algorithm. For recurrent or inoperable tumors, systemic therapy is poorly standardized and evidence-light. Emerging multiomics data suggest fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 driven subsets that could enable targeted approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemic therapy with reproducible tumor control for recurrent/progressive central neurocytoma patients ineligible for further surgery/RT (no consensus chemo regimen)
- Adjuvant post-subtotal resection drug strategy to reduce recurrence/progression risk and spare multi-week fractionated radiotherapy
- FGFR3-targeted therapy for the molecularly defined FGFR3-high central neurocytoma population
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus neurocytoma page; use https://medlineplus.gov/braintumors.html

name: Marginal zone lymphoma | splenic
description: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma is a rare, indolent low grade B cell non Hodgkin lymphoma of marginal zone memory B cells that typically involves spleen and bone marrow, causing splenomegaly with lymphocytosis and sometimes cytopenias and often presenting late in older adults. Care ranges from observation to splenectomy or rituximab with or without chemotherapy, but there is no randomized trial driven standard of care and chemo toxicity limits options in frailer patients. Key unmet needs are well tolerated, durable, low visit disease control and better risk adapted strategies to prevent or treat transformation to aggressive diffuse large B cell lymphoma.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Chemo-free, low-visit first-line regimens for symptomatic SMZL needing systemic therapy (avoid weekly IV anti-CD20 induction and prolonged on-treatment monitoring)
- Higher-depth and longer-duration remissions in relapsed/refractory SMZL post–anti-CD20/BTKi (increase CR rate and durability vs current benchmarks)
- Risk-adapted therapies for biologically high-risk SMZL (e.g., TP53/KLF2/complex karyotype) to prevent/treat aggressive transformation

name: Sinonasal undifferentiated carcinoma
description: Ultra-rare, highly aggressive sinonasal cancer often diagnosed only after invasion into nearby critical structures such as the orbit or brain. Symptoms mimic severe sinus disease with obstruction, epistaxis, and visual changes, and patients are typically middle-aged and male-skewed. Treatment still relies on toxic, variable multimodality surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy, with no firmly established protocol and limited durable control. Key unmet needs are earlier detection, better local and systemic disease control, and biomarker-driven, less morbid regimens including targeted and immunotherapy-based approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral, biomarker-driven IDH inhibition to improve durable benefit/PFS in recurrent/metastatic IDH2‑mutant SNUC
- EZH2 inhibitor–based induction + maintenance strategy to reduce high recurrence and improve outcomes in stage III–IVA SMARCB1 (INI‑1)-deficient sinonasal carcinoma
- Neoadjuvant chemo–immunotherapy to preserve response while lowering toxicity/treatment burden vs legacy platinum‑taxane/5‑FU regimens

name: MOG antibody disease
description: MOG antibody disease is a rare immune mediated central nervous system demyelinating disorder that inflames the optic nerve spinal cord or brain, often presenting with optic neuritis or transverse myelitis and in children acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, with disability driven by relapses. Acute attacks are treated with high dose steroids and sometimes plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin, but there are no Food and Drug Administration approved maintenance therapies, no established guidelines, and no reliable way to predict who will relapse, making steroid sparing relapse prevention the key unmet need.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Proven relapse-prevention maintenance for relapsing MOGAD (esp. higher-relapse-risk optic neuritis/older children) to prevent relapse-driven disability accumulation.
- Rapid-onset, steroid-sparing acute + bridge strategy that avoids prolonged IV/PO steroid exposure used to prevent early relapses.
- Safer, less monitoring- and infusion-intensive long-term therapy reducing reliance on broad immunosuppression and repeated IVIG infusions (cost/shortage/access constraints).

name: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans
description: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans is a rare skin cancer arising in the deep dermis that often starts as a firm plaque and slowly grows into nodules. It rarely metastasizes but is locally aggressive and frequently recurs after excision, forcing wide margin surgery that can be disfiguring or function limiting, especially for large or borderline resectable tumors. Targeted therapy can help in fusion driven disease, but options are limited for fusion negative tumors and for fibrosarcomatous transformation, which carries higher recurrence and meaningful metastatic risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neoadjuvant/local tumor-shrinking therapy to enable complete resection with less disfiguring reconstruction in large/borderline-resectable DFSP.
- Effective systemic options for DFSP that is fusion-negative or not expected to respond to imatinib (e.g., lacking t(17;22)/COL1A1–PDGFB).
- Therapies that prevent metastasis and overcome imatinib resistance in fibrosarcomatous DFSP (FS-DFSP).

name: Osteosarcoma
description: Osteosarcoma is a rare malignant bone tumor of teenagers and young adults, typically arising in long bones around the knee and presenting with weeks to months of progressive bone pain, swelling, limp, and occasional pathologic fracture. Standard chemotherapy plus surgery is often limb sparing, but outcomes remain poor when disease has spread to the lungs, which is present in up to 20% at diagnosis and drives most deaths. Metastatic event free survival is only about 20% to 30%, and unresectable metastatic relapse has under 5% survival, alongside a need to reduce the toxicity and monitoring burden of intensive regimens such as high dose methotrexate.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Metastasis-eradicating systemic therapy that materially improves outcomes in patients with lung-only metastases at diagnosis (pushing 5-year EFS well beyond ~20–25%).
- Active salvage therapy for unresectable metastatic/recurrent osteosarcoma that converts “<5% survival” into meaningfully higher durable-survival rates.
- Chemo-sparing/chemo-protective regimens that preserve cure probability while sharply reducing MAP toxicity (e.g., febrile neutropenia ~54%) and eliminating/mitigating high-dose methotrexate hospital-level monitoring requirements.

name: Parathyroid carcinoma
description: Parathyroid carcinoma is a rare, aggressive endocrine cancer that typically presents in midlife with markedly elevated parathyroid hormone and life threatening hypercalcemia, causing kidney stones, bone disease, fractures, and systemic fatigue. Surgery is the only reliably tumor directed therapy yet 60 to 80 percent recur, and many deaths are driven by refractory hypercalcemia rather than tumor bulk. For unresectable or metastatic disease, evidence for radiotherapy and systemic options is thin, leaving major unmet need for durable disease control and safer, longer lasting calcium management.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-controlling systemic therapy for unresectable/metastatic/recurrent parathyroid carcinoma achieving objective tumor responses (RECIST).
- Safer, more convenient long-term hypercalcemia-control therapy achieving sustained normocalcemia (e.g., corrected Ca <10.3 mg/dL for ≥2 weeks) in inoperable/unresectable disease.
- Precision targeted therapy and/or biomarker-selected immunotherapy for metastatic parathyroid carcinoma with actionable genomic features (e.g., high TMB ~20% or targetable alterations/fusions).

name: Pachyonychia congenita
description: Pachyonychia congenita is a very rare inherited keratin disorder that begins in early childhood, causing thick dystrophic nails and highly painful plantar calluses and blistering that can make walking difficult or impossible, sometimes with oral leukokeratosis and cysts.
