Surgery can be curative but is often limited by proximity to the brainstem or optic nerves, leaving a need for durable tumor control that avoids the long term cognitive and hormonal toxicity of radiation and other therapies.

name: Malignant rhabdoid tumor
description: Malignant rhabdoid tumor is a rare, ultra aggressive cancer of infancy and early childhood, usually arising in the kidney or central nervous system and often presenting at advanced stage with rapid spread to the lungs or brain. It is driven mainly by SMARCB1 loss and is genomically stable and epigenetically driven, making conventional escalation of chemotherapy and local control insufficient. Relapses commonly occur within months and most children still die within about a year, creating urgent need for metastasis active, relapse preventing, less toxic targeted therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS- and lung-metastasis–active systemic therapy for infants/toddlers who frequently present with late-stage/metastatic disease that meaningfully extends survival beyond today’s ~1-year median OS.
- Chemo-sparing regimens that cut severe myelosuppression (e.g., grade 3–5 febrile neutropenia ~58%) and treatment-related mortality (~4.9–5%) versus current intensive cytotoxic backbones.
- Molecularly targeted therapy for SMARCB1/INI1-loss MRT that prevents/controls early relapse (typically within 2 years) and lifts long-term survival beyond ~40%.

name: Nocardiosis
description: Rare opportunistic Nocardia infection starting as subacute pneumonia with frequent hematogenous spread to abscesses, especially in the brain causing headaches, confusion, and seizures in immunocompromised patients; care requires species-level testing and prolonged multi-antibiotic regimens lasting months to a year, yet central nervous system disease remains highly lethal with >80% mortality.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS/disseminated nocardiosis: CNS-penetrant, rapidly bactericidal therapy to reduce very high mortality in brain/spinal cord infection.
- Non-CNS nocardiosis: IV-sparing oral/long-acting regimens that shorten weeks-long IV induction and months-long total therapy while maintaining low relapse.
- Immunocompromised/resistant species: safer, less toxic alternatives to TMP-SMX/linezolid/aminoglycosides with reliable activity against multidrug-resistant strains (e.g., TMP-SMX–resistant N. farcinica).

name: Myxofibrosarcoma
description: Myxofibrosarcoma is a fibroblastic soft tissue sarcoma of older adults that often presents as a slow growing painless superficial limb mass with infiltrative margins that make complete surgery difficult. It has among the highest local recurrence rates in soft tissue sarcoma at roughly 15 to 60 percent within 5 years and recurrences can progress to higher grade disease with greater metastatic potential. Systemic treatment for advanced disease still relies on anthracycline based chemotherapy such as doxorubicin, where intensification adds toxicity without improving overall survival, leaving major unmet need for better perioperative recurrence prevention and more effective, better tolerated systemic options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Peri-operative (neo/adjuvant) drug therapy to reduce very high local-recurrence risk driven by infiltrative growth/margin uncertainty (including out-of-field/multinodular recurrences)
- Adjuvant systemic therapy to prevent local-recurrence–associated grade progression (19–50% of locally recurrent cases) and thereby reduce metastatic risk in intermediate/high-grade disease
- Better-tolerated, more effective 1L regimen for unresectable/metastatic UPS/MFS than doxorubicin±ifosfamide, improving PFS/response without the AI-grade 3/4 toxicity burden

name: Severe congenital neutropenia
description: Severe congenital neutropenia is an inherited bone marrow failure syndrome with profound neutropenia from birth, causing recurrent life threatening bacterial infections beginning in infancy. Chronic granulocyte colony stimulating factor and rapid antibiotic treatment for any fever reduce infections but create a lifelong care burden and do not eliminate risk. A major unmet need is safer disease modifying or curative options that prevent emergency infectious episodes and reduce the 10 to 30 percent lifetime risk of myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- One-time curative therapies (e.g., autologous HSC gene therapy/editing) to replace lifelong G‑CSF and reduce long-term sepsis mortality and MDS/AML transformation risk.
- Non–G‑CSF treatments that demonstrate hard clinical benefit (lower annualized infection rate, reduced antibiotic use/oral ulcers), not just ANC increases.
- Genotype-directed drugs for defined SCN subtypes (e.g., G6PC3 deficiency) with improved tolerability vs current G‑CSF regimens.

name: Tularemia
description: Tularemia is a rare, potentially serious zoonotic infection caused by *Francisella tularensis*, typically acquired via tick or deer fly bites or handling infected animal tissue and often presenting after a 3 to 5 day incubation with an inoculation ulcer and swollen lymph nodes. Inhalational exposure can drive severe pneumonic disease. Care relies on antibiotics, with severe cases requiring parenteral aminoglycosides plus drug level and renal monitoring and limited options in pregnancy and pediatrics. There is no licensed vaccine in the United States, leaving unmet needs for simpler scalable oral regimens, relapse prevention, and robust postexposure prophylaxis and vaccination for preparedness.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Severe/complicated tularemia: reliably curative regimen that avoids initial dual-class therapy and eliminates aminoglycoside IV/IM dosing plus drug-level/renal monitoring
- Children/pregnancy: pediatric- and pregnancy-optimized oral regimen with low relapse risk that avoids doxycycline relapse concerns and fluoroquinolone boxed-warning toxicities
- Bioterrorism/mass exposure & PEP: FDA-approved, stockpile-ready postexposure prophylaxis deployable at scale with activity retained despite engineered-resistance risk

name: Retinoblastoma
description: Retinoblastoma is a rare retinal cancer of early childhood, often first noticed before age 5 as leukocoria in flash photos or new strabismus. When confined to the eye it is frequently curable, but preserving the eye and vision can require enucleation or prolonged, specialized eye salvage with repeated procedures under anesthesia. Key unmet needs include less toxic frontline therapy that avoids carboplatin associated hearing loss, better control of advanced intraocular disease with vitreous or subretinal seeding, and effective options for central nervous system spread and trilateral disease, which still carries dismal outcomes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Hearing-sparing frontline chemoreduction for infants (especially <6 months) to reduce carboplatin/vincristine-associated severe hearing loss.
- Long-acting, seed-penetrant intraocular therapy for advanced intraocular retinoblastoma with vitreous/subretinal seeding (Group D/E) to improve seed control while reducing procedure/EUA burden and reliance on specialized centers.
- More effective, lower–late-effect-burden systemic therapy for intracranial/CNS metastatic and trilateral retinoblastoma to improve survival and reduce reliance on intensive chemo/radiation.

name: Diffuse midline glioma
description: Aggressive, infiltrative pediatric high grade glioma of midline structures especially the pons with rapid onset cranial nerve deficits, long tract signs and ataxia and median survival under 1 year. Surgery is unsafe and radiotherapy offers only temporary palliation, leaving care largely symptom focused and often reliant on dexamethasone despite severe side effects. The biggest gap is disease modifying therapy that can penetrate the blood brain barrier, control diffuse tumor biology and reduce steroid dependence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Frontline therapies that extend OS/PFS beyond radiotherapy alone for newly diagnosed DMG/DIPG.
- Brainstem/BBB-penetrant drugs (or delivery-enabled therapeutics) achieving therapeutic intratumoral exposure and overcoming TMZ resistance (e.g., unmethylated MGMT).
- Steroid-sparing edema/symptom control (e.g., ≥50% dexamethasone reduction) with safer chronic tolerability and less monitoring burden (e.g., avoiding QTc/ECG monitoring).

name: Complex cortical dysplasia with other brain malformations
description: Complex cortical dysplasia with other brain malformations is a neurodevelopmental disorder caused by disrupted neuronal migration and axon guidance, leading to cortical malformations on imaging and early onset seizures with developmental delay, hypotonia or spasticity, and later language, learning, and behavioral problems. First line anti seizure medicines often fail, with only about 1 in 5 achieving good control, and surgery is frequently limited by involvement of eloquent cortex, leaving a major need for durable seizure freedom and therapies that also address neurodevelopmental and behavioral impairment.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunctive therapy achieving meaningful seizure freedom/high responder rates in early-onset MCD/FCD patients with drug-resistant seizures after ≥2 failed anti-seizure medications.
- Treatment that improves neurodevelopmental delay/cognition and behavioral symptoms (and reduces caregiver burden) beyond seizure-count reductions.
- Pediatric-friendly long-term option with fewer serious safety risks/monitoring needs and lower dosing/administration burden than current ASMs.

name: Histiocytoma | malignant fibrous
description: Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma is an aggressive soft tissue or bone cancer, typically in adults in their 50s to 70s, often presenting as a rapidly enlarging extremity mass with high local recurrence and frequent lung metastasis. Treatment relies on wide surgery and radiotherapy, but unresectable or metastatic disease still defaults to doxorubicin based chemotherapy with modest benefit and significant toxicity. A major unmet need is more effective, better tolerated systemic options, including biomarker guided immunotherapy combinations to extend programmed cell death protein 1 inhibitor benefit beyond a small responder subset.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Overall-survival–improving 1L systemic therapy for unresectable/metastatic UPS beyond doxorubicin
- Anthracycline/ifosfamide-sparing regimens with improved tolerability for the typical older UPS population
- Biomarker-guided immunotherapy (and rational combinations) to expand benefit beyond the pembrolizumab responder subset in UPS

name: Early infantile epileptic encephalopathy
description: Early infantile epileptic encephalopathy (Ohtahara syndrome) is a catastrophic neonatal-onset epilepsy marked by very frequent tonic spasms (often in clusters up to hundreds per day) and a burst suppression electroencephalogram pattern with severe neurologic dysfunction. Causes are heterogeneous, often structural or genetic, and seizures are commonly drug resistant with no effective standard therapy, leading to profound developmental disability, reduced survival, and frequent evolution to infantile spasms in later infancy, underscoring the need for disease modifying and etiology matched treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid, durable control of neonatal-onset tonic spasms (often hundreds/day) in drug-resistant patients, improving seizure-free days and motor seizure frequency
- Genotype-stratified precision therapies for SCN2A-spectrum Ohtahara/EIEE that also improve neurodevelopment (e.g., milestone gains) and reduce evolution to West syndrome
- Infant-safe antiseizure options with lower toxicity/monitoring burden than current SoC (e.g., avoiding valproate hepatotoxicity monitoring, vigabatrin vision/REMS, phenobarbital neonatal cardiorespiratory/CNS AEs)

name: Beta thalassemia | transfusion-independent
description: Transfusion independent beta thalassemia is an inherited hemoglobin disorder marked by ineffective red blood cell production and chronic anemia that can cause fatigue, jaundice, growth delay, splenomegaly, and bone changes. Although patients often avoid lifelong regular transfusions, ongoing anemia and hepcidin suppression drive increased intestinal iron absorption, leading to progressive iron overload and organ damage even without transfusions. Management relies on intermittent transfusions for quality of life and iron chelation, leaving a need for disease modifying therapies that sustainably raise hemoglobin while preventing iron loading at its source.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Sustained, non-transfusion anemia correction in symptomatic NTDT patients (Hb <10 g/dL), achieving durable ≥1.0 g/dL Hb rise (ideally Hb ≥10 g/dL) with improved tiredness/weakness.
- Mechanism-based prevention of primary iron overload by modulating the hepcidin/ferroportin axis to reduce intestinal iron absorption and reduce/eliminate chelation dependence.
- Safer, lower-monitoring chronic iron-overload control than deferasirox (avoiding renal/hepatic failure and GI hemorrhage risks) for long-term treatment.

name: Plasma cell leukemia
description: Plasma cell leukemia is a rare, highly aggressive plasma cell cancer (a multiple myeloma variant) marked by malignant plasma cells circulating in blood, often presenting around age 55 with rapid end organ damage and cytopenias. Despite intensive proteasome inhibitor and immunomodulatory based regimens and autologous transplant for eligible patients, median survival is only 7 to 11 months. Progress is hampered by lack of randomized trials and frequent trial exclusion, leaving major unmet needs for rapid, tolerable outpatient cytoreduction, more patients reaching transplant, and biomarker guided options such as BCL-2 targeting in t(11;14) disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Frontline rapid-cytoreduction regimens to prevent early mortality in newly diagnosed pPCL.
- Transplant-sparing, outpatient-manageable backbones with fewer severe complications for transplant-ineligible pPCL.
- Biomarker-selected BCL-2–targeted regimens for t(11;14)-positive pPCL (e.g., venetoclax-based).

name: Erythropoietic protoporphyria
description: Erythropoietic protoporphyria is an inherited heme pathway disorder that usually begins in infancy or childhood, causing rapid, severe phototoxic pain within about 30 minutes of sun or ultraviolet exposure often with minimal visible skin changes, delaying diagnosis and constraining daily life. Treatment is dominated by adult only afamelanotide implants administered every two months with monitoring burdens, leaving major gaps in pediatric ready, self administered photoprotection. A key unmet need is disease modification that lowers circulating protoporphyrin IX to improve light tolerance and reduce hepatobiliary deposition that can rarely progress to liver failure.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pediatric-ready, dose-adjustable photoprotection options for children/adolescents (current fixed-dose afamelanotide implant not suitable).
- Non-invasive/self-administered alternatives to q2‑month HCP-administered implants, avoiding skin-darkening/skin-exam monitoring burden.
- Disease-modifying therapies that lower circulating PPIX (blood ± liver endpoints) to reduce EPP-related liver-failure risk, not just phototoxic symptoms.

name: Myofibromatosis | infantile
description: Rare benign tumor disorder of infancy with firm, usually painless nodules in skin, muscle, and sometimes bone that often regress spontaneously, but a high risk subset develops multifocal visceral lesions that can be life threatening with up to ~70% mortality without therapy and requires chemotherapy. Care is blunt and toxic for infants, and outcomes are poor when organs are involved, creating demand for safer disease controlling options. Molecularly guided targeted therapy is emerging, including kinase inhibition in platelet-derived growth factor receptor beta driven disease and rare RET fusion cases.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-matched PDGFRB inhibition (incl. imatinib-resistant variants) to achieve rapid/complete regression in unresectable/visceral or critical-structure–compressing infantile myofibromatosis, avoiding high-morbidity chemo/surgery in infants.
- Fast-acting systemic therapy for disseminated/multicentric disease with visceral involvement that rapidly reverses cardiopulmonary/GI organ compromise (survival + restored ventilation/oxygenation/GI function).
- Oral, pediatric-feasible targeted options (e.g., RET-altered subset) with materially higher ORR than historical chemotherapy (22%), reducing need for IV MTX/VBL or VAC regimens.

name: Desmoplastic small round cell tumor
description: Desmoplastic small round cell tumor is a very rare, highly aggressive peritoneal abdominal cancer of adolescents and young adults, especially males, driven by an EWSR1 WT1 fusion. Patients often present late with abdominal pain, swelling, and bowel or urinary symptoms, and care relies on toxic multimodal chemotherapy, surgery, and radiotherapy without an agreed standard regimen. Outcomes remain poor with about 15 percent five year survival, so the priority is more effective disease modifying systemic therapy that controls widespread peritoneal disease and reduces relapse and treatment burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Fusion-program–directed systemic therapy achieving durable remissions in adolescents/young adults with DSRCT
- Peritoneal-implant–eradicating therapies to prevent intraperitoneal relapse in peritoneum-dominant DSRCT
- Toxicity-sparing regimens reducing GI/hematologic toxicity and supportive-care burden from intensive multimodal treatment (e.g., WAP-RT)

name: Urethral cancer | adenocarcinoma
description: Primary urethral carcinoma is an exceptionally rare cancer under 1% of genitourinary malignancies. Patients are typically age 50 or older and present with hematuria, dysuria, urinary frequency, and weak stream, often with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections. Tumors invade adjacent structures early and commonly spread to groin or pelvic lymph nodes, so many cases are advanced at diagnosis and require morbid multimodality care such as radical surgery with urinary diversion plus chemotherapy and radiation. The biggest gap is a thin, largely retrospective evidence base with treatments extrapolated from other cancers and unclear criteria for organ preservation or optimal systemic therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adenocarcinoma-tailored systemic regimens that meaningfully improve 5-year survival vs current outcomes
- Evidence-based organ-preserving multimodality strategies with clear patient-selection criteria to avoid exenterative surgery/urinary diversion
- Cisplatin-sparing curative-intent regimens for locally advanced disease that reduce nephrotoxicity and hydration/monitoring burden (esp. renal-impaired/geriatric patients)

name: Transplant rejection | heart
description: Heart transplant rejection is an immune attack on the donated heart that often occurs in the first post transplant year and is frequently silent until heart failure like symptoms appear. Management depends on intensive early endomyocardial biopsy surveillance and lifelong immunosuppression that carries substantial toxicity including chronic kidney disease risk. Longer term outcomes are shaped by chronic injury such as cardiac allograft vasculopathy, driving unmet needs for kidney sparing regimens, better options for antibody mediated rejection, and validated noninvasive monitoring such as donor derived cell free DNA.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNI-sparing/CNI-minimization maintenance immunosuppression to preserve renal function (slow eGFR decline/CKD) without losing rejection control.
- Heart-specific, evidence-based therapies for chronic/late antibody-mediated rejection and persistent donor-specific antibodies to prevent microvascular injury and graft dysfunction.
- Disease-modifying drugs to prevent or treat cardiac allograft vasculopathy (e.g., reduce coronary intimal thickening) to cut late graft failure/mortality.

name: Mycobacterium marinum infection
description: Mycobacterium marinum infection is a chronic, water associated skin and soft tissue infection that follows a cut exposed to contaminated water, often from aquariums, presenting weeks later with papulonodular upper limb lesions that may ulcerate and spread along lymphatics. Disease is usually localized but can involve tendons or joints and require surgery. Care is hampered by delayed diagnosis when routine cultures are negative and by the need for months of multi antibiotic therapy despite limited high quality trial data, creating demand for faster molecular confirmation and shorter, simpler regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course (weeks-not-months) oral regimen for localized cutaneous *M. marinum* that preserves cure rates vs current multi-month therapy
- Safer, low-monitoring alternative to ethambutol/macrolide/rifampin regimens (avoid vision/LFT monitoring and QT-risk constraints)
- Effective option for tetracycline-resistant and complicated/deep-structure infection to reduce failures/need for adjunctive surgery

name: Fibrosarcoma
description: Rare soft tissue sarcoma arising from fibrous connective tissue, often presenting late as a progressively enlarging lump that can cause pain or neurologic symptoms from compression. Care relies on surgery with radiation when feasible, but unresectable or metastatic disease is still treated largely with doxorubicin based chemotherapy where intensified combinations add toxicity without improving overall survival. Key unmet needs are more effective and better tolerated systemic options and reliable preoperative tumor shrinkage to enable functional resections, with targeted tropomyosin receptor kinase inhibitors relevant in ETV6–NTRK3 fusion infantile fibrosarcoma.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Better-tolerated 1L systemic therapy for unresectable/metastatic adult fibrosarcoma that improves outcomes beyond doxorubicin alone.
- Neoadjuvant tumor-shrinkage regimen for large/borderline-resectable extremity fibrosarcoma to increase limb-sparing surgery feasibility.
- Next-generation TRK inhibitor approaches for ETV6–NTRK3 fusion–positive infantile fibrosarcoma to overcome acquired on-target resistance (e.g., NTRK3 G623R).

name: Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy
description: Rare inherited adult-onset myopathy with progressive eyelid ptosis and dysphagia that can lead to malnutrition, choking, and aspiration pneumonia; care is largely supportive and procedure-based, leaving a major need for durable low-burden swallowing and ptosis treatments and PABPN1-directed disease-modifying therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- PABPN1-targeted disease-modifying therapy for genetically confirmed OPMD (including the 5–10% severe early-onset subgroup) to slow/stop ptosis+dysphagia progression and reduce aspiration/malnutrition risk.
- Durable, minimally invasive dysphagia therapy that sustains normal swallowing without repeat injections/surgery or recurrence, with objective swallow-imaging endpoints.
- Non-surgical/low-burden ptosis therapy providing sustained eyelid elevation without repeat operations and avoiding general anesthesia.

name: Hepatoblastoma
description: Hepatoblastoma is a rare malignant liver cancer of infants and toddlers, usually diagnosed before age 3, often noticed as a swollen belly or large abdominal mass with poor appetite, weight loss, and vomiting. Cure still hinges on cisplatin based chemotherapy followed by complete surgical removal or liver transplant, but only about 20 to 30 percent are resectable at diagnosis and up to 20 percent present with lung metastases where outcomes remain poor. Cisplatin can also cause lifelong hearing loss, and the main otoprotective option is labeled only for localized non metastatic disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemic therapies that reliably eradicate pulmonary metastases and reduce relapse in metastatic hepatoblastoma
- Hearing-sparing cisplatin regimens (otoprotection and/or non-ototoxic alternatives) that are safe to use in metastatic disease without compromising cure
- High-risk hepatoblastoma efficacy improvements without chemotherapy dose intensification and added toxicity

name: Aniridia
description: Aniridia is a rare congenital bilateral eye disorder, often from PAX6 haploinsufficiency, marked by partial or complete iris absence with early photophobia, nystagmus and reduced visual acuity from foveal hypoplasia. Vision typically worsens over time as cataracts, refractory glaucoma and common aniridia associated keratopathy from limbal stem cell deficiency drive progressive corneal opacification. Current care is high burden and largely symptomatic, with frequent lubrication and repeated procedures, leaving major unmet need for durable corneal surface disease modification, reliable pediatric intraocular pressure control and treatments that improve foveal development.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying corneal-surface therapy that halts early aniridia‑associated keratopathy progression by restoring/maintaining limbal epithelial stem‑cell function
- Vision-restorative therapy addressing PAX6/foveal hypoplasia to improve visual acuity and nystagmus (incl. genotype-directed options for nonsense mutations)
- Durable pediatric glaucoma therapy providing reliable long-term IOP control and reducing need for high-risk surgical escalation

name: Stiff-person syndrome
description: Stiff-person syndrome is a rare, progressive autoimmune neurologic disease, often antibody associated, marked by worsening axial and proximal limb rigidity and painful stimulus triggered spasms that impair gait and drive falls and avoidance behaviors. Current care relies on intravenous immunoglobulin plus high dose benzodiazepines and baclofen for symptom control, but sedation and incomplete or non durable long term responses leave major unmet need for better tolerated, durable disease modifying immunotherapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, progression-arresting immune therapy for treatment-refractory SPS that avoids IVIG “wear-off” rebound.
- Non-sedating control of stimulus-triggered spasms/falls to improve gait/ADLs without excessive sedation from current antispasmodics.
- IVIG-sparing options with comparable functional benefit but lower infusion burden and improved long-term safety/tolerability.

name: Synovial sarcoma
description: Synovial sarcoma is a rare soft tissue cancer in adolescents and young adults that often presents as a slowly enlarging, painless lump near a joint and is defined by the SS18 SSX t(X;18) translocation. It commonly spreads to the lungs, and advanced disease still relies on anthracycline based chemotherapy where intensified regimens add toxicity without improving overall survival. A first engineered T cell therapy is now available, but access is constrained by human leukocyte antigen A*02 subtype and melanoma associated antigen A4 expression, leaving many patients without durable, broadly applicable systemic control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable life‑prolonging systemic therapy for adults with advanced/metastatic synovial sarcoma
- Higher-response, longer-disease-control options for relapsed/refractory synovial sarcoma in ≥2L/≥3L settings with very low ORR/PFS/OS
- Broader-access, lower-toxicity alternatives to HLA/MAGE‑A4‑restricted engineered T‑cell therapy and inpatient doxorubicin/ifosfamide

name: Choroideremia
description: Rare inherited retinal degeneration mainly affecting males, starting with childhood night blindness and progressing through peripheral field loss and tunnel vision to blindness in late adulthood. Care is supportive only with no approved disease modifying therapy, and treatment development is constrained by challenging ocular delivery into a shrinking, fovea vulnerable target and by the need for sensitive functional and imaging endpoints to detect benefit before visual acuity declines.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-stage choroideremia treatment in adolescents/young adults with endpoints focused on slowing progression (microperimetry/OCT/autofluorescence) rather than ≥15-letter BCVA gains.
- Less invasive ocular delivery that avoids subretinal foveal detachment and reduces postoperative inflammation/immune burden while maintaining photoreceptor/RPE target engagement.
- Vision-restoration therapies for advanced/end-stage patients (NLP/BLP/CF/HM vision) with functional real-world endpoints (mobility, visual field, low-vision QoL).

name: Thymoma
description: Rare thymic epithelial tumor, often silent or presenting as an anterior mediastinal mass with cough, dyspnea, chest pain and frequent autoimmune overlap (myasthenia gravis in ~30–65%). Surgery anchors early disease, but years-long recurrence risk and limited systemic options leave a need for durable disease control in advanced and recurrent cases. Immunotherapy is constrained by high severe immune toxicity (grade ≥3 events reported in 71.4% of thymoma patients in a pembrolizumab phase 2 trial), and low tumor mutational burden complicates typical precision and immune strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, higher-response second-line (post–platinum) therapy for recurrent/metastatic thymoma where no standard of care exists beyond 1L.
- Immunotherapy/immune-modulating regimens that reduce severe irAEs (e.g., myocarditis/myositis/myasthenia gravis) in autoimmune-prone thymoma patients.
- Biomarker-/target-defined, chemo-sparing (ideally oral) therapies for thymoma subsets despite low TMB and few actionable genomic alterations.

name: Lymphoblastic lymphoma
description: Rare, fast growing lymphoma of immature lymphoid cells closely related to acute lymphoblastic leukemia, often in adolescents and young adults with a bulky anterior mediastinal mass causing respiratory symptoms. Standard care uses a long, intensive leukemia style regimen with about 24 months of induction, consolidation, and maintenance. The biggest gaps are poor outcomes after relapse and the toxicity burden of asparaginase heavy therapy, including frequent hepatotoxicity and thromboembolism, creating demand for more effective salvage and safer, potentially asparaginase sparing approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Relapsed/refractory T‑LBL therapies that drive deep CR rates far above today’s <15% salvage benchmark.
- Asparaginase-sparing or markedly safer asparaginase strategies for AYA ALL/LBL that cut hepatotoxicity (~35–60%) and thromboembolism (~15–20%) to prevent toxicity-driven under-dosing.
- Front-line novel agents that lower relapse risk while enabling shorter/less intensive regimens than ~24 months of leukemia-like therapy (without radiotherapy).

name: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 deficiency
description: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 deficiency is a rare inherited urea cycle disorder where the liver cannot clear nitrogen, causing sudden, life threatening hyperammonemia in newborns with rapid cerebral edema, seizures, coma, and high risk of permanent neurodevelopmental injury. Acute care depends on urgent intravenous ammonia scavengers and often dialysis, but treatment is invasive and risky, requiring central access and carrying extravasation injury hazards. Survivors face recurrent metabolic crises triggered by stress or dietary lapses plus lifelong protein restriction and disability. Only early liver transplantation provides durable metabolic correction, yet it cannot reverse established neurologic damage, leaving a premium on faster rescue and earlier liver targeted disease modification.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Peripheral-compatible “neonatal rescue” ammonia-lowering therapy to avert dialysis triggers (>500 μmol/L or non-response within 4 hours)
- Acute parenteral nitrogen-scavenging that avoids central-line–only administration and reduces extravasation injury (burns/skin necrosis)
- Durable liver-targeted CPS1 restoration (e.g., in vivo base editing) to increase protein tolerance and reduce/stop lifelong scavengers and restrictive diet burden

name: Appendix cancer
description: Appendix cancer is an extremely rare malignancy, typically diagnosed around ages 50 to 55 and often discovered incidentally during surgery such as appendicitis operations. Many cases disseminate within the abdomen and mucinous tumors can cause pseudomyxoma peritonei with progressive abdominal distension, pain, and pressure symptoms. Care relies on specialized cytoreductive surgery with heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy and colon cancer style systemic regimens, but there is no appendix specific systemic treatment playbook. Frequent GNAS and KRAS alterations and interest in less morbid regional delivery highlight the need for biomarker guided, disease modifying options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemic therapies that improve OS/PFS beyond current palliative chemo benchmarks in metastatic/unresectable appendiceal adenocarcinoma
- Biomarker-defined strategies (e.g., KRAS/RAS- and GNAS-driven disease) that outperform empiric fluoropyrimidine doublets and address limited EGFR-targeted options
- Non-surgical or less invasive treatments for peritoneal spread/PMP that reduce or replace CRS+HIPEC morbidity/recovery burden and avoid highly disruptive infusion logistics (e.g., 46-hour 5-FU pumps)

name: Myotonia congenita | Becker type
description: Becker type myotonia congenita is an autosomal recessive skeletal muscle chloride channelopathy caused by CLCN1 mutations, usually starting in childhood with leg predominant stiffness and delayed muscle relaxation that improves with repeated movement but leads to clumsiness and falls. Treatment is largely symptomatic and often relies on mexiletine, yet gastrointestinal intolerance and arrhythmia risk requiring electrocardiogram monitoring leave a need for safer, child friendly options that improve day to day function and reduce falls.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that reduce falls and muscle pain and improve real-world function/participation (work/school, home activities, community mobility), not just stiffness
- Anti-myotonia options with lower cardiac pro-arrhythmic risk/monitoring burden and improved GI tolerability vs mexiletine
- Pediatric-/adherence-friendly non-capsule formulations (e.g., syrup/drops) that improve swallowability/palatability and reduce dosing burden

name: Mismatch repair cancer syndrome
description: Constitutional mismatch repair deficiency is a rare inherited cancer predisposition where children develop aggressive early onset malignancies, especially high grade glioma or glioblastoma, leukemia or lymphoma, and colorectal cancer, often alongside neurofibromatosis type 1 like café au lait macules. Survivors face a near certainty of second primary cancers, creating a lifelong cycle of treatment and surveillance. Standard DNA damaging regimens can fail, with temozolomide notably ineffective in mismatch repair deficient brain tumors, raising the premium on durable brain penetrant therapies, immunotherapy enabled control, and credible prevention strategies that reduce new cancers rather than just detecting them earlier.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-penetrant, temozolomide-independent therapies that materially improve survival for pediatric CMMRD-associated high‑grade glioma
- Preventive/maintenance therapeutics that reduce metachronous new primary cancers (not just treat the index tumor)
- Lower-toxicity, lower-burden alternatives to repeated IV checkpoint inhibitor regimens while maintaining efficacy in hypermutated tumors

name: 17-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 3 deficiency
description: Rare inherited 46,XY difference of sex development caused by impaired testosterone synthesis, often presenting with female or ambiguous genitalia at birth and unexpected virilization at puberty with possible primary amenorrhea; care involves irreversible sex assignment decisions, lifelong hormone management with limited evidence, and persistent infertility, creating a need for better disease-modifying and puberty-guiding options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- HSD17B3 functional restoration (gene/mRNA/enzyme replacement) to normalize endogenous testosterone synthesis and improve fertility/paternity potential in 46,XY patients.
- Reversible pharmacologic prevention of pubertal androgenization/virilization for 46,XY individuals raised female.
- Lower-risk, lower-burden long-term sex-steroid replacement minimizing estrogen thromboembolism and testosterone erythrocytosis/hematocrit monitoring.

name: Bartholin gland cancer
description: Ultra-rare Bartholin gland vulvar cancer, typically in postmenopausal women, often first presenting as a unilateral lump misread as a benign cyst or inflammation. Diagnostic delay means many are stage III to IV at diagnosis, with nodal spread and a high risk of recurrence and distant metastasis. Treatment is constrained by scarce disease specific evidence and multiple histologies that likely require different systemic approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Effective systemic (palliative) therapy for metastatic/recurrent Bartholin gland adenocarcinoma that outperforms currently ineffective conventional regimens
- Recurrence-prevention (adjuvant/maintenance) drug strategies after upfront local therapy to reduce frequent distant metastatic relapse
- Biomarker-/histology-driven targeted and immunotherapy options (vs vulvar-cancer extrapolation), e.g., PTEN-loss→mTOR and CCND1-amplified→CDK4/6, and regimens improving on pembrolizumab’s ~10.9% ORR / ~2.1-month median PFS

name: 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency
description: Rare inherited leucine metabolism disorder often found on newborn screening; most patients remain asymptomatic, but some have fasting or illness triggered metabolic crises that can progress to seizures, coma, and death. Care is prevention focused with frequent feeding and supplements plus hospital based rescue during illness, yet it is not curative and cannot fully prevent morbidity, creating demand for reliable at home sick day rescue and enzyme restoring disease modifying therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- At-home sick-day rescue therapy (oral/SC) to prevent fasting/illness/high-protein–triggered metabolic crises and avoid ED IV dextrose + IV bicarbonate escalation
- Disease-modifying MCC enzyme–restoring therapy (gene/mRNA/enzyme/chaperone) for symptomatic/recurrent-crisis patients to normalize leucine-catabolism biomarkers and replace chronic diet/fasting avoidance/carnitine
- Chronic prophylaxis that increases safe fasting tolerance in infants/young children to prevent decompensation-related seizures/coma/brain injury

name: Acro-dermato-ungual-lacrimal-tooth syndrome
description: Ultra-rare autosomal dominant TP63-related ectodermal dysplasia present from birth, combining limb malformations with ectodermal defects of skin, hair, nails, teeth, and tear ducts. Patients face ectrodactyly or syndactyly, nail dysplasia, sparse frontal hair and freckling, lacrimal duct atresia or obstruction with conjunctivitis, and hypodontia or early tooth loss. Care is multispecialty and largely procedural or symptomatic, leaving unmet need for non-surgical tear duct approaches and regenerative or restorative options for teeth, hair, and nail function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drug-based, non-surgical control of lacrimal duct atresia/obstruction to reduce chronic tearing and dry-eye/blepharitis and avoid repeated procedures
- Tooth-regeneration therapy to enable eruption of missing permanent teeth in congenital hypodontia/oligodontia (vs dentures/implants)
- Therapy to restore sparse hair and nail dystrophy with measurable improvements in hair density and nail-plate integrity (vs cosmetic workarounds)

name: Adams-Oliver syndrome
description: Adams Oliver syndrome is a rare congenital disorder marked by scalp aplasia cutis and terminal limb or digit defects, often with broader vasculopathy including cardiac involvement and sometimes life threatening pulmonary hypertension. Management is largely supportive and reconstructive, with severe scalp and skull lesions prone to infection, hemorrhage and cerebrospinal fluid leak, and pulmonary hypertension frequently refractory to standard therapy. With no cure and no formal evidence based guidelines, there is strong unmet need for disease modifying approaches that improve wound regeneration and prevent vascular brain events such as stroke and thrombosis in high risk patients.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Topical/regenerative drug to accelerate healing of severe scalp aplasia cutis and reduce infection/catastrophic hemorrhage/CSF-leak risk (avoiding/reducing graft/flap surgery).
- Therapy to prevent/reverse refractory pulmonary hypertension in the small early-childhood AOS subgroup where standard PH drugs are often ineffective.
- Systemic anti-vasculopathy approach to lower intracranial stroke/thrombosis and fatal hemorrhage risk (e.g., NOTCH1-AOS high-risk patients).

name: Aicardi syndrome
description: Female-predominant neurodevelopmental disorder marked by corpus callosum malformation, chorioretinal lacunae, and infantile-onset spasms progressing to refractory epilepsy and severe lifelong disability; care is largely symptomatic, with seizure control often requiring multiple medication trials and burdened by intensive adrenocorticotropic hormone injections and vigabatrin’s permanent vision-risk, creating a need for safer, injection-sparing disease-modifying options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-life therapies that rapidly stop infantile spasms (EEG response) and prevent progression to multi-type medically refractory epilepsy, reducing need for polypharmacy.
- Steroid/ACTH-sparing first-line regimens for Aicardi-associated infantile spasms that match efficacy while avoiding systemic toxicities and IM injection burden.
- Vision-safe alternatives to vigabatrin (or approaches that markedly limit exposure) that maintain spasm control while avoiding permanent vision loss risk, REMS restrictions, and frequent eye-monitoring.

name: Alagille syndrome
description: Alagille syndrome is a rare inherited multisystem disorder, most often due to JAG1 variants, where too few intrahepatic bile ducts cause cholestasis and progressive liver injury. It typically presents in early infancy with jaundice, pale stools, dark urine, growth failure, fat soluble vitamin deficiencies and severe pruritus that can dominate family life. Care is symptomatic and often involves cycling through therapies with limited or waning itch relief, and there is no cure. Some children progress to fibrosis, portal hypertension, or severe liver or heart disease requiring transplantation, driving demand for better tolerated early life disease modifying treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, deeper pruritus control that normalizes sleep/HRQoL in patients with persistent severe itch
- Disease-modifying liver therapy that improves native-liver survival and prevents portal hypertension/transplant
- Earlier-infant and better-tolerated cholestasis/pruritus therapy (incl. <3 months and <12 months) with fewer GI AEs and no worsening of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency/liver injury risk

name: Åland Island eye disease
description: Very rare X-linked CACNA1F-related retinal disorder presenting in infancy with reduced visual acuity from foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus, astigmatism, impaired dark adaptation and color vision defects, and progressive axial myopia. Management is limited to optical correction, leaving major unmet need for disease modifying retinal therapies and better pediatric control of myopia progression; gene based approaches are promising but constrained by CACNA1F’s large size exceeding single adeno associated virus vector capacity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CACNA1F gene-corrective retinal therapy (gene replacement/editing) to improve visual acuity and dark adaptation beyond optical correction
- Pediatric pharmacotherapy to slow axial-length elongation and prevent progressive axial myopia (vs refractive correction only)
- Pediatric-safe nystagmus-damping drug to increase foveation time and improve best-corrected visual acuity with better tolerability

name: Alexander disease
description: Alexander disease is an ultra rare glial fibrillary acidic protein driven leukodystrophy where Rosenthal fiber buildup in astrocytes disrupts myelin, often starting in infancy with megalencephaly, seizures, developmental delay, and spasticity and progressing to bulbar dysfunction, dysphagia, ataxia, vomiting, and loss of motor function. Care is largely supportive with no cure, leaving a major need for disease modifying therapies that lower glial fibrillary acidic protein and preserve neurologic and autonomic function, with antisense approaches already in Phase 3 testing.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- GFAP-lowering disease-modifying therapy to alter progression/survival in severe early-onset (neonatal) Alexander disease
- Drugs that improve bulbar dysfunction (swallowing/speech) plus GI and autonomic symptom burden beyond supportive care
- Better-tolerated, less burdensome long-term symptomatic regimens that reduce polypharmacy while improving objective function (e.g., gait/gross motor)

name: Alkhumra hemorrhagic fever
description: Alkhumra hemorrhagic fever is a rare, sometimes deadly tick borne viral disease in Saudi Arabia and Egypt linked to livestock exposure. It starts with flu like illness and can progress to cytopenias, liver injury, bleeding, encephalitis, coma, and multi organ failure. With no known person to person spread, the biggest clinical gap is not containment but care. Treatment remains supportive only, leaving high stakes unmet needs for rapid diagnosis, early outpatient antivirals, intensive care rescue options such as antivirals or antibodies, and post exposure prophylaxis for high risk animal and tick exposures.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early (ideally oral) antiviral for suspected AHF to prevent progression to encephalitis and reduce hospitalized mortality.
- Rapidly acting inpatient antiviral/neutralizing biologic for severe AHF to reduce ICU-level supportive measures and shorten hospital stay.
- Post-exposure prophylaxis (oral antiviral or long-acting antibody) for high-risk tick/livestock/raw-meat/unpasteurized-milk exposures and lab incidents.

name: Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome
description: Allan Herndon Dudley syndrome is an ultra rare X linked neurodevelopmental disorder caused by MCT8 thyroid hormone transporter failure that leaves the brain functionally thyroid hormone deficient while peripheral tissues are hyperthyroid. Boys present in infancy with hypotonia and feeding problems, then develop profound intellectual disability and severe motor dysfunction with dystonia and often drug resistant seizures, alongside failure to thrive and tachycardia. Injury begins prenatally with persistent hypomyelination, making deficits hard to reverse. Current care is largely supportive and thyroid lab focused, with limited evidence of neurocognitive benefit, creating a premium on very early diagnosis and brain targeted, disease modifying approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Increase thyroid hormone action in the brain to deliver measurable neurodevelopment gains (e.g., GMFM‑88/Bayley/HINE) without worsening peripheral thyrotoxicosis.
- Prenatal/neonatal “critical window” interventions (including in‑utero strategies) to prevent fetal-stage brain injury and persistent hypomyelination.
- Genotype-stratified MCT8-restoring therapies (pharmacologic chaperones and/or brain-directed gene therapy) to overcome inconsistent benefit/safety limits of conventional thyroid regimens.

name: Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome
description: Alpers Huttenlocher syndrome is a severe POLG related mitochondrial disorder with onset around ages 2 to 4 in previously healthy children, progressing rapidly to intractable seizures, psychomotor regression, and liver failure, with death often within about four years. Care is largely supportive and frequently becomes palliative, with limited options for seizure control and important safety constraints such as avoiding valproic acid due to hepatotoxicity. Advanced disease can require feeding tubes and long term ventilatory support, underscoring the need for disease modifying therapies targeting mitochondrial DNA replication and liver sparing anti seizure regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- POLG/mtDNA-replication restoration in POLG1-mutant infants/toddlers to prevent/delay refractory seizures + psychomotor regression + hepatopathy and extend survival beyond supportive/palliative care.
- Liver-safe, mitochondria-safe anti-seizure therapy reducing observable motor seizures per 28 days and status epilepticus recurrence while avoiding valproate/divalproex-associated hepatic injury.
- Therapy that reduces disease-related hospital/ICU utilization and delays progression to feeding tube + long-term tracheostomy/mechanical ventilation dependence, improving caregiver QoL.

name: Aicardi-Goutières syndrome
description: Aicardi Goutières syndrome is a rare inherited neuroinflammatory interferon driven disorder where aberrant nucleic acid sensing triggers immune attack on brain white matter, causing early infantile encephalopathy with irritability, sterile fevers, seizures, developmental regression, and permanent brain damage. Care is largely supportive with no cure, so the key unmet need is early, central nervous system active, safer suppression of the interferon pathway to prevent irreversible neurodevelopmental injury.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-active therapy that meaningfully improves/stabilizes neurodevelopmental outcomes (e.g., AGS Scale) beyond current JAK inhibitors’ limited neurologic impact.
- Presymptomatic intervention in genetically identified infants that prevents/delays clinical onset despite early interferon activation.
- Safer, upstream interferon-signature suppression (ideally genotype-targeted) that reduces reliance on chronic boxed-warning JAK inhibition and intensive lab monitoring.

name: Andersen-Tawil syndrome
description: Andersen Tawil syndrome is a rare inherited potassium channel disorder, often due to KCNJ2 variants affecting Kir2.1, causing childhood onset episodes of periodic paralysis alongside ventricular arrhythmias including long QT and characteristic dysmorphic or developmental features. Patients may recover between attacks but can accumulate permanent weakness, while cardiac risk persists. Care is largely symptomatic and individualized, with drugs for weakness and rhythm control that can conflict because some cardiac agents worsen muscle symptoms. No standardized guidelines or reliably effective antiarrhythmic therapy exist, creating demand for safer rhythm suppression and disease modifying approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Kir2.1/KCNJ2-targeted therapy for the ~60% with KCNJ2 mutations to reduce both periodic paralysis and ventricular arrhythmias
- Safer, consistently effective ventricular ectopy/VT suppression that reduces 24h ectopy burden and prevents tachycardia-related dilated cardiomyopathy without worsening neuromuscular symptoms
- Disease-modifying neuromuscular therapy to prevent progression to permanent/fixed weakness with more reliable attack prevention than acetazolamide and reduced need for daily potassium supplements

name: Arboleda-Tham syndrome
description: Arboleda Tham syndrome, also called KAT6A syndrome, is an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder driven by heterozygous KAT6A mutations with near universal, typically severe speech delay. Infants often have hypotonia and major feeding problems that can require tube feeding. Reflux and severe constipation reflect intestinal motility dysfunction with meaningful obstruction risk. Sleep disturbance is common and melatonin is sometimes suggested. There are no approved disease specific therapies today, so care stays symptomatic and families often depend on augmentative communication plus intensive gastrointestinal and sleep management.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- KAT6A-pathway disease-modifying therapy that measurably improves the core, persistent expressive communication disability (minimally verbal/non-speaking → functional speech/AAC independence)
- Pediatric-friendly GI motility/feeding pharmacotherapy that reduces NG-feeding need, chronic laxative dependence, and obstruction-risk presentations from severe constipation/reflux
- Sleep-initiation/maintenance therapy beyond melatonin that improves sleep while avoiding next-day impairment in a neurodevelopmentally vulnerable pediatric population

name: Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome
description: Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome is a rare congenital anterior eye development disorder, typically recognized in infancy or childhood with iris and pupil malformations, photophobia, and sometimes dental or other systemic abnormalities. About half develop glaucoma later, but care is largely reactive since eye drops often fail and many children require repeated surgeries, making durable long term pediatric intraocular pressure control and gene informed prevention key unmet needs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-targeted early intervention to prevent/delay glaucoma in ARS children (esp. PITX2/FOXC1-driven disease)
- Pediatric glaucoma drugs that deliver durable IOP control in ARS without requiring surgery
- Adjunct anti-fibrotic/wound-healing therapies to reduce scarring and improve long-term success of trabeculectomy/tube surgery in ARS

name: B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia
description: B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia is a very rare, typically aggressive mature B-cell leukemia of older adults, often presenting with massive splenomegaly, extreme lymphocytosis, and frequent cytopenias. High-risk biology including frequent TP53 or p53 abnormalities drives resistance and short-lived responses, and care is built on non-standardized regimens borrowed from chronic lymphocytic leukemia, sometimes requiring highly immunosuppressive options. Better tolerated, chemo-free targeted therapies that deliver deep, durable remissions remain the central unmet need.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Chemo‑free targeted regimens effective in the high‑risk TP53‑aberrant majority and capable of MRD‑negative durable remissions
- TP53‑abnormal disease control without alemtuzumab‑level immunosuppression/infection and cytopenia burden
- Lower‑burden outpatient (e.g., oral/fixed‑duration) options that avoid q28d infusion chemo‑immunotherapy while rapidly controlling splenomegaly and extreme lymphocytosis

name: Bardet-Biedl syndrome
description: Bardet Biedl syndrome is a rare inherited ciliopathy causing childhood onset multisystem disease marked by early weight gain, polydactyly, progressive retinal degeneration leading to legal blindness by adolescence or early adulthood, and potentially life threatening kidney abnormalities. Management is largely supportive and symptomatic, leaving major unmet need for disease modifying retinal and renal therapies and more effective, durable control of obesity and its metabolic complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Vision-preserving retinal therapy for genetically defined BBS subgroups (e.g., BBS1) to slow rod–cone dystrophy and delay legal blindness.
- Renal-protective disease-modifying therapy for BBS patients with early CKD to prevent progression to kidney failure/ESKD.
- Lower-burden, better-tolerated obesity/hyperphagia therapy vs setmelanotide (avoid daily refrigerated injections; reduce hyperpigmentation/injection-site reactions/nausea-vomiting and mood-risk monitoring).

name: Barre-Lieou syndrome
description: Barré Liéou syndrome (posterior cervical sympathetic syndrome) is a disputed clinical entity defined by occipital headaches with dizziness or vertigo, tinnitus, and sometimes visual symptoms, often triggered by neck movement and historically attributed to cervical sympathetic irritation from cervical arthrosis. With no firmly established etiology, biomarkers, or evidence based treatment, care is largely symptomatic using physical therapy, traction or bracing, medications, and sometimes invasive sympathetic blocks, yet many patients remain refractory, creating demand for safer, durable, noninvasive options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Evidence-based oral/non-procedural therapy that meaningfully reduces the hallmark symptom cluster (occipital headache + head-turn–provoked dizziness/vertigo with tinnitus/reading-limiting visual complaints) in cervical arthritis/spondylosis or post–neck-injury patients.
- Non-invasive alternative to sympathetic blocks/cervical epidural injections with comparable relief but avoiding procedural risks (incl. rare life-threatening events).
- Durable at-home therapy that reduces dependence on multi-week PT/traction/brace regimens and repeat outpatient procedures.

name: Barth syndrome
description: Barth syndrome is an ultra rare X linked mitochondrial disorder in boys, usually presenting in infancy with cardiomyopathy, skeletal muscle weakness, growth delay and neutropenia that drives life threatening heart failure and bacterial infections. Care has largely been symptomatic, often requiring chronic granulocyte colony stimulating factor and intensive cardiac management, and even after the first FDA approved therapy in September 2025 a major gap remains for the most fragile infants and small children because labeling is limited to patients weighing 30 kilograms or more.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Infant-eligible disease-modifying therapy that prevents/reverses early cardiomyopathy/heart-failure mortality (incl. <30 kg/neonates)
- Neutropenia + infection–preventive therapy that reduces pneumonia/sepsis risk and G-CSF dependence
- Oral (or otherwise less burdensome than daily SC injection) mitochondrial/cardiolipin-remodeling therapy to improve fatigue/exercise intolerance and cardioskeletal function

name: Bernard-Soulier syndrome
description: Bernard Soulier syndrome is an ultra rare inherited platelet adhesion disorder caused by loss of the glycoprotein Ib IX V receptor, leading to lifelong macrothrombocytopenia and mucocutaneous bleeding such as bruising, epistaxis, and heavy menstrual bleeding. Care is largely supportive with antifibrinolytics and platelet transfusions for surgery and childbirth, but repeated transfusions can trigger antibodies, refractoriness, and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia risk. The unmet need is durable transfusion independent haemostasis, with interest in one time gene correction of hematopoietic stem cells to restore receptor function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Transfusion-independent hemostasis for major bleeds/procedures in BSS patients with HLA/HPA alloimmunization and platelet refractoriness (including HLA-matched platelet failures)
- Standardizable pregnancy/childbirth and heavy menstrual bleeding prophylaxis that reduces high-frequency platelet support while minimizing maternal/fetal alloimmune complications
- One-time disease-correcting autologous stem-cell gene therapy restoring platelet GPIb-IX-V function to replace lifelong episodic supportive care

name: Bethlem myopathy
description: Bethlem myopathy is a mild collagen VI related muscular dystrophy with early hypotonia and decades long, slowly progressive proximal weakness plus accumulating joint contractures that erode mobility and can lead to later respiratory muscle weakness. Management is supportive with stretching and physical therapy, orthopedic contracture care, and nocturnal ventilation when needed. No disease modifying therapy exists, leaving a need to preserve ambulation, prevent or reverse contractures, and protect long term respiratory function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Mobility-preserving therapy that slows progressive proximal weakness to maintain independent outdoor ambulation and delay walking-aid dependence
- Anti-fibrotic/anti-contracture drug to prevent or reverse adult-onset joint contractures (fingers/elbows/shoulders/ankles/Achilles) and preserve range of motion
- Respiratory-protective therapy that prevents late-onset respiratory muscle weakness to stabilize pulmonary function and delay nocturnal hypoventilation/BiPAP need

name: Blau syndrome
description: Ultra-rare, NOD2-driven autoinflammatory granulomatous disease of early childhood causing dermatitis, boggy arthritis, and often uveitis that can progress to vision loss and joint destruction; current care relies on steroids, immunosuppressants, and biologics but remains inconsistent, creating a need for early steroid-sparing, targeted control that preserves vision and prevents irreversible joint damage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, vision-preserving control of Blau uveitis in the ~60–70% with persistent active uveitis/arthritis despite steroids, immunosuppressants, and biologics.
- Early disease-modifying therapy that prevents progressive granulomatous arthritis from progressing to irreversible joint contractures.
- Steroid-sparing, pediatric-tolerable long-term immunomodulation with simpler administration and lower monitoring burden than chronic multi-agent regimens.

name: Bloch-Sulzberger syndrome
description: Incontinentia pigmenti (Bloch Sulzberger syndrome) is an X linked dominant IKBKG related disorder, usually in girls, with neonatal skin lesions that evolve through staged rashes along Blaschko lines and potentially serious eye and central nervous system involvement. The highest impact is in infancy when retinal neovascular disease and brain vasculopathy can cause vision loss, stroke, seizures, and later neurodevelopmental impairment. Care is largely supportive with screening and ablative eye procedures, leaving a major unmet need for infant safe disease modifying approaches that prevent retinal and neurologic injury.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Long-acting, infant-safe therapy to prevent retinal neovascularization and retinal detachment (vs repeated screening and ablative laser/cryotherapy).
- Early-life vascular-stabilizing/neuroprotective therapy to reduce first-year stroke and seizure morbidity (beyond symptomatic seizure management).
- Steroid-/tacrolimus-sparing topical anti-inflammatory to rapidly control neonatal vesicular lesions and prevent secondary blister infections.

name: Bosch-Boonstra-Schaaf optic atrophy syndrome
description: Bosch Boonstra Schaaf optic atrophy syndrome is an ultra rare NR2F1 related neurodevelopmental disorder that begins in infancy with hypotonia and feeding oromotor dysfunction and is often recognized in early childhood after nystagmus strabismus or poor fixation, alongside developmental delay or intellectual disability and epilepsy. Care is supportive with no cure and seizures are treated with non specific anti seizure drugs, leaving major unmet need for disease modifying therapies that preserve optic nerve and cerebral visual function and improve neurodevelopmental and seizure outcomes, as well as earlier diagnosis and intervention.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- NR2F1 function–restoring therapy to improve optic nerve abnormalities/optic atrophy and meaningfully increase visual function.
- Treatment that reduces DD/ID by accelerating delayed motor and speech milestones.
- Syndrome-specific anti-seizure therapy to better prevent/control epilepsy (incl. infantile spasms) than non-specific ASMs.

name: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay
description: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix Saguenay is a progressive childhood onset neurodegenerative movement disorder where toddlers develop gait unsteadiness that evolves into cerebellar ataxia, lower limb spasticity, and peripheral neuropathy, with many becoming wheelchair dependent in adulthood. Care is supportive rather than disease modifying, leaving a major unmet need for therapies that slow or halt neuron loss and preserve mobility and function. Gene restoration is an emerging direction but full length sacsin is too large for standard delivery, driving interest in mini gene approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying SACS restoration (e.g., gene replacement/editing, incl. AAV “mini‑gene/minisacsin”) started early to slow SARA progression and delay loss of ambulation/wheelchair dependence.
- Axonal/peripheral-nerve–directed neuroprotective therapy to prevent/reverse sensory loss and weakness beyond today’s supportive/spasticity-focused care.
- Better-tolerated, lower-burden symptomatic drugs for pediatric spasticity/bladder dysfunction with less sedation/weakness and anticholinergic effects and reduced multi-dose/procedure burden.

name: Brooke-Spiegler syndrome
description: Brooke Spiegler syndrome (CYLD cutaneous syndrome) is an inherited disorder causing multiple benign appendage skin tumors starting in late childhood or the teens, often on the scalp and face, that accumulate and recur, leading to disfigurement, pain, and psychological burden. Management relies on repeated local procedures with scarring and incomplete control, and there is no curative or disease modifying therapy; occasional malignant transformation and involvement of sensory structures increase clinical risk, creating demand for scalable field treatments that prevent new tumors and reduce procedure burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease‑modifying medical therapy to reduce/prevent new tumor formation and avoid lifelong repeated procedures
- Topical/home “field” therapy that safely treats many small lesions without scarring/large defects and achieves objective lesion response
- Systemic therapy for patients with malignant transformation (e.g., cylindrocarcinoma/spiradenocarcinoma) where surgery alone may be insufficient

name: Brown-Sequard syndrome
description: Rare incomplete spinal cord injury from a one sided cord lesion, usually traumatic, causing ipsilateral weakness and loss of vibration and position sense with contralateral loss of pain and temperature below the lesion, sometimes with bowel bladder dysfunction. Care is supportive with no specific treatment, leaving a premium on neuroprotective or neuroregenerative approaches and better tolerated options for neuropathic pain and spasticity that avoid sedation, fatigue, and monitoring burdens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute neuroprotective/neuroregenerative drug for traumatic incomplete hemicord SCI to improve neurologic + functional recovery on endpoints like ISNCSCI motor score and ambulation measures (Walk Test/SCI‑FAI/LEMS).
- Non-sedating neuropathic-pain therapy for at/below-level SCI pain that is often refractory, reducing dizziness/somnolence discontinuations vs gabapentinoids/SNRIs.
- Spasticity therapy that improves function while avoiding sedation/weakness and reducing hypotension and liver-monitoring burden seen with current oral antispasmodics.

name: Cogan syndrome
description: Rare autoimmune disease affecting eyes and inner ears, typically in young adults, causing interstitial keratitis and rapid Meniere-like vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss that can progress to deafness within 1 to 3 months; may involve aortitis/large-vessel vasculitis. Steroids are first line but 37 to 54 percent have persistent hearing loss, leaving major unmet need for faster hearing preservation, steroid sparing durable control, and cardiovascular protection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute (≤2 weeks) hearing-preservation therapy that reduces the ~50% residual risk of permanent hearing loss despite treatment
- Steroid-sparing, durable disease control for refractory/steroid-dependent patients to enable prednisone taper and avoid long-term steroid toxicities
- Targeted therapy to prevent/treat systemic vasculitis—especially cardiovascular aortitis/aortic insufficiency—in patients with systemic involvement

name: Budd-Chiari syndrome
description: Budd Chiari syndrome is hepatic venous outflow obstruction that traps blood in the liver, causing liver injury and portal hypertension with abdominal pain and progressive ascites and later variceal bleeding. Treatment escalates from lifelong anticoagulation to angioplasty, transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt, or transplant, but medication rarely recanalizes hepatic veins and chronic anticoagulation adds substantial bleeding and monitoring burden. Unmet needs include safer lower burden anticoagulation, pharmacologic vein reopening, and targeted treatment of underlying prothrombotic drivers such as myeloproliferative neoplasms.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer, lower-burden long-term anticoagulation for portal-hypertension/variceal patients (reduced bleeding risk; avoid PT/INR monitoring)
- Pharmacologic recanalization of hepatic venous outflow to prevent progression to angioplasty/TIPS
- Etiology-targeted therapy for the common MPN/JAK2 subgroup to reduce recurrent thrombosis beyond indefinite anticoagulation

name: Burkitt lymphoma
description: Burkitt lymphoma is a rare, highly aggressive MYC driven B cell non Hodgkin lymphoma that often presents suddenly with rapidly progressive extranodal masses such as bulky abdominal disease and can spread to the central nervous system. Cure is possible but treatment is an inpatient emergency requiring months of intensive, toxicity heavy chemotherapy and routine spinal central nervous system prophylaxis. The biggest gaps are safer regimens for older or comorbid adults, and effective chemotherapy sparing options for relapse where choices are few and outcomes worsen.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Chemo-free (or markedly reduced-chemo) salvage therapies that achieve durable remissions in relapsed/refractory Burkitt lymphoma
- Curative-intent first-line regimens for adult/older/comorbid patients that reduce acute toxicity (e.g., severe infections) and inpatient hospitalization burden vs dose-intensive chemo
- Systemic CNS-active therapies that reduce CNS involvement risk while eliminating routine intrathecal methotrexate prophylaxis (4–6 injections)

name: Buruli ulcer disease
description: Buruli ulcer is a chronic toxin mediated skin infection caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans that often begins as a painless nodule or plaque but can progress to extensive tissue destruction, sometimes involving bone, with permanent disfigurement and disability, disproportionately affecting children in rural sub Saharan Africa. Treatment still requires an 8 week antibiotic course plus prolonged wound care, physiotherapy, and often surgery, with recovery taking up to a year and creating major household financial strain. Paradoxical inflammatory worsening can mimic relapse, underscoring the need for shorter, simpler oral regimens that speed durable re epithelialization.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ≤2–4 week (vs 8-week) simplified oral antibiotic regimens achieving complete lesion healing by 52 weeks without relapse and/or surgery, especially for children in remote rural Africa
- Adjunct/novel drugs that accelerate re-epithelialization to reduce prolonged wound-care/debridement/skin-grafting burden and scarring/contracture disability
- Adjunct therapies to prevent/treat paradoxical reactions (8–12%) to shorten time-to-heal and avoid misclassification as treatment failure

name: Buschke-Ollendorff syndrome
description: Rare, usually benign autosomal dominant skin and bone connective tissue disorder with childhood connective tissue nevi and often asymptomatic osteopoikilosis, but frequent diagnostic delay. A subset develops melorheostosis with chronic pain, contractures, limited mobility, and possible orthopedic surgery needs. Care is largely symptomatic, with short-lived pain control and no proven disease-modifying therapy, driving interest in mutation-matched pathway targeting such as MEK1 inhibition in MAP2K1-mutant lesions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Mutation-matched, better-tolerated MEK-pathway inhibition for MAP2K1-positive melorheostosis to slow hyperostosis and reduce chronic pain
- Longer-acting RANKL/bone-turnover modulation to provide months-long pain control vs short-lived (~2-month) denosumab benefit
- Early disease-modifying therapy to prevent irreversible contractures/ROM loss and pediatric limb-length discrepancy in BOS patients with melorheostosis

name: Crigler-Najjar syndrome
description: Crigler Najjar syndrome is a rare inherited failure of hepatic bilirubin clearance caused by UGT1A1 deficiency, presenting with severe neonatal jaundice and risk of kernicterus with irreversible brain injury. Families often rely on 10 to 12 hours a day of phototherapy to control unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and in the most severe form liver transplant remains the only curative option. The central unmet need is rapid, reliable bilirubin control in newborns and durable disease modification that avoids lifelong phototherapy and the risks and constraints of transplantation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Phototherapy-eliminating bilirubin control for severe CNS-I (complete UGT1A1 deficiency).
- Non-transplant definitive disease-modifying therapy for CNS-I to avoid liver-transplant morbidity/cost and lifelong immunosuppression.
- Rapid neonatal rescue bilirubin-lowering (first ~2 weeks) to prevent neurodangerous bilirubin levels and reduce need for exchange transfusion.

name: CD40 ligand deficiency
description: CD40 ligand deficiency (X-linked hyper IgM syndrome) is a rare X-linked primary immunodeficiency in boys where impaired CD40L signaling blocks antibody class switching, causing low IgG, IgA, and IgE with normal or high IgM and early recurrent and opportunistic infections, diarrhea, poor growth, and sometimes neutropenia. Management is largely lifelong immunoglobulin replacement and antimicrobial prophylaxis, with hematopoietic stem cell transplantation the only established cure but limited by timing, access, and risk. Major unmet needs are safer, more accessible durable immune reconstitution and better prevention or eradication of Cryptosporidium to avoid progressive hepatobiliary disease, cirrhosis, and cancer.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable physiologic CD40LG/CD40L pathway restoration enabling discontinuation of chronic Ig replacement and reducing residual opportunistic infection/cancer risk
- Effective Cryptosporidium prophylaxis/eradication to prevent biliary tract disease and sclerosing cholangitis
- Lower-toxicity curative immune reconstitution options for patients who are poor HSCT candidates (e.g., older age, organ damage/severe liver disease, limited donors)

name: Camurati-Engelmann disease
description: Rare inherited sclerosing bone disorder with progressive long bone and skull hyperostosis, usually starting in childhood or early adolescence, causing severe limb pain, proximal muscle weakness, fatigue, and gait impairment; skull base thickening can compress cranial nerves leading to headaches, hearing or vision loss, vertigo, tinnitus, and facial paralysis. Care is largely symptomatic with corticosteroids and analgesics, but long term steroid toxicity and limited evidence for steroid sparing options leave a major unmet need for durable disease modifying control and prevention of neurologic complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- TGFB1-pathway control to prevent/reverse skull-base hyperostosis and avert cranial-nerve compression (hearing/vision deficits, facial paralysis)
- Steroid-sparing long-term control of pain/weakness and mobility in pediatric/teen-onset CED to reduce osteoporosis/fracture risk and monitoring burden
- More reliable, evidence-based relief of severe limb pain and functional impairment in patients refractory to NSAIDs + glucocorticoids (± variable losartan response)

name: Canavan disease
description: Canavan disease is a rare inherited leukodystrophy where impaired breakdown of N-acetylaspartic acid disrupts brain myelin, with infants often normal at birth then developing hypotonia, macrocephaly, feeding and swallowing problems and seizures by 3 to 5 months. Care is largely supportive with no cure, leaving a premium on early, durable disease modification. Gene therapy is an active frontier, but progress is constrained by invasive central nervous system delivery and immune responses that can limit redosing and require immunosuppression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Presymptomatic/early-infant ASPA restoration achieving sustained urine/brain NAA reduction and MRI myelination gains with meaningful motor/neurodevelopmental improvement (e.g., GMFM-88, Bayley-4/Mullen).
- Efficacy in patients treated after typical (late) diagnosis/progression, including those currently excluded from trials due to advanced neurologic features/refractory seizures.
- Lower-burden, safer delivery expanding eligibility by avoiding neurosurgical administration, immunosuppression constraints, and anti-AAV9 antibody screen-outs.

name: Capgras syndrome
description: Capgras syndrome is a delusional misidentification in which a person believes a close familiar, often a spouse, has been replaced by an identical impostor. In dementia with Lewy bodies it often co-occurs with visual hallucinations and anxiety and drives high caregiver burden. Care is adapted from Lewy body dementia psychosis management using cholinesterase inhibitors and very cautious antipsychotics, but neuroleptic sensitivity can worsen cognition, sedation, and parkinsonism and in rare cases cause fatal neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Clozapine adds frequent blood monitoring, leaving a need for safer, low-burden outpatient options that reduce delusions and agitation without dopamine blockade.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer anti-delusional therapy for Capgras-in-DLB/LBD that improves hallucinations+delusions while avoiding DLB neuroleptic sensitivity and dementia-related psychosis mortality risk
- Capgras-in-DLB phenotype–targeted treatment reducing hallucinations/anxiety-driven fear/aggression and lowering caregiver burden (e.g., NPI-Q caregiver distress, Zarit burden)
- Lower-burden outpatient option that avoids clozapine-like ANC monitoring/infrastructure and improves real-world persistence/cost

name: Carney complex
description: Carney complex is a rare inherited multisystem tumor syndrome that typically emerges in the teens or early adulthood with progressive skin lentigines, recurrent cardiac myxomas, and endocrine tumors or overactivity. Cardiac tumors can obstruct blood flow or embolize and may be life threatening, while adrenal disease can cause cortisol excess and Cushing syndrome that often leads to bilateral adrenalectomy. Management is largely lifelong surveillance plus repeated organ specific surgeries and symptomatic treatment, since no etiologic therapy exists, creating a major unmet need for disease modifying options that reduce tumor recurrence, endocrine morbidity, and monitoring burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adrenal-sparing medical control of PPNAD Cushing syndrome (durable cortisol/UFC normalization) to avoid bilateral adrenalectomy and improve on unsafe/monitoring-heavy steroidogenesis inhibitors.
- Pharmacologic prevention of recurrent cardiac myxomas (reduce recurrence up to ~22%) to avoid repeat open-heart resections and lifelong 6–12 month imaging.
- Systemic, pathway-targeted therapy for PRKAR1A/PKA-driven multi-tumor burden to reduce the “treat each tumor separately” paradigm and intensive lifelong multi-organ surveillance.

name: Caroli disease
description: Caroli disease is a rare congenital disorder with non obstructive cystic dilation of the intrahepatic bile ducts that causes bile stasis, stones and recurrent bacterial cholangitis with fever, abdominal pain and jaundice, often diagnosed before age 30. In Caroli syndrome, associated congenital hepatic fibrosis leads to portal hypertension and progressive liver failure, and chronic inflammation raises cholangiocarcinoma risk. Management is largely supportive with ursodeoxycholic acid, antibiotics and endoscopic or surgical procedures, while liver transplantation is the only curative option, underscoring unmet needs for durable infection and stone prevention, antifibrotic disease modification and cancer risk reduction.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Preventive, non-antibiotic therapy to reduce recurrent cholangitis episodes and hepatolithiasis/stone-driven obstruction (reducing ERCP/antibiotic use).
- Anti-fibrotic / portal-hypertension–modifying drugs for Caroli syndrome (type II) to delay cirrhosis and variceal complications.
- Chemopreventive/targeted therapy to reduce elevated cholangiocarcinoma risk in Caroli disease/syndrome.

name: Ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-cleft lip/palate syndrome
