description: Ectrodactyly ectodermal dysplasia cleft lip and palate syndrome is a rare genetic disorder present at birth, marked by split hand or foot malformations, cleft lip or palate, and ectodermal defects of skin, hair, nails, teeth, and glands. Care is largely symptom directed, while progressive ocular surface disease from limbal stem cell deficiency can lead to vision loss or blindness. Exocrine gland dysfunction drives severe dental decay, dry mouth, and poor heat tolerance, leaving major unmet need for vision preserving ocular reconstruction and therapies that restore gland function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Vision-preserving ocular therapy for EEC ocular surface disease/limbal stem cell deficiency beyond lubrication/surgery
- Xerostomia-targeted therapy to restore salivary function and reduce severe dental caries
- Thermoregulation therapy to prevent hypohidrosis-driven hyperthermia (pediatric focus)

name: Ebstein anomaly
description: Rare congenital tricuspid valve malformation with displaced leaflets causing tricuspid regurgitation, right-sided chamber enlargement, cyanosis or heart failure in severe newborns, and later exercise intolerance and arrhythmias. Care is largely intensive neonatal stabilization, surgery, and individualized rhythm management, with limited evidence for right-ventricle–targeted medical benefit, leaving unmet needs for safer neonatal support and more durable, better-tolerated arrhythmia control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer, less resource-intensive neonatal stabilization to reduce pulmonary vascular resistance/hypoxemia and support pulmonary blood flow in cyanotic/heart-failure neonates
- Better-tolerated long-term rhythm control for frequent atrial tachyarrhythmias/accessory-pathway (WPW) disease, minimizing reliance on higher-risk antiarrhythmics
- Right-heart-failure/RV-dysfunction–focused medical therapy beyond symptomatic diuretics/GDMT to improve exercise tolerance and reduce HF decompensations

name: Carrion's disease
description: Carrion’s disease is a neglected sandfly borne Bartonella bacilliformis infection endemic to Andean valleys that can present as acute Oroya fever with severe hemolytic anemia and high untreated mortality or progress to chronic angioproliferative verruga peruana skin lesions. It disproportionately harms children and other vulnerable groups in low resource settings, where treatment relies on antibiotics but optimal regimens are poorly defined and emerging resistance threatens efficacy, driving need for child safe oral options that clear persistent bacteremia and reduce transfusion intensive care.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer, resistance-robust acute-phase (Oroya fever) therapy for children/teens that lowers residual mortality and covers common coinfections without high-toxicity legacy agents
- Sterilizing/curative regimens that eradicate the intraerythrocytic reservoir to prevent persistent bacteremia, relapse, and progression to verruga peruana
- Oral-only or long-acting outpatient regimens that avoid IV antibiotics and transfusion-intensive management in low-infrastructure settings

name: Carvajal syndrome
description: Ultra-rare inherited cardiocutaneous disorder marked by woolly scalp hair from birth and early palmoplantar keratoderma, with dilated left ventricular cardiomyopathy emerging later and leading to arrhythmias, heart failure, and sudden death. Driven by desmosome dysfunction often from desmoplakin variants. Care is supportive with defibrillators, antiarrhythmics, heart-failure therapy, and transplant for end-stage disease. Major unmet need is disease-modifying, ideally pre-symptomatic treatment to prevent malignant ventricular arrhythmias and progressive ventricular failure.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- DSP/Carvajal-targeted disease-modifying therapy that reverses established severe pediatric LV systolic dysfunction and prevents progression to transplant/death.
- Pharmacotherapy that prevents malignant ventricular arrhythmias/sudden cardiac death, reducing reliance on ICDs and avoiding toxic/monitoring-heavy amiodarone.
- Pre-symptomatic therapy initiated in skin-first identified children (woolly hair/early palmoplantar keratoderma) to delay or prevent cardiomyopathy onset.

name: Castleman disease | unicentric
description: Unicentric Castleman disease is a rare immune mediated lymph node overgrowth confined to a single region, often found incidentally in otherwise well adults around their mid 30s. Surgery is usually curative, but unresectable masses may need systemic therapy to shrink lesions enough for resection and to control cytokine driven inflammation. A small high risk subset develops autoimmune paraneoplastic pemphigus with bronchiolitis obliterans where lung disease can progress despite intensive treatment and lead to respiratory failure, underscoring the need for effective medical options that improve operability and stabilize pulmonary outcomes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Medical cytoreduction to convert unresectable UCD to resectable disease (or avoid surgery), with objective imaging response and “non‑resectability status” conversion endpoints.
- Systemic therapy for UCD-associated paraneoplastic pemphigus with bronchiolitis obliterans that improves/stabilizes lung outcomes and reduces BO-related mortality.
- Anti-inflammatory control in inflammation-driven unresectable UCD that reduces reliance on infection-prone IL‑6 blockade and frequent infusion-center dosing (safer and/or more convenient delivery).

name: Chandler syndrome
description: Chandler syndrome is a rare, acquired, usually unilateral iridocorneal endothelial disorder, typically affecting women in early to middle adulthood, where abnormal corneal endothelial cells migrate across the angle and iris causing fluctuating corneal edema with blurred vision and halos and driving secondary angle closure glaucoma. Management is largely reactive and procedural, yet glaucoma surgery can fail as migrating endothelium obstructs drainage, and advanced disease may require keratoplasty with high graft failure and repeat transplants, creating demand for disease modifying endothelial therapy and more durable low burden intraocular pressure control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pathogenesis-targeting therapy to halt ICE membrane/abnormal corneal endothelial proliferation to prevent PAS/angle closure and glaucoma progression.
- Corneal endothelial function restoration to clear Chandler corneal edema and reduce reliance on keratoplasty/redo grafting.
- Durable, less drop-burdensome long-acting glaucoma therapy to achieve sustained IOP control despite membrane-related treatment/surgical failure.

name: Chediak-Higashi syndrome
description: Chédiak Higashi syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive LYST related lysosomal trafficking disorder causing childhood onset immunodeficiency with recurrent severe infections plus oculocutaneous albinism and bleeding tendency, often progressing to an accelerated lymphoproliferative phase with systemic inflammation and cytopenias. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation can correct immune and hematologic complications but does not prevent progressive neurologic decline, leaving major unmet need for brain penetrant disease modifying therapy and safer, more targeted control of the accelerated phase as a bridge to transplant.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-penetrant therapy to prevent/slow progressive neurologic disease that persists post‑HSCT
- Less‑myelosuppressive targeted regimen to rapidly control accelerated‑phase HLH as a safer bridge to HSCT vs HLH‑94 chemo
- LYST/CHS1-directed curative alternative that avoids or markedly reduces allogeneic HSCT conditioning toxicity/fatal-complication risk

name: Erdheim-Chester disease
description: Rare, slow growing histiocytic neoplasm in midlife with osteosclerotic long bone pain and inflammatory fibrotic infiltration of organs such as the pituitary, heart and retroperitoneum, leading to diabetes insipidus and potentially life threatening cardiac or kidney involvement. Targeted therapy helps when mitogen activated protein kinase mutations such as BRAF V600 are present, but treatment is often indefinite with cumulative toxicity, relapse risk off drug, persistent disability despite radiologic response, and limited evidence based options for patients without actionable mutations.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Effective therapies for BRAF‑V600–wild‑type ECD without an identified MAPK mutation (especially acute/life‑threatening cardiac/CNS involvement) beyond empiric MEK inhibition.
- Finite-duration regimens that achieve treatment-free remission and prevent rapid relapse after stopping BRAF inhibition.
- Better-tolerated long-term therapies that reduce AE-driven discontinuation/dose modification while improving persistent fatigue/pain/neurologic symptom burden.

name: Evans syndrome
description: Evans syndrome is a rare acquired autoimmune disorder in which the immune system attacks multiple blood cell lines, typically platelets and red cells, causing relapsing bruising and bleeding alongside hemolytic anemia symptoms like fatigue, shortness of breath, jaundice, and splenomegaly. First line care relies on corticosteroids or intravenous immunoglobulin, yet many patients become refractory or relapse repeatedly and face elevated risks of thrombosis and infection. The key unmet need is durable, steroid sparing control of both cytopenias with safer long term immunomodulation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, steroid-sparing remission for relapsing/refractory adults (sustained control of both thrombocytopenia and hemolysis)
- Lower grade ≥3 infection and thrombosis risk while maintaining cytopenia responses (avoid high-sepsis-risk approaches)
- Rapid, convenient outpatient flare control that is disease-modifying, reducing reliance on IVIg rescue and prolonged steroid courses

name: FG syndrome
description: FG syndrome type 1 is an ultra-rare, X-linked disorder affecting mostly males, marked by early-onset neurodevelopmental disability with hypotonia and frequent gastrointestinal/anal anomalies such as severe constipation and imperforate anus, plus characteristic facial and brain findings. Care is largely supportive across therapies and management of congenital complications, leaving major unmet need for disease-modifying approaches that meaningfully improve cognition and communication and for safer, more effective ways to reduce chronic gastrointestinal morbidity in infants and children.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- MED12 functional restoration for molecularly confirmed FG syndrome type 1 to improve neurodevelopmental outcomes (incl. intellectual disability and language/communication deficits)
- Pediatric-safe GI therapy to materially reduce severe constipation and anal-anomaly–linked morbidity/bowel-management burden
- Infant feeding/GERD-focused therapy to reduce early-life feeding dysfunction and reflux-related complications

name: Fanconi anemia
description: Fanconi anemia is a rare inherited DNA repair disorder, usually diagnosed in childhood, marked by congenital anomalies, progressive bone marrow failure with pancytopenia, and high early cancer risk. Current care is largely supportive, with androgens helping only about half of patients and hematopoietic cell transplantation the only proven cure for marrow aplasia but limited by donor availability and toxicity. Many cancers, especially head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, are hard to treat because DNA damaging chemo and radiation may be unusable, driving demand for safer disease modifying options such as autologous gene corrected stem cell therapy without genotoxic conditioning.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Conditioning-minimized autologous HSC gene therapy for FA-A (FANCA) patients lacking an HLA-identical sibling donor to durably prevent progressive bone marrow failure.
- Safer, durable non-androgen oral therapy for mild–moderate marrow failure/cytopenias to avoid ~50% response/refractoriness and liver toxicity/monitoring burden of androgens.
- Non–DNA-crosslinking systemic treatments (e.g., targeted/IO) for FA-associated aggressive HNSCC/SCC with anti-tumor activity without cisplatin/radiation prohibitive toxicity.

name: Clouston syndrome
description: Clouston syndrome is an autosomal dominant ectodermal dysplasia caused by GJB6 (connexin 30) mutations, presenting from infancy with progressive alopecia, nail dystrophy, and worsening often painful palmoplantar hyperkeratosis while teeth and sweating are usually spared. Management is largely supportive with emollients, keratolytics, mechanical paring, wigs, and analgesics, leaving major unmet need for disease modifying therapies that restore connexin 30 function and provide durable relief of keratoderma and hair loss.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying restoration of GJB6/connexin-30 function (e.g., topical small-molecule modulators or gene-based therapy) for genetically confirmed patients vs supportive-only care
- Sustained reduction of painful palmoplantar keratoderma (hyperkeratosis/fissures) to improve walking/hand function and reduce reliance on repetitive keratolytics/mechanical care/analgesics
- Durable hair-restoration therapy in pediatric/adolescent patients to prevent or reverse progression to total alopecia by puberty

name: Coats disease
description: Coats disease is a rare pediatric retinal vasculopathy, usually unilateral in boys under 8, where leaky telangiectatic and aneurysmal vessels cause exudation that can progress to exudative retinal detachment and severe vision loss, often diagnosed late after strabismus or leukocoria. Care relies on laser or cryotherapy plus selected injections and surgery, but advanced eyes rarely regain vision because persistent detachment and macular fibrosis dominate and anti vascular endothelial growth factor use can worsen fibrosis and traction. Key needs are earlier, fibrosis sparing anti leakage therapies that preserve or restore vision while reducing repeat pediatric procedures under anesthesia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Vision-restorative therapy for advanced Stage 3B (total exudative retinal detachment) patients with poor final visual acuity driven by macular scarring/persistent detachment.
- Anti-exudative pharmacotherapy with lower vitreoretinal fibrosis/tractional retinal detachment risk than adjunctive anti‑VEGF approaches.
- Long-acting, procedure/anesthesia-sparing ocular drug delivery to reduce repeated laser/cryotherapy sessions and pediatric sedation/general anesthesia exposure.

name: Cockayne syndrome
description: Cockayne syndrome is an ultra rare childhood onset neurodegenerative disorder driven by impaired transcription coupled DNA repair, typically presenting in infancy with failure to thrive, microcephaly, developmental delay, photosensitivity, and progressive vision and hearing loss leading to profound disability and often death in the second decade. Care is purely supportive and frequently requires feeding tube support, leaving a premium on early disease modifying therapies that preserve brain myelin, sensory function, and growth rather than managing symptoms alone.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-life (≤2 years) ERCC6/ERCC8-restoring disease-modifying therapy to halt progression from MRI white-matter dysmyelination to progressive cerebral/cerebellar atrophy.
- Vision and hearing preservation therapies to prevent progressive pigmentary retinopathy/optic atrophy and neurosensorial hearing loss (audiogram + ERG/OCT endpoints).
- Anti-cachexia/feeding-function therapeutics to reduce failure-to-thrive and dependence on NG/G-tube feeding or gastrostomy.

name: Coffin-Lowry syndrome
description: Rare multisystem genetic disorder (often severe in males) with early developmental delay and profound intellectual disability, plus progressive skeletal disease and neurologic complications including unpredictable stimulus induced drop episodes that drive injury and loss of mobility. Care is largely symptomatic and supportive with no disease specific therapy, leaving major unmet needs for disease modifying treatment and better control of drop episodes and skeletal progression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- RPS6KA3/RSK2 functional restoration (gene/mRNA/protein-pathway therapy) in infancy/early childhood to prevent or materially reduce severe neurodevelopmental impairment.
- More effective, reliable suppression of stimulus-induced drop episodes/attacks to reduce injuries/falls and wheelchair dependence.
- Pharmacologic prevention/attenuation of progressive skeletal disease (esp. kyphoscoliosis/osteoporosis) to avoid spastic paraplegia and respiratory compromise.

name: Coffin-Siris syndrome
description: Rare congenital BAF complex related neurodevelopmental syndrome causing syndromic intellectual disability with fifth digit hypoplasia, coarse facial features, hypotonia, feeding failure to thrive, infections and frequent epilepsy. Care is supportive only with no cure or disease modifying therapy, leaving high burden feeding support and empiric non syndrome specific seizure control as key unmet needs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ARID1B/BAF-complex disease-modifying therapy (e.g., ASO/gene regulation or gene therapy) targeting core developmental delay/intellectual disability
- Low-burden therapy to reduce severe feeding dysfunction and aspiration risk and avoid/shorten feeding-tube dependence
- Better-tolerated, more effective control of epilepsy and neurobehavioral symptoms without worsening hypotonia/sedation

name: Cogan-Reese syndrome
description: Cogan Reese syndrome is an ultra rare iridocorneal endothelial syndrome that typically affects one eye in young to middle aged women, where abnormal corneal endothelial cells migrate onto the iris and drainage angle causing iris nodules, scarring, corneal edema, and secondary angle closure glaucoma that can progress to severe vision loss or blindness. Management is largely symptomatic with multiple pressure lowering drops and often surgery, but etiology remains unclear, creating unmet need for disease modifying therapy, durable lower burden intraocular pressure control, and approaches that preserve or regenerate corneal endothelium.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Etiology-targeted therapy (e.g., antiviral) for the putative HSV-driven ICE/Cogan–Reese subgroup
- Durable, lower-burden IOP control for ICE/Cogan–Reese secondary glaucoma refractory to multi-drop regimens (ideally sustained-delivery)
- Corneal endothelium–preserving/regenerative pharmacotherapy to prevent corneal decompensation/edema and avoid keratoplasty/repeat grafting

name: Cohen syndrome
description: Cohen syndrome is a VPS13B driven multisystem genetic disorder recognized in childhood with developmental delay or intellectual disability, microcephaly and hypotonia, plus progressive high myopia with retinal dystrophy and chronic neutropenia that drives recurrent infections and aphthous ulcers. With no cure and largely supportive care today, key unmet needs are therapies that preserve vision, more durable infection protection via neutropenia correction, and interventions that materially improve neurodevelopmental outcomes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral/long-acting alternative to injectable G‑CSF for Cohen-syndrome chronic neutropenia that meaningfully raises ANC and reduces infections/antibiotic use/oral ulcers.
- Retina-directed therapy that halts/slows progressive retinochoroidal dystrophy to preserve visual field/nyctalopia and best-corrected visual acuity (esp. deterioration after ~age 30).
- Early-childhood pharmacologic therapy that improves developmental delay/intellectual disability/hypotonia outcomes (motor/speech milestones; adaptive functioning) beyond supportive care.

name: Cornelia de Lange syndrome
description: Cornelia de Lange syndrome is a rare congenital genetic developmental disorder marked by prenatal and postnatal growth restriction, limb malformations, and usually moderate to severe intellectual disability, with early life often dominated by feeding difficulties and severe gastroesophageal reflux that can drive failure to thrive and aspiration pneumonia. Care is largely supportive with medical and surgical management, there is no cure and no validated drug therapy for cognitive or behavioral symptoms, leaving major unmet need for disease modifying approaches and effective treatments for self injury, repetitive behaviors, and other neurobehavioral burdens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Validated pharmacotherapy improving cognition/adaptive functioning in genetically confirmed CdLS (e.g., *NIPBL*), measured by Leiter-R and Vineland
- Non-antipsychotic treatment for repetitive/self-injurious behaviors achieving clinically meaningful reductions while avoiding metabolic/weight/cognitive AEs of antipsychotics
- Drug therapy to reduce severe GERD/esophageal dysmotility and feeding dysfunction, lowering aspiration/failure-to-thrive and need for long-term tube feeding/antireflux surgery

name: Costello syndrome
description: Costello syndrome is a rare, multi system developmental disorder caused by germline gain of function variants in HRAS. It typically presents in fetal life or infancy with polyhydramnios or fetal atrial tachycardia, severe feeding dysfunction and failure to thrive often requiring tube feeding, hypotonia, and characteristic facial and skin features. The most acute unmet need is early, life threatening cardiac disease including hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias that can be fatal in the first two years, alongside safer management of neonatal hyperinsulinism given diazoxide associated pulmonary hypertension risk. No cure exists, and care remains largely supportive, with growing interest in pathway targeted kinase modulation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer, earlier-life disease control for infants with severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and/or multifocal atrial tachycardia (potentially fatal in first 2 years), ideally with less monitoring burden than current MEK inhibition.
- Non-diazoxide therapies for neonatal hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia that maintain euglycemia while avoiding pulmonary-hypertension risk and intensive monitoring.
- Drug therapies that reduce severe infant feeding dysfunction/failure-to-thrive and dependence on NG/G-tube feeding (± fundoplication), with GI-motility options that avoid arrhythmia risk.

name: Cowden syndrome
description: Rare inherited PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome causing multi organ hamartomas and early onset breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancer risk. Care is dominated by lifelong intensive surveillance and repeated procedures such as endoscopy with polyp removal, with major unmet needs for durable medical prevention of cancer and polyp burden and for options addressing neurodevelopmental and social impairment in a subset.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Evidence-backed cancer chemoprevention for PTEN/PHTS carriers to reduce lifetime cancer risk enough to de-intensify lifelong surveillance/risk-reducing surgery.
- Oral/systemic therapy that measurably reduces severe GI/colon polyp burden (polyp number/InSIGHT stage) to lessen colonoscopy/polypectomy burden.
- Safe chronic neurobehavioral therapy that improves PTEN/PHTS social deficits (e.g., Social Responsiveness Scale) for patients with autism/social-impairment phenotypes.

name: Gorham's disease
description: Rare lymphatic driven vanishing bone disorder where abnormal lymphatic vessels proliferate in bone causing progressive osteolysis, pain, swelling, fractures, and sometimes life threatening chylothorax. Care is individualized with no curative surgery and no consensus regimen, and the trial evidence base is sparse, leaving a premium on pediatric tolerable disease modifying therapy that durably arrests bone loss and reliably controls chylothorax.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable radiographic arrest/reversal of progressive osteolysis (prevent fractures/functional decline) in patients refractory to current antiresorptives
- Pharmacologic prevention/resolution of chylothorax/pleural effusions in thoracic/rib/vertebral involvement to reduce high-mortality complications and avoid non–first-line radiation
- Standardized, predictable-efficacy, lower-toxicity long-term regimen (esp. pediatric/adolescent) to address highly variable responses and substantial side effects with current options

name: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
description: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a rare, prion-driven neurodegenerative disorder causing rapidly progressive dementia and early gait disturbance, myoclonus, and visual symptoms in adults typically over 55, with median survival of 4 to 5 months. Care is largely comfort-focused symptom management because no therapy has been shown to stop progression, creating an acute need for disease-modifying treatments with measurable biomarkers and clinically meaningful survival and functional outcomes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prion-protein (PrP)–lowering disease-modifying therapy for confirmed prion disease with measurable CSF PrP reduction (esp. early/moderate impairment).
- Early-stage progression-slowing therapy that prolongs survival and delays key dependency milestones (feeding tube, catheterization/incontinence, akinetic mutism).
- Better-tolerated symptomatic control of myoclonus and delirium/agitation that avoids benzodiazepine-related sedation/ataxia and antipsychotic mortality risk.

name: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever
description: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever is a rare, often fatal tick and bloodborne viral hemorrhagic disease affecting people around livestock and in healthcare settings, with abrupt onset that can progress within days to severe bruising and uncontrolled bleeding. Treatment is largely supportive, with no proven antiviral and ribavirin limited by lack of randomized efficacy and safety concerns, creating a major need for effective, safer antivirals and adjuncts that reduce coagulopathy and mortality.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Randomized-trial–proven antiviral/anti‑CCHFV therapy that accelerates viral clearance (e.g., PCR clearance by Day 5) and reduces Day 14/28 mortality vs optimized supportive care
- Ribavirin-sparing early-treatment/PEP option usable in pregnancy/childbearing-age adults that avoids hemolytic anemia and high-frequency (q6h) dosing
- Adjunct therapy that prevents/reverses coagulopathy and organ dysfunction to reduce transfusions/organ support needs and shorten hospital stay

name: Cronkhite-Canada syndrome
description: Cronkhite Canada syndrome is a rare, nonhereditary gastrointestinal polyposis syndrome in older adults, marked by diffuse polyps with chronic watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, anorexia, weight loss and cachexia plus ectodermal changes like hyperpigmentation, alopecia and nail dystrophy, often complicated by protein losing enteropathy, hypoproteinaemia and edema. Care leans on systemic corticosteroids, but relapses and steroid dependence are common and many patients fail to sustain long term remission, creating demand for steroid sparing maintenance and more durable disease modifying immunomodulation as the underlying inflammatory drivers remain uncertain.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing maintenance that prevents relapse with glucocorticoid taper/cessation while achieving durable endoscopic/histopathologic remission and polyp control.
- Safer long-term immunomodulation than azathioprine for steroid-dependent/refractory CCS, reducing serious infection/myelotoxicity and early discontinuation (esp. in elderly hypoalbuminemic patients).
- Rapid reversal of protein-losing enteropathy/malnutrition (diarrhea, hypoalbuminemia, sarcopenia) to avoid/shorten total parenteral nutrition and stabilize electrolytes.

name: Crouzon syndrome
description: Crouzon syndrome is an FGFR2 driven craniosynostosis where premature skull suture fusion distorts craniofacial growth, causing shallow orbits with proptosis and vision loss risk, midface and maxillary hypoplasia, and complications such as multilevel airway obstruction and hydrocephalus. Treatment is largely repeated, complication driven surgery that reshapes bone but does not address the molecular cause, leaving a major unmet need for early suture targeted disease modifying approaches that prevent airway and neurologic morbidity and reduce lifelong surgical burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-life, suture-targeted FGFR2-pathway suppression in FGFR2 gain-of-function Crouzon infants to prevent premature suture ossification and avoid/defer invasive craniectomy/cranial vault surgery.
- Non-surgical prevention/treatment of intracranial hypertension and hydrocephalus-related morbidity to prevent papilledema → optic atrophy/vision loss and reduce shunting/decompression.
- Medical therapy to improve midface-retrusion–driven airway obstruction/OSA (reduce tracheostomy/CPAP and need for major midface advancement), measured by OSA severity (e.g., AHI/oxygenation).

name: Culler-Jones syndrome
description: Ultra-rare congenital autosomal dominant syndrome marked by congenital hypopituitarism with postaxial polydactyly, often with midline facial defects and neurologic involvement such as seizures and developmental disability. Care is lifelong multi-hormone replacement, but families face high day-to-day treatment burden and safety risk from complex dosing and monitoring including frequent hydrocortisone with stress dosing and emergency injections, desmopressin fluid restriction to avoid hyponatremia, and burdensome daily growth hormone injections, creating demand for simpler, lower-burden regimens and longer-acting options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer central diabetes insipidus control that minimizes desmopressin-related hyponatremia/water intoxication risk and reduces need for strict fluid restriction/monitoring.
- More physiologic, lower-burden cortisol replacement for central adrenal insufficiency that avoids 3x-daily hydrocortisone and reduces stress-dosing/emergency injection reliance.
- Long-acting growth hormone replacement that shifts from 6–7 injections/week to once-weekly dosing while maintaining pediatric growth outcomes.

name: DICER1 syndrome
description: DICER1 syndrome is an inherited tumor predisposition often presenting in infancy as pleuropulmonary blastoma, ranging from cystic type I to aggressive type II/III disease that can rapidly progress and metastasize to the brain. Management relies on surgical resection and, for many, chemotherapy, creating a central tension between preventing progression and limiting treatment toxicity in very young children. Key unmet needs include better risk stratification to identify who truly benefits from systemic therapy and less toxic, more effective disease modifying strategies for higher risk disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-penetrant systemic/maintenance therapy to prevent or treat brain relapse in Type II/III pleuropulmonary blastoma (PPB).
- Targeted/chemo-sparing systemic regimens that improve survival in Type II/III PPB vs current multi-agent sarcoma chemotherapy.
- Progression-preventing medical therapy (chemoprevention/biologic suppression) for DICER1 carriers with early lung cysts/Type I PPB to prevent evolution to Type II/III.

name: Dent disease
description: Rare X linked childhood onset proximal tubule kidney disorder in males causing low molecular weight proteinuria and hypercalciuria with nephrocalcinosis and recurrent kidney stones, often progressing to end stage renal disease in mid adulthood; care lacks standardized protocols and is largely supportive with side effect limited options, leaving a need for tubule targeted disease modifying therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying proximal-tubule–targeted therapy to reduce LMW proteinuria and slow CKD progression (eGFR slope/time-to-ESRD).
- Better-tolerated hypercalciuria control to prevent stones/nephrocalcinosis (thiazide-like >40% urinary Ca reduction) without hypokalemia/volume depletion and with less monitoring.
- Mineral/bone therapy that corrects hypophosphatemia/rickets/osteomalacia without worsening hypercalciuria and reduces vitamin D/calcium monitoring burden.

name: Diamond-Blackfan anemia
description: Diamond-Blackfan anemia is an infant-onset inherited bone marrow failure syndrome where defective erythropoiesis, most often from ribosomal protein gene defects, causes profound anemia and frequent congenital anomalies and growth deficiency. Care still relies on corticosteroids and chronic red blood cell transfusions, with hematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the only curative option. Steroid toxicity, lifelong transfusion burden, and transfusion related iron overload drive the need for durable, steroid sparing ways to achieve transfusion independence via mechanism based therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing hemoglobin maintenance for corticoresistant/corticodependent DBA (esp. pediatrics), keeping chronic prednisone <0.3 mg/kg/day.
- Therapies enabling durable transfusion independence (e.g., Hb >9 g/dL without transfusions) to avoid frequent transfusions and iron-overload/cardiac toxicity.
- Genotype-targeted one-time corrective therapy (e.g., for RPS19-deficient, steroid-resistant, transfusion-dependent children) achieving sustained reticulocyte recovery and Hb ≥8 g/dL ≥90 days post–last transfusion.

name: Dieulafoy lesion
description: Dieulafoy lesion is a developmental gastrointestinal vascular malformation where an abnormally large submucosal artery erodes through normal mucosa, causing sudden, sometimes recurrent and potentially life threatening bleeding (often melena or hematemesis) in patients with significant comorbidities. Diagnosis and treatment hinge on endoscopy, but small, intermittently bleeding lesions and blood filled stomachs often force repeat procedures and reliance on adjuncts like erythromycin with cardiac risk and prolonged high dose proton pump inhibitor infusions. Better ways to rapidly localize and durably stop bleeding are the key unmet needs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct pharmacotherapy to reduce post-endoscopic rebleeding, especially in high-risk patients (e.g., kidney disease or infection)
- Safer rapid pre-endoscopy visualization/clearing agent for severe or ongoing UGI bleeding to replace IV erythromycin (avoid QT/torsade risk)
- Post-hemostasis regimen that matches high-dose PPI efficacy without a 72-hour continuous IV infusion

name: Retinal dystrophy
description: Retinitis pigmentosa is a group of inherited retinal dystrophies in which photoreceptors slowly degenerate, often beginning in childhood with night blindness and progressive peripheral field loss that narrows to tunnel vision and can end in blindness. Treatment is largely supportive, with no cure and only one genotype specific disease modifying option, voretigene neparvovec, limited to patients with biallelic RPE65 mutations and viable retinal cells. The key unmet needs are broadly applicable therapies that can preserve vision across genotypes and stages and less burdensome delivery than surgical subretinal injection plus systemic steroids.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy options for the ~98%+ of RP/IRD patients without biallelic RPE65 mutations.
- Less burdensome delivery than subretinal vitrectomy-based injection, avoiding required systemic oral corticosteroids and reducing ocular adverse events.
- Therapies effective in late-stage disease without sufficient viable retinal cells (beyond Luxturna eligibility).

name: Dravet syndrome
description: Rare genetic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, usually SCN1A related, starting at 6 to 12 months with febrile prolonged tonic clonic or hemiclonic seizures and recurrent status epilepticus, followed by developmental delay and lifelong supportive care needs. Premature mortality is ~15 to 20 percent, often from sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. Current options are limited and burdensome, leaving major unmet need for durable seizure control with fewer side effects and for disease modifying gene based approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early SCN1A/NaV1.1 restoration in SCN1A-positive children with demonstrable neurodevelopmental benefit (e.g., Bayley/Vineland), not just seizure reduction
- Durable elimination of convulsive seizures and prevention of prolonged seizures/status epilepticus to reduce SUDEP-driven mortality
- Better-tolerated, low-monitoring chronic regimens that reduce polytherapy burden and avoid echo/REMS, liver labs, and routine blood-count monitoring

name: Dubin-Johnson syndrome
description: Dubin Johnson syndrome is a rare, benign inherited liver disorder caused by ABCC2 transporter defects that impair bilirubin export into bile, leading to isolated conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and lifelong intermittent jaundice, often triggered by pregnancy, estrogen exposure, illness, fasting, or alcohol. Most patients need no treatment and routine liver tests are normal, but the condition is frequently misdiagnosed, sometimes prompting unnecessary procedures, and there is limited evidence for pharmacologic options in uncommon neonatal cholestasis or recurrent symptomatic flares.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neonatal severe cholestasis rescue therapy that rapidly reduces bilirubin and improves hepatomegaly/cholestasis in rare newborn-onset DJS
- On-demand/prophylactic therapy to prevent/attenuate jaundice flares triggered by pregnancy, oral contraceptives/estrogens, or intercurrent illness
- Safe, evidence-based bilirubin-lowering option for symptomatic adults with recurrent/intermittent jaundice (replacing discouraged phenobarbital; defining role vs rifampicin/UDCA)

name: Ellis-van Creveld syndrome
description: Ellis van Creveld syndrome is a rare inherited ciliopathy causing disproportionate short limb dwarfism, polydactyly and a narrow chest with short ribs, often detected prenatally or at birth. Congenital heart defects are common and drive early cardiopulmonary crises with respiratory distress or heart failure and high mortality in infancy. Management is largely supportive and complication focused, leaving major unmet need for disease modifying therapies that prevent or correct the skeletal and cardiac developmental defects rooted in disrupted primary cilia Hedgehog signaling.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prenatal/neonatal therapies that increase rib-cage/thoracic growth to prevent lung hypoplasia/restrictive lung disease and reduce need for neonatal mechanical ventilation.
- Disease-targeted modulation of the EVC/EVC2→cilia→Hedgehog axis to reduce serious congenital heart defects/heart-failure–driven early mortality.
- Pediatric growth-plate/endochondral-ossification therapies that improve disproportionate short stature/limb shortening beyond supportive care and reduce need for repeated orthopedic surgery.

name: Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy
description: Genetic muscular dystrophy with childhood-onset joint contractures and slowly progressive limb muscle weakness, complicated by often silent cardiac conduction disease and arrhythmias that can cause stroke, heart failure, or sudden death; care is largely supportive with pacemakers sometimes lifesaving, leaving a major unmet need for disease-modifying therapies that preserve mobility and prevent cardiac events to improve lifespan and quality of life.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drug therapy to prevent/reverse early-childhood joint contractures in EDMD.
- Disease-modifying therapy to stabilize/improve humeroperoneal muscle weakness/atrophy and preserve ambulation.
- Cardiac disease-modifying therapy to prevent/delay conduction defects/arrhythmias/cardiomyopathy and reduce pacemaker/antiarrhythmic need and sudden-death risk.

name: Fazio-Londe disease
description: Fazio–Londe disease is a rare riboflavin transporter deficiency neuronopathy caused by SLC52A2 or SLC52A3 mutations, with infant to adult onset and progressive bulbar and peripheral neurodegeneration leading to weakness, dysphagia, vision loss, deafness and often life threatening respiratory failure. High dose riboflavin can be life saving, but outcomes depend on ultra early diagnosis before irreversible neuronal damage, liquid formulations can be hard to obtain, and some patients continue to deteriorate or die despite treatment, leaving a need for more reliably disease modifying therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Ultra-rapid therapy to prevent irreversible diaphragmatic paralysis/respiratory failure in infant-onset disease (improve vital capacity; ventilator-free survival).
- Disease-modifying options for partial/non-responders who continue neurologic/respiratory decline despite high-dose riboflavin (halt/reverse bulbar weakness; reduce ventilator dependence).
- More reliable, less burdensome riboflavin replacement/adjuncts that standardize dose/frequency/delivery and provide “rescue” during illness (fewer daily doses; fewer infection-triggered decompensations).

name: Amyloidosis | Finnish type / Meretoja syndrome
description: Gelsolin-related amyloidosis (Finnish type or lattice corneal dystrophy type II) is an autosomal dominant systemic amyloid disease that typically starts in the 20s with corneal lattice deposits causing clouding, painful erosions, and photophobia, then progresses in the 40s to cranial and peripheral neuropathy with facial palsy and swallowing or chewing difficulty plus lax sagging skin. Care is largely supportive and symptomatic with no cure or disease modifying therapy, leaving major unmet need for treatments that prevent formation or deposition of amyloidogenic gelsolin fragments and preserve vision and neurologic function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying suppression of mutant gelsolin misfolding/proteolytic cleavage (e.g., domain-2 pharmacologic chaperone/kinetic stabilizer) in D187N/Y carriers to prevent amyloidogenic fragment generation.
- Biologic “pathway-blocker” (e.g., nanobody/intrabody) that shields mutant gelsolin intermediates to block furin→MT1-MMP processing into 8/5 kDa amyloid peptides.
- Cornea-targeted anti-amyloid/anti-haze therapy to reduce corneal haze/erosions and decrease reliance on lubrication/IOP monitoring while delaying or avoiding keratoplasty.

name: Fleck corneal dystrophy
description: Ultra-rare, usually benign stromal corneal dystrophy caused by PIKFYVE mutations, marked by bilateral tiny white corneal stromal flecks that are typically nonprogressive and spare visual acuity. Most patients are asymptomatic, with a minority experiencing mild photophobia. Because vision is generally preserved and no specific treatment is needed, the main unmet need is safe symptom relief for the symptomatic few, with longer-term interest in precise molecular or gene-based correction that can justify risk in a largely mild condition.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Topical symptom-control to reduce photophobia/light sensitivity (and improve reduced corneal sensitivity) in the symptomatic minority
- Topical mechanism-targeted therapy to reduce stromal flecks/deposits by addressing the PIKFYVE/PIP5K3 trafficking defect
- Single-administration corneal gene therapy/editing for heterozygous PIKFYVE mutation families (very high safety bar given benign course)
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus condition page/URL for Fleck corneal dystrophy

name: Fraser syndrome
description: Rare prenatal onset congenital malformation syndrome with cryptophthalmos, syndactyly, and genitourinary anomalies often including renal agenesis and laryngeal defects; severe cases are frequently fetal or early neonatal lethal from airway and kidney malformations, and care is mainly reconstructive and supportive with no cure, leaving a major need for earlier developmental intervention to prevent mortality and improve organ function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- In‑utero disease‑modifying therapy to prevent lethal airway obstruction/respiratory insufficiency (laryngeal stenosis/atresia)
- Prenatal organ‑rescue therapy to prevent severe renal/urinary malformations (esp. renal agenesis) linked to early death/stillbirth
- Early developmental ocular‑rescue (regenerative/gene‑based) therapy to prevent cryptophthalmos‑associated blindness

name: Freeman-Sheldon syndrome
description: Ultra rare congenital distal arthrogryposis caused by MYH3 variants that impair fetal muscle relaxation, producing craniofacial and distal limb contractures (whistling face, microstomia) with early feeding and potentially life threatening respiratory complications; care is largely surgical and rehabilitative with repeated procedures, no disease specific pharmacologic therapy, and high anesthesia risk including difficult intubation and malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- MYH3/myosin-3 function–restoring therapy for genetically confirmed patients to normalize impaired muscle relaxation early and prevent fixed contractures/orthopedic sequelae.
- Drug therapy to reduce neonatal/infant dysphagia-related failure-to-thrive and life-threatening breathing complications, minimizing need for NG/G-tube feeding.
- Peri-procedural pharmacologic/anesthesia-adjunct strategy to reduce repeated-surgery anesthetic/surgical complications, including malignant hyperthermia risk and difficult airway/vascular access.

name: Froelich syndrome
description: Fröhlich syndrome or adiposogenital dystrophy is an acquired hypothalamic injury syndrome, often after tumors or treatment near the hypothalamus, where disrupted appetite and pituitary control drive hyperphagia, severe treatment resistant obesity, short stature, delayed puberty, and hypogonadism, sometimes with visual impairment and diabetes insipidus. Care is largely symptomatic and risk management, with persistent gaps in effective weight and hunger control, burdensome hormone replacement that needs close monitoring, and potentially life threatening adrenal crises, leaving a premium on disease modifying approaches that safely restore energy balance and endocrine stability.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable therapy for acquired hypothalamic obesity with hyperphagia in youth after hypothalamic tumor/injury, improving %BMI and hunger/hyperphagia scores long term.
- Antidiuretic replacement for central diabetes insipidus that maintains water balance without desmopressin-associated life-threatening hyponatremia risk and frequent sodium monitoring.
- Lower-burden, safer long-term hypopituitarism hormone replacement (esp. adrenal + GH axes) that reduces adrenal-crisis risk and avoids daily injections/cold-chain logistics.

name: Fuchs' heterochromic uveitis
description: Fuchs uveitis syndrome is a chronic, typically unilateral anterior uveitis that may be quiet for years but progressively impairs vision via cataract, vitreous haze with floaters, and secondary glaucoma. Patients often present in early to mid adulthood with blurred vision or floaters, and management is largely complication driven because corticosteroids are usually ineffective and can worsen cataract and ocular hypertension. Key unmet needs are durable nonsurgical intraocular pressure control and therapies that clear vitreous opacities and address the underlying, possibly rubella linked, low grade inflammation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Etiology-directed local therapy to clear persistent intraocular rubella (rubella+ Fuchs uveitis) and eliminate chronic inflammation where steroids are ineffective.
- IOP-lowering therapy that reliably achieves target IOP in Fuchs-associated secondary glaucoma refractory to maximal medical drops (surgery-sparing).
- Non-surgical local therapy to reduce vitritis/vitreous opacification and improve floater-driven visual function, decreasing reliance on vitrectomy.

name: Legius syndrome
description: Autosomal dominant SPRED1 driven pigmentary and neurodevelopmental condition marked by multiple café au lait macules, sometimes intertriginous freckling, macrocephaly, lipomas, and learning or attention difficulties, but typically without neurofibromas or tumor risk seen in neurofibromatosis type 1. Care is largely supportive with surveillance and symptom management, leaving a need for mechanism based therapies that improve attention and learning outcomes and reduce lifelong pigment and lipoma burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Mechanism-based therapy to reduce ADHD/learning/developmental impairment driven by SPRED1-pathway overactive signaling
- Topical/systemic depigmenting therapy to reduce/prevent progression of café-au-lait macules and freckling burden
- Pharmacotherapy to prevent/shrink subcutaneous lipomas (non-surgical alternative)

name: Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy
description: Rare inherited congenital muscular dystrophy with early infant hypotonia, feeding and bulbar weakness plus cobblestone lissencephaly and frequent seizures; development peaks around age 5 to 6 then regresses, with most never walking and many dying before 20 from respiratory failure and cardiomyopathy. Care is supportive only, leaving a major unmet need for disease modifying therapies that preserve motor and neurologic function and prevent cardio respiratory decline, with antisense splicing correction an emerging mechanistic frontier.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Precision antisense splicing correction for the common FKTN exon-trapping mechanism to restore α-dystroglycan glycosylation and improve gross motor function.
- Disease-modifying therapy that delays/prevents progression to bedridden status and reduces early mortality from respiratory failure/cardiomyopathy (endpoints: ventilator-/tracheostomy-free survival, cardiomyopathy progression).
- CNS-focused, non-sedating seizure control (and neurodevelopmental benefit) for the >50% of FCMD patients with epilepsy.

name: GATAD2B-associated neurodevelopmental disorder
description: GATAD2B-associated neurodevelopmental disorder is an ultra-rare, typically de novo loss-of-function condition that disrupts brain development, with global developmental delay from the first year of life, hypotonia, feeding and reflux problems, and severe lifelong expressive-language impairment. Diagnosis often arrives only in mid-childhood. There is no cure and care is therapy-intensive and symptomatic, leaving major unmet needs for better communication and feeding interventions and disease-modifying approaches that address the underlying GATAD2B loss of function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early GATAD2B-restoration therapy (e.g., gene/mRNA/ASO for haploinsufficiency) to improve global development/adaptive functioning
- Speech-focused therapy for severe expressive-language impairment (incl. non-verbal children), improving functional spoken words and apraxia-of-speech–like features
- Therapy to reduce infant feeding/swallowing dysfunction and GERD burden, improving oral feeding tolerance and reducing reflux/feeding-complication events

name: GM1 gangliosidosis
description: GM1 gangliosidosis is a rare inherited neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorder caused by GLB1 variants that reduce beta galactosidase, leading to toxic substrate buildup in the brain and other organs. The severe infantile form begins around 6 months with developmental slowing then regression, weakness, seizures, hepatosplenomegaly, and skeletal disease, with survival often only two to three years. Care is largely supportive because no approved therapy stops or reverses progression, creating an urgent need for disease modifying treatment that effectively reaches the central nervous system while addressing systemic manifestations.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- BBB-penetrant CNS GLB1 restoration for Type I infants that stabilizes/improves developmental milestones and reduces seizures/psychomotor decline.
- Whole-body (CNS + peripheral) correction that meaningfully treats skeletal dysplasia/progressive skeletal disease and cardiomyopathy, not just neurologic endpoints.
- Lower-burden long-term therapy for Type II/juvenile patients (preferably oral) that slows milestone plateauing/regression and cognitive decline without invasive CNS dosing/immunosuppression complexity.

name: Gaucher's disease | type 1
description: Gaucher disease type 1 is an inherited multisystem lysosomal disorder where lipid laden macrophages accumulate in the spleen, liver, and bone marrow, causing hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, and often disabling bone disease while usually sparing the central nervous system. Current care is effective but burdensome, relying on lifelong intravenous enzyme replacement often every two weeks, with residual skeletal involvement in some patients. Oral substrate reduction reduces infusion burden for selected adults but is limited by CYP2D6 genotype requirements and cardiac risk contraindications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Deeper skeletal/bone-marrow response in ERT-treated GD1 to prevent persistent bone pain, crises, and avascular necrosis
- Non-infusion (or far less frequent/self-administered) disease control to replace q2-week supervised IV ERT
- Genotype-agnostic, DDI-sparing oral therapy for patients ineligible/complicated on eliglustat (CYP2D6 limits; arrhythmia-risk contraindications)

name: Gaucher's disease | type 2
description: Gaucher disease type 2 is a rapidly progressive infantile lysosomal storage disorder caused by inherited glucocerebrosidase deficiency, presenting in the first months of life with hepatosplenomegaly plus severe neurodegeneration including seizures, spasticity, feeding and swallowing failure and aspiration, and is usually fatal by age 2. Enzyme replacement can improve systemic disease but does not cross the blood brain barrier, leaving care largely supportive and a need for central nervous system active, blood brain barrier penetrating disease modifying therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- BBB-penetrant, CNS-active GBA1-targeted therapy to slow/stop progressive neurologic decline (seizures/rigidity) and extend survival in infant-onset GD2.
- Pre-symptomatic (newborn-screen/prenatal) intervention that prevents neuronopathic manifestations rather than only enabling palliative planning.
- Treatments that preserve bulbar/respiratory function (reduce choking/apnea) to avoid/delay feeding-tube placement and tracheostomy/invasive ventilation.

name: Gaucher's disease | type 3
description: Inherited neuronopathic lysosomal disorder caused by glucocerebrosidase deficiency leading to lipid accumulation, with childhood onset hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, bone pain and fractures plus progressive neurologic impairment (eye movement disorders, seizures, cognitive and coordination problems); enzyme replacement controls systemic disease but cannot cross the blood brain barrier and requires lifelong biweekly infusions, leaving major unmet need for brain penetrant disease modifying and less burdensome therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- BBB-penetrant disease-modifying therapy for GD3 to improve/stabilize ataxia and cognition (e.g., SARA and RBANS at ~52 weeks) beyond systemic ERT control.
- Brain-penetrant therapies for GD3-associated progressive myoclonus epilepsy to reduce drug-resistant myoclonic/tonic–clonic seizures and slow cognitive decline.
- ERT-sparing regimens (oral and/or less clinic-dependent) that maintain visceral/hematologic control without q2-week IV infusions and lower infusion hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis risk.

name: Gollop-Wolfgang complex
description: Gollop Wolfgang complex is a very rare congenital limb malformation with bifid femur, absent or hypoplastic tibia, limb shortening, and split or missing digits, presenting antenatally or at birth with profound lifelong disability. Care relies on complex orthopedic reconstruction, prosthetics, and monitoring, but durable function is difficult and limb salvage often fails to deliver a functional knee, forcing high burden choices between repeated surgery and early amputation with prosthetic fitting.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- In utero gene therapy/gene editing post–second-trimester ultrasound diagnosis to prevent tibial agenesis/bifid femur and avoid postnatal amputation/prosthetics.
- Regenerative biologic/cell therapy to create a functional “tibial anlage” + extensor mechanism in complete tibial absence patients to enable reconstruction vs amputation.
- Adjunct molecular therapy to improve limb-salvage procedures (e.g., fibular transfer/tibialization) by reducing high failure/secondary-amputation risk.
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus/MedlinePlus Genetics URL for Gollop-Wolfgang complex

name: Good syndrome
description: Good syndrome is a rare adult onset primary immunodeficiency linked to thymoma, marked by hypogammaglobulinemia with low or absent B cells plus impaired T cell immunity, leading to recurrent sinopulmonary and opportunistic infections and often chronic infectious diarrhea. Thymectomy does not reverse the immune defect, so patients rely on lifelong immunoglobulin replacement and vigilant infection management. Major unmet needs include therapies that restore immune function or reduce infection burden without compounding risk, and safer ways to manage autoimmune hematologic complications such as pure red cell aplasia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Cellular-immunity–restoring/augmenting therapeutics to prevent opportunistic viral/fungal infections (e.g., CMV colitis/retinitis, mucocutaneous candidiasis) not addressed by immunoglobulin replacement.
- Pathogen-directed or pathogen-preventive therapies to achieve durable resolution of the common chronic diarrhea phenotype (often linked to Salmonella/Campylobacter/CMV/Giardia).
- Safer, infection-sparing treatments for thymoma-associated autoimmune/hematologic complications (especially pure red cell aplasia) to reduce reliance on broad immunosuppression.

name: Goodpasture syndrome
description: Anti glomerular basement membrane disease, or Goodpasture syndrome, is a rare autoimmune pulmonary renal syndrome where anti basement membrane antibodies rapidly inflame kidney and lung capillaries, causing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and sometimes life threatening alveolar hemorrhage with hemoptysis. Patients often present abruptly with dyspnea, dark urine, edema, and can deteriorate before diagnosis. Care relies on weeks of plasma exchange plus high dose glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide, which are procedurally burdensome and raise infection risk. Kidney outcomes are frequently determined by how advanced injury is at presentation, leaving a premium on faster antibody lowering and more effective renal rescue.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that improve renal recovery/dialysis-free survival in patients dialysis-dependent at presentation
- Steroid/cyclophosphamide-sparing induction regimens that reduce early severe infections
- Rapid anti-GBM antibody suppression to minimize/avoid plasmapheresis (fewer PLEX sessions)

name: Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome
description: Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome is a congenital GLI3 driven patterning disorder affecting limb, head, and facial development, usually recognized prenatally or at birth with polydactyly, cutaneous syndactyly, macrocephaly, and widely spaced eyes across a wide severity range. Care is largely reconstructive surgery and supportive services rather than disease modifying therapy, leaving unmet need for approaches that prevent malformations, improve long term function, and better predict and monitor the minority who develop neurodevelopmental complications such as seizures or intellectual disability.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Guillain-Barré syndrome
description: Guillain Barré syndrome is a rare post infectious autoimmune attack on peripheral nerves that causes rapidly ascending symmetric tingling and weakness that can progress to life threatening paralysis and respiratory failure, often requiring intensive care. Acute care is limited to plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin, and many patients face prolonged recovery with persistent weakness, fatigue, and pain. The biggest gaps are earlier faster acting immunotherapy, more reliable rescue options when first line treatment fails, and treatments that improve durable functional recovery and reduce long term disability.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early, rapid-onset immunotherapy to prevent progression to respiratory failure/need for mechanical ventilation
- Therapies that improve durable functional recovery (e.g., walking ability at 6 months) and reduce persistent pain/fatigue
- Safer, effective rescue/second-line option for severe/poor-prognosis patients who remain highly disabled after initial IVIg/PLEX

name: Hailey-Hailey disease
description: Hailey Hailey disease is a rare inherited, early adult onset skin disorder causing recurrent painful, itchy, burning erosions and blisters in skin folds that flare with heat, sweat, and friction and are often complicated by malodorous bacterial or fungal infection. Care is largely symptomatic and cyclical, but long term topical antibiotics risk resistance and chronic steroid use weakens already fragile skin. With no curative option and no clearly best systemic therapy, the key unmet need is durable flare prevention and disease modifying approaches targeting the underlying calcium handling defect.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Reproducibly effective systemic therapy for adults with moderate-to-severe, multi-site HHD with meaningful Week-24 PGA and DLQI improvement
- Long-acting sweat/humidity-targeted flare-prevention for intertriginous (axilla/groin) HHD that avoids repeated botulinum-toxin maintenance reinjections
- Steroid/antibiotic-sparing maintenance therapy preventing malodorous, infection-associated (esp. staphylococcus-aggravated) flares while avoiding steroid skin weakening and long-term topical antibiotic resistance

name: Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome
description: Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome is a rodent-borne illness that starts abruptly with fever, severe headache, back and abdominal pain, nausea and blurred vision, and can progress to shock, vascular leakage and acute kidney failure. Care is largely supportive and may require dialysis, with no broadly available disease specific therapy. Intravenous ribavirin may help if given early but is limited by toxicity and logistics, leaving late presenters and survivors with ongoing risks like hematuria, hypertension and proteinuria and a need for kidney protective, easily deployed antivirals and vascular stabilizing adjuncts.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral/strain-agnostic antiviral that reduces oliguria and need for dialysis even when started after presentation (beyond early IV ribavirin)
- Ribavirin-sparing therapy safe in pregnancy, cardiac-risk patients, and renal dysfunction while still reducing mortality/serious AEs
- Kidney/endothelium-protective adjunct that cuts ICU/dialysis needs and prevents long-term sequelae (e.g., hypertension, persistent proteinuria)

name: Haverhill fever
description: Haverhill fever is a North American form of streptobacillary rat bite fever caused by Streptobacillus moniliformis, acquired after rodent bites or ingestion of contaminated food, water, or unpasteurized milk. It presents abruptly with fever, chills, myalgias, headache, and vomiting, followed by an extremity rash and polyarthritis in about half of patients, and can rarely progress to septic arthritis or endocarditis. Care relies on intravenous then oral penicillin, but evidence for optimal regimens is limited and the benefit of post bite antibiotic prophylaxis is uncertain.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral-only or long-acting low-touch curative regimen for uncomplicated disease to avoid ≥7 days IV→oral penicillin and ~2-week course
- Evidence-based, complication-tailored regimens (esp. septic arthritis/endocarditis) with clear duration/combination strategy
- Evidence-based post-exposure chemoprophylaxis for high-risk rodent bites/scratches (prophylaxis efficacy currently unknown)

name: Norrie disease
description: Ultra-rare X-linked NDP-related retinopathy causing congenital bilateral blindness from disrupted retinal development and vascularization, often presenting in newborns with leukocoria, pseudoglioma, and early retinal detachment. Many later develop progressive hearing loss and developmental or behavioral issues. Treatment is largely supportive and complication-driven, with limited surgical ability to restore sight when detachment is complete at birth, leaving a need for very-early vision-preserving therapy, hearing preservation, and durable control of secondary glaucoma and painful elevated eye pressure.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prenatal/neonatal NDP (norrin/Wnt) pathway restoration in genetically diagnosed males to prevent congenital retinal detachment and preserve vision.
- Hearing-loss–preventive therapy to delay/prevent progressive childhood/adolescent SNHL and preserve pure-tone thresholds/speech discrimination.
- Long-acting therapy to prevent/control secondary ocular complications (e.g., elevated IOP/glaucoma) to reduce pain/surgery risk and monitoring burden.

name: Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome
description: Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome is a rare inherited disorder causing oculocutaneous albinism with early visual impairment, platelet-related bleeding, and high-risk progressive pulmonary fibrosis that often begins in the early 30s and can rapidly worsen, sometimes with granulomatous colitis. Management is largely supportive with no established or approved therapies, leaving major unmet need for disease-modifying antifibrotics, safer hemostatic approaches that restore platelet function, and durable colitis control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying anti-fibrotic for HPS pulmonary fibrosis (esp. HPS1/HPS4) that prevents clinically meaningful FVC decline (e.g., avoids ≥10% %predicted FVC drop over 6–12 months).
- Platelet-function–restoring or safer hemostatic prophylaxis to reduce procedure/childbirth/menorrhagia bleeding while minimizing platelet transfusions (alloimmunization) and overcoming variable DDAVP response.
- Targeted therapy for HPS-associated granulomatous colitis/IBD achieving durable remission that is steroid/anti‑TNF‑sparing and reduces progression to bowel resection/colectomy.

name: Papillon-Lefèvre disease
description: Papillon Lefèvre syndrome is an ultra rare autosomal recessive childhood disorder, typically presenting at ages 1 to 5, that combines palm and sole hyperkeratosis with aggressive periodontitis leading to early loss of primary teeth by about age 5 and often permanent teeth by adolescence. Management is largely supportive with intensive antimicrobial dental care and sometimes systemic retinoids, yet periodontal destruction can become refractory and retinoid durability and safety are uncertain. Some patients also face serious recurrent infections such as liver abscesses, underscoring the need for preventive, disease modifying approaches tied to the underlying cathepsin C gene defect.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CTSC activity–restoring disease-modifying therapy (e.g., gene/enzyme replacement) to prevent early-onset periodontitis/alveolar bone loss and preserve dentition into adulthood
- Retinoid-sparing pediatric therapy for keratoderma/periodontal disease with improved long-term safety vs systemic retinoids (avoid growth/skeletal, hepatic/lipid, teratogenic toxicities)
- Infection-/immunology-targeted therapy to reduce recurrent pyogenic infections (including liver abscess risk) and decrease reliance on repeated antibiotic courses

name: Insulin autoimmune syndrome
description: Insulin autoimmune syndrome (Hirata disease) is a rare autoimmune disorder in which antibodies to endogenous insulin cause recurrent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, usually in adults, with neuroglycopenic and adrenergic episodes that can progress to seizures, coma, and fatal outcomes. Some cases resolve after stopping a trigger drug, but many require strict low carbohydrate meal patterning and may need poorly tolerated acarbose or escalation to high dose corticosteroids, plasmapheresis, or rituximab, creating unmet needs for rapid, reliable hypoglycemia prevention and steroid sparing control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid-acting hypoglycemia rescue/prevention to avert severe IAS neuroglycopenic events (e.g., convulsions/coma) and reduce need for continuous IV glucose/inpatient support
- Steroid-sparing, durable insulin autoantibody–lowering immunotherapy for steroid-refractory IAS to avoid prolonged high-dose corticosteroid toxicity and non-durable plasmapheresis
- Better-tolerated outpatient postprandial glucose stabilization to reduce lifelong dependence on frequent low-carb meals/night enteral feeding and avoid acarbose GI intolerance

name: Hodgkin lymphoma | nodular lymphocyte-predominant
description: Rare, slow growing CD20 positive Hodgkin lymphoma subtype, usually early stage with painless peripheral lymph node enlargement and few systemic symptoms; key unmet needs are more durable, toxicity sparing first line control and better prevention of relapse and transformation to aggressive diffuse large B cell lymphoma.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Toxicity-sparing first-line therapy for standard-risk early-stage NLPHL via de-escalated chemo/RT-sparing CD20-directed regimens
- Improve long-term disease control by reducing relapse—especially early progression/relapse within 24 months (POD24)
- Prevent and/or better treat transformation to aggressive NHL (e.g., DLBCL)

name: Holt-Oram syndrome
description: Holt Oram syndrome is a congenital heart hand disorder caused by TBX5 disruption, coupling upper limb malformations with atrial or ventricular septal defects and progressive cardiac conduction disease. Management is largely supportive with defect closure and pacemakers as conduction worsens, but patients remain at risk of arrhythmias, heart failure, and pulmonary hypertension, highlighting the need for therapies that preserve conduction and prevent cardiopulmonary decline.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacotherapy to prevent unpredictable progression of Holt‑Oram cardiac conduction disease (sinus bradycardia/1° AV block → complete heart block ± atrial fibrillation), reducing need for pacemaker implantation
- Drug therapy to prevent clinically significant ASD/VSD from progressing to pulmonary hypertension, congestive heart failure, and Eisenmenger syndrome
- Safer “cardio‑congenital‑compatible” arrhythmia/heart-failure medications with fewer contraindications and reduced monitoring burden (e.g., less need for frequent EKG/Holter surveillance)

name: Glioblastoma | IDH-wildtype
description: Glioblastoma, isocitrate dehydrogenase wildtype, is an invasive infiltrative astrocytic brain cancer typically diagnosed around age 66 that presents with seizures, headaches, nausea or vomiting from raised intracranial pressure, and cognitive or behavioral changes. Standard care remains maximal surgery followed by radiation plus temozolomide, yet cure is rare and many patients, especially those without MGMT promoter methylation, gain limited benefit. Symptom control often relies on dexamethasone for edema despite substantial long term toxicities and immunosuppression, underscoring the need for disease modifying and steroid sparing options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- First-line therapy that meaningfully improves OS in **MGMT-unmethylated, IDH-wildtype glioblastoma** beyond the marginal benefit of TMZ+RT.
- Post-progression/recurrent GBM regimen that extends median OS beyond ~9 months with substantially lower grade 3–5 toxicity and less reliance on q2w IV bevacizumab.
- **Steroid-sparing anti-edema/ICP control** that reduces neurologic symptoms without prolonged dexamethasone exposure and its immunosuppression/toxicity monitoring burden.

name: Patau syndrome
description: Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) is a rare chromosome 13 aneuploidy causing severe multisystem congenital malformations and profound neurodevelopmental impairment, often leading to miscarriage, stillbirth, or death in infancy. With no disease modifying therapy and more than 9 in 10 children dying in the first year, care is largely supportive. The most pressing unmet needs are practical and complication driven, especially stabilizing breathing and apnea, enabling feeding and growth, and preventing or managing seizures alongside complex cardiac and neurologic defects.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacotherapy to reduce recurrent apnea and avoid/limit need for oxygenation, ventilation, intubation or tracheostomy
- Therapeutics to improve feeding tolerance/weight gain (failure to thrive) and reduce need for feeding-tube placement
- Neonatal-optimized anti-seizure therapy with improved safety in medically fragile infants

name: IGSF1 deficiency syndrome
description: IGSF1 deficiency syndrome is an ultra-rare X-linked pituitary disorder causing congenital central hypothyroidism plus later testicular enlargement and delayed pubertal testosterone rise, sometimes with prolactin or growth hormone deficiency and obesity. Many cases are missed by thyroid stimulating hormone based newborn screening and early symptoms can be subtle. Care relies on lifelong levothyroxine with frequent free thyroxine monitoring because thyroid stimulating hormone is unreliable, leaving unmet need for easier monitoring and treatments that address broader metabolic and reproductive morbidity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying pituitary-directed IGSF1 restoration (e.g., gene/RNA therapy) to correct central hypothyroidism plus prolactin/GH abnormalities and prevent the pubertal/gonadal phenotype (delayed testosterone rise + macroorchidism).
- Anti-obesity/cardiometabolic risk–modifying therapy for IGSF1 deficiency patients with increased BMI/waist circumference and dyslipidemia beyond thyroid hormone replacement.
- More “set-and-forget” LT4 replacement for central congenital hypothyroidism (FT4-targeted dosing since TSH is unusable), reducing frequent early-life lab/visit titration burden.

name: Typhus | Queensland tick
description: Queensland tick typhus is a tick borne spotted fever caused by Rickettsia australis in eastern Australia, typically presenting 2 to 14 days after a bite with fever, headache, rash and an eschar, but often missed early due to nonspecific symptoms. Without prompt treatment it can progress to pneumonitis, encephalitis, septic shock, or severe sepsis with multiorgan failure and death. Care relies on a 7 day doxycycline course, leaving gaps in validated alternatives for patients with contraindications or pregnancy and in preventing longer tail postinfective fatigue, malaise, and muscle pain lasting months.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Evidence-based non-tetracycline regimen for patients who cannot take doxycycline (e.g., allergy/intolerance, pregnancy)
- Ultra-short-course therapy (≤3 days or single-dose) that maintains ~48-hour clinical improvement vs 7-day BID doxycycline
- Therapies to prevent/treat severe complications (sepsis/multiorgan failure) and reduce post-infective syndrome lasting months

name: Rocky Mountain spotted fever
description: Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a tick borne infection caused by Rickettsia rickettsii that invades vascular endothelium, driving systemic small vessel injury with abrupt high fever, severe headache, myalgias, and often early gastrointestinal symptoms before the rash appears. It can become fatal within 7 to 9 days, so outcomes depend on starting doxycycline within the first 5 days, yet early diagnosis is difficult when rash is delayed and serology can stay negative for a week. Key gaps include rapid early diagnostics, safer non tetracycline treatment options, and effective prevention since post bite antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-tetracycline oral/IV alternative non-inferior to doxycycline on mortality for patients who can’t receive doxycycline (e.g., severe allergy/pregnancy), avoiding chloramphenicol toxicity/availability limits
- “Late-presenter rescue” regimen that reduces ICU admission and death when treatment starts after illness day 5
- Validated post-exposure prophylaxis/very-early preventive strategy for high-risk tick bites that truly prevents RMSF

name: Jaccoud arthropathy
description: Jaccoud arthropathy is a deforming, typically non erosive joint disorder seen most often in systemic lupus erythematosus, driven by ligament laxity that causes reducible ulnar deviation and metacarpophalangeal subluxation but can progress to fixed fibrosis, contractures, and major functional impairment. Management is largely conservative using standard lupus and arthritis drugs plus splints and hand physiotherapy, with surgery lacking strong evidence, so the key unmet need is earlier disease modifying approaches that prevent irreversible deformity and loss of hand function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-intervention therapy in SLE patients with recurrent arthritis to prevent progression from mild to definite deforming Jaccoud arthropathy.
- Anti-fibrotic/anti-contracture treatment to prevent fixed, non-reversible deformities and preserve joint function in longstanding/severe disease.
- JA-targeted regimen demonstrating meaningful hand-function and quality-of-life improvement beyond current conservative NSAID/low-dose steroid/DMARD symptom control.

name: Jacobsen syndrome
description: Jacobsen syndrome (11q terminal deletion) is a rare multisystem congenital and neurodevelopmental disorder marked by severe congenital malformations, developmental delay, and Paris Trousseau platelet dysfunction with lifelong bleeding risk. Children often face early cardiac surgery and frequent ear and respiratory infections from immune dysfunction. Care is supportive and procedure intensive, but persistent platelet functional defects make perioperative bleeding hard to control, immunodeficiency drives recurrent infections despite vaccination, and there are no disease modifying options to meaningfully improve cognition, behavior, or overall neurodevelopmental outcomes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Platelet-function restoration to prevent Paris‑Trousseau bleeding (esp. infants needing high-risk procedures like neonatal heart surgery)
- Lower-burden immune reconstitution/long-acting infection prevention to reduce recurrent ENT/airway infections and need for prophylactic antibiotics/IgRT
- Neurodevelopmental/behavioral symptom modification to improve cognitive/adaptive outcomes and reduce ADHD/autism-related functional impairment beyond supportive therapies

name: Japanese spotted fever
description: Japanese spotted fever is a tick borne infection caused by Rickettsia japonica, usually affecting older adults after outdoor exposure, with fever, eschar and a spreading rash that can involve palms and soles. A subset progresses rapidly to disseminated intravascular coagulation, multiorgan failure and death, making early empiric tetracycline critical. Care is hampered by limited, nonreimbursed confirmatory testing, few validated alternatives when tetracyclines cannot be used, and a prevention gap since there is no vaccine and antibiotic prophylaxis after exposure is not recommended.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rescue therapy for fulminant/severe Japanese spotted fever that prevents DIC/multi-organ failure/death even with delayed tetracycline initiation.
- Validated non-tetracycline treatment option for tetracycline-allergic/intolerant or pregnant patients (safer than chloramphenicol).
- Prevention-focused therapeutics (vaccine and/or evidence-based post-exposure prophylaxis) for high-risk exposure groups (e.g., agricultural/forestry workers, immunosuppressed).

name: Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome
description: Jervell and Lange Nielsen syndrome is an ultra rare inherited cardio auditory disorder where congenital profound deafness coexists with markedly prolonged QT and stress or exertion triggered syncope with risk of torsades de pointes, ventricular fibrillation, and sudden death in childhood. It is caused by KCNQ1 or KCNE1 potassium channel defects affecting both heart and inner ear. Beta blockers and escalation to implantable defibrillators or sympathetic denervation reduce risk but are not fully protective, with many patients still symptomatic. The unmet need is safer, more reliable pediatric arrhythmia control and disease modifying approaches that address the underlying channel dysfunction.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Breakthrough arrhythmia prevention for high-risk children (e.g., QTc >550 ms and/or early-life syncope) beyond β‑blockers.
- Genotype-directed restoration of KCNQ1/KCNE1 (IKs) function to normalize QTc and reduce arrhythmia risk.
