- Pediatric-safe chronic prophylaxis with fewer β‑blocker limitations (bradycardia/hypotension/bronchospasm/hypoglycemia) and reduced monitoring burden.

name: Joubert syndrome
description: Rare inherited neurodevelopmental brain disorder defined by the magnetic resonance imaging molar tooth sign, with infant hypotonia, episodic hyperpnea or apnea, abnormal eye movements, developmental delay, and ataxia; often multisystem with progressive eye, kidney, and liver involvement. Care is symptom-by-symptom with no cure, leaving major unmet need for disease-modifying therapies that stabilize breathing, improve neurodevelopment, and protect organs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer, more effective pharmacotherapy to reduce episodic infantile hyperpnea/apnea and lessen reliance on apnea monitoring/oxygen/mechanical support
- CNS-active therapy that improves motor/speech milestone acquisition and reduces hypotonia/ataxia and cognitive impairment beyond supportive rehab
- Renal-protective therapy for fibrocystic kidney disease/nephronophthisis to delay/prevent progression to ESRD and reduce need for dialysis/transplant

name: KBG syndrome
description: KBG syndrome is a rare multisystem genetic disorder caused by ANKRD11 loss of function, presenting in childhood with delayed speech and motor milestones, mild to moderate intellectual disability, and a recognizable craniofacial and skeletal phenotype including macrodontia and short stature. Seizures and hearing loss add episodic risk and chronic burden. Management remains symptom directed and multidisciplinary rather than disease modifying, leaving major unmet need for therapies that improve neurodevelopmental outcomes and deliver durable seizure control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ANKRD11-pathway disease-modifying therapy to improve markedly delayed speech/development and core behavioral disturbances
- Seizure therapies targeting the ~27% with drug-resistant epilepsy (≥2 ASM failures)
- Endocrine growth interventions for the ~two-thirds with height <10th centile (beyond limited/short-term GH evidence)

name: Kabuki syndrome
description: Rare congenital multisystem neurodevelopmental syndrome, usually due to KMT2D or KDM6A variants disrupting epigenetic gene regulation, causing early hypotonia and feeding difficulties and lifelong developmental disability with immune vulnerability and recurrent infections. Care is largely symptomatic with no cure, leaving a premium on disease modifying approaches that improve neurodevelopment and reduce infection burden and dependence on intravenous immunoglobulin, plus safer options for neonatal hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia given diazoxide pulmonary hypertension risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying epigenetic/gene-targeted therapy to improve neurodevelopmental outcomes (developmental delay/intellectual disability)
- Immune-restorative therapy for hypogammaglobulinemia/recurrent infections to reduce morbidity and dependence on chronic immunoglobulin replacement
- Safer pharmacologic control of neonatal/infant hyperinsulinism-driven hypoglycemia that avoids diazoxide-associated pulmonary hypertension risk

name: Leukemia | large granular lymphocytic
description: Large granular lymphocytic leukemia is a rare, indolent but chronic clonal expansion of T cells or natural killer cells, typically diagnosed in people in their 60s. Many patients present with persistent cytopenias, especially neutropenia and anemia, driving infections, fatigue and sometimes life threatening pneumonia or sepsis, often alongside autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis. Treatment still relies on slow acting immunosuppressants rather than curative options, creating demand for safer time limited therapies and disease modifying approaches that target Janus kinase and STAT signaling, including STAT3 biology.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid, durable ANC normalization (reducing serious infections) for patients treated for severe neutropenia/recurrent infections
- Safer, time-limited therapy achieving transfusion independence for symptomatic anemia/PRCA (incl. transfusion-dependent patients) vs indefinite immunosuppression
- STAT3/JAK–STAT pathway, clone-eradicating therapy to increase complete remission rates and reduce high relapse vs current first-line immunosuppressives

name: Myotonia congenita | Thomsen type
description: Thomsen type myotonia congenita is an autosomal dominant CLCN1 chloride channel disorder causing childhood-onset muscle stiffness and delayed relaxation, worst after rest but partly relieved by repeated movement. Many children look muscular yet struggle with everyday actions like releasing grip and walking smoothly. Care is lifelong symptom management with repurposed sodium channel blockers such as mexiletine, limited by systemic side effects, monitoring burden, and lack of Food and Drug Administration approved disease-specific therapy, leaving demand for safer, muscle-targeted and chloride channel restoring options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Skeletal-muscle–selective Nav1.4 (SCN4A) blockers for mexiletine nonresponders/intolerant patients, reducing systemic/cardiac risk.
- Better-tolerated, lower-burden dosing/formulations vs mexiletine BID→TID (fewer daily doses, fewer GI/neuro AEs, less monitoring).
- ClC-1/CLCN1 function–restoring/augmenting therapies with pediatric-ready evidence to address the underlying chloride-channel defect.

name: Kaposi sarcoma
description: Kaposi sarcoma is a human herpesvirus 8 driven vascular cancer that emerges with immune suppression, especially in people with human immunodeficiency virus infection or post transplant immunosuppression. It often presents as multifocal red or purple skin lesions with possible mucosal or visceral involvement and many patients feel well at diagnosis. Antiretroviral therapy or reducing immunosuppression can control some cases, but widespread disease often needs intravenous chemotherapy that is hard to deliver safely in profoundly immunocompromised patients, leaving a premium on safer, home manageable disease control and improved targeted or immune based options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer systemic regimens for AIDS-related KS that reduce chemo-associated cytopenias/febrile neutropenia/opportunistic infections.
- Home-manageable (oral and/or field-directed topical) therapy that treats widespread/“systemic-need” KS and reduces infusion-center dependence.
- Post-transplant/iatrogenic KS therapies that control disease without requiring immunosuppression taper (graft rejection risk) or adding chemo-related immunosuppression.

name: Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy
description: Severe collagen VI related congenital muscular dystrophy caused by COL6A1, COL6A2, or COL6A3 variants, with profound early weakness, contractures with distal joint laxity, progressive scoliosis, and respiratory failure often requiring sleep ventilation. Care is largely supportive with no curative or proven disease modifying therapy, leaving major unmet need for treatments that preserve mobility and lung function; a leading frontier is mutation targeted antisense splice correction for recurrent COL6A1 pseudoexon defects.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Splice-switching ASOs to correct the recurrent deep-intronic **COL6A1 c.930+189C>T** pseudo-exon and restore functional collagen VI.
- Drugs that **slow/flatten FVC decline** and **delay/avoid nocturnal NIV dependence** (differentiate on FVC slope/time-to-NIV).
- Pharmacotherapy to **halt progressive large-joint contractures** and **reduce early scoliosis progression/surgery burden** (differentiate on ROM preservation/surgery avoidance).

name: Usher syndrome | type 1
description: Usher syndrome type 1 is a rare inherited deafblindness disorder with congenital severe to profound hearing loss, early balance dysfunction delaying walking, and childhood onset retinitis pigmentosa that starts with night blindness and progresses to tunnel vision and eventual blindness. Care is supportive rather than disease modifying, leaving a premium on early durable treatments that preserve photoreceptors and restore hearing and vestibular function, with gene delivery for large causal genes such as MYO7A remaining a key technical bottleneck.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Retinal disease–modifying therapy for early childhood USH1 (incl. MYO7A/USH1B) that preserves night vision/peripheral field, ideally avoiding subretinal surgery and overcoming AAV MYO7A size limits
- Inner-ear biologic therapy that restores endogenous high-frequency hearing and improves speech-in-noise, reducing reliance on cochlear implants/hearing aids
- Vestibular-restorative therapy for USH1 vestibular areflexia that improves balance/motor milestones (earlier independent walking, fewer falls) beyond supportive care

name: Kearns-Sayre syndrome
description: Kearns Sayre syndrome is a rare mitochondrial DNA deletion disorder with onset typically before age 20, causing progressive external ophthalmoplegia with ptosis, pigmentary retinopathy leading to vision loss, and multisystem complications including ataxia and life threatening cardiac conduction disease that can progress to complete heart block. Care is largely symptomatic and supportive including pacemakers, with no disease modifying therapy, leaving major unmet need for treatments that preserve vision, prevent conduction failure, and improve systemic function via mitochondria targeted approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent/slow progression of cardiac conduction disease/arrhythmias to reduce reliance on prophylactic pacemaker/ICD
- Retinal disease modification to preserve night vision and prevent progressive vision loss from pigmentary retinopathy
- Systemic mitochondrial therapy to meaningfully improve exercise intolerance, fatigue, and muscle weakness/ataxia (e.g., via 6MWT/fatigue scale gains)

name: Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy
description: Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (Kennedy disease) is an X linked adult onset motor neuron disorder causing slowly progressive limb weakness with cramps and falls, followed by bulbar dysarthria and dysphagia, often alongside gynecomastia and infertility from androgen receptor dysfunction. Management remains largely supportive, with late stage aspiration pneumonia and ventilatory failure risk, and no disease modifying therapy. The key unmet need is to slow or halt progression by reducing toxic polyglutamine androgen receptor activity while avoiding hormone manipulation that can worsen disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying slowing of SBMA progression with clinically meaningful ambulatory functional benefit (e.g., less decline/improved 6MWT and SBMA‑FRS over ~48 weeks).
- Therapies that improve bulbar dysfunction/dysphagia and reduce aspiration pneumonia/asphyxiation risk.
- Mutant androgen-receptor toxicity suppression (e.g., lowering mutant AR protein in muscle) without harmful androgen/testosterone manipulation.

name: Kimura disease
description: Rare, benign chronic inflammatory disorder (often in young Asian men) causing painless head and neck soft tissue swelling with lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and high immunoglobulin E; may involve kidneys. Current treatments are often steroid responsive but relapse is common, creating need for durable steroid sparing control and better renal outcomes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing maintenance therapy to prevent relapse during steroid taper/withdrawal
- Renal-involvement–focused therapy achieving durable proteinuria/nephrotic-syndrome control
- Biomarker-guided targeted (Th2/eosinophil/IgE) therapy to reduce recurrence in high eosinophils/IgE patients

name: Kindler syndrome
description: Kindler syndrome is an ultra rare inherited fragility disorder caused by FERMT1 variants that eliminate kindlin 1, leading from infancy to trauma triggered acral blistering that progresses to skin atrophy, photosensitivity, poikiloderma, and worsening mucosal injury such as esophageal stenosis with dysphagia, alongside a high lifetime risk of aggressive squamous cell carcinoma. Care is largely supportive and procedural, leaving major unmet needs for disease modifying therapies that restore kindlin 1 function, prevent or reverse mucosal strictures, and reduce cancer risk beyond surveillance.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Skin + mucosa–directed FERMT1/kindlin‑1 restoration (e.g., topical gene/mRNA/protein) to reduce trauma‑triggered blistering and mucosal fragility
- Mucosal anti‑fibrotic/mucosal‑healing drugs to prevent/reverse esophageal (and anal/urogenital) strictures causing dysphagia and repeated dilations/surgery
- Skin + oral‑mucosa SCC prevention/chemoprevention to reduce high SCC susceptibility currently addressed mainly by surveillance

name: Kleefstra syndrome
description: Kleefstra syndrome is a rare genetic multisystem neurodevelopmental disorder marked by early hypotonia, severe speech impairment, and moderate to severe intellectual disability, often with seizures and congenital anomalies. Adolescence can bring sleep disruption, apathy or catatonia, and episodes of regression and psychosis that raise the stakes for families and caregivers. Management is largely supportive, leaving a major unmet need for disease modifying approaches that preserve function and prevent neuropsychiatric decline. Mechanism based strategies are emerging, including genotype informed synaptic targeting prompted by EHMT1 linked NMDA receptor hyperfunction seen in patient derived neurons.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Mechanism-/genotype-targeted therapies addressing causal *EHMT1* loss-of-function (e.g., enhanced NMDAR signaling) to improve core severe expressive speech deficits beyond supportive care
- Rapid, durable pharmacologic stabilization of adolescent/young-adult sleep disturbance to prevent severe regression and later psychoses
- Effective treatments for post-pubertal neuropsychiatric deterioration (catatonia/extreme apathy) and severe behavioral dysregulation linked to regression

name: Kleine-Levin syndrome
description: Kleine Levin syndrome is a rare relapsing remitting neurologic disorder, typically in adolescent males, marked by sudden episodes lasting days to weeks of extreme hypersomnia of about 15 to 21 hours per day with confusion, apathy, and derealization, separated by normal baseline function. Diagnosis is often by exclusion and there is no definitive therapy, with stimulants and mood stabilizers offering inconsistent benefit and limited impact on cognitive symptoms, leaving a need for safe prophylaxis and rapid on demand treatments that shorten episodes and restore cognition.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Episode-phase therapy that improves disabling cognitive/behavioral symptoms (e.g., derealization, confusion/apathy), not just hypersomnia
- More effective, adolescent-appropriate episode prophylaxis than lithium, without serum-level monitoring/toxicity constraints
- Fast-acting, on-demand episode-abortive treatment to reliably terminate or meaningfully shorten attacks

name: Walker-Warburg syndrome
description: Walker Warburg syndrome is a congenital muscle brain eye disorder presenting at birth or early infancy with profound hypotonia and progressive weakness, cobblestone lissencephaly, hydrocephalus, seizures, and severe eye defects causing vision impairment. It is usually lethal in early childhood, with most children dying before age three. Management is supportive only, leaving an acute unmet need for ultra early disease modifying therapies that address the upstream defect in α dystroglycan glycosylation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying restoration of functional α‑dystroglycan glycosylation (matriglycan) in ribitol‑phosphate–pathway WWS genotypes (e.g., ISPD/CRPPA, FKTN, FKRP).
- Prenatal/very-early intervention to prevent the early neurodevelopmental cascade (neuronal-migration defects → cobblestone lissencephaly/hydrocephalus).
- Improve bulbar/feeding function to reduce need for nasogastric/gastrostomy tube feeding and caregiver dependence vs supportive care.

name: Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome
description: Rare congenital slow flow vascular malformation syndrome causing port wine stain, progressive limb overgrowth and venous or lymphatic disease with pain, swelling, immobility and risks of cellulitis, bleeding and deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism. Often driven by mosaic PIK3CA pathway activation, care still relies on lifelong compression, procedures and selective systemic agents such as sirolimus, leaving a premium on better tolerated oral disease modifying therapies that reduce lesion volume, lymphedema and thrombosis prone coagulopathy and lessen dependence on chronic supportive care.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral, injection-sparing control of localized intravascular coagulopathy (LIC; D‑dimer–high) in extensive venous malformations to prevent thrombosis/VTE/PE while minimizing bleeding/DIC risk
- Systemic lesion-shrinking therapy for symptomatic KTS/PROS achieving MRI volumetric reduction plus pain/fatigue/bleeding/oozing improvement with lower toxicity/monitoring burden than alpelisib/sirolimus
- Drug therapy that reduces chronic limb swelling/lymphedema/venous insufficiency enough to cut reliance on lifelong daily compression garments and home pneumatic compression

name: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
description: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked infant-onset disorder marked by microthrombocytopenia with serious bleeding risk plus immune deficiency, eczema, and recurrent infections, with increasing autoimmunity and lymphoma risk over time. Care is burdensome and largely supportive, while definitive options have been constrained by donor availability and toxicity. The key unmet need is donor-independent, lower-toxicity disease correction that reliably restores immune function and raises platelets to clinically meaningful levels such as above 50,000/µL.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacologic restoration of platelet count (e.g., >50,000/µL) to prevent severe/life‑threatening bleeding in WAS microthrombocytopenia.
- Conditioning-sparing, donor-independent definitive correction for severe WAS patients lacking a suitable HLA-matched related donor (avoiding HSCT conditioning/GVHD and frequent IVIG/prophylaxis burden).
- Steroid/rituximab-sparing targeted control of eczema and autoimmunity (e.g., hemolytic anemia/vasculitis/arthritis) without increasing infection risk.

name: Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome
description: Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome is a rare distal 4p deletion disorder causing prenatal and postnatal growth failure with hypotonia, intellectual disability and epilepsy plus characteristic craniofacial features. Infants often struggle with feeding and weight gain, while seizures can be treatment resistant and drive repeated medical crises. Many children have relatively strong social engagement but limited verbal language and some remain nonverbal and need constant care. Care is largely supportive, leaving major unmet needs for therapies that meaningfully reduce seizure burden, improve nutrition and growth, and strengthen communication and daily functioning.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Infant/early-childhood pharmaco-resistant epilepsy (esp. larger deletions) needing reduced status-epilepticus events and ASM burden
- Severe feeding failure/GI dysfunction (dysmotility/malabsorption) needing reduced tube-feeding dependence
- Persistent verbal language/expressive communication impairment needing CNS therapies that improve communication function

name: Koolen de Vries syndrome
description: Koolen de Vries syndrome is a rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorder caused by KANSL1 haploinsufficiency, most often from a 17q21.31 microdeletion, presenting in infancy with hypotonia and feeding difficulties and near universal speech and language delay. About one third develop epilepsy, often prolonged focal seizures, and care today is largely supportive with no cure. The unmet need is disease modifying therapy that improves early motor and feeding function, enables meaningful communication, and better controls seizures rather than managing symptoms.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-active KANSL1-upregulation therapy to improve the core oral hypotonia/apraxia–driven communication deficit (earlier first words; reduced AAC dependence)
- Drug therapy to reduce neonatal/infant hypotonia-related feeding dysfunction (avoid hospitalization/NG-tube feeding; achieve safe oral feeding/weight gain)
- KdVS-phenotype–targeted epilepsy therapy for prolonged childhood-onset focal seizures with autonomic features (better seizure duration/frequency control than generic ASMs)

name: Krabbe disease
description: Krabbe disease is a rare, devastating demyelinating leukodystrophy that usually begins in infancy with irritability, feeding difficulties, unexplained fevers, stiffness, and developmental delay, and most children with the classic form die by age 2. Treatment remains largely supportive, with hematopoietic cell transplantation only for very early disease and carrying significant risk, leaving a premium on therapies that can be delivered presymptomatically and broadly restore function across both the central and peripheral nervous systems. Early stage gene transfer approaches are beginning clinical testing.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy for symptomatic early-infantile patients (>1–9 months; symptom onset <6 months) that improves survival plus neurodevelopmental milestones vs HSCT/natural history
- Therapies that control both CNS and progressive PNS disease with measurable improvements/maintenance in peripheral nerve conduction
- Transplant-free or conditioning-minimized options to reduce HSCT toxicity and expand access beyond newborn-screened populations

name: Kyasanur forest disease
description: Tick-borne viral haemorrhagic fever endemic to India’s Western Ghats, causing abrupt febrile illness and sometimes biphasic neurologic relapse in ~20% with 2–10% fatality; care is largely supportive with no definitive antivirals, and prevention relies on a multi-year booster vaccine with suboptimal durability and acceptability, leaving a need for easy-to-deploy therapeutics and simpler, longer-lasting prophylaxis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early, easy-to-deploy antiviral therapy to reduce KFD mortality (~3–10%) vs supportive care only
- Treatment to prevent/mitigate the ~10–20% second-phase meningoencephalitis (tremors/convulsions/coma)
- Single-visit seasonal prophylaxis/post-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk forest/tribal populations to replace multi-dose, variably effective vaccine

name: Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia | tarda
description: Rare TRAPPC2 related X-linked skeletal dysplasia with normal early growth followed by mid-childhood onset (about ages 6 to 10) disproportionate short trunk stature, platyspondyly and spinal deformity, hip deformity and progressive back and joint pain. Burden escalates into early degenerative osteoarthritis and disability, sometimes requiring hip replacement by around age 40. Care is largely symptomatic and orthopedic, leaving a need for disease modifying approaches that preserve growth, cartilage and joint function and reduce lifelong surgeries and pain.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- TRAPPC2-targeted disease modification in the X‑linked (typically male) population initiated during the ~6–8y growth-slowing window to preserve spine/trunk growth.
- Disease-modifying chondroprotection to prevent/slow early-adulthood osteoarthritis (hips/knees/shoulders), delaying/avoiding arthroplasty (e.g., hip replacement by ~40y).
- Pharmacologic reduction of scoliosis/kyphoscoliosis progression to reduce need for corrective spine surgery and ongoing orthopedic surveillance burden.

name: Xia-Gibbs Syndrome
description: Xia-Gibbs syndrome is a rare, underdiagnosed AHDC1-related neurodevelopmental disorder starting in infancy with hypotonia, feeding problems, and common obstructive sleep apnea, followed by delayed motor milestones, intellectual disability, and markedly impaired expressive language with occasional seizures. Management is largely supportive and symptomatic, relying on therapy services plus standard epilepsy care and burdensome apnea interventions such as continuous positive airway pressure or adenotonsillectomy. The central unmet need is a disease modifying approach that targets the underlying biology while improving pharmacologic options for sleep disordered breathing and better tolerated, evidence based seizure control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- AHDC1-deficiency–targeted therapy (drug/genome editing) to improve core neurodevelopment—meaningful expressive-language gains (incl. achieving speech) and improved motor milestones.
- Pharmacologic reduction of obstructive sleep apnea / sleep-related breathing pauses to reduce reliance on surgery and CPAP.
- XGS-specific epilepsy control that reduces seizure burden with good developmental tolerability (no added cognitive/motor impairment).

name: Lafora disease
description: Lafora disease is a rare autosomal recessive teenage onset progressive myoclonus epilepsy marked by occipital visual seizures, worsening myoclonus, cognitive decline and ataxia. Aberrant glycogen metabolism drives accumulation of insoluble polyglucosan Lafora bodies, leading to drug resistant seizures, frequent status epilepticus, rapid loss of independence by the mid twenties, and death within about a decade. Current anti seizure medicines may briefly suppress generalized seizures but do not slow neurodegeneration, leaving major unmet need for disease modifying therapies that reduce Lafora bodies and provide durable, better tolerated seizure control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying Lafora-body reduction/clearance in teen-onset disease to delay disability progression.
- Durable control of pharmacoresistant myoclonus/seizures (including status epilepticus) to prevent early functional collapse.
- Better-tolerated, less burdensome long-term therapy than current polypharmacy, avoiding cognitive/GI toxicity and invasive/frequent intrathecal or IV dosing.

name: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
description: Lambert Eaton myasthenic syndrome is a rare autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder where antibodies against presynaptic P/Q type voltage gated calcium channels reduce acetylcholine release, causing progressive proximal weakness with autonomic symptoms that can severely impair mobility. Up to 60 percent of cases are paraneoplastic, most often linked to small cell lung cancer, and neuromuscular symptoms may precede cancer detection. Treatment remains largely symptomatic and burdensome, with amifampridine requiring 3 to 5 daily doses and carrying seizure risk, while severe disease often relies on broad immunosuppression or high dose immunoglobulins rather than targeted durable control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- All‑day (≤BID) symptomatic control with objective mobility/strength benefit to replace short‑acting amifampridine requiring 3–4×/day dosing
- Seizure‑safe symptomatic alternative for patients with seizure history who cannot use amifampridine
- Targeted non–broadly immunosuppressive disease‑control therapy that reduces anti‑VGCC autoimmunity and improves persistent autonomic/QoL impairment while avoiding chronic steroids/azathioprine and IVIG/plasmapheresis rescue (esp. SCLC‑LEMS)

name: Landau-Kleffner syndrome
description: Rare childhood epilepsy-aphasia syndrome with normal early development followed by acquired language loss (speech and comprehension), sleep-activated electroencephalogram abnormalities and often sleep seizures. Care is largely empirical using steroids, benzodiazepines and other antiseizure medicines plus urgent speech therapy, but durable language recovery is inconsistent, driving unmet need for steroid-sparing, evidence-based and genotype-guided treatments including for GRIN2A-related disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid, durable suppression of sleep‑activated spike‑wave activity to prevent permanent receptive→expressive language disability.
- Steroid‑sparing anti‑inflammatory regimens with steroid‑like efficacy but lower toxicity/discontinuation burden.
- Precision, non‑sedating genotype‑guided treatments for the ~20% GRIN2A‑positive subgroup to improve EEG/language outcomes and reduce benzodiazepine burden.

name: Langerhans-cell histiocytosis
description: Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a rare clonal disorder of immature dendritic Langerhans cells with presentations ranging from isolated painful bone lesions or scalp rash to disseminated multisystem disease. Frontline care still relies on vinblastine plus prednisone, but relapses and late sequelae are common, including central diabetes insipidus and severe neurodegenerative central nervous system involvement. The biggest needs are more durable first line control with less steroid and chemotherapy toxicity, earlier recognition when skin disease mimics benign rashes, and central nervous system active targeted options for molecular subsets such as BRAF V600E.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Improve frontline systemic efficacy in multisystem/disseminated LCH (raise 12‑month “no active disease”/cure rate above ~48% and reduce need for salvage therapy).
- Steroid/vinblastine/6‑MP–sparing (ideally oral) regimens to avoid key toxicities and reduce prolonged injection/maintenance burden.
- CNS‑penetrant therapy for neurodegenerative LCH to stabilize/improve MRI T2/FLAIR lesions and prevent progressive neurologic decline.

name: Laron syndrome
description: Laron syndrome is a rare pediatric growth hormone insensitivity caused by growth hormone receptor dysfunction, with near normal birth size followed by profound postnatal growth failure and severe short stature, sometimes with infant hypoglycemia and delayed puberty. Insulin-like growth factor 1 replacement can help but is burdensome, requiring strict meal-timed dosing and hypoglycemia vigilance, and even with long-term treatment many patients still end well below normal adult height.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Lower-burden IGF‑1–pathway therapy that avoids twice‑daily, meal/snack‑timed injections and refrigerated multi‑dose vial logistics.
- Growth promotion with materially reduced hypoglycemia risk/monitoring burden (and less need for food-coupled dosing/withholding).
- Therapies that deliver meaningfully better near‑adult/final adult height outcomes than current rhIGF‑1 (mecasermin).

name: Larsen syndrome
description: Rare congenital genetic skeletal disorder with large joint dislocations and clubfoot at birth; cervical spine dysplasia can cause spinal cord injury and paralysis risk. Care is symptom-directed with casting or traction in infancy, frequent orthopedic surgeries and sometimes cervical fusion, plus long-term therapy, and patients may develop osteoarthritis later in life; major unmet need is safer, disease-modifying approaches that reduce early neurologic risk and lifelong orthopedic burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-life (prenatal→neonatal/infant) disease-modifying therapy to reduce congenital large-joint dislocations enough to avoid serial casting/traction and later operative reductions
- Non-surgical cervical-spine–stabilizing therapy to prevent neonatal cervical instability and reduce myelopathy risk (fewer fusions/arthrodeses)
- Joint-protective pharmacotherapy for adolescents/adults with painful/dislocated joints to delay/avoid early hip/knee arthroplasty (improve pain/function; extend time-to-replacement)

name: Laurence-Moon syndrome
description: Ultra-rare autosomal recessive PNPLA6 related multisystem disorder causing childhood onset progressive ataxia, peripheral neuropathy and spastic paraplegia with chorioretinal dystrophy driven vision loss and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Care is symptomatic only with physical therapy and visual aids, leaving a major unmet need for disease modifying therapy that preserves vision and slows neurologic decline.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that prevent/slow chorioretinal dystrophy–driven retinal atrophy to preserve BCVA, visual fields, and OCT structure.
- Disease-modifying treatment that slows progression of ataxia/spastic paraplegia/peripheral neuropathy with improved SARA and SPRS trajectories.
- Restorative endocrine therapies that normalize pituitary/gonadal function to achieve puberty/sex-steroid milestones without lifelong hormone replacement.

name: Leber congenital amaurosis
description: Leber congenital amaurosis is a retinal disorder present from birth causing severe vision loss in infancy with nystagmus, abnormal pupillary light responses, and characteristic eye rubbing. It is genetically heterogeneous with around 20 causal genes, but the only approved gene therapy is limited to biallelic RPE65 disease and requires subretinal surgery, systemic steroids, and carries ocular risks such as cataract and retinal tears, with no recommended use under 12 months. This leaves major unmet need for earlier, safer, simpler, genotype-specific treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapies delivering BCVA/functional-vision benefit for LCA genotypes beyond biallelic *RPE65* (Luxturna-ineligible patients).
- Less invasive, simpler delivery than subretinal injection (ideally avoiding staged bilateral surgery/systemic steroids) with lower ocular complication burden.
- Safe, effective treatment options for infants <12 months to enable earlier retinal rescue before loss of viable retinal cells.

name: Lemierre syndrome
description: Rare, life threatening post anginal sepsis in otherwise healthy adolescents or young adults, progressing within days from sore throat to internal jugular vein septic thrombophlebitis and metastatic septic emboli often to the lungs. Treatment relies on prolonged broad anaerobe active antibiotics for 4 to 6 weeks and often inpatient care, with limited ability to target therapy or shorten courses. Management of thrombosis is inconsistent because anticoagulation remains controversial and lacks controlled trial evidence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Validated short-course, outpatient-friendly *Fusobacterium*-active therapy (oral and/or long-acting parenteral) to replace typical 4–6-week antibiotics and reduce ~3-week hospitalization.
- Narrow-spectrum regimen with predictable activity vs beta-lactamase–producing/penicillin-nonsusceptible *F. necrophorum* to avoid penicillin failures and reduce broad empiric coverage.
- Adjunct therapy for septic thrombophlebitis (e.g., anticoagulant and/or anti-thromboinflammatory/anti-virulence) proven to reduce thrombus extension and embolic complications.

name: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome
description: Rare X linked purine metabolism disorder in boys caused by hypoxanthine guanine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency, leading to uric acid overproduction with gout and kidney stones plus infant onset dystonia and later compulsive self injury. Uric acid lowering with allopurinol helps renal and gout complications but not the neurologic or behavioral disease and must be balanced to avoid xanthine stones, leaving a major need for disease modifying therapies that preserve mobility and prevent self harm.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Infancy-onset therapy that meaningfully reduces generalized dystonia to preserve functional mobility (standing/walking endpoint).
- Pharmacologic therapy around tooth eruption that reduces self-injurious biting frequency/severity and avoids restraints/dental extraction.
- Urate-lowering strategy that prevents renal failure/stones while minimizing xanthine lithiasis without requiring highly precise dosing.

name: Leydig cell tumor
description: Rare sex cord–stromal testicular tumor arising from testosterone producing Leydig cells, typically in men 30 to 60, presenting with painless testicular swelling and endocrine effects such as gynecomastia, infertility, or hypogonadism. Most are benign and cured with orchiectomy or testis sparing surgery, but the malignant metastatic subset is chemo radiation resistant with no standard systemic therapy and risk of late metastases, creating a need for effective drugs, relapse prevention, and fertility preserving approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable effective systemic therapy for metastatic/malignant Leydig cell tumor (objective responses and survival benefit in chemo/radiation–resistant disease).
- Adjuvant/neoadjuvant drug therapy for high-risk localized tumors to prevent late relapse/metastasis and reduce prolonged surveillance needs.
- Testis-preserving medical tumor control that maintains fertility/endocrine function and avoids orchiectomy-associated hypogonadism/long-term testosterone replacement.

name: Loeffler endocarditis
description: Uncommon eosinophil mediated restrictive cardiomyopathy linked to hypereosinophilic syndromes that progresses from necrotic injury to intracardiac thrombosis and endomyocardial fibrosis, causing diastolic dysfunction, heart failure symptoms, arrhythmias, and embolic events. Care centers on controlling eosinophilia and anticoagulating documented thrombus, but outcomes hinge on catching disease before irreversible fibrosis, when effective medical options are limited. Key unmet needs include earlier recognition, faster and safer clot control, and therapies that prevent or reverse cardiac fibrosis and restore function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid thrombus-resolution/embolism-prevention therapies for LV thrombus despite warfarin + steroids
- Anti-fibrotic/reverse-remodeling agents to improve restrictive filling/heart-failure physiology in fibrotic-stage disease
- Steroid-sparing eosinophil-directed therapies that rapidly reduce eosinophils and prevent progression to fibrosis (esp. steroid-nonresponsive patients)

name: Loeys-Dietz syndrome
description: Loeys-Dietz syndrome is a genetic connective tissue disorder driven by transforming growth factor beta pathway variants, marked by aggressive aortic and systemic arterial aneurysms and dissections plus craniofacial features and frequent allergic or inflammatory disease. Management relies on lifelong whole-arterial-tree imaging and blood pressure lowering drugs, yet dissections can occur at younger ages and smaller diameters, there is no trial proven best pharmacotherapy to slow progression, and immune comorbidities complicate treatment choices such as beta blocker use in asthma.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Randomized-trial–proven pharmacotherapy that slows aortic growth and reduces dissection/rupture risk in high-risk LDS patients who dissect at young age/small diameters
- Whole-arterial-tree aneurysm-prevention therapy that reduces clinically meaningful events (prophylactic repair/dissection/rupture), including cerebral aneurysms
- Targeted immunomodulatory therapy for LDS-associated allergic/inflammatory disease (e.g., asthma/eczema/food allergy/eosinophilic esophagitis/IBD)

name: Lown-Ganong-Levine syndrome
description: Extremely rare, controversial cardiac conduction phenotype marked by a short PR interval with normal QRS and intermittent atrial tachyarrhythmias causing sudden palpitations, dyspnea, and sometimes presyncope or syncope, with patients often well between attacks. Care relies on vagal maneuvers and monitored intravenous adenosine for acute termination, plus atrioventricular node blocking drugs or catheter ablation for prevention, leaving unmet need for fast, reliable self administered rescue and better tolerated long term control despite heterogeneous underlying mechanisms.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- At-home, non‑IV rescue therapy to terminate regular PSVT within ~1–2 minutes without syncope risk
- Preventive therapy reducing recurrent PSVT episodes without AV‑nodal–blocker hypotension/bradycardia limits or verapamil contraindications in accessory‑pathway settings (incl. LGL)
- Lower‑proarrhythmia rhythm‑control option for disabling/refractory PSVT to improve safety vs class Ic agents (e.g., flecainide) and reduce need for ablation/daily meds

name: Ludwig’s angina
description: Ludwig’s angina is a rapidly progressive, life threatening deep neck cellulitis of the floor of mouth, usually arising from lower molar odontogenic infection, that can rapidly cause brawny submandibular swelling, dysphagia, and airway compromise. Management is high acuity with airway protection, broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and sometimes drainage or tooth extraction, often requiring intensive care. Key unmet needs include earlier, more reliable control of edema to prevent invasive airway procedures and simpler, safer empiric regimens with predictable coverage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer single-regimen empiric antibiotic covering mixed oral aerobes/anaerobes plus MRSA-risk patients while lowering C. difficile/colitis and AKI risk vs current multi-drug regimens
- Evidence-backed anti-edema adjunct that rapidly reduces airway/floor-of-mouth swelling early enough to prevent within-hours airway obstruction and reduce invasive airway procedures
- Therapy/strategy enabling earlier step-down or outpatient completion by reducing the need for ICU/OR-level airway readiness and intense observation

name: MASA syndrome
description: MASA syndrome is a monogenic X linked L1CAM related neurodevelopmental disorder affecting mostly males, with early hypotonia and developmental delay that progresses to spasticity or spastic paraplegia, delayed speech, adducted thumbs, and ventriculomegaly or hydrocephalus. Care is lifelong and symptom focused such as therapies, spasticity management and cerebrospinal fluid shunting when needed, but there is no cure and no proven way to prevent or delay progression, creating a major unmet need for disease modifying treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- L1CAM-targeted disease-modifying therapy in neonatal-onset MASA to prevent hypotonia→spastic paraplegia and improve intellectual disability/speech outcomes beyond supportive care.
- Better-tolerated spasticity drugs with less drowsiness/weakness and lower habit-forming/respiratory-depression risk than baclofen/tizanidine/diazepam (and safer alternatives to botulinum toxin where appropriate).
- Lower-burden spasticity regimens (e.g., long-acting formulations/routes) that reduce frequent dosing (multiple times daily) and repeat botulinum toxin visits.

name: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers
description: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers (MERRF) is a childhood or adolescent onset multisystem mitochondrial disorder affecting brain and muscle, marked by progressive myoclonus, myopathy, seizures, ataxia, neuropathy and cognitive decline, sometimes with hearing loss, optic atrophy and cardiomyopathy. Care is largely symptomatic with no disease modifying therapy, and even seizure management is limited by mitochondrial toxicity risks such as avoiding valproic acid. The major unmet need is safe treatments that slow progression and improve neurologic and muscular function, ideally targeted to common MT-TK mutations such as m.8344A>G.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- MT‑TK (m.8344A>G) mutation–targeted disease modification for the ~80% of MERRF patients in this genotype subgroup
- Mitochondrial-safe control of action myoclonus and generalized seizures that avoids valproate and other myoclonus-worsening ASMs
- Disease-specific therapies to prevent/treat MERRF cardiac arrhythmia/ventricular dysfunction and reduce cardiac failure/sudden-death risk beyond standard cardiology care

name: Maffucci syndrome
description: Maffucci syndrome is a very rare childhood-onset disorder of bone and skin marked by multiple benign cartilage tumors in bone that cause asymmetric deformity, limb shortening, and fractures, alongside vascular malformations such as blue subcutaneous hemangiomas. A core clinical and commercial challenge is lifelong risk of malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma and other cancers, driving ongoing surveillance and repeated, complication-driven procedures. With no specific medical therapy and surgery as the mainstay when complications arise, there is a major unmet need for disease-modifying treatments, particularly those that can leverage common somatic IDH1 or IDH2 mutations.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral, disease-modifying targeted therapy for IDH1/IDH2‑mutant enchondromas that reduces pain and radiographic lesion burden and delays fractures/orthopedic resections
- Non-surgical pharmacologic control of venous malformations/hemangiomas that reduces lesion size/symptoms enough to avoid repeat sclerotherapy and surgery
- Therapies that lower malignant transformation risk and/or treat early IDH‑mutant malignant change (e.g., chondrosarcoma) with endpoints like incidence/time-to-malignancy

name: Mahvash disease
description: Ultra-rare inherited pancreatic tumor syndrome from loss of glucagon receptor function, causing pancreatic alpha-cell hyperplasia and neuroendocrine tumors with extreme hyperglucagonemia but no classic glucagonoma syndrome and occasional hypoglycemia. Patients often present with nonspecific abdominal symptoms and pancreatic enlargement or masses, then enter long-term surveillance with repeat imaging and procedures. Care is largely watchful waiting for small lesions and surgery for larger ones; somatostatin analogues can lower glucagon but are an imperfect bridge, leaving a major need for pancreas-sparing, disease-modifying strategies that prevent progression and metastasis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-transplant restoration of hepatic glucagon receptor (GCGR) signaling to durably normalize glucagon and reverse pancreatic hypertrophy/α-cell hyperplasia.
- Better-tolerated, evidence-backed chronic hyperglucagonemia control vs octreotide (lower burden than monthly long-acting injections) with sustained plasma glucagon lowering.
- Pancreas-sparing medical control of Mahvash-associated PNETs to avoid size-threshold resections/total pancreatectomy, measured by radiographic stabilization/shrinkage and reduced pancreatectomy rates.

name: Marinesco-Sjogren syndrome
description: Marinesco Sjögren syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive multisystem neuromuscular disorder that begins in infancy with hypotonia and evolves into progressive myopathy, early cataracts, and cerebellar ataxia that can severely limit mobility and function. Most cases are caused by SIL1 mutations linked to impaired protein folding and endoplasmic reticulum stress. Care is largely supportive and surgical, with cataracts often requiring lens extraction in childhood, and there are no disease modifying therapies, leaving a major unmet need for treatments that preserve vision and slow neurologic and muscle decline.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- SIL1-targeted disease modification (e.g., gene/mRNA/protein replacement or pathway restoration) for genetically confirmed MSS to prevent progressive myopathy/ataxia-related ambulatory disability.
- Non-surgical drug therapy to prevent/delay early-life rapidly progressive cataracts to avoid or meaningfully delay pediatric lens-extraction surgery.
- Better-tolerated, lower-burden hypertonia/dystonia control (less sedating; less frequent dosing/procedure dependence) to reduce reliance on baclofen/tizanidine/botulinum toxins.

name: McCune Albright syndrome
description: McCune Albright syndrome is a rare, non inherited mosaic disorder caused by postzygotic GNAS variants that affects bone, skin, and endocrine tissues, often presenting in childhood with café au lait macules, peripheral precocious puberty, and fibrous dysplasia leading to fractures, deformity, limp, craniofacial asymmetry, and chronic pain. Care is largely symptomatic with no cure or approved disease modifying therapy, leaving major unmet needs in controlling bone lesions, achieving safer durable hormone suppression, and improving long term pain management.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Fibrous-dysplasia lesion–modifying therapy that reduces lesion progression/activity on imaging (e.g., Na18F-PET/CT; skeletal burden score) and lowers fracture/deformity risk
- More reliable, ovary-safe pharmacotherapy for MAS-associated peripheral precocious puberty in girls that stops recurrent vaginal bleeding and prevents bone-age advancement/adult-height compromise
- Non-bisphosphonate options for sustained, clinically meaningful FD/MAS bone-pain reduction in patients with persistent moderate–severe pain and/or bisphosphonate non-response, ideally with less burdensome administration than IV antiresorptives

name: Meckel syndrome
description: Meckel syndrome is a rare, lethal autosomal recessive ciliopathy typically detected on first trimester ultrasound with cystic kidneys, occipital encephalocele, and polydactyly, often leading to oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia and death before or shortly after birth from respiratory failure or kidney failure. There is no treatment, leaving a premium on early prenatal confirmation and ultimately in utero, gene agnostic interventions that preserve fetal renal function and amniotic fluid to prevent lung hypoplasia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- In‑utero (≥12 gestational weeks) mutation‑targeted therapy restoring primary‑cilium function across genetically heterogeneous MKS genes to prevent lethal multi‑organ malformations.
- Fetal renal cystic‑dysplasia disease modification to preserve fetal renal function/amniotic fluid (prevent oligohydramnios) and avert pulmonary hypoplasia/kidney-failure–driven early death.
- Early‑gestation correction of cilia‑dependent embryonic signaling (e.g., Wnt/Shh) to reduce CNS malformations (e.g., occipital encephalocele) contributing to non‑viability.

name: Menkes disease
description: Menkes disease is an infantile onset X linked ATP7A copper transport disorder causing systemic copper deficiency and rapid neurodegeneration. Infants often appear normal at birth then develop hypotonia, seizures, failure to thrive and characteristic brittle kinky hair within weeks, with high mortality by early childhood. Copper histidinate can help but only when started in the neonatal window, and brain delivery across the blood brain barrier remains a bottleneck. Key unmet needs are newborn era diagnosis, safer and less burdensome long term therapy, and disease modifying approaches that restore ATP7A function and prevent irreversible central nervous system injury.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-effective treatment that improves neurodevelopment and survival in infants treated after symptom onset/late diagnosis (>1 month)
- ATP7A function–restoring therapies (e.g., gene/splice/molecular rescue) for copper-nonresponsive, genotype-dependent nonresponders
- Long-acting/less toxic copper replacement that reduces twice-daily injections, monitoring burden, and copper-accumulation toxicity risk

name: Merkel cell carcinoma
description: Merkel cell carcinoma is a rare, highly aggressive neuroendocrine skin cancer of older adults, often presenting as a rapidly growing painless violaceous nodule on sun exposed skin, driven by ultraviolet damage, immunosuppression, and Merkel cell polyomavirus. It metastasizes early to lymph nodes and beyond. Immune checkpoint inhibitors improved outcomes, but many patients still relapse or lack durable control, and evidence is limited for immunosuppressed populations often excluded from trials, leaving a need for more durable and broadly usable systemic and perioperative therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable tumor control for PD-(L)1–refractory advanced MCC (primary/acquired resistance).
- Systemic therapies for immunosuppressed MCC patients excluded from ICI trials (e.g., CLL; transplant) that avoid severe toxicity such as graft failure.
- Effective adjuvant/neoadjuvant systemic therapy for high-risk resected MCC to prevent early systemic recurrence.

name: Middle East respiratory syndrome
description: Middle East respiratory syndrome is a zoonotic coronavirus infection that can spill over from camels and amplify via person to person transmission, especially in hospitals. It ranges from fever, cough, and shortness of breath to pneumonia and respiratory or multi organ failure requiring intensive care, with roughly one third mortality in reported cases. Severe disease concentrates in older adults and people with chronic comorbidities. With no licensed vaccine or specific therapy, management remains supportive, leaving major unmet needs for rapid acting antivirals or antibodies, post exposure prophylaxis for healthcare workers and close contacts, and ICU rescue options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early, outpatient-startable antiviral/neutralizing therapy for high‑risk patients (>65 and/or major comorbidities) to prevent progression to pneumonia and hospitalization/ICU
- Hospital/ICU rescue therapy that reduces mortality and increases organ‑support–free days in severe MERS with respiratory/organ failure
- Post‑exposure prophylaxis (e.g., long‑acting mAb) for healthcare workers/close contacts to block healthcare‑amplified transmission

name: Mikulicz disease
description: IgG4 related Mikulicz disease is a fibroinflammatory disorder causing persistent, usually painless bilateral swelling of lacrimal and major salivary glands with dry eyes and dry mouth, often in middle aged to older women and sometimes part of systemic IgG4 related disease. Steroids induce initial control, but relapses are common after taper and progressive fibrosis can become hard to reverse, leaving a need for durable steroid sparing therapies that prevent flares and preserve gland structure and function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing maintenance to achieve durable flare-free, corticosteroid-free remission after glucocorticoid taper/discontinuation
- Anti-fibrotic/anti-scarring control that preserves lacrimal/salivary gland structure and function (beyond transient swelling reduction)
- Long-term remission strategies with improved safety vs chronic systemic immunosuppression (e.g., lower infection risk, less prolonged low-dose steroid exposure)

name: Miller Fisher syndrome
description: Rare post-infectious autoimmune Guillain-Barré variant causing ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, and areflexia (often anti-GQ1b positive) with risk of respiratory compromise; usually self-limited with near-full recovery in 2–3 months, but care relies on hospitalization and empiric intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange despite limited evidence and no randomized placebo-controlled trials.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that measurably shorten time to functional recovery (e.g., faster resolution of ataxia/ophthalmoplegia) versus current uncertain immunotherapy benefit.
- Early high-efficacy treatment for the first-week “overlap” subgroup to prevent progression to severe weakness/respiratory failure.
- Lower-burden outpatient immunomodulation (avoiding multi-day IVIg/serial plasmapheresis), ideally targeting anti‑GQ1b/complement-mediated injury.

name: Miller-Dieker syndrome
description: Miller Dieker syndrome is a rare 17p13.3 deletion disorder often involving PAFAH1B1 and YWHAE that disrupts brain development and causes severe lissencephaly with profound developmental delay, hypotonia, and hard to control seizures. Infants frequently develop dysphagia, reflux, failure to thrive, and aspiration requiring tube feeding and respiratory support. Care is largely palliative and symptom focused, with no curative or disease modifying therapy, creating major unmet needs for safer seizure control, swallow sparing supportive care, and gene informed approaches that change the course of disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer, lower-burden control of drug‑resistant infantile spasms in MDS (rapid spasm cessation without vigabatrin vision-loss/REMS or ACTH infection–hypertension toxicity).
- Swallowing/feeding-directed therapeutics that avoid gastrostomy/tube feeding and reduce aspiration events/aspiration pneumonia.
- Root-cause molecular therapies for 17p13.3 deletion MDS (e.g., JAK/STAT3 or mTOR modulation) to improve neurodevelopmental milestone attainment and multi-symptom severity beyond seizure palliation.

name: Miyoshi muscular dystrophy
description: Miyoshi muscular dystrophy is an inherited distal myopathy, usually from DYSF or ANO5 mutations, starting in young adulthood with calf weakness and atrophy that makes running or standing on tiptoe difficult and slowly spreads proximally to impair stairs and longer walks, sometimes progressing to wheelchair use. Creatine kinase is typically markedly elevated. Care remains symptomatic with no approved disease modifying therapy, and corticosteroids may be harmful, leaving a premium on treatments that preserve muscle function and address the technical challenge of restoring dysferlin, a gene too large for single adeno-associated virus delivery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemic dysferlin restoration (e.g., IV gene transfer) to achieve meaningful DYSF protein expression and improve early function (tiptoe/toe-walking, stair climbing) to delay wheelchair dependence.
- Genotype-targeted dysferlin “rescue” for missense DYSF variants to boost functional protein via proteostasis approaches and provide a non-steroid option (avoiding detrimental prednisone exposure).
- ANO5-targeted therapy for distal anoctaminopathy (ANO5-mutant Miyoshi myopathy) to slow distal calf weakness/declining walking endurance and reduce progression to wheelchair need.

name: Melanoma | acral lentiginous
description: Uncommon melanoma of the palms, soles, or nail unit that is often misdiagnosed and diagnosed late, so few patients present at stage I; advanced disease responds less well to standard immune checkpoint inhibitors and has limited actionable targets beyond a minority with KIT mutations, creating a need for better early detection and alternative systemic options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Metastatic ALM therapies that substantially improve response and durability vs current PD‑1–based regimens, especially in nail‑apparatus ALM (very low ORR)
- Targeted therapies for ALM beyond BRAF/MEK that address copy-number/amplification-driven biology (e.g., CCND1/MDM2) and KIT-mutant (~15%) precision subgroup
- ALM-specific validated perioperative (adjuvant/neoadjuvant) systemic strategies for resectable high-risk disease (not extrapolated from cutaneous melanoma trials)

name: Moebius syndrome
description: Moebius syndrome is a rare congenital neurologic disorder, often due to underdeveloped cranial nerves VI and VII, causing facial paralysis and impaired eye movement with early-life feeding problems, drooling and exposure-related eye damage. Care is largely multidisciplinary and symptomatic, with no disease-modifying therapy, leaving unmet needs for nerve-restoring approaches plus more durable ocular surface protection and safer long-acting control of drooling.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-life neuroregenerative/gene-based therapy to restore cranial nerve VI/VII function (ocular abduction + facial expression)
- Safer, longer-acting sialorrhea control to reduce aspiration risk without systemic anticholinergic toxicity
- Long-duration ocular-surface protection to prevent exposure keratopathy/corneal ulceration while reducing hourly drops + nightly taping

name: Mooren's ulcer
description: Mooren’s ulcer is an ultra rare idiopathic corneal ulcer diagnosed by exclusion, causing severe pain, photophobia, tearing and a red eye as a peripheral ulcer spreads circumferentially and centrally with perforation risk. Care starts with topical corticosteroids and may escalate to immunosuppression and surgery, but relapse is common at about 25.6% after procedures and most recurrences occur within 2 to 6 months. Steroid toxicity and weak comparative evidence leave a need for rapid anti melt rescue and durable steroid sparing control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable relapse-prevention/maintenance therapy to reduce postoperative recurrence (~25.6%), especially in the high-risk first 2–6 months
- Rapid “anti-melt” therapy for severe progressive disease (e.g., bilateral, >50% stromal loss/impending perforation) to prevent perforation/vision loss without inpatient high-dose systemic steroids
- Steroid-/systemic-immunosuppression–sparing long-acting local therapy that controls inflammation while avoiding topical steroid toxicities (IOP/glaucoma, cataract, delayed healing) and systemic immunosuppression risks

name: Mowat-Wilson syndrome
description: Mowat-Wilson syndrome is a rare ZEB2-driven multisystem genetic disorder presenting at birth or early childhood with severe developmental delay, profound expressive language impairment, frequent childhood seizures, and major gastrointestinal morbidity including Hirschsprung disease and refractory constipation. Care is largely supportive rather than disease modifying, leaving high unmet need for therapies that meaningfully improve communication, epilepsy control, and gut motility.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Expressive-language/communication–improving therapeutics to move children beyond absent/few-word speech toward functional communication.
- Childhood epilepsy/ESES therapies that reliably control difficult-to-treat seizures and prevent ESES-associated developmental/physical skill loss.
- GI motility/enteric-function drugs to substantially reduce severe constipation/obstructive symptoms, including constipation persisting post–Hirschsprung surgery.

name: Moyamoya disease
description: Moyamoya disease is a rare, progressive cerebrovascular disorder in which the internal carotid and branch arteries progressively narrow, reducing cerebral blood flow and triggering fragile collateral vessels. It often presents in school age children with recurrent transient ischemic attacks or strokes causing episodic weakness, speech problems, and potential cognitive or developmental disability. Revascularization surgery can reduce future stroke risk, but untreated disease accumulates permanent injury and there are no disease modifying drugs, with medical strategies like antiplatelets showing uncertain benefit for preventing ischemic stroke.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Progression‑modifying drug that slows/halts intracranial stenosis/CBV‑reserve decline and reduces recurrent ischemic events (non‑surgical alternative).
- CBF‑normalizing/hemodynamic‑augmenting therapy (standalone or peri/post‑revascularization) that improves pediatric neurocognitive outcomes (IQ/executive function).
- Proven next‑gen antithrombotic for non‑hemorrhagic Moyamoya with net ischemic‑event reduction and minimized ICH/bleeding risk vs empiric aspirin.

name: Muckle-Wells syndrome
description: Muckle-Wells syndrome is an ultra-rare cryopyrin-associated autoinflammatory disease that typically starts in infancy or early childhood with recurrent inflammatory flares of non-itchy rash, fever, painful swollen joints, and sometimes conjunctivitis. The long-term stakes are preventing irreversible organ damage, especially progressive sensorineural hearing loss that often becomes apparent in the teen years and amyloid driven kidney disease in about one-third of patients. Even with anti interleukin 1 biologics, some patients continue to lose hearing or have residual symptoms, keeping demand high for durable disease control with lower treatment burden, including oral small-molecule NLR family pyrin domain containing 3 inhibition.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Eliminate persistent fatigue/cognitive fatigue in “inactive” MWS/CAPS and stabilize or reverse progressive high‑frequency sensorineural hearing loss
- Prevent and ideally reverse AA amyloidosis–driven renal damage (proteinuria/eGFR decline)
- Oral (non-injectable) NLRP3/IL‑1–pathway inhibition matching biologic disease control with lower treatment burden and improved safety (e.g., fewer serious infections)

name: Muir-Torre syndrome
description: Autosomal dominant Lynch syndrome variant caused by DNA mismatch repair defects, marked by recurrent sebaceous skin tumors and high risk of internal cancers, especially colorectal. Typical presentation is midlife, slightly more common in men, with painless slow growing yellow papules or nodules that drive repeated procedures and prompt intensive lifelong cancer screening. Key gaps include imperfect chemoprevention, uncertainty around practical long term aspirin dosing, and no established systemic standard for metastatic sebaceous carcinoma.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer, dose-optimized chemoprevention that reduces both colorectal and non-colorectal Lynch-spectrum cancers in Muir–Torre carriers.
- Durable systemic therapy for unresectable/metastatic sebaceous carcinoma with predictable responses beyond case reports.
- Long-term, well-tolerated pharmacologic suppression of recurrent/new sebaceous neoplasms to reduce repeated excisions/cryotherapy and disfigurement.

name: Acute myeloid leukemia | promyelocytic
description: Acute promyelocytic leukemia is an acute myeloid leukemia subtype driven by the t(15;17) PML RARA fusion that blocks myeloid differentiation, causing marrow failure and an emergency bleeding phenotype. Adults are often diagnosed around age 40 with fatigue, infections, bruising, and mucosal bleeding. Despite high cure rates, early death from disseminated intravascular coagulation and hyperfibrinolysis remains the key unmet need, alongside preventing and managing differentiation syndrome. Current arsenic trioxide based regimens also impose major daily intravenous treatment burden, sustaining demand for faster coagulopathy control, safer supportive care, and convenient oral outpatient arsenic options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct to rapidly neutralize APL thrombohemorrhagic coagulopathy in the first ~2 induction weeks to reduce 30‑day early death from fatal hemorrhage.
- Differentiation-syndrome–sparing prophylaxis/early-intervention strategy for high-risk patients to prevent DS on ATO+ATRA regimens.
- Fully oral/outpatient ATO+ATRA regimen to eliminate daily IV ATO infusions and central-line complications/treatment burden.

name: Factitious disorder imposed on another
description: Factitious disorder imposed on another is a rare form of medical child abuse where a caregiver fabricates or induces illness in a dependent, driving repeated healthcare encounters, extensive testing, and iatrogenic harm. It typically affects very young children and is often recognized late, with diagnostic delays around two years, because clinicians must disentangle deception from true disease and symptoms may improve in hospital then recur at home. Care focuses on child protection and trauma support, but there are no well validated, evidence based treatments for perpetrators, leaving a major unmet need for scalable behavior change interventions and structured deprescribing and recovery toolkits.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Perpetrator-directed pharmacotherapy that reliably reduces/halts FDIA/FII deception/induction behaviors
- Pediatric-safe medications that meaningfully reduce victims’ post-abuse depression/anxiety/PTSD symptom burden
- Pharmacologic “deprescribing + recovery” toolkits to enable rapid, safe cessation of unnecessary meds/treatments (e.g., withdrawal mitigation/iatrogenic-injury treatment)

name: Natural killer cell deficiency
description: Rare primary immunodeficiency with impaired natural killer cell function, leading to severe or recurrent herpesvirus and papillomavirus infections, warts, and elevated cancer risk, often emerging in adolescence. Care is largely continuous antiviral prophylaxis and treatment with agents like acyclovir or ganciclovir, but papillomavirus disease responds poorly and antivirals such as valganciclovir carry serious hematologic toxicity, leaving a major unmet need for durable immune restoration and safer long term antiviral options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- NK-cell immune restoration that increases NK number/function to prevent recurrent/severe herpesvirus infections and reduce reliance on lifelong antiviral prophylaxis
- Non-myelosuppressive CMV therapy/prophylaxis to replace valganciclovir and avoid severe hematologic toxicity/ANC monitoring burdens
- Effective systemic anti-HPV (wart-clearing) therapy for extensive/recalcitrant cutaneous warts to reduce downstream EBV/HPV-driven malignancy risk

name: NUT carcinoma
description: NUT carcinoma is a rare, highly aggressive squamous cancer driven by NUTM1 fusion oncoproteins, typically arising in the lung or head and neck and presenting after only weeks of symptoms like cough or nasal obstruction and epistaxis. It is frequently misdiagnosed as a more common tumor, delaying molecular confirmation. There is no standard of care and treatment relies on multimodality surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy with poor durability, with average survival around 10 months. Key unmet needs are earlier diagnosis and effective targeted systemic therapies that produce durable responses.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemic therapies that materially extend survival for the common metastatic/thoracic-presenting subgroup (beyond ~6–10 month median/average OS; improve ~30% 2‑year survival)
- NUTM1-fusion/BET-axis–directed therapies delivering durable responses across heterogeneous fusion partners (BRD4 and non‑BRD4)
- Better-tolerated, outpatient-friendly regimens (e.g., single-agent immunotherapy or oral targeted therapy) to reduce reliance on intensive surgery+radiation+chemotherapy
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus URL for NUT carcinoma

name: Nance-Horan syndrome
description: Nance-Horan syndrome is a rare X linked disorder where boys are born with severe bilateral congenital cataracts and microcornea causing early profound vision loss with nystagmus and sometimes strabismus, often alongside dental and facial anomalies and occasional intellectual disability. Care is supportive with early cataract surgery, but visual outcomes are often poor and complications such as glaucoma and retinal detachment can further erode sight, leaving a major unmet need for eye targeted disease modifying approaches that preserve vision.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neonatal, eye-targeted NHS gene restoration to prevent congenital cataracts/microcornea with poor surgical outcomes.
- Long-acting (drop-sparing) glaucoma prevention/IOP control for common post–infant cataract-surgery glaucoma.
- Retina-targeted therapy to prevent retinal detachment/degeneration driving poor vision despite early cataract surgery.

name: Nasu-Hakola disease
description: Nasu Hakola disease (polycystic lipomembranous osteodysplasia with sclerosing leukoencephalopathy) is a rare inherited TYROBP or TREM2 disorder where osteoclast and microglia dysfunction drives early adult bone pain and recurrent extremity fractures followed by frontal lobe behavioral change and rapidly progressive presenile dementia, often fatal before 50. Care is supportive only, leaving a major need for disease modifying therapy that stabilizes bone early and slows white matter neurodegeneration before irreversible disability.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying microglia/white-matter therapy targeting biallelic TREM2/TYROBP Nasu-Hakola to halt progression to profound dementia/death.
- Osteoclast/bone-remodeling–normalizing therapy in the osseous stage (~age 20–30) to reduce cystic bone changes, pain, and frequent limb fractures.
- Better-tolerated neuropsychiatric + antiseizure symptom control in early neurologic stage, avoiding antipsychotic-associated parkinsonism.

name: Naxos disease
description: Rare inherited cardiocutaneous syndrome marked by woolly hair from birth and early palmoplantar keratoderma, progressing in adolescence to arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy with malignant ventricular arrhythmias, syncope, sudden death, and eventual right heart failure. There is no cure and care is largely preventive with implantable defibrillators, antiarrhythmics, and heart failure therapy, leaving major unmet need for disease modifying approaches and safer durable rhythm control beyond devices and transplant.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-directed disease modification that prevents/slows Naxos (ARVC-spectrum) progression from fibro-fatty replacement to ventricular arrhythmias and RV (±LV) failure.
- Safer chronic ventricular arrhythmia suppression that reduces VT burden/ICD shocks without amiodarone toxicity or sotalol proarrhythmia/monitoring burden.
- RV-predominant heart-failure therapies specifically validated in Naxos/ACM to delay RV (±LV) failure and reduce need for advanced HF support/transplant.

name: Nelson syndrome
description: Rare post–bilateral adrenalectomy complication of Cushing disease where a corticotroph pituitary tumor progresses and overproduces adrenocorticotropic hormone, causing hyperpigmentation and sometimes invasive mass effects such as headaches, pituitary failure, and vision loss; care relies on pituitary surgery and radiation, with no established medical therapy and an unmet need for durable tumor control and reliable hormone suppression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical, tumor-targeted medical therapy achieving durable radiologic control (MRI tumor stabilization/shrinkage) for patients progressing after surgery ± radiotherapy.
- Reliable ACTH suppression to reverse deep hyperpigmentation and other ACTH-driven morbidity in patients with persistently high ACTH.
- Better-tolerated (non-alkylating) systemic option for aggressive/refractory Nelson’s that improves on temozolomide’s inconsistent efficacy and reduces myelosuppression monitoring burden.

name: Netherton syndrome
description: Netherton syndrome is a rare inherited disorder of skin, hair, and immune function caused by SPINK5 variants, presenting at birth with severe barrier failure, red scaly skin, and chronic itch. Infants can lose fluid and heat and are prone to recurrent skin infections and life threatening sepsis with poor growth. Care remains largely symptomatic, and the compromised barrier makes even topical therapy risky due to high systemic absorption. The largest gap is safe, durable disease modifying treatment that restores barrier integrity and controls inflammation, with interest growing in targeted immune modulation and protease inhibition approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neonatal barrier stabilization to prevent dehydration/sepsis/failure-to-thrive (e.g., TEWL improvement as PD readout)
- Durable itch + skin-severity control (e.g., WI-NRS/IGA/SCORAD) without increasing bacterial/fungal infections
- Whole-body topical anti-inflammatory options safe in severe barrier-defect skin/young children (avoid excess systemic exposure/HPA-axis suppression)

name: Niemann-Pick disease | type A
description: Niemann Pick disease type A is an infant onset lysosomal storage disorder caused by SMPD1 mutations that reduce acid sphingomyelinase, leading to sphingomyelin buildup, hepatosplenomegaly, failure to thrive, progressive neurodegeneration, lung disease, and death usually by age 3. Care is largely supportive, and even enzyme replacement for non central nervous system manifestations does not reach the brain, leaving a major need for brain penetrating disease modification plus safer, less burdensome lifelong treatment for fragile infants.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-penetrant therapy to prevent rapid neurodegeneration/early childhood death (BBB delivery)
- Safer, less burdensome systemic therapy for infants (reduce q2wk IV infusion + IAR/hypersensitivity)
- Type-A–specific development framework (validated endpoints/assessment criteria; real-world data to guide trials)

name: Andermann syndrome
description: Andermann syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by SLC12A6 variants that disrupt the KCC3 potassium chloride cotransporter, leading to infancy onset progressive sensorimotor neuropathy with hypotonia and areflexia plus corpus callosum malformation. Children often learn to walk late and lose ambulation in adolescence, with added disability from psychiatric symptoms and life limiting respiratory insufficiency. Care is largely supportive, creating a premium for disease modifying therapies that preserve mobility, prevent respiratory decline, and safely control psychosis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-life restoration of SLC12A6/KCC3 function to prevent progressive neuropathy and preserve ambulation
- Therapies that prevent or meaningfully delay respiratory insufficiency (life-limiting complication)
- Better-tolerated treatments to control adolescent-onset psychotic/psychiatric episodes (~39% after age 15)

name: Aggressive natural killer-cell leukemia
description: Aggressive natural killer cell leukemia is an ultra-rare, Epstein Barr virus linked leukemia of mature natural killer cells that presents abruptly in adults with fever, liver dysfunction, hepatosplenomegaly, and severe cytopenias, often complicated by hemophagocytic syndrome and disseminated intravascular coagulation with rapid multiorgan failure. Current care relies on intensive L asparaginase based chemotherapy and allogeneic stem cell transplantation, yet median survival is often under three months and durable remissions are uncommon. Key unmet needs are faster, deeper, better tolerated regimens that overcome multidrug resistance, clear circulating Epstein Barr virus DNA, and target core Janus kinase signal transducer and activator of transcription biology.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid induction regimens achieving deep remission (CR with EBV-DNA clearance) to reliably bridge more patients to early allo-HSCT.
- Lower-toxicity frontline options usable in patients presenting with DIC/HLH/multiorgan failure that reduce severe cytopenias/sepsis and organ toxicity vs SMILE.
- Targeted/immune therapies against EBV-driven disease and JAK/STAT (e.g., STAT3/STAT5B) lesions to overcome P-gp–mediated multidrug resistance.

name: Digital papillary adenocarcinoma
description: Ultra-rare malignant eccrine sweat gland cancer of the fingers and toes, typically a slow-growing painless nodule in men 50 to 70 that often looks benign and is diagnosed late; even after surgery it has high local recurrence and meaningful metastatic risk (often lung), pushing wide excision or amputation and long surveillance. There are no clear guidelines or proven systemic therapies and chemotherapy has been ineffective, leaving a major unmet need for disease-modifying treatments for recurrent or metastatic disease, with emerging interest in human papillomavirus 42-directed and immunologic approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemic therapy with meaningful objective responses for metastatic/unresectable DPA (especially lung-metastatic disease)
- Neoadjuvant/adjuvant systemic therapy to enable digit-sparing surgery while reducing recurrence and distant metastasis risk
- HPV42-directed therapies (e.g., therapeutic vaccination/HPV-targeted immunotherapy) for HPV42+ DPA to prevent late relapse

name: Niemann-Pick disease | type B
description: Niemann-Pick disease type B is a later-onset chronic visceral acid sphingomyelinase deficiency caused by SMPD1-related enzyme loss, leading to progressive sphingomyelin buildup in spleen, liver, and lungs. It often presents in mid-childhood with hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, short stature, and recurrent lung infections, usually without central nervous system signs. Key unmet needs include preventing or reversing advanced organ damage such as established liver fibrosis or cirrhosis and reducing treatment burden, since current enzyme replacement requires lifelong every-two-week intravenous infusions and carries hypersensitivity or anaphylaxis risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that restore lung/liver function in patients with extensive lung fibrosis and/or liver cirrhosis (e.g., improving %predicted DLCO and fibrosis/ILD).
- Therapies that achieve deeper visceral correction—near-normal spleen volume and reversal of hypersplenism/cytopenias—beyond residual splenomegaly on current ERT.
- Lower-burden and safer alternatives to chronic q2-week multi-hour IV ERT (reduced infusion time/frequency and hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis risk).

name: Niemann-Pick disease | type C
description: Niemann Pick disease type C is a rare inherited lysosomal lipid trafficking disorder driven by NPC1 or NPC2 dysfunction, causing lipid buildup in the liver, spleen, and brain and progressive neurodegeneration. Children often develop ataxia, abnormal vertical eye movements, learning decline, then worsening speech and swallowing, feeding problems, and seizures, with a typically fatal course often before age 20. Care is largely supportive, and available therapy is not curative, leaving major unmet need for earlier diagnosis and truly disease modifying treatments that reach the brain and address systemic disease with lower treatment burden.
