Care is constrained by frequent resistance to venetoclax plus azacitidine in monocytic disease, the need for deeper genotype guided remissions in nucleophosmin 1 mutated or KMT2A rearranged leukemia, and persistent sanctuary site risk including central nervous system involvement.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Overcome high primary refractoriness to VEN+AZA in FAB‑M5 by targeting MCL1‑dependent (BCL2-low) resistance biology.
- Precision therapy for monocytic-enriched genotypes (KMT2A‑rearranged and/or NPM1‑mutated AML) with menin-pathway targeted agents to achieve deeper remissions.
- Systemic therapies with CNS/extramedullary penetration to prevent/treat sanctuary-site disease (CNS/skin/gingiva/meninges) common in monocytic AML.

name: Acute retinal necrosis
description: Acute retinal necrosis is a rare, rapidly progressive herpesvirus retinitis often in immunocompetent patients, causing sudden unilateral painful vision loss with prominent intraocular inflammation, necrotizing retinitis, and occlusive vasculitis. Despite intensive systemic and intravitreal antiviral therapy followed by prolonged prophylaxis, outcomes remain poor, with retinal detachment common and ongoing risk of fellow eye involvement. Key unmet needs are faster, more reliably vision sparing disease control, prevention of retinal detachment and bilateral disease, and treatment strategies supported by stronger evidence in this rare condition.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that reduce the ~50–75% retinal detachment risk (mostly within ~3 months) and improve visual outcomes beyond current antivirals.
- Durable prophylaxis that prevents contralateral/fellow-eye involvement (3–35%) without months-to-lifelong oral antiviral suppression.
- Safer, less burdensome antiviral regimens that avoid very high-dose oral induction and repeated intravitreal injections while reducing renal/cytopenia toxicity.

name: Adamantinoma
description: Adamantinoma is a rare, low grade malignant bone tumor that usually arises in the anterior tibial shaft of adolescents and young adults, presenting as a slow growing swelling or pain and occasionally fracture, with a risk of late local recurrence and lung metastases. Treatment is essentially surgical, requiring wide margin resection and often complex limb salvage reconstruction with substantial complication risk, while chemotherapy and radiotherapy offer little benefit. The unmet need is for less morbid local control and effective systemic options for recurrent or metastatic disease, with early signals limited to case reports of targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemic tumor-shrinkage therapy for unresectable/metastatic adamantinoma (esp. pulmonary metastases) achieving objective responses/durable control despite chemo/radiation non-responsiveness
- Peri-operative/adjuvant therapy to reduce late local recurrence/metastasis after limb-salvage wide resection and lessen the need for repeat resections/long surveillance
- Pharmacologic adjuncts to improve limb-salvage reconstruction outcomes (e.g., reduce nonunion/fracture and related complications)

name: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency
description: Inherited adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency drives 2,8-dihydroxyadenine crystal formation, causing recurrent radiolucent kidney stones and crystalline nephropathy that can progress to kidney failure. Symptoms often begin in adulthood and diagnosis is frequently delayed, leaving some patients already in end-stage kidney disease. Care relies on lifelong xanthine oxidase inhibition with limited alternatives, little benefit from urine alkalinization, and high stakes after transplant where recurrence can destroy the allograft, creating demand for earlier diagnosis, objective monitoring, and more durable crystal-suppressing or crystal-clearing therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Kidney-/transplant-safe alternatives to high-dose xanthine oxidoreductase inhibition that fully suppress urinary 2,8‑DHA while avoiding allopurinol SCAR/febuxostat CV risk and azathioprine/6‑MP interactions.
- Drugs that rapidly clear/dissolve established intratubular 2,8‑DHA crystals to treat crystalline nephropathy (native kidney or graft), since urine alkalinization is ineffective.
- Long-acting/adherence-independent control with more objective monitoring than crystalluria microscopy (imprecise/interobserver variability) for lifelong therapy, including post-transplant.

name: Adenosarcoma
description: Uterine adenosarcoma is a rare biphasic uterine tumor with malignant sarcomatous stroma and benign-appearing glands, often presenting in postmenopausal women as a polypoid endometrial mass with abnormal vaginal bleeding. Even when diagnosed at early stage, recurrence is common (about 25 to 40%), and care remains dominated by surgery with limited, non–evidence-rich systemic options for recurrent or metastatic disease, largely relying on sarcoma-style cytotoxic chemotherapy and case-series supported hormone therapy in receptor-positive low-grade tumors.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Recurrence-preventing adjuvant/maintenance systemic therapy for stage I uterine adenosarcoma with sarcomatous overgrowth
- Prospective, biomarker-driven endocrine/ER-targeted therapy for ER/PR+ low-grade disease (chemo-sparing durability)
- Genomically matched targeted therapy (e.g., PI3K/MAPK and cell-cycle axis) to outperform modest chemo in recurrent/metastatic disease

name: Severe combined immunodeficiency | ADA deficiency
description: Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes toxic purine metabolite buildup that destroys developing lymphocytes, leading to early infancy severe combined immunodeficiency with profound T cell, B cell, and natural killer cell deficits and life threatening infections. Without rapid immune restoration, survival beyond 1 to 2 years is rare. Enzyme replacement can stabilize patients but requires lifelong at least weekly intramuscular dosing and often delivers incomplete immune reconstitution, while definitive transplant or gene based approaches are complex and center dependent. Neurologic and hearing complications frequently persist, highlighting the need for safer, scalable, durable immune correction that also protects the brain.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent/ameliorate persistent or emergent neurodevelopmental/behavioral complications (incl. sensorineural hearing loss) not reliably addressed by current ERT/HSCT/gene therapy.
- Provide curative immune reconstitution with lower genotoxicity/oncogenesis risk and reduced/avoided chemotherapy conditioning toxicity.
- Reduce treatment burden and access barriers vs frequent IM ERT dosing and specialist-center-dependent gene therapy (e.g., fewer-visit, outpatient-scalable options).

name: Breast cancer | HR-positive, HER2-negative
description: Hormone receptor positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 negative breast cancer is the most common breast cancer subtype, often diagnosed in the early 60s and frequently localized at presentation. Endocrine therapy is foundational but resistance such as estrogen receptor 1 mutations drives progression, creating demand for convenient oral estrogen receptor degraders versus intramuscular fulvestrant. After progression, targeted add ons can add significant monitoring and metabolic toxicity burdens, and brain metastases remain difficult to treat due to limited drug delivery across the blood brain barrier and lack of effective strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral ER-targeting therapies that overcome ESR1-driven endocrine resistance and avoid IM fulvestrant
- Better-defined, more tolerable post‑CDK4/6 progression regimens (vs PI3Kα inhibitor toxicity/monitoring burden)
- CNS-penetrant systemic therapies with proven intracranial activity for ER+/HER2− brain metastases, including symptomatic/untreated patients

name: Colorectal cancer | adenosquamous carcinoma
description: Ultra-rare colorectal cancer histotype with mixed glandular and squamous components that presents like typical colorectal cancer but is often advanced and metastatic with poor differentiation. Surgery is the mainstay, yet evidence for adjuvant chemotherapy or radiation is limited so clinicians extrapolate from other cancers, leaving high risk of early relapse and a need for validated perioperative regimens and biomarker guided targeted options based on recurring mutations such as TP53, APC, KRAS and BRAF.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Peri-operative (neo/adjuvant) systemic therapy to extend DFS beyond ~6 months and prevent early relapse/metastasis post-resection
- Biomarker-driven systemic options for predominantly stage III–IV disease to improve OS beyond ~14 months (esp. KRAS-mutant and dMMR subsets)
- Lower-toxicity, lower-burden regimens reducing grade ≥3 AEs/discontinuations and avoiding 46-hour infusional pump logistics vs FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab

name: Gallbladder cancer | adenosquamous carcinoma
description: Rare, hard-to-detect gallbladder cancer that often presents late with nonspecific biliary symptoms in older women with gallstones; aggressive variants like adenosquamous carcinoma invade locally, and current first-line chemoimmunotherapy requires frequent infusions with high grade 3 to 4 toxicity, underscoring need for earlier detection and safer, more effective systemic options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Histology-specific efficacy lift beyond 1L durvalumab+GemCis outcomes in adenosquamous gallbladder carcinoma.
- Lower severe toxicity vs current immunochemotherapy (reduce ~76% grade 3–4 AEs and ~13% AE-driven discontinuation).
- Reduced administration burden with chemo-sparing/less frequent IV visit regimens (avoid day 1 & 8 q21d induction cycles).

name: Adrenal gland cancer
description: Adrenocortical carcinoma is an ultra rare adrenal gland malignancy that often presents in adults in their 40s and 50s with hormone excess syndromes such as Cushing syndrome or virilization and nonspecific abdominal pain. Only a minority are localized at diagnosis and surgery is the lone curative option yet relapse after complete resection is frequent. In advanced disease mitotane based regimens have low response rates and are commonly limited by gastrointestinal and neurologic toxicity leaving a clear need for more effective and better tolerated systemic therapies that control both tumor growth and debilitating hormone symptoms.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- First-line advanced/metastatic ACC regimens that meaningfully improve ORR/PFS/OS vs EDP–mitotane.
- Mitotane-sparing (or safer/faster) adrenolytic therapy that avoids prolonged titration and frequent drug-level monitoring while reducing adrenal-crisis/QoL burden.
- Effective 2L/3L systemic therapies for ACC after progression on EDP–mitotane.

name: Testicular adrenal rest tumor
description: Testicular adrenal rest tumours are benign adrenal-like lesions in males with classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia that often go undetected without scrotal ultrasound and can progressively impair spermatogenesis, causing azoospermia and infertility. Management leans on intensifying glucocorticoids to suppress adrenocorticotropic hormone driven growth, but tumour shrinkage is inconsistent and higher steroid doses increase iatrogenic Cushing risk, leaving a need for better hormone control and fertility preserving options when lesions become steroid unresponsive.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-steroidal ACTH suppression to shrink/prevent TART while avoiding supraphysiologic glucocorticoid toxicity
- Effective therapy for late-stage fibrotic/steroid-refractory TART (Stage 4–5) to prevent obstruction/irreversible testicular damage and infertility
- More convenient long-acting/once-daily regimens that reduce multi-dose steroid burden and frequency of ultrasound surveillance

name: Adrenocortical carcinoma
description: Adrenocortical carcinoma is a rare, often hormone secreting adrenal cortex cancer that typically presents in midlife with cortisol and or sex steroid excess and large tumors, with over half diagnosed at locally advanced or metastatic stages. Treatment options for unresectable or metastatic disease remain limited, with mitotane the only approved drug and modest response rates plus significant toxicity and monitoring burden. Key unmet needs include more effective first line systemic therapies, broader biomarker guided immunotherapy beyond the small microsatellite instability subset, and safer faster control of hypercortisolism.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- First-line systemic therapy that meaningfully extends survival vs EDP–mitotane while reducing serious toxicity/mitotane dependence
- Biomarker-enriched checkpoint strategies (e.g., MSI-H/MMR-D/Lynch “immune-hot” ACC) to improve durable response rates
- Rapid, titratable control of cortisol excess in functional ACC with less monitoring/toxicity than mitotane

name: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma
description: Rare, highly aggressive HTLV-1–driven mature T-cell malignancy of older adults (often late 60s) with multiorgan disease, hypercalcemia, and profound immunosuppression; aggressive subtypes frequently relapse or are refractory to conventional therapy and have overall survival under 1 year, underscoring need for durable disease control and infection-risk reduction.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Frontline regimens for aggressive (acute/lymphoma) ATLL—especially older/transplant-ineligible patients—that prevent rapid post-CR relapse and improve OS beyond ~9–13 months.
- Relapsed/refractory ATLL treatments that deliver durable responses with meaningfully longer OS (vs early relapse/primary refractory disease and months-level survival).
- Systemic therapies (or add-ons) that reduce severe infections and infection-related deaths associated with current chemotherapy/immunosuppression.

name: Ankyrin-B syndrome
description: Rare autosomal dominant ANK2 channel-targeting disorder causing bradycardia, conduction disease, and stress-triggered atrial and ventricular arrhythmias with syncope and sudden-death risk; current care is constrained by rate-slowing drugs and often progresses to pacemaker dependence, leaving a need for disease-modifying therapies that restore ankyrin-B biology.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Heart-rate–neutral suppression of exercise/stress-triggered ventricular tachyarrhythmias in Ankyrin-B syndrome patients with concomitant sinus-node dysfunction/bradycardia
- Therapies that prevent/delay progression to pacemaker/ICD dependence by treating sinus-node dysfunction and conduction disease/heart block
- ANK2/ankyrin-B–restorative gene/RNA therapies to correct ion-channel mislocalization and reduce the full arrhythmia spectrum (AF/VF, CPVT-like VT) and sudden-death risk

name: Anodontia
description: Anodontia is a congenital condition defined by complete absence of teeth, often occurring with ectodermal dysplasias affecting hair, nails, and sweat glands. It causes major functional and developmental burdens including impaired chewing and speech, gum damage, and inadequate jawbone growth. Care is largely prosthetic with dentures and implants, but children often need repeated refits and limited bone growth can preclude implants, leaving persistently suboptimal function. Emerging approaches aim to modify development early in syndromic disease and to regenerate teeth by targeting pathways such as USAG-1.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying tooth regeneration for severe congenital partial anodontia (≥6 missing permanent teeth) via USAG‑1 neutralization to activate dormant tooth buds and erupt new teeth.
- Prenatal rescue to prevent syndromic anodontia in unborn XLHED males (intra‑amniotic ER004), improving dental development measured by number of erupted teeth and tooth germs.
- Whole-tooth regeneration for complete anodontia/edentulism by stimulating “third dentition/third dental crest” (e.g., targeted molecular/siRNA/antibody DDS or gene therapy) beyond implants/dentures.

name: Anal cancer | adenocarcinoma
description: Rare anal cancer subtype (5%–10% of anal canal malignancies) with poor prognosis, typically presenting in older adults with rectal bleeding, anal pain or pressure, and bowel habit change that can be mistaken for hemorrhoids. Treatment often requires prolonged chemoradiation and sometimes colostomy creating surgery, yet complete responses can be very low (reported as low as 7%), leaving a premium on better systemic control, more organ preserving cures, and shorter, less toxic regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemic (neo/adjuvant) regimens that reduce both local relapse and distant metastasis.
- Neoadjuvant therapy with much higher complete response rates to enable organ preservation (avoid APR/colostomy).
- Less-burdensome curative-intent strategies that replace or shorten long-course chemoradiation (improved convenience/tolerability).

name: Generalized arterial calcification of infancy
description: Rare autosomal recessive infant-onset disorder where ENPP1-related loss of pyrophosphate drives diffuse arterial calcification plus intimal thickening and stenosis, causing severe hypertension, heart failure, and frequent early death from myocardial infarction or stroke. Care is largely supportive with uncertain bisphosphonate benefit and potential skeletal toxicity plus heavy imaging surveillance, and there is no targeted medical therapy for the occlusive arteriopathy and myointimal hyperplasia that drive morbidity, creating high unmet need for disease-modifying ENPP1 or pyrophosphate restoration approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prenatal-to-neonatal disease‑modifying PPi restoration (e.g., ENPP1/PPi replacement) to prevent diffuse arterial calcification/stenosis and cut very high early mortality.
- Therapies that halt/reverse coronary and renal‑artery luminal narrowing from intimal hyperplasia (not just calcification regression) to prevent ischemia/heart failure and refractory hypertension.
- Infant‑safe, lower‑burden regimens that avoid bisphosphonate toxicity/uncertain benefit and reduce intensive monitoring/high‑frequency co‑therapies.

name: Optic neuropathy | arteritic anterior ischemic
description: Giant cell arteritis is a granulomatous medium to large vessel vasculitis in older adults where inflamed narrowed arteries can abruptly cut off optic nerve perfusion, causing arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy and permanent blindness. Patients often present with sudden painless vision loss plus headache, scalp tenderness, and jaw claudication, and the other eye can be lost within days without urgent corticosteroids. Treatment is time critical but usually cannot restore vision once lost and often requires one to two years of steroids with substantial toxicity, creating a need for faster diagnosis, true vision sparing rescue options, and safer disease control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Vision-restoring “rescue” therapy for patients presenting after AAION-related vision loss.
- Ultra-rapid acute therapy to prevent fellow-eye involvement/bilateral blindness in the first days–week after presentation.
- Safer, lower-burden steroid-sparing regimens for older GCA/AAION patients (reduced toxicity/infection risk and less monitoring/clinic burden).

name: Afferent loop syndrome
description: Uncommon post surgical complication after Billroth II Roux en Y or Whipple reconstruction where distal obstruction traps bile and pancreatic secretions causing afferent limb distension with acute abdominal pain nausea vomiting or chronic postprandial fullness relieved by bilious emesis and risks pancreatitis cholangitis perforation. Management is largely surgical leaving a need for less invasive durable decompression in frail postoperative patients with endoscopic ultrasound guided entero enterostomy emerging as a promising approach.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Agammaglobulinemia
description: Agammaglobulinemia, usually X linked, is an inherited failure of B cell development that leaves infants unprotected once maternal antibodies wane, leading to recurrent ear, sinus, and lung infections and progressive complications such as bronchiectasis. Lifelong immunoglobulin replacement and frequent antibiotics reduce infections but are not curative, impose chronic treatment burden, and still allow irreversible lung damage. The key unmet need is a durable disease modifying approach that restores antibody production and prevents long term organ injury, with Bruton tyrosine kinase correction strategies such as stem cell gene therapy representing the main curative frontier.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent/reverse progressive bronchiectasis/chronic lung disease despite IgRT (lung-function preservation), potentially by addressing mucosal-immunity gaps (IgA/IgM)
- Reduce residual encapsulated-bacteria sinopulmonary infections that persist despite gammaglobulin substitution (esp. refractory ~10%), to avoid repeated antibiotics/hospitalizations
- Durable/curative BTK-restoring therapy (e.g., gene therapy) to eliminate dependence on lifelong weekly SCIG or q2–4-week IVIG

name: Aspartylglucosaminuria
description: Aspartylglucosaminuria is a progressive lysosomal storage disorder caused by AGA gene variants, with children often appearing normal at birth before developmental delay, speech and motor decline, infections and later loss of speech and seizures. Care is supportive with no cure or disease modifying therapy, and even intensive options like bone marrow transplant have not helped. The unmet need is for treatments that restore enzyme activity in the brain and slow neurodegeneration, with gene therapy and biomarker guided monitoring emerging as a key frontier.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Single-dose, CNS-effective AGA enzyme–restoration therapy (e.g., scAAV9/AGA gene therapy) with biomarker (glycoasparagine/AGA activity) reduction and functional improvement
- Non-transplant disease-modifying therapy effective beyond the narrow early-life window to slow cognitive decline in later-diagnosed symptomatic children
- BBB-penetrant, low-burden chronic therapy (ideally oral; e.g., chaperone or substrate-reduction) startable early (incl. post–newborn screening) to reduce CNS substrate accumulation

name: Asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy
description: Asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy (Jeune syndrome) is a rare inherited skeletal ciliopathy in which a narrow bell shaped chest and short ribs restrict lung growth, causing neonatal respiratory distress and high early mortality, with survivors at risk of progressive kidney failure. Care is mainly supportive with infection management, organ monitoring, and in severe thoracic insufficiency repeated surgical thoracic expansion using adjustable implanted ribs, leaving a major unmet need for disease modifying therapies that improve early lung development and protect long term renal function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prenatal/neonatal disease-modifying therapy that increases lung growth/expansion to reduce life-threatening neonatal respiratory failure in infants with severely narrow bell-shaped thorax
- Renoprotective therapy in post-infancy survivors to prevent progression to kidney malfunction/failure (ideally targeting nephronophthisis biology)
- Non-surgical systemic or locally delivered therapy that reduces/eliminates the need for repeated thoracic expansion procedures (e.g., frequent VEPTR adjustments)

name: Alkaptonuria
description: Rare inherited inborn error of metabolism where homogentisic acid accumulates and deposits as ochronotic pigment in connective tissue, causing dark urine early and later progressive spine and large joint arthritis, pigmentation, stones, and sometimes cardiac valve disease. Patients are often diagnosed around age 40 when joint damage is advanced and many ultimately need joint replacement. Treatment remains largely symptomatic and surgical. Nitisinone can lower homogentisic acid but raises tyrosine, creating ocular toxicity risk and a need for careful monitoring, and it may be most beneficial if started early.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- HGA-lowering therapy that avoids nitisinone’s tyrosine-related keratopathy risk and frequent ocular/tyrosine monitoring
- Treatments that modify established adult disease by preventing progression to end-stage ochronotic arthropathy (delay/avoid major joint replacement; preserve function)
- Preventive therapy for pre-symptomatic/pediatric patients to stop early cartilage/tendon damage before adult arthropathy

name: Atrophoderma vermiculata
description: Rare childhood onset follicular skin disorder where facial keratotic papules and erythema slowly progress to permanent honeycomb pitted atrophic scarring, often asymptomatic but psychologically distressing. Treatment is largely cosmetic and often unrewarding, relying on topical keratolytics retinoids and procedural scar approaches, while systemic retinoids are constrained in children due to growth plate risks.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early pediatric disease‑modifying therapy preventing progression to facial “honeycomb” atrophy/atrophic scarring (no new pitted scars)
- Safer pediatric alternative to systemic isotretinoin that halts progression without growth‑plate/premature epiphyseal closure risk
- Non‑procedural pharmacotherapy to remodel established pitted/atrophic facial scars and reduce reliance on temporary laser/IPL or abrasive procedures

name: Allescheriosis
description: Allescheriosis is a life-threatening opportunistic mould infection in immunocompromised patients, usually starting in the lungs and often spreading to the brain and other organs. Care is constrained by broad antifungal resistance and high mortality (50–70%), while standard azole therapy such as voriconazole demands intensive therapeutic drug monitoring and toxicity surveillance, limiting outpatient use. The biggest gaps are better tolerated, resistance breaking agents with reliable central nervous system activity that can be deployed earlier and stepped down more easily.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-penetrant, resistance-breaking antifungal that improves survival in disseminated/CNS allescheriosis/scedosporiosis (esp. immunocompromised patients)
- Voriconazole-sparing option with better tolerability and reduced safety monitoring burden (LFT/QT/visual/photosensitivity)
- Oral-first therapy with predictable PK requiring minimal TDM/drug–drug interaction management for step-down/outpatient use

name: Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome
description: Rare inherited immune dysregulation from impaired FAS mediated apoptosis causing early childhood chronic lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, later autoimmune cytopenias and high lymphoma risk. Management relies on corticosteroids and other immunosuppression while avoiding splenectomy and rituximab associated prolonged hypogammaglobulinemia, leaving a need for durable steroid sparing pathway targeted disease modifying therapies now in Phase 2 trials.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing, non–B-cell-depleting control of refractory autoimmune cytopenias (ITP/AIHA) that avoids rituximab-associated prolonged hypogammaglobulinemia/neutropenia and reduces need for splenectomy.
- Oral targeted therapy that objectively debulks lymphoproliferation (spleen/lymph node volume reduction), improves cytopenias, and enables prednisone dose reduction without burdensome monitoring.
- Non-transplant, disease-modifying restoration of FAS-pathway apoptosis/lymphocyte homeostasis to reduce long-term lymphoma risk and reliance on splenectomy/HSCT.

name: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome
description: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 is a rare inherited childhood-onset disorder marked by chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and autoimmune endocrine failure, classically hypoparathyroidism and adrenal insufficiency, with frequent multi-organ autoimmunity including hepatitis and enteropathy. Care is largely supportive with hormone replacement, long-term antifungals, and immunosuppression rather than disease-modifying therapy. Key unmet needs include safer, more physiologic parathyroid hormone replacement to avoid renal complications from calcium and active vitamin D, durable Candida control without driving azole resistance, and steroid-sparing immune control for severe non-endocrine disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Physiologic PTH replacement for APS‑1 hypoparathyroidism that stabilizes serum calcium while lowering 24‑hour urine calcium excretion (reducing hypercalciuria/nephrocalcinosis and hypocalcemic events).
- Durable, resistance-sparing control of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis that avoids prolonged systemic antifungals and reduces antifungal resistance/species selection.
- Targeted, steroid-sparing immunomodulators for severe non-endocrine APS‑1 autoimmunity (esp. enteropathy/malabsorption and autoimmune hepatitis) with efficacy tracked by validated GI/enteritis scores.

name: Alpha thalassemia-X-linked intellectual disability syndrome
description: Alpha thalassemia X linked intellectual disability syndrome is a rare inherited multisystem disorder in males caused by ATRX variants disrupting gene regulation, presenting in infancy with hypotonia, feeding difficulties, and profound delays in speech and walking. The anemia is usually mild, but neurologic disability, seizures, reflux, and swallowing problems drive morbidity and can lead to fatal aspiration. Care is largely supportive and multidisciplinary, leaving a major unmet need for disease modifying approaches that improve neurodevelopment and safer, more effective control of feeding and gastrointestinal complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neurodevelopmental restoration to achieve meaningful expressive-language gains and enable independent walking vs supportive care
- Pharmacologic control of GERD/swallowing to prevent aspiration events/hospitalizations and reduce need for fundoplication/gastrostomy
- Non-sedating, GI-sparing management of seizures/spasticity/drooling for the ~1/3 with seizures, avoiding anticholinergic GI-motility risks

name: Alpha-mannosidosis
description: Alpha mannosidosis is a rare inherited multisystem lysosomal storage disease, typically recognized in childhood, driven by MAN2B1 mutations that cause oligosaccharide buildup and progressive dysfunction including hearing loss, immunodeficiency with recurrent infections, developmental delay or intellectual disability, ataxia, and skeletal disease. Current enzyme replacement therapy is limited to non neurological manifestations, requires weekly intravenous infusions, and can trigger infusion reactions, leaving a gap for brain active, lower burden treatments that deliver meaningful functional improvement.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-penetrant therapy to improve cognition/learning disability and other neurologic manifestations (e.g., hearing loss, ataxia)
- Treatment that can reverse established/late-presenting disease and deliver clinically meaningful disability/functional gains
- Lower-burden, safer alternative to weekly IV ERT that reduces severe hypersensitivity/infusion-reaction risk and monitoring requirements

name: Craniometaphyseal dysplasia
description: Ultra-rare genetic skeletal disorder with lifelong craniofacial bone overgrowth and metaphyseal widening that can present in infancy with airway and feeding obstruction and later cause cranial nerve compression with facial palsy, blindness, or deafness. Care is largely supportive and surgical decompression or contouring is technically difficult with frequent bone regrowth, creating a need for safe disease-modifying therapy to prevent early craniofacial overgrowth and foraminal narrowing.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy to prevent early craniofacial overgrowth and maintain nasal/choanal airway patency (reduce infant breathing/feeding compromise).
- Therapy to halt/reverse cranial foramina narrowing to prevent cranial nerve compression (facial palsy, blindness, deafness) and reduce need for decompressive surgery.
- Safe long-term systemic bone-remodeling drug that improves long-bone metaphyseal deformity and prevents post-surgical craniofacial regrowth/recurrence.

name: Distal hereditary motor neuronopathy
description: Ultra rare inherited lower motor neuron disorder causing slowly progressive distal weakness and lower leg atrophy with gait disturbance and foot deformity, usually starting in adolescence to mid adulthood and with little sensory involvement; care is supportive only, creating a need for genotype targeted disease modifying therapies (eg sorbitol lowering in SORD deficiency, restoring axonal transport in HSPB1 disease, reducing endoplasmic reticulum stress in BSCL2).
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Sorbitol-lowering disease-modifying therapy for genetically confirmed CMT‑SORD/dHMN patients (e.g., aldose reductase inhibition).
- Axonal-transport–restoring small molecules (e.g., HDAC6 inhibitors) for HSPB1- and GARS1-related axonal dHMN/CMT2 lacking human-proven therapies.
- Proteostasis/ER-stress–modulating therapeutics for BSCL2-related dHMN type V to reduce cold-triggered hand cramps and slow progression to gait disturbance/foot drop.

name: Alternating hemiplegia of childhood
description: Ultra-rare (≈1 in 1 million) neurodevelopmental disorder with infancy-onset episodes of alternating paralysis lasting minutes to days, often with dystonia and abnormal eye movements that remit during sleep but recur on waking; most patients develop developmental delay and progressive cognitive decline. Care is symptomatic with highly variable benefit and no specific therapy, leaving a need for durable attack prevention, rapid at-home abortive options, and disease-modifying treatments targeting the ATP1A3 genetic cause.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable prophylaxis that consistently reduces AHC attack frequency and duration (minutes–days) despite high inter-patient variability
- Rapid, at-home acute abortive therapy that stops dystonic/plegic attacks within ~30 minutes without sedative/benzodiazepine sleep-induction burden
- Neuroprotective/disease-modifying therapy that prevents developmental regression and preserves milestones/cognition beyond attack suppression

name: Alveolar echinococcosis
description: Alveolar echinococcosis is a rare, slow-growing Echinococcus multilocularis infection that incubates silently for 5 to 15 years then behaves like an invasive liver tumor, so diagnosis is often late in older adults with abdominal pain, weight loss, malaise, and sometimes hepatic failure. Curative surgery is only possible in a subset, and many patients require long term, often lifelong albendazole that is parasitostatic, hepatotoxic in some, and prone to relapse when stopped. High value needs are finite, parasiticidal regimens and validated imaging or blood viability markers to guide safe treatment withdrawal.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Parasiticidal, finite-duration therapy for inoperable/nonresectable AE enabling safe treatment withdrawal via objective stop rules (e.g., PET/CT + serology/viability markers)
- Better-tolerated benzimidazole-sparing/add-on regimens for patients with benzimidazole toxicity/ineffectiveness (avoiding liver dysfunction/cytopenias)
- Simplified long-term oral regimens/high-bioavailability formulations to reduce lifelong dosing burden and QoL impact

name: Epilepsy | autosomal dominant sleep-related hypermotor
description: Rare focal epilepsy with brief, clustered hypermotor seizures during sleep, often starting before age 20; high nightly seizure burden fragments sleep and impairs daytime function, can be misdiagnosed as parasomnias, and ~30% become drug resistant, driving need for better diagnosis and durable night-time seizure control and genotype-informed options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapy achieving sustained seizure freedom or ≥50% reduction in the ~30% of ADSHE patients with medication-resistant seizures.
- Genotype-directed precision treatments for genetically defined ADSHE subsets (~19% identifiable; incl. KCNT1 ~1%).
- Night-focused therapy reducing very high nocturnal seizure burden/cluster events (1–20 attacks/night) to improve sleep quality and daytime functioning.

name: Urethral diverticulum
description: Female urethral diverticulum is a usually benign periurethral outpouching that traps urine and causes years of irritative urinary symptoms and recurrent urinary tract infections, often with delayed diagnosis. Magnetic resonance imaging and transvaginal diverticulectomy are standard, but recovery and complications such as stress urinary incontinence, recurrence, fistula, stricture, and persistent urgency are common, and conservative care may rely on antibiotic prophylaxis, creating demand for antibiotic sparing symptom control and nonsurgical anatomy correcting options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical anatomy-correcting therapy to eliminate/obliterate the urethral diverticulum “pocket” for symptomatic patients seeking to avoid excision.
- Peri-/post-op local pharmacologic adjuncts to reduce reconstructive complications (e.g., urethrovaginal fistula/stricture) and shorten catheter/VCUG leakage-management burden.
- Non-antibiotic (antibiotic-sparing) options to control chronic infection/irritative LUTS in conservatively managed or persistent/recurrent-symptom patients.

name: Rhabdoid tumor predisposition syndrome
description: Rare inherited pediatric cancer predisposition, usually SMARCB1 driven, causing aggressive rhabdoid tumors often presenting in infancy in the brain and kidney, sometimes multifocal. Outcomes remain poor despite intensive chemotherapy and radiotherapy, while radiation in very young children can impair brain development, leaving a premium on disease modifying, less genotoxic approaches such as targeted epigenetic therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-penetrant targeted/epigenetic therapy added up front (e.g., EZH2/PRC2-pathway inhibition) to prevent early chemo-refractory progression and improve infant EFS/OS
- Radiotherapy-sparing (or RT-delaying) systemic regimens for very young AT/RT patients to preserve neurocognition and avoid RT-related radionecrosis risk
- Non–DNA-damaging maintenance/secondary-prevention therapy post-remission (or short-course prophylaxis in RTPS carriers) to prevent recurrent/synchronous/metachronous tumors while reducing cumulative genotoxic exposure/secondary AML risk

name: Rhinosporidiosis
description: Rhinosporidiosis is a chronic granulomatous infection of the nasal and nasopharyngeal mucosa caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi, often in adult men with freshwater exposure, presenting with bleeding and nasal obstruction from a polypoidal mass. Care relies on surgical excision with cauterization but relapse is common from sporangia seeding, with reported recurrence rates of 10 to 70 percent, and there is no reliably curative medical therapy. Dapsone is sometimes used as an adjunct but carries rare fatal hematologic toxicity and requires intensive blood count monitoring.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct anti-*Rhinosporidium* therapy that reliably prevents post-excision relapse in mucosal disease (materially lowering the 5–67% recurrence range; addressing extreme recurrence in disseminated disease).
- A true systemic sterilizing regimen targeting “remaining reservoirs” (blood/lymphatics) to prevent relapse/dissemination beyond surgery-only control.
- A safer alternative to long-course oral dapsone that avoids severe hematologic toxicity/monitoring burden while retaining anti-recurrence benefit.
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus page available (no MedlinePlus URL)

name: Ring chromosome 20 syndrome
description: Ring chromosome 20 syndrome is an ultra-rare developmental epileptic encephalopathy with childhood-onset seizures that are often drug resistant and marked by prolonged nonconvulsive status epilepticus causing confusional episodes. Children may initially appear typical, but epilepsy onset can trigger cognitive and behavioral decline with frontal-lobe–pattern dysfunction, attention and learning problems, and difficult behaviors. Care is largely symptomatic, with no specific treatment regimen and limited procedural options, leaving major unmet need for therapies that reliably control status episodes, shorten the diagnostic odyssey, and preserve long-term cognition.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-sedating, reliably effective abortive/preventive therapy for recurrent non-convulsive status epilepticus (confusional episodes)
- Sustained long-term seizure control (ideally seizure freedom) in medication-refractory ring(20) without ineffective side-effect–driving polytherapy
- Therapy to prevent or reverse post-epilepsy-onset cognitive/behavioral decline (e.g., aggression, autistic features, psychosis, loss of social skills)

name: Scimitar syndrome
description: Rare congenital cardiopulmonary malformation where right lung pulmonary veins drain to the inferior vena cava with right lung hypoplasia and systemic arterial supply, causing a left to right shunt. Often presents in early infancy with pulmonary hypertension, respiratory distress, heart failure and failure to thrive, with mortality reported up to 45%. Care is staged medical stabilization, catheter occlusion of systemic collaterals, and surgical rerouting, but postoperative venous obstruction and residual stenosis frequently drive reinterventions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neonatal/infant PAH-targeted bridge therapy that safely lowers PVR/PAP and stabilizes infantile scimitar syndrome (severe PAH/CHF, high mortality) pre-repair.
- Anti-proliferative/anti-fibrotic therapy (systemic or local) to prevent/treat post-repair scimitar venous restenosis/pulmonary venous obstruction and reduce reinterventions.
- Pharmacologic reduction of aortopulmonary collateral flow/shunt (↓Qp:Qs, ↓PAP) to reduce reliance on catheter-based collateral embolization.
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus page for Scimitar syndrome; closest: https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001114.htm

name: Dystonia | focal / segmental
description: Cervical dystonia is a focal neurologic dystonia in which neck muscles contract involuntarily, twisting or pulling the head into abnormal postures, typically with slow midlife onset and a female-skewing patient population. There is no cure and care is largely symptomatic, dominated by repeat botulinum toxin injections. Key gaps include long diagnostic delays, end of cycle symptom return under fixed roughly 12 week dosing intervals, dose limiting adverse effects such as dysphagia and neck weakness, and secondary loss of response in some patients due to neutralizing antibodies, underscoring demand for more durable, better tolerated, disease modifying options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Full-cycle, predictable symptom control through the standard ≥12‑week interval to prevent common mid‑cycle wearing‑off.
- BoNT-like efficacy with lower bulbar/weakness toxicity, especially reduced dysphagia and swallowing/breathing risk.
- Effective therapies for secondary non-response/immunoresistance after repeated BoNT cycles.

name: Sitosterolemia
description: Rare inherited sterol-transport disorder where ABCG5/ABCG8 mutations cause dietary plant sterols to accumulate, producing familial hypercholesterolemia-like disease with childhood xanthomas, premature atherosclerosis, and hemolytic anemia with macrothrombocytopenia. Management relies on strict low-plant-sterol diets plus ezetimibe and sometimes bile acid sequestrants, but sterol reductions are often only partial, pediatric experience is limited, and diagnosis is frequently delayed because routine lipid panels do not measure plant sterols.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Near-complete sitosterol/campesterol normalization to prevent early ASCVD/CHD risk despite diet + ezetimibe ± resins
- Therapies that reverse hematologic membrane pathology (hemolytic anemia/stomatocytosis/macrothrombocytopenia) beyond routine lab improvement
- Lower-burden, adherence-friendly regimens effective in infants/children <2 years, reducing reliance on strict diet and long-term bile-acid sequestrants

name: Plasmacytoma | solitary osseous
description: Solitary plasmacytoma of bone is a rare, localized plasma cell tumor in midlife (median ~55, male predominant) that typically presents with focal bone pain and may cause pathologic fractures or spinal cord compression, without myeloma defining systemic organ damage at diagnosis. Radiotherapy provides local control, but many patients later progress to multiple myeloma, especially with limited marrow involvement or persistent monoclonal protein. The central unmet need is risk stratification and a risk adapted systemic approach after local therapy to deepen remission and prevent systemic progression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Post-radiotherapy systemic therapy to clear persistent M-protein/normalize serum free-light chain ratio (achieve CR) to reduce progression to multiple myeloma.
- Early systemic therapy for “solitary plasmacytoma with minimal bone marrow involvement” (<10% monoclonal plasma cells) to cut high early MM progression risk.
- Adjunct systemic regimens compatible with few-session SBRT to preserve local control while improving long-term PFS/MM-free survival.

name: Melanoma | uveal
description: Uveal melanoma is an adult eye cancer of the uveal tract, typically diagnosed around age 60 and often found incidentally or with painless visual symptoms. Most cases are localized initially, but up to half later develop metastases predominantly to the liver, where outcomes are poor. Care is fragmented, with tebentafusp limited to HLA-A*02:01 positive patients and burdensome weekly infusions with monitoring, while liver perfusion melphalan fits only selected liver-limited disease and carries procedural risk. There is no consensus first-line systemic option for HLA-A*02:01 negative metastatic disease, driving interest in adjuvant and pathway-targeted approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Overall-survival–improving systemic therapy for HLA‑A*02:01‑negative metastatic uveal melanoma (no consensus 1L option), ideally without weekly IV and prolonged monitoring.
- Liver-metastasis control (hepatic response/hepatic PFS) with less invasive, non‑REMS delivery and better tolerability than melphalan hepatic perfusion, and usable beyond the <50% liver-involvement population.
- Adjuvant systemic therapy to improve recurrence‑free survival in high‑risk non‑metastatic uveal melanoma post-local therapy where observation is current standard of care and relapse is common.

name: Heerfordt syndrome
description: Heerfordt syndrome (uveoparotid fever) is a rare acute presentation of systemic sarcoidosis marked by uveitis with parotid swelling, fever, and facial nerve palsy; the central unmet need is durable, vision preserving control as sight threatening cystoid macular edema can develop and care often relies on systemic corticosteroids that may be inadequate or toxic, requiring steroid sparing immunosuppressants and tumor necrosis factor alpha inhibitors.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable vision-preserving control of Heerfordt/sarcoid uveitis (esp. posterior/macular disease with cystoid macular oedema), achieving visual acuity/inflammation improvement with ≥50% systemic steroid taper without relapse.
- Steroid-sparing systemic therapy to avoid long-term corticosteroid toxicities (e.g., diabetes/HTN/osteoporosis; cataract/glaucoma) in patients needing prolonged systemic steroids.
- Safer, lower-burden alternatives to anti-TNF biologics for steroid-refractory ocular sarcoidosis/uveitis (fewer serious infections/interruptions, less relapse after discontinuation, and less IV/SC administration burden).

name: Oropharyngeal cancer | HPV-negative
description: HPV negative oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma is a tobacco and heavy alcohol associated cancer of the tonsil and base of tongue, typically in older men, presenting with persistent sore throat, painful swallowing, and neck nodes. Care relies on surgery and radiotherapy with systemic therapy, often concurrent cisplatin, but outcomes are poorer than HPV positive disease and many patients cannot tolerate cisplatin due to age, frailty, renal dysfunction, or hearing loss. Treatment can also leave lasting oral mucositis and debilitating dysphagia, making less toxic regimens that preserve speech and swallowing a major need.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Improve OS/recurrence outcomes specifically in p16-negative oropharyngeal cancer
- Develop cisplatin-sparing concurrent systemic therapy/radiosensitizer for cisplatin-ineligible patients
- Create swallowing-/mucositis-sparing regimens to reduce severe acute toxicity and long-term dysphagia/functional sequelae

name: Variegate porphyria
description: Variegate porphyria is a rare inherited heme metabolism disorder caused by PPOX deficiency leading to porphyrin buildup, with postpubertal photosensitive blistering skin disease and intermittent acute neurovisceral attacks. Management is largely trigger avoidance and hospital based intravenous dextrose and hemin for attacks, but many patients still require hospitalization, chronic intravenous hemin carries central line, infection, and iron overload risks, and hemin or glucose do not reliably control chronic cutaneous symptoms, leaving a need for safer disease modifying options that reduce attacks and skin burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drug to materially reduce photosensitivity-driven blistering/skin fragility with slow-healing scarring in cutaneous-dominant (incl. skin-only) VP
- Home-usable, non-IV acute-attack rescue that aborts neurovisceral attacks without multi-day inpatient IV hemin
- Long-term prophylaxis with givosiran-like attack reduction but fewer hepatic/renal safety monitoring burdens and less clinician-administered monthly injection (incl. broader than adults-only)

name: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis
description: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is a rare, aggressive chronic kidney infection driven by obstructing stones and ongoing bacterial infection that can mimic renal cancer and progressively destroys the kidney, often leaving it nonfunctioning. It typically affects middle aged women with urolithiasis and recurrent urinary tract infections who present with flank pain, fever, malaise and sometimes weight loss or a palpable mass. Antibiotics are necessary but rarely curative, so care frequently ends in radical nephrectomy. Key unmet needs are earlier accurate diagnosis and kidney sparing approaches when viable parenchyma remains.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Kidney-sparing medical cure for focal/early XGP with salvageable renal function to avoid nephrectomy.
- Stone-/obstruction-/biofilm-directed anti-infective therapy for staghorn-calculus XGP to prevent progression to a nonfunctioning destroyed kidney.
- Resistance-robust, safer antimicrobial regimens (ideally oral/shorter IV) targeting common XGP pathogens to reduce treatment failure and surgical morbidity/mortality.

name: Yellow nail syndrome
description: Yellow nail syndrome is an ultra-rare, usually late-onset disorder driven by lymphatic drainage dysfunction, presenting with slow-growing thick yellow-green dystrophic nails, chronic respiratory disease including recurrent infections, bronchiectasis and pleural effusions, and often lower-limb lymphedema. Care is largely supportive with no specific therapy, pleural effusions frequently recur after drainage, and nail-directed treatments like high-dose vitamin E or empiric antifungals are inconsistently effective, leaving a premium on disease-modifying approaches that restore lymphatic function and prevent recurrent effusions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Faster, higher-complete-response nail therapy for xanthonychia/thickening that avoids year-long fluconazole+vitamin E courses
- Drug therapy to prevent recurrent pleural effusions and reduce need for repeated thoracentesis/definitive pleural interventions
- Disease-modifying therapy improving lymphatic drainage dysfunction to reduce chronic lymphedema and multisystem morbidity

name: Spiradenoma
description: Spiradenoma is a benign sweat gland skin tumor, typically a solitary blue gray or purple nodule in young to middle aged adults, notable for severe pain and often managed with surgical excision. The biggest unmet need is durable nonsurgical control and pain relief, especially for patients with CYLD cutaneous syndrome who develop multiple recurring lesions requiring repeated procedures. Malignant transformation is rare, but metastatic spiradenocarcinoma is high stakes and lacks clear treatment guidelines.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical tumor-burden suppression for *CYLD* cutaneous syndrome patients with multiple spiradenomas/cylindromas to durably reduce new lesions and repeat excisions.
- Effective systemic therapy for metastatic/high-grade spiradenocarcinoma (carcinoma arising from spiradenoma) to achieve objective responses and prevent/slow metastasis.
- Non-opioid, lesion-directed analgesic therapy to rapidly and durably reduce pain without requiring excision (esp. patients with multiple lesions).

name: Splenic infarction
description: Splenic infarction is ischemic necrosis of splenic tissue from interrupted blood flow, typically in adults over 40 with thromboembolism or hypercoagulability, presenting with acute left upper abdominal pain plus fever or nausea. Care is largely supportive and pain driven, with inconsistent use of anticoagulation when thrombosis is suspected, and complications like abscess, hemorrhage, or rupture can require urgent escalation. Key unmet needs include an established treatment pathway, safer antithrombotic strategies that balance clot control with bleeding risk, and opioid sparing symptom control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer/more effective antithrombotic regimens that reduce high 1‑year recurrent thrombosis while limiting major bleeding.
- Non‑opioid/NSAID‑sparing symptom control that shortens the typical 7–14 day pain course and enables earlier discharge/outpatient management.
- Medical prevention of splenic-infarct complications (e.g., abscess, hemorrhage, rupture, pseudocyst) to avoid escalation to emergent/surgical management.

name: Spontaneous tension pneumothorax
description: Spontaneous pneumothorax is air leaking into the pleural space, usually from ruptured blebs, causing sudden pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath often at rest. Tension physiology can rapidly become fatal from impaired venous return, making prompt recognition and decompression critical. Even after initial management, 25 to 50 percent recur within a year and some develop persistent air leaks, while options like pleurodesis can be poorly tolerated. The practical unmet need is safer, faster leak closure and durable recurrence prevention with less pain, hospitalization, and procedure burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Low-pain, low-ARDS-risk recurrence-prevention therapy for first-episode PSP presenting with tension physiology that reduces ~25–30% recurrence
- Drain-delivered “seal-the-leak” therapy for persistent air leak that enables chest drain removal within ≤5 days
- Safer rapid procedural analgesia/anxiolysis + local anesthesia for emergency decompression/chest tube insertion that preserves ventilation/hemodynamics

name: Subcorneal pustular dermatosis
description: Rare chronic relapsing neutrophilic dermatosis with recurrent sterile pustules on the trunk and skin folds, typically in women over 40 and otherwise systemically well. Dapsone often clears lesions but long term control is limited by hematologic toxicity and the need for prolonged monitoring for paraproteinemia or progression to myeloma. Key unmet needs are safer durable disease control and therapies that reduce relapse and long term surveillance burden, with cytokine pathway targeting such as interleukin 1 blockade under exploration.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Dapsone-sparing maintenance control that reduces hemolysis/methemoglobinemia risk and high-frequency CBC monitoring while preventing relapse
- Mechanism-targeted therapies for dapsone-refractory disease with objective endpoints for development
- Long-term control compatible with hematologic comorbidity surveillance (e.g., paraproteinemia/myeloma risk) without added myelosuppression complexity

name: Subdural empyema
description: Subdural empyema is a loculated pus collection between the dura and arachnoid, often arising from sinus or middle ear infection in young males, causing fever and headache that can rapidly progress to vomiting, altered mental status, seizures, and focal deficits. Care requires urgent neurosurgical drainage plus weeks of broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics, yet hemiparesis, seizures, and persistent neurologic disability remain common, creating unmet need for faster diagnosis, safer shorter antimicrobial courses, and adjuncts that prevent long term neurologic damage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-oral or long-acting antimicrobial regimens that maintain cure while avoiding/shortening 3–6+ weeks of IV antibiotics (reduced OPAT burden).
- Adjunct neuroprotective/anti-epileptogenic therapy to reduce persistent seizures and long-term neurologic deficits after infection control.
- Less-toxic broad-spectrum alternatives to common multi-week components (e.g., vancomycin- and prolonged metronidazole-sparing) while preserving MRSA/anaerobe coverage.

name: Syringocystadenoma papilliferum
description: Ultra-rare, usually benign apocrine or eccrine sweat gland tumor presenting at birth or around puberty as a pink, sometimes exudative scalp or head and neck papule or plaque that may itch, hurt, or bleed; managed with complete surgical excision but recurrence is common, and lesions in nevus sebaceus carry some basal cell carcinoma risk, creating demand for durable non-surgical local control, better surveillance, and mutation-informed approaches (for example RAS–mitogen-activated protein kinase alterations such as BRAF V600E or HRAS).
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Mutation-guided topical/intralesional RAS–MAPK inhibition (e.g., BRAF V600E/HRAS-driven) to clear lesions non-surgically.
- Drug-based strategy for durable local control and recurrence prevention to avoid repeat procedures.
- Chemoprevention/field therapy to reduce BCC/malignant-transformation risk in nevus-sebaceus–associated SCAP.

name: Thanatophoric dysplasia
description: Thanatophoric dysplasia is a rare, usually perinatally lethal skeletal dysplasia caused by activating fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 mutations, typically detected on mid pregnancy ultrasound with profound limb shortening and a narrow chest. Most infants die shortly after birth from respiratory failure due to reduced thoracic capacity or brainstem compression, and the few who survive require invasive long term ventilation and often neurosurgical decompression. Care is supportive only, leaving a premium on disease modifying fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 pathway therapies that can be started prenatally or immediately after birth to prevent lethal respiratory compromise and reduce lifelong intensive support.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prenatal (maternal/transplacental) FGFR3‑pathway therapy started immediately after early diagnosis to prevent lethal early respiratory failure and avoid long-term trach/vent dependence.
- Postnatal disease-modifying therapy for long-term TD survivors delivering clinically meaningful pulmonary benefit (e.g., large vital-capacity gains) with acceptable tolerability to reduce reliance on aggressive ventilatory support.
- Precision FGFR3 therapy to reduce foramen magnum narrowing/brain-stem compression (and downstream invasive procedures), ideally as an oral formulation.

name: Thelaziasis
description: Fly transmitted zoonotic eyeworm infection where Thelazia nematodes inhabit the conjunctival sac and lacrimal ducts, causing conjunctivitis like irritation with tearing, itching and foreign body sensation that can progress to keratitis, corneal ulceration and even blindness. Humans are usually incidental hosts and diagnosis is often missed because larvae can hide in lacrimal ducts and mimic allergic conjunctivitis. Care still relies on mechanical removal, leaving a need for practical topical or short course therapies that clear adults and larvae and for prevention that reduces repeat exposure to vector flies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Topical, self-administered ocular anthelmintic that clears adult worms + larvae without manual extraction
- Ocular-penetrant anti-Thelazia therapy for severe keratitis/corneal ulceration or intraocular invasion to prevent sight-threatening complications
- Post-removal adjunct larvicidal/anthelmintic (topical or short-course systemic) to prevent recurrence from residual/newly acquired worms

name: Thrombocytopenia-absent radius syndrome
description: Thrombocytopenia absent radius syndrome is a congenital disorder with absent forearm radii but preserved thumbs and severe infant thrombocytopenia, creating high risk of life threatening bleeding especially intracranial hemorrhage in the first year. Platelet counts often improve over time, but care is largely supportive with platelet or blood product transfusions that carry alloimmunization and infection risks. Cow’s milk reactions can exacerbate thrombocytopenia and some infants also have heart or kidney malformations, underscoring the need for safer transfusion sparing ways to stabilize platelets early in life.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid, durable platelet-count rescue in neonates/infants to prevent first-year catastrophic hemorrhage (esp. intracranial)
- Transfusion-sparing outpatient platelet maintenance to reduce platelet-transfusion dependence, central-line use, and alloimmunization/infection risk
- Targeted therapy for cow’s-milk–allergy/intolerance phenotype to prevent cow’s-milk–triggered thrombocytopenic flares (± eosinophilic/leukemoid episodes) beyond dietary avoidance

name: Adenoma | thyroid, toxic
description: Toxic thyroid adenoma is usually a single benign thyroid nodule that autonomously produces thyroid hormone, causing hyperthyroidism with symptoms like palpitations, heat intolerance, and weight loss and raising risks such as atrial fibrillation and bone loss. Medications and beta blockers can control symptoms but are not curative and relapse is expected when stopped. Definitive treatment is typically surgery or radioactive iodine, which can take months to work, may result in hypothyroidism needing lifelong replacement, and is contraindicated in pregnancy and lactation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable nodule-targeted pharmacotherapy achieving sustained euthyroidism in solitary toxic adenoma without relapse after stopping therapy and avoiding surgery/I‑131–induced hypothyroidism.
- Rapid-onset, safer medical control of autonomous (subclinical→overt) hyperthyroidism—especially in older adults—to reduce AF/fracture/mortality risk while awaiting slow I‑131 effect.
- Pregnancy-/lactation-compatible definitive therapy (non-radioactive, non-teratogenic), avoiding I‑131 contraindication and thionamide fetal-risk tradeoffs.

name: Tooth and nail syndrome
description: Tooth and nail syndrome (Witkop syndrome) is a rare inherited ectodermal dysplasia caused by disrupted MSX1 driven development, typically recognized in mid childhood when primary teeth persist and permanent teeth fail to erupt, leaving missing or small conical teeth plus thin brittle ridged nails often worse in toenails. Management is supportive with ongoing dental rehabilitation and prosthetic replacement rather than disease modification, creating unmet need for earlier diagnosis, reduced lifelong functional aesthetic and psychosocial burden, and ultimately biologic tooth repair or regenerative living tooth replacement beyond implants and dentures.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Injectable therapy to regenerate/induce eruption of missing permanent teeth to reduce reliance on prosthetics/braces/surgery
- MSX1 restoration (gene replacement/editing or functional rescue) early in development to prevent tooth+nail defects
- Local regenerative nail therapy (topical/targeted) to normalize thin/brittle/koilonychia toenails by improving nail thickness/strength and growth

name: Dystonia | DYT-type (Genetic)
description: Early onset monogenic dystonias such as TOR1A dystonia are childhood onset movement disorders with task triggered limb spasms that can spread over months to years into disabling twisting postures and tremor despite preserved cognition. Treatment is symptomatic with repeated botulinum toxin injections that wear off in about three months and can cause function limiting weakness, oral drugs often limited by sleepiness and confusion, and invasive deep brain stimulation. Key unmet needs are durable, gene informed therapies that prevent generalization and provide long lasting control without weakness or surgery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-targeted early therapy in childhood/adolescent limb-onset DYT (e.g., DYT1/TOR1A) to prevent spread/generalization and downstream disability.
- Longer-lasting focal treatment than current botulinum toxin (beyond 3–4 month retreatment cycles) with less weakness and reduced antibody-related loss of response.
- Durable, cognitively sparing oral systemic therapy for generalized/medically refractory dystonia with sustained improvement on severity scales (e.g., BFM-DRS).

name: Trimethylaminuria
description: Rare metabolic disorder where impaired trimethylamine breakdown causes fluctuating rotten fish odor in sweat, urine, and breath, with major social and psychological burden despite otherwise normal health. Management is high burden and inconsistent using diet restriction, binders, intermittent antibiotics, and riboflavin, and there is no cure, creating demand for durable low burden odor control, non antibiotic gut trimethylamine suppression, and approaches that restore flavin containing monooxygenase 3 function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Longer‑acting, lower‑burden oral TMA sequestrants to reduce urinary free TMA with fewer daily doses than current charcoal/chlorophyllin regimens
- Targeted, non‑antibiotic gut‑metabolism therapies to suppress TMA production (e.g., choline→TMA blockade or TMA‑lowering microbes) with more consistent efficacy than antibiotics/probiotics
- FMO3‑function augmentation/restoration for primary genetic TMAU to address hepatic FMO3 deficiency beyond residual‑activity support (e.g., riboflavin)

name: Triple A syndrome
description: Triple A (Allgrove) syndrome is a rare inherited AAAS gene disorder causing early alacrima, later esophageal achalasia with severe feeding and weight loss, and adrenocorticotropic hormone resistant adrenal insufficiency with risk of hypoglycemia, seizures, and adrenal crisis, often followed by dysautonomia and progressive neurologic decline. Treatment is fragmented and supportive only with artificial tears, lifelong steroid replacement, and dilation or surgery for often refractory achalasia, leaving no way to modify the underlying disease course or reliably prevent life threatening crises.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- AAAS/ALADIN-targeted disease-modifying therapy to prevent/slow progressive autonomic/neurodegenerative dysfunction (dysautonomia/neuropathy, dysphagia)
- Better prevention of life-threatening adrenal crises beyond steroid replacement (lower reliance on complex stress-dosing and emergency IM/SC hydrocortisone)
- Pharmacologic therapy for Triple A–associated achalasia to reduce need for esophageal dilatation/myotomy and severe feeding/weight-loss complications

name: Complement component 8 deficiency | type 1
description: Rare inherited immunodeficiency where loss of complement component 8 prevents membrane attack complex formation, leaving patients prone to invasive Neisseria meningitidis infections often first presenting in adolescence or young adulthood with meningococcal meningitis. Management is prevention focused with meningococcal vaccination and sometimes long term antibiotics, but vaccines do not fully eliminate risk and there is no disease correcting therapy, creating demand for durable protection that restores complement function with lower prophylaxis burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable terminal-complement (MAC) restoration (e.g., long-acting C8 replacement or C8A gene therapy) to correct complement-dependent bactericidal defects in C5–C8 deficiencies.
- Complement-independent meningococcal prophylaxis (e.g., broadly bactericidal anti-meningococcal mAb) to prevent breakthrough IMD despite vaccination/high antibody titres.
- Lower-burden, resistance-sparing long-term prevention to replace frequent MenB boosters and chronic antibiotic prophylaxis.

name: Complement component 8 deficiency | type 2
description: Rare inherited C8B driven terminal complement (membrane attack complex) deficiency causing susceptibility to recurrent invasive Neisseria meningitidis infections and meningitis, often first recognized after a meningitis episode after age 10; care relies on vaccination and antibiotics but risk persists, prophylaxis is inconsistent, and there is no durable complement restorative therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Complement-independent prophylaxis to prevent recurrent invasive meningococcal disease despite MenACWY/MenB vaccination
- Durable restoration of terminal complement (MAC) function (e.g., C8B “replacement-like” or gene therapy) without frequent infusions/anti-protein antibodies
- Evidence-backed, resistance-sparing long-term prophylaxis to replace chronic penicillin/cotrimoxazole-style prevention

name: Tyrosinemia | type 1
description: Hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 is a rare fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency in tyrosine metabolism where toxic metabolites drive early life progressive liver and kidney damage, with risks of neurologic crises and hepatocellular carcinoma. Newborn screening plus nitisinone and a low tyrosine diet yields high survival but leaves major burdens from lifelong dietary restriction and frequent monitoring, plus residual cancer risk, eye complications from elevated tyrosine, and neurocognitive impairment in some patients. A key frontier is liver directed gene therapy or editing aiming for one time metabolic correction.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- FAH-restoring disease-correction (e.g., liver-directed gene therapy/editing) to eliminate residual HCC risk and reduce late-treated patients’ need for liver transplant.
- Neurocognitive-protective adjuncts/curative approaches that maintain physiologic tyrosine/phenylalanine exposure to prevent learning/cognitive sequelae despite nitisinone.
- Lower-burden chronic management (or curative alternative) enabling diet liberalization while reducing monitoring needs and tyrosine-driven ocular-toxicity risk vs nitisinone.

name: Verruciform xanthoma
description: Uncommon benign reactive histiocytic lesion of the oral mucosa, typically a slow growing asymptomatic solitary papillary or verrucous plaque under 1.5 cm on gingiva or hard palate in older adults, often arising in chronically inflamed or traumatized mucosa and frequently misdiagnosed; treated mainly by surgical excision but recurs in about 12 percent, creating need for non surgical clearance and field directed options in patients with inflammatory oral disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Topical/intralesional non-surgical therapy achieving complete verruciform xanthoma lesion clearance without excision.
- Post-excision adjunct to reduce recurrence risk (~12%), especially for trauma-prone masticatory-site lesions.
- Field-directed anti-inflammatory/immune-modulating therapy to prevent new lesions in multifocal disease linked to chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., chronic GVHD/oral lichen planus).

name: Verrucous carcinoma
description: Verrucous carcinoma is a rare, slow growing, highly differentiated exophytic squamous cell carcinoma most often in the oral cavity of older men. It is typically nonmetastasizing but can be locally infiltrative and destructive, causing warty masses, pain, halitosis, and difficulty chewing or swallowing. Management relies on surgical excision, yet margins and recurrence are highly variable, making durable local control and tissue sparing approaches in sensitive head and neck sites a key unmet need. Systemic options for extensive unresectable disease remain ill defined.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Function-/cosmesis-sparing topical or intralesional drug therapy to avoid traumatic/deforming wide excision in patients unable/unwilling to undergo surgery.
- Adjuvant (post-excision) recurrence-prevention therapy to reduce local recurrence and support close/positive (“margin-challenged”) resections without re-operation.
- Effective systemic therapy for locally advanced unresectable or metastatic (incl. HPV-related) verrucous carcinoma to achieve objective responses and reduce reliance on radiotherapy/chemoradiation.
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus page; see https://medlineplus.gov/oralcancer.html and https://medlineplus.gov/headandneckcancer.html

name: White sponge nevus
description: Rare inherited oral mucosal keratin disorder (KRT4/KRT13) causing early childhood onset, bilateral non removable white spongy plaques on the buccal mucosa that are usually painless but can cause discomfort and cosmetic bother; frequently misdiagnosed as thrush leading to unnecessary antifungals, with unmet need for earlier accurate diagnosis and safe disease modifying therapy to durably reduce plaque burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- KRT4/KRT13-targeted disease-modifying therapy to correct keratin-filament defect and prevent/clear oral mucosal plaques
- Durable reduction of plaque thickness/extent and improved mouth texture/appearance without chronic maintenance antibiotics
- Safe, non-antibiotic approach for early-onset patients to prevent secondary infection/discomfort and reduce unnecessary antifungal exposure from thrush misdiagnosis

name: Cherubism
description: Cherubism is a childhood onset autoinflammatory jaw bone disorder in which the mandible and maxilla are replaced by painless cyst like fibroosseous lesions, causing progressive bilateral facial swelling and severe dental eruption and occlusion problems. Lesions typically expand from ages two to seven through puberty then often regress, but some children develop airway, speech, swallowing, or eye complications. Care is largely observation, orthodontics, and surgery, with evolving protocols, possible recurrence, and procedures that may not halt progression, creating demand for safe pediatric medical therapy that arrests lesions early and preserves dentition.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pediatric, non-surgical therapy that halts active jaw-lesion growth pre‑puberty to avoid/reduce surgery and recurrence
- Therapy that preserves dentition/eruption (prevents displaced/unerupted/absent “free‑floating” teeth) rather than deferring orthodontics until after regression
- Pediatric-authorized targeted regimen (e.g., antiresorptive/anti‑inflammatory) with standardized dosing/monitoring and improved safety vs today’s off‑label options

name: Anisakiasis
description: Anisakiasis is a foodborne nematode infection from eating raw or undercooked fish or squid, where larvae embed in the gastrointestinal wall and trigger abrupt severe epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting within hours. Diagnosis and cure for gastric disease often require endoscopic visualization and removal, while intestinal or extraintestinal cases are harder to diagnose and can escalate to obstruction or peritonitis requiring urgent surgery. Allergic manifestations from hives to rare anaphylaxis add risk, highlighting unmet needs for endoscopy sparing short course oral therapy, more reliable systemic medical options for complicated disease, and approaches that prevent severe allergic reactions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Endoscopy-sparing short-course oral therapy that definitively clears larvae and rapidly relieves symptoms in gastric anisakiasis.
- Proven systemic regimen for intestinal/extraintestinal anisakiasis that prevents obstruction/peritonitis and reduces need for urgent surgery.
- Anisakis-specific allergen/IgE-pathway preventive or abortive therapy to prevent severe urticaria/angioedema/anaphylaxis in sensitized patients after seafood exposure.

name: Anthrax
description: Anthrax is a high consequence infection caused by Bacillus anthracis, typically acquired from infected animals or contaminated animal products. Most cases are cutaneous, presenting as a painless lesion that evolves over days into a black eschar with surrounding edema, but inhalational or systemic disease can rapidly progress to meningitis with over 90 percent mortality despite treatment. Key gaps include delayed recognition and the burden of post exposure prophylaxis requiring multiple vaccine doses plus up to 60 days of antibiotics, motivating interest in simpler long acting prophylaxis and better central nervous system active antitoxin approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- “Set-and-forget” post‑exposure prophylaxis covering the full ≥60‑day spore‑dormancy window without 60‑day twice‑daily antibiotics and multi‑visit vaccination.
- CNS‑effective adjuncts for anthrax meningitis (BBB‑penetrant anti‑toxin/anti‑virulence) to reduce ~90% fatality.
- Rapidly deployable, non‑infusion anti‑toxin/anti‑virulence therapy (IM/SC/oral) for severe inhalational/systemic anthrax to enable scalable administration vs monitored IV infusions.

name: Botulism
description: Botulism is a rare neurotoxin mediated paralytic illness that can progress from cranial nerve palsies to respiratory failure, with flaccid weakness lasting weeks to months. Infant botulism typically affects babies 6 weeks to 6 months old after ingested spores colonize the gut and produce toxin, starting with constipation and poor feeding and potentially evolving to bulbar weakness and ventilatory failure. Care is largely supportive plus time critical antitoxin that cannot reverse established paralysis, leaving prolonged intensive care risk. Key gaps include faster, safer, broader antitoxin access and adjuncts that accelerate functional recovery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct therapies that reverse/accelerate recovery from established paralysis to reduce ventilator days and weeks–months of post-onset weakness
- Immediate-start antitoxin/anti-toxin-pathway treatments that eliminate centralized-release delays and enable first-hours dosing in any ER/ICU
- Fully human/recombinant, scalable broad-serotype antitoxins (including infant-appropriate) that reduce equine hypersensitivity/serum-sickness risk and expand beyond BabyBIG’s A/B infant limitation

name: Angioma serpiginosum
description: Rare benign superficial vascular skin disorder causing childhood-onset clustered pinpoint red to violaceous macules, usually on buttocks and legs, mainly affecting girls and young women; medically harmless but cosmetically and psychosocially burdensome, with limited evidence-based topical options and reliance on multiple-session laser therapy for fading.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Proven-effective topical pharmacotherapy (e.g., beta‑blocker class) to fade lesions in angioma serpiginosum (esp. females <20y)
- Short-course drug option achieving near-complete cosmetic clearance without repeated/multi-session laser visits
- Pigment-sparing, pain-minimizing medical alternative with low iatrogenic risk for this benign/cosmetic condition

name: Angiostrongyliasis
description: Angiostrongyliasis is rat lungworm infection in which Angiostrongylus cantonensis larvae enter the brain and trigger eosinophilic meningitis, causing severe headache, nausea or vomiting, neck stiffness, and neurologic symptoms after eating raw or undercooked infected snails or slugs. Care is largely supportive with analgesics, corticosteroids, and sometimes serial lumbar punctures, with optional albendazole. The key unmet need is a proven, safe anthelmintic regimen since worm killing may worsen neurologic inflammation, and patients can have weeks to months of symptoms and chronic neuropathic pain.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Proven CNS-active anthelmintic regimen that improves outcomes without neurologic worsening from “dying-worm” inflammatory reactions.
- Steroid-sparing anti-inflammatory therapy that preserves headache/LP benefit while improving safety in high-risk patients (e.g., diabetes/glucose intolerance).
- Adjunct therapy to reduce serial lumbar punctures/CSF removal and prevent chronic neurologic sequelae (chronic pain, weakness, cognitive issues, recurrent headache).

name: Argininosuccinic aciduria
