description: Argininosuccinic aciduria is a rare inherited urea cycle disorder where argininosuccinate lyase deficiency drives toxic ammonia buildup, causing newborn metabolic crashes and long term brain injury. Babies may appear normal for 24 to 48 hours then rapidly develop hyperammonemia with poor feeding, vomiting, tachypnea, seizures, coma, and death if untreated. Care depends on lifelong protein restriction, arginine, nitrogen scavengers, and sometimes dialysis, yet many patients still develop neurocognitive deficits, liver disease, and hypertension, highlighting the need for disease modifying therapies beyond crisis prevention.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neurocognitive-outcome–modifying therapy that improves attention/learning disability/seizures beyond hyperammonemic crisis control.
- Liver- and vascular-complication–modifying therapy (e.g., fibrosis/cirrhosis and hypertension endpoints) beyond ammonia scavenging.
- Crisis-prevention + care-burden–reducing therapy that cuts ICU-level hyperammonemic episodes and need for dialysis/hemofiltration (ideally with less restrictive diet/less scavenger use).

name: Atypical autosomal dominant adult-onset demyelinating leukodystrophy
description: Rare, slowly progressive adult-onset demyelinating leukodystrophy with cerebral and corticospinal white-matter involvement and cerebellar sparing, causing spastic weakness, dysarthria, and worsening gait that can progress to paralysis and swallowing problems. Treatment is symptomatic with no disease-modifying therapy; early gene-silencing antisense oligonucleotides are entering human testing.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- LMNB1-directed disease modification (e.g., ASO/RNAi) to slow functional gait decline and MRI brain atrophy beyond symptomatic care
- Non-sedating, strength-sparing spasticity treatments that avoid CNS AEs (e.g., baclofen drowsiness; tizanidine AE-driven discontinuation)
- Remyelination/neuroprotection targeting cerebral + corticospinal-tract white matter with differentiation tracked by MRI progression biomarkers and gait endpoints

name: Chronic myeloid leukemia | atypical
description: Rare BCR-ABL1 negative myelodysplastic myeloproliferative overlap leukemia in older adults, marked by neutrophilic leukocytosis, organomegaly and dysgranulopoiesis with fatigue and bleeding or bruising. No established standard of care and commonly used cytoreduction such as hydroxyurea delivers only short lived control, leaving patients at ongoing risk of progression and leukemic transformation and creating demand for durable, mutation informed disease modifying therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable disease control that improves survival and reduces AML transformation (beyond short-lived hydroxyurea cytoreduction).
- Molecularly matched targeted therapies for genetically defined subsets (e.g., CSF3R/JAK2-, RAS-mutated) to achieve deep remissions.
- Transfusion-sparing, better-tolerated options for older, cytopenia-prone patients ineligible for allo-HSCT (avoiding interferon-limiting toxicity).

name: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease
description: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease is an inherited kidney tubule disorder causing slowly progressive chronic kidney disease with bland urinalysis and often normal imaging, frequently first detected by incidentally elevated creatinine and advancing to dialysis or transplant in adulthood. Key subtypes are driven by intracellular retention of misprocessed proteins such as mutant uromodulin or mucin 1 frameshift, yet there are no disease specific treatments for major forms like ADTKD MUC1. Unmet needs center on earlier genetic diagnosis and disease modifying therapies that can slow non proteinuric decline before end stage renal disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ADTKD‑MUC1: kidney-targeted clearance of ERGIC-accumulating MUC1fs to slow eGFR decline/time to ESKD beyond supportive CKD care
- ADTKD‑UMOD: therapies that reduce mutant UMOD ER retention/ER-stress (better than failed chemical chaperones) while improving urine-concentrating defect/hyperuricemia
- Pan‑ADTKD: renoprotective/anti-fibrotic drug proven to slow non‑proteinuric CKD progression beyond standard CKD management (classes like SGLT2i not well validated)

name: Dystonia | dopa-responsive
description: Very rare, genetically driven dopamine-deficiency disorder that typically begins in childhood with foot and leg dystonia causing gait disturbance and diurnal worsening with sleep benefit, sometimes progressing to parkinsonism and mood or sleep issues. Low-dose levodopa can be dramatically effective, but many patients are underdiagnosed or misdiagnosed and miss years of reversible disability. Related recessive dopamine-pathway forms can include neurodevelopmental impairment and broader non-motor burden, leaving a need for earlier, more reliable diagnosis and treatments that address residual cognitive and psychiatric impact.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy for severe autosomal-recessive/infantile encephalopathic DRD (e.g., TH/SPR) where levodopa is dose-limited or ineffective.
- Adjuncts that improve non-motor burden in GCH1-deficient DRD (psychiatric symptoms, sleep disturbance, fatigue/cognitive issues) beyond motor response to levodopa.
- Long-acting dopaminergic delivery to cover diurnal worsening while reducing multi-dose schedules and minimizing start-up dyskinesia/missed-dose relapse.

name: Ichthyosis | congenital
description: Congenital ichthyosis is a heterogeneous group of inherited disorders of skin cornification, often presenting at birth with a collodion membrane, ectropion, and eclabium. When the membrane cracks, barrier failure can cause dehydration, temperature instability, and infection risk. Survivors often face lifelong plate like scaling, painful fissures, heat intolerance, and hours of daily skin care. Treatment is mostly topical barrier repair and keratolytics, with systemic retinoids limited by toxicity, leaving a need for safer disease modifying options such as topical gene therapy and targeted immunomodulation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neonatal barrier-restoring therapy to reduce dehydration/hypernatremia/electrolyte imbalance and lower infection/sepsis risk enough to shorten NICU humidified-incubator dependence.
- Genotype-corrective treatment for TGM1-deficient ARCI/lamellar ichthyosis with objective endpoints (e.g., IGA/VIIS scaling response and TGM1 restoration in skin).
- Retinoid-sparing long-term therapy that improves painful/itchy fissures and hypohidrosis/heat intolerance while reducing reliance on daily emollients/keratolytics and avoiding systemic-retinoid toxicities.

name: Distal renal tubular acidosis
description: Distal renal tubular acidosis is a rare disorder where the distal kidney cannot excrete acid, causing chronic metabolic acidosis that often begins in infancy with poor growth, vomiting, polyuria, dehydration, and hypokalemia, and can lead to nephrocalcinosis, kidney stones, and declining kidney function. Care relies on lifelong alkali replacement, but current formulations often require 2 to 6 doses daily, are limited by adherence and gastrointestinal intolerance, and sodium loads can worsen urinary calcium. In some inherited forms, progressive sensorineural hearing loss continues despite treatment, underscoring the need for better tolerated, longer acting, and disease modifying options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Once-/twice-daily alkali regimen that maintains 24-hour serum bicarbonate targets and hypokalemia control (vs ideal q6h dosing) to improve adherence.
- Kidney-protective adjunct to reduce nephrocalcinosis/nephrolithiasis and slow CKD progression beyond alkali replacement, without sodium-driven hypercalciuria.
- Disease-modifying therapy for autosomal-recessive dRTA with progressive sensorineural hearing loss not reversed by alkali therapy.

name: Epilepsy | benign familial neonatal
description: Benign familial neonatal seizures is an autosomal dominant KCNQ2 or KCNQ3 channelopathy causing seizures starting around day 3 of life that typically remit within 1 to 4 months, often with tonic stiffening and apnea followed by clonic jerking. Most infants develop normally, but a subset has intellectual disability and about 15 percent later develop recurrent epilepsy. Acute care still often relies on phenobarbital, which can cause cardiorespiratory depression and potential neurotoxicity, creating demand for safer seizure control and rapid genetic diagnosis to guide treatment and counseling.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-first (KCNQ2/KCNQ3) precision antiseizure therapy optimized for rapid neonatal electrographic seizure freedom to shorten hospitalization.
- Non–phenobarbital acute seizure regimens that maintain control while reducing hypotension/respiratory depression and minimizing exposure linked to worse neurodevelopment.
- Preventive therapies for the ~15% with later-life epilepsy recurrence and subsets with developmental sequelae, with endpoints beyond neonatal seizure cessation.

name: Mesothelioma
description: Mesothelioma is a rare, asbestos linked cancer of the mesothelial lining most often affecting the pleura, typically diagnosed after long latency in older exposed people and presenting with breathlessness, cough, chest pain and weight loss. Many patients are advanced or too frail for curative surgery. First line chemotherapy or immunotherapy can extend survival, but relapse is common and second line options remain disappointing, leaving a need for deeper durable disease control, better tolerated later line therapies, and biomarker guided targeted approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Higher-efficacy 1L systemic therapy (especially for epithelioid MPM) that improves disease control beyond current ORR (~40%) and median PFS (~6.8 months) while reducing long-duration IV burden
- Effective, tolerable 2L/3L options after progression (post-platinum+pemetrexed ± IO) given very low response/short disease control and high toxicity with salvage chemo
- Biomarker-selected targeted therapies for large molecular subgroups (e.g., MTAP-deleted and/or BAP1-inactivated) to deliver differentiated benefit vs non-selective IO/chemo

name: Biotin deficiency
description: Biotinidase deficiency is a rare inherited failure to recycle biotin that can present in early infancy with seizures, hypotonia, rash, alopecia, developmental delay, and metabolic decompensation. Newborn screening and prompt biotin can preserve normal development, but late diagnosis can leave irreversible vision, hearing, or neurodevelopmental deficits despite lifelong therapy, creating a premium on early detection and adherence. High dose biotin also interferes with some lab assays, including troponin, risking dangerous false negative results.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that restore (not just stabilize) vision/hearing/neurodevelopment in late-diagnosed symptomatic patients with optic atrophy, hearing loss, and/or developmental delay at biotin initiation
- Adherence-proof long-acting/one-time approaches to avoid relapse from missed lifelong daily oral biotin
- Metabolically effective “lab-interference–safe” alternatives that avoid high free biotin exposure causing false lab results (e.g., falsely low troponin)

name: Biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease
description: Ultra rare autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder with impaired brain thiamine transport causing illness triggered encephalopathic crises with seizures and dystonia that can progress to coma or death; early lifelong biotin plus thiamine can rapidly reverse episodes, but missed diagnosis, poor adherence, and severe infantile forms with refractory respiratory failure leave major unmet need for faster recognition, better acute rescue, and more durable disease modifying maintenance.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS SLC19A3 transporter-restoration (e.g., gene/mRNA/protein replacement) for early-infantile/severe BTBGD with poor or fatal outcomes despite biotin+thiamine
- Rapid crisis “rescue” that maintains CNS thiamine delivery during fever/stress decompensations to avoid ICU/ventilation needs
- Adherence-proof long-acting maintenance (e.g., once-daily fixed-dose combo/depot) to prevent rapid relapse/metabolic crises after dosing interruption

name: Bladder cancer | adenocarcinoma
description: Bladder adenocarcinoma is a very rare malignancy (about 0.5 to 2 percent of bladder cancers) arising from mucus secreting glandular cells, typically affecting men in their 60s to 70s and presenting with hematuria and irritative urinary symptoms. Early lesions can be clinically silent, especially in urachal disease, so many patients present with locally advanced or metastatic disease. Treatment is dominated by major surgery, while systemic therapy is extrapolated from other cancers with no established chemotherapy standard and generally poor outcomes, creating a premium on biomarker guided approaches in targetable subsets such as ERBB2 amplification.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Biomarker-selected targeted therapy (esp. HER2/ERBB2+) for the ~7% of bladder adenocarcinomas (incl. urachal) with ERBB2 amplification/overexpression.
- More effective systemic therapy for advanced/metastatic disease to improve on modest chemo activity (low ORR/short median survival).
- Lower-toxicity and lower-burden regimens versus current 5‑FU/platinum backbones (avoid cisplatin toxicity and prolonged multi-day infusion logistics).

name: Bladder cancer | small cell carcinoma
description: Small cell carcinoma of the bladder is a rare, poorly differentiated neuroendocrine bladder cancer that is highly aggressive and often diagnosed at advanced stage, typically presenting with hematuria in older men with a smoking history. Treatment is largely extrapolated from small cell lung cancer, centered on platinum etoposide chemotherapy, but outcomes are poor in recurrent or metastatic disease and there is little prospective evidence, leaving major unmet need for validated, better tolerated post platinum options and well designed trials.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable first-line systemic therapy that meaningfully improves OS in node-positive/metastatic SCCB (N1–3/M1)
- Validated 2L+ post-platinum treatments for recurrent/metastatic SCCB (vs extrapolated SCLC regimens)
- Safer, less clinic-intensive alternatives to multi-day platinum–etoposide that reduce severe myelosuppression/infections and avoid cisplatin renal/ototoxicity

name: Blepharochalasis
description: Blepharochalasis is a rare eyelid disorder starting in childhood or early adolescence with recurrent, painless eyelid swelling lasting a few days several times per year; repeated flares leave thin, lax “tissue paper” eyelid skin that can obstruct vision and often ultimately requires surgery. There are no standardized, proven medical therapies to abort flares or alter disease course, and surgery is typically delayed until quiescence and may need revision, leaving a major unmet need for effective disease modifying and flare controlling treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute, on-demand flare-abort therapy to reliably shorten 2–3 day eyelid-edema attacks and prevent transient visual obstruction
- Steroid-sparing prophylaxis to materially reduce early-course flare frequency (~3–4 episodes/year) to prevent cumulative tissue stretching/atrophy and later ptosis/dermatochalasis
- Local disease-modifying therapy targeting elastic-fiber degradation pathways (e.g., MMP/IgA-linked elastolysis) to prevent irreversible eyelid laxity/ptosis and reduce reliance on revision-prone surgery

name: Blue cone monochromacy
description: Rare X linked retinal cone disorder causing loss of red and green cone function from infancy, leaving rod and blue cone vision with severe lifelong color vision loss, reduced acuity, photophobia, nystagmus, and often marked myopia. Care is symptomatic only with no disease modifying therapy, creating a premium on durable restoration of cone mediated vision and better daylight function. Gene therapy is a key frontier but is constrained by safety, as subretinal delivery may require foveal detachment, shifting focus to safer less invasive intravitreal approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-targeted L/M-cone functional restoration for X‑linked BCM (*OPN1LW/OPN1MW*) to improve L/M‑cone–mediated vision/BCVA.
- Therapeutics that reduce disabling photophobia and improve contrast sensitivity/daylight vision beyond tinted lenses/low-vision aids.
- Less invasive, safer and durable retinal delivery (ideally intravitreal) that avoids subretinal/subfoveal surgery and works despite progressive cone loss/retinal thinning.

name: Branchiootorenal syndrome
description: Inherited developmental syndrome causing branchial cleft and neck anomalies plus ear malformations with often progressive hearing loss and variable congenital kidney and urinary tract defects that can progress to end stage kidney disease; care is largely supportive, leaving unmet need for disease modifying, genotype targeted therapies to preserve hearing and prevent renal decline.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-targeted disease-modifying therapy restoring EYA1/SIX1/SIX5 pathways for genetically confirmed BOR (esp. EYA1-variant patients).
- Hearing-preservation therapy that halts progressive hearing loss (stabilizes serial audiometry) to avoid escalation to cochlear implantation.
- Kidney-protective therapy that prevents/delays progression of BOR-associated renal disease to ESRD/ESKD (dialysis/transplant).

name: Breast cancer | triple-negative
description: Triple-negative breast cancer is an aggressive invasive breast cancer subtype lacking estrogen and progesterone receptors and with little or no HER2, leaving few biomarker targets and making chemotherapy the backbone. It often presents as a new breast lump or change and disproportionately affects younger patients, Black women, and people with BRCA1 or BRCA2 changes. Despite initial chemo sensitivity, rapid growth, early relapse, and a predilection for visceral and brain metastases drive high morbidity and mortality. Key unmet needs are chemo-sparing curative regimens and more durable systemic and intracranial control in metastatic disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Chemo-sparing perioperative regimens for high-risk early-stage TNBC with KEYNOTE-522–level efficacy but lower serious toxicity/discontinuation and shorter treatment duration
- Systemic therapies with proven intracranial activity for metastatic TNBC patients with brain metastases
- More effective later-line metastatic TNBC agents for patients relapsing early/resistant to anthracycline/taxane/platinum-capecitabine backbones, where options are very limited

name: Bacillary angiomatosis
description: Opportunistic Bartonella (B. henselae/B. quintana) infection in immunocompromised patients that often starts with bleeding, ulcerating skin papules or nodules and can disseminate with systemic symptoms and fatal disease if untreated; care is constrained by long antibiotic courses (at least 3 months), frequent relapse requiring prolonged suppression in advanced human immunodeficiency virus, and drug interaction risk with rifamycins via cytochrome P450 induction.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course, relapse-resistant eradication in advanced HIV (esp. CD4 <200) to avoid ≥3-month courses and long-term suppressive therapy after relapse
- ARV-compatible therapy for CNS/severe or decompensated disease that avoids rifamycin (DDIs) and reduces need for initial IV treatment
- Lower-burden administration (simpler dosing + fewer total months on therapy) to improve adherence in immunocompromised patients

name: Bejel
description: Bejel is a neglected nonsexually transmitted treponemal infection of children in arid endemic regions, spread by close mouth or skin contact and shared utensils, with early painless oral lesions often missed until secondary rash, mucosal disease, lymphadenopathy, and painful bone involvement appear. It is curable with antibiotics, but control is constrained by the logistics of single visit intramuscular benzathine penicillin in low resource settings and the lack of durable, simple oral options given macrolide resistance risk, alongside weak surveillance and no dedicated eradication strategy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral non‑macrolide rescue therapy for azithromycin‑resistant/failed bejel in children (2–15y), avoiding IM benzathine penicillin fallback
- Needle‑free, field‑deployable oral regimen to replace benzathine penicillin when azithromycin can’t be used (no cold chain/injection logistics)
- AMR‑sparing mass‑treatment option that avoids driving macrolide resistance while maintaining single‑visit cure rates

name: Benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis
description: Benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis is an inherited liver disorder with intermittent failures of bile secretion, typically starting in the teens or twenties, causing weeks to months long attacks of severe pruritus followed by jaundice, with patients often well between episodes. Care is largely symptomatic and itch control is often inconsistent and burdensome, sometimes escalating to procedures. Key needs include reliable therapies to abort attacks, control pruritus, and genotype guided treatments for BRIC1 and BRIC2 that restore bile transport and prevent progression toward progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Attack-abortive therapy that reliably induces remission and shortens BRIC pruritus/jaundice bouts (weeks–months).
- Better-tolerated, low-burden pruritus control to replace cholestyramine powder and rifampin (minimal interactions/monitoring; convenient oral pill).
- Genotype-directed preventive therapy for BRIC1 (ATP8B1) and BRIC2 (ABCB11/BSEP) to restore bile secretion and prevent recurrent attacks/progression.

name: Benign shuddering attacks
description: Benign shuddering attacks are frequent, brief nonepileptic shivering spells beginning in infancy, often triggered by feeding or tasks, with preserved awareness and rapid recovery, and they usually remit spontaneously. The main unmet need is fast infant safe diagnostic closure and reassurance to avoid misdiagnosis as epilepsy, family anxiety, unnecessary testing, and anticonvulsant exposure.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid-onset, infant-safe symptomatic suppression for rare high-frequency attacks that impair feeding/dressing (endpoint: attack cessation or major frequency reduction within days)
- Time-limited therapy achieving durable off-treatment remission after discontinuation (vs chronic suppression)
- Non-antiepileptic, non-sedating option for trigger-provoked clusters (e.g., during eating) to reduce episodes during predictable windows and avoid unnecessary antiseizure exposure

name: Teratoma | immature
description: Immature ovarian teratoma is a malignant ovarian germ cell tumor with immature, often primitive neuroectodermal tissue that mainly affects adolescents and very young women and presents as a rapidly enlarging unilateral ovarian mass causing abdominal or pelvic pain and distention. Surgery is often curative, but management hinges on accurately selecting patients for surveillance versus adjuvant bleomycin etoposide cisplatin chemotherapy to avoid long term toxicity in those likely cured, while outcomes remain poor for platinum refractory or relapsed disease where care still relies on intensive salvage including high dose regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Chemo-sparing, risk-adapted post-op management (active surveillance vs adjuvant BEP) for completely resected stage I low-risk disease
- BEP toxicity reduction for cured AYA patients via bleomycin- and/or cisplatin-sparing regimens that preserve cure rates but reduce long-term harms (e.g., fertility impairment)
- New effective systemic options for relapsed/cisplatin-refractory disease to reduce reliance on intensive salvage (e.g., high-dose chemo + autologous stem cell transplant)

name: Birdshot chorioretinopathy
description: Rare, chronic, progressive bilateral posterior uveitis strongly linked to HLA-A29, typically affecting white adults aged 40–60; causes floaters and blurred vision with early night blindness, contrast sensitivity and peripheral field loss despite preserved central acuity, and vision-threatening cystoid macular edema. Care often requires long-term systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppressants yet retinal function may still decline, with key gaps in timely diagnosis, comprehensive functional monitoring beyond eye-chart acuity, and durable steroid-sparing disease control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Predictable, safer steroid‑sparing disease control that reduces systemic corticosteroid burden and avoids trial‑and‑error immunomodulator regimens
- Treat‑to‑target therapies that preserve peripheral visual field/ERG function and contrast sensitivity (beyond Snellen visual acuity)
- Durable control of cystoid macular edema (CME)—preferably local/non‑steroid options for CME persisting despite systemic therapy

name: Piedra | black
description: Black piedra is a superficial fungal infection of the hair shaft caused by Piedraia hortae that forms hard black gritty nodules on hairs, typically in people with long hair in hot humid tropical settings. It is often asymptomatic but chronic, can weaken hair leading to breakage or alopecia, and is mainly a cosmetic and adherence problem. Shaving is most curative but frequently unacceptable, while medicated shampoos require prolonged regimens and some cases need oral antifungals, leaving unmet need for effective, convenient leave on topical eradication.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-shaving, cosmetically acceptable topical/leave-on therapy that fully clears adherent hair-shaft nodules
- Short-course, low-frequency regimen that eradicates *P. hortae* while preventing hair-shaft breakage/alopecia
- High-efficacy non-systemic option for widespread/refractory disease (incl. immunocompromised) to avoid oral antifungal exposure

name: Bladder cancer | squamous cell carcinoma
description: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder is a rare, inflammation linked subtype that typically presents in older adults with hematuria and painful, frequent urination. Localized disease is usually managed with radical cystectomy, while metastatic disease responds poorly to systemic therapy and treatment is often extrapolated from urothelial cancer due to scarce squamous specific evidence. Older, comorbid patients are frequently cisplatin ineligible, reinforcing the need for better tolerated, disease specific systemic and perioperative options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Metastatic bladder squamous cell carcinoma: novel systemic regimens beyond chemo/IO extrapolation to achieve meaningful ORR and durable PFS/OS.
- Muscle-invasive localized bladder SCC: evidence-based perioperative (neo/adjuvant) systemic standard with SCC-specific endpoints (e.g., pathologic downstaging/ypT0) and survival benefit.
- Older/frail, cisplatin-ineligible patients: less toxic, lower-burden systemic options that avoid cisplatin nephrotoxicity/hydration logistics, reduce myelosuppression, and decrease frequent IV clinic visits (e.g., q2w maintenance IO).

name: Adenoma | bronchial
description: Bronchial carcinoids are rare, well differentiated lung neuroendocrine tumors that often arise as central airway lesions in midlife, causing cough, wheeze, hemoptysis, dyspnea, chest pain, and recurrent infections and are sometimes misdiagnosed as asthma. Localized disease is often curable with surgery, but metastatic disease is limited by mostly disease stabilizing systemic options and radioligand therapy that depends on somatostatin receptor uptake. Uncommon brain metastases have poor prognosis, driving demand for durable tumor shrinkage beyond receptor positive disease and in the brain.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non–SSTR-targeted systemic options for metastatic bronchial carcinoid/lung NET with heterogeneous or absent SSTR expression (PRRT-ineligible/suboptimal)
- Objective-response–driven agents achieving durable tumor shrinkage for progressive metastatic pulmonary carcinoid (vs largely cytostatic, low-ORR therapies)
- CNS-penetrant systemic therapies for pulmonary carcinoid patients with brain metastases

name: Bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma
description: Epidermolytic ichthyosis is a congenital keratin fragility disorder caused by KRT1 or KRT10 mutations, marked at birth by erythroderma and severe blistering with dehydration and sepsis risk, evolving into chronic hyperkeratosis, odor and functional limitation. Care is largely symptomatic and intensive early on, with retinoids and other measures that can reduce scale but may worsen fragility and blistering, leaving a major unmet need for safer long term control and durable mutation level, disease modifying correction.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neonatal barrier-stabilizing therapy to reduce denuded-skin infection/sepsis and electrolyte-imbalance risk enough to avoid/shorten NICU-level monitoring
- Hyperkeratosis/scale control that does not worsen blistering/skin fragility and reduces severe pain and mobility limitation from fissures/blistering (esp. hands/feet)
- Mutation-targeted corrective therapy for dominant KRT1/KRT10 (e.g., topical/ex vivo mutant-allele inactivation) to restore keratin filament stability beyond symptomatic care

name: Capillariasis
description: Intestinal capillariasis (usually Capillaria philippinensis) is a fishborne roundworm infection acquired from raw or undercooked freshwater fish that can amplify via hyperinfection, causing months to years of profuse watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, hypoalbuminemia and edema, and in severe cases fatal dehydration and cachexia. Current care relies on 10 to 20 day benzimidazole courses plus relapse follow up and supportive rescue, but pregnancy restrictions and lab monitoring burdens leave a need for shorter, safer, relapse proof regimens and faster physiologic stabilization.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ≤3-day, relapse-/autoinfection-proof regimen to replace 20–30-day BID benzimidazole courses
- Pregnancy- and pediatric-safer alternative to benzimidazoles with minimal monitoring and fewer serious toxicities/DDIs
- Rapid “rescue” therapy proven to reverse protein/electrolyte wasting (hypoalbuminemia/hypokalemia) and prevent cardiomyopathy/death in severe disease

name: Plague | bubonic
description: Bubonic plague is an acute Yersinia pestis infection typically acquired from flea exposed rodents, presenting after 2–8 days with fever and a painful swollen lymph node bubo and risking progression to septicemic or pneumonic disease. Outcomes hinge on immediate empiric antibiotics, as untreated mortality is high. Key gaps include drug regimens that reliably penetrate bubo abscesses, outbreak ready oral options, preparedness for engineered antimicrobial resistance, and the absence of a routinely available vaccine.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rescue therapeutics for delayed-treatment bubonic plague (≥3 days after symptom onset) that cut fatality toward early-treated outcomes
- Bubo-targeted agents with reliable abscess/lymph-node penetration and activity at acidic pH to speed bubo resolution/pain control and avoid alternative/dual therapy
- Mass-outbreak–ready oral regimens (no nephrotoxicity/therapeutic drug monitoring) effective against engineered multi-drug-resistant *Y. pestis* to reduce reliance on empiric dual-class therapy

name: Cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome
description: Cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome is an ultra rare RAS mitogen activated protein kinase pathway disorder that disrupts early development, typically presenting in infancy with congenital heart disease, hypotonia, feeding difficulty, and failure to thrive and later with seizures and neurodevelopmental disability. Treatment is largely supportive, so major unmet needs are disease modifying options that prevent severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and heart failure, control often refractory epilepsy without heavy polypharmacy, and reduce gastrointestinal and feeding complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Targeted RAS/MAPK-pathway therapy for CFC-associated hypertrophic cardiomyopathy/heart failure to reduce major cardiac events
- Precision therapy for BRAF-driven drug-resistant epilepsy/epileptic encephalopathy achieving seizure freedom/EEG normalization with less reliance on high-risk ASMs
- Therapies reducing severe feeding dysfunction/GERD and prolonged NG/G-tube dependence (preventing or shortening enteral feeding)

name: Hemangioma | cavernous, cerebral
description: Cerebral cavernous malformation is a brain vascular lesion of enlarged, irregular, thin walled capillaries prone to leakage that can cause seizures, headaches, and cerebral hemorrhage, and is often found incidentally on imaging. Care is largely symptom management and lifelong monitoring, with surgery typically avoided for asymptomatic non-hemorrhaged lesions, leaving major unmet need for disease modifying medical therapy, better seizure prevention, and biomarkers to track risk and progression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacologic option for CCMs in asymptomatic/eloquent or otherwise non-surgical lesions, differentiated by lowering clinically meaningful hemorrhage/neurologic-event risk
- Disease-modifying therapy for familial/multifocal CCM to prevent increasing lesion number and stabilize lesion size over time
- Improved medical therapy for CCM-related epilepsy with seizures recurring despite anti-epileptic drugs, differentiated by reduced seizure recurrence/frequency

name: Caudal regression syndrome
description: Rare congenital malformation of the lower spine affecting legs plus genitourinary and gastrointestinal function, often detected prenatally or at birth. Lifelong bladder and bowel dysfunction and orthopedic disability are common, with neurogenic bladder driving recurrent urinary tract infections and reflux that can damage kidneys and progress to kidney failure. Management is multidisciplinary but largely symptomatic and not disease modifying, and standard catheterization and antimuscarinic regimens may be insufficient, leaving a key unmet need for more effective kidney protective bladder strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Renal-protective neurogenic-bladder pharmacotherapy to prevent UTIs/vesicoureteral reflux → progressive kidney failure while reducing CIC burden and antimuscarinic side effects (dry mouth/constipation).
- Neurogenic-bowel therapies to deliver reliable bowel control/continence while reducing dependence on daily enema programs and laxative adverse effects (cramps/diarrhoea, electrolyte imbalance).
- Microbiome/motility-directed rescue therapeutics for refractory “enema non-responder” cases to restore continence and bowel-program responsiveness.

name: Central pontine myelinolysis
description: Central pontine myelinolysis is a rare, often iatrogenic brainstem demyelination syndrome triggered by overly rapid correction of hyponatremia, disproportionately affecting malnourished patients and those with alcohol use disorder or chronic liver disease. Neurologic decline is often delayed by days and can progress to dysarthria, dysphagia, spastic quadriparesis, or locked-in syndrome and coma. Care is largely prevention with intensive sodium monitoring and controlled correction, with no proven curative therapy once injury is established and only inconsistent case-report rescue options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying drug for established ODS initiated after delayed deterioration window to improve functional outcomes.
- Pharmacologic late-rescue therapy targeting circulating myelinotoxic/inflammatory drivers beyond supportive care/variable-benefit plasmapheresis.
- Lower-burden, safer prevention “correction-clamp” alternative to DDAVP + D5W relowering for high-risk chronic hyponatremia patients that reduces intensive sodium-monitoring needs.

name: Central retinal artery occlusion
description: Central retinal artery occlusion is a retinal infarction that functions like an acute ischemic stroke, presenting as sudden painless loss of vision in one eye, typically in older patients with vascular risk factors. Visual recovery is uncommon and there are no effective evidence based therapies, leaving an extremely narrow window for reperfusion approaches and a need for treatments that can salvage retina in late presenters, prevent complications such as iris neovascularization, and reduce the high subsequent cerebrovascular and cardiovascular event risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute, rapidly deployable reperfusion for non‑arteritic CRAO within ≤4.5 hours that restores functional vision.
- Neuroprotective/retinal‑rescue therapy (ideally intravitreal) that improves BCVA/visual field in late-presenting or thrombolysis-ineligible CRAO.
- Pharmacologic prevention of post‑CRAO ischemia-driven neovascular complications to preserve remaining vision and reduce reactive interventions.

name: Cerebral creatine deficiency syndrome
description: Ultra-orphan neurometabolic disorders causing brain creatine deficiency, typically presenting in early childhood with developmental delay, intellectual disability and severe speech impairment, often with autism-like behaviors and seizures. Oral creatine can help biosynthesis defects, but creatine transporter deficiency remains largely untreatable because creatine reaches blood but not brain, while GAMT deficiency requires burdensome high-dose multi-agent regimens to suppress neurotoxic guanidinoacetate. Key unmet needs are disease-modifying brain creatine restoration and easier, more effective therapies, with interest in transporter-independent creatine delivery and gene therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Transporter-independent, BBB/CNS-effective creatine restoration for SLC6A8/creatine transporter deficiency (CTD) that improves neurodevelopmental outcomes
- More complete suppression/normalization of neurotoxic guanidinoacetate (GAA) in GAMT deficiency to improve seizure/DEE control and protect neurodevelopment
- Lower-burden, more adherent treatment regimen vs current high-frequency multi-dose supplementation (e.g., long-acting/palatable formulations, reduced monitoring burden)

name: Cervical cancer | adenosquamous carcinoma
description: Cervical adenosquamous carcinoma is a rare, human papillomavirus driven cervical cancer with mixed glandular and squamous histology, often found on screening or presenting with abnormal vaginal bleeding, discharge, and pelvic pain. Standard care centers on cisplatin or carboplatin based chemoradiation and, in recurrence, options like pembrolizumab and bevacizumab. Outcomes are poorer than squamous disease after definitive radiotherapy and anti angiogenic therapy can be limited by fistula risk in previously irradiated patients, leaving a premium on safer, more effective systemic and histology tailored approaches including emerging biomarker defined subsets such as HER2 mutated tumors.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Relapse-prevention systemic therapy for cervical adeno/adenosquamous patients after definitive chemoradiation (higher relapse risk/worse outcomes vs squamous histology).
- Bevacizumab-sparing (or safer anti-angiogenic) regimens for previously irradiated recurrent/metastatic patients to reduce fistula risk.
- ERBB2/HER2-targeted therapy for ERBB2-mutant cervical adenosquamous carcinoma (~7.6%) to improve post-chemo outcomes.

name: Cervical cancer | small cell carcinoma
description: Rare, high grade human papillomavirus associated cervical neuroendocrine cancer typically diagnosed in the late 40s that often presents with vaginal bleeding or pelvic symptoms and bulky disease. It grows quickly and spreads early, so even aggressive multimodal care such as platinum plus etoposide chemoradiotherapy leaves poor outcomes, with a premium on stronger upfront systemic control and more durable options at recurrence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable disease control (e.g., improved PFS6/response durability) for recurrent/metastatic SCNEC after platinum-based therapy failure.
- Up-front systemic strategies that reduce early distant metastasis and improve survival beyond current multimodality EP chemoradiation outcomes.
- HPV-targeted, chemo-sparing systemic options (e.g., vaccine/T-cell/ICI combinations) for the predominantly HPV-positive SCNEC population.

name: Acute myeloid leukemia | megakaryoblastic
description: Rare early childhood acute myeloid leukemia subtype driven by malignant megakaryoblasts, often with fibrotic marrow that complicates diagnosis and presents with pancytopenia. Care still relies on intensive cytarabine and anthracycline chemotherapy that causes prolonged neutropenia, infection and bleeding risk, and long hospital stays, yet high risk non Down syndrome CBFA2T3 GLIS2 disease often remains minimal residual disease positive with poor survival. Biggest needs are safer disease modifying approaches that reliably clear residual leukemia, including fusion stratified immunotherapy such as folate receptor alpha targeting.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Fusion‑stratified, MRD‑eradicating targeted therapy for non‑Down‑syndrome pediatric AMKL (<3y) with CBFA2T3::GLIS2 (e.g., FOLR1‑directed ADC/CAR‑T).
- Toxicity‑sparing (incl. anthracycline‑sparing) regimens that maintain remission while reducing severe myelosuppression, infections, and critical‑care needs.
- Convenience‑differentiated approaches that shorten neutropenia and inpatient hospitalization (enabling more outpatient delivery/maintenance).

name: Chorea-acanthocytosis
description: Chorea acanthocytosis (VPS13A disease) is an ultra rare inherited basal ganglia neurodegenerative disorder starting around age 30 with progressive chorea and dystonia, prominent self injurious orofacial movements and feeding dystonia, dysarthria and dysphagia with aspiration risk, plus seizures and neuropsychiatric and cognitive changes. Care is largely supportive and symptomatic with no cure or disease modifying therapy, and major unmet needs include controlling disabling swallowing and orofacial symptoms and translating mechanistic leads such as Lyn kinase and autophagy targeting into effective treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- VPS13A (chorein) functional restoration (e.g., gene/ASO/mRNA) for genetically confirmed VPS13A loss‑of‑function patients to halt/slow progression.
- BBB‑penetrant Lyn kinase inhibition/autophagy restoration as a mechanism-based (potentially disease-modifying) approach.
- Safer, more effective pharmacologic control of feeding dystonia/orofacial dyskinesia (tongue protrusion/biting, dysphagia) to reduce aspiration risk vs current symptomatic therapy liabilities.

name: Autism spectrum disorder | level 2
description: Autism spectrum disorder level 2 is a behaviorally defined neurodevelopmental condition with persistent social communication deficits plus restricted and repetitive behaviors such as sensory sensitivities and rigidity with routines, typically diagnosed around age 4. Children require substantial support because impairments remain prominent even with existing services. Current medications mainly address associated irritability or hyperactivity and can cause weight gain or sedation, while stimulants help only about half and are often poorly tolerated, leaving core social communication and functional outcomes largely untreated and creating demand for better tolerated, disease relevant therapies with validated endpoints.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Medication that improves core ASD Level 2 symptoms (social-communication deficits and restricted/repetitive behaviors), with validated endpoint gains (e.g., SRS)
- Weight-neutral, non-sedating alternative for ASD-associated irritability/aggression that maintains ABC-I benefit vs risperidone/aripiprazole
- Better-tolerated treatment for comorbid hyperactivity/inattention in ASD than methylphenidate (higher response, far fewer AE discontinuations, no irritability worsening)

name: Eosinophilic pneumonia | chronic
description: Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia is a rare eosinophil driven lung disease, often in nonsmoking midlife women with asthma or atopy, causing weeks to months of cough and progressive breathlessness with wheeze, fever, night sweats, and weight loss. Corticosteroids usually produce rapid improvement, but relapse is common during tapering or after stopping, leaving many patients on years of maintenance and exposed to steroid toxicity. Key unmet needs are durable steroid sparing control and stronger evidence for targeted biologic maintenance therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Relapse-prevention maintenance therapy enabling safe discontinuation of systemic steroids (improved relapse-free survival after taper/stop)
- Steroid-sparing long-term control for patients requiring months–years of prednisone/prednisolone to avoid systemic steroid toxicities
- Evidence-based use of biologics (severe-asthma pathway) for CEP+asthma/frequent-relapser patients to reduce/replace maintenance steroids

name: Cholesterol ester storage disease
description: Cholesterol ester storage disease is a later onset lysosomal acid lipase deficiency caused by LIPA mutations that impair lysosomal fat breakdown, leading to cholesteryl ester and triglyceride buildup in the liver and vasculature. Patients often present from childhood with hepatomegaly, persistent transaminase elevation, and mixed dyslipidemia, with progression to fibrosis or cirrhosis and premature atherosclerosis that raises heart attack and stroke risk. Enzyme replacement requires ongoing intravenous infusions and while it improves biomarkers, it has not yet shown definitive prevention of cirrhosis or hard cardiovascular outcomes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-infusion/lower-burden disease-modifying therapy to replace biweekly multi-hour IV ERT and mitigate hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis risk
- Therapy proven to prevent/reverse liver fibrosis/cirrhosis (fibrosis-stage or liver-failure outcomes)
- Therapy proven to reduce premature atherosclerosis and hard CV events (MI/stroke) beyond lab lipid improvements

name: Chondroblastoma
description: Rare benign epiphyseal bone tumor near joints in adolescents and young adults, causing chronic pain, stiffness, and swelling. Treatment is surgical curettage with graft or cement, but 10–35% recur and lesions can damage cartilage and growth plate leading to long term arthritis. Rare lung metastases and limited systemic options make recurrence sparing local adjuncts and targeted approaches based on K36M and osteoclast driven RANKL biology an important frontier.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neo/adjuvant drug therapy to reduce post-surgical local recurrence while enabling physis/cartilage-sparing local control
- Chondroprotective/anti-degenerative therapy to prevent cartilage injury and secondary osteoarthritis from local adjuvants/treatment
- Systemic targeted therapy for unresectable/metastatic chondroblastoma (e.g., RANKL/denosumab-like and/or H3.3K36M-driven approaches) with endpoints like surgery avoidance, radiologic control, and pain reduction

name: Chondrodysplasia punctata
description: Congenital skeletal dysplasia spectrum with stippled epiphyses, limb shortening and contractures, and early cataracts, often with multisystem disease. Severe rhizomelic cases arise from peroxisome defects that impair plasmalogen synthesis, leading to profound neurodevelopmental disability, recurrent life threatening respiratory disease, and early childhood mortality. Care is largely supportive, creating urgent demand for disease modifying therapies that correct the metabolic pathway and preserve breathing and vision. X linked type 2 stems from disrupted cholesterol synthesis and adds ichthyosis and cataracts, highlighting the need for mechanism based skin and eye treatments beyond symptomatic care.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying plasmalogen restoration for severe RCDP (PEX7/GNPAT/AGPS-related) to reduce respiratory-complication–driven early mortality.
- Pharmacologic prevention/delay of early progressive congenital cataracts in classic severe PEX7-RCDP to preserve vision and avoid infant surgery.
- Cholesterol-biosynthesis pathway correction for CDPX2/Conradi–Hünermann skin disease to improve ichthyosis plaque severity/extent (e.g., PGAS, %TBSA) vs symptomatic topicals.

name: Chordoma | chondroid
description: Rare, slow growing but locally aggressive malignant tumor from notochord remnants, often at the spheno occipital skull base; adult onset with headaches and diplopia. Managed with maximal safe surgery plus focused radiotherapy often proton or carbon ion, but complete resection is often impossible leading to frequent local recurrence and about 40% metastasis. No approved systemic drugs for advanced disease, creating a major need for effective disease modifying medical therapies and better durable local control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemic therapy for locally advanced/metastatic chordoma that achieves meaningful RECIST tumor shrinkage and durable disease control.
- Post-resection (adjuvant) systemic therapy to prevent late loco-regional relapse after macroscopic complete resection ± radiotherapy.
- Radiosensitizing/immunotherapy add-ons for inoperable/residual localized chordoma receiving definitive high-dose RT (≥70 Gy) to improve RECIST ORR/local control and reduce prolonged proton-therapy burden.

name: Choroid plexus papilloma
description: Choroid plexus papilloma is a rare World Health Organization grade I intraventricular tumor in young children that often causes hydrocephalus by blocking and overproducing cerebrospinal fluid, leading to increased intracranial pressure with vomiting, lethargy, and infant macrocephaly. Complete surgical resection can be curative, but operations are high risk due to major bleeding from tumor vascularity, and hydrocephalus can persist with ongoing shunt dependence even after removal. When tumors are unresectable or recur, systemic therapy options are limited and largely experimental, motivating better perioperative devascularization and drugs that reduce cerebrospinal fluid secretion.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pre-op drug cytoreduction/devascularization for hypervascular pediatric CPP to reduce intraoperative blood loss/hemorrhage risk.
- CSF hypersecretion/hydrocephalus–targeted therapy (e.g., AQP1 pathway) to prevent persistent hydrocephalus and reduce VP-shunt dependence.
- More effective, less toxic systemic therapy for progressive/inoperable residual or metastatic CPP (improving remission rates while minimizing cycles and avoiding radiotherapy).

name: Colorectal cancer | small cell carcinoma
description: Ultra-rare, high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma of the colon/rectum with very high proliferative activity that often presents around age 60 with nonspecific colorectal cancer-like symptoms but is frequently metastatic at diagnosis. There is no standard management, so care is extrapolated and outcomes are poor, with median survival around 9 months for stage IV disease. Post-platinum options are especially weak, with second-line progression-free survival typically about 2 to 3 months, creating a major need for better first-line control and credible therapies after platinum.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- First-line regimen for metastatic-at-diagnosis colorectal HGNEC that improves median OS beyond ~8.7 months.
- A validated post-platinum (2L+) standard that exceeds typical median PFS ~2.3 months and OS ~6.2 months.
- Less myelosuppressive, biomarker-driven alternatives to multi-day IV platinum doublets (e.g., targeted options for BRAF V600E–mutant tumors).

name: Colorectal cancer | squamous cell carcinoma
description: An uncommon anorectal squamous cell carcinoma, often human papillomavirus linked, typically presenting with rectal bleeding, pain or pressure, bowel habit changes, and weight loss. First line curative intent care is fluorouracil plus mitomycin with radiation, but relapse can force radical salvage surgery with permanent colostomy. In metastatic or recurrent disease, chemotherapy and checkpoint inhibitors are usually palliative and rarely curative, creating demand for more durable, organ sparing disease control and more effective systemic options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer, less clinic‑intensive organ‑preserving curative alternative to definitive 5‑FU+mitomycin chemoradiation.
- Peri‑CRT/consolidation systemic therapy to cut post‑CRT relapse/local failure and improve durable CR/DFS and stoma‑free survival.
- More effective systemic options for recurrent/metastatic HPV‑associated disease beyond PD‑1 monotherapy for the majority of non‑responders.

name: Chromosome 9p deletion syndrome
description: Chromosome 9p deletion syndrome is an ultra rare contiguous gene disorder caused by loss of genetic material on chromosome 9p, typically presenting prenatally or in infancy with trigonocephaly and other congenital anomalies, hypotonia, feeding and swallowing problems sometimes requiring tube feeds, and lifelong neurodevelopmental impairment with prominent speech and language delay. Care is supportive and symptom directed, including anticonvulsants for seizures, leaving a premium on disease modifying approaches that improve cognition and communication and on lower burden, more durable solutions for feeding difficulties and seizure control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-targeted neurodevelopment therapy to improve severe speech/language impairment and broader cognitive/developmental outcomes (e.g., targeting distal 9pter haploinsufficiency such as FOXD4).
- Pharmacologic therapies to improve infant feeding/swallowing coordination and reduce reflux/aspiration to reduce tube-feeding and avoid escalation to gastrostomy/fundoplication.
- Better anti-seizure therapies tailored to 9p deletion syndrome to improve seizure prevention/control while reducing overall supportive-care complexity.

name: Chromosome Xp21 deletion syndrome
description: Rare X linked contiguous gene deletion syndrome in males combining congenital adrenal hypoplasia with glycerol kinase deficiency and sometimes Duchenne muscular dystrophy plus neurodevelopmental disability. Presents early with life threatening adrenal crises and catabolic stress related metabolic decompensation, requiring lifelong steroid replacement and careful sick day management. Key unmet needs are lower burden, more physiologic hormone delivery and disease modifying approaches that restore missing gene function across endocrine, metabolic, and muscle manifestations.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Lower-burden, more physiologic adrenal hormone replacement (e.g., long-acting/continuous hydrocortisone with robust stress-dosing coverage) to reduce early-life adrenal crises.
- Mutation-agnostic dystrophin restoration for Xp21 deletion patients with DMD not eligible for genotype-specific exon-skipping therapies.
- GK-directed therapy to prevent fasting/illness-triggered metabolic decompensation and reduce reliance on frequent carbohydrate-rich meals.

name: Chronic NK-cell lymphocytosis
description: Chronic lymphoproliferative disorder of natural killer cells is an ultra rare, indolent large granular lymphocyte leukemia characterized by persistent natural killer cell lymphocytosis, often found incidentally in older predominantly male patients. When symptomatic it can drive fatigue, systemic symptoms, autoimmune complications, splenomegaly, cytopenias and recurrent infections from neutropenia. Treatment is typically immunosuppressive rather than clone eradicating and there is no clearly defined optimal regimen, creating a need for more durable, targeted disease control informed by emerging biology such as STAT3 and STAT5B mutations.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- STAT3/JAK–STAT–directed, clone-eradicating therapy achieving molecular remission (e.g., STAT3 mutation clearance) in STAT3-driven CLPD‑NK
- Durable correction of severe neutropenia (ANC <0.5×10^9/L) to reduce recurrent infections
- Better-tolerated therapies for symptomatic cytopenias (esp. anemia/bi‑pancytopenia) to reduce multi-line treatment dependence

name: Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis
description: Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, also called chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis, is a pediatric autoinflammatory disease causing sterile bone inflammation and often insidious, sometimes nocturnal pain that can limit function. Whole body magnetic resonance imaging frequently uncovers additional silent lesions, including spinal involvement that may be painless yet lead to irreversible vertebral height loss, raising the stakes for early detection and control. Care typically starts with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and escalates to immunomodulators or bisphosphonates, but there are no licensed therapies and limited randomized evidence, leaving a premium on safer, durable, evidence based options for refractory and spinal disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Deep suppression of asymptomatic vertebral lesions to prevent vertebral fractures/vertebra plana/deformity (reduce reliance on frequent whole‑body MRI surveillance).
- Evidence-based, licensed 2nd/3rd-line therapy for NSAID-refractory and/or active spinal-lesion CRMO with sustained pain control plus whole‑body MRI lesion healing.
- Safer long-term disease control for children needing escalation that lowers serious-AE risk and monitoring/treatment burden versus current empiric immunomodulation.

name: Cicatricial pemphigoid
description: Cicatricial pemphigoid, also called mucous membrane pemphigoid, is a very rare autoimmune blistering disease of mucosal linings often diagnosed in women over 60, with ocular involvement causing chronic conjunctival inflammation that can progress to irreversible scarring and blindness. Early symptoms are nonspecific so diagnosis is frequently delayed, and 20 to 30 percent of patients continue to worsen despite systemic immunomodulators. There are no U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved therapies and off label immunosuppression can carry serious toxicity, creating demand for safer treatments that halt fibrosis earlier and preserve vision beyond salvage surgery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent progressive conjunctival cicatrization/vision loss in the ~20–30% who still progress despite systemic therapy, including “quiet eye but ongoing fibrosis” patients
- Anti-fibrotic/regenerative therapy that can revert established cicatricial ocular-surface damage (e.g., fornix shortening/symblepharon), not just suppress inflammation
- Safer, more convenient steroid-/cyclophosphamide-/dapsone-sparing systemic therapy with reduced severe toxicities and less monitoring/infusion burden

name: Citrullinemia | type 1
description: Citrullinemia type 1 is a rare inherited urea cycle disorder caused by deficient argininosuccinate synthase 1, leading to rapid, toxic ammonia buildup that can make a previously well newborn crash within days with poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, seizures, and coma. Survivors often live with neurologic impairment and a lifelong regimen of protein restriction, chronic nitrogen scavengers, and arginine, yet still face unpredictable, life threatening metabolic decompensations requiring intensive acute rescue such as dialysis. The key unmet need is faster crisis control and durable liver targeted correction that prevents hyperammonemic episodes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ER/ICU-sparing acute rescue to rapidly lower ammonia in classic neonatal hyperammonemic crises without central-line IV scavengers/hemodialysis.
- Early (≤1 year) disease-correcting therapy restoring hepatic ASS1 activity to prevent irreversible neurocognitive injury and avoid lifelong diet/scavengers.
- Lower-burden chronic nitrogen disposal maintaining ammonia control with improved palatability, lower sodium load, smaller volume, and fewer daily doses vs current scavengers.

name: Congenital afibrinogenemia
description: Congenital afibrinogenemia is an ultra rare inherited bleeding disorder caused by complete absence of fibrinogen, often presenting at birth with persistent umbilical stump bleeding and sometimes fatal intracranial hemorrhage, with recurrent mucosal and joint bleeds over life. Women face heavy menstrual bleeding and pregnancy loss without prophylaxis. Care relies on repeated intravenous fibrinogen replacement titrated to lab targets, but prophylaxis in infants is poorly defined, treatment is burdensome, and management is complicated by paradoxical thrombosis risk and safety issues with non virus inactivated products, leaving demand for durable lower burden prophylaxis and better peripartum strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Practical long‑term prophylaxis to prevent catastrophic CNS bleeding in severe congenital afibrinogenemia with reliable maintenance of fibrinogen activity >50 mg/dL without highly individualized repeat dosing
- Pregnancy/peripartum prophylaxis that reduces fetal loss and postpartum hemorrhage while managing simultaneous thrombotic risk despite fibrinogen replacement
- Safer, lower-burden fibrinogen replacement that reduces infection/hypersensitivity and viral-transmission concerns while minimizing traumatic/inconvenient IV access needs (esp. in children)

name: Cleidocranial dysplasia
description: Cleidocranial dysplasia is an ultra rare inherited RUNX2 related disorder of bone and tooth development, typically recognized in childhood with persistently open skull soft spots, underdeveloped clavicles and severe dental anomalies including delayed eruption and extra teeth. Morbidity is driven by repeated surgeries and intensive dental orthodontic care, plus hearing loss and recurrent sinus or ear infections, with early onset low bone density increasing fracture risk. There is no cure and management is supportive, creating unmet need for safe disease modifying approaches that normalize ossification and tooth eruption and protect long term bone health.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- RUNX2-pathway disease-modifying therapeutics for RUNX2-haploinsufficient CCD that improve cranial-suture closure and skeletal growth/ossification.
- Pharmacotherapy to correct delayed/absent permanent-tooth eruption and severe dental anomalies to reduce painful/expensive surgical–orthodontic interventions.
- Orthodontic-compatible bone-health therapy for CCD patients with osteopenia/osteoporosis that increases DXA BMD and reduces fractures without impairing tooth movement.

name: Coenzyme Q10 deficiency disease
description: Ultra rare inherited coenzyme Q10 biosynthesis disorder causing mitochondrial energy failure with prominent neurologic and renal disease, often presenting in childhood with progressive ataxia, seizures, hypotonia, or nephrotic syndrome that can progress to kidney failure. High dose oral coenzyme Q10 is standard but response is genotype dependent and often poor, with major unmet needs for earlier diagnosis, consistent pharmaceutical grade bioavailable formulations, and better brain and kidney delivery before irreversible damage occurs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neurologic efficacy in COQ8A/ADCK3 ataxia patients who respond poorly to high-dose oral CoQ10
- Durable renal disease modification in CoQ10-deficiency SRNS (sustained proteinuria reduction and prevention/delay of ESKD)
- High-bioavailability, CNS/kidney–penetrant CoQ10 replacement or pathway-bypass therapies that lower very high, frequent oral dosing burden

name: Ogilvie syndrome
description: Ogilvie syndrome is an acute colonic pseudo-obstruction caused by failure of bowel motility, leading to abdominal distention and obstructive symptoms in older, medically complex inpatients often after surgery or trauma. Treatment is time sensitive to prevent ischemia and perforation, but neostigmine requires cardiac monitoring due to bradycardia and arrhythmia risk, and endoscopic decompression, while effective, has a narrow window and can itself cause perforation. Key unmet needs are safer, lower-burden medical decompression options and better prevention of recurrence and complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neostigmine-like rapid decompression that’s safe/usable in high-risk or contraindicated inpatients (e.g., bradycardia/asthma/renal insufficiency/recent MI) without requiring atropine-ready continuous cardiopulmonary monitoring
- Lower-burden administration (e.g., subcutaneous/alternative route) that maintains rapid radiographic decompression while reducing bradycardia/bronchospasm risk that drives monitored-setting use
- Medical recurrence-prevention/rescue strategy that materially reduces recurrence and avoids repeat neostigmine dosing and endoscopic decompression risks

name: Complement component 5 deficiency
description: Rare inherited terminal complement (C5) deficiency impairs membrane attack complex killing, driving adolescent-onset risk of invasive, often recurrent meningococcal infections including meningitis. Management relies on vaccination with response monitoring plus antibiotics and emergency planning, yet 40 to 50% have recurrent disease and vaccine escape is reported, while complement replacement is not routine, leaving a need for durable prevention and functional restoration.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- C5/MAC functional restoration (e.g., C5 replacement or gene therapy) to prevent recurrent invasive meningococcal disease in hereditary terminal-complement (C5–C9) deficiency
- Complement-independent, long-acting prophylaxis to replace lifelong daily antibiotic chemoprophylaxis
- Prevention of breakthrough disease from nongroupable/uncommon meningococci and reduced acquisition/transmission (e.g., decolonization or passive-immunity for patients/household contacts)

name: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome
description: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome is a rare genetic failure of automatic breathing, usually recognized in newborns when sleep triggers shallow breathing with hypoxemia and carbon dioxide retention. Reduced or absent brainstem responses to high carbon dioxide and low oxygen mean patients may not feel dyspnea even when dangerously under ventilating. With no medication proven to reliably replace assisted ventilation, care becomes lifelong dependence on mechanical ventilation or diaphragm pacing, sometimes 24 hours a day, plus monitoring and treatment of autonomic complications such as sinus pauses that can require cardiac pacing. Key unmet needs are ventilator free sleep and reduced autonomic cardiac risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-acting therapy that restores CO₂/hypoxia responsiveness enough to reduce/eliminate mechanical ventilation (ventilator-free sleep)
- PHOX2B-targeted disease-modifying therapy for ~90% with PHOX2B mutations to remove lifelong ventilator/technology dependence
- Therapy for CCHS autonomic cardiac rhythm instability (sinus pauses/asystoles) to prevent pacemaker implantation/sudden-death risk

name: Congenital tufting enteropathy
description: Congenital tufting enteropathy is a rare autosomal recessive intestinal epithelial disorder that presents in the first days of life with profuse watery diarrhea, dehydration, electrolyte derangements, and growth failure that persists despite bowel rest. Most children require long term parenteral nutrition, which carries substantial iatrogenic risk including sepsis, thrombosis, and liver disease, and some progress to intestinal transplant. With no approved drug therapies, the key unmet need is disease modifying treatment for EPCAM or SPINT2 driven disease and effective intestinal rehabilitation that reduces parenteral nutrition dependence and enables enteral autonomy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Mutation-targeted therapy for EPCAM/SPINT2 CTE that enables sustained enteral feeding and achieves enteral autonomy (PN-free)
- Intestinal adaptation/absorption pharmacotherapy (e.g., GLP-2 agonist class) to reduce PN volume/days and enable weaning
- PN-sparing and/or PN-complication–prevention therapies that reduce catheter sepsis/thrombosis and PN-associated liver disease to avoid transplant

name: Congenital dyserythropoietic anemia | type 1
description: Rare inherited red cell development disorder causing lifelong macrocytic anemia from infancy with jaundice and splenomegaly and sometimes fetal hydrops. Patients accumulate iron overload even without transfusions due to suppressed hepcidin, risking end organ damage. Care depends on frequent interferon injections, transfusions in severe cases, and lifelong iron chelation, with transplant reserved for refractory disease, leaving a premium on durable disease modifying and iron absorption targeted therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non‑interferon anemia therapy achieving transfusion independence and/or hemoglobin normalization in interferon‑refractory/transfusion‑dependent CDA‑I
- Hepcidin/iron‑absorption–targeted therapy to prevent progressive iron overload even in non‑transfused CDA‑I patients
- Safer, less burdensome long‑term iron‑overload treatment than current chelators (lower toxicity, less monitoring, simpler administration)

name: Congenital dyserythropoietic anemia | type 2
description: Congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type II is an ultra rare inherited red blood cell maturation disorder causing ineffective erythropoiesis and hemolysis, typically starting in infancy or childhood but sometimes diagnosed in adulthood. Patients live with chronic anemia causing fatigue and weakness plus intermittent jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly and gallstones, and about 20 percent require regular transfusions. The burden is compounded by iron overload that can occur even without transfusions and lead to organ damage. Treatment is largely supportive with transfusion and long term iron removal, while splenectomy yields only modest hemoglobin gains and curative transplant is rarely used.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Transfusion-eliminating anemia correction (raise Hb to reduce/eliminate RBC transfusions in transfusion-dependent CDA II)
- Iron-overload control without lifelong chelation (prevent/reverse iron overload and organ damage, including in transfusion-independent patients)
- Non-splenectomy control of hypersplenism/splenomegaly-driven hemolysis (avoid splenectomy while improving Hb)

name: Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles
description: Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles is a rare genetic cranial nerve development disorder causing congenital, largely non progressive restriction of eye movements, often with strabismus and ptosis that limits vision and forces compensatory head postures. The biggest clinical risk is childhood amblyopia from misalignment, refractive error, and lid droop, which can lead to permanent vision loss without early detection. Care is symptomatic and high burden, relying on patching or daily atropine plus repeated strabismus and ptosis surgeries that improve alignment but cannot correct the underlying dysinnervation or reliably normalize motility, leaving a need for disease modifying, gene informed approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neurodevelopmental/axon-guidance restoration therapy for genetically defined CFEOM (e.g., KIF21A/TUBB3/PHOX2A) to increase extraocular range of motion (esp. upgaze) and primary-position alignment
- Surgery-sparing therapy to reduce restrictive strabismus/ptosis and ocular-surface complications, lowering repeat/stepwise procedure burden
- Better-tolerated, lower-burden drug-based amblyopia prevention/treatment to reduce patching/atropine dependence and intensive monitoring

name: Congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy
description: Congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy is a rare autosomal recessive corneal endothelial disorder presenting at birth with bilateral corneal edema and ground glass clouding that can severely impair vision and cause amblyopia or nystagmus if treatment is delayed. Medical therapy is limited to supportive measures such as hypertonic sodium chloride for mild cases, while meaningful visual rehabilitation typically requires corneal transplantation in infancy, bringing graft failure, repeat procedures, and anesthesia risk. Key unmet needs are disease modifying, less invasive options that preserve or restore endothelial function, including SLC4A11 targeted pharmacologic rescue, gene based approaches, and endothelial protective strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early intracameral SLC4A11 gene supplementation in biallelic SLC4A11 CHED infants/children to rapidly reverse corneal edema and prevent amblyopia.
- Topical mutation-rescue therapy for SLC4A11 misfolding/trafficking defects to improve corneal transparency/thickness and visual acuity without keratoplasty.
- Endothelial-protective disease-pathway therapy beyond temporary hypertonic dehydration (e.g., mitochondrial-targeted antioxidants) to slow progression and reduce reliance on corneal transplant/anesthesia.

name: Congenital mesoblastic nephroma
description: Rare spindle cell kidney tumor of very early infancy, often presenting as a unilateral abdominal mass (sometimes detected prenatally) with occasional hypertension or hematuria; outcomes are usually excellent after complete surgical resection, but a small high risk subset (cellular or stage III, often lacking ETV6 NTRK3 fusion) can relapse, creating demand for less toxic, molecularly guided and targeted therapy such as NTRK inhibitors in fusion driven recurrences.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- TRK-inhibitor, chemo-/surgery-sparing regimens for recurrent/refractory or unresectable ETV6::NTRK3/NTRK-fusion CMN.
- Relapse-prevention therapy for highest-risk CMN (stage III cellular and/or translocation-negative tumors) with persistently inferior RFS on current surgery ± Wilms-style chemo.
- Molecularly matched kinase inhibitors beyond NTRK (e.g., EGFR-ITD, ALK-fusion, BRAF-fusion) for recurrent/metastatic or unresectable CMN where conventional chemo benefit is unclear.

name: Congenital mirror movement disorder
description: Rare lifelong neurodevelopmental motor control disorder where intentional movement in one hand triggers involuntary mirrored movement in the other, impairing independent bimanual tasks and sometimes causing arm pain; care is mainly accommodations since symptom-suppressing options risk weakness, creating demand for safe strength-sparing symptomatic and circuit-level neuromodulation approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Strength-sparing symptomatic therapy that reduces mirror hand/finger movements to enable pure unimanual movements and skilled bimanual coordination (safer than botulinum toxin).
- Therapy that prevents/treats upper-limb pain/discomfort triggered by sustained or repetitive hand use.
- Early disease-modifying intervention targeting neurodevelopmental wiring/axon-growth defects (e.g., DCC/NTN1/RAD51 pathways) to prevent bilateral motor signal transmission.

name: Cyclic hematopoiesis
description: Cyclic neutropenia is a rare, usually ELANE driven bone marrow rhythm disorder starting in infancy with predictable neutrophil crashes about every 21 days lasting 3 to 5 days, causing recurrent fevers, painful mouth ulcers, gingivitis and pharyngitis, and sinus, respiratory, and skin infections with relative wellness between episodes. Care is largely supportive with granulocyte colony stimulating factor to blunt nadirs, but it often requires frequent subcutaneous injections and can cause bone or muscle pain and splenomegaly, leaving unmet need for less burdensome, better tolerated therapies that prevent nadirs and oral morbidity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent predictable ~21-day neutropenic nadirs and associated infection/oral-ulcer flares without chronic (daily/alternate-day) injections.
- Neutrophil-restoring therapy with improved tolerability vs G-CSF (less bone pain/headache/splenomegaly/osteoporosis) without worse pain seen with pegylated/large-dose less-frequent regimens.
- More complete suppression of oral/periodontal morbidity and clinically meaningful febrile/infectious events (fewer mouth-ulcer days, febrile episodes, serious infections).

name: Cystadenofibroma
description: Ovarian cystadenofibroma is a rare, usually benign epithelial ovarian tumor with a prominent fibrous component, often found incidentally but sometimes causing pelvic or abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding. The main unmet need is diagnostic confidence because imaging can mimic ovarian malignancy, leading to overly aggressive surgery, so better preoperative and intraoperative diagnostic algorithms and decision support are needed to avoid unnecessary extensive procedures.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Delta beta thalassemia
description: Delta beta thalassemia is a rare inherited hemoglobin disorder caused by deletion of the delta and beta globin genes, leading to compensatory fetal hemoglobin production and a trait like microcytic anemia or an intermedia like phenotype. Care is largely supportive, and patients can still develop iron overload from ineffective erythropoiesis even without regular transfusions, leaving a premium on therapies that safely raise hemoglobin while reducing transfusion dependence and avoiding the heavy monitoring and tolerability burden of current iron chelators.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Transfusion-sparing hemoglobin improvement for δβ/β-thalassemia intermedia patients (raise Hb into safer range and reduce intermittent transfusions)
- Hepcidin/iron-absorption pathway modulation to prevent non-transfusional iron overload (reduce liver iron and need for chelation)
- Safer, lower-monitoring, lower-burden iron-overload therapies vs current chelators (avoid severe toxicity, reduce lab surveillance and infusion/oral burden)

name: Congenital stationary night blindness
description: Congenital stationary night blindness is a non progressive inherited retinal disorder where rod to bipolar signaling is impaired, causing lifelong night blindness plus photophobia, reduced visual acuity, high myopia, nystagmus, and strabismus. Management is largely supportive with refractive correction and occasional strabismus surgery, leaving patients without disease modifying options. The key unmet need is a therapy that restores rod mediated function and meaningfully improves vision across genetically heterogeneous forms, translating active preclinical gene based work into effective clinical treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ON‑bipolar–cell–targeted therapy to restore rod-mediated night vision/dark adaptation (scotopic ERG b‑wave; real‑world scotopic navigation)
- Pharmacologic improvement of daytime visual morbidity beyond supportive care (visual acuity loss, photophobia, high myopia, nystagmus/strabismus)
- Mutation‑agnostic or multi‑gene/multi‑variant therapies to address CSNB genetic heterogeneity without bespoke per‑mutation products

name: Symblepharon | congenital
description: Congenital symblepharon is a birth defect where the eyelid lining abnormally adheres to the eye surface and in abortive cryptophthalmos the upper lid may be absent with skin fused to the cornea, causing restricted eye movement, photophobia, and potentially sight threatening corneal keratinization and vascularization. Care is largely surgical release with fornix reconstruction and tissue grafts, followed by prolonged postoperative drops and conformer use, yet recurrence from scarring is common and anti scarring adjuncts like mitomycin C carry serious ocular toxicity risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Anti-adhesion/anti-fibrotic therapy to prevent post-surgical re-adhesion (recurrence) and fornix foreshortening, improving fornix depth and corneal/vision outcomes.
- Safer intraoperative scar-suppression adjunct to replace mitomycin C with similar or better anti-fibrosis efficacy but less tissue toxicity.
- Pediatric-friendly long-acting topical/local depot regimen to reduce multi-week, high-frequency post-op drops and reliance on rings/conformers/contact lenses while preventing recurrence.

name: Craniofrontonasal syndrome
description: Rare congenital EFNB1 related craniofacial malformation syndrome causing premature skull suture fusion, with coronal craniosynostosis, hypertelorism, bifid nasal tip and split nails. Management is individualized, staged surgery in infancy and childhood to prevent raised intracranial pressure and neurodevelopmental harm, but procedures carry high bleeding and transfusion burden. No disease modifying therapy exists, leaving unmet need for earlier biology driven prevention and safer blood sparing perioperative approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
