- Prenatal/neonatal EFNB1/ephrin‑B1 restoration or Eph/ephrin pathway modulation to prevent coronal craniosynostosis and avoid first‑year skull surgery
- Medical therapy to prevent/mitigate craniosynostosis‑associated elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) as an alternative/bridge to surgery
- Perioperative hemostatic/antifibrinolytic pharmacotherapy to reduce extreme blood loss and transfusion exposure during infant craniosynostosis operations

name: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy
description: Dentatorubral pallidoluysian atrophy is a rare autosomal dominant ATN1 driven neurodegenerative disorder, often starting around age 30, marked by progressive ataxia, involuntary movements, psychiatric symptoms and dementia, with earlier onset cases dominated by myoclonus and severe seizures. Care is supportive with no cure, so patients face relentless neurologic decline plus high risk complications including sudden unexpected death in epilepsy and late stage dysphagia leading to aspiration pneumonia, creating a premium for disease modifying therapies that reduce seizure burden and preserve swallowing and cognition.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ATN1 CAG-expansion–targeted disease-modifying therapy that slows progression with measurable improvement/slowed decline in ataxia/mobility (e.g., SARA) and reduced polypharmacy burden.
- Juvenile-onset DRPLA progressive myoclonus epilepsy therapy that reduces severe seizure frequency/length (and SUDEP risk) with fewer antiseizure-medication side effects/burden.
- Adult-onset DRPLA bulbar/swallow-function–preserving therapy that reduces dysphagia and aspiration pneumonia events with quantifiable swallow-test improvement (e.g., MBSS).

name: Dentin dysplasia
description: Ultra rare inherited dentin formation disorder (about 1 in 100,000) presenting in childhood with clinically normal crowns but radiographic pulp obliteration, short or absent roots, tooth mobility, abscesses, and early tooth loss; care is largely reactive salvage, extractions, and later prosthetic or implant reconstruction because endodontics is often not feasible, leaving a need for disease modifying approaches that preserve roots, pulp vitality, and jaw bone.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Odontoblast-targeted DSPP-pathway restoration to prevent the short/rootless-root phenotype and premature tooth loss in DD‑I
- Local pulp-preservation/anti-obliteration therapy to maintain pulp-space patency and reduce periapical radiolucencies/abscesses where endodontic rescue is often not feasible
- Local jaw-bone preservation/regeneration pharmacotherapy to prevent early exfoliation–linked maxillomandibular bony atrophy and reduce need for later reconstructive procedures

name: Desquamative interstitial pneumonia
description: Desquamative interstitial pneumonia is an uncommon, largely smoking related interstitial lung disease marked by alveolar macrophage accumulation, chronic dry cough, and exertional breathlessness with lower lobe ground glass opacities and reduced diffusion capacity. Management hinges on exposure removal and smoking cessation, but treatment evidence is thin and practice often relies on corticosteroids or other immunosuppression with uncertain benefit. Around a quarter of patients progress despite steroids, developing pulmonary fibrosis, creating a need for steroid sparing disease control and therapies that reliably prevent fibrotic progression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Evidence-based, steroid-sparing disease control for patients who deteriorate despite glucocorticoids
- Anti-fibrotic/anti-progression therapy for progressive/chronic fibrosing DIP to reduce annual FVC decline with improved tolerability
- Targeted therapy for higher-risk subgroups (non-smokers—especially women—and occupational-exposure–associated DIP) to prevent fibrotic progression to chronic respiratory failure

name: Diabetes insipidus | dipsogenic
description: Dipsogenic diabetes insipidus is a rare, non psychiatric disorder of thirst regulation with a pathologically low thirst set point that drives compulsive drinking, polyuria, and sleep disruption. Excess water intake can cause symptomatic hyponatremia, yet standard antidiuretic therapy risks water intoxication when thirst persists. Care is largely behavioral with few established outpatient options, creating demand for safe thirst suppression and hyponatremia prevention, with early signals around glucagon like peptide 1 receptor agonists.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacologic suppression of pathologic thirst to reduce excessive fluid intake and downstream polyuria/nocturia (e.g., GLP‑1R agonist–class hypodipsic therapy).
- Safer, scalable antidiuretic symptom-relief in confirmed dipsogenic polydipsia that lowers osmolality below the thirst threshold without strict fluid restriction, while minimizing desmopressin-related hyponatremia risk from misdiagnosis.
- Outpatient pharmacologic prevention of dilutional hyponatremia/water intoxication episodes in excessive drinkers when free-water excretion is impaired (illness/meds/low solute intake).

name: Dirofilariasis
description: Mosquito-borne zoonotic filarial infection where humans are dead end hosts, typically presenting with an incidental pulmonary coin lesion that mimics cancer or a tender sometimes migratory subcutaneous or periocular nodule; limited routine diagnostics mean confirmation and definitive management often require invasive biopsy or surgical excision, with ocular disease sometimes needing higher risk procedures, creating need for noninvasive diagnosis and practical systemic options to reduce repeat interventions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course systemic therapy to eradicate suspected pulmonary “coin lesion”/subcutaneous dirofilariasis and avoid invasive diagnostic/curative excision
- Rapid anti-migration regimen for ocular/subcutaneous disease to stop/localize worms and prevent procedure-related complications (e.g., facial nerve injury)
- Evidence-based systemic clearance regimen for rare microfilaremic/systemic-risk cases where surgery is insufficient (blood microfilariae clearance, fewer repeat/invasive procedures)
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus topic page for Dirofilariasis (mentioned on https://medlineplus.gov/eyeliddisorders.html)

name: Dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria
description: Rare inherited pigmentary genodermatosis (ADAR1 related) with mottled hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules on hands and feet starting in infancy or early childhood that stabilize but persist lifelong. Usually benign and asymptomatic, yet cosmetically burdensome with no effective or definitive treatment, and a minority develop neurologic complications such as dystonia and cognitive decline, creating need for durable pigment normalization and disease modifying options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Skin-delivered ADAR1 restoration for genetically confirmed childhood-onset DSH to durably reduce acral hyper/hypopigmented macule area/contrast beyond supportive photoprotection.
- Lesion-type–aware pigmentation normalizers that repigment hypopigmented macules without worsening hyperpigmentation (endpoints: colorimetry + symmetry).
- Systemic/CNS-penetrant ADAR1-pathway therapeutics for the subset with neurologic manifestations (e.g., dystonia/mental deterioration) not addressed by skin-only care.

name: Dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria
description: Rare inherited childhood-onset skin pigmentation disorder causing generalized reticulate hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules across the body; usually medically benign but highly visible with significant cosmetic and psychological burden. Pathophysiology appears to involve disrupted melanosome production and distribution, with genetic subtypes such as SASH1 and ABCB6. Care is largely reassurance and supportive counseling, with no definitive disease-modifying therapy, creating unmet need for safe long-term whole-body treatments that can normalize both hypo and hyperpigmentation, ideally tailored to genotype.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Whole-body pharmacologic normalization of both hypo- and hyperpigmented macules to improve cosmetic appearance and psychosocial burden.
- Genotype-/mechanism-directed therapy for DUH subgroups with ABCB6 and/or SASH1 mutations (pathway-targeted, disease-modifying approach).
- Pediatric-suitable, long-term safe, non-scarring/non-UV drug option that reduces reliance on high-burden procedures (phototherapy/lasers) for generalized disease.
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus page; GARD URL: https://rarediseases.info.nih.gov/diseases/1996/dyschromatosis-universalis-hereditaria

name: Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor
description: Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor is a benign cortical glioneuronal tumor in children and young adults, usually presenting with long-standing focal seizures that are often medication resistant. Seizures are nearly universal and long-term control depends on gross total surgical resection, leaving patients with unresectable or subtotally resected lesions facing years of anti-seizure drugs and associated cognitive and developmental toxicity. Frequent fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 alterations suggest a path toward targeted, brain-penetrant options for recurrent or difficult-to-excise disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-penetrant FGFR-pathway targeted therapy for FGFR1-altered DNET (esp. recurrent/difficult-to-excise tumors) to reduce tumor burden and seizures
- Adjunct anti-epileptogenic/seizure-control therapy for patients where gross-total resection is infeasible to achieve durable seizure freedom
- Neurocognitively sparing long-term antiseizure therapy (or tumor-directed therapy enabling ASM withdrawal) that reduces pediatric tolerability-limiting toxicities

name: Dysgerminoma
description: Rare malignant ovarian germ cell cancer in adolescents and young women, typically a rapidly growing unilateral mass causing abdominal or pelvic pain. Most patients are cured with fertility sparing surgery and platinum based chemotherapy, but treatment toxicity and prolonged surveillance complicate long term health and family planning. The hardest gap is relapse, where chemo resistant disease remains difficult to treat, driving interest in de escalating therapy without sacrificing cure and in biomarker and target driven approaches such as KIT.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Bleomycin-/platinum-sparing curative regimens that maintain BEP-level cure while reducing pulmonary and long-term toxicities.
- More effective, less-toxic salvage therapies for relapsed/refractory (incl. platinum-resistant) disease vs TIP/VIP and high-dose chemo.
- Low-toxicity adjuvant/maintenance options after fertility-sparing Stage I management to reduce long, intensive surveillance and the 2-year pregnancy delay.

name: Dyskeratosis congenita
description: Rare inherited telomere biology disorder from impaired telomere maintenance causing short telomeres, often diagnosed in childhood with nail dystrophy, reticular skin pigmentation, and oral leukoplakia, then progressing to bone marrow failure with risks of pulmonary fibrosis and malignancy. Care is largely supportive, with marrow failure treated mainly by toxic androgens or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation that corrects blood defects but not systemic disease, leaving major need for safer non-androgen hematologic options and disease modifying telomere and antifibrotic therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-androgen therapy for DC marrow failure that achieves durable hematologic responses/transfusion-independence without virilization or liver toxicity
- Disease-modifying anti-fibrotic/telomere-pathway therapy for DC pulmonary fibrosis/liver disease that stabilizes objective lung-function endpoints (e.g., FVC/DLCO) and is safe with concurrent marrow failure
- Curative-intent marrow-failure correction via non-genotoxic conditioning/transplant-alternative approaches that avoid worsening lung/liver dysfunction and cancer risk versus HSCT

name: Ehrlichiosis
description: Ehrlichiosis is an acute tick borne intracellular bacterial infection of white blood cells that typically presents 1 to 2 weeks after a bite with abrupt flu like fever, chills, headache, myalgias, nausea and characteristic cytopenias and elevated liver enzymes. Because rash is often absent, early cases are easily missed and delays in doxycycline can lead to meningoencephalitis, respiratory failure, organ failure or death. Unmet needs include faster recognition and treatment pathways, limited validated alternatives when doxycycline cannot be used, no vaccine or post bite prophylaxis to prevent disease, and persistent fatigue and constitutional symptoms in some patients despite therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Clinically validated non‑tetracycline acute therapy for patients with doxycycline allergy/intolerance (and select pregnancy cases) matching doxycycline’s 24–48h defervescence.
- Vaccine and/or evidence‑based post‑exposure prophylaxis for high‑risk tick‑exposed individuals (no vaccine; prophylaxis not recommended).
- Treatments for persistent post‑treatment symptom syndromes after documented ehrlichiosis, improving functional/symptom scores over months.

name: Eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome
description: Eosinophilia myalgia syndrome is a rare, abrupt onset inflammatory illness first recognized in the 1989 L tryptophan associated epidemic, defined by eosinophilia and disabling generalized myalgia with intense extremity pain. Many patients develop edema and skin induration, cough or dyspnea, and neurologic injury such as polyneuropathy and cognitive impairment that can persist despite steroids. Care remains empiric, typically corticosteroids, but relapse during tapering is common, leaving major unmet needs for steroid sparing disease control and durable relief of chronic pain and neurotoxicity beyond laboratory eosinophil response.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute-phase therapy that meaningfully reduces severe myalgia/cramps even when eosinophilia improves (beyond eosinophil-count response).
- Disease-modifying, steroid-sparing early regimen that reduces symptom severity/duration without high-dose corticosteroids.
- Later-phase treatment for persistent neurologic sequelae, especially unchanged peripheral neuropathy and worsening cognitive changes.

name: Epidermolysis bullosa | acquisita
description: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita is a rare, chronic, incurable autoimmune blistering disease in middle-aged adults where antibodies against type VII collagen cause skin fragility with trauma-site blisters, erosions, scarring and milia, sometimes with inflammatory flares and disabling mucosal involvement. Treatment is unsatisfactory and often requires years to lifelong immunosuppression with significant complications and costly options like intravenous immunoglobulin, leaving a need for durable, steroid-sparing control that prevents scarring and functional decline.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable reduction/neutralization of pathogenic anti–type VII collagen (C7) autoantibodies to enable sustained blister control and steroid-/immunosuppressant-free remission in refractory adult EBA
- Anti-fibrotic/anti-cicatricial therapies for mucosal/ocular EBA to prevent conjunctival scarring/blindness and esophageal strictures
- Safer long-term maintenance alternatives to chronic systemic immunosuppression that reduce morbidity/monitoring burden and avoid clinic-intensive IVIG rescue

name: Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis
description: Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (epidermolytic ichthyosis) is an ultra rare congenital keratin disorder caused by KRT1 or KRT10 mutations that make skin cells fragile, leading to blistering and erythroderma at birth with dehydration and sepsis risk, then lifelong progressive hyperkeratosis with odor and psychosocial burden. Treatment is symptomatic and labor intensive with emollients, keratolytics and retinoids, with no cure or disease modifying option. Key unmet needs include neonatal barrier stabilization, safer durable control of hyperkeratosis and infection, and mutation targeting approaches such as allele suppression or gene based therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neonatal-onset barrier–stabilizing therapy to prevent dehydration/electrolyte imbalance and systemic infection/sepsis in EI/EHK newborns.
- Non-retinoid hyperkeratosis-reduction therapy that improves thick scale without worsening blistering/fragility or causing irritation/toxicity seen with current keratolytics/retinoids.
- Mutation-targeting restorative therapy for dominant KRT1/KRT10 disease (e.g., allele disruption/correction) to deliver durable keratin-filament stabilization vs lifelong symptomatic care.

name: Wilms tumor | anaplastic
description: Anaplastic Wilms tumor is a high risk childhood kidney cancer, typically diagnosed at ages 2 to 5, often presenting as a large painless abdominal or flank mass sometimes with hematuria or hypertension. Diffuse anaplasia is linked to TP53 disruption, relative resistance to standard chemotherapy, and about 50 percent recurrence frequently in the lungs. Outcomes are often pursued by intensifying multiagent chemotherapy and radiotherapy, but late effects such as heart failure, infertility, kidney failure, and second cancers rise with treatment intensity, creating a need for more durable disease control with less toxicity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Overcome TP53-linked treatment resistance in stage III/IV diffuse anaplastic Wilms tumor to reduce relapse/death.
- Prevent and more effectively treat recurrence in anaplastic-histology Wilms tumor (high recurrence; very poor prognosis after recurrence in stage II–IV).
- Maintain/improve disease control while materially reducing acute/late toxicity and overall treatment burden of intensified multi-agent chemo + radiotherapy.

name: Acute myeloid leukemia | erythroleukemia
description: Erythroleukemia, or acute erythroid leukemia, is a rare, aggressive acute myeloid leukemia dominated by erythroid precursors, often arising after myelodysplastic syndromes or prior cytotoxic therapy and frequently driven by complex cytogenetics with biallelic TP53 loss. It presents over weeks with marrow failure causing fatigue, fever, and bleeding or bruising. Current chemotherapy or hypomethylating agent based care is toxic and infection prone, responses are short lived, and outcomes after frontline hypomethylating agent plus venetoclax failure are dire, leaving a pressing need for durable, tolerable disease modifying and salvage options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- TP53-mutant/complex-karyotype pure erythroid leukemia therapy that improves survival despite high-risk genetics
- Effective salvage regimens for patients relapsing after venetoclax+azacitidine (post-relapse survival ~2 months)
- Lower-toxicity, lower-monitoring frontline alternatives to venetoclax+azacitidine that reduce severe infection/cytopenia and simplify dosing

name: Esophageal cancer | adenosquamous carcinoma
description: Esophageal adenosquamous carcinoma is a rare mixed adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma that skews to men over 50 and often presents late with dysphagia, pain, and weight loss, when disease is already deeply invasive or metastatic. Outcomes are poor and evidence is thin, leaving reliance on palliative measures like stents for obstruction and intensive multi day fluorouracil plus platinum chemoimmunotherapy backbones. Key unmet needs are faster, more durable dysphagia control and better biomarker guided, less burdensome systemic options for this often HER2 negative aggressive subtype.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Biomarker-driven targeted options for HER2-negative esophageal ASC (e.g., EGFR-directed for squamous-component disease and/or CLDN18.2-directed for GEJ/adeno-like biology).
- Regimens that meaningfully improve 1L outcomes and relieve dysphagia/obstruction faster than current chemo-IO.
- Pump/central-line–sparing systemic therapy with fewer serious AEs and lower AE-driven discontinuation versus cisplatin + 120-hour continuous-infusion 5-FU–based chemo-IO.

name: Esophageal cancer | small cell carcinoma
description: Rare, aggressive neuroendocrine esophageal cancer often diagnosed after a short course of dysphagia and weight loss, frequently metastatic at presentation. Care is largely extrapolated from small cell lung cancer with platinum based chemotherapy plus or minus radiation, but the evidence base is thin and guidelines are unclear. Outcomes are poor and toxicity is high, leaving a premium on more durable benefit beyond first line platinum, credible post platinum options, and better tolerated outpatient regimens, with early exploration of immune checkpoint combinations.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable OS-improving systemic therapy for extensive-stage/metastatic small-cell esophageal carcinoma (meaningfully beyond ~7–12 months median OS)
- Effective, standardized post-platinum (relapsed/refractory) option with clinically meaningful ORR and durable PFS/OS
- Lower-toxicity, lower-visit-burden alternatives to platinum–etoposide ± chemoradiation, especially for older patients

name: Essential fructosuria
description: Essential fructosuria is an ultra rare, autosomal recessive fructokinase deficiency causing intermittent fructose in blood and urine after fructose, sucrose, or sorbitol intake but it is clinically benign and asymptomatic. Most patients are found incidentally when urine tests show a non glucose reducing sugar. The main unmet need is practical recognition and counseling to avoid unnecessary diagnostic workups and inappropriate dietary restriction, rather than disease modifying therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus topic URL (use search: https://vsearch.nlm.nih.gov/vivisimo/cgi-bin/query-meta?v:project=medlineplus&query=Essential+fructosuria)

name: Plasmacytoma | extramedullary
description: Extramedullary plasmacytoma is a solitary soft tissue plasma cell tumor with minimal or no bone marrow involvement, most often in the head and neck where mass effects like dysphagia can occur. Radiotherapy is the mainstay, but 10 to 30 percent recur locally or progress to multiple myeloma, and there is no standard systemic therapy, leaving a need for disease modifying approaches that reduce progression risk while avoiding head and neck radiotherapy toxicities such as mucositis and xerostomia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjuvant/consolidation systemic therapy for “high-risk” extramedullary plasmacytoma to reduce the ~10–30% risk of local recurrence and/or transformation to multiple myeloma after local therapy (e.g., abnormal FLC ratio and/or residual M‑protein).
- Effective, well-tolerated systemic options for bulky and/or radiotherapy-nonresponsive extramedullary plasmacytoma where chemotherapy use is limited/controversial.
- Radiation-sparing or RT-deintensifying drug approaches that preserve curative local control while reducing RT toxicities (e.g., mucositis/xerostomia) and long-course treatment burden.

name: Diastrophic dysplasia
description: Rare congenital cartilage and bone dysplasia caused by impaired sulfate transport leading to undersulfated cartilage matrix, with disproportionate short-limb stature, clubfoot, spinal deformity, hitchhiker thumbs, frequent cleft palate and ear swelling, progressive contractures and early osteoarthritis that impair mobility; care is largely symptomatic and supportive, leaving a major need for disease-modifying and durable non-opioid joint-preserving therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prenatal/early-postnatal sulfate-donor therapy to restore cartilage/GAG sulfation and improve skeletal growth/phenotype.
- Chondrocyte pathway modulation (e.g., FGFR3 pathway inhibition) to improve cartilage growth and reduce progression of cervical kyphosis/kyphoscoliosis and contractures.
- Joint-protective, non-opioid pharmacotherapy for early-onset osteoarthritis pain (esp. hip) to preserve mobility and delay early arthroplasty.

name: Neurocutaneous melanosis
description: Neurocutaneous melanosis is an ultra rare disorder where melanin producing cells accumulate in the brain and spinal cord alongside congenital melanocytic nevi, often large or giant with many satellites at birth. In infancy or early childhood it can rapidly cause hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure, seizures, vomiting, and developmental delay, with high early mortality once symptomatic. Care is largely supportive with shunts and antiseizure drugs, with no definitive disease modifying therapy and limited benefit from chemotherapy or radiation. NRAS and mitogen activated protein kinase pathway biology highlights the need for durable brain penetrating targeted treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, CNS-penetrant MAPK-pathway targeted therapy for symptomatic (esp. NRAS-driven) leptomeningeal NCM that sustains neurologic/ICP/seizure control beyond transient MEK-inhibitor benefit.
- Targeted systemic therapy for NCM-associated (often CNS/leptomeningeal) melanoma where no targeted option exists today.
- Non-surgical medical therapy to prevent/treat hydrocephalus/raised ICP by controlling leptomeningeal nevomelanocyte proliferation and reducing VP-shunt dependence/clogging risk.

name: Astrocytoma | fibrillary
description: WHO grade 2 diffuse astrocytoma that grows slowly but infiltrates brain, often presenting with seizures plus subtle cognitive or mood changes and headaches; key unmet needs are durable tumor control that delays progression to higher grade disease while minimizing long term cognitive toxicity from radiotherapy and reducing chronic seizure burden, with growing interest in isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 targeted therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent malignant transformation and recurrence by reducing progression from grade 2 astrocytoma to higher-grade glioma.
- Achieve seizure freedom/major seizure reduction to address tumor-related, often refractory epilepsy and QoL burden.
- Maintain tumor control while reducing long-term toxicity and monitoring burden vs RT/PCV/TMZ and IDH-inhibitor LFT monitoring.

name: Focal dermal hypoplasia
description: Ultra rare X linked dominant PORCN related disorder, usually in girls, with congenital linear dermal hypoplasia, fat herniation and telangiectasia causing painful pruritic infection prone skin lesions plus multisystem malformations and progressive mucocutaneous or aerodigestive papillomas that can impair swallowing or breathing. Care is symptomatic and procedural with major unmet needs for disease modifying therapy and better control and prevention of skin pain, itch, infections and recurrent papillomas.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Infant-safe topical therapy that meaningfully reduces painful/pruritic skin disease and secondary skin infections beyond today’s nonspecific creams/dressings and intermittent procedure-based management
- Non-surgical anti-papillomatosis therapy to prevent/shrink aerodigestive papillomas that drive dysphagia and breathing/sleep problems (incl. peri-anesthesia airway risk/OSA), reducing repeated surgical interventions
- PORCN/WNT-pathway targeted molecular therapy (gene/RNA/small-molecule) correcting the underlying PORCN-mediated WNT secretion defect, with efficacy tied to dermal integrity endpoints (e.g., skin hypoplasia/fat herniation/telangiectasia burden)

name: Distal myopathy
description: Rare, mostly genetic, slowly progressive muscle diseases causing distal weakness starting in feet and ankles and sometimes hands with foot drop, high stepping gait and fine motor difficulty but preserved sensation and cognition; care is largely supportive with rehabilitation and bracing, and key subtypes still lack disease modifying therapy, making preservation of strength and ambulation the core unmet need as gene linked trials emerge.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- GNE-myopathy substrate/pathway replacement to slow distal strength loss (e.g., ankle dorsiflexion) and preserve ambulation/6MWT to delay wheelchair dependence.
- Dysferlinopathy disease-modifying dysferlin restoration/repair targeting the distal anterior-tibial (foot-drop) phenotype beyond symptomatic supports.
- Muscle-function therapy preventing early ankle dorsiflexion loss/steppage gait to reduce falls/balance impairment and delay reliance on AFOs/canes/walkers/wheelchairs.

name: Dominant optic atrophy | plus syndrome
description: Rare inherited OPA1 driven mitochondrial neuro-ophthalmic disorder causing progressive bilateral optic atrophy in childhood, often later complicated by hearing loss and neuromuscular features; care is largely supportive with no efficient treatment, creating a major unmet need for disease modifying therapies that preserve vision and prevent multisystem progression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early disease-modifying ocular therapy that halts first-decade onset progressive central visual loss in OPA1 DOA/DOA+.
- Systemic therapy to prevent/delay progression to DOA+ multisystem disease, especially 2nd–3rd decade sensorineural deafness and later neuromuscular disability.
- Convenient oral neuroprotective therapy showing measurable stabilization/improvement in optic-nerve function/structure within ~6 months (e.g., PhNR/OCT endpoints).

name: Dystransthyretinemic hyperthyroxinemia
description: Dystransthyretinemic hyperthyroxinemia is a rare inherited, benign thyroid lab phenotype in which a transthyretin variant binds thyroxine too tightly, raising total and sometimes apparent free thyroxine despite normal thyroid stimulating hormone and no symptoms. It is usually found incidentally and does not require treatment, but misread results can trigger unnecessary workups or therapy. Key needs are clinician awareness plus access to confirmatory testing and more reliable free thyroxine assays to avoid spurious elevations and overtreatment.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Acrospiroma | eccrine
description: Eccrine acrospiroma (nodular hidradenoma) is a rare, usually benign sweat gland tumor presenting as a slow growing, freely movable 0.5 to 2 cm dermal nodule, often in women. Excision is typically curative, but incomplete removal can recur in up to 10% and rare malignant transformation to aggressive hidradenocarcinoma creates the main unmet need, since there are no uniform systemic guidelines for metastatic disease. Emerging directions include biomarker guided targeted therapy based on EGFR or HER2 expression and PI3K AKT alterations, and immunotherapy with PD-1 inhibitors in selected advanced cases.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- HER2-directed systemic/adjuvant therapy for HER2/neu-positive malignant nodular hidradenoma/hidradenocarcinoma
- Biomarker-driven anti–PD-1 immunotherapy for advanced/metastatic hidradenocarcinoma (e.g., TMB-H/MSI/high PD-L1)
- Targeted therapy for molecularly defined disease with high EGFR expression and PI3K/AKT alterations

name: Eccrine carcinoma
description: Eccrine porocarcinoma is an ultra-rare malignant sweat-duct skin cancer, typically slow-growing in adults over 60 on the lower limbs or head and neck. Surgery can cure early disease, but around 20% recur and around 20% metastasize to lymph nodes, where mortality is high and there are no proven systemic therapies. Key unmet needs are durable systemic control for metastatic disease, perioperative therapy for high-risk lesions, and surgery-sparing local treatments, with progress mainly coming through rare-tumor basket immunotherapy trials.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable systemic therapy for metastatic/recurrent eccrine carcinoma/porocarcinoma to achieve meaningful objective responses and extend survival beyond ~5–24 months.
- Adjuvant/neoadjuvant drug therapy for high-risk resectable disease to cut the ~20% recurrence/metastasis rate and prevent progression to high-mortality nodal disease.
- Surgery-sparing local pharmacologic options (topical/intralesional) to eradicate/downstage early/local lesions in older or poor-surgical-candidate patients.
medlineUrl: No specific MedlinePlus URL; closest: https://medlineplus.gov/skincancer.html

name: Early-onset ataxia with ocular motor apraxia and hypoalbuminemia
description: Ataxia oculomotor apraxia type 1 is a rare autosomal recessive childhood onset neurodegenerative ataxia caused by APTX mutations impairing DNA single strand break repair. Children develop progressive gait and limb ataxia with oculomotor apraxia and severe axonal neuropathy, often becoming wheelchair dependent within about 7 to 15 years. Hypoalbuminemia with hypercholesterolemia adds cardiovascular risk on top of relentless neurologic decline. Management is supportive with no disease modifying therapy, leaving a premium on treatments that slow disability and on biomarkers that track meaningful clinical benefit.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- APTX/aprataxin-targeted disease-modifying therapy in childhood-onset AOA1 to delay loss of ambulation/wheelchair dependence (~7–10 years post-onset)
- Neuroprotective therapy that prevents/slows severe axonal motor-sensory peripheral neuropathy driving quadriplegia and disability
- Biomarker-anchored therapy that stabilizes/corrects hypoalbuminemia (± hypercholesterolemia) with demonstrated improvement on validated ataxia/neurologic endpoints

name: Ectodermal dysplasia with immune deficiency
description: Rare genetic ectodermal dysplasia immunodeficiency presenting soon after birth with abnormal skin, hair, teeth, and sweat glands plus severe immune dysfunction causing recurrent, sometimes life threatening infections and early childhood mortality. Current care is largely supportive with immunoglobulin and antimicrobial prophylaxis, while susceptibility to mycobacteria and complications like hyperthermia from impaired sweating and inflammatory bowel disease persist. Even hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may not resolve gastrointestinal disease, leaving a major need for safe disease modifying approaches that prevent infections and address barrier inflammation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Immune reconstitution that restores protective anti-pneumococcal (and broader) antibody function to reduce reliance on chronic Ig replacement plus multi-drug prophylaxis.
- Therapies for NEMO-related colitis/IBD and epithelial-barrier dysfunction that can persist even after HSCT.
- Targeted prevention/treatment for the mycobacterial-/BCG-susceptible subset, including HSCT-bridging strategies to improve transplant outcomes.

name: Endocardial fibroelastosis
description: Endocardial fibroelastosis is a rare infant and childhood heart disorder marked by fibroelastic thickening of the endocardial lining, typically presenting between 4 and 12 months with rapid-onset heart failure symptoms such as dyspnea, poor feeding, sweating, and failure to thrive. Management is essentially standard chronic heart failure care, with no disease-specific curative therapy, and severe cases may progress to heart transplantation. Maternal autoantibody-associated fetal disease can be especially aggressive, highlighting the need for earlier diagnosis and disease-modifying, potentially immunologically targeted approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying anti-fibroelastosis therapy (e.g., anti-EndMT/anti-fibrotic) to prevent/regress the de novo fibroelastic endocardial layer rather than symptomatic HF control.
- Rapid “transplant-avoidance” rescue therapy for acutely decompensated infants to quickly restore LV function/cardiac output and improve transplant-free survival.
- Targeted fetal EFE immunomodulation for maternal anti-Ro/anti-La cases that reverses fetal EFE with better benefit–risk than systemic steroids (and options for steroid-nonresponsive seronegative EFE).

name: Endometrial cancer | stromal
description: Rare malignant uterine tumor in women 40–55 presenting with abnormal uterine bleeding and pelvic pain; surgery is the cornerstone, with hormone therapy for low grade disease but frequent late recurrences (up to ~50%), while high grade disease is often advanced with poor survival (median ~11–24 months), leaving a need for durable relapse prevention and molecularly guided systemic options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemic adjuvant relapse-prevention for Stage I low‑grade ESS post‑surgery to reduce high, delayed recurrence risk.
- Next‑gen endocrine therapies/combos for metastatic/recurrent ER/PR+ low‑grade ESS with aromatase‑inhibitor resistance (e.g., ESR1‑mutant) to extend PFS and delay chemotherapy.
- Molecularly targeted drugs for aggressive high‑grade ESS subsets (e.g., BCOR/YWHAE) to improve response and durability versus chemotherapy-centric care.

name: Eosinophilic meningitis
description: Eosinophilic meningitis is most often rat lungworm neuroangiostrongyliasis, where Angiostrongylus cantonensis larvae invade the central nervous system after ingestion of infected snails or slugs or contaminated produce, triggering intense meningeal inflammation with severe headache, raised cerebrospinal fluid pressure, and neurologic symptoms that can persist for months and rarely progress to coma or death. Management is largely supportive with corticosteroids, analgesia, and sometimes repeated lumbar punctures, and the major gap is the lack of a proven, low risk antiparasitic that clears infection without worsening inflammation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing intracranial-pressure/headache control that eliminates serial therapeutic lumbar punctures
- Proven CNS-penetrant anti-parasitic that clears *A. cantonensis* without inflammatory worsening and works despite uncertain timing of exposure
- Therapies that prevent/treat chronic post-acute neurologic sequelae (e.g., persistent neuropathic pain/paresthesias) and reduce severe pediatric complications

name: Epidermodysplasia verruciformis
description: Rare inherited genodermatosis with intrinsic susceptibility to cutaneous human papillomavirus, causing childhood-onset disseminated, treatment-resistant wart-like and pityriasis versicolor-like lesions and a high lifetime risk of non-melanoma skin cancer, especially cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Care is largely non-curative and focused on photoprotection and lifelong surveillance, leaving a need for durable lesion control and safe long-term chemoprevention of malignant transformation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable β‑HPV lesion clearance/prevention for inherited EV (TMC6/TMC8/CIB1 pathway) with sustained control of disseminated, treatment‑recalcitrant lesions
- Drug chemoprevention that meaningfully reduces EV’s high lifetime cutaneous SCC/non‑melanoma skin-cancer risk beyond photoprotection/surveillance/excision
- Non‑teratogenic, pediatric/adolescent-suitable long‑term maintenance with lower relapse and reduced monitoring burden vs systemic retinoids/topical field therapies

name: Erythrokeratodermia variabilis
description: Rare inherited skin disorder starting at birth or infancy, driven by connexin gap junction dysfunction, causing fixed hyperkeratotic plaques plus transient migratory erythematous flares often triggered by temperature change, stress, or irritation and sometimes burning or itching. Management is symptomatic and often incomplete, with emollients limited and systemic retinoids reducing scale more than redness and constrained by adverse effects and teratogenicity, leaving need for safe lifelong erythema control and mechanism based therapies targeting connexin or gap junctions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Complete suppression of the erythematous/inflammatory (migratory red patch) component that persists despite retinoids
- Non-retinoid long-term therapy safe for lifelong use starting in childhood and feasible for women of childbearing potential (avoid retinoid teratogenicity/bone-growth risks)
- Genotype-/mechanism-directed disease modification for connexin-variant EKVP (e.g., GJB3/GJB4/GJA1) via variant correction/ablation

name: Parry–Romberg syndrome
description: Parry Romberg syndrome is a rare acquired disorder, usually beginning in childhood or adolescence, in which one side of the face slowly loses skin, fat and soft tissue, often with pigment changes, enophthalmos and neurologic pain or headache. Care in active disease often relies on broad immunosuppression such as methotrexate plus corticosteroids, but there is no cure, no standard of care and little randomized evidence. Definitive reconstruction is typically delayed until the disease quiets, leaving patients with years of progressive disfigurement and variable outcomes, with early regenerative fat grafting approaches still nascent.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- RCT-validated disease-modifying therapy to reliably halt progression during the pediatric active phase, with objective imaging endpoints to measure response
- Safer pediatric-friendly steroid/MTX-sparing targeted immunomodulator with proven long-term benefit and tolerability vs broad immunosuppression
- Injectable regenerative biologic/cell therapy that delivers durable facial volume restoration to reduce dependence on reconstructive procedures
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus page (no standalone medlineplus.gov URL)

name: Factor V deficiency
description: Ultra-rare inherited or acquired bleeding disorder caused by factor V loss or inhibition, leading to mucocutaneous and post-procedure bleeding and occasional life-threatening hemorrhage; care relies on fresh frozen plasma that provides only temporary correction and carries transfusion burden and risks, with no commercial factor V concentrate and limited options for inhibitor-driven cases beyond immunosuppression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Commercially available factor V replacement (vs FFP) to reliably maintain FV activity ≥25–30% for bleeds/procedures (higher for life‑threatening hemorrhage)
- Non‑plasma/low‑volume hemostatic option to avoid plasma transfusion complications (TRALI, TACO, allergic reactions) and enable safer repeat dosing
- Inhibitor‑focused strategy for acquired FV deficiency (inhibitor‑tolerant replacement and/or targeted inhibitor eradication) to control bleeding without broad immunosuppression/high‑risk bypassing therapy

name: Factor VII deficiency
description: Ultra-rare inherited factor VII clotting disorder causing variable bleeding from asymptomatic disease to mucosal, menstrual, and post‑procedure hemorrhage and occasionally life‑threatening intracranial or gastrointestinal bleeding. Management relies on intravenous recombinant factor VIIa, fresh frozen plasma, and antifibrinolytics, but short factor VII half life drives frequent repeat dosing that makes prophylaxis and perioperative coverage burdensome, while thrombosis risk constrains use. Key unmet needs are longer-acting, safer hemostatic options that provide durable bleed prevention with fewer infusions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Long-acting (ideally SC) prophylaxis for severe congenital FVII deficiency patients with recurrent/severe bleeding to avoid frequent rFVIIa dosing.
- Simplified peri-procedural/major-bleed regimens that reduce intensive IV rFVIIa schedules (e.g., q2h dosing for surgery).
- Thrombosis-sparing hemostatic options usable in patients with thrombotic risk factors and without concomitant PCC/aPCC.

name: Factor X deficiency
description: Rare inherited factor X deficiency causes impaired coagulation and variable bleeding from neonatal umbilical bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage risk to joint and muscle bleeds and heavy menstrual and postpartum hemorrhage. Care is largely intravenous replacement with plasma or factor concentrates such as COAGADEX, while some patients rely on variable prothrombin complex concentrates that carry thrombosis risk. The main gaps are simpler, safer prophylaxis and lower burden options that reliably prevent life threatening bleeds in infants and support women through pregnancy and childbirth.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Low-frequency, non‑IV prophylaxis (e.g., long‑acting/subcutaneous or gene-based) to maintain protective FX troughs and prevent early-life CNS/intracranial bleeding
- Safer, standardized FX-only replacement to replace variable PCC/FFP use and reduce thromboembolism/volume-transfusion risks
- Women-focused bleeding control (menorrhagia plus peripartum/postpartum hemorrhage) to reduce blood-product use and intensive monitoring

name: Factor XII deficiency
description: Rare autosomal recessive factor XII (Hageman factor) deficiency causing isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time but typically no clinical bleeding, often found incidentally on preoperative labs. Biggest need is avoiding misdiagnosis and unnecessary perioperative delays or plasma, while clarifying whether any thromboembolism risk is real and who might benefit from prevention.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Factor XIII deficiency
description: Ultra rare inherited Factor XIII clot stability disorder causing delayed bleeding despite normal routine coagulation tests, often first seen as newborn umbilical stump bleeding, with risks of poor wound healing, recurrent miscarriage, and fatal spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage; managed mainly with lifelong intravenous factor replacement every 3 to 4 weeks, leaving unmet needs in earlier diagnosis, reduced infusion burden, and broader prophylaxis options beyond A subunit deficiency.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non‑IV, lower-burden prophylaxis that maintains FXIII trough ≥10% (vs monthly/q28d IV prophylaxis)
- Non–plasma-derived therapy effective for FXIII‑B subunit (F13B) deficiency (catridecacog is A‑subunit only)
- Pregnancy‑optimized prophylaxis to prevent high miscarriage risk without routine FXIII supplementation

name: Fallopian tube cancer | endometrioid
description: Exceptionally rare epithelial fallopian tube cancer, usually in peri or postmenopausal women, clinically grouped with ovarian and primary peritoneal cancer and often presenting with vague abdominal or pelvic symptoms and late spread. Managed with surgery plus platinum chemotherapy, sometimes with bevacizumab or poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor maintenance, but relapse is common. The key unmet need is durable options for recurrent, platinum resistant disease where standard monotherapy delivers only about 10 to 15 percent response rates and roughly 3.5 months median progression free survival.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- HRD-negative/BRCA–wild-type maintenance that materially lowers recurrence risk vs bevacizumab/observation
- Platinum-resistant recurrent disease therapies that beat ~10–20% single-agent cytotoxic ORR and extend duration of response
- Lower-toxicity, lower-burden long-term regimens that reduce marrow-suppression dose modifications/discontinuations and avoid prolonged q3-week IV maintenance

name: Gallbladder cancer | squamous cell carcinoma
description: Gallbladder squamous cell carcinoma is a profoundly rare, highly aggressive gallbladder cancer subtype that is usually diagnosed late in older women often with gallstones, presenting with abdominal pain, jaundice, and weight loss. With no routine screening and limited effectiveness of chemoradiation and systemic therapy for unresectable disease, prognosis is very poor with median survival measured in months. The key need is earlier detection and more effective treatments that increase rates of complete surgical resection and meaningfully extend survival.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Conversion-enabling systemic therapy with much higher ORR than 1L GemCis±durvalumab to downstage unresectable gallbladder SCC to R0 resection.
- Regimens that materially improve durability/OS beyond current 1L chemo‑IO benchmarks for advanced gallbladder SCC.
- Chemo-sparing biomarker-driven targeted therapies (e.g., EGFR/HER2) to reduce GemCis-based chemo‑IO serious-toxicity burden.

name: Gastric dilatation
description: Acute gastric dilatation is a rare emergency in which the stomach becomes massively enlarged, typically from gastric outlet obstruction or dysmotility such as eating disorders and gastroparesis, causing progressive distention with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Delayed recognition can rapidly lead to ischemia and perforation, so care hinges on urgent decompression, often with nasogastric tube placement, and surgery when obstruction or ischemia is suspected. Key unmet needs include faster, less invasive decompression, gastric wall protection, and safer durable prokinetics given limits of metoclopramide and macrolides.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid ED-administered pharmacologic “medical decompression” to reverse early acute gastric dilatation and reduce need for NGT decompression/emergent laparotomy
- Adjunct “gastric wall rescue” therapy to prevent progression to ischemia/necrosis/perforation (fewer perforations/gastrectomies/deaths)
- Safe long-term recurrence prevention in high-risk dysmotility settings via motility agents avoiding metoclopramide (tardive dyskinesia/≤12-week limit) and erythromycin (tachyphylaxis/QT risk) limitations

name: Epilepsy | familial focal with variable foci
description: Rare inherited focal epilepsy with variable seizure onset regions; many have preserved awareness and normal function between seizures. Anti-seizure medications help most, but up to ~30% have drug-resistant seizures, especially with focal cortical dysplasia. Common drivers include DEPDC5, NPRL2, and NPRL3 variants disrupting GATOR1 control of mTOR complex 1 signaling, leaving a need for durable seizure freedom and pathway-informed precision therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- mTORC1-pathway precision therapy for genetically defined FFEVF (DEPDC5/NPRL2/NPRL3→GATOR1)
- Therapies that achieve sustained seizure freedom in drug-resistant focal epilepsy (after ≥2 ASM failures), especially FCD-associated cases
- Better-tolerated long-term ASMs (fewer behavioral AEs vs levetiracetam; lower hyponatremia/monitoring burden vs oxcarbazepine), particularly for adolescents

name: Familial glucocorticoid deficiency
description: Familial glucocorticoid deficiency is a genetic primary adrenal insufficiency in which infants and young children cannot produce cortisol, leading to hypoglycemia, failure to thrive, recurrent infections, and hyperpigmentation, with risk of seizures, neurologic injury, and death if missed. Management is lifelong hydrocortisone replacement plus rapid parenteral stress dosing during illness, but today’s immediate release regimens cannot mimic circadian cortisol and pediatric dosing often relies on inaccurate compounding, driving avoidable under or over replacement and ongoing adrenal crisis risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Circadian-mimicking glucocorticoid replacement (modified-release hydrocortisone or pump chronotherapy) to better replicate physiologic cortisol rhythms vs immediate-release dosing.
- Ready-to-use emergency stress-dose hydrocortisone (prefilled autoinjector/EMS-available) to reduce illness/vomiting-triggered adrenal crises.
- Infant-precision low-strength oral hydrocortisone formulations (e.g., stable suspensions/minitablets/granules) to enable fine titration and reduce long-term harms from over/under-replacement.

name: Posner–Schlossman syndrome
description: Rare episodic inflammatory glaucoma causing recurrent, usually unilateral spikes of very high intraocular pressure (often 40s to 50s mmHg) with only mild anterior uveitis, leading to blurred vision and halos and cumulative glaucomatous optic nerve damage. Care is largely reactive and drop heavy with pressure lowering agents plus topical steroids and, when cytomegalovirus is implicated, ganciclovir or valganciclovir. Key unmet needs are durable recurrence prevention, sustained antiviral control given relapse after stopping therapy, steroid sparing inflammation control because steroids can raise intraocular pressure, and simpler management that reduces urgent monitoring burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable/virucidal CMV-directed control in CMV-associated PSS to prevent post-treatment relapse after valganciclovir cessation
- Steroid-sparing inflammation control for steroid-dependent PSS to enable steroid withdrawal while reducing steroid-induced ocular hypertension risk
- Faster, simpler acute control of IOP/inflammation with fewer daily drops and fewer urgent follow-ups to reduce cumulative glaucomatous damage from recurrences
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus page for Posner–Schlossman syndrome (PSS); related: https://medlineplus.gov/glaucoma.html; https://medlineplus.gov/uveitis.html

name: Glioblastoma | mesenchymal
description: Mesenchymal glioblastoma is an aggressive World Health Organization grade 4 brain cancer that typically presents with headaches, seizures, nausea or vomiting, and cognitive or personality changes. Despite maximal surgery plus radiotherapy and temozolomide, cure is rare and recurrence is expected because infiltrative tumor margins retain an intact blood brain barrier that limits drug delivery. Benefit from temozolomide is minimal in O6-methylguanine DNA methyltransferase promoter unmethylated disease. The mesenchymal state is necrosis rich and microenvironment driven with heavy macrophage and microglia infiltration, while steroid use for edema can blunt antitumor immunity, reinforcing the need for better delivery and steroid sparing, immune compatible therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- TMZ-sparing/non-alkylator regimens with clinically meaningful OS benefit in MGMT promoter–unmethylated (TMZ-resistant) newly diagnosed GBM.
- Mesenchymal-subtype therapies that reprogram/deplete TAM–microglia biology while enabling steroid-sparing (minimized dexamethasone) immune-compatible treatment.
- BBB-penetrant/BBB-modulating delivery that reaches infiltrative invasive margins (intact BBB) to prevent/treat post-local-therapy recurrence.

name: Glomus tumor
description: Glomus tumors are rare, usually benign vascular tumors of the glomus apparatus, most often under the fingernail, causing severe focal fingertip pain with cold sensitivity and point tenderness. They are frequently missed for years, with an average diagnostic delay around 7 years. Definitive treatment is complete surgical excision, but recurrence and post operative nail deformity are common practical concerns. Malignant variants are exceedingly rare yet can be locally aggressive and metastatic, and evidence for effective systemic therapies is limited.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, non-opioid pain control to bridge years-long diagnostic delays in patients with severe cold-triggered paroxysmal digital pain.
- Nail-sparing, non-surgical intralesional/chemical ablation (e.g., sclerotherapy) for subungual lesions to reduce nail deformity and recurrence vs excision.
- Systemic targeted/anti-angiogenic therapy for multifocal/recurrent (e.g., NF1-associated) or malignant/metastatic glomus tumors where no established non-surgical strategy exists.

name: Vitamin E deficiency | familial isolated
description: Familial isolated vitamin E deficiency (ataxia with vitamin E deficiency) is a TTPA driven failure to use dietary vitamin E causing progressive childhood onset neurodegeneration with ataxia, sensory loss, and areflexia. Lifelong high dose oral vitamin E can prevent disease if started presymptomatically, but later treatment often leaves persistent gait and proprioceptive deficits and carries a bleeding risk at high exposure, creating unmet need for earlier diagnosis and safer lower burden disease modifying approaches that restore function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- One-time/infrequent causal *TTPA* correction to prevent AVED in presymptomatic siblings (vs daily lifelong high-dose vitamin E + monitoring)
- Therapies that restore neurologic function (proprioception/gait) in late-treated symptomatic patients beyond mere stabilization
- Lower-burden/safer vitamin E replacement that maintains efficacy while reducing bleeding risk and anticoagulant/antiplatelet interactions

name: Hypoparathyroidism | familial isolated
description: Rare genetic disorder with impaired parathyroid hormone secretion causing hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, often presenting in childhood with tingling, tetany, or seizures. Care relies on calcium and active vitamin D, but patients frequently develop hypercalciuria with kidney stones, nephrocalcinosis, and renal impairment, and phosphate control and daily treatment burden remain challenging. A premium remains for more physiologic, lower burden approaches that stabilize calcium and phosphate while protecting the kidneys, including strategies that restore endogenous parathyroid hormone signaling such as calcium sensing receptor modulators.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Renal-safe physiologic control that prevents symptomatic hypocalcemia while lowering urinary calcium (reduce hypercalciuria-driven stones/nephrocalcinosis/CKD vs calcium + active vitamin D).
- Phosphate-centric control that reliably lowers hyperphosphatemia/calcium–phosphate product without escalating calcium/active vitamin D (limit ectopic calcifications).
- Low-burden regimen that reduces multi-dose daily calcium/meal-timing complexity and demonstrates improved patient-reported QoL vs conventional therapy.

name: Familial multiple lipomatosis
description: Rare inherited disorder (often autosomal dominant) causing numerous benign subcutaneous lipomas on the trunk and extremities that emerge in adulthood and can accumulate over decades. Lesions are usually painless but can become large and disfiguring, driving quality of life burden. Care is largely repeated procedures such as surgical excision or liposuction, which trade clearance for scarring or incomplete removal. With causal genetics and biology still uncertain, there are no disease modifying options to prevent new lipomas or reduce long term procedural burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Office-based, minimally invasive therapy to clear numerous lipomas with ≥90% reduction and minimal scarring/downtime (vs surgery/liposuction)
- Systemic or field-directed therapy that prevents/slows formation and growth of new lipomas in autosomal-dominant FML
- Pathway-targeted agents against lipoma-driving adipocyte proliferation biology (e.g., HMGA axis) for durable control beyond debulking

name: Tumor of the follicular infundibulum
description: Rare, benign hair follicle adnexal tumor in older adults, typically a slow asymptomatic scaly papule or scar-like hypopigmented macule on the head and neck or trunk that often mimics basal cell carcinoma and requires biopsy. Eruptive cases can cause multiple field lesions. Key unmet needs are effective non-scarring, field-directed treatments and practical surveillance, since medical options are limited and destructive procedures can leave cosmetically troubling scars, with rare malignant transformation reported in very high-burden patients.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-scarring topical lesion clearance for cosmetically sensitive tumors of the follicular infundibulum (TFI).
- Field-directed therapy achieving durable clearance in eruptive/multiple infundibulomatosis.
- Medical prevention/stabilization for high-burden patients at rare risk of basal cell carcinoma (BCC) transformation.

name: Follicular mucinosis
description: Follicular mucinosis (alopecia mucinosa) is a rare disorder marked by mucin accumulation around hair follicles, causing follicular papules or plaques and non scarring hair loss often on the face, neck, or scalp. Younger patients may have localized disease that can spontaneously resolve, while adults over 40 can develop widespread, persistent disease with a clinically important overlap with cutaneous T cell lymphoma. Care is limited by the lack of any proven effective therapy, frequent incomplete responses, and the ongoing burden of repeat biopsies and close surveillance.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CTCL-directed systemic therapy that reliably clears lesions and restores hair growth in adult/secondary (CTCL-associated) follicular mucinosis
- Evidence-based, consistently effective regimen for primary follicular mucinosis with durable complete responses
- Low-burden maintenance therapy to prevent relapse and reduce need for long-term surveillance/serial biopsies

name: Thyroid cancer | follicular
description: Follicular thyroid cancer is a midlife, female-predominant differentiated thyroid cancer often presenting as a thyroid nodule and treated initially with surgery plus radioactive iodine when appropriate. The major unmet need is metastatic disease with hematogenous spread to bone and lung, especially once tumors become radioactive iodine refractory, where multi-target kinase inhibitors offer progression control but limited overall survival and quality-of-life benefit with substantial, dose-limiting toxicity and resistance. A key frontier is biomarker-guided redifferentiation to restore iodine sensitivity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Overall-survival–improving systemic therapy for metastatic radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer (incl. follicular)
- Better-tolerated alternatives to chronic VEGFR/MKI therapy that reduce hypertension/proteinuria-driven dose modification and discontinuation
- Biomarker-directed short-course redifferentiation to restore actionable radioiodine uptake (e.g., MAPK-pathway targeting in RAS-pathway tumors) to enable therapeutic I-131 vs indefinite MKI exposure

name: Glycine encephalopathy
description: Glycine encephalopathy (nonketotic hyperglycinemia) is a rare autosomal recessive defect of the glycine cleavage system that causes toxic glycine buildup in the brain, often presenting in the first days of life with lethargy progressing to coma, profound hypotonia, myoclonic seizures, and life threatening apnea. Care today is largely symptomatic, using glycine lowering (for example sodium benzoate) and N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonists, but severe cases still progress to profound developmental disability and intractable epilepsy. The key unmet need is early started disease modifying therapy that changes the natural history.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early disease-modifying GLDC/AMT restoration (liver + CNS) for severe neonatal NKH to prevent irreversible neurodevelopmental injury.
- Safer glycine-lowering therapy with wider therapeutic window than high-dose sodium benzoate (reduced toxicity/monitoring burden).
- More effective and safer control of CNS excitotoxicity/intractable epilepsy in severe NKH beyond current NMDA antagonists/polypharmacy ASMs.

name: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency
description: Ultra-rare autosomal recessive gluconeogenesis disorder causing fasting or illness triggered crises of ketotic hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis that can lead to apnea, seizures, or coma. Patients are usually well between episodes but require strict avoidance of prolonged fasting, frequent carbohydrate intake, and rapid access to rescue glucose, with severe episodes needing intravenous dextrose and sometimes bicarbonate, creating high caregiver burden and limited disease-modifying options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- FBPase restoration therapy (gene/mRNA/enzyme replacement) to enable safe overnight fasting beyond the current ~8–10h fasting limit.
- Standardized at-home “sick day” rescue product triggered by early warning signs (e.g., ketonuria) to abort crises and avoid hospital IV dextrose ± bicarbonate.
- Long-acting oral prophylactic extended-release glucose polymer to reduce frequent feeding during illness and simplify/standardize dietary management (incl. uncertainty around sucrose/fructose restriction and cornstarch use).

name: Glycogen storage disease | type 1
description: Inherited glycogen metabolism disorder causing glycogen buildup in liver and kidneys, presenting in early infancy with fasting intolerance and life threatening hypoglycemia plus metabolic derangements. Management relies on strict carbohydrate replacement with uncooked cornstarch and often overnight tube feeding, yet patients still face limited overnight fasting tolerance, progressive liver disease with adenomas that can transform into hepatocellular carcinoma, and in type Ib neutropenia with recurrent infections and inflammatory bowel disease, underscoring the need for durable disease modifying therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Restore ~8-hour overnight fasting tolerance with reliable euglycemia to eliminate middle-of-the-night cornstarch/tube feeds and reduce severe hypoglycemia risk.
- Prevent/treat hepatic adenomas and block malignant transformation to hepatocellular carcinoma.
- In GSD-Ib, mechanism-based correction of neutropenia/neutrophil dysfunction to reduce infections/IBD and lessen reliance on chronic G-CSF injections.

name: Glycogen storage disease | type 9
description: Glycogen storage disease type IX is an inherited phosphorylase kinase deficiency that impairs glycogen breakdown, typically presenting in early childhood with enlarged liver, growth delay, and fasting triggered ketotic hypoglycemia. Management is largely dietary with frequent meals and cornstarch, yet overnight fasting often tops out at 6 to 8 hours, forcing nighttime dosing, sleep disruption, and ongoing risk of hypoglycemia. Despite supportive care, some patients develop liver fibrosis or cirrhosis, and rarer muscle forms cause exercise intolerance and myoglobinuria, underscoring the need for more durable metabolic control and disease modifying options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that extend overnight fasting tolerance beyond ~6–8 hours while maintaining biochemical control (glucose 70–100 mg/dL; βOHB 0.0–0.2 mmol/L), reducing q6h/bedtime/night cornstarch burden and overtreatment toxicities.
- Liver disease–modifying therapy to prevent/reverse progressive hepatic fibrosis/cirrhosis and reduce adenoma/HCC risk (notably in GSD IXc).
- Therapies targeting muscle-involved GSD IX (IXd/PHKA1 and mixed phenotypes) to reduce exercise intolerance/cramps/myoglobinuria and prevent progressive muscle weakness.

name: Fundus albipunctatus
description: Fundus albipunctatus is a rare autosomal recessive retinal disorder, usually due to RDH5 visual cycle dysfunction, causing early night blindness with hours long delayed dark adaptation and characteristic white yellow retinal flecks while daytime vision is often preserved. Some patients later develop macular degeneration with cone loss. Management is largely supportive with no broadly proven disease modifying or vision restoring therapy, leaving a need for treatments that normalize visual cycle biochemistry, improve dark adaptation, and prevent central retinal degeneration.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid, durable reversal of hours-long delayed dark adaptation/night blindness via visual-cycle/RDH5 pathway restoration (e.g., chromophore replacement), measurable by dark adaptometry/scotopic ERG.
- Prevention of progression in the non-stationary subset with cone dysfunction/macular degeneration, preserving photopic function/visual acuity.
- A clinically validated, well-tolerated pharmacologic treatment beyond supportive care (improving on ad-hoc high-dose beta-carotene and stalled Phase 1 retinoid/chromophore approaches).

name: Galactokinase deficiency
description: Galactokinase deficiency (galactosemia type II) is a mild inherited galactose metabolism disorder where galactitol accumulation in the lens causes early bilateral oil droplet cataracts, sometimes with infant feeding difficulty after milk exposure. Care is largely lifelong galactose and lactose restriction with supplements, and late diagnosis can still mean cataract surgery. The key unmet need is a disease modifying option that reduces galactitol and reliance on strict diet, with aldose reductase inhibitors and enzyme restoration approaches (pharmacological chaperones, GALK1 messenger ribonucleic acid) as emerging directions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral aldose-reductase pathway inhibition to suppress lens galactitol and meaningfully liberalize lifelong galactose/lactose restriction while maintaining cataract-free outcomes
- Rapid-acting systemic/ocular pharmacotherapy to reverse or halt cataracts in late-diagnosed infants/children and avoid or reduce cataract surgery
- Long-acting restoration of GALK1 activity (e.g., pharmacologic chaperone or GALK1 mRNA) to normalize biomarkers and eliminate lifelong dietary restriction/monitoring

name: Ganglioneuroma
description: Rare benign, well differentiated neural crest tumor of the sympathetic nervous system, often incidental but can cause compressive or hormone related symptoms; treatment is mainly surgery with no effective chemotherapy, leaving a need for medical options to manage high risk unresectable or residual disease and reduce long surveillance burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neoadjuvant, well-tolerated tumor-shrinking drug therapy (e.g., mTOR-pathway inhibition) for large/encasing ganglioneuromas to reduce tumor size/extent pre-op and lower surgical morbidity.
- Therapies that reliably control hormone-mediated syndromes (e.g., diarrhea and hypertension) in functional ganglioneuroma patients to reduce symptom burden and peri-operative instability.
- Disease-control drugs for patients under observation or after subtotal resection with major residual tumor (>2 cm) to prevent local progression and reduce long-term surveillance/re-operation.

name: Clostridial gas gangrene
description: Clostridial gas gangrene, or clostridial myonecrosis, is a rare, hyperacute necrotizing soft tissue infection that typically follows trauma or surgery, where anaerobic clostridia release gas and potent exotoxins that rapidly destroy muscle and drive systemic toxicity, shock, and organ failure. Treatment is a race against time with urgent surgical exploration and debridement, high dose intravenous antibiotics, and sometimes amputation, yet mortality can be extreme. Key unmet needs are earlier, clearer diagnosis in the initial phase when it mimics necrotizing fasciitis and adjuncts that neutralize toxins to reduce death and limb loss.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Up-front exotoxin neutralization (e.g., anti-toxin mAbs/inhibitors/decoy peptides) to prevent early toxin-driven septic shock/death.
- Rapid bacterial-load reduction in devitalized/anaerobic muscle (e.g., phage or other fast-acting modalities) to slow 24-hour progression and reduce amputations/extensive debridement.
- Broad-spectrum ICU empiric regimens that maintain coverage while lowering AKI risk vs vancomycin+piperacillin/tazobactam and lowering CDI risk vs clindamycin-containing therapy.

name: Germinoma
description: Ultra-orphan midline brain tumor of adolescents, typically in the suprasellar or pineal region, presenting with diabetes insipidus and endocrine deficits or with hydrocephalus symptoms like headache, nausea, diplopia and Parinaud syndrome. Cure is usually achieved with chemotherapy plus radiotherapy, but survivorship is dominated by permanent endocrinopathies and radiation related neurocognitive and vascular toxicity, second tumors, and late recurrence risk. The key unmet need is maintaining high cure rates while de escalating radiation dose and field to reduce lifelong morbidity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Radiation-sparing systemic therapy for localized pediatric/AYA CNS germinoma that preserves ~95% 3-year PFS/EFS while reducing long-term endocrine/vascular/neurocognitive/second-cancer toxicities.
- CNS-penetrant therapies for disseminated CNS germinoma that avoid craniospinal irradiation while maintaining cure rates and lowering late radiation toxicities.
- Less-toxic, effective salvage therapies for recurrent/relapsed CNS germinoma that reduce reliance on high-dose chemotherapy with autologous stem-cell rescue ± additional radiation.

name: Choriocarcinoma | gestational
description: Gestational choriocarcinoma is a fast growing uterine cancer that arises after pregnancy, often presenting with persistent abnormal vaginal bleeding and markedly elevated human chorionic gonadotropin, and can rapidly metastasize to the lungs or brain with pulmonary or neurologic symptoms. Chemotherapy cures most patients, but around one in five high risk cases fail first line multi agent regimens and treatment can carry long term toxicity including early menopause and secondary leukemia risk. Key needs include more durable options for resistant disease, such as immunotherapy, and less visit intensive monitoring that preserves cure rates.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Immunotherapy (± combinations) that delivers sustained β‑hCG normalization enabling discontinuation in the ~25–30% chemo-/polychemotherapy‑resistant high‑risk GTN.
- Chemo‑sparing, non‑genotoxic alternatives to etoposide‑containing multi‑agent regimens (e.g., EMA‑CO) that reduce premature menopause and secondary leukemia risk.
- Regimens that reduce the q14‑day EMA‑CO visit intensity and prolonged β‑hCG monitoring/consolidation cycles, including chemo‑avoidance strategies in selected patients.

name: Giant cell reparative granuloma
description: Benign but locally aggressive osteolytic jaw lesion (usually mandible) in mostly young, often female patients, causing painless swelling and facial asymmetry; key unmet needs are less mutilating options for aggressive pediatric disease, lower-burden conservative therapy, and safer antiresorptives given rebound hypercalcemia and jaw osteonecrosis risks with denosumab, alongside sparse prospective evidence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjuvant/neoadjuvant therapy to reduce high post-curettage recurrence in aggressive jaw CGCG while avoiding morbid radical surgery (tissue/tooth loss).
- Pediatric-safe denosumab/bisphosphonate alternative that controls lesions without rebound hypercalcemia, MRONJ risk, or long skeletal retention.
- Low-burden systemic/long-acting option that avoids multiple weekly intralesional injections and prolonged high-compliance regimens while maintaining low recurrence.

name: Gingival fibromatosis
description: Gingival fibromatosis is a rare, often inherited disorder of slowly progressive collagen rich gum overgrowth that can cover teeth and cause chewing, speech, occlusion, esthetic, and psychosocial problems, typically presenting around tooth eruption in childhood. Care is largely invasive gum surgery, but recurrence is common at about 33.85 percent after gingivectomy, creating demand for durable, noninvasive, mechanism based therapies for genetic forms such as those linked to SOS1 variants.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical (or post‑gingivectomy adjunct) therapy that prevents recurrent gingival overgrowth and reduces high post‑surgery recurrence (~34.92%).
- Pediatric disease-control therapy that reduces gingival tissue enough to allow normal tooth emergence and improves speech/chewing function.
- Genotype-/mechanism-directed therapy for SOS1‑driven hereditary gingival fibromatosis that counteracts the overactive growth signal to stop gingival cell proliferation.

name: Glucose-galactose malabsorption
description: Rare inherited SLC5A1 (sodium glucose cotransporter 1) defect causing neonatal onset, feed triggered glucose and galactose malabsorption with severe watery diarrhea, dehydration, weight loss, and metabolic acidosis that can be life threatening. Care is strict lifelong avoidance of glucose, galactose, and lactose using fructose based formulas, but adherence becomes harder with age and accidental exposure triggers immediate relapse. Unmet needs include safer, less burdensome disease control, rapid rescue options during exposures, and disease modifying approaches that restore transporter function and prevent chronic dehydration complications such as kidney stones.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable SGLT1 (SLC5A1) functional restoration enabling neonates to tolerate breast milk/standard formula without life-threatening diarrhea/dehydration relapse
- On-demand oral “rescue” therapy to rapidly stop diarrhea after accidental glucose/galactose/lactose exposure and avoid feed cessation/IV-level care
- Long-term adjunct therapy to reduce reliance on extreme fructose-centered high-fat/high-protein diets while lowering dehydration and renal-complication risk (nephrocalcinosis/kidney stones)

name: Glycogen storage disease | type 6
description: Glycogen storage disease type VI (Hers disease) is an ultra rare inherited liver glycogen breakdown disorder starting in infancy or early childhood with hepatomegaly, fasting intolerance, and ketotic hypoglycemia with slowed growth. Care is largely intensive dietary management with frequent meals and repeated cornstarch dosing including bedtime doses, yet many patients still face hepatic fibrosis risk and bone complications with imperfect metabolic control. The key unmet need is longer acting metabolic stabilization and liver directed disease modifying options such as gene or messenger RNA based approaches to prevent progression and reduce treatment burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Long-acting therapy to maintain overnight metabolic stability (glucose 75–100 mg/dL; β-hydroxybutyrate ≤0.3 mmol/L) in infants/toddlers (<5y) without middle-of-night feeds/cornstarch.
- Hepatocyte-directed PYGL restoration and/or anti-fibrotic therapy to prevent/slow early hepatic fibrosis and reduce adenoma/HCC risk.
- Ketosis/acidosis-reducing therapy (esp. during illness/stress in young children) to prevent growth delay and osteopenia/osteoporosis beyond diet titration.

name: Granulomatous endometritis
description: Granulomatous endometritis is a chronic inflammatory injury of the uterine lining, often driven by genital tuberculosis in endemic settings and typically discovered during infertility or secondary amenorrhea workups. Symptoms can be subtle, including pelvic discomfort, spotting, and vaginal discharge, so diagnosis is often delayed. Even after standard six month multidrug tuberculosis therapy, endometrial damage may progress to scarring with intrauterine adhesions and Asherman syndrome that may not improve in higher grade disease, leaving persistent infertility. Treatment also carries toxicity and monitoring burdens, notably liver and vision monitoring, underscoring the need for safer, shorter regimens and approaches that prevent or reverse fibrosis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Anti‑fibrotic/regenerative therapies to reverse tuberculous endometritis–driven intrauterine adhesions/Asherman’s syndrome (especially higher‑grade adhesions nonresponsive to ATT) and restore fertility.
- Host‑directed anti‑inflammatory/immunomodulatory adjuncts to improve endometrial receptivity and raise pregnancy outcomes beyond ATT‑only.
- Shorter‑course, lower‑toxicity anti‑mycobacterial regimens for genital TB (incl. MDR) to reduce duration and hepatotoxicity/ocular‑toxicity monitoring burden.

name: Granulomatous myositis
description: Granulomatous myositis is a rare, biopsy defined inflammatory myopathy with non caseating granulomas, often linked to systemic sarcoidosis, typically affecting midlife to older women with proximal weakness and sometimes dysphagia. Management relies on prolonged corticosteroids and other immunosuppression, but relapse is common and steroid toxicity accumulates, with some patients progressing to severe disability especially with distal weakness and amyotrophy. Normal creatine kinase in chronic disease can delay recognition and complicate monitoring, reinforcing the need for durable steroid sparing disease control and better ways to track and prevent functional decline.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Relapse-free maintenance of muscle response after initial corticosteroid improvement
- Therapies that prevent/slow progression to severe disability in the “severe GM” phenotype (notably distal weakness + amyotrophy)
- Steroid-sparing, lower-toxicity and more convenient regimens that keep prednisone <10–15 mg/day and reduce reliance on infusion anti-TNF

name: Guanidinoacetate methyltransferase deficiency
description: Guanidinoacetate methyltransferase deficiency is a rare inherited creatine synthesis disorder affecting brain and muscle, typically presenting in infancy to early childhood with developmental delay, severe expressive language impairment, and often intractable seizures. Treatment is lifelong multi dose oral creatine plus ornithine and sometimes arginine restriction, which can improve seizures and behavior but cannot reverse established neurocognitive injury from delayed diagnosis. The key unmet needs are presymptomatic detection and durable central nervous system restoration that goes beyond supplementation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- One-time/infrequent CNS-targeted GAMT enzyme restoration to normalize creatine and GAA, replacing chronic supplement/diet regimens
