- Drug approaches that reduce neurogenic dysphagia/aspiration and failure-to-thrive enough to avoid long-term tube feeding/gastrostomy dependence.
- Genotype-targeted (ideally prenatal/very-early) therapies for NDE1-related microlissencephaly/LIS4 to address underlying neurodevelopmental mechanisms.

name: Cholesterol granuloma
description: Cholesterol granuloma is an expansile cystic inflammatory lesion in aerated temporal bone spaces, most often the petrous apex, driven by hemorrhage and outflow obstruction that leave blood products provoking chronic granulomatous inflammation and bony erosion. Patients may be incidental findings or present with hearing loss and a blue tympanic membrane, and petrous apex disease can add tinnitus, vertigo, headache, or cranial nerve deficits. Management is observation when asymptomatic or surgical drainage with stenting, but drainage pathways often re-obstruct from bony regrowth and fibrous blockage, leading to recurrence and repeat procedures.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical medical therapy achieving MRI-documented petrous apex cholesterol granuloma shrinkage with symptomatic improvement (e.g., headache/cranial neuropathies)
- Adjunct local anti-inflammatory/anti-restenosis drug delivery post-drainage to maintain patency and reduce recurrence/re-operation
- Prophylactic/maintenance medical option for “wait-and-scan” patients to prevent lesion growth/symptom conversion and reduce long-term serial MRI surveillance

name: Mitochondrial trifunctional protein deficiency
description: Mitochondrial trifunctional protein deficiency is a rare inherited long chain fatty acid oxidation disorder in which infants can decompensate during fasting or common infections, causing hypoketotic hypoglycemia, liver dysfunction, encephalopathy, cardiomyopathy, coma, and sudden death. Survivors often accrue chronic neuropathy and retinopathy with episodic rhabdomyolysis and multisystem injury. Care is largely preventive and burdensome, centered on strict avoidance of fasting, frequent feeds, and medium chain triglycerides or triheptanoin, which requires multiple daily doses and is limited by gastrointestinal side effects, leaving a need for simpler, more tolerable metabolic protection and disease modifying therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prevent fasting/illness–precipitated hypoketotic hypoglycemia/metabolic acidosis in neonatal–infantile MTP deficiency (reduce dependence on strict “no-missed-meals” management)
- Modify long-term disease to prevent peripheral polyneuropathy/pigmentary retinopathy and reduce episodic rhabdomyolysis (and respiratory failure) in later-onset survivors
- Improve on triheptanoin with markedly better GI tolerability and simpler dosing than ≥4 doses/day mixed into food

name: Monilethrix
description: Monilethrix is a rare inherited hair shaft disorder with infant onset, where structurally abnormal beaded hairs narrow and break, causing short sparse scalp hair and patchy alopecia often with follicular keratosis. Most cases are due to keratin or desmoglein 4 gene mutations, but care is largely supportive because there is no established disease modifying therapy. Evidence for treatments such as topical minoxidil or retinoids is limited to isolated reports, with relapse after stopping retinoids, leaving a need for safe pediatric therapies that durably reduce breakage and ultimately follicle targeted genetic approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-directed follicle-targeted gene replacement/editing/allele silencing for monilethrix patients with *KRT81/KRT83/KRT86* (AD) or *DSG4* (AR) mutations.
- Pediatric-first topical therapy with proven improvements in hair density and reduced shaft fragility/breakage vs limited non-RCT minoxidil evidence.
- Safer, durable therapy for severe alopecia with hyperkeratosis/keratosis pilaris to avoid long-course systemic retinoid tolerability issues and relapse after discontinuation.

name: Mpox
description: Mpox is a close contact transmitted orthopoxvirus infection driving a global clade II outbreak since May 2022, disproportionately affecting gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men. It typically causes painful vesiculopustular skin and mucosal lesions often anogenital, sometimes with proctitis, lasting 2 to 4 weeks and severe pain can prompt hospitalization. Current antivirals are operationally imperfect, leaving unmet need for faster lesion healing, rapid pain relief, and more reliable viral clearance especially for immunocompromised patients.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapy that shortens lesion/mucosal healing time and rapidly reduces severe anogenital/proctitis pain
- High-barrier-to-resistance regimen for severely immunocompromised/protracted or life-threatening mpox (e.g., advanced HIV) achieving durable viral clearance
- Safer, simpler outpatient option/formulation that avoids tecovirimat’s high-fat meal requirement and reliance on cidofovir/brincidofovir

name: Cystadenocarcinoma | mucinous
description: Rare epithelial ovarian cancer subtype (2–3% of new ovarian cancers), often in women under 40, presenting with a large mucus producing ovarian mass causing bloating and pain. Most cases are diagnosed at stage 1 with good prognosis, but advanced or recurrent disease responds poorly to standard chemotherapy (12–35% response) and lacks clear systemic guidelines, creating demand for chemo sparing precision options especially for tumors with KRAS mutations or HER2 amplification.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Chemo-sparing systemic therapy that improves outcomes in advanced/recurrent primary mucinous ovarian carcinoma despite platinum/taxane resistance while reducing IV chemotherapy toxicity burden.
- HER2/ERBB2-directed therapy (e.g., trastuzumab-based regimens/maintenance or HER2 ADCs) for the ERBB2-amplified mucinous ovarian carcinoma subset (~20–38%) to achieve durable remission.
- RAS/MAPK-pathway precision therapy for KRAS/RAS-altered mucinous ovarian carcinoma (KRAS mutations ~40–65%) to deliver superior ORR/PFS versus empiric chemotherapy.

name: Mucolipidosis II alpha/beta
description: Mucolipidosis II alpha/beta (I-cell disease) is a severe early-onset lysosomal storage disorder caused by GNPTAB-related failure of mannose 6 phosphate enzyme tagging, leading to multisystem substrate accumulation. Newborns present with hypotonia, weak cry, growth failure, dysmorphic features, progressive skeletal disease, airway narrowing, and cardiac valve insufficiency, with most children dying in early childhood. Treatment is supportive only, leaving an acute unmet need for safe neonatal disease-modifying therapy that reaches bone and cardiopulmonary connective tissue; exploratory efforts have included hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neonatal/early-infant systemic GNPTAB-restoring therapy that safely extends survival beyond current natural history.
- Bone/cartilage-penetrant disease modification to prevent/reverse osteopenia and dysostosis multiplex and preserve ambulation.
- Cardio‑airway/connective-tissue control to prevent airway narrowing and mitral/aortic valve insufficiency and reduce respiratory-insufficiency deaths/anesthesia risk.

name: Mucolipidosis III alpha/beta
description: Rare GNPTAB related lysosomal storage disorder with gradual onset around age 3 causing progressive skeletal disease including growth slowing, joint contractures, painful hip degeneration, osteoporosis and worsening bone pain often initially mistaken for rheumatologic disease. No curative or disease modifying therapy exists so care is supportive with physical therapy, orthopedic procedures, analgesics and intravenous bisphosphonates such as pamidronate. The key unmet need is treatment that restores lysosomal enzyme targeting to prevent irreversible joint destruction and preserve mobility.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease‑modifying GNPTAB‑restoring therapy (e.g., gene/mRNA) to correct the upstream lysosomal trafficking defect vs supportive-only care
- Therapy to prevent progressive joint destruction/contractures, preserving mobility and reducing need for repeat orthopedic surgeries
- Safer, lower‑burden osteoporosis/bone therapy that meaningfully reduces severe bone pain and improves mobility/BMD vs intermittent long IV bisphosphonate infusions

name: Mucolipidosis III gamma
description: Mucolipidosis III gamma is a slowly progressive genetic lysosomal storage disorder caused by GNPTG mutations that impair mannose-6-phosphate enzyme targeting, leading to lysosomal macromolecule accumulation. Symptoms typically begin around age 3 with short stature and joint stiffness, then progress to osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, chronic pain, and major functional disability. Current management is symptomatic and supportive, and there is no cure or disease-modifying therapy to prevent progressive joint and mobility decline.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Joint-mobility–preserving therapy for early-childhood ML IIIγ to maintain/improve ROM and slow progression to functional impairment.
- Safer long-term bone + pain disease-control therapy that reduces osteoporosis-related fracture risk and progressive pain without bisphosphonate-associated femoral fractures.
- Hip/joint-structure–preserving therapy to prevent rapidly progressive osteoarthritis/cartilage destruction and delay/avoid total hip replacement.

name: Multiple sulfatase deficiency
description: Multiple sulfatase deficiency is an ultra rare inherited lysosomal storage disorder caused by SUMF1 mutations that prevent activation of multiple sulfatases, leading to toxic substrate buildup and progressive neurodevelopmental regression plus seizures and movement problems with multisystem disease affecting skin and skeleton including ichthyosis, coarse facies, hepatosplenomegaly, and skeletal abnormalities. Care is largely supportive with no approved therapy that reverses or meaningfully slows progression, making early diagnosis and disease modifying approaches that reach the brain a central unmet need.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Presymptomatic (infant) CNS + systemic SUMF1 restoration to preserve ambulation and verbal development with a single-administration disease-modifying therapy
- Disease-modifying therapy with measurable CNS benefit even when initiated after symptom onset, via scalable delivery (e.g., intrathecal/CSF ± systemic dosing)
- Genotype-tailored small-molecule FGE stabilizers/chaperones for non-null (residual FGE expression) patients to raise sulfatase activity and reduce storage burden

name: Multiple endocrine neoplasia | type 2B
description: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B is a RET driven syndrome marked by early mucosal neuromas, alacrima, and gastrointestinal ganglioneuromatosis alongside aggressive infant onset medullary thyroid carcinoma and frequent pheochromocytoma. Because many cases arise de novo, recognition is often delayed despite early bowel symptoms, yet cure hinges on thyroidectomy in the first year of life before rapid metastatic spread. For metastatic disease, kinase inhibitors including selective RET inhibitors can control tumors, but toxicity, quality of life tradeoffs, and emerging drug resistance limit durability.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Resistance-robust RET-directed regimens for metastatic MEN2B/RET-mutant MTC that deliver deeper/durable responses (higher CR) and retain activity vs solvent-front resistance (e.g., RET G810).
- Long-term systemic options with materially improved safety/convenience vs current TKIs (reduced QT/perforation/hemorrhage risks and intensive monitoring), especially suitable for chronic/pediatric use.
- Therapies that directly treat MEN2B diffuse GI ganglioneuromatosis (infant-onset constipation/diarrhea/megacolon) rather than supportive care alone.

name: Biotinidase deficiency
description: Biotinidase deficiency is an inherited failure to recycle biotin that, without treatment, can cause early onset neurologic and multisystem complications including seizures, hypotonia, breathing problems, rashes, alopecia, and hearing or vision loss. Most patients are identified presymptomatically via newborn screening and do well on lifelong biotin, but missed or late diagnosis can leave irreversible optic and hearing damage. Chronic high dose biotin also interferes with some laboratory assays such as troponin, creating safety and workflow risk and motivating enzyme restoring and biotin sparing approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- One-time restoration of biotinidase activity (e.g., gene therapy/ERT) to eliminate lifelong biotin dependence and adherence-related relapse
- Neuro/sensory “rescue” for late-diagnosed symptomatic patients to prevent/reverse optic atrophy, hearing loss, and developmental delay that persist despite biotin
- Biotin-sparing regimens that maintain metabolic control while avoiding biotin–streptavidin lab-test interference (e.g., troponin immunoassays)

name: Multiple synostoses syndrome
description: Ultra-rare autosomal dominant childhood-onset developmental bone disorder where excess bone morphogenetic protein signaling drives progressive joint fusions from fingers and toes into larger joints, often with conductive hearing loss from stapes fixation. Care is largely surgical and supportive because there is no medical way to treat ankylosis, leaving major unmet need for disease-modifying approaches that prevent new fusions, preserve mobility and quality of life, and protect hearing beyond stapes surgery and hearing aids.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-life BMP-pathway modulation to prevent progressive multi-joint ankylosis/synostosis (preserve ROM/hand function and prevent new radiographic fusions)
- Therapy to prevent/reverse stapes-fixation hearing loss (improve air–bone gap/conductive thresholds)
- Anti-fusion strategy for hindfoot/subtalar synostosis to prevent rigid varus/valgus deformity and childhood pain/instability (delay/avoid arthrodesis; improve gait)

name: Multisystem proteinopathy
description: Multisystem proteinopathy, often VCP associated, is a rare inherited disorder of impaired protein degradation that causes progressive adult onset muscle weakness with loss of mobility and possible respiratory failure, plus Paget bone disease in about half and frontotemporal dementia in about one third that can end in loss of speech and self care. Care is largely symptomatic, with bisphosphonates easing bone pain but no therapies that meaningfully slow or reverse neuromuscular decline or neurodegeneration, leaving a premium on disease modifying treatments that preserve function across muscle, brain, and bone.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- VCP-targeted disease-modifying therapy to slow limb-girdle weakness and delay loss of ambulation/wheelchair dependence and respiratory involvement
- FTD-modifying therapy to prevent/slow rapidly progressive behavioral/executive/language decline in the ~30% who develop FTD
- Safer non-bisphosphonate option for Paget bone disease in patients who can’t take bisphosphonates, avoiding calcitonin long-term cancer-risk concerns while controlling bone pain

name: Oculocerebrorenal syndrome
description: Lowe syndrome is a rare X-linked disorder affecting the eyes, brain, and kidneys, usually in males, beginning in infancy with congenital cataracts often followed by glaucoma, hypotonia, and developmental impairment. Renal Fanconi syndrome causes polyuria, dehydration, metabolic acidosis, electrolyte wasting, poor growth, and rickets, with progressive decline to end-stage renal disease. Management is intensive but supportive, relying on eye procedures and chronic alkali, phosphate, and vitamin D supplementation, without a curative option. The key unmet need is disease-modifying therapy that preserves renal function, vision, and neurodevelopment, with gene therapy and kidney-directed approaches emerging.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Kidney/proximal-tubule restorative therapy to correct Fanconi dysfunction and delay CKD→ESRD, reducing chronic electrolyte/phosphate/calcitriol supplementation burden
- Vision-preserving therapy to prevent/control severe early infantile glaucoma (in boys with congenital cataracts) and reduce need for repeated procedures
- Early-life neuromuscular/neurodevelopment therapy to improve neonatal hypotonia–related feeding/respiratory dysfunction and reduce tube-feeding dependence

name: Myoepithelioma
description: Rare salivary gland tumor (usually benign) presenting as a slow growing painless parotid or palate mass in midlife; treatment is surgical but constrained by facial nerve morbidity and recurrence if margins are inadequate. Malignant myoepithelial carcinoma often recurs and can metastasize, and advanced disease lacks effective systemic options, creating need for better local control and biomarker guided therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neoadjuvant/local drug therapy to shrink tumors pre-op and enable less-morbid nerve‑sparing parotid surgery.
- Adjuvant/locoregional pharmacotherapy to prevent local recurrence in margin‑positive or recurrent/persistent tumors.
- Biomarker-driven systemic therapy for unresectable/recurrent/metastatic myoepithelial carcinoma to improve durable responses (e.g., RECIST/PFS).

name: Myofibrillar myopathy
description: Myofibrillar myopathy is a genetically heterogeneous, usually adult onset progressive muscle disease marked by myofibril breakdown and toxic protein aggregates, often starting with distal weakness and progressing to pain and neuropathy. Beyond loss of mobility, cardiomyopathy with arrhythmias and respiratory muscle failure can drive disability and mortality. Care is largely supportive with rehabilitation, assistive devices, and cardiac and respiratory monitoring and interventions, but there are no curative or disease modifying therapies, creating a premium for subtype specific treatments that slow progression and protect heart and lung function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Skeletal-muscle disease-modifying therapy targeting myofibril disintegration/protein inclusions to delay functional decline (e.g., gait-aid/wheelchair milestones), especially in high-burden subtypes like DES/desminopathy.
- MFM-directed cardioprotective/anti-arrhythmic therapy to prevent arrhythmias/conduction defects/cardiomyopathy-related deaths beyond standard heart-failure medications.
- Therapy to preserve respiratory-muscle function and prevent progression to respiratory failure in patients developing respiratory involvement within years of onset.

name: Myofibroma
description: Myofibroma or infantile myofibromatosis is a rare tumor of infancy that typically presents at birth or in the first two years as firm, painless skin or soft tissue nodules that often regress spontaneously. The high stakes cases are multicentric or visceral disease, where organ compression can cause cardiopulmonary or gastrointestinal failure and high mortality without therapy. Management ranges from observation to systemic treatment, but current regimens often rely on cytotoxic pediatric chemotherapy with significant toxicity in neonates. A key unmet need is safer, biomarker guided targeted options such as kinase inhibition in actionable platelet derived growth factor receptor beta or RET altered disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Low-toxicity systemic therapy to rapidly debulk neonatal/infant multicentric/visceral disease (organ-compression risk), avoiding high-morbidity surgery/chemotherapy and with clear benefit beyond spontaneous regression uncertainty
- Prospective, molecularly guided PDGFRB-pathway inhibition (oral pediatric TKI) for PDGFRB gain-of-function/rearranged disease to drive objective regression while avoiding cytotoxic chemotherapy
- Biomarker-defined RET-altered infantile myofibromatosis treated with an oral selective RET inhibitor (e.g., selpercatinib), differentiated by RECIST-based ORR and pediatric dosing feasibility (≥6 months)

name: Myositis ossificans
description: Rare post traumatic heterotopic bone formation within injured muscle, typically in young athletic males, causing a painful hard mass and reduced range of motion weeks after a contusion; care is largely rest, physical therapy and nonsteroidal anti inflammatory drugs with delayed surgical excision for refractory cases, leaving unmet need for reliable post injury prevention and non surgical reversal of established lesions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course prophylaxis (ideally local) for high-risk severe muscle contusions/large intramuscular hematomas with early ROM loss (e.g., knee flexion <120°) to prevent MO.
- Non-surgical “de-ossification” therapy for symptomatic lesions (intractable pain, neurovascular compression, functional limitation) to shrink heterotopic bone and restore ROM.
- NSAID-sparing outpatient/home-usable pain/anti-inflammatory control to avoid prolonged systemic NSAID exposure.

name: Ependymoma | myxopapillary (WHO Grade 2)
description: Myxopapillary ependymoma is a rare, slow growing glial tumor of the lower spine that often presents in adults after months or years of low back and radicular pain, with weakness and bowel or bladder dysfunction as nerve roots become compressed. Despite surgery and radiation, recurrence and leptomeningeal spread remain meaningful risks, driving lifelong imaging surveillance and repeat interventions. When disease returns or disseminates, systemic salvage options are limited and only modestly durable, leaving a premium on safer, more effective disease modifying therapies that improve local control and reduce neuraxis wide progression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjuvant post-op systemic therapy for high-recurrence surgical subgroups (capsular violation or STR/piecemeal resection) to improve long-term control.
- CSF/neuraxis-penetrant systemic therapy for disseminated disease to reduce dependence on craniospinal/whole-spine irradiation and prolonged neuraxis surveillance.
- More effective, safer systemic salvage than temozolomide + lapatinib to extend disease control beyond ~8 months and reduce serious toxicity.
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus URL; relevant pages: https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001403.htm; https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/007222.htm

name: Necrotizing fasciitis
description: Rare, rapidly progressive bacterial infection that destroys deep soft tissue and can mimic cellulitis early but causes severe pain out of proportion; within 24 to 48 hours can progress to gangrene, sepsis, shock, organ failure, and death. Treatment requires urgent intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics plus aggressive surgical debridement, yet devitalized tissue limits antibiotic penetration. Key unmet needs are faster early diagnosis, toxin targeted adjuncts, perfusion independent or local anti infectives, and safer broad coverage options that reduce acute kidney injury risk while maintaining methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus and polymicrobial coverage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunctive anti-toxin/host-response therapy for ICU-level NSTI to improve Day-28 survival and organ-failure recovery
- Perfusion-independent or locally delivered anti-infective adjuncts to cut repeat debridements and prevent post–first-debridement amputations
- Broad-spectrum regimens that maintain MRSA/polymicrobial coverage while reducing AKI risk (e.g., vanc + pip/tazo) and C. difficile colitis risk (e.g., clindamycin)

name: Necrotizing sialometaplasia
description: Necrotizing sialometaplasia is a rare, benign, self-limited ischemic injury of minor salivary glands that presents as a painful posterior palatal ulcer and often mimics oral cancer, driving biopsy and occasional overtreatment. Lesions typically heal over 4 to 10 weeks with supportive care, so key gaps are better diagnostic certainty to avoid unnecessary surgery and workups, plus improved local pain control and pro-healing options to shorten recovery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid topical/local analgesia to control intense palatal pain/odynophagia during ulcer formation
- Locally delivered pro-healing therapy to achieve complete mucosal healing in ≤2 weeks (vs ~3–12 weeks natural course), including severe cases with palatal perforation/large defects
- Mechanism-based anti-inflammatory/pro-resolution therapy with proven clinical benefit to replace empiric antibiotics/corticosteroids (no established active-treatment protocol)

name: Nemaline myopathy
description: Nemaline myopathy is a rare inherited skeletal muscle disorder marked by nemaline bodies and diffuse weakness, often worst in the face, neck, trunk, and proximal limbs, with feeding, swallowing, and sometimes life threatening respiratory failure. Care is supportive only, commonly requiring ventilation for hypoventilation and tube feeding, and the biggest unmet need is disease modifying therapy that restores thin filament muscle biology to preserve bulbar and breathing function, the main drivers of morbidity and mortality.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-targeted restoration of sarcomere/thin-filament function in high-prevalence NM subtypes (esp. NEB-related mini‑nebulin/protein-stitching approaches; ACTA1 universal AAV) to drive objective motor/strength gains (e.g., MFM32, 6MWT).
- Therapies that prevent/reverse nocturnal hypoventilation (hypercapnia) and reduce dependence on home NIV/mechanical ventilation, including in patients with minimal limb weakness.
- Bulbar/swallowing therapies that reduce aspiration/pneumonia and eliminate persistent dysphagia to avoid long-term gastrostomy/tube feeding.

name: Diabetes mellitus | neonatal
description: Rare, usually genetic diabetes presenting in the first 6 months of life with severe hyperglycemia, dehydration, and poor growth. Some forms are transient and resolve by ~18 months, others are lifelong. Treatment is highly genotype dependent; some infants can switch from insulin injections to oral sulfonylureas, but many still face delayed genetic diagnosis, limited options for nonresponders, and persistent neurologic comorbidity such as developmental delay and epilepsy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Infant-optimized, precisely titratable oral sulfonylurea formulations (e.g., glibenclamide liquid micro-dosing) for KCNJ11/ABCC8 neonatal diabetes to replace insulin injections while maintaining HbA1c control and minimizing hypoglycemia during transfer/remission
- Non-insulin, genotype-specific therapies for INS-mutation (and other insulin-requiring) permanent neonatal diabetes to avoid neonatal insulin dosing/feeding-variability hypoglycemia risk while providing stable glycemic control
- Neurodevelopment-targeted treatments for KCNJ11/ABCC8 neonatal diabetes with DEND-spectrum neurologic phenotypes to improve developmental/epilepsy outcomes beyond glycemia, including in sulfonylurea non-responders

name: Myasthenia gravis | neonatal
description: Transient neonatal weakness in infants of mothers with myasthenia gravis, caused by placental transfer of maternal autoantibodies that impair neuromuscular junction signaling. Presents 3 to 72 hours after birth with poor feeding, weak cry, hypotonia, facial and bulbar weakness and sometimes respiratory distress requiring intensive support. Most recover within weeks, but the course is hard to predict, driving 48 to 72 hour inpatient observation and disruption to breastfeeding. Key unmet needs are better risk prediction and preventive or faster antibody clearing approaches that reduce neonatal intensive care use and enable earlier safe discharge.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid maternal-IgG neutralization/clearance to prevent progression to severe neonatal respiratory weakness and reduce need for mechanical ventilation
- Bulbar-strength restoration to normalize suck/swallow, avoid gavage/tube feeding, and prevent breastfeeding failure
- Peripartum prophylaxis/early-acting therapy to enable safe early discharge and eliminate ≥48–72h (often ≥3 days) routine in-hospital observation

name: Neonatal thyrotoxicosis
description: Rare, potentially life-threatening neonatal hyperthyroidism, usually transient from transplacental thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibodies in maternal Graves disease, presenting in the first days to weeks with tachycardia, irritability, feeding problems, and poor weight gain and risking arrhythmias and heart failure if control is delayed. Care is monitoring intensive with frequent thyroid labs plus methimazole and beta blockers, sometimes iodine or glucocorticoids, largely bridging infants through a 2 to 3 month antibody clearance window; unmet needs include faster stabilization, reduced intensive monitoring burden, and mechanism based receptor blockade for rare permanent activating receptor mutation cases.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Same‑day control of severe neonatal thyrotoxicosis to prevent tachycardia/arrhythmia/heart‑failure complications.
- TRAb (IgG) neutralization/depletion for high‑TRAb at‑risk neonates (or late‑pregnancy prophylaxis) to shorten disease duration and reduce intensive monitoring.
- Targeted therapy (e.g., TSHR antagonists/inverse agonists) for permanent non‑autoimmune congenital hyperthyroidism due to activating TSHR mutations, avoiding lifelong thionamides/ablation.

name: Adenoma | nephrogenic
description: Nephrogenic adenoma is a rare, benign bladder lesion that arises after chronic urothelial irritation, often in older men with catheterization or recurrent urinary tract infections, causing irritative urinary symptoms and hematuria and frequently mimicking malignancy. Care is usually transurethral resection, but recurrence is common (reported 37% to 88%) and there are no clear management or follow-up guidelines, creating a need for durable post-procedure strategies that reduce recurrence and repeated procedures when the underlying irritation persists.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Post‑TUR maintenance therapy that materially lowers nephrogenic adenoma bladder recurrence below the reported 37%–88% range.
- Intravesical/medical non‑surgical eradication option for diffuse/multifocal disease to avoid repeated fulgurations/endoscopic procedures.
- Preventive or regressive therapy for high‑risk ongoing‑injury populations (e.g., chronic catheterization/recurrent UTI, renal‑transplant/immunosuppressed) when drivers can’t be removed.

name: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
description: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is a rare kidney water balance disorder where renal tubules resist vasopressin, driving extreme polyuria and chronic thirst with high dehydration and hypernatremia risk. Congenital disease needs lifelong management and acquired disease is often lithium related and may be slow to reverse or irreversible. Care remains largely symptomatic with low sodium diet, thiazides, and sometimes indomethacin or amiloride, so the major unmet need is disease modifying therapy that restores urine concentrating capacity by bypassing receptor signaling and improving downstream water channel function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Targeted therapy for X‑linked congenital NDI (AVPR2/V2R mutations) that meaningfully increases urine osmolality and reduces 24‑h urine volume to lower hypernatraemic dehydration risk (esp. infants).
- Kidney‑sparing therapy for lithium‑induced NDI that reverses the urine‑concentrating defect and reduces polyuria/nocturia/thirst without amiloride‑associated hyperkalemia/monitoring burden.
- Durable long‑term polyuria control beyond partial thiazide ± NSAID benefit, via non‑NSAID mechanisms that avoid boxed‑warning GI/CV risks and reduce thiazide electrolyte‑monitoring burden.

name: Nephronophthisis
description: Inherited cystic tubulointerstitial kidney disease causing early loss of urine concentrating ability, with childhood polyuria and polydipsia, salt wasting, growth restriction and iron resistant anemia, progressing to end stage kidney disease often in adolescence around median age 13. Care is supportive until dialysis or transplant, with no disease modifying treatment, creating demand for kidney targeted therapies including gene based approaches and for options that address syndromic complications such as retinal degeneration and liver fibrosis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying renal therapy that delays progression to ESRD/renal replacement therapy in juvenile nephronophthisis (ESRD ~age 13).
- Kidney-targeted gene-based therapy for high-frequency genetic subgroups (e.g., NPHP1-deletion juvenile NPH ~25%), delivered early to delay/prevent dialysis/transplant.
- Therapies that prevent/treat syndromic extra-renal morbidity (especially retinal degeneration/vision loss and liver fibrosis) in the ~10–20% with ciliopathy features.

name: Ovarian tumor | sex cord-stromal tumor
description: Rare ovarian sex cord stromal tumors, often hormone producing, present with pelvic mass and endocrine symptoms such as postmenopausal bleeding. Most adult granulosa cell tumors are diagnosed early with good survival, yet 20 to 30% recur years later, creating prolonged surveillance and treatment needs. In advanced or recurrent disease, evidence is sparse and care is borrowed from epithelial ovarian cancer chemotherapies with limited tailored options, driving demand for better systemic therapies and biomarker guided endocrine or targeted approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjuvant/maintenance therapy for early-stage disease that prevents very late relapse so lifelong surveillance isn’t needed.
- Biomarker-driven systemic therapy for relapsed/recurrent disease (no standard regimen) that improves objective response vs current chemo/endocrine options.
- Chemo-sparing, less-toxic regimens for advanced/recurrent patients that reduce severe (grade ≥3) toxicity vs BEP/platinum-taxane backbones.

name: Pancreatic cancer | adenosquamous carcinoma
description: Pancreatic adenosquamous carcinoma is a rare pancreatic cancer with mixed squamous and ductal components that is more aggressive than typical pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, often diagnosed late due to few early symptoms and frequently metastatic, with median survival under 1 year. Standard care relies on toxic, infusion heavy chemotherapy that many patients cannot tolerate, and evidence is thin because this histology is often excluded from trials. Key needs include earlier detection and disease modifying, better tolerated therapies, with interest in biomarker guided approaches such as immunotherapy in PD-L1 high tumors and targeted options where actionable alterations exist.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- PD‑1/PD‑L1–based therapy for the PD‑L1–enriched PASC subgroup to achieve durable responses
- KRAS/RAS‑pathway targeted therapy (ideally oral) for KRAS‑mutant PASC beyond non‑selective cytotoxic backbones
- Lower‑toxicity, lower‑clinic‑burden regimens that reduce AE‑driven discontinuation and avoid prolonged infusion/take‑home pump logistics vs IV chemo

name: Paramyotonia congenita | Von Eulenburg subtype
description: Paramyotonia congenita is a rare SCN4A related skeletal muscle sodium channel disorder starting in infancy or early childhood in which cold and exercise trigger paradoxical myotonia that worsens with repeated movement and can progress to hours long weakness, affecting daily function and sometimes breathing. Management is largely trigger avoidance plus symptomatic sodium channel blockers such as mexiletine or lamotrigine and sometimes acetazolamide. There is no cure or disease modifying therapy, responses are inconsistent, and up to one third of patients develop gastrointestinal side effects on mexiletine, with limited pediatric evidence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Attack-prevention therapy for cold/exercise-triggered weakness episodes that can persist for hours (even after rewarming)
- Better-tolerated mexiletine alternative for the ~30% with poor tolerability/contraindications/limited efficacy (notably GI dyspepsia)
- Pediatric-validated pharmacotherapy (child-appropriate formulation + safety/efficacy evidence) given frequent first-decade onset and adult-only RCT data

name: Partial androgen insensitivity syndrome
description: Partial androgen insensitivity syndrome is an X linked androgen receptor disorder in 46,XY individuals where testes make typical androgen levels but body tissues respond incompletely, leading to undermasculinized genitalia such as micropenis, severe hypospadias, bifid scrotum and sometimes undescended testes. Puberty commonly brings gynecomastia and impaired sperm production, and care often involves difficult sex assignment decisions, staged urologic surgery and lifelong hormone management. A major unmet need is better ability to predict phenotype and long term outcomes from genotype to guide early decisions and reduce invasive, irreversible interventions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype‑stratified AR‑pathway therapeutics to achieve predictable virilization in male‑reared PAIS (beyond empiric testosterone/DHT).
- Fertility/spermatogenesis restoration therapies for PAIS males (not addressed by sex‑steroid replacement).
- Safer, more convenient non‑aromatizable androgen options (e.g., improved DHT delivery) to reduce gynecomastia risk and avoid topical‑gel hazards.

name: Kaeser syndrome
description: Ultra-rare autosomal dominant DES related neuromuscular disease with adult onset scapuloperoneal weakness progressing from foot drop to shoulder involvement often with facial weakness dysphagia and gynecomastia and potential cardiac and respiratory complications including sudden death risk; care is supportive with no disease modifying therapy, creating need for treatments that reduce desmin protein aggregation and prevent cardiopulmonary failure.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Proteostasis/aggregate-clearance therapy to reduce mutant-desmin aggregation and slow progression to severe motor disability (tetraparesis/wheelchair dependence)
- Cardiac disease–modifying therapy to reduce conduction block/arrhythmia progression and sudden cardiac death risk (avoiding pacemaker dependence)
- Respiratory-muscle disease–modifying therapy to prevent respiratory insufficiency–driven disability/death and reduce need for ventilatory support

name: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
description: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a rare, life-threatening reaction to antipsychotic or neuroleptic drugs that typically emerges early in treatment and rapidly evolves over days with fever, severe rigidity, delirium, and autonomic instability, often complicated by rhabdomyolysis and kidney injury. Care hinges on stopping the offending drug and intensive supportive management, but adjunct medications lack trial-proven efficacy, leaving an unmet need for fast, reliably reversing acute therapies that prevent organ damage while allowing ongoing psychiatric care.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid-onset, clinically proven “reversal” therapy that reliably controls hyperthermia/rigidity during the first ~72 hours when NMS severity peaks
- Renal-protective/rhabdomyolysis-targeted therapy to prevent myoglobinuric AKI in high-CK patients and reduce dialysis/death
- Safer, easier-to-administer acute agent that reduces reliance on high-burden adjuncts (e.g., avoids high‑pH IV dantrolene extravasation/tissue necrosis and benzo–opioid respiratory-depression risk)
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus URL; primary resource: https://rarediseases.info.nih.gov/diseases/7195/neuroleptic-malignant-syndrome

name: Neuronal intestinal dysplasia | type A
description: Ultra rare congenital enteric neuropathy with hypoplasia or aplasia of sympathetic intestinal innervation causing severe neonatal dysmotility that mimics Hirschsprung disease and can be fatal if untreated. Newborns present with lower intestinal obstruction or diarrhea with bloody stools. Management is largely supportive with laxatives and enemas and often escalates to procedure heavy surgery, leaving a major unmet need for neonatal safe, durable pharmacologic motility control that prevents obstruction and avoids resection or stomas.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid, neonatal-safe pharmacologic control of autonomic imbalance (sympathetic hypoplasia → focal colon spasms) in IND‑A to prevent acute obstruction/hemorrhagic stools and fatal untreated disease.
- Durable medical alternative to prolonged laxatives/enemas that avoids escalation to invasive surgery (e.g., myectomy/sphincterotomy, colonic resection, temporary colostomy) in refractory patients.
- Effective (ideally oral/enteral) prokinetic therapy for diffuse dysmotility that reduces dependence on procedure-based bowel programs (e.g., cecostomy/antegrade enemas) and improves objective bowel endpoints (evacuations/week, distension, enema requirement, bowel function score).

name: Neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease
description: Neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease is a slowly progressive neurodegenerative disorder affecting central, peripheral, and autonomic nervous systems, causing progressive disability with adult dementia and episodes such as encephalitis-like altered consciousness, autonomic dysfunction, and sometimes severe gastrointestinal dysmotility with weight loss. There is no cure or disease modifying therapy, and treatment is largely symptomatic with empiric corticosteroids for some episodic or gastrointestinal symptoms on limited evidence. Key unmet needs are reliable diagnosis and therapies that slow progression or target the NOTCH2NLC GGC repeat expansion, where repeat directed antisense approaches are an emerging frontier.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- NOTCH2NLC GGC repeat–targeted disease-modifying therapy (e.g., CNS-delivered ASO) to reduce polyG pathology and slow dementia-dominant decline in genetically confirmed NIID.
- Steroid-sparing agents to prevent/abort paroxysmal encephalopathy/unconsciousness episodes where steroids lack clear prognostic benefit.
- Durable non-steroid treatments for severe autonomic/GI disability (e.g., refractory nausea/vomiting and neurogenic bladder) to avoid relapse and long-term steroid dependence.
medlineUrl: No MedlinePlus NIID page (no dedicated MedlinePlus URL)

name: Ganglioneuroblastoma
description: Intermediate neuroblastic tumor from nerve tissue in young children often presenting as an abdominal mass; high risk cases can be metastatic with long term survival under 50% and poor outcomes after relapse despite intensive multimodal therapy, which carries substantial toxicity, leaving a need for more effective and better tolerated disease modifying options such as next generation immune cell therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Frontline/relapse regimens that improve ORR/OS/EFS in high‑risk metastatic ganglioneuroblastoma (stage 4, >18 months) where survival and post‑recurrence outcomes remain poor.
- Safer anti‑GD2 (or alternative) therapies that reduce severe infusion reactions/capillary leak and lessen long‑term toxicities (e.g., hearing loss) from intensive chemo/immunotherapy.
- More outpatient‑friendly approaches that maintain efficacy while reducing transplant intensity/length of hospitalization and shortening prolonged multi‑day anti‑GD2 infusions.

name: Pityriasis rubra pilaris
description: Pityriasis rubra pilaris is a rare inflammatory skin disorder that often emerges in mid to late adulthood and can rapidly spread over weeks to near whole body redness and scaling with distinctive islands of spared skin. Severe itch, thickened palms and soles, and painful fissures can make walking and using the hands difficult, driving major quality of life and functional impairment. Treatment is largely empirical and off label with oral retinoids or methotrexate, backed by limited controlled trial data and unpredictable responses, leaving a premium on safe, durable disease control and more targeted options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, consistently effective systemic control for moderate-to-severe PRP (e.g., PASI ≥10/BSA ≥10%) achieving PASI75–PASI90-level responses
- Safer long-term systemic therapy with less toxicity and lab/teratogenic monitoring burden than retinoids/immunosuppressants
- Rapid relief for severe erythrodermic PRP with intense symptoms/palmoplantar disability, supported by PRP-specific endpoints and responder predictors

name: Scabies | crusted (Norwegian)
description: Crusted scabies is a severe, highly contagious hyperinfestation with scabies mites causing thick scaly plaques often on palms, soles, and under nails, with itch sometimes minimal so diagnosis is missed until late. It disproportionately affects people with impaired immune or mechanical defenses such as older adults in institutional settings, where a single case can trigger outbreaks. The clinical stakes are secondary bacterial infection that can progress to cellulitis and sepsis. Management is resource intensive, often requiring prolonged combination therapy with keratolytics, topical scabicides, and multi dose systemic ivermectin, creating major operational and adherence challenges.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Standardized short-course systemic regimen (ideally ≤2 doses/single-dose) to replace today’s variable multi-dose ivermectin + frequent topical permethrin schedules
- Scabicide with strong crust/nail penetration and rapid mite-burden debulking to speed time-to-negative scrapings and reduce complication risk
- Resistance-/failure-ready therapy (new mechanism and/or validated combination) to reliably cure refractory cases and reduce relapse/re-treatment cycles

name: Ependymoma | posterior fossa group A
description: Posterior fossa ependymoma group A is an aggressive pediatric brain tumor usually arising in the fourth ventricle in infants and young children, often presenting with obstructive hydrocephalus, raised intracranial pressure, and ataxia. It is biologically defined by loss of histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation, with chromosome 1q gain marking especially poor prognosis. Care still hinges on maximal safe surgery followed by weeks of focal radiotherapy, frequently requiring anesthesia, while chemotherapy benefit remains uncertain. The biggest gaps are durable disease control without debilitating late neurocognitive and endocrine toxicity, driving demand for molecularly stratified systemic options and radiation sparing approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Biomarker-stratified systemic therapy for PF‑EPN‑A (H3K27me3-loss) to improve disease control and reduce distant relapse in high-risk 1q‑gain patients
- Neuroprotective and/or radiation-sparing adjunct drug strategies to prevent radiotherapy-associated neurocognitive decline
- Drug regimens that enable shorter-course/reduced-frequency radiotherapy (or omission) to reduce the ~30-session treatment burden and repeated anesthesia exposure

name: Ependymoma | posterior fossa group B
description: Posterior fossa ependymoma group B is a molecular subtype of ependymoma arising near the fourth ventricle, typically in adolescents and adults, and often presenting with obstructed cerebrospinal fluid symptoms such as headache, nausea, and vomiting. Care centers on maximal safe resection with focal radiotherapy, but many patients can be cured with complete resection, creating pressure to safely de escalate radiation. The major gaps are late relapses and lack of durable systemic options, since chemotherapy responses are often short lived and relapse can drive repeat local therapy or invasive intraventricular drug delivery, highlighting the need for blood brain barrier penetrant treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Radiation-sparing adjuvant therapy enabling observation/no focal RT after GTR in PF‑EPN‑B AYA patients without compromising control.
- BBB-penetrant systemic salvage therapies achieving objective, durable responses for late-recurrent posterior fossa ependymoma (incl. PF‑EPN‑B).
- Systemic outpatient (oral/IV) options to replace invasive intraventricular/intrathecal drug delivery regimens in relapsed disease.

name: Pulmonary sclerosing pneumocytoma
description: Pulmonary sclerosing pneumocytoma is a rare, usually benign epithelial lung tumor arising from type II pneumocytes that typically appears as an incidental solitary pulmonary nodule in middle aged women, often never smokers. Surgery is generally curative, but preoperative diagnosis is challenging and the lesion can mimic malignancy, driving unnecessary lung resection. A small subset shows multifocal, recurrent, or metastatic behavior including nodal spread, where there is no established systemic therapy despite frequent PI3K AKT mTOR pathway alterations and limited benefit reported with mTOR inhibition.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Evidence-based systemic therapy with durable objective responses for rare metastatic/recurrent pulmonary sclerosing pneumocytoma, where cytotoxic chemotherapy is typically poor
- Genotype-directed targeted therapy for AKT/PI3K–mTOR–altered PSP (e.g., AKT1 E17K) to achieve radiographic tumor shrinkage in unresectable/metastatic disease
- Non-surgical drug options that avoid or downstage lung resection (especially multifocal/hilar/endobronchial/mediastinal presentations) to preserve lung function

name: Purpura fulminans
description: Purpura fulminans is a life threatening hematologic emergency marked by rapidly progressive purpura from small vessel thrombosis and hemorrhagic skin necrosis with a highly thrombotic disseminated intravascular coagulation phenotype, often in pediatric sepsis or neonates with severe protein C deficiency. Despite prompt antibiotics and supportive anticoagulant, anticoagulation, and transfusion care, patients can deteriorate to peripheral gangrene, amputations, and 30 to 60 percent mortality, underscoring the need for treatments that restore protein C pathway cytoprotection while controlling microvascular clotting without excess bleeding.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Ultra-rapid limb-salvage adjuncts for acute infectious/meningococcal purpura fulminans to halt microvascular thrombosis within 24–48h and reduce amputation/skin-graft rates.
- Protein C–pathway cytoprotective (PAR-1–biased/APC-mutant) therapies for septic PF that preserve endothelial/barrier function without anticoagulant-related bleeding.
- Longer-acting, lower-monitoring-burden protein C replacement for congenital protein C deficiency/neonatal PF to reduce frequent IV dosing and q6h activity checks.

name: Ochronosis
description: Ochronosis in alkaptonuria is a progressive connective tissue disorder caused by homogentisic acid accumulation, with dark urine and blue black pigment deposition that becomes evident after age 30 and is often diagnosed around age 40 when spine and large joint arthritis drives pain, stiffness, declining mobility, and eventual joint replacement. Treatment is largely palliative, and while nitisinone lowers homogentisic acid, its long term use is constrained by marked tyrosine elevation, keratopathy risk, and the burden of monitoring and dietary restriction. Major unmet needs are safer early disease modification before irreversible tissue damage and therapies that restore function in established arthropathy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- HGA-lowering therapy that avoids nitisinone-associated tyrosine elevation/keratopathy and eliminates burdensome diet + frequent monitoring.
- Pediatric/presymptomatic disease-modifying treatment (0–18 years) to prevent irreversible ochronosis before symptoms.
- Therapies that deliver meaningful pain and mobility improvement in established ochronotic arthropathy (beyond merely slowing progression), delaying/avoiding joint/spine procedures.

name: Oculodentodigital dysplasia
description: Rare (usually autosomal dominant) GJA1 (connexin 43) developmental disorder causing congenital eye, dental, craniofacial, and limb anomalies and sometimes progressive neurologic involvement; care is mainly multidisciplinary monitoring and supportive or surgical management, with unmet need for disease modifying therapies that preserve vision and dentition and prevent or slow neurologic progression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- GJA1/connexin-43–restoring disease modification to normalize gap-junction communication early in development
- Ocular-protective therapy to prevent glaucoma-driven blindness (ideally reducing chronic topical anti-glaucoma treatment burden)
- Neuroprotective therapy for the ~30% with neurologic disease (spasticity/ataxia + leukodystrophy) to prevent/slow late-onset progression

name: Oculopharyngodistal myopathy
description: Rare, slowly progressive adult-onset genetic neuromuscular disease causing ptosis and ophthalmoparesis with facial and pharyngeal weakness leading to dysarthria and dysphagia, followed by distal limb weakness and common respiratory involvement. Care is supportive only, with no disease-modifying therapy, so preventing aspiration pneumonia and preserving respiratory function are the key unmet needs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Genotype-targeted therapy for repeat-expansion OPDM (e.g., LRP12/GIPC1/NOTCH2NLC/RILPL1/ABCD3) to suppress repeat-driven toxicity and slow progression.
- Pharmacologic bulbar-weakness/dysphagia treatment that reduces aspiration events/aspiration pneumonia.
- Respiratory muscle–preserving therapy to maintain pulmonary function and delay/avoid need for NIPPV/ventilatory support (ideally at-home regimen).
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus page/URL for OPDM

name: Pycnodysostosis
description: Ultra-rare autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia from CTSK mutations that impair osteoclast remodeling, causing short stature with osteosclerosis yet fragile, fracture-prone bones plus craniofacial and dental anomalies; care is supportive only, leaving major unmet needs for disease-modifying therapy to reduce fractures and delayed healing and to better manage severe childhood obstructive sleep apnea.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CTSK/osteoclast-function restoration to reduce bone fragility (fewer fractures) and improve delayed fracture healing
- Non-surgical drug therapy to meaningfully reduce severe pediatric OSA/hypoventilation and dependence on noninvasive ventilation/CPAP
- Reduced-burden therapy for short stature (e.g., longer-acting alternative to daily somatropin) while preserving height benefit

name: Rhabdomyosarcoma
description: Rare pediatric soft tissue sarcoma arising from skeletal muscle, often presenting as a progressively enlarging mass in the head and neck or genitourinary tract. Despite relatively infrequent overt metastasis at diagnosis, presumed micrometastatic spread drives year long chemotherapy plus surgery and radiation with major toxicity. Survival remains poor in high risk metastatic and relapsed or refractory disease, and there is demand for biomarker guided systemic therapies, better salvage options, and less myelotoxic regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Biomarker-selected systemic therapy to improve survival in metastatic/high-risk RMS, especially FOXO1 fusion–positive disease.
- Effective salvage regimen for relapsed/refractory RMS (including early relapse/progression) where no accepted standard exists.
- Chemo-/radiation-sparing, less myelotoxic outpatient-friendly regimens that reduce severe hematologic/infectious toxicity and treatment burden.

name: Plasma cell granuloma
description: Plasma cell granuloma of the orbit is a tumor-like inflammatory, often fibrosing orbital mass that can encase the optic nerve and extraocular muscles, causing pain, diplopia, and progressive vision loss. Care relies on systemic corticosteroids and empiric immunosuppression, but durable control is difficult with frequent relapse, creating demand for steroid-sparing maintenance and more precise, biology-guided approaches. In the subset on the inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor spectrum with actionable drivers such as anaplastic lymphoma kinase fusions, targeted therapy is an emerging option for recurrent or inoperable disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing maintenance therapy to reduce high relapse/recurrence while avoiding prolonged high-dose systemic steroid toxicities
- Therapies optimized for high-risk orbital phenotypes (e.g., diffuse/deep disease, optic disc edema) to prevent steroid-dependent relapse and flares on low-dose taper
- Biomarker-driven targeted therapy for IMT/plasma cell granuloma (e.g., oral ALK inhibitors for ALK-fusion–positive cases) to reduce empiric immunosuppression/resection

name: Ossifying fibromyxoid tumor
description: Ossifying fibromyxoid tumor is a rare, typically slow growing soft tissue neoplasm of intermediate malignant potential, often presenting around age 50 as a painless lower extremity mass with long diagnostic delay. Surgery is usually curative, but recurrence and metastasis can occur and follow up is prolonged. For advanced disease there is little prospective evidence and systemic options are limited with modest chemotherapy activity, leaving a premium on biomarker led approaches informed by common PHF1 fusions and epigenetic dysregulation and on better strategies to prevent relapse after resection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Effective systemic therapy for unresectable/metastatic malignant OFMT delivering durable ORR/PFS beyond limited doxorubicin benefit
- Biomarker-selected targeted/epigenetic therapies for PHF1-rearranged OFMT (e.g., PHF1::EP400, PHF1::TFE3)
- Evidence-based adjuvant/maintenance systemic therapy post-resection of atypical/malignant OFMT to reduce late recurrence/metastasis
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus URL (no OFMT health topic page)

name: Osteoblastoma
description: Osteoblastoma is a rare benign bone tumor, often in the spine, typically affecting males aged 10 to 30, causing progressive dull pain and sometimes neurologic symptoms or scoliosis. Treatment is largely surgical, yet hypervascular bleeding and difficult anatomy can prevent complete resection, driving local recurrence rates reported up to 25%. There is no established adjuvant systemic option, with chemotherapy and radiotherapy lacking a defined role and radiation generally reserved for unresectable or high risk cases.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Surgery-sparing systemic control for unresectable/“too risky to operate” spinal osteoblastoma (radiologic response, pain improvement, and surgery avoidance).
- Post-op adjuvant therapy to reduce local recurrence/regrowth after curettage/resection in anatomically constrained spine/pelvis lesions.
- Neoadjuvant/perioperative medical strategies to reduce hypervascular bleeding and enable less extensive resection (less instrumentation/fusion).

name: Sebaceous carcinoma
description: Rare aggressive sebaceous gland skin cancer, usually arising in eyelid meibomian glands in adults aged 60 to 80, often misdiagnosed as chalazion and diagnosed late with conjunctival spread and nodal metastasis risk; surgery controls localized disease but metastatic cases lack an established systemic standard, creating demand for biomarker guided immunotherapy in microsatellite instability or high tumor mutational burden tumors and targeted options such as HER2 amplified disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prospective-trial–proven systemic therapy for unresectable/recurrent/metastatic sebaceous carcinoma (esp. microsatellite-stable) that delivers meaningful objective responses
- Predictive biomarkers/strategies to better select patients likely to respond to PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint blockade
- Biomarker-selected targeted options for advanced ocular sebaceous carcinoma (e.g., HER2-overexpressing or PI3K–mTOR–pathway–driven tumors)

name: Otopalatodigital syndrome spectrum disorder
description: FLNA-related otopalatodigital spectrum disorders are congenital skeletal dysplasias with craniofacial and palate anomalies, limb malformations, and conductive hearing loss from ossicle defects; severe OPD2 in males often leads to death in the first year from thoracic hypoplasia and pulmonary insufficiency. Care is largely surgical and supportive, leaving major unmet needs for disease-modifying approaches that prevent lethal respiratory compromise, reduce progressive scoliosis, and enable safer, more effective hearing restoration than current hearing aids or risky, often unsuccessful ossicular surgery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prenatal/neonatal disease-modifying therapy to prevent thoracic-hypoplasia–driven pulmonary insufficiency and first-year mortality in male FLNA-OPD2
- Systemic skeletal-modifying therapy to halt progressive scoliosis (and related functional decline), reducing reliance on bracing/surgery and chronic PT
- Non-surgical hearing restoration for conductive hearing loss due to fused/misshapen ossicles (where ossicular surgery is usually unsuccessful/high-risk)

name: Pancreatic cancer | intraductal papillary mucinous carcinoma
description: Intraductal papillary mucinous carcinoma is invasive pancreatic cancer arising from mucin producing ductal cysts that are often found incidentally until pain, weight loss, jaundice, or pancreatitis like episodes appear. Management centers on long term imaging surveillance and major pancreatic surgery, yet there is no proven medical therapy to prevent progression, making risk stratification and chemoprevention a key unmet need. Once invasion occurs, outcomes hinge on better peri and postoperative systemic therapy and biomarker guided targeting for molecular subsets such as GNAS mutated disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Peri-/post-operative systemic therapy for resected invasive IPMC that reduces recurrence and improves OS vs surgery alone
- Non-surgical chemoprevention for “high-risk” IPMN on surveillance to prolong Kyoto-guideline-defined progression-free survival and delay/avoid pancreatectomy
- Biomarker-defined targeted therapies for invasive IPMC/IPMN and recurrence (e.g., GNAS-codon-201 or RNF43-mutant subsets)

name: Pemphigus | paraneoplastic
description: Paraneoplastic pemphigus is a rare cancer associated autoimmune blistering disease that typically starts with severe, painful oral mucositis and can progress to polymorphous skin lesions and life threatening lung disease such as bronchiolitis obliterans. Current care relies on high dose corticosteroids and other broad immunosuppression with variable efficacy and high infection risk in oncology patients. Key unmet needs are durable control of treatment resistant mucositis and infection sparing disease control that prevents bronchiolitis obliterans and reduces mortality.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable control of chronic, severe (often steroid-refractory) mucositis
- Prevention/attenuation of bronchiolitis obliterans to reduce respiratory-failure mortality
- Oncology-compatible, infection-sparing immunomodulation to replace high-dose systemic steroids

name: Peliosis hepatis
description: Peliosis hepatis is a rare vascular liver disorder marked by randomly scattered blood filled cavities, often found incidentally in asymptomatic adults but sometimes progressing to portal hypertension, liver failure, or fatal hemorrhage if lesions rupture. It is frequently secondary to drugs such as anabolic steroids, oral contraceptives, or azathioprine, or to Bartonella infection in immunocompromised patients. Care is largely trigger removal or prolonged antibiotics, with limited evidence, frequent relapse, drug interaction constraints, and no consensus on monitoring or disease modifying strategies to stabilize lesions and prevent bleeding.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course, relapse-resistant Bartonella therapy for bacillary peliosis hepatis that avoids rifamycin–antiretroviral DDIs
- Disease-directed lesion regression therapy for drug-associated peliosis (e.g., azathioprine-associated in kidney transplant recipients) beyond simple causative-drug withdrawal
- Pharmacologic lesion-stabilization/hemostatic strategies to prevent or rapidly control rupture-related hemorrhage/death risk

name: Pemphigus | foliaceus
description: Rare autoimmune blistering skin disease driven by anti desmoglein 1 autoantibodies, causing fragile superficial blisters that become scaly crusted erosions on scalp face and trunk with mucosal sparing; diagnosis can be delayed and long term immunosuppression controls disease but adds infection risk, leaving a need for durable steroid sparing remission via targeted autoantibody suppression and depletion.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Anti‑Dsg1–targeted, fast‑onset induction to rapidly achieve disease control and CRmin in skin‑only pemphigus foliaceus.
- Durable maintenance/relapse‑prevention (including post‑rituximab) to reduce frequent relapses after induction.
- Steroid‑sparing therapy for mild/limited PF (BSA <5% and/or PDAI ≤15) to prevent escalation to systemic prednisone and long‑term steroid toxicities.

name: Pemphigus | gestationis
description: Rare pregnancy associated autoimmune blistering disorder driven by immunoglobulin G autoantibodies to BP180 causing severe periumbilical itch and urticaria like plaques that can progress to widespread tense blisters, often flaring at delivery and recurring in later pregnancies. Management relies on topical or systemic corticosteroids and antihistamines used sparingly in pregnancy, with limited trial grade evidence and persistent need for pregnancy safe steroid sparing control, postpartum flare prevention, and better protection against prematurity and fetal growth restriction.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing systemic therapy for severe/widespread PG (>10% BSA) to rapidly stop new blisters/itch while avoiding maternal–fetal risks of systemic prednisolone and potent topical steroids.
- Peripartum/postpartum maintenance to prevent common postpartum flares (~75%) and reduce prolonged postpartum activity and high recurrence in subsequent pregnancies (~90%).
- Prospectively validated, pregnancy-safe immunomodulators (beyond case reports) to control debilitating pruritus and reduce PG-associated prematurity/preterm birth and fetal growth restriction.

name: Penicilliosis
description: Talaromycosis (formerly penicilliosis) is an invasive fungal infection caused by Talaromyces marneffei, concentrated in Southeast Asia, southern China, and India, and most often affecting people with advanced HIV and very low CD4 counts. It presents as disseminated disease with fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms, and sometimes characteristic papular skin lesions, and is near universally fatal if untreated. Care relies on two weeks of intravenous amphotericin followed by prolonged oral azoles and maintenance, leaving major unmet needs around amphotericin toxicity and access, complex azole absorption and drug interactions, monitoring burden, and relapse prevention with simpler, safer regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course induction (e.g., single-dose liposomal amphotericin strategies ± new partner drugs) to preserve amphotericin-like survival while reducing IV burden and toxicities (renal/electrolytes/anemia/infusion reactions).
- Simplified oral step-down/maintenance therapy that avoids itraconazole’s pH/food-dependent dosing, routine therapeutic drug monitoring, and major antiretroviral drug–drug interactions.
- Relapse-prevention approaches that shorten/simplify secondary prophylaxis vs prolonged itraconazole until CD4 >100 for ≥6 months, without increasing relapse risk.

name: Penile cancer | basaloid carcinoma
description: Basaloid penile squamous cell carcinoma is a rare, human papillomavirus associated and often aggressive penile cancer, typically presenting in men aged 50 to 70 with a persistent glans or foreskin lump or ulcer that can progress to bleeding, foul discharge, and early inguinal node spread. Outcomes hinge on nodal burden, with pelvic node involvement marking a steep survival drop. Treatment still relies on disfiguring surgery plus cisplatin based chemotherapy, while single agent immune checkpoint therapy has a low ceiling, driving demand for better tolerated neoadjuvant approaches and effective post platinum, biomarker guided or human papillomavirus directed options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Less toxic, higher-pCR neoadjuvant/induction systemic therapy for bulky node-positive (cN2–N3) basaloid penile cancer vs current platinum triplets.
- Evidence-based 2L+ systemic option after platinum failure that meaningfully improves survival/response in metastatic/recurrent disease.
- HPV/p16-biomarker-selected therapies for basaloid tumors (HPV-directed and/or immune-based) to outperform modest single-agent checkpoint inhibitor activity.

name: Perineurioma
description: Intraneural perineurioma is a rare, benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor of perineurial cells that typically presents in childhood or young adulthood as a slowly progressive, painless, motor-predominant mononeuropathy with focal weakness and muscle atrophy. Underdiagnosis and delayed recognition are common, and management is largely observation or surgery, but long-segment lesions make operative approaches potentially function-sacrificing. With no proven disease-modifying therapy, the unmet need is for earlier diagnosis plus non-surgical strategies that stabilize nerves and restore innervation rather than simply adapt to progressive denervation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- TRAF7 WD40 mutation–biomarker–driven disease‑modifying therapy to prevent/slow progressive focal extremity weakness
- Pharmacotherapy to restore nerve/muscle function (neuroregeneration/reinnervation) for patients with severe motor deficits (e.g., MRC ≤2)
- Non‑surgical disease stabilization for long‑segment pediatric/adolescent lesions compatible with watchful waiting

name: Phaeohyphomycosis
description: Phaeohyphomycosis is a rare infection from melanized black fungi, often starting after minor trauma as indolent subcutaneous lesions on exposed extremities but sometimes progressing to deep disease such as brain abscess with very high mortality. Care is hampered by delayed diagnosis, lack of standardized regimens, and the need for prolonged azole or amphotericin based combinations that carry toxicity and drug interaction burdens. The biggest unmet need is safer fungicidal therapies with reliable central nervous system penetration plus clearer evidence based treatment pathways for severe and disseminated disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-penetrant, fungicidal antifungal for cerebral phaeohyphomycosis (Cladophialophora brain abscess) to reduce very high mortality
- Standardized systemic regimen that can cure severe non-resectable brain abscesses/disseminated disease (esp. immunocompromised) without radical surgery + prolonged combo therapy
- Safer, low–drug-interaction salvage option for refractory/resistant or antifungal-intolerant patients (incl. organ dysfunction) with shorter courses/less monitoring

name: Pineoblastoma
description: Pineoblastoma is a fast growing grade 4 malignant pineal region tumor that mainly affects children, often presenting with obstructive hydrocephalus symptoms and frequent dissemination at diagnosis. Treatment relies on maximal resection plus craniospinal irradiation and intensive chemotherapy, but toxicity is high and infants often cannot receive radiation and still fare poorly, especially in high risk molecular subgroups. Relapsed disease has no standard salvage options, driving demand for less toxic central nervous system penetrant systemic therapies and standardized maintenance or salvage strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Radiation-sparing curative therapy for infants/young children (<3 years) where radiation is often deferred
- CNS-penetrant systemic therapy for metastatic/high-risk molecular subtypes (e.g., PB-MYC/FOXR2, PB-RB1)
- Standardized, less-toxic salvage/maintenance regimen for relapsed/refractory pineoblastoma to improve PFS/OS
medlineUrl: No specific MedlinePlus Health Topic URL for pineoblastoma

name: Pinta disease
description: Pinta is a nonsexually transmitted Treponema skin infection spread by close skin to skin contact in poor rural tropical communities, mainly affecting children and young adults in Latin America. It causes itchy plaques that enlarge and later leave persistent pigment changes that can stigmatize patients even after antibiotic cure. Care is straightforward when single dose first line therapy is available, but access and adherence become harder when alternatives like multi day doxycycline are needed, and there are no treatments that reliably speed clearance or reverse late dyschromia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course oral alternative for patients intolerant/allergic to penicillin/azithromycin or with treatment failure, avoiding 14-day doxycycline fallback and providing an azithromycin-resistance–robust option.
- Adjunct therapies to prevent or reverse permanent late-stage dyschromic plaques/depigmented patches that persist despite antibiotic cure.
- Treatments that accelerate lesion clearance (vs 6–12 months to ~1 year) and reduce residual scarring.

name: Fibromatosis | plantar fascial
description: Plantar fibromatosis (Ledderhose disease) is a rare benign overgrowth of the plantar fascia that forms hard 1 to 2 cm nodules in the foot arch, sometimes in both feet, causing pain and difficulty walking. Care is largely symptom focused with orthotics, anti inflammatory drugs, injections, or radiation, and surgery for severe cases. The key unmet need is a durable, nonsurgical way to shrink nodules and prevent relapse, since recurrence after surgery is common and injections can require repeats and carry rupture risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable (≥3-year) non-surgical nodule regression/softening that reduces pain with ambulation
- Adjuvant recurrence-prevention therapy to reduce ~60% post-surgery recurrence (esp. bilateral disease/multiple nodules/family history)
- Lower-burden alternatives to 3–5 serial intralesional steroid injections that avoid fascial/tendon rupture risk while improving pain/function

name: Plasminogen deficiency | type 1
description: Ultra-rare autosomal recessive PLG-related fibrinolysis disorder where low plasminogen drives fibrin buildup and recurrent woody mucosal pseudomembranes, often starting in infancy, commonly affecting the eyes with risk of vision loss and sometimes the airway with life-threatening obstruction. Current care remains burdensome and imperfect despite plasminogen replacement, requiring intravenous infusions every 2 to 4 days with bleeding risk, while fresh frozen plasma is inefficient and can cause fluid overload or allergic reactions, leaving a need for safer, longer-acting and more convenient disease control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable plasminogen restoration that avoids chronic high-frequency IV replacement (q2–4 days)
- Safer therapy for high-risk mucosal disease (esp. airway lesions) with lower bleeding/tissue-sloughing/obstruction risk and non–blood-derived product
- Practical, licensed ocular/local mucosal therapy that prevents relapse and protects vision without intensive plasma-based regimens

name: Platelet storage pool deficiency
description: Rare platelet function disorder caused by abnormal or depleted platelet granules, leading to delayed clot formation and lifelong mild to moderate mucocutaneous bleeding such as easy bruising, nosebleeds and heavy menstrual bleeding that can cause iron deficiency anemia. Routine coagulation tests are often normal so diagnosis is delayed. Management is supportive with antifibrinolytics and desmopressin, but peri procedural and obstetric bleeding control remains unreliable due to tachyphylaxis, hyponatremia and tradeoffs with platelet transfusions or procoagulants.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Contraception-compatible, low-thrombosis-risk control of heavy menstrual bleeding in PSPD
- Peri-procedural prophylaxis with predictable efficacy without DDAVP hyponatremia monitoring burden/tachyphylaxis
- Transfusion-sparing rescue therapy for major bleeding/postpartum hemorrhage that avoids platelet-transfusion immunization limits and rFVIIa thrombosis risk

name: Pleuropulmonary blastoma
description: Pleuropulmonary blastoma is a rare childhood lung tumor, often linked to germline DICER1 variants, that can present like pneumonia or pneumothorax and may progress from cystic Type I to aggressive disease. Cure depends on complete surgical resection, with chemotherapy and sometimes radiation for Type II and III, but there is no single standard regimen. High rates of relapse and spread to the brain and the long term toxicity of intensive therapy in very young children create strong demand for better risk stratification, central nervous system directed control, and treatment de escalation for low risk patients.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-penetrant systemic therapy to prevent/treat brain metastases in Type II/III pleuropulmonary blastoma (PPB)
- Less-myelosuppressive alternatives (or protective combinations) to IVADo→IVA that reduce severe cytopenias/infection risk
- Biomarker-driven risk-adapted adjuvant therapy for Type I PPB to avoid overtreatment while preventing progression/recurrence to Type II/III

name: Ependymoma | spinal cord, NF2-mutant
description: NF2 related schwannomatosis is a hereditary tumor syndrome that typically begins in late adolescence or early adulthood and often features multiple spinal tumors including intramedullary ependymomas that may be asymptomatic until growth causes pain, numbness, and weakness. Care is dominated by surveillance and high stakes spinal surgery, with radiotherapy sometimes used after incomplete resection but constrained by an elevated long term malignancy risk. The central gap is durable, radiation sparing systemic tumor control for multifocal disease, since standard chemotherapy has little role and drug approaches remain investigational.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical, CNS-penetrant therapy for progressive/symptomatic NF2 spinal ependymomas with objective MRI response and durable PFS.
- Systemic therapy that controls multifocal NF2 spinal ependymoma burden to reduce serial procedures and neurologic harm from intramedullary surgery.
- Radiation-sparing medical option for residual/inoperable NF2-associated tumors (incl. ependymomas) to avoid radiotherapy-linked CNS malignant transformation risk while maintaining tumor control.

name: Popliteal pterygium syndrome
description: Popliteal pterygium syndrome is an autosomal dominant IRF6-related congenital disorder marked by cleft lip and or palate, popliteal skin webbing with knee contractures, and sometimes intraoral bands that can threaten the neonatal airway. Care is largely multi stage surgery, but procedures are high burden and technically risky because major nerves may course through the web, and contractures can recur. Key unmet needs include safer less invasive tissue remodeling approaches, better prevention of recontracture, and rapid options to relieve mouth opening and airway compromise in newborns.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical tissue-remodeling therapy to reduce popliteal webbing/knee flexion contracture and restore ambulation while avoiding high-risk neurovascular dissection
- Rapid-acting therapy to prevent/lyse neonatal oral synechiae (syngnathia) to avoid emergent release/tracheotomy and reduce feeding/respiratory compromise at birth
- Adjunct anti-fibrotic/anti-recontracture therapy post-correction to reduce growth-associated recurrence and repeat operations plus prolonged casting/bracing

name: Spinal muscular atrophy | type 3
description: Spinal muscular atrophy type 3 is a later onset, ambulatory motor neuron disease driven by survival motor neuron protein deficiency, causing progressive proximal muscle weakness, gait impairment, and fatigue that often erodes walking and stair climbing and can lead to wheelchair use later in life. Despite disease modifying options, key unmet needs are more durable strength and endurance preservation with lower treatment burden than repeated lumbar punctures or lifelong daily dosing.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that deliver sustained improvements in fatigue and ambulatory endurance (e.g., Fatigue Severity Scale and 6-minute walk test) in SMA type 3.
- Treatments that meaningfully delay or reverse loss of ambulation and restore proximal motor function beyond stabilization, including on top of SMN-targeted therapy.
- Lower-burden, safer disease-modifying options that avoid repeated intrathecal lumbar punctures/intensive monitoring and enable durable dosing for later-onset patients.

name: Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia | congenita
