description: Rare congenital COL2A1 related skeletal dysplasia causing disproportionate short stature with spine hip and knee malformations plus vision and hearing issues; major morbidity from cervical spine instability with spinal cord injury risk, early airway and restrictive breathing complications, and early arthritis with loss of mobility. Care is largely supportive and surgical, leaving a need for disease modifying approaches that prevent cervical injury, preserve joints and function, and reduce early respiratory complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying cartilage/spine therapy that prevents cervical-spine instability and lowers spinal-cord injury risk (reducing need for C1–C2 fixation).
- Joint/cartilage-protective therapy that delays early-onset arthritis and preserves joint mobility (reducing chronic pain/stiffness and major joint surgeries).
- Airway/respiratory-targeted therapy that reduces tracheo(laryngo)malacia-driven breathing morbidity in infancy (reducing CPAP/ventilation needs).

name: Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia
description: Rare spondylometaphyseal skeletal dysplasia causing disproportionate short stature, progressive scoliosis and kyphosis, hip and knee deformity, waddling gait, chronic pain and early arthritis from early childhood; severe kyphoscoliosis can impair breathing and cervical instability raises spinal cord injury risk. Care is largely supportive and orthopedic surgery based, with no disease modifying therapy, and some axial subtypes add rapid retinal degeneration, underscoring need for disease modification and vision preservation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying skeletal therapy to prevent progressive kyphoscoliosis/respiratory compromise, cervical-spine instability/spinal-cord injury risk, and hip deformity–driven gait impairment (reducing repeated orthopedic surgeries).
- Vision-preserving therapy for axial spondylometaphyseal dysplasia (SMDAX) to halt early-life, rapidly progressive retinal degeneration (RP/cone-rod dystrophy).
- Pediatric-suitable long-term analgesic/anti-arthritic strategy for chronic joint pain/contractures and early-onset arthritis with lower cumulative NSAID GI-ulcer risk.

name: Struma ovarii
description: Struma ovarii is a very rare ovarian teratoma dominated by thyroid tissue, usually unilateral and often found incidentally or after pelvic pain, distension, or ascites, with true hyperthyroidism in only a small minority. Malignant transformation is uncommon and hard to diagnose preoperatively, so treatment ranges from fertility sparing oophorectomy to extensive pelvic surgery plus thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine. The key unmet need is advanced disease with extraovarian spread or radioiodine resistant mutation driven tumors, where systemic targeted therapy is considered despite a thin evidence base.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable systemic therapy for metastatic malignant struma ovarii that is radioiodine- and chemotherapy-refractory, with improved tolerability to avoid AE-driven interruptions.
- Genotype-guided targeted options (e.g., BRAF/MEK, RET, NTRK) for advanced/radioiodine-refractory disease, including therapies for NRAS/RAS-like tumors with no direct targeted option.
- Fertility-/QoL-sparing alternatives to prolonged TSH suppression and high-intensity I-131 management with less reproductive toxicity and pregnancy-delay burden.

name: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis
description: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is a rare, progressive, usually fatal brain disorder caused by persistent measles virus infection years after measles, typically presenting in late childhood or adolescence with cognitive decline and myoclonic jerks that advance to seizures, dementia, coma, and death over months to years. There is no cure, and today’s empiric antiviral or immune based approaches offer only modest response rates around 30 to 35 percent and can be invasive or hard to sustain in pediatric patients, leaving a premium on durable, better tolerated, noninvasive disease modifying therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Clinically validated measles-virus–targeted agents (e.g., RNA-targeting/siRNA or membrane-fusion blockade) that deliver durable neurologic stabilization and survival benefit in pediatric SSPE.
- Non-invasive (systemic/oral) CNS-active regimens that avoid intrathecal/intraventricular interferon delivery while maintaining/improving stabilization rates.
- Higher-response, better-tolerated long-term therapy that exceeds the ~one‑third benefit rate and reduces regimen toxicities/complications in children/adolescents.

name: Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency
description: Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency is an ultra rare inherited neurometabolic disorder caused by biallelic ALDH5A1 variants that impair gamma aminobutyric acid breakdown leading to excess gamma aminobutyric acid and gamma hydroxybutyrate in the brain. It presents in early childhood with hypotonia and delayed development and often evolves into lifelong intellectual disability, epilepsy, ataxia, sleep disturbance, and autism like or anxiety and obsessive compulsive symptoms. Treatment is largely supportive with no cure, leaving a premium on disease modifying approaches plus safer seizure control and improvements in language, adaptive function, sleep, and behavior.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ALDH5A1-targeted disease-modifying therapy (gene/enzyme replacement) to lower urine/CSF GHB and related GABA-pathway metabolites
- SSADHD-appropriate antiseizure therapy for ~50% with epilepsy that reduces seizure burden/SUDEP risk while avoiding tiagabine/vigabatrin and minimizing valproate
- Treatments that improve expressive language/adaptive function (e.g., ABAS) and reduce sleep + neuropsychiatric symptoms (ASD/attention/anxiety/OCD), reducing reliance on symptomatic polypharmacy

name: Sudden infant death syndrome
description: Sudden infant death syndrome is the sudden, sleep associated death of an apparently healthy infant under 1 year that remains unexplained after autopsy and scene investigation, with risk concentrated in the first 6 months and peaking at 2 to 4 months. Care is largely limited to safe sleep practices, but clinicians still cannot prospectively identify vulnerable infants or intervene in time. Key unmet needs are validated biomarkers and screening plus targeted physiologic protections, including approaches informed by brainstem serotonin mediated arousal failures and a potentially preventable arrhythmia subset such as long QT syndrome.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Caffeine/adenosine-antagonist prophylaxis to reduce intermittent-hypoxia–triggered severe desaturation events in high-risk infants.
- Serotonergic/arousal-pathway restoration to improve arousal/autoresuscitation responses in infants with brainstem serotonergic vulnerability.
- Genotype-guided antiarrhythmic prophylaxis (e.g., beta-blockers) for LQTS/channelopathy-associated SIDS risk.

name: Pachydermoperiostosis
description: Ultra-orphan, hereditary primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy driven by impaired prostaglandin E2 clearance, usually presenting around puberty in males with digital clubbing, thickened skin, periosteal new bone formation and painful polyarthritis, sometimes complicated by small intestinal ulcers with bleeding and anemia. Care is largely symptomatic with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, analgesics, bisphosphonates and selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors, but there is no definitive disease modifying therapy and benefits can be incomplete, particularly for periostosis, while gastrointestinal disease and drug side effects can limit treatment.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying PGE2 normalization in genetically defined PHO (HPGD/SLCO2A1) to halt periostosis/digital clubbing progression using urinary PGE2/PGE‑M and objective swelling/structure endpoints.
- Therapies for SLCO2A1-associated enteropathy (PHOAR2/CEAS overlap) to heal small-intestinal ulcers and reduce GI bleeding–driven anemia/hypoproteinemia.
- Long-term, puberty-onset-compatible control of bone/joint pain/swelling plus skin/hyperhidrosis with lower safety/monitoring burden than COX-2 inhibitors and systemic retinoids.

name: Tetanus | neonatal
description: Generalized tetanus in newborns, typically presenting at 3–14 days with inability to suck or breastfeed and excessive crying progressing to rigidity and stimulus triggered spasms that can cause respiratory compromise; largely driven by nonsterile umbilical cord cutting or contaminated stump care where maternal immunization is low, and treatment is constrained because antitoxin cannot reverse neuron bound toxin, leaving major needs for effective post onset therapies and less resource intensive spasm control, ventilation, and management of autonomic instability.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neuron/CNS-targeted anti-toxin that neutralizes tetanospasmin already bound to nerve endings (effective after symptom onset)
- Ventilation-sparing, neonate-appropriate spasm control that reduces the need/duration of mechanical ventilation
- Low-monitoring drug approach to prevent/treat autonomic instability (labile BP/tachycardia) without invasive ICU-style titration

name: Progressive bulbar palsy
description: Progressive bulbar palsy is a bulbar onset motor neuron disorder causing early, worsening dysarthria and dysphagia with tongue atrophy and high near term risk of choking and aspiration pneumonia, often evolving into amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with rapid progression and poor prognosis. Care is largely supportive with limited disease modifying options, leaving a premium on therapies that preserve bulbar function and safer secretion control since standard anticholinergics are often stopped due to systemic side effects including constipation, urinary retention, sedation, delirium, and cognitive dysfunction.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Bulbar-function–targeted disease modification that slows ALSFRS‑R bulbar decline (speech/salivation/swallowing) and reduces aspiration/aspiration‑pneumonia events
- Safer, more effective sialorrhea/secretion control that reduces drooling/choking without anticholinergic toxicity (e.g., delirium/arrhythmias/falls) in older patients
- Dysphagia-friendly, low-monitoring regimens (liquid/PEG-compatible or long-acting non-oral delivery) to reduce dosing/monitoring burdens (e.g., riluzole fasting + liver labs; Nuedexta ECG/QT; baclofen sedation)

name: Prolidase deficiency
description: Prolidase deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive PEPD enzyme disorder causing multisystem disease from infancy, dominated by recurrent skin and potentially fatal respiratory infections and severe chronic painful lower leg ulcers that often do not heal and can lead to infection or amputation. Management is largely supportive with wound care and aggressive infection control, with limited benefit from topical amino acid approaches in some patients, leaving a major unmet need for disease modifying, enzyme restoring therapies that deliver durable ulcer closure and reduce serious infections.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prolidase/PEPD activity–restoring therapy to prevent adolescent-onset ulcers and improve long-term survival.
- Durable complete ulcer closure/ulcer-free survival for severe chronic recalcitrant lower-extremity ulcers, reducing dressing-change burden and amputation risk.
- Steroid-sparing strategy that reduces recurrent (potentially fatal) respiratory/skin infections and need for antibiotic prophylaxis.

name: Prune belly syndrome
description: Prune belly syndrome is a rare congenital disorder, usually in boys, marked by weak abdominal muscles, urinary tract malformations and genital anomalies. Poor bladder emptying causes urinary stasis, recurrent infections and progressive risk of chronic kidney disease, sometimes severe and life limiting. Care is largely supportive with early corrective surgeries, urinary diversion and long term antibiotic prophylaxis, leaving major unmet needs for better bladder drainage and function, non antibiotic infection prevention and kidney protective disease modifying approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-antibiotic UTI prevention to reduce long-term prophylaxis and antimicrobial-resistance risk in prune-belly patients with chronic urinary stasis
- Bladder-emptying pharmacotherapy to reduce urinary stasis/UTIs and avoid catheterization-based management
- Renal-function preservation/anti-progression therapy to prevent pediatric CKD/renal failure in high-risk prune-belly patients

name: Pseudoachondroplasia
description: Pseudoachondroplasia is a rare genetic skeletal dysplasia caused by COMP mutations that trap misfolded cartilage oligomeric matrix protein inside growth plate chondrocytes, triggering endoplasmic reticulum stress, cell death, impaired bone growth, and disproportionate short-limb short stature. Children typically present around walking age with a waddling gait and growth faltering by about age two, then develop joint hyperextensibility, progressive pain, and early osteoarthritis, with many eventually needing hip replacement. Care is supportive only, leaving major unmet needs for disease modifying therapies that reduce intracellular protein stress and for effective long-term, standardized pain control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early post-diagnosis (~18–24 months) disease-modifying therapy that clears mutant COMP/reduces ER stress to preserve growth-plate chondrocytes and improve long-bone growth/height trajectory.
- Joint-sparing systemic therapy to slow/stop progressive multi-joint degeneration and reduce the ~50% lifetime hip-replacement burden.
- NSAID-sparing chronic pain therapy that improves Numeric Pain Rating Scale pain and SF-36 QoL while avoiding long-term NSAID GI/CV risks.

name: Pseudohypoaldosteronism
description: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 is a rare infant onset aldosterone resistance disorder that causes renal and sometimes multi organ salt wasting with dehydration and failure to thrive plus life threatening hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis despite high aldosterone. Management is largely supportive and intensive with extreme sodium and bicarbonate replacement and potassium binding resins that can require feeding tubes and carry neonatal safety constraints. Key unmet needs are safer neonate ready hyperkalemia control and disease modifying approaches that reduce lifelong electrolyte instability, monitoring, and the salt supplementation burden, particularly in systemic disease with pulmonary complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer, neonate-ready hyperkalemia control that avoids polystyrene-sulfonate resins while reliably preventing life-threatening K+ spikes in PHA1 crises.
- Therapies that reduce the extreme sodium-replacement and monitoring burden by decreasing salt-wasting severity/frequency (fewer urgent electrolyte-correction episodes/hospitalizations).
- Systemic/generalized PHA1 (AR ENaC-subunit) functional rescue addressing multi-organ disease (incl. lung) with outcomes beyond electrolytes (reduced chronic pulmonary morbidity plus fewer salt-loss episodes).

name: Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism
description: Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism is a rare GNAS related imprinting disorder marked by the Albright hereditary osteodystrophy phenotype without parathyroid hormone resistance, leaving patients with short stature, brachydactyly, and painful subcutaneous heterotopic ossifications that can be trauma triggered and recur after surgery. Care is largely supportive because there are no effective medical therapies to prevent or treat new ossifications, and functional burden is often compounded by high rates of carpal tunnel syndrome, creating a need for lesion preventing, function preserving treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacologic prophylaxis to prevent new ectopic/subcutaneous ossifications (including pressure/trauma-triggered lesions) and reduce pain/QoL decline
- Medical alternative or peri-surgical adjunct to shrink/stabilize painful ossifications and prevent post-excision regrowth/complications
- Therapy to prevent/mitigate brachydactyly-associated hand disability and reduce high carpal-tunnel burden in PPHP

name: Nodular fasciitis
description: Nodular fasciitis is a benign, self limited fibroblastic or myofibroblastic soft tissue neoplasm, typically a small rapidly growing superficial mass in young adults, often USP6 fusion driven and sometimes tender or painful. Its malignant appearing growth pattern leads to frequent sarcoma misdiagnosis and unnecessary biopsy or excision. Key unmet needs are more confident scar sparing diagnosis and conservative local control, especially for cosmetically sensitive sites or lesions causing nerve compression, using molecular confirmation such as USP6 translocation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Scar-sparing, non-surgical local therapy for facial/cosmetically sensitive nodular fasciitis to avoid excision-related scarring and high post-excision recurrence.
- Faster, predictable lesion involution vs watchful waiting (e.g., ≥50% tumor-volume shrinkage within ~2–4 weeks).
- Non-surgical, rapid symptom control for painful/nerve-compressive lesions to avoid outpatient excision.
medlineUrl: No MedlinePlus page/URL for nodular fasciitis

name: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum
description: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum is a rare, progressive inherited disorder in which calcium mineralization of elastic fibers damages skin, retina, and blood vessels. Patients often present in adolescence or young adulthood with yellow papules and retinal angioid streaks that can progress to macular neovascularization and vision loss, alongside systemic vascular complications. Management is largely monitoring and complication control such as intravitreal anti angiogenic injections, with no disease modifying therapy, creating a major unmet need for systemic treatments that restore pyrophosphate biology and slow ectopic calcification.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemic PPi restoration to slow ectopic vascular calcification (CT arterial calcification score/volume) and improve PAD function (ABI/6‑minute walk)
- Ocular therapies that preserve vision beyond CNV by preventing retinal atrophy/fibrosis and inner retinal degeneration (e.g., microperimetry light sensitivity)
- Longer-acting CNV control to reduce anti‑VEGF injection/visit burden (e.g., durable anti‑VEGF or port delivery systems)

name: Tick-borne encephalitis
description: Tick-borne encephalitis is a tick-borne viral central nervous system infection that often has a biphasic course and can progress to meningitis or meningoencephalitis, leaving up to half of adults with long term neurologic sequelae. There is no specific antiviral treatment and care is supportive once neurologic disease begins, with no recommended post exposure prophylaxis after a tick bite. Prevention relies on vaccination but immune responses are reduced in older adults, creating demand for faster, more reliable protection and disability preventing options such as passive antibody approaches entering first in human trials.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS/BBB-penetrant direct-acting antiviral that is effective when patients present in the neurologic (second) phase and reduces long-term neurologic sequelae.
- Safe, reliable post-exposure prophylaxis after tick bite despite very early transmission (better than historical immunoglobulin PEP).
- Improved/rapid vaccine-based protection in known low-responders (older adults >50 and obese individuals) and fast time-to-immunity for travelers.

name: Tinea nigra
description: Tinea nigra is a rare, superficial fungal infection of the stratum corneum, typically causing a solitary dark brown to black patch on the palm or sole with minimal symptoms and fine scaling, more common in tropical settings and in people with sweaty palms. It is readily curable with topical antifungals over 2 to 4 weeks, but care is constrained by frequent diagnostic confusion with melanoma and other pigmented lesions, leading to anxiety and sometimes unnecessary procedures, and by the need for shorter, durable topical regimens that hold up on high friction, high perspiration acral skin.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Single-application or ≤7‑day topical achieving cure vs typical 2–4 week courses
- Sweat-resistant long-wear palmar/plantar formulation (e.g., film-forming/patch) for patients with hyperhidrosis
- Non-systemic topical salvage option for refractory cases, resilient to emerging antifungal resistance to avoid toxic systemic agents

name: Tinea profunda
description: Tinea profunda (Majocchi granuloma) is a deep, persistent dermatophyte infection of hair follicles, usually on the lower leg, causing scaly plaques with follicular papules, pustules, and nodules, often triggered by shaving, topical steroid use, or immunosuppression. Because fungi invade deep in follicles, topical antifungals often fail and treatment requires 4 to 6 weeks of systemic therapy. Key unmet needs are rising antifungal resistance with relapses and failures, and the safety and monitoring burdens of oral agents such as liver testing for terbinafine and cardiac risk with itraconazole.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemic antifungal(s) that reliably achieve clinical + mycologic cure in Majocchi granuloma caused by terbinafine-resistant Trichophyton (e.g., T. indotineae)
- Safer systemic (or targeted local) therapy that avoids terbinafine hepatotoxicity/monitoring burden and avoids itraconazole CHF risk/drug–drug interaction constraints
- Shorter-course and/or follicle-penetrating therapy that reduces prolonged systemic-treatment requirements and overcomes topical monotherapy’s poor deep-dermal/subcutaneous penetration

name: Tolosa-hunt syndrome
description: Tolosa-Hunt syndrome is a rare inflammatory disorder of the cavernous sinus and superior orbital fissure causing acute unilateral periorbital pain with painful ophthalmoplegia and cranial nerve palsies. Attacks last days to weeks and can remit spontaneously but often recur, with relapses in roughly 40 to 50 percent. Corticosteroids usually relieve pain within 24 to 72 hours, yet cranial nerve deficits may take weeks to recover and frequent relapses drive prolonged or repeated steroid use, creating unmet need for steroid sparing maintenance therapies and faster, more complete neurologic recovery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing maintenance to prevent relapses/durable remission in the high-recurrence subgroup (~40–50% relapse rate).
- Treatments that improve cranial-nerve palsy recovery (faster/more complete ophthalmoplegia/diplopia resolution) beyond pain relief.
- Lower-toxicity, more convenient steroid-minimizing induction/taper regimens that reduce weeks–months steroid exposure and cumulative steroid complications.

name: Pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis
description: Rare inherited interstitial lung disease where calcium phosphate microliths accumulate in the alveoli due to SLC34A2 related impaired phosphate clearance, often found incidentally before age 40 and slowly progressing to fibrosis and respiratory failure. No proven disease modifying medical therapy exists and lung transplantation is the only established effective option, creating demand for treatments that restore phosphate homeostasis or dissolve microliths such as gene correction, phosphate lowering, or chelation approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Lung-directed genetic correction restoring SLC34A2/NPT2b function to reduce microlith burden as a disease-modifying therapy
- Pharmacologic phosphate-lowering approach that prevents and reverses microlith accumulation in early-stage PAM
- Microlith clearance/dissolution drug (e.g., calcium chelation) that reproducibly reduces established stone burden in humans

name: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis
description: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is an ultrarare lung disease where surfactant rich material accumulates in the alveoli, progressively impairing oxygen transfer and causing dyspnea and cough that can be mild early or life threatening. About 90 percent of adult cases are autoimmune, driven by anti granulocyte macrophage colony stimulating factor antibodies that disable alveolar macrophage clearance. Care still relies on whole lung lavage under general anesthesia, often needing repeat procedures yearly or even monthly, underscoring demand for durable disease modifying therapies that prevent reaccumulation and address secondary and congenital subtypes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable pharmacologic control of surfactant reaccumulation to reduce/eliminate repeat whole-lung lavage under general anesthesia.
- Clinically meaningful, durable improvements beyond prior inhaled GM‑CSF (e.g., DLCO/A–aDO2 plus symptoms/QoL).
- Etiology-specific therapies for congenital/hereditary and secondary PAP where GM‑CSF is ineffective and WLL/underlying-disease treatment is not curative.

name: Idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis
description: Very rare pediatric lung disease with recurrent diffuse alveolar hemorrhage causing iron deficiency anemia and progressive lung damage including fibrosis; symptoms often include dyspnea, cough and anemia with hemoptysis variably present. No cure and care relies on steroids and immunosuppressants, creating a need for durable steroid sparing control of bleeding and lung protective strategies to prevent irreversible scarring and severe flares.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing long-term maintenance therapy to prevent recurrent diffuse alveolar hemorrhage while avoiding chronic systemic steroid toxicity.
- Rapid-acting rescue treatment to halt acute massive pulmonary hemorrhage early (reducing ICU escalation and transfusion/anemia burden).
- Lung-protective control that prevents/slows progression to pulmonary scarring/fibrosis and chronic progressive pulmonary insufficiency.

name: Pulmonary venoocclusive disease
description: Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease is an ultra-rare, rapidly progressive form of pulmonary hypertension caused by fibrotic blockage of small pulmonary veins, leading to exertional dyspnea, fatigue, hypoxemia, pulmonary edema, and right-sided heart failure with poor survival after diagnosis. Treatment is constrained because standard pulmonary arterial hypertension vasodilators can trigger life-threatening pulmonary edema, leaving largely supportive care and lung transplantation as the only proven cure. Major unmet needs include earlier recognition and disease-modifying therapies that reverse venous fibrosis and improve oxygen delivery without worsening edema.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy for heritable PVOD (EIF2AK4-driven) that prevents/reverses pulmonary venule fibrotic occlusion to extend transplant-free survival.
- Pulmonary-edema–sparing pulmonary vascular therapy that lowers PVR/mPAP and improves exercise capacity (e.g., 6MWD) without triggering pulmonary edema.
- Therapy that improves gas exchange to reduce continuous oxygen dependence (raise oxygenation/low DLCO phenotype).

name: Relapsing polychondritis
description: Relapsing polychondritis is a rare autoimmune disease with recurrent inflammation of ear, nose, and airway cartilage, typically presenting in midlife with painful auricular chondritis and inflammatory arthritis. Diagnosis is often delayed, and about half of patients develop airway involvement that can progress to tracheobronchomalacia and life threatening airway collapse. Care is largely empirical and steroid dependent, with no standard, trial proven disease modifying therapy and a strong need for steroid sparing control and earlier, more precise treatment, including in VEXAS overlap associated with higher mortality.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Airway-protective disease control to prevent laryngotracheobronchial collapse/respiratory failure in RP patients with airway involvement
- Steroid-sparing therapy achieving durable remission (~6 months) and reducing flare recurrence in mild–moderately active RP
- Precision therapy for VEXAS/UBA1-mutant RP enabling prednisone tapering below ~10–20 mg/day while controlling inflammatory and hematologic manifestations

name: Renal coloboma syndrome
description: Childhood-onset PAX2-related disorder causing congenital kidney hypoplasia that can progress to end-stage renal disease and optic nerve malformations with variable vision loss and retinal detachment risk; current care is supportive (blood pressure and reflux control, dialysis or transplant, low-vision aids) with major unmet need for disease-modifying therapies that preserve renal function and prevent irreversible vision loss.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying renal therapy targeting the underlying PAX2 defect to delay/prevent progression from renal hypoplasia/hypodysplasia to ESRD (especially pediatric-onset).
- Vision-preservation therapy that reduces retinal detachment risk and preserves visual acuity in optic nerve dysplasia/coloboma beyond supportive measures.
- Renoprotective therapy that durably controls proteinuria/hypertension and mitigates progression to glomerulosclerosis/fibrosis while reducing monitoring/clinic-visit burden.

name: Renal cysts and diabetes syndrome
description: Autosomal dominant HNF1B disorder linking congenital/cystic kidney disease with slowly progressive tubulointerstitial renal failure and early onset non autoimmune diabetes often with pancreatic atrophy and genital tract anomalies. Management is interdisciplinary but largely symptomatic with chronic electrolyte and metabolic burden and no disease modifying or gene therapy options, leaving a need for treatments that preserve kidney function and simplify glycemic control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Kidney-directed HNF1B pathway–restoring therapy to slow eGFR decline and delay ESKD/dialysis in genetically confirmed HNF1B/RCAD.
- Genotype-stratified non-insulin glucose-lowering therapy achieving durable HbA1c control with lower injection/monitoring burden (and less hypoglycemia risk) in HNF1B‑MODY5/RCAD.
- Therapy that reduces renal magnesium wasting to sustainably normalize serum magnesium beyond chronic oral supplementation/pill burden.

name: Renal oncocytoma
description: Benign kidney tumor, typically an incidental renal mass in older adults (often men), but hard to distinguish from renal cell carcinoma on imaging, leading to biopsy, surveillance, ablation, or nephrectomy and a major unmet need for diagnostic confidence to avoid overtreatment while preserving kidney function (especially in hereditary Birt-Hogg-Dubé).
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Noninvasive pharmacologic tumor control/cytoreduction to keep biopsy-proven renal oncocytoma patients on active surveillance and avoid ablation/partial–radical nephrectomy.
- Chemoprevention/chronic growth suppression for hereditary multifocal/bilateral oncocytic renal tumors (e.g., Birt-Hogg-Dubé) to reduce repeated imaging and delay nephron-sparing surgery triggers.
- Low-toxicity systemic therapy for rare metastatic/advanced oncocytoma (or misclassified oncocytic neoplasm) when local excision isn’t curative.

name: Cardiomyopathy | restrictive
description: Restrictive cardiomyopathy is a rare condition where stiff, rigid ventricles cannot relax and fill, progressively reducing cardiac output and causing late presenting heart failure, edema, fatigue, dyspnea, and arrhythmias, often driven in older adults by cardiac amyloidosis from extracellular amyloid fibril deposition. Management is constrained by a fixed stroke volume that makes diuresis and decongestion precarious and by high thromboembolism risk with uncertain anticoagulation choices, leaving a premium on disease modifying approaches that go beyond symptom control toward amyloid fibril clearance.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapies that clear existing cardiac amyloid (not just stabilize TTR) and improve functional/QoL endpoints (e.g., 6MWT, KCCQ) and amyloid burden biomarkers (e.g., myocardial ECV).
- Hemodynamically “safe” decongestion/diastolic symptom control that reduces filling pressures without causing hypotension or low-output states in preload-dependent patients.
- Better-defined, safer thromboembolism prevention in cardiac amyloidosis/RCM atrial disease (high clot risk even without AF) with clearer DOAC vs warfarin selection and lower net bleeding risk.

name: Reticulohistiocytoma
description: Reticulohistiocytoma is a rare non Langerhans histiocytic skin lesion, typically a solitary red brown dermal nodule in young adults where surgical excision is curative. Its systemic form, multicentric reticulohistiocytosis, is a macrophage driven disorder marked by papulonodular skin disease and rapidly destructive erosive arthritis, often presenting in midlife and sometimes as a paraneoplastic syndrome. The major unmet need is for reliably effective, disease modifying therapy that can halt joint destruction and control systemic inflammation since conventional rheumatology agents often fail and no consistently effective treatment is established.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying systemic therapy for multicentric reticulohistiocytosis that prevents rapid progression to severe destructive arthritis/joint deformity (incl. arthritis mutilans).
- Trial-validated, guideline-defining targeted systemic therapy for MRH (vs case-report-driven trial-and-error), e.g., targeting TNFα/IL‑1β/IL‑6 or RANKL/osteoclast pathways.
- Scar-sparing topical/intralesional pharmacologic alternative to surgical excision for solitary cutaneous reticulohistiocytoma.
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus page (as of Apr 2026)

name: Tracheal cancer | squamous cell carcinoma
description: Ultra-rare airway cancer in older male smokers that often goes misdiagnosed as asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease until dyspnea, wheeze or stridor, cough, or hemoptysis signal critical obstruction; few patients are eligible for complete resection and radiotherapy, leaving many reliant on empiric platinum chemoradiation and palliative stenting amid sparse evidence and no standardized guidelines, driving unmet need for durable systemic control and actionable sequencing-guided options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ICI-based regimens that deliver multi-year complete remissions and improve survival beyond chemoradiation/palliative outcomes.
- NGS-guided targeted therapy for actionable TSCC subsets (e.g., PIK3CA/FGFR1 alterations) to move beyond empiric platinum.
- Rapid, procedure-sparing relief of malignant airway obstruction via systemic or locoregional endobronchial therapies to avoid stenting/repeated debulking.

name: Tracheal cancer | carcinoma
description: Ultra rare tracheal windpipe cancer, often smoking associated squamous cell carcinoma in men in their 60s to 70s. Symptoms emerge only after major airway narrowing and are often mistaken for asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, so diagnosis is late and many patients cannot undergo curative surgery. Chemoradiation is common but relapse risk is high, with a premium on durable systemic control and effective post treatment maintenance, including emerging checkpoint immunotherapy strategies now being tested in small phase 2 studies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable-response systemic regimen for unresectable/recurrent tracheal SCC (e.g., achieving ≥2-year CR)
- Consolidation/maintenance immunotherapy after definitive chemoradiotherapy for unresectable tracheal SCC to prevent early metastatic relapse
- Neoadjuvant/downstaging drug therapy to convert initially unresectable tracheal tumors into surgical candidates (or comparable survival)

name: Trench fever
description: Trench fever is a louse borne Bartonella quintana infection concentrated in people experiencing homelessness, marked by relapsing five day fevers with severe headache, dizziness, and shin pain and sometimes rash or splenomegaly. The biggest clinical and public health gap is durable eradication since bacteremia can smolder for months and lead to endocarditis. Standard regimens often require weeks of doxycycline plus two weeks of intravenous gentamicin, which is hard to deliver where access and adherence are limited and carries nephrotoxicity and usually irreversible ototoxicity risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course (≤7–14 day) all-oral or long-acting regimen enabling durable eradication in homeless/low-access patients vs 1‑month + 14‑day IV therapy
- Gentamicin-sparing curative regimen for bacteremia/endocarditis that avoids nephrotoxicity/irreversible ototoxicity and monitoring burden
- Therapies that clear persistent/intraerythrocytic infection to prevent prolonged/relapsing bacteremia and downstream culture-negative endocarditis risk

name: Trichorhinophalangeal syndrome | type 1
description: Trichorhinophalangeal syndrome type 1 is an ultra-rare autosomal dominant TRPS1-related skeletal dysplasia causing short stature, sparse hair, distinctive facial features, and hand and foot abnormalities, with progressive hip dysplasia and joint degeneration that can lead to chronic pain, limited mobility, and even early adult hip replacement. Care is largely supportive with physiotherapy and analgesics such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, leaving a major unmet need for disease-modifying therapies that preserve hip joint integrity and function and for safer long-term pain control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- TRPS1-targeted disease modification to prevent/slow progressive hip dysplasia and joint degeneration, delaying/avoiding early hip replacement.
- Safer long-term non-NSAID therapy for chronic joint pain that preserves mobility/hip range of motion.
- Short-stature therapy with fewer injections and more predictable height gain vs daily somatropin regimens with variable response.

name: Leprosy | tuberculoid
description: Localized paucibacillary Hansen disease with 1–5 well defined hypopigmented lesions and marked sensory loss from peripheral nerve involvement. Disability is driven by immune reactions and neuritis, with reliance on prolonged multidrug antibiotics and prednisone for reactions. Key unmet needs are safer shorter self administered regimens, alternatives for dapsone intolerance and clofazimine discoloration, and steroid sparing control to prevent irreversible nerve damage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing immunomodulators for severe reversal reaction/acute neuritis to prevent rapid irreversible nerve damage
- PB/TT-curative antimicrobial regimens safe for dapsone-intolerant/G6PD-deficient patients and avoiding clofazimine pigmentation/dryness–driven discontinuation
- Ultra-short-course and/or fully self-administered PB regimens that eliminate months-long daily dosing plus monthly supervised dosing

name: Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma
description: Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma is a fast growing, unresectable pediatric brainstem tumor of the pons that typically presents at ages 5 to 10 with rapid cranial nerve deficits, dysphagia and ataxia. Radiation offers only temporary control and median survival remains under 12 months, while symptom management often relies on dexamethasone with major quality of life costs. The biggest bottlenecks are tumor biology and drug delivery across the blood brain barrier, driving demand for disease modifying therapies and steroid sparing approaches that can reach the pons safely.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Radiation-sparing or post-radiotherapy maintenance therapy to prevent the typical 6–12 month post-diagnosis regrowth and extend survival beyond ~11-month median OS.
- Steroid-sparing control of tumor-related edema/symptoms to reduce corticosteroid toxicities that substantially compromise quality of life.
- CNS-penetrant, genotype-selected targeted therapies (e.g., H3K27M, ACVR1/ALK2 subsets) that overcome poor chemo efficacy and blood–brain barrier–limited drug exposure.

name: Harlequin Ichthyosis
description: Severe autosomal recessive ABCA12 driven congenital ichthyosis presenting at birth with thick plate like skin and deep fissures causing ectropion and eclabium and high early risk of dehydration infection sepsis and respiratory failure. Care is largely NICU based supportive management with emollients and sometimes systemic retinoids so major unmet needs are durable skin barrier restoration and disease modifying molecular correction such as gene therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying ABCA12 restoration in neonates (gene/mRNA or gene-corrected skin approach) to re-establish lipid-barrier function and prevent dehydration/infection/respiratory-failure deaths.
- Long-acting, NICU-compatible topical barrier/keratolytic therapy to reduce first-weeks care burden (humidified incubator, close monitoring, 3–8×/day emollients, daily bathing).
- Retinoid-sparing (or skin-restricted) plate/scale-softening therapy that preserves survival benefit while avoiding systemic retinoid toxicities and lab monitoring.

name: Uncombable Hair Syndrome
description: Rare childhood scalp hair shaft disorder causing dry, frizzy, unmanageable hair that will not lie flat due to structural defects often from PADI3, TGM3, or TCHH variants. Symptoms are mainly cosmetic and psychosocial, typically improving by adolescence, but there is no proven therapy beyond gentle hair care and anecdotal biotin, and an unresolved mutation negative subgroup limits targeted treatment options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Follicle-targeted therapy restoring trichohyalin–keratin cross-linking to normalize hair-shaft geometry in genetically defined (PADI3/TGM3/TCHH) UHS.
- Early-childhood treatment providing rapid, cosmetically meaningful improvement (vs waiting for spontaneous improvement by adolescence).
- Pediatric-safe, evidence-backed topical regimen to replace current “no effective treatment”/anecdotal biotin-plus-avoidance care, including an approach for mutation-negative cases.

name: Urbach-Wiethe Disease
description: Urbach Wiethe disease (lipoid proteinosis) is an ultra rare autosomal recessive ECM1 loss disorder causing hyaline like deposits in skin and upper aerodigestive tissues. Infants often present with a weak hoarse cry, then develop fragile blistering skin and mucosal lesions that scar and characteristic beaded eyelid papules. Many patients also develop temporal lobe calcifications with seizures and neurobehavioral symptoms, while progressive laryngeal and airway involvement can drive dysphagia, aphonia and obstruction requiring repeat procedures. Care is largely symptomatic with no established curative or disease modifying therapy and no approved treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical, durable reduction of laryngeal hyaline deposits to improve hoarseness/airway patency and avoid microlaryngoscopic excision/tracheostomy
- Early-life anti-deposition/anti-scarring therapy to prevent vesiculobullous/crusted skin lesions from healing with pock-like/acneiform scars (face/extremities)
- CNS-penetrant therapy targeting temporal-lobe calcification–associated epilepsy/neuropsychiatric sequelae, especially in anti-seizure–refractory patients

name: Spinal muscular atrophy | type 1
description: Infant-onset spinal motor neuron disease caused by SMN1 loss, leading to progressive muscle weakness and wasting with early bulbar and respiratory failure; untreated infants often cannot sit and may die before age 2. Despite disease-modifying therapies, it remains non-curative, and key unmet needs are durable bulbar and respiratory preservation with safer, lower-burden delivery than intrathecal dosing with frequent labs, one-time gene therapy with serious liver toxicity monitoring, or lifelong daily oral treatment.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- SMN-independent add-on (muscle/NMJ-directed) therapy to improve late-treated SMA type 1 infants’ motor milestone attainment (standing/walking).
- Bulbar/respiratory-targeted pharmacotherapy to reduce permanent ventilation and tube-feeding/alternative nutrition in symptomatic SMA type 1.
- Safer, lower-burden, re-dosable disease-modifying approach that avoids intrathecal dosing/monitoring and mitigates gene-therapy hepatic risk/re-dosing limits.

name: Hypercholesterolemia | familial homozygous
description: Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia is a severe inherited disorder causing extremely high low-density lipoprotein cholesterol from infancy, with childhood xanthomas and rapid early atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease including myocardial infarction and aortic stenosis. Even with intensive lipid lowering, many patients cannot reach guideline targets and remain reliant on frequent, time-consuming lipoprotein apheresis. Treatment is further constrained by hepatotoxicity monitoring requirements for some agents and limited efficacy of receptor-dependent drugs in low-density lipoprotein receptor null disease, driving demand for durable low-density lipoprotein receptor independent therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Deeper LDL‑C lowering to reliably reach guideline targets (<100 mg/dL; <70 mg/dL if clinical ASCVD) on therapy.
- LDLR‑null/receptor‑negative options (LDLR‑independent or LDLR‑restoring, incl. gene therapy) for PCSK9‑inhibitor nonresponders.
- Safer, lower‑burden regimens that reduce/avoid weekly/biweekly multi‑hour apheresis and avoid lomitapide hepatotoxicity/REMS monitoring.

name: Glanzmann thrombasthenia
description: Rare congenital platelet aggregation disorder (ITGA2B/ITGB3) causing lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding from infancy, including heavy menstrual bleeding; care is largely reactive with antifibrinolytics, recombinant factor VIIa and platelet transfusions complicated by alloimmunization and refractoriness, leaving a need for durable disease modifying or curative options such as gene therapy or stem cell transplantation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Home-administered prophylaxis that materially lowers annualized bleed rate/severe bleeds (no effective GT prophylaxis today)
- Platelet-transfusion–independent hemostasis for major bleeds/surgery in alloimmunized or platelet-refractory patients
- Menorrhagia-targeted bleeding control that reduces reliance on continuous hormone therapy and lowers iron-deficiency/anemia risk

name: Idiopathic giant cell myocarditis
description: Idiopathic giant cell myocarditis is a rare, immune mediated myocarditis with myocardial necrosis and fibrosis plus multinucleated giant cells that can progress within months to fulminant heart failure, cardiogenic shock, malignant ventricular arrhythmias, heart block, or sudden death, often in young and middle aged adults. Diagnosis requires endomyocardial biopsy, and even with combination immunosuppression many patients still need transplant and face relapse including post transplant, creating demand for rapid ICU compatible disease control and durable maintenance therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid, ICU-compatible disease control for fulminant giant cell myocarditis with cardiogenic shock and incessant ventricular arrhythmias to improve death/transplant/LVAD outcomes
- Steroid- and calcineurin-inhibitor–sparing regimens to reduce nephrotoxicity and infection complications from intensified immunosuppression
- Durable long-term relapse/recurrence prevention in native heart and post-transplant giant cell myocarditis with a clearly defined maintenance regimen

name: Ventricular fibrillation | idiopathic
description: Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation is a diagnosis of exclusion after resuscitated ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest in patients without identifiable structural or secondary causes, often in otherwise healthy adults around their 40s. Recurrence is common and unpredictable, so implantable cardioverter defibrillators are first line but do not prevent future episodes and shocks. Key unmet needs include better substrate modifying prevention, effective trigger identification and ablation, and reliable, well tolerated chronic and rescue pharmacotherapy given largely empirical drug options, quinidine tolerability and access limits, and mixed evidence for isoproterenol in electrical storm.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Chronic VF-suppression specifically for short‑coupled idiopathic VF (PVC coupling interval <350 ms; often DPP6 haplotype) to reduce recurrences/electrical storm and ICD shocks beyond empiric verapamil/quinidine.
- Quinidine-replacement chronic therapy retaining anti‑VF efficacy but with improved tolerability/safety (less QTc prolongation/torsades risk and GI intolerance).
- Rapid, safer rescue pharmacotherapy for electrical storm (≥3 VF/PVT episodes/24h) that reduces reliance on ICU-level IV isoproterenol infusion while reliably terminating clustered events.

name: Glycogen storage disease | type 4
description: Glycogen storage disease type IV is an inherited glycogen branching enzyme disorder where abnormal glycogen accumulates in cells and progressively damages high energy tissues, especially liver and muscle. Many infants present with failure to thrive and hepatomegaly that can rapidly progress to irreversible cirrhosis and early childhood liver failure. There is no specific disease modifying treatment, leaving supportive care and liver transplantation for progressive hepatic disease, while extrahepatic complications such as cardiomyopathy and later onset neurologic disease can continue to progress. Emerging approaches aim to restore enzyme activity or reduce glycogen burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Liver-directed therapies that restore GBE function and/or reduce glycogen synthesis to prevent progressive cirrhosis and avoid liver transplantation in infantile progressive hepatic GSD IV.
- Heart-directed/systemic disease-modifying therapies to prevent or slow cardiomyopathy/arrhythmias (including post–liver transplant progression).
- CNS/PNS-active, mutation-targeted therapies (e.g., ASOs for deep intronic GBE1 variants) to reduce polyglucosan accumulation and progression in adult polyglucosan body disease (APBD).

name: Isobutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency
description: Rare inherited disorder of valine breakdown caused by ACAD8 deficiency, usually detected on newborn screening (elevated C4 acylcarnitine) with most infants asymptomatic. A small unpredictable subset develops hypotonia, vomiting, developmental delay, anemia, and cardiomyopathy. Key unmet needs are clearer natural history and risk stratification and an evidence based, standardized care pathway beyond monitoring, selective L carnitine, and low valine or low protein diet.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable ACAD8 enzyme restoration (e.g., liver-directed gene/mRNA/enzyme replacement) for the rare severe subgroup with cardiomyopathy/hypoglycemia
- Oral ACAD8 pharmacologic chaperone/activator for variants that impair folding/stability
- Substrate-reduction/anti-catabolic therapies to reduce illness/prolonged-fasting vulnerability and relax valine/protein restriction

name: AA amyloidosis
description: AA amyloidosis is a rare secondary amyloidosis driven by chronic inflammation that raises serum amyloid A, leading to AA fibril deposition most often in the kidneys. Typical patients have long standing inflammatory disease such as rheumatoid arthritis and present with proteinuria that can progress to nephrotic syndrome, edema, and end stage kidney disease requiring dialysis. Management largely focuses on controlling the underlying inflammatory or infectious driver, but once renal function is significantly impaired it rarely recovers, underscoring the need for disease modifying therapies that clear deposits and preserve kidney function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drugs that actively clear established AA amyloid deposits to reverse organ dysfunction (vs inflammation control alone)
- Renal-protective therapies that reduce proteinuria and preserve eGFR/CrCL to delay/prevent ESRD/ESKD
- Biologic-sparing long-term SAA suppression with lower infection risk and less frequent/non-injectable dosing burden

name: Alström syndrome
description: Rare autosomal recessive multisystem genetic disorder beginning in infancy with nystagmus and photophobia and progressive retinal degeneration leading to blindness in the second decade, plus hearing loss, obesity and type 2 diabetes, and sometimes early dilated cardiomyopathy with later liver, kidney, bladder, and lung disease; no disease specific therapy, so major unmet needs are disease modifying treatments and better preservation of vision and cardiac function with improved appetite and weight control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Vision-preserving retinal/ciliary therapy to maintain cone–rod function into adulthood (delay/avoid blindness by ~age 20).
- Cardiomyopathy-modifying therapy for genetically diagnosed infants (onset ~3 weeks–4 months) to prevent irreversible heart failure/early death and later recurrent CHF.
- Appetite/weight-loss plus insulin-sensitizing therapy for hyperphagic children/adolescents with early-onset obesity to achieve ≥10% 52-week weight loss, reduce hunger, and lessen need for multi-daily insulin injections.

name: Bietti crystalline dystrophy
description: Bietti crystalline dystrophy is an autosomal recessive, CYP4V2 driven retinal degeneration where lipid crystals accumulate in the retina, causing progressive night blindness, peripheral field loss, and declining acuity beginning in the teens or twenties and often leading to legal blindness by midlife. It is currently untreatable and vision loss is not correctable with glasses, creating a premium for disease modifying therapy delivered early enough to preserve remaining retina and accessible to patients too advanced for subretinal gene therapy eligibility.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Preserve rod-driven night vision and peripheral visual field (not just BCVA) in teens–30s with CYP4V2-confirmed BCD to delay driving-eligibility loss/legal blindness
- Vision-restorative options for advanced BCD with severe retinal degeneration/low photoreceptor reserve excluded from current gene-replacement trials (e.g., retinal thickness <100 μm)
- Less invasive delivery than subretinal injection (e.g., non-surgical) that enables earlier treatment and broader eligible populations

name: Gnathostomiasis
description: Gnathostomiasis is a foodborne nematode infection from eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish and other hosts, often in travelers or people in endemic areas. Weeks after exposure, larvae migrate through tissue causing recurrent, migratory, painful or itchy non pitting subcutaneous swellings with eosinophilia that can relapse for months or years and occasionally invade the eyes or nervous system with severe outcomes. Treatment relies on albendazole or ivermectin, but relapses are common and some series report first course cure rates as low as 40%, creating demand for short course, relapse free oral therapy and safer options for ocular and neurologic disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course (≤2 days) oral therapy achieving durable relapse-free cure through ≥26 months for cutaneous gnathostomiasis.
- CNS/ocular-active antihelminthic (± adjunct) that can be treated without provoking larval migration/flare to prevent death/permanent neurologic deficit.
- New-mechanism antihelminthic (or rational combination) for recurrent/relapsing disease to overcome incomplete cure and potential drug resistance beyond albendazole/ivermectin.

name: Vibrio vulnificus infection
description: Vibrio vulnificus infection is a fulminant seafood or seawater borne bacterial disease that in high risk adults with liver disease, diabetes, or immunocompromise can progress within about 24 hours from cellulitis to necrotizing soft tissue infection, septic shock, and limb loss. Outcomes remain poor despite antibiotics and aggressive surgery, with about 20% mortality overall and septicemia fatality over 50%, creating unmet needs for faster diagnosis, resistance robust antimicrobials, and adjunctive therapies that blunt toxin driven tissue destruction and dissemination.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct anti-toxin/anti-virulence therapy (e.g., neutralizing MARTX/rtxA1 and/or VvhA) to prevent rapid toxin-driven tissue necrosis/dissemination despite antibiotics
- Resistance-robust “immediate-start” therapy for septic presentations to improve survival beyond current outcomes where mortality remains high even with timely antibiotics
- Simplified, safer regimen (ideally single-dose/once-daily + oral step-down) to replace q8h parenteral ceftazidime + doxycycline multi-day therapy, especially in renal/hepatic dysfunction

name: Yersiniosis
description: Foodborne diarrheal illness (Yersinia enterocolitica or Yersinia pseudotuberculosis) most common in young children, causing fever, abdominal pain and sometimes bloody diarrhea lasting weeks; treated mainly with rehydration and supportive care with antibiotics for severe cases, but current therapy does not prevent postinfectious sequelae such as reactive arthritis and erythema nodosum, leaving gaps in prevention and faster pediatric symptom control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct/prophylactic therapy that prevents post‑infectious reactive arthritis and/or erythema nodosum (antibiotics don’t prevent sequelae)
- Oral pediatric therapy that shortens prolonged diarrhea and reduces rapid dehydration risk beyond supportive care
- Short‑course, outpatient‑feasible regimen for severe/invasive yersiniosis in iron‑overload patients to avoid prolonged IV ceftriaxone + gentamicin

name: Nephropathy | C1q-mediated
description: C1q nephropathy is a rare, biopsy-defined glomerular disease seen often in older children and young adults, driven by dominant mesangial C1q immune deposits without systemic lupus erythematosus. Patients may be asymptomatic or develop heavy proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome with edema, sometimes hematuria, hypertension, and declining kidney function. Care is empiric, relying on corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants, but steroid resistance is common and evidence is limited by a lack of randomized trials. Even with treatment, some patients progress to chronic kidney disease and end stage renal disease, underscoring the need for more reliable, disease modifying options that sustain remission and preserve renal function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable complete remission/proteinuria control in steroid-resistant nephrotic-syndrome patients (esp. FSGS-pattern disease) to prevent CKD/ESRD progression
- Mechanism-/subtype-directed therapy (e.g., targeting C1q-driven immune activation) for the immune-complex/proliferative-GN subtype
- Steroid/CNI-sparing regimens that maintain remission with lower toxicity and less monitoring/infusion burden

name: C3 glomerulopathy
description: C3 glomerulopathy is an ultra rare kidney disease driven by dysregulated alternative complement activation that deposits C3 in the glomeruli, causing hematuria, heavy proteinuria, edema, hypertension, and progressive loss of kidney function. About half of patients reach end stage kidney failure within 10 years and recurrence after kidney transplant is common, so dialysis and graft loss remain real risks. Complement inhibitors are an emerging approach but long term use is constrained by serious encapsulated bacterial infection risk plus vaccination and restricted access requirements, keeping demand high for safer, durable kidney and graft protection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- True disease‑modifying kidney protection (improve eGFR slope; prevent kidney failure and graft loss), including reducing post‑transplant C3G recurrence
- Improved efficacy in biologically defined hard‑to‑treat C3G (e.g., genetic‑mutation–driven disease and/or dense deposit disease) with less relapse after stopping therapy
- Complement therapies with lower serious infection/REMS burden and simpler administration vs current oral BID and SC twice‑weekly regimens

name: Fibrillary glomerulonephritis
description: Fibrillary glomerulonephritis is a rare glomerular kidney disease marked by Congo red negative fibril deposits that cause heavy proteinuria, hematuria, hypertension, and progressive loss of renal function, often in middle aged patients. Despite improved diagnosis with DNAJB9 testing, there is no disease specific therapy and nearly half progress to kidney failure within about four years, leaving transplantation as a last resort. Graft recurrence is common, and secondary forms linked to monoclonal gammopathy, autoimmune disease, or malignancy are often excluded from trials, underscoring the need for disease modifying and recurrence preventing strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Renal-response disease modification in primary/idiopathic FGN (durable proteinuria remission with stable eGFR).
- Clone/driver-targeted therapies for secondary FGN (esp. monoclonal protein/MGRS) populations excluded from idiopathic trials.
- Pharmacologic prevention/treatment of post–kidney-transplant FGN recurrence to protect graft function.
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus page for fibrillary glomerulonephritis; closest: https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000484.htm

name: Hepatic glomerulopathy
description: Kidney glomerular injury seen in cirrhosis and portal hypertension, typically hepatic immunoglobulin A nephropathy causing mesangial immunoglobulin A deposition with microscopic hematuria and proteinuria; a minority progress to nephrotic syndrome or renal impairment. Treatment is limited by decompensated cirrhosis, where infection risk is high and standard antiproteinuric or portal pressure therapies can worsen hypotension and renal perfusion, creating demand for renal perfusion neutral, infection sparing approaches and portal hypertension targeted disease modification.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Infection-sparing, non-steroid therapy for the high-risk “intrinsic AKI + heavy proteinuria/MPGN-like” cirrhosis-IgAN subset, reducing AKI/dialysis events and mortality.
- Renal-perfusion–neutral antiproteinuric therapy usable in decompensated cirrhosis/ascites where ACEi/ARB are often avoided, improving hematuria/proteinuria without hypotension/AKI.
- Portal-hypertension–targeted therapy that improves proteinuria/hematuria without the renal-perfusion penalty/risk of hepatorenal syndrome seen with nonselective beta-blockade in advanced disease.

name: Hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis
description: Rare immune complex small vessel vasculitis marked by chronic urticaria and low complement, often with anti-C1q antibodies, typically in middle aged women. Painful hives can persist beyond 24 hours and bruise as they heal. Multisystem involvement is common with joint, eye, lung, and kidney disease, with pulmonary involvement a major driver of morbidity and mortality. Management relies on long term glucocorticoids and other immunosuppressants, creating unmet need for durable steroid sparing control that prevents organ damage, especially in lungs and kidneys.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Complement/anti‑C1q–pathway, steroid‑sparing therapy that prevents or reverses pulmonary involvement (COPD/emphysema) in HUVS.
- Kidney‑protective, steroid/cytotoxic‑sparing therapy for HUV patients with glomerulonephritis (proteinuria/hematuria) at risk of renal failure.
- Durable steroid‑sparing disease control that prevents relapse during taper/discontinuation and reduces polypharmacy (≥3 drugs), ideally improving UVAS7.

name: Lightwood-Albright Syndrome
description: Lightwood–Albright syndrome is a neonatal, often transient distal renal tubular acidosis causing impaired kidney acidification with infant failure to thrive, vomiting and constipation, and risk of nephrocalcinosis and kidney stones. Care relies on oral alkali (bicarbonate or citrate) and sometimes potassium, but metabolic control is often suboptimal because dosing is frequent and formulations are hard to tolerate, leaving need for better sustained acid control and kidney protection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Palatable, pediatric-ready alkali therapy that reduces q3–6h (incl. overnight) administration to ≤BID dosing in neonates/infants
- Sustained biochemical control of metabolic acidosis (target serum bicarbonate thresholds ± potassium) despite current adherence/tolerability limits
- Kidney-protective adjuncts to prevent and ideally reverse nephrocalcinosis/nephrolithiasis and downstream renal damage

name: Malakoplakia
description: Malakoplakia is a rare chronic granulomatous inflammatory disease, typically in immunocompromised patients, driven by defective macrophage bacterial killing and causing bladder plaques or masses that mimic cancer with hematuria, recurrent urinary tract infections, and obstruction that can progress to hydronephrosis. Treatment relies on prolonged intracellularly active antibiotics plus procedures such as excision or stenting, but guidelines and optimal duration are unclear, leaving unmet needs for organ sparing, immunosuppression compatible, macrophage restoring approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Macrophage-targeted intracellular eradication (restore phagocyte killing/cGMP defect) to avoid prolonged, uncertain-duration antibiotics
- Organ-sparing medical control for aggressive upper-urinary-tract disease to preserve renal function and avoid nephrectomy/stenting/resection
- Long-term-tolerable regimens compatible with ongoing immunosuppression with fewer severe AEs/interactions and reduced monitoring burden
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus URL for Malakoplakia

name: Monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance
description: Monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance is kidney injury from a nephrotoxic monoclonal immunoglobulin made by a small plasma cell or B cell clone that does not meet myeloma or lymphoma criteria, typically presenting later in life with unexplained proteinuria, microscopic hematuria, and progressive renal impairment requiring biopsy for diagnosis. Treatment is clone directed but heterogeneous biology and thin evidence mean kidney recovery is unreliable even with deep hematologic responses, leaving strong unmet need for kidney safe disease modifying options that consistently reduce proteinuria and preserve renal function, including in complement mediated lesions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Renal-response–restoring therapies for MGRS lesions (esp. PGNMID/C3GN) that reliably reduce proteinuria and preserve/improve eGFR.
- Deep, durable B‑cell–clone control beyond rituximab backbones (e.g., IgM/B‑cell–driven MGRS).
- Kidney-compatible, lower-toxicity and lower-visit-burden alternatives to current clone-directed regimens used in MGRS.
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus URL for MGRS

name: Pseudoporphyria
description: Pseudoporphyria is a porphyria cutanea tarda like blistering photodermatosis with normal porphyrin tests, often in chronic kidney disease patients on dialysis, causing sun exposed skin fragility and tense blisters on hands and feet that can scar and form milia. Care is mainly trigger withdrawal and strict photoprotection, but symptoms can persist and haemodialysis associated disease has no specific, standardized therapy, leaving a need for renal safe treatments that rapidly clear lesions and prevent scarring.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Faster blister/lesion clearance with prevention of scarring and milia vs trigger-withdrawal + photoprotection
- Renal-safe therapy for dialysis/CKD-associated pseudoporphyria when the trigger can’t be removed and/or N-acetylcysteine fails
- Trigger-agnostic prophylaxis/maintenance that reduces reliance on strict photoprotection and daily sun-avoidance measures

name: Retroperitoneal fibrosis
description: Rare immune mediated fibroinflammatory disorder where a retroperitoneal mass progressively encases the ureters, often in middle aged men, causing insidious abdominal or flank pain and high risk of hydronephrosis and kidney failure. Treatment relies on corticosteroids plus urgent decompression with ureteral stents or nephrostomy, but relapse during steroid taper is common and many patients remain device dependent, creating demand for faster, steroid sparing therapies that durably shrink the mass and preserve renal function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing induction/maintenance that prevents relapse during/after prednisone tapering while reducing glucocorticoid toxicity
- Rapid regression of retroperitoneal mass to relieve ureteric obstruction and achieve freedom from ureteric stent/nephrostomy
- Better-tolerated targeted therapy for relapsing/refractory idiopathic or IgG4-related RPF after steroid failure with lower serious infection risk and improved device-free outcomes

name: Tumor lysis syndrome
description: Tumor lysis syndrome is an acute metabolic emergency after rapid cancer cell breakdown, typically following therapy for high burden chemosensitive blood cancers, causing hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, and hypocalcemia that can quickly progress to acute kidney injury, arrhythmias, seizures, and death. Care depends on aggressive hydration, close inpatient level monitoring, and urate and electrolyte control, but current options are constrained by slow urate reduction with allopurinol and contraindication of rasburicase in glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, leaving a need for faster, safer urate lowering and less burdensome monitoring that enables safer outpatient treatment ramps.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- G6PD-safe “rasburicase-equivalent” rapid urate control for TLS patients contraindicated for rasburicase
- Rapid therapies to prevent/severely reduce ICU/dialysis escalation by quickly controlling hyperphosphatemia/hyperkalemia and protecting kidneys (AKI/renal replacement therapy)
- Outpatient-enabling, rapid-onset prophylaxis for malignancy-associated (secondary) hyperuricemia/TLS risk (faster than XO inhibitors; label-supported in malignant disease settings)

name: Ureteritis cystica
description: Ureteritis cystica is a rare, benign reactive change in the ureter lining caused by chronic urothelial irritation, most often from recurrent urinary tract infections or kidney stones, and is frequently found incidentally in otherwise asymptomatic patients. Lesions can mimic urothelial cancer on imaging, driving invasive workups and diagnostic uncertainty. With no disease specific guidelines, care centers on treating and preventing the underlying triggers, creating unmet needs for better noninvasive risk stratification and antibiotic sparing strategies to reduce recurrent infection and stone related irritation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Antibiotic-sparing prevention of recurrent cystitis/UTIs (e.g., methenamine hippurate or other non-antibiotic prophylaxis) in the chronic-UTI phenotype linked to ureteritis cystica
- Stone-prevention/stone-dissolution pharmacotherapy for ureteritis cystica patients with recurrent nephrolithiasis to reduce chronic urothelial irritation
- Ureter-directed anti-inflammatory/anti-fibrotic therapy for the rare obstructive/painful phenotype to prevent cyst/scar-related obstruction

name: Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia | symptomatic
description: Symptomatic Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a rare, indolent lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma of older adults where marrow cells overproduce immunoglobulin M, causing fatigue from anemia, peripheral neuropathy, and hyperviscosity with bleeding and neurologic or visual symptoms. Management is chronic rather than curative, with needs for faster immunoglobulin M debulking without rituximab related flare, safer sequencing to prevent rebound hyperviscosity after Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor interruption, and more durable options for molecular subgroups such as MYD88 wild type disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Effective salvage options after covalent BTK inhibitor resistance/intolerance (e.g., BTK C481S/PLCG2) to avoid dangerous IgM rebound/hyperviscosity after ibrutinib discontinuation.
- Regimens that deliver major, durable responses in genotype-defined poor responders (MYD88-wild-type and CXCR4-mutated WM).
- Rapid, deep IgM debulking for high-IgM patients without rituximab-associated IgM flare/hyperviscosity (reducing need for prophylactic/urgent plasmapheresis).

name: Birt-Hogg-Dubé Syndrome
description: Birt Hogg Dubé syndrome is a rare inherited folliculin gene disorder that causes recurrent facial and neck skin papules, lung cysts with spontaneous pneumothorax, and an elevated risk of kidney tumors. Management is largely lifelong surveillance and repeated procedures such as serial renal imaging and nephron sparing intervention around a 3 cm tumor threshold, since lesions often recur. The key unmet needs are disease modifying therapies that prevent or slow lung cyst formation and pneumothorax and reduce the chronic burden of recurrent skin and renal interventions, beyond monitoring and surgery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Renal tumor chemoprevention/growth-control to keep tumors <3 cm and delay/avoid nephron-sparing intervention
- Pulmonary disease-modifying therapy to reduce new lung cysts and lower spontaneous pneumothorax recurrence/time-to-recurrence
- Durable topical/systemic therapy for fibrofolliculomas to sustainably reduce lesion size/count and prevent recurrence without repeated procedures

name: Nephrotic syndrome | congenital
description: Rare infant onset kidney disease, usually genetic podocyte defects such as NPHS1, that disrupts the glomerular filtration barrier and causes massive protein loss with edema and ascites, infection and thrombosis risk, poor growth, and rapid progression to kidney failure in early childhood. Care is largely supportive and high burden, often requiring months of daily intravenous albumin via central lines with line related complications, followed by dialysis and kidney transplant. A major unmet need is safe disease modifying therapy that reduces proteinuria and delays or avoids renal replacement therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Podocyte/genetic-defect–targeted disease modification to prevent/delay progression to ESRD (~2–3 years in Finnish type) and avoid/meaningfully delay transplant.
- Sustained proteinuria suppression that eliminates chronic parenteral albumin + IV diuretic replacement via central venous catheters.
- Infant-safe reduction of thrombosis/infection risk by avoiding central venous lines and/or reducing need for prolonged prophylactic anticoagulation/hospitalization.

name: Diffuse mesangial sclerosis
description: Rare infantile glomerular disorder marked by progressive mesangial scarring causing congenital nephrotic syndrome with heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and edema in utero or in the first 3 months of life, often progressing to kidney failure within weeks to months. Management is largely supportive and high burden, sometimes requiring daily albumin infusions via central venous lines with infection and thrombosis risk and variable antiproteinuric control, highlighting the need for infant-safe disease modifying, mechanism targeted therapies that can delay or avoid dialysis and transplant.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- WT1/PLCE1 genotype-/mechanism-targeted therapy to delay/avoid ESRD (dialysis-/transplant-free survival) in infants
- Antiproteinuric efficacy sufficient to eliminate near-daily IV albumin infusions and central venous line dependence
- Non-immunosuppressive, infant-safe therapy that reduces need for nephrectomy/dialysis/transplant and intensive monitoring

name: Nephropathy | mesoamerican
description: Mesoamerican nephropathy is an epidemic of chronic kidney disease of unknown cause in Pacific coast Central America, disproportionately affecting young male agricultural workers such as sugarcane cutters who often lack diabetes or hypertension and show a low protein, tubulointerstitial phenotype with electrolyte and urate abnormalities. The disease is thought to be driven by recurrent heat stress and dehydration, potentially compounded by environmental exposures, and is often detected only when creatinine is elevated on pre harvest screening. There are no proven disease modifying drugs to slow progression, making scalable prevention, early detection, and kidney protective interventions the key unmet needs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Harvest-season prophylaxis for sugarcane cutters/high-heat agricultural workers that blocks heat/dehydration injury pathways to prevent recurrent subclinical AKI and CKD progression
- Uric-acid/urate-crystalluria–targeted therapy for the tubulointerstitial MeN/CKDu phenotype to reduce inflammation and slow kidney-function decline
- Dehydration-safe outpatient drug strategy to prevent recurrent symptomatic hypokalemia (cramps/weakness) and reduce repeat emergency visits

name: Nephropathy | MUC1-associated
description: Autosomal dominant MUC1 driven tubulointerstitial kidney disease with a bland urinalysis and often silent onset in late teens or early adulthood, progressing steadily to end stage renal disease requiring dialysis or transplant. Care today is supportive chronic kidney disease management because there are no disease specific therapies, and diagnosis often depends on genetic testing. Key unmet needs are earlier scalable biomarkers and disease modifying approaches that clear the toxic MUC1 frameshift protein and dampen downstream stress signaling to slow progression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- MUC1fs-directed therapies that slow eGFR decline and delay progression to ESRD/dialysis/transplant.
- Cytoprotective agents that blunt MUC1fs-driven ER-stress/UPR signaling (e.g., ATF6) to prevent tubular cell loss.
- Treat-early enablement via specialized MUC1‑VNTR variant diagnostics plus scalable blood/urine pharmacodynamic biomarkers.

name: Scleroderma renal crisis
description: Scleroderma renal crisis is a life threatening kidney emergency in systemic sclerosis marked by abrupt severe hypertension and rapidly progressive renal failure, often early in diffuse disease and enriched in anti RNA polymerase III positive patients. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors are essential once crisis begins but do not prevent it, and many patients still require dialysis with substantial early mortality. The unmet need is earlier risk prediction and prevention, plus kidney protective and rescue approaches for thrombotic microangiopathy, potentially including complement targeted strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- True prophylactic therapy (non-ACEi) to prevent SRC in anti–RNA polymerase III–positive systemic-sclerosis patients
- Add-on renal vasculoprotective therapy beyond ACE inhibitors to improve 6–12 month renal function and dialysis-free survival
- Targeted anti-TMA/complement-pathway rescue for high-risk normotensive SRC to improve renal outcomes and survival

name: Lymphoma | Sézary syndrome
description: Rare, aggressive leukemic cutaneous T cell lymphoma with malignant T cells in blood, skin, and lymph nodes; typically affects adults 50+ and often presents with near whole body erythroderma and severe itch, sleep disruption, and high infection risk. No curative standard and many need lifelong therapy, leaving unmet need for durable multi compartment disease control with rapid itch relief and fewer toxicities and clinic burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable multi-compartment (skin/lymph node/blood) disease control that improves survival in leukemic/blood-involved Sézary syndrome
- Rapid, sustained reduction of erythroderma and severe pruritus (itch/QoL) in the typical ≥80% BSA red/itchy phenotype
- Safer, less clinic-intensive systemic therapy for older/frail patients (lower serious infection/skin toxicity and reduced IV infusion burden)

name: Medullary cystic kidney disease | type 2
description: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease due to UMOD is a hereditary, slowly progressive tubulointerstitial nephropathy that typically begins in adolescence or early adulthood, often with polyuria and polydipsia plus hyperuricemia and gout despite a bland urinalysis. Patients gradually lose kidney function and many ultimately require dialysis or transplant. Care today is largely supportive since there are no specific disease modifying treatments, leaving a premium on mechanism based therapies that preserve renal function by addressing UMOD protein misfolding and endoplasmic reticulum stress, while reducing the lifelong gout and hydration burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Kidney-function–preserving, mechanism-targeted therapy for ADTKD‑UMOD that slows eGFR decline/delays ESKD
- Therapy to improve urinary concentrating defect (isosthenuria) and reduce dehydration risk without worsening hyperuricemia
- Safer, more convenient lifelong urate-lowering/gout-prevention options (including for allopurinol intolerance) with lower hypersensitivity risk

name: Nephropathic cystinosis
