description: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is a congenital cardiac conduction disorder caused by an accessory pathway that bypasses the atrioventricular node, leading to abrupt episodes of supraventricular tachycardia with palpitations, dyspnea, chest discomfort, and sometimes syncope. The central unmet need is preventing rare but catastrophic pre-excited atrial fibrillation that can trigger ventricular fibrillation and sudden death, especially because common atrioventricular node blocking drugs are contraindicated. Catheter ablation can be curative, but procedural risk is higher for some pathway locations, leaving a subset reliant on imperfect long-term antiarrhythmic control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer acute conversion for hemodynamically stable pre-excited AF without torsades/proarrhythmia risk or need for continuous ECG-monitored IV infusion.
- Non-ablative chronic suppression for higher-ablation-risk pathways (esp. pediatric anteroseptal/midseptal) that reduces recurrence without iatrogenic AV block.
- Fast, non-IV episode-abort therapy for recurrent orthodromic AVRT/SVT usable outpatient/prehospital to avoid ED-only IV workflows.

name: Spasm of accommodation
description: Spasm of accommodation is a rare, often stress triggered functional focusing disorder in children and adolescents where ciliary muscle overconstriction causes episodic pseudomyopia with distance blur, headaches, eye pain and sometimes miosis with acute inward eye turn. Diagnosis hinges on cycloplegic refraction showing reduced myopia. Treatment relies on cycloplegic drops, but photophobia, blurred vision and systemic side effects like flushing, fever and drowsiness limit use and adherence, and relapses are common with anxiety and near work. Better tolerated, pupil sparing, fast offset therapies with durable relapse prevention are needed.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pupil-sparing, rapid-offset accommodative-relaxant drop to clear pseudomyopic distance blur without prolonged near-vision impairment/photophobia
- Pediatric-optimized therapy with minimal systemic/CNS toxicity (esp. children/neurologically vulnerable) vs atropine/cyclopentolate risks
- Durable relapse-prevention therapy for recurrent/trigger-associated disease (near-work and stress/anxiety) with standardized regimen

name: Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis
description: Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis is a rapidly onset, painful viral conjunctivitis marked by tearing, lid swelling, and subconjunctival hemorrhage, most often from enterovirus 70 or coxsackievirus A24 variant, and it spreads efficiently via hand to eye contact with high attack rates in crowded settings. Illness typically resolves in 10 to 14 days, but outbreaks disrupt schools and workplaces. Care is largely supportive, leaving a premium on topical antivirals or virucidals that shorten disease, reduce contagiousness, and provide steroid sparing symptom control plus practical prophylaxis to curb epidemics.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Etiology-targeted topical antivirals/virucidals for enteroviral AHC (CA24v/EV70) to shorten illness duration/time off work or school vs supportive care.
- Steroid-sparing topical anti-inflammatory/analgesic to rapidly reduce pain/swelling/hemorrhage in severe cases where corticosteroids are contraindicated.
- Outbreak-ready post-exposure prophylaxis (e.g., once-daily virucidal drops) for household/school contacts to lower secondary transmission/attack rates.

name: Adenomyoma
description: Adenomyoma is a focal form of adenomyosis where endometrial tissue grows into the uterine muscle, thickening the wall and often mimicking fibroids. It typically affects premenopausal multiparous women and causes heavy menstrual bleeding, worsening painful periods, and pelvic pain, with possible links to infertility. Current care is largely symptomatic with hormones and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and severe cases often progress to hysterectomy, leaving a major gap for uterus sparing, fertility compatible options that reliably control symptoms and preserve reproductive potential.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Fertility-compatible, non-hormonal control of heavy bleeding and pain for patients inadequately controlled on hormones or who want to avoid hormones and still conceive.
- A fertility-outcomes–driven medical regimen for adenomyosis/adenomyoma-associated subfertility/IVF with endpoints like pregnancy and live birth.
- A uterus-sparing, disease-modifying therapy that delivers durable symptom relief plus objective lesion/uterine-burden reduction to avoid hysterectomy.

name: Otitis media | adhesive
description: Adhesive otitis media is an advanced inflammation driven middle ear disorder where a thinned, retracted tympanic membrane adheres to the middle ear wall, locking the ossicular chain and causing conductive hearing loss, aural fullness, otorrhea, otalgia, and tinnitus. Often arising from Eustachian tube dysfunction and persistent effusion, it can be subtle in children yet impair hearing enough to affect speech and language development. Progression risks include ossicular erosion and cholesteatoma, but management remains largely procedural with tubes, tympanoplasty, and reconstruction because medical therapies are inconsistent and durable anti adhesion options are lacking.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying medical therapy targeting persistent OME drivers (e.g., Eustachian tube dysfunction/inflammation) to prevent adhesive disease and deliver durable hearing normalization.
- Local middle-ear anti-adhesion/anti-remodeling therapy for established adhesive otitis media to prevent ossicular destruction/cholesteatoma and improve conductive hearing without surgery.
- Long-acting, low-burden ototopical therapy to prevent/treat post-grommet otorrhea with fewer dosing days and no systemic antibiotics.

name: Advanced sleep phase syndrome
description: Advanced sleep phase syndrome is a circadian rhythm disorder where an “early bird” internal clock drives sleepiness in the late afternoon, early evening bedtimes, and very early morning awakenings, often impairing work and social life and being mistaken for insomnia or depression. Management relies on evening bright light therapy and precisely timed melatonin, which can be burdensome and timing sensitive, with relapse when treatment stops. Key unmet needs include convenient, durable phase delaying treatments and genotype informed options for familial forms linked to PER2 and casein kinase 1 delta.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Once-daily, non-sedating circadian phase–delayer that reliably shifts sleep onset/offset ≥2 hours later to reduce early-morning/maintenance insomnia and evening sleepiness.
- Genotype-directed therapy for familial ASPS (e.g., PER2 S662G or CSNK1D mutations) that normalizes clock protein phosphorylation/period.
- Non-photic phase-shifting drug alternative for patients who can’t tolerate/should avoid bright-light therapy (e.g., ocular disease/photosensitizers or bipolar mania risk) with low neuropsychiatric activation and ocular safety.

name: Atrophic glossitis
description: Atrophic glossitis is a “bald tongue” condition marked by partial or complete loss of dorsal tongue papillae, leaving a smooth glossy surface and often causing burning and taste changes. It is commonly secondary to hematinic deficiencies such as iron, folate, and vitamin B12 deficiency and to local drivers like dry mouth and oral candidiasis. Care is largely indirect and burdensome, with malabsorption related vitamin B12 deficiency often requiring lifelong injections and antifungal therapy relying on frequent dosing and difficult administration, leaving a need for easier long term nutrient replacement, saliva restoring therapies, and longer acting anti Candida options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-injectable vitamin B12 replacement matching rapid (~2-week) symptom normalization for pernicious anemia/malabsorption patients who otherwise need frequent/lifelong IM injections.
- More effective/better-tolerated saliva-restoring pharmacotherapy for medication/radiation/chronic-condition–associated hyposalivation to reduce xerostomia-driven recurrence.
- Long-acting, high-retention topical anti–C. albicans therapy to reduce adherence burden vs QID nystatin regimens (incl. post-dose fasting).

name: Atrophic rhinitis
description: Atrophic rhinitis (ozena) is a chronic nasal disease marked by progressive atrophy of the nasal mucosa and underlying bone, widening the nasal cavities and causing severe dryness, crusting, foul smelling discharge, obstruction, loss of smell, and nosebleeds that can be socially disabling, often in women in early to mid adulthood. Management is largely burdensome maintenance with frequent irrigation and intermittent antibiotics, but crusting commonly recurs and no durable therapy restores mucosa or reliably controls infection, leaving unmet need for long lasting hydration, targeted local antibacterial control, and nonsurgical mucosal regeneration.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical mucosal-regeneration/secretory-restoration therapy for patients with persistent crusting/ozena to reduce recurrence.
- Targeted *Klebsiella ozaenae* eradication (preferably local/topical, anti-recurrence) to improve cacosmia/crusting without prolonged systemic antibiotics.
- Long-acting intranasal hydration/anti-crusting therapy to replace 3–4×/day irrigations while maintaining crusting/odor control.

name: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
description: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity driven, immune mediated airway disease from Aspergillus fumigatus colonization, usually in people with asthma or cystic fibrosis, causing wheeze, dyspnea, mucus plugging and transient infiltrates. Delayed recognition can allow irreversible bronchiectasis and lung function decline. Care still relies on systemic steroids and oral azole antifungals, but long term control is limited by steroid toxicity plus frequent drug interactions and therapeutic drug monitoring with azoles, driving demand for safer steroid sparing anti inflammatory therapies and more practical ways to reduce airway fungal burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-steroidal (or truly steroid-sparing) acute ABPA control matching systemic glucocorticoids while avoiding high steroid toxicity.
- Maintenance therapy for treatment-dependent/recurrent ABPA to prevent exacerbations, reduce steroid exposure, and slow bronchiectasis progression.
- Airway-directed antifungal/antigen-burden reduction that avoids systemic azole drug–drug interactions and hepatotoxicity/TDM monitoring burden (incl. ICS–azole Cushing’s risk).

name: Testicular atrophy
description: Testicular atrophy is a clinically meaningful reduction in testicular volume, often arising after infarction, inflammation, varicocele, cryptorchidism, or trauma and commonly discovered during infertility evaluation with hypogonadal symptoms such as low libido. The condition reduces spermatogenesis and fertility, yet treatment is constrained by a core tradeoff. Testosterone replacement can improve androgen deficiency but suppresses sperm production, while fertility preserving hormonal induction relies on frequent self injected gonadotropins and regular lab monitoring. For primary testicular failure there are still no approved drugs that reliably restore spermatogenesis, leaving a major unmet need for disease modifying, fertility sparing therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Fertility-preserving androgen restoration that raises testosterone without suppressing spermatogenesis in men trying to conceive
- Long-acting/oral spermatogenesis-induction regimens to reduce frequent injections/monitoring vs current gonadotropin protocols
- Testis-protective/regenerative drug therapies to improve testicular volume and sperm output after post-injury or post-infectious atrophy

name: Autism spectrum disorder | level 3
description: Autism spectrum disorder is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition marked by persistent social communication deficits and restricted or repetitive behaviors. Severe Level 3 cases often have minimal social initiation and response, few intelligible words, and extreme inflexibility that disrupts daily functioning. Needs typically become evident by ages 2 to 3, and about 30 percent remain minimally verbal despite years of intervention. Current drugs mainly target irritability and can cause weight gain and somnolence, leaving major unmet need for weight neutral, non sedating options that improve functional communication and reduce rigidity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Clinically meaningful functional expressive-communication gains for the ~30% of children with ASD who remain minimally verbal despite years of intervention.
- Non-sedating, weight-neutral pharmacologic control of irritability/aggression/self-injury comparable to risperidone/aripiprazole but without metabolic/somnolence burden.
- Meaningful reduction of restricted/repetitive behaviors and rigidity on validated RRB scales (e.g., CY-BOCS-PDD, RBS-R).

name: Gastritis | autoimmune
description: Autoimmune metaplastic atrophic gastritis is a chronic immune-mediated destruction of parietal cells in the gastric corpus and fundus, leading to low or absent acid and intrinsic factor deficiency. It often presents in women around age 60 and is discovered after unexplained anemia, with patients requiring lifelong parenteral vitamin B12 and often iron plus periodic endoscopic surveillance. Ongoing hypergastrinemia increases risk of type 1 gastric neuroendocrine tumors and higher gastric adenocarcinoma risk, yet care remains largely supportive, underscoring the need for disease-modifying therapies that address autoimmunity and downstream neoplasia risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Gastric-targeted immunotherapy/anti-inflammatory to halt autoimmune oxyntic inflammation and prevent progression to parietal-cell atrophy/achlorhydria.
- Chronic gastrin/CCK2-axis therapy to suppress hypergastrinemia-driven ECL hyperplasia and prevent recurrent type 1 gastric NETs.
- More convenient/tolerable deficiency correction: alternatives to lifelong hydroxocobalamin injections and iron products with fewer GI side effects to improve adherence.

name: Alpha-gal syndrome
description: Acquired tick bite associated allergy to the carbohydrate alpha gal, causing delayed 2 to 6 hour reactions after red meat or other mammal derived exposures. Symptoms range from hives and anaphylaxis to severe gastrointestinal pain and diarrhea, often with hidden triggers such as gelatin coated medications that raise the vigilance burden. Diagnosis is frequently delayed, especially when gastrointestinal symptoms dominate and mimic other disorders. Care is largely strict avoidance plus emergency readiness, with no vaccine to prevent the condition and limited options to prevent reactions beyond symptomatic control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prophylactic anti‑IgE/biologic therapy to prevent severe reactions from unavoidable/“hidden” alpha‑gal exposures (incl. meds/medical products) in refractory patients.
- Gut‑directed mast‑cell–targeted therapy for GI‑predominant AGS (cramping/diarrhea/GERD) with validated symptom-score improvement despite avoidance.
- Preventive vaccine or post‑tick‑bite immunotherapy to block tick‑bite–driven sensitization/reactivation and prevent new-onset AGS.

name: Rheumatic heart disease
description: Rheumatic heart disease is permanent, irreversible heart valve scarring after rheumatic fever triggered by an autoimmune response to group A streptococcal throat infection, often starting in childhood in low resource settings and presenting later with breathlessness, heart failure, arrhythmias, or stroke. Care is largely preventive and supportive with no cure, relying on painful, years long benzathine penicillin injections that are vulnerable to adherence barriers and global shortages, plus complex anticoagulation requiring frequent international normalized ratio monitoring. The biggest gaps are scalable primary prevention, especially a safe, affordable group A streptococcus vaccine, and simpler anticoagulation options that preserve outcomes without intensive monitoring.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safe, broadly protective Group A Streptococcus (GAS) vaccine for childhood immunization in endemic LMICs to prevent GAS infections and downstream rheumatic fever/RHD
- Less burdensome secondary prophylaxis replacing IM benzathine penicillin G every 3–4 weeks with a multi-month and/or non-injectable regimen to improve adherence despite pain/fear, travel barriers, and supply shortages
- Warfarin-sparing anticoagulation for RHD-associated AF (esp. moderate–severe rheumatic mitral stenosis) that avoids routine INR monitoring/major bleeding while maintaining warfarin-level stroke prevention

name: Angioma
description: Cherry angiomas are benign acquired vascular skin growths that become common in midlife, usually asymptomatic but prone to traumatic bleeding. Management is typically observation, with in office destructive removal for cosmetic concerns or recurrent bleeding via cryotherapy, electrosurgery, laser, or shave excision. Key unmet needs center on safer, pigment sparing options that minimize scarring and can treat multiple lesions or clusters, ideally as convenient self applied field therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Self-applied topical “field therapy” to clear multiple/grouped cherry angiomas without in-office destructive procedures.
- Pigment- and scar-sparing treatment for darker skin types and cosmetically sensitive sites to minimize dyspigmentation/scarring.
- Lesion-stabilizing/bleed-prevention therapy for trauma-prone angiomas that frequently bleed, avoiding removal-related scarring/anesthesia.

name: Selective IgA deficiency disease
description: Selective immunoglobulin A deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency, defined after age four by very low serum immunoglobulin A with normal immunoglobulin G and M. Many patients are asymptomatic, but others develop recurrent sinopulmonary infections and chronic diarrhea, sometimes progressing to bronchiectasis and long term lung morbidity. Management is largely supportive with antibiotics and infection prevention, since no immunoglobulin A enriched replacement therapy is available, leaving a major unmet need for disease targeted mucosal immunoglobulin A restoration and better prophylaxis to prevent chronic respiratory and gastrointestinal damage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Mucosal IgA functional replacement (e.g., IgA‑enriched/secretory‑IgA therapy) to reduce recurrent sinopulmonary/GI infections in symptomatic SIgAD patients
- Bronchiectasis prevention/attenuation in SIgAD patients with recurrent sinopulmonary infections (fewer pulmonary exacerbations/preserved lung function vs episodic/prophylactic antibiotics)
- Anti-parasitic/GI-directed therapies that reliably clear and prevent recurrence of Giardia-associated chronic diarrhea/malabsorption in SIgAD (including metronidazole-refractory cases)

name: Sialolithiasis
description: Sialolithiasis is a benign blockage from calcified stones in salivary ducts, usually the submandibular gland, causing cyclical meal triggered pain and unilateral swelling that can progress to infection. Treatment is largely conservative care and, when stones do not pass, endoscopic or surgical removal and sometimes gland excision. Recurrence and the need for antibiotics or invasive procedures leave a premium on noninvasive clearance of large or proximal stones and better prevention to reduce repeat obstruction, infection, and surgery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacologic chemodissolution/expulsion to clear large and/or difficult-location salivary stones (e.g., proximal/hilar or >7–10 mm) and avoid invasive procedures/gland excision.
- Preventive therapy to reduce recurrent/new stone formation in “repeat-stone” patients to avoid progression to salivary gland removal.
- Targeted local anti-infective/anti-inflammatory therapy to prevent or rapidly abort obstruction-associated sialadenitis and reduce systemic antibiotic use.

name: Sick sinus syndrome
description: Progressive sinus node dysfunction in older adults causing bradycardia, pauses, and tachy brady swings often with atrial fibrillation, leading to fatigue, dizziness, palpitations, and syncope; care relies on permanent pacemakers and rhythm drugs, but device costs, battery limits, infections, and other complications leave a need for more physiologic, less burdensome pacing alternatives and better tolerated oral chronotropic options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Autonomically responsive “biological pacemaker” therapy (gene/cell) to restore physiologic chronotropic modulation and avoid device infection/replacement burdens.
- Tachy‑brady/AF “decoupling” therapy to reduce atrial tachyarrhythmia burden without worsening sinus pauses/syncope that drives pacemaker implantation.
- Better‑tolerated chronic oral chronotropic to raise resting HR and improve exertional tolerance in symptomatic SND patients not eligible for/declining pacing.

name: Vestibular neuritis
description: Vestibular neuritis is an acute inflammatory injury of the vestibular nerve causing sudden, severe vertigo with nausea, vomiting and nystagmus but typically no hearing loss or tinnitus, most often in adults 30 to 60. Treatment is largely supportive and time sensitive since prolonged vestibular suppressants can slow central compensation. With no curative therapy, a substantial subset develop chronic dizziness, unsteadiness and spatial disorientation, creating demand for early disease modifying options and non sedating symptom control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute disease‑modifying therapy (within 24–72h) that improves long‑term vestibular recovery and reduces persistent deficits
- Non‑sedating, “compensation‑sparing” vertigo/nausea control that can be used beyond the first few days without slowing recovery
- Evidence‑based etiology‑targeted drug therapy (e.g., antiviral/anti‑inflammatory/immunomodulatory) that reliably shortens course and improves outcomes

name: Beriberi | wet
description: Wet beriberi is the cardiovascular form of thiamine deficiency, causing tachycardia, high output heart failure, edema, and sometimes fulminant Shoshin beriberi with lactic acidosis and cardiogenic shock that can rapidly reverse with intravenous thiamine. The core unmet need is operational, earlier recognition and emergency ready parenteral thiamine, since oral absorption is capped and alcohol use can impair uptake, along with routine magnesium co repletion to avoid apparent treatment failure.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ED/ICU-ready ultra-rapid “rescue” parenteral thiamine to reverse fulminant Shoshin wet beriberi shock and lactic acidosis within hours.
- Absorption-enhanced/high-bioavailability thiamine (e.g., prodrugs/transporter-bypass) for alcohol use disorder or malabsorption patients where oral thiamine is inadequate.
- Longer-acting and/or non-IV thiamine regimens to reduce frequent IV dosing/monitoring burden and mitigate nonresponse from cofactor deficiency (e.g., magnesium co-repletion).

name: Xanthomatosis | eruptive
description: Eruptive xanthomatosis is a sudden crop of small yellow red papules on extensor surfaces that signals severe hypertriglyceridemia often with poorly controlled diabetes. The lesions can itch or be tender but the real danger is acute pancreatitis when triglycerides surge above about 1000 mg/dL. Management hinges on rapidly lowering triglycerides yet standard lipid drugs may be ineffective in familial chylomicronemia syndrome, and newer apolipoprotein C-III targeting options can carry significant monitoring burdens such as platelet surveillance.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid outpatient “rescue” TG-lowering to <500 mg/dL within ~48–72h to prevent pancreatitis without multi-day inpatient NPO + IV insulin
- Durable TG control in familial chylomicronemia syndrome (FCS) patients who can’t sustain ultra–low-fat diets and respond poorly to fibrates/omega-3/niacin (target TG ≤500 mg/dL and fewer pancreatitis events)
- Platelet-sparing/low-monitoring APOC3-pathway therapies that avoid volanesorsen-associated thrombocytopenia while maintaining TG lowering

name: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome
description: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome is a rare anatomy driven duodenal obstruction from compression between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery, often after rapid weight loss or scoliosis surgery. Patients develop postprandial pain, early satiety, nausea or vomiting and worsening malnutrition. Care can escalate to nasogastric decompression and intravenous total parenteral nutrition, underscoring the need for outpatient options that restore oral intake and weight more reliably and for safer motility support given metoclopramide’s boxed warning for potentially irreversible tardive dyskinesia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Outpatient pharmacologic option that rapidly restores reliable oral intake in acute symptomatic SMAS to avoid NG decompression and TPN
- Safer prokinetic alternative to metoclopramide that preserves motility benefit without boxed-warning risk of often-irreversible tardive dyskinesia
- Drug-enabled “weight restoration accelerator” for rapid weight-loss–triggered SMAS (esp. post-scoliosis surgery in younger patients) to speed mesenteric fat-pad recovery and reduce progression to surgical bypass

name: Syndactyly
description: Syndactyly is a congenital webbing or fusion of two or more fingers or toes, usually diagnosed at birth, with functionally important cases typically involving the hand. Treatment is surgical separation around ages 1 to 2 and often requires skin grafts or substitutes. Outcomes can be undermined by scarring and web creep that may necessitate reoperation, while postoperative pain control in pediatric upper extremity surgery can still default to opioids, leaving unmet needs for graft sparing, scar modulating, and opioid sparing adjuncts.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Perioperative anti-fibrotic/scar-modulating therapy to prevent post-release web creep and contracture-driven functional relapse (esp. infants operated early).
- Regenerative/topical pharmacologic approach that reduces or eliminates the need for skin grafting to lower web creep/contracture and cosmetic/donor-site morbidity.
- Opioid-sparing perioperative analgesic adjuncts to reduce post-surgical pain and 24-hour opioid exposure in pediatric syndactyly surgery.

name: Syringoma
description: Syringoma is a benign eccrine sweat duct tumor causing clusters of small firm papules, most often around the lower eyelids and cheeks, and while medically harmless it can be cosmetically distressing and sometimes itchy. Treatment is mainly procedural or topical retinoids, but real world clearance is often limited by recurrence from deep dermal involvement and by scarring or post inflammatory pigment changes, especially in darker skin, leaving a need for durable non scarring therapies that prevent regrowth.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Dermis-penetrant, non-scarring lesion-clearance therapy for cosmetically bothersome (often periorbital) syringomas achieving high cosmetic response with minimal scarring/PIH.
- Durable recurrence-preventing medical therapy that eradicates deep-dermal disease drivers to achieve long recurrence-free clearance.
- Non-invasive antipruritic + lesion-reducing therapy for symptomatic and/or widespread syringoma (generalized/eruptive or vulvar) where repeated procedures are impractical and scarring is unacceptable.
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus Syringoma page; https://medlineplus.gov/benigntumors.html (or https://medlineplus.gov/skinconditions.html)

name: Taeniasis
description: Taeniasis is an intestinal tapeworm infection acquired from eating raw or undercooked beef or pork, often asymptomatic or mild until patients notice moving worm segments in stool. While treatment is typically straightforward with a single oral dose, the key unmet need is field safe preventive treatment that can be deployed in low sanitation settings to reduce transmission without triggering seizures in people with occult cysticercosis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Single-dose taenicide suitable for mass drug administration that minimizes neurologic/seizure risk in people with possible occult neurocysticercosis
- US-available, pediatric-validated alternative to praziquantel addressing access/regulatory gaps
- Evidence-backed preventive-chemotherapy drug/regimen optimized for field efficacy and transmission interruption (best drug/dose balancing efficacy vs adverse effects)

name: Neutropenia | transient neonatal
description: Transient neonatal neutropenia is a low neutrophil count seen mainly in premature or critically ill newborns, often linked to maternal hypertension or preeclampsia, sepsis, or alloimmune causes. Most cases resolve spontaneously, but a subset is prolonged and leaves infants vulnerable to serious infection, driving empiric broad spectrum antibiotics in the neonatal intensive care unit. Current rescue options such as granulocyte colony stimulating factor or intravenous immune globulin have mixed efficacy and meaningful safety burdens, creating demand for antibiotic sparing approaches and short, targeted neutrophil restoration that demonstrably reduces culture proven infections.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course neutrophil restoration in highest-risk neonatal neutropenia (e.g., maternal hypertension/preeclampsia–associated; ANC <500/µL persisting) that demonstrably reduces culture-proven sepsis (not just raises ANC)
- Antibiotic-sparing/non-aminoglycoside empiric infection-control options for neutropenic neonates that maintain early-onset sepsis coverage while avoiding gentamicin nephrotoxicity/irreversible ototoxicity and therapeutic drug monitoring
- Targeted alternative to IVIG for neonatal alloimmune neutropenia refractory to G-CSF that avoids IVIG thrombosis/renal failure risks and repeated dosing

name: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia
description: Fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia is a rare pregnancy disorder where maternal antibodies attack fetal platelets, often first detected after delivery when an otherwise healthy newborn presents with petechiae or bleeding. The major clinical risk is intracranial hemorrhage, reported in roughly 10 to 20 percent of affected fetuses or newborns. Care is hindered by lack of routine prenatal screening and underdiagnosis, and current management relies on burdensome maternal intravenous immunoglobulin with or without corticosteroids plus access to compatible platelet transfusions. Key unmet needs include earlier identification, true prevention, and therapies that block placental transfer of pathogenic antibodies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- More reliable antenatal prevention of severe fetal/neonatal bleeding and very severe thrombocytopenia (<30×10^9/L in first week) in high-risk HPA-1a–alloimmunized pregnancies than weekly high-dose IVIG ± steroids.
- Targeted immunoprophylaxis for HPA-1a–negative mothers to prevent initial HPA-1a alloimmunization (prevent first affected pregnancy/recurrence).
- Rapid postnatal pharmacologic platelet “rescue” to quickly raise/stabilize neonatal platelet counts and reduce reliance on antigen-negative platelet transfusions and repeat monitoring.

name: Ureterocele
description: Congenital ballooning of the distal ureter at the bladder that obstructs urine outflow and can cause reflux, recurrent febrile urinary tract infections in infancy, and permanent kidney damage; care relies on prolonged antibiotic prophylaxis and endoscopic or reconstructive surgery, but postsurgical reflux and uncertain prophylaxis benefit leave unmet need for antibiotic sparing infection prevention, reflux resistant decompression, and kidney protective approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Antibiotic-sparing UTI prevention for neonates with ureterocele + hydroureteronephrosis started on continuous antibiotic prophylaxis
- Renal-protective adjuncts to prevent kidney damage/scarring (and nephrectomy) in large/obstructive ureteroceles despite infection/obstruction management
- Post-decompression anti-reflux/anti-infection strategies to reduce de novo VUR and repeat surgery after ureterocele puncture/incision

name: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction
description: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction is a blockage where the kidney meets the ureter that traps urine, causing hydronephrosis and potential kidney damage, often detected on prenatal ultrasound and frequently asymptomatic early. Care is largely watchful waiting with repeat imaging, sometimes antibiotic prophylaxis in severe hydronephrosis, and surgery if drainage does not improve, but there are no precise predictors for which infants will silently lose renal function, creating a major need for better risk stratification and kidney preserving interventions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapy that prevents renal scarring and preserves differential renal function in UPJ/obstructive UTD patients at risk of deterioration on surveillance
- Non-antibiotic febrile-UTI prevention for high-risk antenatal hydronephrosis/UPJ-like UTD to avoid prolonged continuous antibiotic prophylaxis
- Pharmacologic restoration of UPJ drainage (e.g., anti-fibrotic/ECM or pro-peristalsis) to reduce the observe→serial imaging→surgery pathway

name: Vulvar cancer | keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma
description: Keratinizing vulvar squamous cell carcinoma is a rare, often slow growing vulvar cancer that can evolve from vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia and typically affects postmenopausal women with lichen sclerosus, causing persistent itch, pain, bleeding, dysuria, and visible vulvar lesions. Treatment is usually surgical, but groin lymph node dissection can lead to lymphoedema, and advanced or recurrent disease has few effective systemic options, with pembrolizumab monotherapy responses around 10 percent, driving demand for biomarker guided targeted approaches and less morbid regional node strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Substantially higher ORR and longer PFS/OS than anti–PD-1 monotherapy for previously treated advanced/recurrent vulvar SCC
- Biomarker-driven targeted therapies for HPV-unrelated/keratinizing-pathway VSCC (lichen sclerosus → dVIN–driven; e.g., TP53/CDKN2A/NOTCH1/HRAS alterations)
- (Neo)adjuvant systemic regimens enabling lymphadenectomy-sparing management in higher-risk patients (e.g., >4 cm or multifocal tumors)

name: Angiodysplasia
description: Angiodysplasia is an aging related, right sided colonic vascular malformation with painless, often occult gastrointestinal bleeding that commonly presents as iron deficiency anemia. Endoscopic coagulation can control acute bleeding but lesions recur and about one third rebleed, driving repeat procedures, chronic iron, and sometimes transfusions. Medical options remain limited by tolerability and long term use issues, leaving a need for safer, durable therapies that reduce bleeding recurrence and the procedural and transfusion burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct drug to prevent post-argon plasma coagulation rebleeding/recurrence and reduce repeat endoscopies + chronic iron therapy
- Therapy for transfusion-dependent, endoscopy-refractory patients achieving ≥50% reduction in RBC transfusions and/or IV iron
- Thalidomide-like anti-bleeding option suitable for chronic use without dose-/duration-limiting neurologic toxicity (e.g., peripheral neuropathy)

name: Angiokeratoma
description: Angiokeratoma is a benign superficial vascular lesion presenting as small blue red hyperkeratotic papules, often on genital skin in older men. While frequently asymptomatic, lesions can itch, bleed after minor trauma, and cause cosmetic and psychological distress. They do not resolve spontaneously and can become more warty over time. Current management is mainly reassurance or office based destruction with cautery, cryotherapy, or vascular lasers, which can be painful and may leave persistent lesions. Key unmet needs are durable clearance with minimal pain, low recurrence, and convenient at home topical options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- At-home, non-procedural therapy for symptomatic/cosmetically distressing angiokeratomas (esp. scrotal/vulvar) that controls bleeding/itching/pain while avoiding painful, scarring in-office destruction.
- Durable, low-recurrence treatment for patients with multiple or recurrent lesions to reduce retreatment and multi-session laser courses.
- Drug delivery that effectively penetrates thick/hyperkeratotic and/or deeper lesions to treat vessels beyond the reach of superficial energy-based approaches.

name: Angiolipoma
description: Angiolipoma is a benign subcutaneous tumor of fat and small blood vessels, often presenting in young adults as multiple tender or painful nodules on the forearms. Although noncancerous, lesions can be chronic and painful, sometimes poorly responsive to simple analgesics, and multiplicity makes repeated procedures common. Management is largely surgical excision, creating unmet need for scar sparing debulking approaches, more effective pain control, and potential genotype guided options as PRKD2 and PIK3CA alterations have been reported.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical, scar-sparing debulking for patients with multiple painful subcutaneous angiolipomas to avoid repeat excisions/liposuction
- Genotype-selected therapy (e.g., PRKD2/PIK3CA-mutant) to drive lesion regression and prevent new-lesion formation
- Non-NSAID pain control options for painful/tender lesions, including for patients with NSAID contraindications

name: Angiomyolipoma
description: Renal angiomyolipoma is a usually benign kidney tumor of abnormal blood vessels, smooth muscle, and fat, often found incidentally in asymptomatic middle aged women but with a subset at risk of hematuria, pain, and sudden life threatening retroperitoneal hemorrhage. Management for higher risk lesions still leans on procedures such as selective arterial embolization, while systemic options can be limited by toxicity and the need for ongoing therapy because stopping can trigger tumor regrowth, leaving a need for durable, well tolerated noninvasive disease control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Finite-course therapy achieving ≥50% renal angiomyolipoma volume reduction with durable control after stopping treatment.
- Everolimus-like lesion shrinkage with materially improved tolerability (lower stomatitis/mucositis; fewer dose interruptions/reductions).
- First effective systemic drug option for sporadic high-rupture-risk AML (e.g., >4 cm and/or intralesional aneurysms >5 mm) to avoid procedures.

name: Angular cheilitis
description: Angular cheilitis is an inflammatory eruption at one or both mouth corners causing erythema, maceration, and painful cracking that can bleed, often in denture wearers and drooling children and in the very old or very young. Saliva pooling drives irritation and fosters mixed Candida and bacterial infection, so care relies on topical antifungals or antibiotics plus steroids and barrier ointments. High recurrence, reported up to 80 percent, and the need for continuous barrier maintenance leave a clear unmet need for more durable relapse prevention and lower burden long term control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable relapse-prevention therapy for patients with persistent saliva pooling/anatomic drivers (e.g., deep commissural furrows, denture-related changes)
- Etiology-targeted, biofilm-active topical that clears mixed Candida–bacterial colonization and prevents re-colonization/relapse
- Adherence-friendly once-daily or sustained-release barrier + antimicrobial ± anti-inflammatory regimens to replace frequent multi-application courses

name: Anhidrosis
description: Anhidrosis is failure to sweat, causing heat intolerance with fatigue, dizziness and flushing, and potentially life threatening overheating and heatstroke risk. Care is largely avoidance and cooling, with limited evidence for immunosuppression and secretagogues that may not restore sweating in affected skin, and no established sweat gland regenerative therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing immunomodulatory therapy that restores whole-body sweating in severe/generalized AIGA (reducing heatstroke risk).
- Better-tolerated, more targeted sweat secretagogues than pilocarpine that induce sweating in anhidrotic (not just normal) areas.
- Disease-modifying developmental/regenerative therapy to establish functional eccrine sweat glands in congenital anhidrosis (e.g., XLHED/HED; CIPA).

name: Aneurysm | aortic
description: Aortic aneurysm is a weakening and ballooning of the aorta that is often silent until rupture causes life threatening bleeding, typically affecting older men with smoking and hypertension. Management relies on screening and surveillance imaging plus cardiovascular risk control, with procedural repair the only proven way to prevent rupture and aneurysm related death. The key unmet need is a disease modifying therapy that slows aneurysm growth and reduces the need for surgery during years of monitoring.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy for small-to-medium AAAs under surveillance that slows aortic diameter growth (mm/year) and delays/avoids reaching repair thresholds.
- Women-specific therapy to reduce rupture risk at smaller AAA diameters (≈42–50 mm) to safely delay repair.
- Safer long-term vascular risk-reduction alternatives to chronic aspirin/antiplatelet use that maintain protection with lower major-bleeding risk.

name: Apolipoprotein C-III deficiency
description: Apolipoprotein C-III deficiency is a rare APOC3 loss-of-function state characterized by very low triglycerides and a generally healthy, cardioprotective lipid profile, so it is often detected incidentally on routine lipid panels rather than through symptoms. The practical gap is not disease treatment but clinical guidance on how to interpret and manage unexpectedly low triglycerides and associated lipid patterns in otherwise well adults, while the main frontier is leveraging APOC3 biology for therapeutics that lower triglycerides and reduce residual cardiovascular risk.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Breast papilloma
description: Breast papilloma is a benign growth in a breast milk duct, typically in women aged 35 to 55, presenting with unilateral clear or bloody nipple discharge and sometimes a small lump behind the nipple. Because some lesions can harbor atypical cells and multiple papillomas slightly raise breast cancer risk, diagnosis often escalates to imaging and needle biopsy followed by duct excision or minimally invasive vacuum assisted excision, or long term imaging surveillance. Key unmet needs are better risk stratification to avoid unnecessary duct removing surgery while reliably identifying lesions that warrant intervention.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Duct-preserving pharmacotherapy for symptomatic central intraductal papilloma to stop clear/bloody unilateral nipple discharge and avoid open duct excision.
- Medical suppression/eradication for multiple papillomas/papillomatosis to reduce progression to extensive surgery (incl. mastectomy consideration) and mitigate elevated breast-cancer risk.
- Targeted risk-reduction therapy for intraductal papilloma with atypia/atypical papillary lesions to lower upgrade to DCIS/invasive cancer and reduce excision-driven morbidity.

name: Bladder calculus
description: Bladder calculi are mineral stones that form when urine is retained from incomplete emptying, often in men with benign prostatic hyperplasia, neurogenic bladder, infection, or catheters. They cause urinary frequency, terminal hematuria, dysuria or suprapubic pain and sometimes recurrent urinary tract infections alone. Care is largely procedural with cystoscopic fragmentation and removal, while chemolysis is mostly limited to uric acid stones, leaving a need for nonprocedural dissolution and better prevention of recurrence in infected or catheterized bladders where urease driven stones can block catheters and shelter bacteria.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-procedural chemolysis effective for non–uric-acid (incl. large) bladder stones to avoid anesthesia-based removal
- Drug-based recurrence prevention for patients with uncorrectable drivers (e.g., catheter-dependent/neurogenic bladder)
- Anti-infection/anti-biofilm/urease-targeted therapies to prevent/treat struvite stones and catheter encrustation without chronic irrigations

name: Azoospermia
description: Azoospermia is male-factor infertility with no measurable sperm in the ejaculate, typically found during infertility workups and confirmed on two semen analyses. It is either obstructive or due to impaired testicular production. In nonobstructive disease, sperm production is often focal, making surgical retrieval probabilistic and leaving couples dependent on invasive procedures and assisted reproduction. In hormonally driven cases, gonadotropin treatment can require frequent injections for 9 to 18 months with ongoing monitoring, creating a strong need for more reliable sperm production and lower-burden, disease-modifying options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying induction of spermatogenesis that produces sperm in ejaculate for intrinsic-testicular-impairment non‑obstructive azoospermia (NOA).
- Adjunct “testicular optimization” therapies that raise micro‑TESE/TESE sperm retrieval rates in NOA where many still have no sperm retrieved.
- Lower-burden spermatogenesis induction for hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism–associated azoospermia (e.g., oral/long‑acting regimens replacing frequent hCG/FSH injections and monitoring).

name: Balanitis xerotica obliterans
description: Male genital lichen sclerosus causing white atrophic plaques on the foreskin and glans that can progress to phimosis, meatal stenosis, and urethral stricture with urinary obstruction; care relies on ultrapotent topical steroids and sometimes surgery, but durable steroid sparing disease control is needed to prevent scarring and reduce penile cancer risk, with late stage nonsteroid topical options emerging.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Stricture-/fibrosis-modifying drug therapy to prevent/reverse meatal/urethral stenosis and reduce need for dilation/meatoplasty/urethroplasty.
- Steroid-sparing option for steroid-refractory BXO/penile LS achieving remission and symptom control without circumcision.
- Long-term maintenance therapy that sustains disease control and lowers malignancy risk without chronic safety tradeoffs of topical steroids/TCIs.

name: Balantidiasis
description: Intestinal protozoan infection caused by Balantidium coli, acquired via fecally contaminated food or water often in pig raising settings; ranges from asymptomatic to severe colitis with diarrhea and dysentery and can progress to fatal disease or colonic perforation in debilitated or immunocompromised patients. Current therapy uses multi dose courses of tetracycline, metronidazole, or iodoquinol, but tolerability and contraindications in pregnancy and young children and adherence to frequent dosing leave a need for safer, short course oral options effective in high risk patients.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pregnancy- and <8-years-old–safe oral therapy with demonstrated parasitologic cure
- Ultra-short, low-frequency (≤BID, ≤3-day) oral regimen with minimal timing constraints
- Therapy specifically validated for debilitated/immunocompromised patients (rapid symptom control + complication prevention)

name: Tuberculosis | active
description: Active pulmonary tuberculosis is an airborne bacterial lung infection that can disseminate, causing chronic cough (sometimes with blood), fever, night sweats, fatigue, and weight loss; treatment still relies on multi drug regimens for 6 months or longer with high pill burden, adherence sensitive resistance risk, major drug drug interaction constraints in people on human immunodeficiency virus therapy, and toxicity limited options for drug resistant disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Universal ≤4‑month, all‑oral DS‑TB regimen effective and usable in key excluded groups (children <12, pregnancy/breastfeeding, most extrapulmonary TB, interacting meds/ART)
- Rifamycin‑sparing (non–CYP‑inducing) sterilizing regimens that maintain cure while minimizing drug–drug interactions, especially enabling modern HIV ART without switching
- Linezolid‑sparing (or markedly lower‑toxicity) MDR/RR‑TB/pre‑XDR regimens with BPaLM‑like simplicity but far less peripheral neuropathy and myelosuppression/anemia

name: Carbuncle
description: Carbuncle is a deep, pus forming skin infection where multiple adjacent boils merge around hair follicles, often on the back of the neck and linked to diabetes risk. It can cause fever, chills, and permanent scarring. Care centers on incision and drainage, with antibiotics mainly when systemic illness is present, but methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus is common, raising pressure to avoid unnecessary systemic antibiotics. Recurrence remains a key gap, driving interest in simple decolonization and prevention regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct therapy that accelerates healing and reduces permanent scarring after required incision & drainage
- MRSA-active treatment with less systemic antibiotic exposure (fewer GI AEs/diarrhea, lower resistance pressure), especially in febrile/systemically unwell or immunocompromised/diabetic patients
- Convenient recurrence-prevention/decolonization regimen to reduce recurrent lesions and repeat antibiotic courses (incl. household transmission risk)

name: Sleep apnea | central
description: Central sleep apnea is recurrent sleep-time breathing pauses due to impaired brain drive to the respiratory muscles, typically in older men and often linked to heart failure, stroke, or opioid use. Treatment is constrained by heterogeneity and safety and tolerability tradeoffs, including increased mortality with adaptive servo ventilation in reduced ejection fraction heart failure and only modest, side effect limited benefit with acetazolamide. Implantable phrenic nerve stimulation offers an option but leaves demand for durable, low burden, cardio safe and better tolerated therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Cardio-safe pharmacotherapy for CSA in HFrEF (LVEF ≤45%) that reduces CAI/AHI without increasing all-cause/cardiovascular mortality.
- Rapid-onset oral therapy for opioid-associated CSA (e.g., methadone/buprenorphine/chronic opioids) delivering clinically meaningful CAI reduction on PSG within ~1 week plus symptom/physiology benefit.
- Better-tolerated, monitoring-light alternative to acetazolamide with durable CSA control and improved patient-reported outcomes.

name: Cercarial dermatitis
description: Cercarial dermatitis, or swimmer’s itch, is a highly pruritic rash after swimming in waters where infected snails release parasite larvae from birds and mammals; the larvae penetrate skin but do not mature in humans. Symptoms begin within minutes to days and evolve into itchy papules or small blisters that usually resolve in 1 to 2 weeks, but scratching can cause secondary bacterial infection and repeat exposures can be more intense. Care is largely symptomatic because treatments have not been evaluated in clinical trials, creating demand for pre-swim barriers and faster, non-sedating itch control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pre‑swim, water‑resistant topical anti‑penetrant prophylaxis that remains protective after extended immersion (esp. for high‑exposure shoreline/kids).
- Trial‑validated acute post‑exposure therapy that rapidly reduces pruritus and shortens the typical ~1–2 week symptom course (esp. repeat‑exposure swimmers).
- Non‑sedating itch control that reduces scratching and secondary bacterial infection/antibiotic use.

name: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy
description: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is an age related small vessel brain disorder where amyloid beta deposits in cortical vessel walls, weakening them and causing lobar intracerebral hemorrhage, microbleeds, and cognitive decline in older adults. Care is largely secondary prevention with blood pressure control and avoiding bleeding promoting drugs, yet there are no disease modifying therapies and recurrence after a first hemorrhage is high at about 7.4 percent per year. The inflammatory subtype often responds to high dose corticosteroids but relapses are common, underscoring demand for safer, durable treatments that prevent bleeding and preserve cognition.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Recurrent lobar ICH prevention in MRI-high-risk CAA survivors (e.g., lobar microbleeds and/or disseminated cortical superficial siderosis), materially lowering the ~7.39%/year recurrent ICH rate and reducing new microbleeds/cSS progression.
- Disease-modifying therapy that slows CAA progression and cognitive decline using objective endpoints (e.g., cerebrovascular vasoreactivity/WMH burden and validated cognitive scales) while avoiding ARIA liabilities in high-CAA-burden patients.
- Steroid-sparing, relapse-preventing therapy for CAA-related inflammation (CAA-ri) to reduce prolonged high-dose corticosteroid exposure and lower ~38%–40% 3-year relapse rates.

name: Cervical cancer | adenocarcinoma
description: Cervical adenocarcinoma arises from mucus producing gland cells of the endocervix and is often silent early, later causing abnormal vaginal bleeding and persistent watery or bloody discharge. A key unmet need is better control of aggressive human papillomavirus independent gastric type disease that can be radioresistant, alongside more biomarker guided options given a meaningful HER2 positive subset. In advanced settings, regimen choices are constrained by toxicity such as bevacizumab associated fistulas, underscoring the need for safer, more effective disease modifying and targeted therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Locoregional control/RT-sensitization strategies for locally advanced cervical adenocarcinoma (esp. gastric-type/HPV-independent) with low complete response to definitive radiotherapy.
- Biomarker-matched targeted/ADC therapies for HPV-independent cervical adenocarcinoma subgroups (e.g., ERBB2/HER2-amplified) not addressed by stage-based standard care.
- Less toxic, more tolerable systemic regimens for persistent/recurrent/metastatic disease to reduce grade 3–5 AEs/discontinuation vs chemo-IO±bevacizumab and avoid anti-VEGF fistula risk.

name: Oral cavity cancer | squamous cell carcinoma
description: Oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma is a tobacco and alcohol linked cancer that typically affects older men and presents with persistent oral red or white patches or a nonhealing ulcer, progressing to dysphagia and cervical lymphadenopathy. Standard care for advanced disease relies on surgery plus multi week daily radiation, often with cisplatin based chemoradiation that many patients struggle to tolerate. Recurrence and metastasis are common and outcomes are poor, with limited survival benefit from systemic chemotherapy, creating demand for better relapse prevention and more tolerable, more deliverable locoregional regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Perioperative/adjuvant systemic regimens that improve event-free survival by preventing early/post-op relapse beyond surgery + PORT±cisplatin in resectable locally advanced oral cavity SCC.
- Effective systemic therapies with meaningful OS/ORR benefit for PD‑L1–negative (CPS<1%) and/or post‑platinum recurrent/metastatic SCCHN.
- Lower-toxicity, more deliverable radiosensitization/adjuvant alternatives to high-dose cisplatin-CRT (and ideally reduced treatment/visit burden vs ~7-week daily RT).

name: Chromosome 22q11.2 duplication syndrome
description: Chromosome 22q11.2 duplication syndrome is a highly variable pediatric chromosomal disorder from an extra 22q11.2 segment, often presenting with hypotonia and developmental delay and sometimes heart or palatal defects, with longer term impact driven by neurodevelopmental and neurologic comorbidities such as autism spectrum disorder and seizures. Care is supportive and symptom based with early intervention therapies, leaving major unmet need for disease modifying approaches that improve motor and neurobehavioral outcomes and reduce seizure burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pediatric drug therapy to improve hypotonia-driven gross-motor milestone delays (roll/sit/walk) in symptomatic 22q11.2 duplication
- Better-tolerated treatment to reduce ASD/ADHD/anxiety-related functional impairment, especially in the ASD-associated subgroup (~14–25%)
- Tailored seizure prevention/control addressing both hypocalcemia-related and non–calcium-related seizure disorders, reducing chronic antiepileptic exposure

name: Cholesteatoma
description: Cholesteatoma is a noncancerous skin cyst in the middle ear and mastoid that typically affects one ear, causing persistent foul smelling drainage and progressive hearing loss as it erodes the eardrum, ossicles, and surrounding bone, with rare but serious intracranial complications. Treatment is largely surgical excision with long term surveillance, yet recurrence and residual disease often require second look and repeat procedures. Biofilm associated infection and inflammatory bone destruction pathways limit the durability of topical antibiotics and leave a need for adjuncts that improve local control and prevent erosion.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Locally delivered intra-/post-operative sustained-release adjuncts to neutralize residual microscopic disease and reduce postoperative recurrence.
- Local osteoclast-axis inhibition (e.g., anti-RANKL or anti-activin A/INHBA) for aggressive bone-erosion endotypes to preserve ossicles/temporal bone and hearing outcomes.
- Middle-ear–retained anti-biofilm therapies and/or sequencing-guided antimicrobials in mucoadhesive carriers to overcome biofilm-limited antibiotic penetration and reduce persistence/recurrence.

name: Embolism | cholesterol
description: Cholesterol embolization syndrome occurs when cholesterol crystals break off atherosclerotic plaques, lodge in small arteries, and trigger ischemic and inflammatory end organ injury, often after vascular procedures in older patients with acute kidney failure and skin ischemia such as livedo reticularis or blue toe. Management is largely supportive with no proven disease modifying therapy, leaving a major unmet need for treatments that prevent progression to permanent renal damage and dialysis. A key emerging frontier is targeting inflammasome driven interleukin 1 inflammation to blunt ongoing injury, including options compatible with necessary anticoagulation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early, steroid-sparing NLRP3/IL‑1–axis blockade to prevent renal failure/dialysis after iatrogenic CES
- Crystal-/micro-occlusion–clearing therapy to directly remove/neutralize cholesterol crystals causing end-organ ischemia
- CES therapy compatible with continued anticoagulation (e.g., AF/LV thrombus) to prevent ongoing micro-embolization without increasing thrombotic risk

name: Clubfoot
description: Clubfoot is an uncommon congenital deformity where a newborn is born with one or both feet curved into an abnormal, stiff position. It is usually painless in infancy but, untreated, can leave the foot deformed and impair normal walking. Standard Ponseti care requires weeks of serial casting, an Achilles tenotomy for most infants, and years of brace wear, with relapse strongly driven by poor adherence and reported recurrence up to 50%. Key unmet needs include reducing tenotomy burden, improving relapse prevention and brace compliance, and streamlining in clinic pain control for percutaneous procedures.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct injectable to overcome early-infancy “hindfoot stall” equinus and achieve ≥15° dorsiflexion without Achilles tenotomy/additional procedures
- Relapse-prevention pharmacotherapy to shorten/replace multi-year foot-abduction bracing, especially for families with brace intolerance/skin injury risk
- Faster in-clinic analgesia for percutaneous Achilles tenotomy that lowers infant pain (FLACC) and reduces visit time vs 30–60 min topical anesthetic creams

name: Chondroma
description: Chondromas are benign cartilage tumors, most often enchondromas inside bone, that can be asymptomatic or cause pain, swelling, deformity, and pathologic fracture and are typically monitored or treated with curettage and bone grafting. The toughest gaps are diagnostic and risk stratification since benign lesions and grade 1 chondrosarcoma can be nearly indistinguishable, and in syndromic multiple enchondromas such as Ollier disease where cumulative deformity and fractures combine with high malignancy risk. Better molecularly informed surveillance and less morbid local options like ablation are key needs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying systemic/targeted therapy (e.g., IDH1/IDH2-driven) to reduce enchondromatosis lesion burden and prevent deformity/limb-length discrepancy/pathologic fractures.
- Chemoprevention/early-intervention to reduce malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma in high-risk multiple enchondroma (Ollier/Maffucci) patients.
- Local non-surgical/minimally invasive drug delivery to ablate/stabilize painful enchondromas and avoid curettage/bone graft surgery (improve pain and recovery time).

name: Chorioangioma
description: Placental chorioangioma is a benign vascular tumor of the placenta, typically found on second trimester ultrasound near the umbilical cord insertion. Most are asymptomatic, but larger lesions over 4 cm can create arteriovenous shunting that drives polyhydramnios, fetal anemia, heart failure and hydrops, and maternal mirror syndrome with preeclampsia. Management is surveillance plus procedure heavy fetal therapy such as amnioreduction, intrauterine transfusion, and fetoscopic laser devascularization. Key unmet needs include safer pharmacologic control of polyhydramnios and less invasive, placenta targeted approaches that reduce fetal and maternal risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Placenta/tumor-targeted pharmacologic devascularization to halt AV‑shunting–driven fetal heart failure/hydrops in clinically significant (often >4 cm) chorioangiomas.
- Safer anti‑polyhydramnios drug to reduce amniotic fluid without indomethacin-associated fetal ductal constriction/neonatal risks and reduce need for repeated amniodrainage.
- Maternal therapy to prevent/treat mirror syndrome–preeclampsia physiology in large chorioangioma pregnancies to enable pregnancy prolongation when severe fetal complications arise in late 2nd trimester.

name: Glaucoma | chronic, closed-angle
description: Chronic primary angle closure glaucoma is often silent as repeated iris contact scars the drainage angle shut, blocking aqueous outflow and raising intraocular pressure until optic nerve damage causes progressive peripheral vision loss and eventual blindness. It is most common in older adults, especially women, and in anatomically predisposed eyes such as shallow anterior chambers and hyperopia. Care is pressure centric with laser iridotomy, long term drops, and sometimes angle surgery, but lost vision cannot be restored and damage may continue despite good pressure control. Key gaps are pressure independent neuroprotection and drop sparing, better tolerated delivery to address adherence and preservative related ocular surface disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- IOP-independent neuroprotection/neurorecovery to prevent ongoing retinal ganglion cell damage and visual-field loss in patients progressing despite substantial IOP reduction.
- Outflow-/structure-modifying therapies that reduce/eliminate trabecular meshwork “structural blockage” to provide durable IOP control in chronic angle-closure glaucoma.
- Drop-sparing, better-tolerated chronic therapy (e.g., sustained-release and/or preservative-free/ocular-surface–sparing options) to improve adherence and reduce toxicity/contraindication burden (e.g., beta-blocker–intolerant patients).

name: Hydrocephalus | communicating
description: Communicating hydrocephalus is cerebrospinal fluid buildup from impaired circulation or absorption after it leaves the ventricles, often presenting in older adults as normal pressure hydrocephalus with progressive gait disturbance, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence. The condition is frequently misdiagnosed as Alzheimer’s or Parkinson’s and an estimated over 80 percent of cases go unrecognized or untreated. Care is dominated by surgical shunting, which carries risks such as malfunction, infection, and subdural hematoma and often yields uneven symptom recovery. A key unmet need is safer, non-surgical, disease modifying therapies that restore cerebrospinal fluid absorption, including approaches targeting post hemorrhagic or post infectious inflammation and fibrosis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical pharmacologic option that improves gait enough to delay/avoid shunt implantation in newly diagnosed NPH/iNPH
- Adjunct drug therapy that reliably improves cognitive and urinary outcomes (not just gait) in shunt-treated iNPH
- Anti-inflammatory/anti-fibrotic therapy to prevent or reverse post-hemorrhagic/post-infectious CSF malabsorption by targeting arachnoid-granulation dysfunction

name: Chronic intestinal vascular insufficiency
description: Chronic mesenteric ischemia is a rare, usually atherosclerotic, multivessel reduction in intestinal blood flow that often presents late with postprandial abdominal pain, weight loss, and food aversion, leading to malnutrition and potential progression to acute ischemia. Treatment depends on revascularization plus long term antiplatelet or antithrombotic therapy, but outcomes are constrained by high in stent restenosis and repeat interventions, an evidence thin and bleeding limited antithrombotic strategy, and a lack of fast acting, nonprocedural bridge therapies since symptomatic drugs offer only temporary, noncurative relief.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Anti-restenosis adjunct to cut 12‑month in‑stent restenosis (~39%) and symptom recurrence (~17%) after mesenteric artery stenting.
- Bleeding-sparing antithrombotic regimen that preserves stent patency/thrombosis protection while reducing bleeding risk vs ≥1 month DAPT then lifelong antiplatelet.
- Non-procedural/bridge drug therapy to rapidly relieve postprandial pain/food fear–driven weight loss and prevent bowel infarction in symptomatic patients who cannot undergo (or are awaiting) revascularization.

name: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy
description: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy is a progressive neurodegenerative brain disease linked to repeated head impacts, marked by abnormal tau buildup and worsening cognitive, mood, and behavioral symptoms that can disrupt daily functioning. Diagnosis is still only confirmable at autopsy, which limits patient identification and trial endpoint validation. There is no cure and no disease modifying therapy, leaving major unmet needs for accurate in life diagnostics, biomarkers to track progression, and treatments that slow decline while safely managing neuropsychiatric symptoms.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying anti-tau/anti-neuroinflammation therapy that measurably slows cognitive/functional decline in living TES patients
- Safer, more effective neuropsychiatric therapy for mood/behavior-predominant TES (impulsivity/aggression + depression/anxiety) without increasing suicidality risk
- Convenient (ideally oral), well-tolerated therapy that meaningfully improves executive function/working memory and everyday function beyond supportive/off-label care

name: Cyclothymic disorder
description: Cyclothymic disorder is a chronic, fluctuating bipolar spectrum condition marked by recurrent subthreshold hypomanic and depressive symptoms for at least two years, often beginning in adolescence or young adulthood and disrupting work, schooling, and relationships. Treatment is largely off label and monitoring heavy, with no United States Food and Drug Administration recommended medications and a risk that antidepressants can trigger hypomania, mixed states, and rapid cycling. The key need is safer, disease tailored maintenance options that stabilize mood, improve day to day function, and reduce progression to bipolar I or II.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Cyclothymia-indicated pharmacotherapy that measurably improves social/work/school functioning and reduces progression to bipolar I/II.
- Treatment for depressive/anxiety symptoms that avoids antidepressant-induced symptom worsening and hypomanic/mixed switches.
- Long-term maintenance option (esp. youth/young adults) with lower monitoring/titration burden and fewer serious safety/tolerability liabilities than off-label mood stabilizers/antipsychotics.

name: Cyclotropia
description: Cyclotropia is a torsional (rotatory) strabismus often due to superior oblique palsy, causing twisted vertical double vision and compensatory head tilt that can make reading and navigating stairs difficult. Care is largely symptomatic with temporary prisms, botulinum toxin, or surgery, but torsion is poorly prism correctable and chemodenervation can induce transient ptosis or vertical deviation, leaving a need for safer, more reliable correction of torsional misalignment and functional vision.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical, torsion-correcting drug therapy for acute symptomatic cyclodiplopia/cyclotropia that restores single vision in primary gaze without occlusion and avoids surgery.
- Longer-acting local neuromuscular modulator vs botulinum toxin that maintains alignment ≥6 months to reduce frequent re-treatment.
- Precision-delivered/low-diffusion chemodenervation to reduce off-target ocular AEs (e.g., ptosis/vertical deviation) and systemic toxin-spread risk.

name: Congenital nystagmus
description: Congenital or early onset nystagmus is a lifelong neurovisual disorder beginning in infancy with involuntary eye movements that blur vision, slow reading, and increase fatigue. It is often linked to underlying sensory pathway disease such as albinism or retinal dystrophies, so reducing the oscillation does not reliably restore vision. Today care is largely supportive with glasses, prisms, and surgery to reduce abnormal head posture but no cure and no treatment that stops nystagmus. Chronic drug suppression is difficult to justify in children due to lifelong dosing and side effects, driving demand for pediatric safe therapies that improve real world visual function and for disease modifying approaches for retinal causes including gene therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pediatric (incl. <12y) non-sedating therapy that meaningfully improves BCVA (logMAR) and foveation time/nystagmus intensity without systemic AE burden
- Treatments for INS with afferent visual system anomalies (e.g., foveal/optic nerve hypoplasia, albinism/retinal disease) that deliver meaningful vision gains beyond nystagmus suppression
- Durable, disease-modifying approaches with long-term benefit (e.g., retinal gene/vision-restoration therapies) vs lifelong symptomatic dosing

name: Delayed sleep-wake phase disorder
description: Delayed sleep-wake phase disorder is a circadian rhythm condition, common in adolescents, where the main sleep period shifts late so patients cannot fall asleep at conventional bedtimes and struggle to wake for school or work, yet sleep is typically normal when allowed to follow the delayed schedule. Current care relies on precisely timed melatonin and light and behavioral interventions that are operationally hard to execute and relapse prone, compounded by variable over the counter melatonin quality. Key unmet needs include durable, easier to use phase advancing therapies that can be taken near bedtime, pharmaceutical grade melatonin like exposure, and precision options for biologically defined subtypes such as CRY1 related delayed sleep.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Bedtime-dosed circadian phase–advancing drug that avoids hours-before-bed melatonin timing and reduces reliance on daily morning light-box therapy
- Precision therapy for biologically driven (e.g., CRY1Δ11) DSWPD with objective, durable phase correction beyond melatonin
- Pharmaceutical-grade alternative to OTC melatonin with predictable exposure and proven long-term endocrine/pubertal safety (esp. adolescents)

name: Ptosis | congenital
description: Congenital ptosis is upper eyelid drooping present at birth or in the first year, often from levator muscle dysfunction, and can obstruct vision so infants adopt a chin up posture. Management is mainly surgery, with urgent repair when the visual axis is threatened to prevent amblyopia. Today’s biggest gaps are procedure burden and complications like incomplete eyelid closure and recurrence, with many children needing repeat operations as they grow, creating demand for a safe pediatric nonsurgical eyelid lift that is durable and vision sparing.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pediatric, non-surgical eyelid-elevating drug that rapidly clears the visual axis in infants with vision-threatening congenital ptosis (high amblyopia risk/ocular torticollis).
- Medical alternative for poor-levator-function congenital ptosis (≤4 mm) that avoids post-surgical lagophthalmos/exposure keratopathy.
- Durable, growth-accommodating therapy that maintains eyelid-height symmetry through childhood and reduces repeat operations (recurrence/undercorrection/revision).

name: Craniosynostosis
description: Congenital premature fusion of skull sutures in infancy, restricting skull expansion during rapid brain growth and causing head-shape deformity and sometimes increased intracranial pressure; care is still surgery-centric, often before age 1 and sometimes across multiple operations, with major burdens from perioperative blood loss and transfusions and prolonged post-operative helmet therapy (about 23 hours per day for around a year), highlighting the need for safer, less invasive and more durable treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-life disease‑modifying therapy for syndromic/genetic craniosynostosis to prevent premature suture fusion and reduce/replace repeated surgeries.
- Perioperative hemostatic pharmacotherapy to materially reduce blood loss, transfusions, and ICU/hospital stay during infant craniosynostosis surgery.
- Adjunct therapy to shorten or eliminate prolonged post‑endoscopic helmeting while preserving head-shape outcomes.

name: Diphyllobothriasis
description: Long lasting intestinal fish tapeworm infection acquired from raw or undercooked fish, usually asymptomatic but can cause gastrointestinal symptoms and vitamin B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anemia; treatment is typically single dose oral praziquantel, with limited United States alternatives and need for post treatment cure confirmation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- FDA-approved, US-available labeled therapy (or new agent class) to replace current off-label/limited options
- Pediatric-optimized/dispersible oral formulation with established safety/labeling for children <4 years
- More reliable single-dose cure for high-worm-burden or prior-treatment-failure cases with fewer systemic adverse events

name: Cryptorchidism
description: Cryptorchidism is a common congenital condition where one or both testes fail to descend, usually noticed on newborn exam as an empty scrotum, especially in premature infants. While often asymptomatic early, persistent undescended testes raise long term risks of infertility, testicular cancer, torsion, and inguinal hernia, making timely correction critical. Care is largely surgical orchiopexy with referral if descent has not occurred by six months, and hormone based descent therapy is discouraged due to low and non durable response. Unmet needs include effective non surgical options and approaches that better preserve future fertility and reduce procedure burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, non-surgical pharmacotherapy achieving scrotal descent in palpable/inguinal undescended testes (vs low/undurable hCG/GnRH response).
- Peri-operative/early-life adjunct that preserves germ cells and improves later fertility outcomes in high-risk boys (e.g., bilateral UDT or delayed correction >15–18 months).
- Post-orchiopexy analgesic regimen maximizing opioid-free recovery at 48 hours and 10–14 days while maintaining pain control.

name: Macular edema | cystoid
description: Pseudophakic cystoid macular edema, or Irvine Gass syndrome, is cystic fluid swelling in the macula after cataract surgery that can blur central vision and peaks around six weeks post op. It is a common cause of postoperative visual loss and a meaningful minority do not fully regain 6/6 vision. Care typically starts with topical nonsteroidal anti inflammatory and steroid drops, but persistent and high risk cases such as patients with diabetes face limited evidence based guidance and tradeoffs including steroid related intraocular pressure elevation and rare nonsteroidal anti inflammatory drug associated corneal melt.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid‑sparing therapy for persistent/refractory Irvine–Gass (pseudophakic) CME that reliably restores 6/6 vision
- Validated prevention regimen for diabetic patients with NPDR undergoing cataract surgery where optimal anti‑inflammatory prophylaxis is unknown
- Drop‑minimizing/depot (“dropless”) anti‑inflammatory strategy to replace QID topical NSAID+steroid while reducing NSAID corneal toxicity and steroid IOP/glaucoma risk

name: Ovarian cyst
description: Ovarian cysts are common, usually benign fluid filled sacs that often form during ovulation and resolve within one to two menstrual cycles, so many are found incidentally. When larger they can cause pelvic pain pressure and bloating, and occasionally rupture or torsion with acute severe pain and bleeding. Care is dominated by ultrasound surveillance and surgery for large symptomatic or suspicious cysts, while hormonal contraception may prevent new cysts but does not shrink existing ones, leaving an unmet need for non surgical cyst resolving and fertility sparing options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Active, non-surgical cyst-resolution drug for symptomatic/persistent simple/functional ovarian cysts that speeds ultrasound-confirmed remission vs 2–3-cycle watchful waiting and reduces need for cystectomy/oophorectomy.
- Non-hormonal prophylaxis for recurrent functional ovarian cysts that prevents new cysts without combined-hormonal (e.g., clot) risks.
- Fertility-sparing medical therapy for ovarian endometriomas that reduces cyst size/recurrence and pain while avoiding ovarian-reserve loss and repeat-surgery risk.

name: Discrete subaortic stenosis
description: Discrete subaortic stenosis is a progressive congenital left ventricular outflow tract obstruction just below the aortic valve, usually from a fibrous subaortic membrane. It is often found in otherwise asymptomatic children after an incidental murmur, confirmed on echocardiography. Turbulent flow progressively injures the aortic valve, leading to aortic regurgitation. Surgery relieves obstruction but is not curative and recurrence is common, creating an unmet need for durable disease control that prevents repeat operations and long term valve damage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Medical therapy to reverse/stop discrete subaortic stenosis progression (delay/avoid surgery)
- Adjunct therapy to prevent post-resection subaortic membrane recurrence and reduce reoperations
- Valve-protection therapy to prevent/provide slower progression of aortic regurgitation/insufficiency and reduce valve repair/replacement need

name: Eczema herpeticum
description: Eczema herpeticum, or Kaposi varicelliform eruption, is a rapidly spreading herpes simplex virus skin infection most often complicating atopic dermatitis, causing fever and clusters of blisters or punched out erosions. It can extend to the eyes with risk of permanent vision loss or rarely disseminate systemically with meaningful mortality if untreated, making early recognition and treatment time critical. Care is burdensome with frequent oral antiviral dosing and escalation to hospital intravenous therapy in severe cases. Recurrence, antiviral resistance, and nephrotoxic second line options keep prevention and simpler outpatient grade regimens a key unmet need.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Targeted antiviral prophylaxis for eczema‑herpeticum–high‑risk atopic dermatitis patients (esp. starting JAK inhibitors/systemic immunosuppression) with recurrent HSV to prevent EH flares.
