- Hospital‑avoiding, simplified acute anti‑HSV regimens (long‑acting parenteral or once/twice‑daily oral) that match inpatient IV acyclovir outcomes while reducing dosing/infusion burden.
- Non‑nephrotoxic, resistance‑robust anti‑HSV therapies for severe/complicated EH (infants/immunocompromised), including effective options for acyclovir‑resistant HSV.

name: Empty sella syndrome
description: Empty sella syndrome is a radiologic finding where cerebrospinal fluid fills the sella turcica and flattens the pituitary, often found incidentally with preserved pituitary function. When symptomatic, it commonly affects middle aged obese hypertensive women and can cause chronic headaches, visual changes, or pituitary hormone deficits. Care is largely symptomatic, and unmet needs center on better tolerated intracranial pressure control and safer, more physiologic long term hormone replacement when endocrine axes are affected.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Better-tolerated intracranial-pressure–lowering therapy for ESS patients with intracranial hypertension/headache to reduce reliance on acetazolamide adverse effects and avoid progression to shunt procedures
- Safer antidiuretic replacement for ESS patients with central diabetes insipidus that preserves efficacy while materially lowering desmopressin-associated hyponatremia risk and sodium-monitoring burden
- Physiologic/circadian glucocorticoid replacement for ESS-associated adrenal-axis insufficiency to reduce under/over-replacement from immediate-release hydrocortisone and improve fatigue/QoL

name: Endometrial cancer | adenosquamous carcinoma
description: Endometrial cancer is the predominant uterine malignancy, usually presenting in postmenopausal women around age 60 with abnormal vaginal bleeding, which helps many endometrioid tumors get caught early and cured by hysterectomy. The hardest clinical problem is the smaller set of aggressive histologies such as uterine serous carcinoma, often HER2 high, that drive a disproportionate share of deaths, plus ultra rare adenosquamous variants where evidence and standardized protocols are thin. In advanced or recurrent disease after platinum chemotherapy, current options like lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab are frequently limited by toxicity and discontinuation, leaving demand for better tolerated, more durable targeted approaches including HER2 directed antibody drug conjugates.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Better-tolerated alternatives to lenvatinib+pembrolizumab for post‑platinum pMMR/MSS advanced/recurrent disease while maintaining efficacy
- More effective/durable HER2‑targeted regimens (including next‑gen HER2 ADCs) for HER2/neu‑positive high‑risk endometrial cancer (esp. uterine serous)
- Standardized, evidence‑based systemic therapy options for rare adenosquamous endometrial cancer (incl. glassy‑cell variants), ideally biomarker‑driven/basket‑trial enabled

name: Endomyocardial fibrosis
description: Tropical restrictive cardiomyopathy caused by subendocardial scarring of ventricular apices and inflow tracts, limiting filling and often causing valvular regurgitation, heart failure, arrhythmias, and thromboembolism. Disproportionately affects impoverished children and young adults in tropical and subtropical regions. Care is largely late stage symptom management because patients often present after the potentially modifiable inflammatory phase, and definitive surgery is scarce and high risk in endemic settings.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying anti-fibrotic to halt endocardial scarring in chronic/advanced EMF and reduce reliance on high-risk/inaccessible endocardectomy/valve surgery.
- Trial-validated early-stage immunomodulation (acute eosinophilic myocarditis/transitional thrombus phase) to prevent progression to dense fibrosis.
- Affordable, monitoring-light anticoagulation for EMF patients with AF/mural thrombus that avoids warfarin INR burden and closes the DOAC evidence/access gap.

name: Exfoliation syndrome
description: Exfoliation syndrome is an age related extracellular matrix disorder that deposits abnormal fibrillary material in the eye, usually in people over 60 and often found incidentally. The main clinical and commercial burden is secondary open angle glaucoma with very high and asymmetric intraocular pressures that can spike outside office hours and may be more resistant to standard drops, pushing patients toward earlier surgery. There is no therapy that halts material deposition, and zonular weakness and poor pupil dilation increase cataract and glaucoma procedure risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease‑modifying topical/intraocular therapy that halts PEX material deposition and prevents progression to ocular hypertension/glaucoma
- IOP‑lowering therapy that reliably suppresses large 24‑hour IOP fluctuations/peaks (including outside office hours) in pseudoexfoliative glaucoma
- Long‑acting, adherence‑friendly, ocular‑surface‑sparing delivery that reduces multi‑drop burden and dependence on accurate self‑instillation in older patients

name: Filariasis
description: Lymphatic filariasis is a mosquito-borne parasitic infection acquired in childhood that damages lymphatic vessels and later presents in adults with chronic limb swelling, scrotal hydrocele, and recurrent painful inflammatory attacks. Mass drug administration suppresses microfilariae but has limited impact on adult worms, requiring annual rounds for 4 to 6 years and regimen changes in Loa loa co-endemic areas. Once chronic lymphedema or hydrocele is established it is often not reversed by antiparasitics, leaving unmet need for safe adult-worm sterilizing therapies and better morbidity-modifying care.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course macrofilaricidal/sterilizing regimen that reliably eliminates adult worms (not just microfilariae), reducing need for ≥4–6 years of annual MDA.
- Safer, broadly deployable treatment for co-endemic areas (onchocerciasis/Loa loa) without DEC-linked severe reactions/toxicities.
- Morbidity-modifying therapy that improves established lymphedema/lymphatic dysfunction (and ideally hydrocele), since chronic disease is not improved by antiparasitics.

name: Flat ductal epithelial atypia
description: Flat epithelial atypia is a microscopic, noninvasive breast duct lining lesion usually found on image guided core biopsy after screening mammography shows microcalcifications. The clinical burden is uncertainty about malignant potential and frequent coexistence with more advanced lesions, historically driving surgical excision despite many patients having low upgrade risk. Key unmet needs are better risk stratification to avoid overtreatment while not missing cancer, and more acceptable prevention options since uptake of oral anti estrogen chemoprevention is very low due to side effects, spurring interest in lower dose and breast targeted endocrine delivery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Low-toxicity oral endocrine chemoprevention (e.g., low-dose tamoxifen) for FEA patients with elevated breast-cancer risk to improve uptake while maintaining prevention benefit
- Breast-localized antiestrogen delivery (topical/transdermal endoxifen or potent metabolites) to preserve efficacy with lower systemic exposure/toxicity
- Risk-stratified chemoprevention targeting only the high-upgrade-risk subset of isolated FEA, with early response/surrogate readouts to avoid overtreatment

name: Beriberi | dry
description: Dry beriberi is the neurologic form of thiamine deficiency, often arising within weeks in people with diets heavy in refined carbohydrates, alcohol use disorder, or malabsorption after bariatric surgery. It typically causes a symmetric distal sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy with burning feet, pins and needles, cramps, weakness, and diminished reflexes that can progress to wasting and disability. Thiamine replacement can be dramatic, but diagnosis is often missed and treatment delayed, especially around glucose or refeeding, and recovery may take months or be incomplete. Key needs are earlier recognition, parenteral dosing when absorption is impaired, and fail-safe inpatient protocols to prevent irreversible neurologic injury.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neuro-repair add-on therapy to accelerate/complete motor–sensory recovery in late/severe dry beriberi neuropathy where deficits can persist for months or become permanent
- Absorption/transport-independent thiamine delivery (or thiamine-equivalents) for high-risk patients with impaired GI uptake/storage (e.g., alcohol use disorder, gastric bypass, congenital malabsorption)
- Fail-safe parenteral thiamine prophylaxis products/protocols ensuring dosing before/with glucose or refeeding in malnourished/high-risk patients to prevent residual neurologic morbidity

name: Dumping syndrome
description: Dumping syndrome is a post meal symptom complex caused by rapid gastric emptying, usually after stomach or esophagus surgery. Early episodes within 30 minutes cause gastrointestinal distress and vasomotor symptoms, while late episodes 1 to 3 hours later are driven by hypoglycemia from insulin over secretion. Many patients remain symptomatic despite diet changes, acarbose, and somatostatin analogues that can be injection burdensome. A key emerging approach is glucagon like peptide 1 receptor antagonism to blunt reactive hypoglycemia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- GLP‑1 receptor antagonists to prevent severe PBH/late dumping hypoglycemia (reduce Level 2–3 events; SMBG <54 mg/dL/severe requiring assistance).
- Oral, non-injectable options (e.g., SGLT2 inhibition) to blunt post‑meal glucose excursions and reduce peak→nadir swings/hypoglycemia risk.
- Long-term therapies that control both early + late dumping while avoiding frequent pre‑meal injections/injection-site pain seen with short-acting somatostatin analogs.

name: Syphilis | congenital
description: Congenital syphilis is a multisystem Treponema pallidum infection transmitted from an untreated or inadequately treated pregnant person to the fetus in utero or at birth. Many infants appear well initially but later develop rash on palms and soles, nasal discharge, jaundice with hepatosplenomegaly and anemia, and painful bone disease, with risks of stillbirth, neonatal death, and long term neurologic, hearing, vision, and bone damage. Care remains dependent on injectable penicillin with fragile multi day dosing and limited evidence backed alternatives during shortages.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pregnancy-safe non-penicillin regimen proven to treat fetal infection/prevent congenital syphilis for penicillin-allergic or penicillin-unavailable patients.
- Simplified neonatal congenital-syphilis therapy (e.g., single-encounter long-acting IM or oral/DOT) non-inferior to 10-day parenteral penicillin regimens and avoiding restart penalties for missed doses.
- Shortage-resilient access to pediatric-appropriate benzathine penicillin G (or a true substitute) to prevent care gaps during Bicillin L-A recalls/shortages.

name: Thyroid eye disease
description: Thyroid eye disease is a chronic autoimmune orbitopathy usually linked to Graves disease where autoantibody driven inflammation enlarges extraocular muscles and orbital fat, causing proptosis, pain, irritation, light sensitivity and diplopia that can progress to vision threatening optic neuropathy. The active inflammatory phase can last two years or more and often burns out into scarring, leaving persistent disfigurement and functional impairment. Despite teprotumumab, treatment is burdensome with eight intravenous infusions and risks such as hyperglycemia and sometimes permanent hearing loss, many patients still need staged orbital, strabismus or eyelid surgery and recurrences occur.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, relapse-resistant correction of proptosis and diplopia (sustained long-term benefit with minimal need for re-treatment)
- Effective medical therapy for chronic/inactive or long-duration TED (e.g., >18 months/low CAS) to reduce reliance on rehabilitative surgery
- Safer, more convenient options vs infusion-based teprotumumab (avoid hearing loss/hyperglycemia; shorten/simplify administration)

name: Entropion
description: Entropion is a turned in eyelid, most often the lower lid in older adults, that makes lashes rub the ocular surface causing foreign body sensation, tearing, redness, discharge, discomfort and blurry vision and can progress to corneal abrasion, ulceration or even perforation. Lubricants, taping and botulinum toxin offer only temporary relief, so definitive care usually requires surgery. Outcomes are worse and recurrence is higher in cicatricial disease with severe conjunctival scarring, highlighting unmet need for longer acting nonsurgical correction, anti scarring adjuncts and better corneal protective healing therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, non-surgical lid-eversion pharmacotherapy (e.g., long-acting neuromodulator) for involutional lower-lid entropion in poor surgical candidates
- Anti-fibrotic/anti-scarring adjunct therapy for cicatricial/trachomatous entropion to reduce long-term post-surgical recurrence
- Corneal-protective/epithelial-healing topical therapy to prevent friction-driven ulceration/scarring while awaiting definitive lid correction

name: Epidemic pleurodynia
description: Epidemic pleurodynia (Bornholm disease) is a contagious, usually Coxsackie B viral illness most common in people under 30 that causes abrupt inflammation of the chest wall muscles with severe pleuritic chest or upper abdominal pain plus fever and viral symptoms, often appearing in clusters. Care is essentially supportive and pain focused, with no specific antiviral therapy, and prevention is limited by the lack of a vaccine.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early oral Coxsackie B/enterovirus-targeted antiviral to shorten pleurodynia’s painful course vs supportive-only care.
- Pediatric-safe, opioid-sparing acute analgesia for excruciating pleuritic/epigastric pain (avoiding codeine and invasive nerve blocks).
- Coxsackie B immunization/prophylaxis for close-contact outbreaks to reduce incidence rather than just treating symptoms.
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus page; covered under https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001340.htm

name: Epidermal nevus
description: Epidermal nevus is a benign mosaic overgrowth of epidermal cells that typically appears at birth or in infancy as linear tan to brown or velvety plaques along the lines of Blaschko and may thicken into wart like lesions. Some patients have eye bone or nervous system involvement or inflammatory variants with intense itch. Medical therapy is largely ineffective and topical responses are often poor while procedures can scar and frequently recur, creating demand for durable genotype guided and itch relieving targeted treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pediatric, genotype-guided topical pathway inhibition (e.g., mTOR/PI3K/FGFR-axis) to measurably flatten mosaic epidermal nevi (↓ lesion thickness/volume)
- Scar-sparing durable medical alternative/adjuvant to ablative procedures that reduces recurrence and iatrogenic scarring (esp. ILVEN or large lesions)
- Targeted anti–IL-17/IL-12/23 (psoriasis-pathway) therapy for CARD14/psoriasis-like ILVEN to achieve rapid, meaningful itch relief and inflammatory plaque improvement

name: Esophageal diverticulosis
description: Esophageal intramural pseudodiverticulosis is a rare disorder of dilated submucosal gland ducts that typically presents in older adults with slowly progressive solid food dysphagia from upper or mid esophageal strictures, often with intermittent food impaction and weight loss. It is linked to reflux, diabetes, tobacco or alcohol exposure, and esophageal Candida. Care is largely supportive with acid suppression, antifungals when needed, and repeated endoscopic dilations, but pseudodiverticula and fibrosis related strictures often persist or recur, driving a need for durable medical therapies that prevent restenosis, reduce Candida relapses, and address coexisting motility disorders.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Anti-fibrotic/anti-inflammatory drug therapy to prevent or slow fibrosis-driven stricture recurrence and extend dysphagia-free intervals (reduce repeat dilation dependence)
- Non-systemic (swallowed/topical) antifungal ± mucosal-protective therapy for suspected/confirmed Candida-associated cases to reduce dysphagia/relapse while avoiding long-term systemic azole exposure
- Manometry-guided motility-modulating oral therapy for the subset with co-existing motility disorders (e.g., achalasia/jackhammer) to improve dysphagia beyond mechanical dilation

name: Factitious disorder
description: Factitious disorder is a rare psychiatric condition where people deliberately fake or induce illness to occupy the sick role, often cycling through dramatic, unexplained presentations and repeated evaluations that can lead to iatrogenic harm. Care is hard because patients frequently deny the behavior and disengage, and there are no clearly effective treatments beyond psychotherapy and careful management to avoid unnecessary tests and procedures.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacotherapy that reduces/blocks the core “sick-role” drive (symptom falsification/induction) to prevent recurrent unnecessary tests/procedures/surgeries and iatrogenic harm.
- Adjunctive medication to improve sustained engagement (reduce denial/hostility/avoidance) so psychotherapy can be delivered in patients who refuse treatment and “doctor-hop.”
- Comorbidity-focused meds (depression/anxiety) with low misuse/abuse potential and minimal monitoring burden for a population at high risk of harmful medication misuse/substance abuse/suicidality.

name: Fasciolopsiasis
description: Fasciolopsiasis is a foodborne intestinal fluke infection caused by Fasciolopsis buski, acquired from contaminated aquatic plants or water. Many infections are asymptomatic, but heavier worm burdens, often in children in endemic Asian settings, cause abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhea that can progress to malabsorption with protein loss leading to edema and ascites, and occasionally intestinal obstruction. Praziquantel is effective, but real-world care is constrained by pediatric delivery, multi-dose regimens and the need for supportive management in severe cases, leaving room for simpler child-friendly dosing and faster stabilization in high-burden presentations.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pediatric-ready, child-friendly anti-*F. buski* regimen with established safety/PK in children <4 years
- Bioavailability-improved praziquantel (or new oral flukicide) to deliver more consistent exposure and reduce retreatment/meal-timed multi-dose complexity
- Rapid-acting regimen/adjunct for severe/heavy-burden or obstructive/ectopic disease to reduce surgery-first management
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus URL (not indexed as a standalone topic)

name: Adenoma | gallbladder
description: Gallbladder adenomas are usually asymptomatic mucosal polyps found incidentally but can cause intermittent right upper quadrant pain with nausea or vomiting and carry malignant potential. The major bottleneck is risk stratification since imaging cannot reliably separate benign from malignant lesions, pushing care toward repeated ultrasound surveillance for small polyps and prophylactic cholecystectomy at size thresholds, which can still lead to unnecessary follow up and surgery. Better diagnostic tools and non-surgical options are key unmet needs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical drug to shrink surveillance-eligible small gallbladder polyps (esp. 6–9 mm) enough to stop serial ultrasound follow-up.
- Chemopreventive/anti-neoplastic therapy for true adenomatous (neoplastic) gallbladder polyps to avoid prophylactic cholecystectomy triggers (e.g., ≥10 mm or PSC-associated pathways).
- Symptom-targeted medical option for polypoid lesions with biliary-type symptoms that reduces symptoms and stabilizes polyp growth to avoid cholecystectomy.

name: Gastric cancer | adenocarcinoma
description: Gastric adenocarcinoma starts in the stomach’s inner lining and often causes nonspecific early symptoms such as early satiety, fatigue, and weight loss, so ~58% of cases are diagnosed at regional or metastatic stage. Current care relies on surgery when feasible and systemic chemotherapy that can prolong survival but is rarely curative, with peritoneal metastases particularly hard to treat and typically managed palliatively. Immunotherapy benefit is concentrated in tumors with higher programmed death ligand 1 expression, leaving many patients needing broadly effective, lower toxicity regimens with less burdensome administration than prolonged fluorouracil infusions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- First-line regimens that deliver clear OS benefit in PD‑L1–low gastric/GEJ cancer (CPS <5) where chemo±PD‑1 shows minimal incremental gain.
- Peritoneal-directed/peritoneal-penetrant therapies for gastric cancer with peritoneal metastasis (incl. diffuse-type, immune-cold tumors) where systemic therapy performs poorly.
- Lower-toxicity, lower-discontinuation regimens that also reduce administration burden (avoid 46‑hour 5‑FU pumps and prolonged BID capecitabine schedules) via simpler oral/SC-based care.

name: Stroke | hemorrhagic
description: Hemorrhagic stroke is bleeding in or around the brain from a ruptured vessel, often in older adults with hypertension, causing sudden neurologic deficits. Outcomes are difficult to improve because hematomas expand rapidly in the first hours and there is no proven therapy that reliably prevents expansion and improves function. In aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, delayed cerebral ischemia remains a major driver of deterioration, while nimodipine is burdensome and can cause hypotension. Anticoagulant associated bleeds add urgency but reversal options carry thromboembolic risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Hyperacute ICH hematoma-expansion arrest (≤2 hours from onset) that improves 180-day functional outcomes (mRS), not just CT hematoma volume.
- aSAH delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) prevention with continuous prophylaxis/non-vasospasm mechanisms that avoid nimodipine-related hypotension/BP-driven interruptions and reduce q4h/21-day dosing burden.
- Safer, outcomes-improving reversal for Factor Xa–inhibitor–associated ICH that avoids andexanet’s thrombosis risk and addresses the post-Andexxa U.S. access gap.

name: Hydrocephalus
description: Hydrocephalus is a buildup of cerebrospinal fluid that compresses the brain, presenting in infants with enlarged head and bulging fontanelle and in older adults as slowly progressive gait impairment, cognitive slowing, and urinary incontinence. Care is still largely surgical via shunts, but durability is poor due to frequent blockage and infection, with about half of pediatric shunts failing within two years and driving repeat operations. Major unmet needs include longer lasting fluid control and effective non surgical options for shunt nonresponders and patients who are poor surgical candidates.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drugs/biologics that prevent VP shunt obstruction and infection to extend revision-free shunt survival
- Anti-inflammatory/anti-fibrotic therapies to prevent post-hemorrhagic/post-infectious hydrocephalus progressing to shunt dependence
- Non-surgical pharmacotherapy for NPH/iNPH that improves cognition and urinary symptoms and treats non-responders/poor surgical candidates

name: Hymenolepiasis
description: Hymenolepiasis is a worldwide intestinal infection caused by the dwarf tapeworm, typically acquired from egg contaminated food or water and concentrated in children and institutional settings with poor sanitation. Most cases are asymptomatic, but heavy infections can cause pruritus ani, sleep disruption, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and anorexia, and autoinfection can rapidly amplify worm burden. Management is complicated by easy person to person spread, the need for repeat dosing and cure confirmation, limited treatment alternatives in the United States, and an evidence gap for praziquantel safety in children under 4.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Single-course regimens that reliably break internal autoinfection/reinfection and improve ≥1‑month stool-clearance durability in high-risk (often pediatric/family-cluster) settings.
- Infant/toddler-ready oral therapy with established safety and dosing in children <4 years (ideally including ≤1 year).
- US-available alternative to praziquantel with a simpler, shorter regimen than multi-day niclosamide/nitazoxanide courses.

name: Infectious mononucleosis
description: Infectious mononucleosis is a contagious Epstein Barr virus illness that disproportionately affects teenagers and young adults, causing extreme fatigue, fever, and sore throat. Most recover in 2 to 4 weeks but fatigue can persist for months, and spleen enlargement can force about a month away from contact sports due to rupture risk. With no vaccine and no disease targeted therapy beyond supportive care, key unmet needs are preventing infection and shortening the prolonged fatigue and return to activity window.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- EBV prophylactic vaccine to prevent symptomatic infectious mononucleosis in EBV‑seronegative adolescents/young adults.
- Early-start, short-course oral anti‑EBV therapy to shorten recovery/time off school-work and reduce risk of prolonged post‑IM fatigue (≥6 months).
- Therapy to rapidly reverse splenomegaly and lower spleen-rupture risk to shorten the ~4-week restriction from vigorous/contact sports.

name: Heterophyiasis
description: Fish borne intestinal fluke infection acquired from eating raw or undercooked contaminated fish in endemic regions, often asymptomatic or causing intermittent abdominal pain and diarrhea but heavy infections can lead to ectopic egg migration with potentially fatal cardiac and reported brain involvement. Care relies on praziquantel yet some patients need multiple courses and use is constrained in infants under 1 year and by required breastfeeding interruption, creating demand for better tolerated, practical regimens for high burden disease and vulnerable populations.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Lower-toxicity, higher-bioavailability oral flukicide that preserves single-dose cure while reducing common praziquantel AEs (esp. in heavy worm burden)
- One-course curative regimen for heavy/diffuse or mixed trematode infections that currently may require multiple praziquantel courses/steroid adjuncts
- Infant- and breastfeeding-compatible therapy without current praziquantel age floor (<1 year) or breastfeeding interruption

name: Human granulocytic anaplasmosis
description: Tick-borne infection (Anaplasma phagocytophilum) causing acute febrile illness with cytopenias and elevated liver enzymes, often in older adults in the US Midwest and Northeast; treatment depends on rapid doxycycline initiation despite frequent missed bite history, with no recommended post-bite prophylaxis and limited evidence-based alternatives for pregnancy or tetracycline allergy, making delayed diagnosis a key driver of rare but severe organ failure complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-tetracycline regimen with proven in‑vivo efficacy and pregnancy safety for pregnant patients or those with severe tetracycline allergy.
- True post‑tick‑bite prophylaxis (e.g., single‑dose/long‑acting) for high‑risk exposures (≥65 or immunocompromised).
- Rescue therapy (antibiotic or adjunct) that prevents progression to late/severe disease (respiratory failure, bleeding, organ failure) despite delayed treatment.

name: Hypertensive heart disease
description: Hypertensive heart disease is cumulative cardiac end organ damage from long standing high blood pressure, often detected late after silent remodeling into left ventricular hypertrophy and interstitial fibrosis with dyspnea, palpitations, and edema progressing to heart failure; key unmet needs are earlier detection and disease modifying approaches that prevent or reverse myocardial fibrosis beyond blood pressure control, with current add ons like spironolactone limited by hyperkalemia and lab monitoring burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drugs that reverse myocardial fibrosis/histologic remodeling beyond BP control/LVH regression (including patients who develop LVH despite well-controlled BP).
- Therapies that prevent progression from LVH/diastolic dysfunction to overt HF (HFpEF/HFrEF) and reduce HF events in HHD.
- Cardio-protective add-ons (e.g., safer MR-pathway options) that avoid hyperkalemia risk and reduce/obviate potassium-monitoring requirements limiting MRA use.

name: Keratoacanthoma
description: Rapidly growing, locally destructive sun related skin tumor in older fair skinned men, presenting as a 1 to 2 cm nodule with a central keratin plug on the face or upper limbs that may regress over months but often scars. Diagnostic overlap with squamous cell carcinoma makes watchful waiting risky so most patients undergo excision or Mohs surgery, creating unmet need for accurate diagnosis and scar sparing, well tolerated topical or intralesional options especially for multiple or recurrent lesions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Scar-sparing non-surgical lesion clearance for solitary/recurrent KA in cosmetically sensitive or hard-to-excise sites (e.g., nose/face) and in poor surgical candidates
- “Diagnostic-ambiguity–proof” drug option usable when partial biopsy can’t reliably distinguish KA from invasive SCC
- Better-tolerated systemic/field therapy for high-lesion-burden KA (e.g., generalized eruptive disease) to reduce scarring without limiting systemic toxicity

name: Renal papillary necrosis
description: Renal papillary necrosis is death of part or all of the kidney papillae, often triggered by analgesic overuse, diabetes related kidney disease, infection, sickle cell disease, or urinary tract obstruction, and presents with flank pain, hematuria, fever and dysuria, sometimes with tissue in the urine. Sloughed papillae can obstruct the ureter causing renal colic, acute kidney injury and urosepsis. Care is largely supportive and cause directed, with no disease specific therapy, leaving a need for treatments that prevent papillary ischemia, limit sloughing and better protect kidney function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Renal-medullary “papilla salvage” cytoprotective therapy for high-risk etiologies (e.g., diabetes/NSAID exposure) to halt ongoing damage and prevent progression to kidney failure/dialysis/transplant
- Anti-necrosis/anti-sloughing therapy to reduce papillary sloughing (hematuria/ureteral colic) and prevent obstruction-driven infection and post-renal AKI
- Kidney-safe anti-infective or host-directed adjunct to prevent/tamp down severe RPN infections that can be fatal

name: Allergy | legume
description: Immunoglobulin E mediated allergy to legumes such as lentils and chickpeas, typically starting in early childhood, that can rapidly cause hives or swelling, vomiting, coughing or wheezing, and occasionally life threatening anaphylaxis. Management is still strict avoidance plus rescue epinephrine, yet accidental exposures and cross reactivity between legumes make avoidance unreliable and can broaden dietary restriction. There is no cure and approved immunotherapy is largely peanut specific, leaving demand for dose standardized legume immunotherapy and preventive biologics such as anti immunoglobulin E to reduce severe reactions after accidental exposure.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Licensed, dose-standardized lentil/chickpea/pea immunotherapy (e.g., OIT/EPIT) with validated protocols to reduce reactions after accidental exposure
- Multi-legume desensitization (or proven cross-desensitization) to reduce cascade avoidance in patients allergic to ≥2 legumes
- Biologic prophylaxis/adjunct (anti-IgE) to lower Type I/anaphylaxis risk from accidental exposure and enable safer, faster desensitization

name: Leptospirosis
description: Leptospirosis is a zoonotic bacterial infection acquired from water or soil contaminated with animal urine, often after flooding, ranging from a flu-like illness to severe multi-organ failure with jaundice, renal failure, hemorrhage, meningitis, and potentially fatal pulmonary hemorrhage. Key gaps are rapid, widely available diagnostics, better adjunctive care for severe lung involvement, simpler outpatient antibiotic regimens with fewer treatment reactions, and vaccines that provide durable cross-serovar protection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct therapy that reduces mortality/ventilator days in severe leptospirosis with pulmonary hemorrhage/involvement.
- Simplified short-course oral antibiotic regimen for mild/outpatient leptospirosis with low failure and fewer adverse/Jarisch–Herxheimer reactions.
- Broadly protective, high-safety human vaccine for high-risk exposure groups (e.g., occupational/flood).

name: Loiasis
description: Loiasis is a deerfly transmitted filarial infection in West and Central African rainforests where adult worms live in subcutaneous tissues and symptoms are often silent until episodic Calabar swellings or visible eye worm migration. The clinical bottleneck is treatment safety because rapid parasite killing in patients with high microfilarial loads can trigger severe neurologic toxicity, forcing quantitative blood smears, careful risk stratification, and slow load reduction or apheresis before diethylcarbamazine. This leaves demand for practical short course oral regimens that quickly reduce microfilaremia and clear adult worms with fewer inflammatory reactions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-encephalopathy-inducing microfilaricidal/macrofilariacidal therapy for hypermicrofilaremic patients (≥8,000 mf/mL) to avoid apheresis/monitoring-intensive pre-reduction.
- Short-course (3–5 day) oral microfilaremia-reducing regimen to replace slow/long pretreatment approaches.
- Low-reaction parasiticidal drugs or adjuncts to prevent treatment-triggered inflammatory syndromes (e.g., Calabar swelling/pruritus/eosinophilia) and reduce need for steroids/antihistamines.
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus URL for loiasis

name: Ideomotor apraxia
description: Ideomotor apraxia is an acquired disorder of skilled action, often after stroke or early neurodegeneration, where patients cannot perform learned movements on request despite intact strength and comprehension. It undermines independence in everyday self care and tool use through breakdowns in multistep tasks. Care is largely occupational and other rehabilitation rather than disease modifying therapy, and benefits are often task specific with limited durable transfer to real world function. Key unmet needs are scalable treatments that produce lasting, generalizable improvements across daily activities, with adjunct approaches like noninvasive neuromodulation emerging.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Restorative symptomatic drug therapy for post–left-hemisphere stroke ideomotor/limb apraxia that reduces basic ADL dependency (grooming/bathing/toileting)
- Adjunct drug delivering durable, task-generalizable improvements that transfer to untrained daily activities
- Home-administered therapy that reduces the time/logistics burden of intensive rehab while maintaining functional gains

name: Idiopathic progressive polyneuropathy
description: Idiopathic progressive polyneuropathy is a chronic, slowly progressive peripheral nerve disorder in older adults with no identifiable cause despite testing, causing extremity numbness and tingling, burning or shooting pain, and balance loss that drives falls and functional decline. Care is largely symptomatic with neuropathic pain agents that often cause drowsiness or dizziness, leaving major unmet need for disease modifying neuroprotection and better tolerated pain control that preserves mobility and daily function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy that slows axonal neuropathy progression and improves mobility/balance and basic ADLs in late-adulthood CIAP/CSPN.
- Analgesics for painful CIAP/CSPN that achieve substantially higher ≥50% pain-responder rates with fewer discontinuations than current oral standards.
- Better-tolerated, simpler-to-use options for older adults (non-sedating/peripherally restricted, fewer daily doses; potentially localized/topical).

name: Non-small cell lung cancer | non-squamous
description: Metastatic nonsquamous non-small cell lung cancer is a common lung adenocarcinoma of older adults (median age ~71) that causes progressive cough, dyspnea, chest pain and weight loss. First-line chemo-immunotherapy has improved outcomes, but many patients have few effective options after progression and brain metastases are frequent and difficult to control due to blood–brain barrier limits and resistance. Hard-to-treat molecular subsets such as STK11 or KEAP1 altered tumors have poor prognosis, underscoring the need for more durable systemic control and effective therapies in the central nervous system.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Higher-ORR/OS 2L+ therapies post–chemo-immunotherapy (esp. poor-prognosis STK11/KEAP1 subsets) vs modest docetaxel outcomes
- Systemic NSCLC treatments with reliable, durable intracranial responses for patients with brain metastases
- 1L regimens matching KEYNOTE-189 efficacy with fewer serious AEs/discontinuations and simpler (less burdensome) administration than multi-drug Q3W IV chemo-IO

name: Gastritis | lymphocytic
description: Rare, biopsy defined inflammatory stomach disorder marked by increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, often associated with celiac disease or Helicobacter pylori but idiopathic in some cases. Symptoms are nonspecific such as dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss and iron deficiency anemia, and endoscopy may appear normal. Treatment is largely symptomatic acid suppression and treating underlying triggers when found, with a thin prospective evidence base and limited options for durable histologic remission or refractory anemia and malabsorption when the trigger is unclear.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Histology-normalizing, durable-remission therapy for idiopathic/unknown-etiology lymphocytic gastritis
- Lower-pill-burden H. pylori eradication strategy for LG patients with proven infection
- Complication-directed therapy for refractory LG with iron-deficiency anemia/malabsorption

name: Macular hole
description: Macular hole is a full thickness defect of the fovea causing painless, progressive central vision loss with distortion and a central scotoma, most often in women over 65. Treatment is largely surgical pars plana vitrectomy with internal limiting membrane peeling and gas tamponade, but many patients face postoperative burden such as days of face down positioning and complications like cataract, and larger holes are more likely to fail closure, leaving a need for less burdensome, more reliable repair especially for large or recurrent holes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical pharmacologic closure for VMT-associated small full-thickness macular holes to avoid vitrectomy.
- Adjunct/regenerative therapies to improve closure and visual outcomes in “difficult” holes (large, chronic, high-myopia, RD-associated, or refractory/failed surgery).
- Therapies that reduce post-vitrectomy morbidity and recovery burden (notably cataract prevention/delay and less face-down posturing).

name: Intestinal impaction
description: Fecal impaction is a large, hard stool mass lodged in the rectum, disproportionately affecting frail hospitalized or institutionalized older adults and causing total constipation with abdominal distension and pain, sometimes with overflow diarrhea. Care is often invasive, relying on enemas and manual disimpaction, and can be risky in comorbid patients since some enemas, such as sodium phosphate, can trigger serious toxicity including phosphate nephropathy, underscoring the need for safer, easier, less traumatic options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid, non-invasive disimpaction drug for elderly hospitalized/institutionalized patients to avoid repeated enemas/manual or OR/anesthesia removal
- Fast-onset “enema-equivalent” disimpaction option safer than sodium-phosphate (usable in ≥55 and renal/cardiac/dehydration-risk patients)
- Post-disimpaction maintenance therapy to prevent recurrent impaction in high-risk frail elderly (esp. opioid-exposed/bedridden)

name: Stroke | acute ischemic
description: Acute ischemic stroke is caused by a clot blocking a brain blood vessel, cutting off oxygen so brain cells begin dying within minutes and leaving a high risk of lasting disability or death, especially in older adults with risk factors such as high blood pressure and diabetes. The central unmet need is faster, more reliable reperfusion and neuroprotection that can be delivered broadly and safely, since many patients arrive too late or are ineligible for current acute interventions and outcomes depend heavily on minutes-to-treatment.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prehospital/ED neuroprotection scalable to AIS patients who never receive reperfusion
- Next-gen thrombolytic/adjunct that maintains reperfusion benefit but lowers symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage risk
- Add-on neuroprotection or reperfusion-injury mitigation to improve 90-day functional independence (mRS 0–2) after EVT/IVT

name: Kleptomania
description: Kleptomania is a chronic psychiatric impulse control disorder marked by recurrent, irresistible urges to steal unneeded items, often cycling from mounting tension to brief relief and then guilt and shame. Patients frequently present late, after legal consequences, and commonly have comorbid depression, anxiety, substance misuse, and suicidality that complicate care. Treatment relies on psychotherapy and off label medications, but there is no Food and Drug Administration approved drug and no standard regimen, leaving a clear unmet need for scalable, evidence based, disease targeted interventions that reliably reduce urges and prevent relapse.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- First FDA-approved pharmacotherapy with durable symptom control (sustained K‑YBOCS/K‑SAS and reduced real-world stealing)
- Medications proven safe/effective in high-comorbidity, higher-risk patients (incl. SUD and suicidality)
- Better-tolerated, lower-burden long-term options that reduce reliance on frequent psychotherapy and minimize adverse effects (e.g., nausea)

name: Kwashiorkor
description: Kwashiorkor is an edematous form of severe acute malnutrition typically emerging around weaning onto protein poor diets, causing swelling, distended abdomen, diarrhea, skin and hair changes, lethargy, and frequent infections, and can be fatal or leave disability if treated late. Care is largely protocolized nutritional rehabilitation plus empiric infection and electrolyte management, yet early deaths still cluster around clinically silent infection, dehydration, and electrolyte shifts during refeeding. Longer term, many children relapse or fail to regain durable gut and developmental health after ready to use therapeutic foods stop, driving interest in adjuncts targeting oxidative stress and the gut microbiome.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drug-like adjuncts to prevent early stabilization-phase mortality from diarrhea/malabsorption and refeeding-syndrome electrolyte shifts, shortening time-to-stabilization vs F-75 protocols.
- Redox/antioxidant small-molecule adjuncts (e.g., cysteine/N-acetylcysteine) to correct glutathione depletion and speed kwashiorkor edema/skin-sign resolution vs nutrition-only rehab.
- Microbiome-directed therapeutics (e.g., defined live biotherapeutics) to prevent relapse after RUTF and improve durable neurodevelopmental/cognitive outcomes beyond short-term anthropometrics.

name: Lateral medullary syndrome
description: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome is a posterior circulation brainstem stroke from vertebral or posterior inferior cerebellar artery infarction, causing vertigo, ataxia, crossed sensory loss and frequent dysphagia with dysphonia. Treatment is constrained by the narrow reperfusion window and imaging selected extensions, leaving many patients managed supportively. Dysphagia affects roughly 51 to 94 percent and drives aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, increased mortality and poor quality of life, underscoring the need for better acute identification and durable swallowing restorative therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-hemorrhagic acute reperfusion/penumbral-salvage therapy for lateral medullary infarction usable beyond the <4.5h IV alteplase window.
- Swallow-restoring drug therapy for severe post–lateral medullary syndrome dysphagia to reduce aspiration-pneumonia risk and accelerate return to oral diet.
- Neurorecovery adjunct to improve 1-year functional independence (shift mRS outcomes) in high-risk patients (e.g., presenting with dysphagia).

name: Lichen nitidus
description: Lichen nitidus is a rare inflammatory dermatosis, usually in children or young adults, causing crops of tiny shiny flat topped skin colored papules on the forearms and hands, trunk, and sometimes genital skin, often asymptomatic aside from mild itch but cosmetically distressing. Many cases self resolve, yet generalized or persistent disease can be unpredictable, and today’s empiric options such as topical corticosteroids, topical tacrolimus, and phototherapy have inconsistent responses and meaningful treatment burden, creating demand for reliable evidence backed steroid sparing therapies that can clear extensive disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Predictable, evidence-backed therapy that rapidly clears generalized/persistent lichen nitidus (vs years-long spontaneous resolution) and relieves itch/cosmetic distress.
- Steroid-sparing topical suitable for pediatric + genital/thin-skin disease to avoid topical-corticosteroid toxicity.
- Convenient drug alternative to replace burdensome multi-session phototherapy (e.g., NB‑UVB/PUVA) for extensive/generalized disease.

name: Lingual-facial-buccal dyskinesia
description: Classic orofacial tardive dyskinesia from chronic dopamine receptor blocking drugs, often appearing months to years after exposure and persisting despite stopping. Repetitive lip, tongue, and jaw movements can disrupt speaking, chewing, and swallowing, with weight loss and aspiration risk. Biggest gaps are durable symptom control and therapies that fit older, polypharmacy heavy patients given vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitor tradeoffs such as sedation, QT prolongation risk, drug induced parkinsonism, and dosing or interaction burdens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Restore speech/chewing/swallowing function and reduce aspiration/weight-loss risk in lingual–facial–buccal tardive dyskinesia (beyond AIMS score improvement)
- Avoid VMAT2-inhibitor liabilities (somnolence/sedation, QT prolongation constraints, drug-induced parkinsonism) to enable safer use in older/comorbid polypharmacy patients
- Minimize CYP2D6/CYP3A4 interaction-driven dose limits and simplify dosing/administration (no with-food/divided-dose requirements) to improve compatibility with psychiatric comedications

name: Measles
description: Measles is a highly contagious airborne viral infection with fever, cough, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, then a spreading maculopapular rash and risk of severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis. Despite being vaccine preventable, outbreaks still cause substantial mortality, largely in unvaccinated young children. Care is mainly supportive with no Food and Drug Administration approved antiviral, so high risk patients depend on narrow post exposure windows for measles mumps rubella vaccine or short lived immune globulin that can be logistically hard to deliver.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- FDA-approved acute measles antiviral (ideally oral/early-start) that reduces severe complications (e.g., pneumonia/encephalitis) in high-risk patients (children <5, pregnant, immunocompromised).
- Long-acting measles-neutralizing monoclonal antibody/passive immunization for those who can’t receive MMR, providing longer protection than current immune globulin (~3–4 weeks) and usable at outbreak scale.
- Scalable post-exposure prophylaxis that relaxes tight timing windows (MMR ≤72h; IG ≤6d) and avoids high-volume IM injections or hospital IVIG workflows.

name: Median rhomboid glossitis
description: Localized midline tongue lesion, often in men 30 to 50, usually asymptomatic and Candida associated; recurs after antifungals and is hampered by high burden topical dosing and systemic azole safety risks, leaving need for more durable low burden non azole options, especially for refractory or potentially resistant cases
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Once-daily “set-and-forget” topical therapy matching antifungal clearance vs multi-dose regimens (e.g., nystatin 4×/day, clotrimazole 5×/day)
- Non-azole (resistance-robust) therapy effective in refractory/azole-resistant Candida-associated cases, especially in immunosuppressed patients
- Safer systemic option vs fluconazole with fewer hepatic toxicity, QT, and drug–drug interaction risks while maintaining minimal systemic exposure

name: Allergy | milk
description: Cow’s milk allergy typically begins in early infancy, days to weeks after cow milk based formula or other exposure, with immunoglobulin E mediated reactions ranging from hives and wheeze to anaphylaxis and delayed gastrointestinal symptoms like diarrhea, colic, and bloody stools. Care is still centered on strict avoidance and emergency epinephrine, but milk’s ubiquity and unpredictable severity make accidental exposure hard to prevent. Oral immunotherapy can raise reaction thresholds, yet it is not curative and can still trigger severe reactions, sustaining demand for safer, durable tolerance and lower burden prevention.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable immune tolerance (sustained unresponsiveness after stopping therapy), not just ongoing-exposure desensitization.
- Safer, lower-burden at-home “threshold-raising” therapy to meaningfully reduce accidental reaction risk.
- Prophylaxis that reduces anaphylaxis risk and is validated in infants <1 year, ideally enabling dietary liberalization beyond strict avoidance.

name: Metagonimiasis
description: Metagonimiasis is a food borne intestinal fluke infection from eating undercooked or improperly processed fish, often asymptomatic or causing nonspecific diarrhea and crampy abdominal pain but with rare serious complications from egg migration to organs such as the heart or brain. Treatment relies on praziquantel, yet single dose cure rates are only in the mid 80 percent range and tolerability issues including dizziness plus driving and machinery restrictions raise the bar for a better tolerated, truly single administration cure.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Single-administration therapy achieving near-100% “complete radical cure” without needing repeat dosing vs ~85–88% cure with single-dose praziquantel.
- Stage-agnostic flukicidal therapy active against immature flukes (not mainly adult-stage activity) to enable earlier, more definitive clearance and prevent extraintestinal egg-migration sequelae (heart/brain).
- Better-tolerated non-praziquantel option that reduces CNS/GI adverse effects and avoids post-dose driving/machinery restrictions, especially in high worm-burden infections.
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus page for metagonimiasis

name: Valve disease | mitral stenosis
description: Mitral stenosis is usually rheumatic mitral valve narrowing that restricts left atrial to left ventricular blood flow, often presenting with atrial fibrillation, breathlessness, pulmonary hypertension, and high stroke risk. Care is still dominated by mechanical fixes and chronic management, with key gaps including reliance on vitamin K antagonists rather than simpler oral anticoagulants in rheumatic atrial fibrillation, the long painful course of benzathine penicillin injections to prevent recurrence, and persistent pulmonary hypertension and restenosis in some patients even after valvotomy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- INR-free oral anticoagulation for adults with moderate–severe rheumatic mitral stenosis + atrial fibrillation proven vs warfarin on stroke/systemic embolism with lower major bleeding.
- Longer-acting and/or non-intramuscular secondary prophylaxis for rheumatic fever/RHD that avoids painful frequent benzathine penicillin G injections.
- Targeted therapy to prevent/treat persistent pulmonary hypertension after balloon mitral valvotomy (e.g., PASP ≥40 mmHg at 1 year) to reduce HF events/restenosis/reintervention.

name: Monofixation syndrome
description: Small-angle strabismus state with a central (foveal) suppression scotoma that preserves peripheral fusion, so patients often look normal but have reduced fine stereopsis and mild to moderate amblyopia; care is mostly observation plus amblyopia penalization, yet binocular suppression and stereoacuity rarely normalize and a minority later decompensate with diplopia, leaving demand for therapies that restore central fusion and more controllable, shorter-acting penalization.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Binocular-scotoma reversal to restore fine stereopsis (stereoacuity) in monofixation syndrome
- Pharmacologic prevention of adult decompensation/diplopia by preserving fusional vergence (alignment stability) in established MFS
- Shorter-acting, low-photophobia penalization alternative to atropine for the amblyopia subset of MFS

name: Mucocele
description: Benign mucus filled minor salivary gland cysts, typically triggered by duct rupture after lip biting or other trauma, presenting as a painless clear to bluish dome shaped oral bump that may self rupture but recur. Care is often watchful waiting or local procedures like cryotherapy, laser, or excision, with unmet need for fast low burden treatments that reduce recurrence and avoid procedure related scarring, numbness, disfigurement, and duct injury, especially in younger patients.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Low-burden local drug that reliably clears superficial mucoceles in children/adolescents within days–1 week
- Validated nonsurgical intralesional pharmacotherapy for persistent/recurrent symptomatic oral mucoceles to avoid excision-related recovery/duct injury/scarring
- Safer, more predictable sclerosing-agent strategy for deep/recurrent mucoceles (ranula-spectrum) to cut recurrence while avoiding excision/dissection nerve-risk and OK-432 safety limits

name: Aphasia | nominal
description: Acquired language disorder most often after stroke, where word finding (anomia) can persist into chronic aphasia and disrupt work and relationships; care relies on speech language therapy, but high dose intensive programs are hard to deliver at scale and there is no consensus on optimal dosing, leaving a need for scalable adjuncts that boost recovery and reduce session burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral neuroplasticity-enhancing adjunct to improve chronic (>1 year) post-stroke anomia/word-finding (naming performance/language severity).
- Therapy that delivers meaningful gains with far fewer sessions than intensive high-dose speech-language therapy (≥20h total; ≥3h/week; ≥4 days/week).
- Well-tolerated agent broadly usable in typical older stroke survivors with comorbidities (fewer contraindications/exclusions than prior trials).

name: Neonatal abstinence syndrome
description: Neonatal abstinence syndrome or neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome is withdrawal in a newborn after in utero opioid exposure, marked by central nervous system and gastrointestinal instability such as high pitched crying, tremors, poor feeding, vomiting or diarrhea and autonomic symptoms. Symptoms usually start 1 to 3 days after birth but can appear up to a week, driving prolonged hospital observation and sometimes weeks to months of inpatient weaning. Care is still anchored in supportive nonpharmacologic measures with opioids and sedating adjuncts for severe cases, leaving a major need for safer approaches that control symptoms while shortening costly hospital stays and avoiding outpatient opioid tapers.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Low-burden inpatient pharmacotherapy that reduces dosing/monitoring intensity and length of stay vs q3h morphine-style regimens/ESC alone
- Safer, non-sedating rescue/adjunct for severe or refractory NOWS (esp. polysubstance exposure) that also treats GI symptoms without clonidine-like hemodynamic monitoring
- Therapy enabling early discharge without prolonged outpatient opioid exposure and downstream utilization (e.g., ED visits)

name: Adenoma | arathyroid
description: Parathyroid adenoma is a benign parathyroid tumor that often causes primary hyperparathyroidism, typically discovered incidentally in postmenopausal women with hypercalcemia and elevated or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone. Disease can progress from mild biochemical changes to kidney stones and osteoporosis. Surgery is curative but many patients are not surgical candidates, leaving a gap for tolerable, disease modifying medical therapy since cinacalcet is limited by nausea and vomiting and bone agents do not correct persistent hypercalcemia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable non-surgical outpatient therapy achieving sustained normocalcemia and meaningful PTH suppression for PHPT patients who cannot/will not undergo parathyroidectomy.
- Single agent or fixed-combo that normalizes calcium and delivers proven fracture-risk reduction (and ideally kidney benefits), not just BMD surrogates, in PHPT with osteoporosis.
- Better-tolerated, lower-burden long-term medical management vs cinacalcet/antiresorptives (fewer GI discontinuations, less monitoring/dosing friction).

name: Paratyphoid fever
description: Paratyphoid fever is an enteric fever caused by Salmonella Paratyphi, usually acquired via contaminated food or water in poor sanitation settings, causing several days of high fever with systemic and gastrointestinal symptoms. Antibiotics are effective but rising antimicrobial resistance and limited access to susceptibility testing increasingly constrain reliable treatment. Ongoing shedding and difficult-to-eradicate gallbladder carriage can persist for weeks to months after therapy, sustaining relapse and transmission and creating a need for resistance-robust, transmission-limiting approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral, resistance-robust acute therapy effective despite fluoroquinolone non-susceptibility and emerging ceftriaxone/azithromycin resistance
- Carbapenem-sparing outpatient regimen for complicated/severe disease to avoid IV ceftriaxone/meropenem hospitalization
- Anti-relapse/transmission-blocking eradication therapy that clears gallbladder biofilm-associated persistence and chronic carriage

name: Fetal alcohol syndrome
description: Fetal alcohol syndrome is the severe end of fetal alcohol spectrum disorders caused by prenatal alcohol exposure, with characteristic facial and growth abnormalities plus central nervous system injury leading to lifelong cognitive, attention, behavioral, sleep, and feeding problems. There is no cure and treatment is largely early supportive services and symptom management, leaving a major unmet need for disease modifying or reliably effective interventions that improve cognition, attention control, and sleep.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-targeted neurocognitive therapy improving executive function and memory in children with FASD
- More reliable ADHD symptom control specifically in FASD (inattention/hyperactivity/impulsivity) on validated rater scales
- Sleep-focused therapy for insomnia/sleep fragmentation in children with FASD to improve daytime behavior/adaptive function

name: Neurogenic bowel dysfunction
description: Neurogenic bowel dysfunction is loss of normal nerve control of colon and rectum after neurologic injury or disease, common in spinal cord injury and multiple sclerosis, causing constipation, difficult rectal evacuation, fecal incontinence, and bloating or pain. Care relies on long term, time intensive bowel routines that can still leave patients dependent and may trigger autonomic dysreflexia in higher spinal cord injury, creating demand for more predictable, less burdensome bowel emptying and continence options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Fast, predictable pharmacologic evacuation trigger to shorten bowel-care time and reduce need for digital rectal stimulation/manual evacuation
- Continence-focused therapy for areflexic NBD to reduce unplanned bowel evacuations/fecal incontinence and avoid at-least-daily bowel care
- Regimen for SCI at/above T6 that prevents bowel-care–triggered autonomic dysreflexia by avoiding rectal stretching/digital evacuation/suppositories

name: Pentosuria
description: Essential pentosuria is a benign autosomal recessive DCXR related metabolic trait causing urinary L xylulose excretion, typically found incidentally on urine reducing substance tests. Patients are otherwise healthy and need no treatment, but the key unmet need is accurate recognition and confirmatory testing so it is not mistaken for diabetes and does not trigger unnecessary workup or insulin therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Perianal hematoma
description: Perianal hematoma is an acutely thrombosed external hemorrhoid that presents as a sudden, exquisitely painful blue purple lump at the anal verge, often making sitting or walking difficult. Management is usually burdensome conservative care such as sitz baths, stool softeners, and oral or topical analgesics, while surgical excision relieves symptoms much faster at about 3.9 vs 24 days. Key unmet needs are a simple at home local therapy that matches excision speed and avoids headache limited glyceryl trinitrate.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid-onset, non-surgical local therapy achieving excision-like symptom resolution speed (~4 days vs ~24 days with conservative care).
- GTN/nitroglycerin-sparing topical agent for pain/spasm/congestion relief with fewer headaches than current nitrate options.
- Low-burden, simplified at-home regimen that replaces frequent sitz baths (3–4/day) and multi-agent supportive care with once-daily/single-application use.

name: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
description: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is an early respiratory failure of prematurity driven by surfactant deficiency, with symptoms within minutes of birth and worsening over 48 to 72 hours. Care relies on airway surfactant plus continuous positive airway pressure or ventilation, but treatment itself can cause lung injury and bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Key unmet needs are effective support that avoids iatrogenic harm and long term chronic lung disease, with momentum toward less invasive and aerosolized surfactant delivery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-/less-invasive surfactant delivery for spontaneously breathing preterm infants on CPAP (e.g., aerosolized surfactant or LISA/MIST) to avoid intubation-related injury/complications
- Adjunct therapies for extremely preterm/VLBW infants to prevent bronchopulmonary dysplasia (reduce death or BPD at ~36 weeks PMA), not just improve short-term oxygenation
- Improved surfactant formulations/dosing (e.g., protein-containing/protein-analog synthetics) to reduce redosing needs and downstream morbidity/mortality in very preterm infants

name: Melanoma | nodular
description: Nodular melanoma is an aggressive melanoma subtype with early vertical growth, often in men over 50, that can rapidly deepen, ulcerate or bleed, and frequently lacks classic ABCDE warning signs, leading to late thick diagnoses and high relapse risk even after complete surgery. Key gaps include preventing recurrence in very high risk resected stage IIB and IIC disease and providing effective, practical options after anti PD 1 therapy that avoid intensive cell therapy style regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjuvant relapse-prevention intensification for completely resected stage IIB/C nodular melanoma with very high‑risk thick/ulcerated primaries (e.g., T4b).
- Off‑the‑shelf systemic salvage after PD‑1 failure that substantially improves response rates without the operational burden of TIL therapy (lymphodepletion + IL‑2).
- Adjuvant PD‑1–based therapy with comparable relapse protection but fewer infusions/interruptions and lower risk of severe/fatal immune‑mediated toxicities.

name: Phlyctenulosis
description: Phlyctenulosis or phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis is a pediatric predominant immune hypersensitivity inflammation of the conjunctiva and cornea most often triggered in the US by Staphylococcus aureus antigens, often alongside blepharitis. It causes painful photophobic nodules at the limbus or cornea and tends to recur, with repeat flares risking corneal scarring, neovascularization, amblyopia, and vision loss. Topical steroids are effective but repeated exposure in children raises safety concerns such as increased intraocular pressure, leaving a need for durable steroid sparing control that prevents recurrent corneal injury.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing control of phlyctenular inflammation in children without topical corticosteroid toxicities (IOP rise/glaucoma, cataract) or steroid-dependence/recurrence.
- Therapies that reduce vision-threatening corneal sequelae (scarring/neovascularization) and downstream amblyopia/visual-acuity loss.
- Lower-burden, pediatric-fit regimens for chronic/recurrent disease (longer-acting/less frequent dosing; avoid prolonged systemic antibiotics and age-limited tetracyclines).

name: Pityriasis rosea
description: Pityriasis rosea is an acute, self-limiting papulosquamous rash typically affecting 10 to 35 year olds, often starting with a herald patch and spreading in a Christmas tree pattern with sometimes severe itch. Most cases resolve in 6 to 10 weeks, but post-inflammatory pigment changes can persist for months, making symptom relief and cosmetic impact key unmet needs. Care is largely supportive with topical corticosteroids and oral antihistamines, with limited escalation options such as aciclovir or narrowband ultraviolet B. Early pregnancy is a special concern given reports of fetal harm.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Convenient (≤BID) rapid-clearance therapy for severe/widespread or persistent pityriasis rosea, avoiding high-burden acyclovir 5×/day and frequent phototherapy visits.
- Pregnancy-focused therapy for PR onset <15 weeks’ gestation with proven reduction in miscarriage/prematurity risk vs current off-label/conflicting antiviral evidence.
- Therapy that prevents or materially shortens post-rash hypo/hyperpigmentation (especially in darker skin) by accelerating clearance and/or reducing inflammation.

name: Placenta accreta
description: Placenta accreta spectrum is abnormal placental invasion into the uterine muscle, often at a prior cesarean scar and frequently with placenta previa, and can cause life threatening hemorrhage requiring transfusion. Diagnosis is usually imaging based, and care commonly requires planned cesarean hysterectomy with placenta left in situ to avoid catastrophic bleeding, leaving major unmet needs in hemorrhage prevention, earlier more reliable antenatal detection, and credible uterus sparing options since fertility preserving approaches remain investigational.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- PAS-specific perioperative hemostatic pharmacotherapy to reduce intraoperative blood loss and massive transfusion during planned cesarean hysterectomy
- Uterus-preserving “placenta left in situ” drug regimen to safely accelerate placental involution and prevent bleeding-/infection-driven failure and sepsis (vs methotrexate)
- PAS-specific uterotonic/uterine-tone modulation to reduce bleeding without provoking placental disruption/hemorrhage

name: Thrombophilia | Protein C deficiency
description: Protein C deficiency is an inherited thrombophilia where reduced protein C anticoagulant activity leads to venous clots ranging from adult onset deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism often triggered by surgery, immobility, or pregnancy to rare neonatal purpura fulminans with microvascular thrombosis, skin necrosis, and bleeding. Care is dominated by long term anticoagulation and, in severe congenital disease, intravenous protein C replacement that is temporary and burdensome, leaving a premium on safer, more durable protein C restoration and simpler lifelong clot prevention.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Protein C function restoration (replacement/long-acting biologic or gene-based) for mild protein C deficiency with recurrent VTE risk to reduce/avoid long-term anticoagulation
- Long-acting, non-IV (ideally subcutaneous) protein C replacement for severe congenital protein C deficiency/neonatal purpura fulminans to avoid frequent IV dosing/venous access and plasma-related fluid overload
- Pregnancy/postpartum-safe anticoagulation for protein C deficiency–associated thrombosis risk that avoids daily LMWH injections and overcomes DOAC pregnancy/breastfeeding restrictions

name: Thrombophilia | Protein S deficiency
description: Protein S deficiency is a rare inherited thrombophilia where low protein S leaves coagulation poorly controlled, predisposing to deep vein thrombosis and potentially fatal pulmonary embolism, often first presenting in young adulthood and triggered by surgery, immobility, or pregnancy. Management is largely long term anticoagulation with meaningful bleeding risk and complex peripartum switching. The sharpest unmet need is severe neonatal disease such as purpura fulminans that can require fresh frozen plasma every 8 to 12 hours, with limited access to more durable protein replacement concentrates.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Long-term thromboprophylaxis for protein S deficiency that materially lowers major bleeding risk vs current indefinite anticoagulation while preventing recurrent VTE.
- Pregnancy + postpartum prophylaxis that improves live-birth outcomes while reducing LMWH injection burden and hemorrhagic complications.
- Rapid, durable protein S restoration for neonatal purpura fulminans to avoid q8–12h fresh-frozen plasma infusions and related complications.

name: Nephropathy | obstructive
description: Obstructive nephropathy is kidney injury from blocked urinary outflow, often in older men with benign prostatic hyperplasia, causing lower urinary tract symptoms and sometimes postrenal acute kidney injury. Care still hinges on urgent catheter based drainage, yet renal recovery is unpredictable as obstruction can trigger fibrosis and chronic kidney disease. Current preventive drugs are limited by orthostasis with alpha blockers, slow onset with 5 alpha reductase inhibitors, and sexual side effects, leaving a need for catheter sparing decompression, better prevention of acute obstruction, and renal protective adjuncts.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute “catheter-sparing” pharmacologic decompression to rapidly reverse bladder outlet obstruction in acute urinary retention/postrenal AKI
- Renal recovery/anti-fibrosis adjunct started at or immediately after obstruction relief to prevent irreversible tubulointerstitial injury/CKD progression
- Better-tolerated, faster-acting medical therapy to prevent progression to acute urinary retention/obstruction without α1-blocker orthostasis/falls and without 5-ARI slow onset/sexual adverse effects

name: Ophthalmia nodosa
description: Rare inflammatory eye injury from embedded insect hairs (often caterpillar setae) or plant material that can migrate deeper, causing painful red foreign body sensation and corneal abrasions and, in severe cases, vision threatening posterior inflammation (vitritis, macular edema, scarring). Care is procedure intensive with irrigation, hair removal, and antibiotic steroid drops, but complete clearance is difficult, leaving unmet need for better removal and steroid sparing control that prevents migration and late complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing control of posterior-segment/Type V ophthalmia nodosa (retained setae in vitreous causing recurrent uveitis/CME) to avoid prolonged corticosteroids and reduce need for vitrectomy.
- Anti-migration/anti-toxin adjunct for incompletely removable intracorneal setae to prevent delayed posterior migration and chronic toxin-driven inflammation.
- Long-acting outpatient anti-inflammatory + anti-infective drug delivery to replace high-frequency multi-drop regimens and reduce repeat visits for hair removal.

name: Pyloric stenosis
description: Early-life gastric outlet obstruction caused by hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle, typically presenting at 2 to 6 weeks with progressively forceful non-bilious projectile vomiting despite persistent hunger, leading to dehydration and weight loss. Care is highly effective but procedure centered, requiring preoperative fluid and electrolyte correction and normalization of metabolic alkalosis to reduce anesthesia related apnea risk. When surgery is high risk, atropine can be used but is less effective and prolongs hospitalization, leaving room for faster, reliable non-surgical options and perioperative adjuncts.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- High-success non-surgical pharmacologic option for infants unfit for general anesthesia/surgery
- Faster, short-course medical regimen that reverses pyloric hypertrophy in days rather than weeks–months
- Adjunct peri-operative pharmacotherapy to reduce post-pyloromyotomy recovery burden (pain/discomfort, time to feeds, length of stay)

name: Optic disk drusen
description: Optic disc drusen are benign calcified protein deposits in the optic nerve head, often found incidentally when they mimic optic disc swelling. Most patients are asymptomatic, but some develop transient visual obscurations and slow peripheral visual field loss and rare ischemic or neovascular complications can threaten vision. There is no proven therapy to prevent drusen growth or treat progressive field loss, so care is largely monitoring and reactive management of complications, leaving a need for disease modifying approaches that prevent progression and preserve vision.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Anti-calcification/decalcification therapy to prevent optic disc drusen growth and consequent progressive visual-field loss.
- Neuroprotective therapy that slows peripheral visual-field progression in patients with established/measurable field deficits.
- Durable, lower-burden therapy to prevent/treat vision-threatening vascular complications (e.g., peripapillary/choroidal neovascularization, NAION) beyond reactive intravitreal anti-VEGF/laser/PDT.

name: Orthostatic proteinuria
description: Benign, posture related proteinuria in otherwise healthy adolescents with higher urinary protein when upright that normalizes overnight; typically an incidental urinalysis finding. Key unmet need is clear, low burden diagnosis and sensible follow up to avoid anxiety and unnecessary invasive kidney workups such as biopsy rather than new therapeutics.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Rubella
description: Rubella is a contagious viral infection that is often mild or asymptomatic, typically causing low grade fever, a maculopapular rash, lymphadenopathy, and sometimes arthralgia in adult women, so cases are easily missed. The high stakes are in pregnancy, where early infection can cause miscarriage or stillbirth or congenital rubella syndrome with lifelong cataracts, heart defects, and hearing loss. Prevention relies on a live measles mumps and rubella vaccine that cannot be given during pregnancy or in severe immunodeficiency, and there is no cure or proven post exposure prophylaxis to prevent fetal infection once exposure occurs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pregnancy post-exposure prophylaxis that prevents maternal infection/viremia and fetal transmission (CRS) after confirmed rubella exposure in non-immune pregnant patients.
- Non-live rubella immunization/prophylaxis (e.g., mAb or non-replicating vaccine) for patients who cannot receive live MMR/MMRV, especially pregnancy and severe immunodeficiency.
- Direct-acting antiviral therapy usable in pregnancy to treat acute rubella and reduce congenital rubella syndrome risk.

name: Typhus | scrub
description: Scrub typhus is an acute chigger-borne Orientia infection common in rural Asia-Pacific that starts as nonspecific fever with headache and myalgia and can progress to vasculitis with acute respiratory distress syndrome, encephalitis, multiorgan failure, and death if antibiotics are delayed. Because eschars are often absent and early symptoms mimic other tropical fevers, diagnosis and timely treatment are unreliable in many settings. Key gaps include rapid point-of-care diagnostics, tetracycline-sparing options validated in pregnancy, relapse-proof ultra-short oral regimens, rapid intravenous therapies for severe disease, and prevention tools such as a vaccine.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Severe/ICU scrub typhus: IV (or rapid-acting) regimen that improves day‑7 organ complications and day‑28 mortality vs monotherapy.
- Uncomplicated outpatient scrub typhus: relapse-proof ultrashort oral regimen (≤3 days/single dose) maintaining rapid fever clearance.
- Pregnancy: pregnancy-safe, tetracycline-sparing regimen with demonstrated maternal cure and fetal safety.

name: Otosclerosis
description: Otosclerosis is a slowly progressive hearing disorder caused by abnormal bone remodeling in the middle ear that impairs sound transmission, often starting as unilateral conductive hearing loss and progressing to bilateral loss, with tinnitus and occasional dizziness. Patients rely on hearing aids and stapes surgery, but there is no effective drug therapy and surgery only fixes the conductive component, leaving inner ear hearing loss and progression unaddressed and with rare risk of worsening hearing. Key unmet needs are disease modifying treatments that preserve cochlear function and safer perioperative otoprotection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying pharmacotherapy to slow/stop otosclerotic bone remodeling early to prevent progressive conductive hearing loss.
- Therapy for cochlear/inner-ear otosclerosis to preserve or improve sensorineural (bone-conduction) hearing in patients with SNHL/mixed loss.
- Peri-operative otoprotective adjunct pharmacotherapy to reduce iatrogenic SNHL/high-frequency loss and postoperative complications (e.g., vertigo/tinnitus) after stapes surgery.

name: Cystadenoma | ovarian
description: Ovarian cystadenomas are common benign epithelial ovarian tumors, often found incidentally in midlife but sometimes causing pelvic pain and bloating or acute symptoms with rupture or torsion. Management is largely procedural with cystectomy or removal of the affected ovary and tube, since hormonal therapy may prevent new cysts but does not shrink existing ones. Key unmet needs are non surgical options that relieve symptoms, reduce recurrence, preserve ovarian tissue and fertility, and improve confidence in ruling out malignancy without operative intervention.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical drug therapy that shrinks existing benign ovarian cystadenomas to avoid surgery/anesthesia
- Pharmacologic reduction/prevention of cyst growth in large (≥4–5 cm) cysts to lower torsion risk and emergency surgery
- Fertility/ovarian-reserve–preserving cyst control that avoids oophorectomy and minimizes AMH/AFC decline vs cystectomy

name: Parovarian cyst
description: Paraovarian or paratubal cysts are usually benign, epithelium lined fluid filled adnexal cysts beside the ovary or fallopian tube, often found incidentally on ultrasound in women aged 20 to 40. Most need only observation, but enlargement can cause pelvic pain, constipation, or frequent urination and rare torsion or rupture can require urgent surgery. Care hinges on deciding who can be safely monitored versus operated on, yet these lesions are often hard to distinguish from ovarian masses and malignancy is rare but possible, driving a need for better imaging based triage.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Patulous eustachian tube
description: Patulous eustachian tube dysfunction is a rare disorder where the eustachian tube stays abnormally open, letting voice and breathing sounds transmit into the middle ear and causing distressing autophony and ear fullness that often fluctuates, worsens with exercise, and improves when lying down. Triggers can include weight loss, though many cases have no clear precipitant.
