- Ritonavir-free oral outpatient antiviral maintaining Day-28 hospitalization/death reduction while avoiding Paxlovid drug–drug interactions
- Variant-resilient, long-acting pre-exposure prophylaxis for moderately/severely immunocompromised patients (not compromised by emerging non-susceptible variants)
- Long COVID prevention/treatment improving meaningful functional outcomes (e.g., reducing activity limitation)

name: Primary hyperaldosteronism
description: Primary hyperaldosteronism is excess adrenal aldosterone, often presenting as difficult to control hypertension even without low potassium, with fatigue, headache, and muscle weakness in some patients. Care centers on adrenalectomy for tumor driven disease or mineralocorticoid receptor blockade, but steroidal antagonists carry hyperkalemia monitoring burden and endocrine side effects such as gynecomastia, limiting long term use and adherence. A key frontier is reducing aldosterone at the source via aldosterone synthase inhibition to improve blood pressure control while potentially lowering hyperkalemia risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Aldosterone-synthase (CYP11B2) inhibition to control BP while normalizing renin/RAAS (vs persistent suppressed renin on MRAs).
- Anti-androgen–sparing MR antagonists enabling higher/true max-tolerated aldosterone blockade without spironolactone endocrine AEs (e.g., gynecomastia/sexual dysfunction).
- Potassium/renal-sparing therapies with lower hyperkalemia risk and reduced lab-monitoring/titration burden, including suitability for patients with reduced eGFR or higher baseline K.

name: Trichomoniasis | Trichomonas vaginalis
description: Trichomoniasis is a common sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis, often asymptomatic but in women can cause vaginitis with painful urination and yellow green or gray discharge. Untreated infection can persist for months or years and increases risk of human immunodeficiency virus transmission and adverse pregnancy outcomes such as preterm birth. Treatment is constrained because nitroimidazoles are the only proven effective class, resistance occurs in about 4% to 10%, and true allergy can require desensitization, leaving a need for reliable non nitroimidazole cures and simpler partner treatment to prevent reinfection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral non‑nitroimidazole systemic cure for recurrent/persistent (incl. metronidazole‑resistant) trichomoniasis.
- Non‑nitroimidazole systemic alternative for patients with true 5‑nitroimidazole allergy/intolerance (avoid desensitization).
- Single‑visit/observed regimen (incl. partner treatment) that matches multidose efficacy and reduces reinfection/recurrence.

name: Lyme disease
description: Lyme disease is a blacklegged tick transmitted Borrelia burgdorferi infection that often begins within 3 to 30 days with erythema migrans and flu like symptoms, and can progress to joint, cardiac, and neurologic involvement. While most patients recover with a 2 to 4 week oral antibiotic course, a meaningful minority develop persistent fatigue, pain, cognitive symptoms, or refractory arthritis where extended antibiotics do not help, leaving a need for better diagnostics, non antibiotic symptom and immune targeted options, and improved prevention beyond a narrow 72 hour post exposure window and without an available human vaccine.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-antibiotic symptom-control therapies for PTLDS (persistent fatigue/pain/cognitive symptoms) with measurable improvements on FSS/GSQ-30/SF-36.
- Immunomodulatory options for post-antibiotic Lyme arthritis after oral+IV antibiotic failure to resolve synovitis and avoid DMARDs/biologics/steroids/synovectomy.
- Alternative post–tick-bite prophylaxis effective beyond the 72-hour window and/or usable when doxycycline is contraindicated (e.g., pregnancy/lactation/allergy).

name: Malaria | Plasmodium falciparum
description: Plasmodium falciparum malaria is a mosquito borne infection causing an acute febrile illness that can deteriorate to severe disease and death within 24 hours if untreated. Treatment relies on artemisinin based combination therapy, but emerging artemisinin resistance in parts of Africa, multi dose food dependent regimens that are fragile in real world use, and limited safe first trimester pregnancy options leave major unmet needs for resistance resilient, simpler, rapidly curative therapies that are pregnancy ready.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Resistance-resilient cures for artemisinin-partial-resistant (PfKelch13-mutant) P. falciparum in Africa that maintain Day-28 PCR-corrected cure/ACPR despite partner-drug vulnerability.
- Single-dose (or ultra-short-course) oral regimens that eliminate food-dependent, multi-dose ACT adherence barriers and reduce incomplete-course–driven resistance.
- First-trimester pregnancy–optimized therapies with robust early-pregnancy safety and practical regimens, reducing reliance on prolonged quinine+clindamycin and filling evidence gaps for non-AL options.

name: Acanthosis nigricans
description: Acanthosis nigricans causes dark, thick, velvety plaques in skin folds, most often reflecting obesity related insulin resistance and serving as a visible marker of metabolic risk. Management largely hinges on treating the underlying driver such as weight loss, with topicals like ammonium lactate or tretinoin used mainly for cosmetic benefit, but results are inconsistent because no reliably effective condition specific therapy exists. A small but critical subgroup presents with sudden, widespread or mucosal disease that can rarely signal internal malignancy, especially gastric cancer, creating a need for better lesion directed options and clearer risk stratification.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non‑irritating, lesion‑directed topical that reliably clears hyperpigmentation + thickening with objective melanin/ANSC and QoL (DLQI) improvement in ~8–12 weeks.
- Better‑tolerated systemic insulin‑lowering therapy for obesity/insulin‑resistance–associated AN in children/adolescents that improves Burke severity and fasting insulin/HOMA‑IR within ~12–24 weeks.
- Evidence‑based antiproliferative/anti–tumor‑factor drug for rare malignant/paraneoplastic rapid‑onset AN (often mucosal) to regress lesions while underlying cancer is treated.

name: Actinic keratosis
description: Sun driven precancerous skin lesions on chronically exposed areas in older fair skinned or immunosuppressed patients, with a small risk of progression to squamous cell carcinoma; the key unmet need is durable field control since subclinical disease continually seeds new lesions and current field therapies are burdensome with inflammatory local reactions that limit adherence and repeatability.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable, safe field-directed therapy that clears visible + subclinical AK and lowers recurrence/new-lesion formation (and SCC progression risk), especially in immunosuppressed/organ-transplant patients.
- Low-pain/low-inflammation field treatment (incl. PDT alternatives) that patients can complete and repeat.
- Adherence-friendly, home-based, short-course regimens that can cover large contiguous areas and reduce reliance on clinic-only modalities.

name: Acute stress disorder
description: Trauma triggered condition with distressing, function impairing intrusion, avoidance, hyperarousal and dissociation symptoms lasting 3 days to 1 month post event; care favors trauma focused cognitive behavioral psychotherapy, with no evidence supported pharmacotherapy and a need for brief, easily deployed stepped care options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ED-initiated, brief-course pharmacotherapy during the 3-days–1-month ASD window that prevents progression to PTSD.
- Rapid, non-benzodiazepine control of intrusion/nightmares, hyperarousal, and dissociation in early ASD.
- Low-visit-burden pharmacologic options for patients unable to access/complete multi-session trauma-focused CBT.

name: Adenoid hypertrophy
description: Adenoid hypertrophy is common in children and causes nasal obstruction with mouth breathing, snoring and restless sleep, sometimes progressing to pediatric obstructive sleep apnea and recurrent ear infections with middle ear fluid and hearing impact. Care starts with nasal steroid sprays or antibiotics but many children ultimately need adenoidectomy, with occasional regrowth. The unmet need is for safe, effective medical options that reduce symptoms and sleep disruption and prevent ear complications while avoiding surgery and drug safety tradeoffs such as montelukast’s neuropsychiatric risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Surgery-sparing pharmacotherapy for ages ~1–6 that reduces objective adenoid obstruction (e.g., A/C grade or A/N ratio) and improves sleep-disordered breathing/OSA symptoms without montelukast-class neuropsychiatric risk
- Drug therapy that prevents/resolves adenoid-driven Eustachian tube dysfunction/glue ear with improved objective hearing/effusion endpoints (e.g., tympanometry) and reduced need for tubes/surgery
- Post-adenoidectomy adjunct for high-risk children (<5 years, frequent postoperative antibiotics) that prevents adenoidal regrowth/recurrence and persistent nasal obstruction

name: Arteriolosclerosis
description: Arteriolosclerosis is small vessel disease marked by hyaline thickening and stiffening of arteriolar walls from serum protein deposition, narrowing the lumen and impairing renal autoregulation. Patients are often clinically silent until slowly progressive hypertensive nephrosclerosis develops with little or no proteinuria, and end organ signs like hypertensive retinopathy. Care is mostly risk factor control, especially blood pressure, but key gaps are therapies that reverse microvascular hyalinosis, restore renal microvascular function, and sustain renoprotection when hyperkalemia limits renin angiotensin aldosterone system inhibitor use.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-targeted reversal of afferent-arteriolar hyalinosis/medial thickening to restore renal autoregulation and prevent single-nephron glomerular hypertension/ischemia (vs systemic BP lowering alone)
- Potassium-neutral renoprotection (or dedicated K+ control) to enable maximal-dose ACEi/ARB continuation without hyperkalemia-driven down-titration/discontinuation
- Stratified therapies for ischemia-dominant vs glomerular-hypertension-dominant nephrosclerosis, particularly in low-proteinuria patients (<0.22 g/gCr)

name: Conjunctivitis | allergic
description: Allergic conjunctivitis is a common immunoglobulin E mediated ocular allergy causing intense itching, redness, and watery or stringy discharge, usually starting before age 20 and often impairing daily quality of life despite rarely threatening vision. Most patients rely on chronic antihistamine and mast cell stabilizer drops, with severe vernal or atopic disease risking corneal damage and flares that drive steroid use. Steroids are constrained by monitoring burden and cataract and glaucoma risk, and frequent preserved drop exposure can worsen ocular surface toxicity, leaving a premium on durable, steroid sparing control with better tolerability.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing long-term control for severe VKC/AKC (often pediatric/atopic; corneal involvement) to avoid steroid vision risks (IOP/glaucoma/cataract)
- Faster + longer-lasting itch/redness control with simpler dosing (ideally once-daily) vs slow-onset prophylactic drops
- BAK-free/preservative-free (or sustained-release) ocular-allergy therapy for chronic/frequent users and contact-lens wearers to reduce ocular-surface toxicity and handling burden

name: Contact dermatitis | allergic
description: Allergic contact dermatitis is an eczema caused by delayed type IV hypersensitivity after skin sensitization to an external allergen, typically flaring 24 to 72 hours after exposure with a well demarcated intensely itchy rash that may blister or weep then become chronic and lichenified, often on the hands or face. Key unmet needs are reliable allergen identification and avoidance since patch testing is required and ubiquitous triggers like nickel and even tiny exposures can drive recurrence, plus safer steroid sparing options for sensitive areas where topical corticosteroid overuse can thin skin.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Steroid-sparing high-potency topical option for severe hand ACD (including safer use on periocular/facial sites).
- Systemic steroid–sparing therapy for severe acute/chronic ACD to prevent relapse and avoid long-term systemic steroid or chronic immunosuppressant toxicity.
- Allergen-specific tolerance/desensitization for hard-to-avoid allergens (especially nickel) to reduce flares despite minimal exposure.

name: Riboflavin deficiency
description: Riboflavin deficiency is a vitamin B2 shortfall that impairs flavin dependent energy metabolism and mucosal integrity, typically causing painful oral fissures and cheilitis, glossitis with a magenta tongue, dermatitis, itchy red eyes, fatigue, and normocytic anemia. While oral riboflavin can rapidly reverse early disease, durable repletion often fails in nutritionally vulnerable patients with poor adherence, malabsorption, or dialysis related losses, leading to predictable recurrence unless the driver is corrected. A high stakes subgroup is riboflavin transporter deficiency, where delayed recognition can mean progressive neurologic decline and empiric high dose therapy may be lifesaving.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Long-acting IM “depot” riboflavin (≥30-day coverage) for patients unable to adhere to daily oral dosing.
- Malabsorption-robust riboflavin replacement (formulations/routes that bypass impaired GI uptake) for diarrhea/malabsorption or dialysis-driven secondary deficiency.
- Rapid-start, high-dose riboflavin protocols for suspected riboflavin transporter deficiency (SLC52A2/SLC52A3; BVVL/RTD) prior to genetic confirmation.

name: Selective IgD deficiency disease
description: Rare antibody deficiency with low or undetectable serum immunoglobulin D, usually an incidental lab finding with minimal symptoms and no clear infection predisposition; management is mainly surveillance and ruling out broader humoral immunodeficiencies rather than disease specific therapy, leaving an unmet need for better diagnostic confidence and risk stratification.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus URL for Selective IgD deficiency

name: Skin tag
description: Skin tags are very common, usually harmless, soft skin growths that hang off the skin in high friction folds like the neck, underarms, eyelids, and groin, becoming more frequent with age and in people with obesity or type 2 diabetes. They are mainly a cosmetic and nuisance issue, but irritation and bleeding drive removal. Current office procedures often require out of pocket payment and can cause infection, bleeding, scarring, or hyperpigmentation, especially in Black or Brown skin, creating demand for safer, self applied, pigment sparing at home removal and supportive post removal care.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Self-applied, non-procedural topical therapy to remove bothersome skin tags safely at home (avoiding in-office freezing/cutting/heat and DIY infection/bleeding/scarring risks)
- Pigment- and scar-sparing removal approach, especially for Black/Brown skin, minimizing post-procedure hyperpigmentation/dyschromia
- Post-removal topical hemostatic + wound-healing/anti-infective regimen to reduce bleeding-management burden and postoperative infection risk

name: Varicocele
description: Varicocele is an enlargement of scrotal veins with blood pooling, usually arising around puberty and often left sided, commonly asymptomatic or causing a dull ache and a palpable bag of worms mass. Management is mostly observation and pain control, with surgery or embolization when fertility or testicular growth is threatened, but there are no drugs and post repair fertility benefit is inconsistent. Key unmet needs include better patient selection and mechanism based approaches that address oxidative stress and sperm DNA damage rather than anatomy alone.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral/non-surgical therapy for primary infertile men with clinically evident varicocele to improve semen parameters and demonstrate pregnancy/live-birth benefit.
- Adolescent-focused disease-modifying therapy to prevent/correct progressive testicular hypotrophy in high-grade varicocele (>20% testis size discrepancy).
- Mechanism-based therapy targeting oxidative stress/elevated sperm DNA fragmentation with consistent, predictive benefit beyond inconsistent antioxidant approaches.

name: Vitreous detachment
description: Age-related separation of the vitreous from the retina, typically after age 50, causing sudden floaters and peripheral flashes. Most cases are observed, but symptoms require urgent dilated exams to rule out retinal tears or detachment. Persistent floaters have no proven medical therapy and surgical options carry risk, creating unmet need for safe pharmacologic treatments that reduce symptoms and traction related complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical pharmacologic option to meaningfully reduce persistent PVD-related floaters/visual obstruction (vs observation/no treatment).
- Prophylactic/early-intervention drug for acute symptomatic PVD patients at highest tear risk (e.g., myopic and/or lattice degeneration) to reduce delayed retinal tears.
- Therapy that reduces prolonged monitoring/return-visit burden by safely stabilizing vitreoretinal traction and lowering post-diagnosis complication risk.

name: Squamous blepharitis
description: Squamous blepharitis is an anterior eyelid margin inflammation with dandruff-like debris at the lash base, causing gritty or burning discomfort, tearing, crusting, and morning lid sticking in a relapsing course. Management is chronic and hygiene driven with episodic antibiotics, but it cannot be permanently fixed and long term steroid use is constrained by intraocular pressure and cataract risk, creating demand for relapse preventing maintenance options and steroid sparing anti inflammatory therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Relapse-preventing maintenance drug therapy that reduces/replaces lifelong daily lid hygiene.
- Therapies achieving “complete cure” of anterior blepharitis signs/symptoms (lid-margin erythema, debris, discomfort), not just partial relief.
- Steroid-sparing anti-inflammatory control for flares suitable for longer use without glaucoma/cataract/infection risk or IOP-monitoring burden.

name: Toxicodendron dermatitis
description: Urushiol triggered allergic contact dermatitis from poison ivy oak or sumac causing delayed onset linear intensely pruritic blistering rash lasting about 2 to 3 weeks. Most cases self resolve but severe widespread eruptions often require systemic corticosteroids with rebound risk if under treated. Prevention is largely avoidance since barrier lotions are short acting, leaving unmet need for durable prophylaxis, practical post exposure prevention, and steroid sparing therapies including immunotherapy approaches.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Post-exposure “rash-prevention” topical that remains effective beyond ~30 minutes after urushiol contact
- Steroid-sparing therapy for severe/widespread (>20% BSA) rhus dermatitis providing rapid relief without a 2–3 week prednisone taper/rebound risk
- Season-long prophylaxis for repeatedly exposed high-risk people that outlasts ~4-hour bentoquatam barrier protection

name: Toxocariasis
description: Toxocariasis is a zoonotic roundworm infection from dog or cat feces, typically acquired when eggs in contaminated soil reach the mouth, with severe disease most often in young children. Many infections are asymptomatic, but larvae can trigger multi organ inflammation or cause unilateral ocular disease that may lead to permanent vision loss. Antiparasitics can kill the parasite, yet ocular cases are hard to manage because inflammation must be controlled and patients often present after irreversible eye damage, with limited data guiding optimal treatment.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Eye-penetrant larvicidal + steroid-sparing regimen for ocular toxocariasis that prevents progressive vision loss without triggering sight-threatening inflammatory flares.
- Standardized, evidence-backed systemic regimen for visceral/covert toxocariasis with defined dose/duration and clinically meaningful (non-surrogate) outcomes.
- Age-appropriate (esp. <2y), ultra-short/single-dose pediatric regimen with clear safety to reduce need for prolonged albendazole exposure/monitoring.

name: Ulcerative blepharitis
description: Ulcerative blepharitis is a chronic, usually staphylococcal eyelid margin infection and inflammation causing scaling, crusting and redness with gritty, itchy eyes and morning lid sticking. Management relies on ongoing lid hygiene and episodic topical antibiotics, but durable cure is uncommon and symptoms recur when treatment stops. Persistent lid margin biofilm and the risk of antimicrobial resistance with long term antibiotics drive unmet need for non antibiotic, biofilm disrupting options that reduce daily hygiene burden and prevent flares and complications.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable complete cure (score 0 redness + debris + discomfort) with longer off-treatment remission for staphylococcal/ulcerative blepharitis flares
- Non-antibiotic anti-biofilm/anti-virulence therapy to disrupt lid-margin biofilm, reduce recurrence, and avoid resistance from prolonged antibiotics
- Therapies that reduce the need for frequent, lifelong lid hygiene (warm compresses + lid cleaning; up to 2–4×/day during flares)

name: Ulcerative stomatitis
description: Ulcerative stomatitis is painful, often recurrent inflammation and ulceration of the oral mucosa that can quickly disrupt eating, swallowing, and speaking, sometimes causing dehydration or undernutrition. Care is largely symptomatic and steroid centric with limited high quality evidence and adjuncts like chlorhexidine carry tolerability tradeoffs. The unmet need is fast, durable local control and convenient maintenance that reduces flare frequency and pain without chronic steroid exposure.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Fast-acting local therapy that rapidly restores ability to drink/eat (and speak) during painful ulcer flares.
- Maintenance/prophylactic therapy that meaningfully reduces outbreak frequency and prolongs ulcer-free periods in frequent/continuous disease.
- Steroid-sparing, long-contact local anti-inflammatory option with improved tolerability and less burdensome administration (e.g., fewer rinse/paste/NPO constraints).

name: Urolithiasis
description: Urolithiasis is the formation of kidney or ureter stones, usually calcium, causing severe intermittent flank pain that can radiate to the groin with blood in urine, urinary urgency, nausea or vomiting and sometimes fever or chills. Recurrence is common with 35 to 50 percent developing another stone within 10 years. Care is still largely reactive with limited medical dissolution beyond uric acid stones, mixed evidence for alpha blockers outside distal ureter stones, pain control constrained by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug risks in renal insufficiency, and frequent need for procedures when obstruction threatens infection or kidney damage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical chemolysis that can dissolve/shrink calcium oxalate/phosphate stones (imaging-confirmed clearance) to avoid URS/SWL.
- More effective medical expulsive therapy for middle/proximal ureteral stones ≤10 mm (esp. 5–10 mm) to improve passage rates and reduce pain/ED revisits vs alpha-blockers.
- Renal-safe, opioid-sparing acute renal colic (and stent/post-URS) analgesia for patients with NSAID contraindications (e.g., renal insufficiency).

name: Vitreous syneresis
description: Age related vitreous degeneration often presenting after age 60 with sudden floaters and flashes from posterior vitreous detachment; most cases are observed but there is a small delayed retinal tear risk requiring follow up. Persistent, visually significant floaters have limited options beyond procedures such as laser vitreolysis with an immature evidence base or vitrectomy with meaningful complication risks, driving interest in safer pharmacologic symptom relief such as low dose atropine drops.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical floater-clearing drug for persistent, debilitating PVD-related floaters that improves contrast sensitivity/vision-related QoL without vitrectomy-level cataract/retinal tear/detachment risk
- Vitreoretinal-traction modulator for acute symptomatic PVD (no break on initial exam) to lower ~2% delayed-retinal-break risk and reduce 4–6 week follow-up burden
- Home/office-administered (e.g., topical) therapy with durable symptom improvement on validated patient-reported visual function measures to replace Nd:YAG vitreolysis

name: Astigmatism
description: Astigmatism is a common refractive error from an irregularly shaped cornea or lens that blurs or distorts vision at all distances, often causing eye strain, headaches, squinting, and glare or halos especially at night. The biggest gap is early detection and sustained, low burden correction since children may not notice symptoms and delayed treatment can contribute to amblyopia with irreversible vision loss.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Hypertension | essential
description: Essential hypertension is usually asymptomatic and often only detected on routine blood pressure checks, yet chronic elevation drives cumulative vascular and organ damage leading to heart attack, stroke, heart failure, and kidney failure. The hardest-to-treat segment is resistant hypertension, where patients remain above goal despite three antihypertensive classes including a diuretic or require four or more drugs. Polypharmacy, side effects, frequent titration, and poor real-world adherence in a largely symptomless disease leave a premium on durable blood pressure control with better tolerability and adherence assurance.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- True resistant-hypertension BP control (above-goal BP despite 3 classes incl diuretic and/or needing ≥4 drugs)
- Adherence-proof regimens for an asymptomatic disease (long-acting and/or single-pill/fixed-dose strategies to reduce pill burden)
- BP-lowering with fewer adverse effects and less lab/visit monitoring (e.g., less edema/angioedema risk; less electrolyte monitoring)

name: Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis
description: HPV-6/11 driven disease where benign papillomas repeatedly regrow in the airway, usually the larynx, causing hoarseness and sometimes obstructive stridor. Often begins in young children ages 2 to 6 and requires frequent repeat surgeries because there is no cure and no consistently effective medical therapy. Major unmet need is durable pediatric safe treatments that reduce procedure burden and control aggressive or distal disease including rare lung spread.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Surgery-sparing medical therapy that meaningfully reduces annual debulking rates/extends inter-surgical interval in RRP.
- Effective systemic therapy for aggressive high-recurrence and/or distal spread (larynx/trachea/lungs) disease with objective lesion-burden and surgery-rate endpoints.
- Pediatric-appropriate labeled therapy with established safety/efficacy in children and less procedure-coupled regimens.

name: Breast fibroadenoma
description: Benign breast tumor in women ages 15 to 35, typically a firm, rubbery, painless, mobile lump that can grow with pregnancy and shrink after menopause; often managed with imaging and watchful waiting or removal for growth or pain, but surgery can alter breast appearance and new lumps may form, creating demand for predictable non-surgical shrinkage and broader access to image-guided ablation such as cryoablation or radiofrequency ablation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical breast-targeted therapy to shrink symptomatic/large/growing fibroadenomas enough to avoid excision.
- Pharmacologic prevention/limitation of recurrent or multiple fibroadenomas in high-burden subgroups (juvenile 10–18; giant >5 cm) to reduce repeat procedures.
- Short-course, better-tolerated medical therapy for painful fibroadenoma/non-cyclic mastalgia that reduces pain vs tamoxifen-like side effects and helps avoid surgery for discomfort.

name: Fibrocystic breast changes
description: Common benign breast tissue changes causing cyclic breast pain, lumpiness and cysts (sometimes nonbloody green or brown discharge), most often in women 30 to 50. The biggest burden is recurrent nodules that drive imaging and biopsies to rule out cancer, plus symptoms that conservative care often fails to control. Effective escalation options exist but are systemic and risk limited, creating demand for durable breast directed therapies that reduce pain and lump burden without hormonal safety trade offs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drug option for premenopausal women with moderate–severe refractory cyclic mastalgia (despite conservative measures/OTC analgesics) achieving meaningful VAS/Cardiff pain improvement and lowering recurrence
- Non-systemic/local breast-directed alternative with danazol/tamoxifen-like efficacy but avoiding systemic hormonal risks (e.g., danazol androgenic AEs/fetal effects; tamoxifen VTE risk and time-limited use)
- Therapy that reduces nodularity/cyst/lump burden (palpation/ultrasound) in addition to pain, with durable benefit after stopping treatment

name: Chondromalacia
description: Chondromalacia patella is patellofemoral knee pain caused by softening and breakdown of the cartilage under the kneecap, often from uneven joint loading. It typically affects active teens and young adults, especially women, with anterior knee pain worsened by stairs, squatting, or prolonged sitting and sometimes grinding. Management is largely rest, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and physical therapy, with surgery mainly for alignment problems, leaving many patients without durable symptom relief. Key gaps include safer long term pain control and cartilage protective approaches to prevent progression toward arthritis.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable symptom control for adolescents/young adults with patellofemoral/chondromalacia pain refractory or recurrent despite conservative care (improve VAS + Kujala score).
- Cartilage-protective/repair therapy in early-stage patellar cartilage disease to prevent progression and reduce patellofemoral OA risk (MRI cartilage thickness/Outerbridge endpoints).
- NSAID-sparing long-acting/local (non-systemic) anti-inflammatory analgesia that matches pain/swelling relief while reducing GI/CV risks.

name: Cobblestone retinal degeneration
description: Cobblestone or paving stone degeneration is a common, usually benign peripheral retinal finding marked by discrete yellow white depigmented patches and retinal thinning between the ora serrata and equator, often discovered incidentally in older adults and sometimes associated with high axial myopia. It is typically asymptomatic and not linked to increased retinal detachment risk, so the key unmet need is accurate recognition and patient counseling to avoid unnecessary intervention while still reinforcing warning signs of true retinal tear or detachment.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Adenoma | colorectal
description: Colorectal adenomas are usually benign gland-like polyps found incidentally on screening colonoscopy but can progress to colorectal cancer, so they are removed and often trigger intensive surveillance such as repeat colonoscopy at 3 years for higher risk findings. The central unmet need is safe, scalable chemoprevention that reduces adenoma recurrence and the burden of frequent procedures since effective options like celecoxib are limited by cardiovascular risk and aspirin offers only modest benefit and an unclear risk benefit profile. Low toxicity prevention and better risk stratification remain key frontiers.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Low-toxicity oral chemoprevention for “high-risk adenoma” patients that reduces metachronous high-risk adenoma recurrence enough to extend surveillance beyond 3 years.
- Gut-restricted (colon-targeted) COX-2–pathway agent with celecoxib-like recurrence reduction but without systemic cardiovascular risk.
- Biomarker/genotype-guided “precision prevention” to identify responders to chemopreventives (e.g., aspirin/NSAIDs/metformin) and avoid unnecessary long-term exposure in non-responders.

name: Complement component 4b deficiency
description: Complement component 4B deficiency is an inherited defect in the classical complement pathway that impairs opsonization and immune complex clearance, leading to recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections including meningitis and a lupus like immune complex autoimmunity with complications such as vasculitis and renal disease. Management is mainly preventive vaccinations and antibiotics, since protein replacement is impractical, leaving major unmet need for complement restoring therapies, antibiotic sparing prophylaxis, and safer control of immune complex driven inflammation.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- C4B functional restoration (replacement/gene/mRNA) to normalize CH50 and reduce encapsulated-bacteria infections plus autoimmune/vasculitic burden
- Complement-independent, antibiotic-sparing prophylaxis (e.g., long-acting passive immunization) against S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and N. meningitidis
- Steroid-sparing control of immune-complex autoimmunity (esp. SLE/IgA vasculitis/kidney disease) that preserves infection safety in C4B-deficient patients

name: Conjunctival concretion
description: Conjunctival concretions are benign yellowish white deposits on the inner eyelid, more common with aging and chronic ocular surface inflammation. Most are incidental, but when they erode through the conjunctiva they can cause focal foreign body sensation, irritation, tearing, redness, and photophobia. Management is largely reactive in office removal with a needle or forceps, sometimes followed by antibiotic drops, and recurrence is driven by uncontrolled underlying inflammation or allergy, highlighting unmet need for durable anti inflammatory control and faster epithelial healing to reduce repeated extractions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Topical concretion‑dissolving/loosening therapy to clear symptomatic conjunctival concretions without in‑office needle/forceps extraction
- Chronic ocular‑surface anti‑inflammatory/anti‑allergy therapy to prevent recurrence in patients with inflammation/allergy‑associated concretions
- Ocular‑surface protective/epithelial‑healing therapy to prevent or rapidly resolve corneal abrasion–driven symptoms (foreign‑body sensation, tearing, redness, photophobia, blur)

name: Conjunctivochalasis
description: Age related ocular surface disorder where loose, redundant bulbar conjunctival folds destabilize the tear film and can block tear drainage, causing dry eye like irritation and tearing that often persists despite lubricants and anti inflammatory drops and may require surgery; key needs are drop sparing, better tolerated therapies that restore tear outflow and target inflammatory matrix metalloproteinase driven tissue breakdown to slow progression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non‑surgical relief of epiphora/tear‑outflow obstruction in stage‑2 (medium/severe) CCh, especially nasal/medial disease where folds mechanically block the punctum.
- Disease‑modifying topical therapy to slow/reverse conjunctival laxity by interrupting inflammatory cytokine→MMP signaling to reduce fold severity/progression.
- Better‑tolerated, drop‑sparing anti‑inflammatory symptom control to reduce local irritation and the medical‑failure→surgery funnel.

name: Dysgraphia
description: Dysgraphia is a childhood learning disorder where writing is disproportionately impaired, causing poor handwriting, spelling, and organization plus slow, effortful transcription that can lead to fatigue and avoidance. Care is largely school based accommodations and remediation, but these workarounds often fail to address core deficits in handwriting automaticity, motor sequencing, and the working memory load of transcription, leaving a need for more direct interventions that improve writing fluency and output quality.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pharmacologic enhancement of orthographic-coding/working-memory deficits to improve spelling accuracy and written-output fluency in dysgraphia.
- Therapeutics that improve sequential finger-movement planning to increase handwriting speed/quality (automatization).
- Adjunct medication producing direct handwriting gains in dysgraphia with ADHD comorbidity beyond indirect benefits from treating inattention.

name: Epithelial basement membrane dystrophy
description: Epithelial basement membrane dystrophy is an anterior corneal surface disorder marked by map dot fingerprint changes that destabilize vision and predispose to recurrent corneal erosions, often with sudden morning pain, tearing, photophobia, and blurred vision in adults. Care is largely lubricants and hypertonic saline with escalation to procedures, but there is no cure or proven way to prevent symptoms, creating demand for durable non surgical prophylaxis and vision stabilizing therapy.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical prophylaxis to prevent recurrent corneal erosions in refractory EBMD/RCE patients despite artificial tears, hypertonic saline, or bandage lenses.
- Vision-stabilizing therapy to reduce EBMD-related periodic blurred vision from altered corneal curvature and avoid escalation to debridement/superficial keratectomy/PTK.
- Long-acting ocular-surface therapy that reduces frequent daytime preservative-free tears plus bedtime ointment/hypertonic ointment and avoids escalation to oral doxycycline + topical steroids (e.g., via targeted MMP-9/adhesion biology without systemic exposure).

name: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
description: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency is a malabsorption disorder from inadequate pancreatic enzyme delivery to the intestine, causing fat maldigestion with steatorrhea, bloating, weight loss, and fat soluble vitamin deficiencies and malnutrition. Care relies on pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with every meal and snack, often multiple capsules, yet symptoms and nutritional gaps can persist and products are largely porcine derived, creating burden, acid stability issues, and acceptability constraints that drive need for more reliable, lower burden, non porcine, stomach stable enzymes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Enzyme therapy that reliably eliminates residual steatorrhea and normalizes fat absorption/nutrition (e.g., CFA, fat‑soluble vitamins, weight).
- Lower-burden dosing that reduces “with every meal + snack” administration and high capsule/tablet counts.
- Non‑porcine and/or acid‑stable alternative to avoid pork-derived barriers and reduce reliance on PPI/H2 co-therapy.

name: Exostosis
description: Exostosis is most often osteochondroma, a benign bone and cartilage outgrowth from the growth plate that presents in childhood or adolescence as a painless hard bump near joints like the knee or shoulder, sometimes causing activity related pain or nerve compression symptoms. In hereditary multiple osteochondromas, multiple lesions by early adolescence can disrupt growth, limit motion, and cause recurrent pain, with a 2 to 10 percent lifetime risk of malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma. Management is mainly surveillance and repeated surgical excision, leaving a key unmet need for disease modifying therapies that prevent new tumors and reduce pain and cancer risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying prevention of new osteochondromas in pediatric HMO/MHE (e.g., reduced annualized rate/volume of new lesions on whole-body MRI)
- Non-surgical control of chronic pain/deformity and nerve-compression morbidity to reduce repeat operations
- Chemoprevention/early-intervention to reduce malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma in MHE

name: Diaphragmatic eventration
description: Diaphragmatic eventration is an abnormally elevated but intact hemidiaphragm caused by congenital muscle deficiency or acquired phrenic nerve dysfunction. Many patients are incidentally diagnosed and asymptomatic, but symptomatic adults and children can develop dyspnea, orthopnea, recurrent respiratory infections, atelectasis, and reflux type symptoms, with some neonates progressing to life threatening ventilator dependent respiratory distress. Management is usually supportive, escalating to surgical diaphragm plication for severe disease, yet plication relieves mechanics without restoring diaphragm function, leaving a gap for function restoring, non surgical options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical therapy that improves dyspnea/orthopnea and objective lung function (e.g., FEV1/FVC) to plication-like gains while avoiding operative morbidity.
- Ventilation-sparing medical therapy for severe neonatal congenital eventration to prevent/shorten mechanical ventilation.
- Function-restoring therapy for acquired eventration due to phrenic nerve injury (beyond mechanical benefit of plication).

name: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis
description: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis is a progressive, usually noninflammatory disorder of abnormal ligament and enthesis calcification and ossification that forms flowing bony bridges along the spine, typically in older men with obesity, diabetes, or metabolic syndrome, causing chronic back or neck pain, morning stiffness, and reduced mobility. Care is largely conservative with physical therapy, activity modification, and analgesics, with surgery for severe cervical complications like dysphagia or airway compromise. The central unmet need is a safe disease modifying therapy that can slow or reverse new bone formation and reduce osteophyte burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy to prevent/inhibit soft-tissue ossification and slow radiographic bridging in DISH
- Non-NSAID option for high-symptom/clinically active DISH (e.g., BASDAI ≥6) with meaningful pain/stiffness relief without NSAID CV/GI toxicity
- Medical alternative to surgery for cervical DISH complications (dysphagia/airway obstruction) by reducing osteophyte burden/local drivers

name: Dyslexia
description: Dyslexia is a common, brain based learning disability marked by persistent slow and inaccurate word reading and spelling due to inefficient sound to letter mapping, often emerging in the early grades and compounding into comprehension, confidence, and long term academic and employment impacts. Care relies on early, intensive structured literacy instruction that is hard to scale, and there are no medications for the core disorder, leaving major unmet need for scalable, durable ways to build fluent reading while addressing frequent comorbid attention and mental health issues.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Adjunct pharmacotherapy that accelerates early structured-literacy response (decoding/word recognition) in primary-grade children needing high-intensity intervention
- Therapeutics that close the persistent fluency/automaticity gap (reading speed) in adolescents/adults who remain slow readers despite prior intervention
- Adjunct pharmacotherapy for dyslexia with comorbid ADHD/inattention to improve attention/response inhibition and increase treatability

name: Erythema infectiosum
description: Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) is a usually mild parvovirus B19 infection in children causing flu-like symptoms followed by a slapped-cheek, sometimes lacy rash, but it can be dangerous in pregnancy and in patients with hemolytic disorders or immunocompromise where it can cause severe fetal anemia, miscarriage, or aplastic anemia. There is no vaccine, preventive therapy, or antiviral, leaving a key unmet need for protection and virus-clearing treatments in high-risk groups.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Prophylactic parvovirus B19 vaccine for seronegative women of childbearing potential/high-exposure groups to prevent infection
- Post-exposure prophylaxis/early acute therapy (e.g., neutralizing antibody/antiviral) for pregnancy and other high-risk exposures
- Virus-clearing targeted therapy (oral antiviral and/or long-acting neutralizing antibody) for chronic infection/chronic anemia in immunocompromised patients and aplastic anemia in high-risk hematologic disorders

name: Fibroma
description: Oral irritation fibroma is a common benign, scar like reactive overgrowth of oral mucosal fibrous tissue caused by chronic local trauma such as cheek or lip biting, rough teeth, or dentures. It usually appears in midlife or older adults as a solitary firm smooth 1 to 2 cm nodule along the buccal bite line, often asymptomatic but sometimes ulcerated or painful and can interfere with chewing or speech. Care is largely procedure centric since surgical excision with removal of the irritant is the main option, and lesions can recur when irritation persists, creating unmet need for non surgical local therapies that reduce inflammation, speed mucosal healing, and prevent recurrence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Local non-surgical (topical/intralesional) therapy that achieves complete lesion resolution (avoids excision)
- Locally delivered adjunct that improves 12-month recurrence-free rate in patients with ongoing irritation/repeated trauma
- Oral topical for the painful/ulcerated subset that reduces bite-trauma pain and accelerates mucosal/ulcer healing to restore chewing/speech

name: Gingival recession
description: Gingival recession is common in middle and older adults, where the gum margin migrates down the tooth to expose root surfaces, making teeth look longer and driving thermal and tactile sensitivity plus higher risk of root caries. First line care focuses on plaque control and desensitising agents but often does not restore lost tissue. Predictable root coverage typically requires graft based surgery, sometimes with palatal donor tissue, creating a need for durable, less invasive regenerative options that avoid donor site morbidity while protecting exposed roots.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Regenerative root-coverage drug/biologic alternative (or adjunct) achieving predictable mean/complete root coverage for RT1/RT2 defects without palatal donor-site morbidity (esp. multiple defects, smokers)
- Long-acting dentin-hypersensitivity control for exposed-root patients with inadequate relief from desensitizing toothpastes
- Combined sensitivity + root-caries/cervical-lesion prevention therapy tailored to exposed root surfaces (often older adults)

name: Cystitis glandularis
description: Cystitis glandularis is a glandular metaplasia of the bladder mucosa, usually arising from chronic irritation or inflammation and often found incidentally or during workup for irritative urinary symptoms and hematuria. Lesions commonly involve the bladder neck or trigone and can mimic malignancy, requiring cystoscopy with biopsy or resection. Management is largely procedural and surveillance based, yet recurrence can drive repeat interventions and, in extensive disease, ureteric obstruction may progress to hydroureteronephrosis and renal impairment, leaving a need for durable local, disease modifying therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Post‑TUR adjuvant drug therapy to reduce high cystitis glandularis recurrence and need for repeat endoscopic resection/surveillance.
- Kidney‑protective medical therapy that prevents ureteric‑orifice involvement/upper‑tract obstruction in patients with upper‑tract changes.
- Bladder‑local, non‑antibiotic symptom‑modifying therapy (e.g., microbiome/mucosal remodeling) for high‑risk phenotypes such as pelvic‑lipomatosis–associated CG.

name: Hairy tongue
description: Hairy tongue is a temporary, usually benign condition where keratin accumulates on elongated tongue papillae, trapping debris and microbes that discolor the surface and can cause halitosis, taste changes, burning, or gagging. It is more common in older men and often triggered by antibiotics, tobacco, or irritant mouthwashes. Management relies on oral hygiene and mechanical tongue scraping, which can be hard for patients with sensitive gag reflexes or recurrent disease, creating demand for convenient topical therapies that reliably clear papillae and quickly control breath and taste symptoms.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Standardized topical therapy to reliably normalize elongated papillae and prevent recurrence in refractory/recurrent hairy/black hairy tongue when hygiene fails
- Non-mechanical, gag-reflex–friendly topical (rinse/film/lozenge) that achieves scraping-equivalent clearance for patients unable to brush/scrape
- Targeted topical antimicrobial/anti-odor treatment to rapidly reduce halitosis, dysgeusia, and burning linked to bacteria/yeast/debris accumulation

name: Hepatitis A
description: Hepatitis A is an acute, highly contagious liver infection spread fecal orally, typically causing abrupt fever, malaise, nausea, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, and jaundice, and usually resolves within 2 months though 10% to 15% relapse or persist up to 6 months. Care is largely supportive with no specific antiviral, leaving high risk patients such as older adults and those with chronic liver disease vulnerable. Recent US outbreaks in under-immunized groups highlight gaps in prevention, since immune globulin must be given within 2 weeks of exposure and long term vaccine protection requires a second dose 6 months later.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Short-course antiviral/active therapy for acute HAV to shorten weeks–months symptoms and reduce severe outcomes in high-risk adults (older, chronic liver disease)
- Standardized long-acting passive immunization (e.g., mAb) for PEP/pre-exposure in vulnerable contacts to overcome IG potency drift and >2-week post-exposure efficacy gap
- Single-visit rapid outbreak prophylaxis with durable protection for PWUD, people experiencing homelessness, and MSM (avoiding 6-month return for second vaccine dose)

name: Hepatitis E
description: Hepatitis E is an inflammation of the liver caused by hepatitis E virus, usually an acute self limited hepatitis with fever, nausea, abdominal pain and jaundice. The highest stakes are severe fulminant liver failure and very high mortality in pregnancy in the second or third trimester, while immunosuppressed patients such as transplant recipients can develop chronic infection. Care is largely supportive for acute disease with no specific antiviral, and ribavirin is not an option in pregnancy due to teratogenicity, leaving major unmet needs for pregnancy safe antivirals, durable viral clearance in chronic infection, and broader prevention through vaccination.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pregnancy-safe antiviral for acute HEV in 2nd/3rd trimester to prevent acute liver failure and reduce maternal mortality
- Short-course, non-ribavirin antiviral achieving sustained HEV RNA clearance in chronic HEV in immunosuppressed/solid-organ transplant patients (incl. ribavirin non-response/relapse)
- Therapy that improves survival in HEV-triggered severe acute hepatitis/acute-on-chronic liver failure where ribavirin benefit and dosing are uncertain

name: Hyperopia
description: Hyperopia is a refractive error where the eye is too short or underpowered so light focuses behind the retina, blurring near vision and causing eyestrain and headaches during close work. Children may compensate but high hyperopia can lead to amblyopia and strabismus if not corrected. Care is dominated by glasses, contact lenses, or refractive surgery, leaving a need for safer non-surgical options that reduce device dependence and avoid contact lens complications such as eye infections while protecting developing near vision.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-device, non-surgical topical therapy producing clinically meaningful hyperopic refractive shift (MRSE toward emmetropia) to reduce dependence on glasses/contacts and associated keratitis/ulcer risk.
- Adherence-independent pediatric intervention for preschoolers with moderate/high hyperopia (≥+4.0 D) to prevent amblyopia/strabismus and irreversible vision impairment.
- Therapy targeting accommodative/near-vision function (not just distance acuity) for children with functional deficits despite normal distance VA, reducing accommodative load and improving binocular near performance.

name: Intestinal disaccharidase deficiency
description: Rare inherited small intestinal brush border enzyme deficiency, typically congenital sucrase isomaltase deficiency, causing post weaning intolerance to sucrose and starch with watery diarrhea, bloating, gas, abdominal pain, dehydration and failure to thrive. Current yeast derived sacrosidase must be taken with every meal or snack and does not replace isomaltase, leaving ongoing starch restriction plus handling and allergy burdens and a need for safer, lower burden enzyme therapy with broader carbohydrate coverage.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Therapy addressing isomaltase/starch maldigestion so patients can be symptom-free without ongoing starch restriction.
- Lower-burden alternative to per-meal/snack split dosing and cold/room-temp mixing constraints.
- Non-yeast/less immunogenic option to reduce severe hypersensitivity risk and enable use in yeast-sensitive patients.

name: Microsporidiosis
description: Opportunistic intracellular spore forming microsporidia infection in advanced immunosuppression, especially HIV, causing chronic diarrhea with malabsorption, weight loss and wasting and sometimes ocular biliary or disseminated fatal disease; management relies on antiretroviral immune restoration and supportive care, with no specific therapy for Enterocytozoon bieneusi and effective options like fumagillin limited by serious hematologic toxicity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Orally available, *Enterocytozoon bieneusi*–active therapy that reliably resolves diarrhea and achieves microbiologic eradication in advanced/low-CD4 HIV.
- Fumagillin replacement/analog that maintains *E. bieneusi* clearance while avoiding dose-limiting hematologic toxicity (thrombocytopenia/neutropenia) and hospitalization burden.
- Solid-organ-transplant–compatible regimen that controls *E. bieneusi* without requiring immunosuppression tapering (minimizing graft-rejection risk/drug–drug interactions).
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus page for Microsporidiosis

name: Mongolian spot
description: Congenital dermal melanocytosis is a common benign newborn birthmark of flat blue or blue gray patches, usually on the back or buttocks, caused by melanocytes in deeper skin layers and typically fading in early childhood. The main unmet need is accurate recognition and documentation, since lesions can be mistaken for bruises and trigger child abuse evaluations. Extensive or atypical cases rarely merit workup for associated inborn errors of metabolism.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Otitis media | non-suppurative
description: Otitis media with effusion (glue ear) is thick, sticky fluid behind the eardrum without acute infection, affecting ~90% of children by age 5 and causing temporary hearing loss that can impair speech and school progress when persistent. Care is largely watchful waiting, with guidelines recommending against systemic antibiotics and steroids, yet there is no effective long term medical therapy to clear middle ear fluid and biofilms drive recurrence, leaving a need for safe non antibiotic, disease modifying treatments that speed clearance and prevent persistent effusion and tube placement.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non‑antibiotic, non‑steroid drug that clears middle‑ear effusion and improves hearing in children with persistent bilateral OME + hearing loss at ~3‑month reassessment.
- Local (intratympanic/topical) anti‑biofilm therapy for biofilm‑driven chronic OME to reduce post‑tympanostomy recurrence/repeat procedures.
- Noninvasive Eustachian‑tube function/mucus‑clearance modulator (e.g., intranasal) to prevent sticky mucus build‑up and persistent OME‑related hearing loss.

name: Periapical granuloma
description: Chronic inflammatory lesion at the root tip of a nonvital, infected tooth, often asymptomatic and detected as a periapical radiolucency. Definitive care is procedural via root canal therapy or extraction, but failures persist because complex canal anatomy and biofilm protected pathogens can evade standard instrumentation and irrigation, making eradication of deep infection and predictable healing a key unmet need.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Deep-tubule/apical anti-biofilm intracanal antimicrobial to eradicate persistent intraradicular infection (incl. *E. faecalis*) without caustic periapical toxicity.
- Pro-healing/bone-regenerative adjunct to accelerate periapical bone repair and shorten radiographic healing timelines (PAI improvement).
- Fast-acting intracanal medicament/disinfection adjunct enabling predictable single-visit root canal care to reduce multi-appointment burden.

name: Leukoedema | oral
description: Oral leukoedema is a very common, benign, asymptomatic oral mucosal change that appears as diffuse milky gray white nonwipeable buccal plaques that fade with stretching, likely due to intracellular edema. It has no malignant potential and needs no treatment, so the key unmet need is diagnostic confidence to distinguish it from higher risk oral white lesions and avoid unnecessary biopsies and anxiety.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Retinal degeneration | lattice
description: Lattice degeneration is a common peripheral retinal degeneration marked by localized retinal thinning with vitreous liquefaction and vitreoretinal adhesion, usually asymptomatic and found incidentally, especially in myopic eyes. Most patients never need treatment, but lesions can predispose to retinal tears and detachments with sudden vision loss. Management is largely surveillance because routine prophylactic laser or cryotherapy is rarely used and lacks randomized evidence of benefit, leaving uncertainty about who truly benefits from prevention and how best to reduce detachment risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Proven medical prophylaxis for high‑risk lattice degeneration eyes (e.g., fellow eye after retinal detachment, high myopia >6 D) to reduce future retinal tear/RRD vs observation.
- Non‑scarring pharmacologic alternative to laser/cryotherapy that strengthens peripheral retina without increasing vitreoretinal adhesion/traction.
- Therapy that prevents new tears/breaks outside visible lattice (including in previously healthy peripheral retina) to reduce failure of lesion‑targeted prophylaxis and lessen surveillance burden.

name: Adenoma | pituitary
description: Pituitary adenomas are usually benign and often incidental, but larger tumors can cause headaches, progressive visual field loss, and hormone excess syndromes such as acromegaly or Cushing disease. Surgery is central, yet major unmet needs include dopamine agonist resistant prolactinomas (about 10 percent cabergoline resistant) with monitoring burdens, acromegaly where about 40 percent remain uncontrolled with high treatment burden and incomplete quality of life recovery, and recurrent Cushing disease where pasireotide can worsen glycemic control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical, tumor-shrinking options for cabergoline-resistant prolactinomas (~10%) achieving normoprolactinemia and ≥30% macroadenoma shrinkage without prolonged high-dose cabergoline/valvular monitoring.
- Self-administered (ideally oral) acromegaly therapies that deliver durable GH/IGF‑1 biochemical control beyond first-generation SRLs and reduce injection/storage/HCP-administration burden.
- Persistent/recurrent Cushing disease treatments post-surgery that increase UFC normalization/response rates versus pasireotide while avoiding significant hyperglycemia/metabolic adverse effects.

name: Cherry angioma
description: Cherry angiomas are common benign vascular skin growths that appear in adulthood as multiple small bright red papules, usually asymptomatic but often removed for cosmetic reasons or trauma related bleeding. Care relies on destructive procedures such as electrosurgery, cryotherapy, laser, or shave excision, which can leave scars and pigment changes that are especially problematic in darker skin. A key unmet need is less destructive, cosmetically safer treatment, with emerging biology pointing to somatic mutations in vascular signaling genes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Scar-free non-ablative topical/local drug clearance of lesions to avoid scarring from destructive removal
- Pigment-safe therapy for skin of color with low risk of hypo/hyperpigmentation
- Local vessel-stabilizing/anti-bleeding therapy for trauma-prone lesions that bleed frequently

name: Prostate stones
description: Age related calcium phosphate prostate calcifications, usually incidental after age 50, but in chronic prostatitis can drive pelvic pain and relapsing infection by sheltering bacteria in biofilms. Management is mostly watchful waiting or endoscopic removal when symptomatic, and antibiotics often fail to clear biofilm protected reservoirs, leaving unmet need for biofilm active anti infectives, less invasive clearance, and prevention of recurrent calcification.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Biofilm-active anti-infective regimens to eradicate bacteria sheltered in prostatic calculi and prevent relapse/recurrence
- Non-endoscopic “stone elimination” therapy for symptomatic large/multiple or inflammation-associated calculi causing LUTS/chronic pelvic pain, reducing reliance on procedures
- Prevention of stone genesis/progression in chronic prostatic inflammation by targeting biofilm-driven calcification surfaces to avoid persistent infection reservoirs and resistance selection

name: Pterygium
description: Pterygium is a noncancerous conjunctival growth that can extend onto the cornea, often linked to chronic ultraviolet light, wind, and dust exposure, causing irritation, inflammation, and sometimes astigmatism and vision loss. Drops can relieve symptoms, but definitive care is surgical and recurrence remains the central challenge, typically within months. Current anti-recurrence adjuncts can be toxic, and prolonged steroid use can raise eye pressure and contribute to cataracts, creating demand for safer, steroid sparing approaches that durably prevent regrowth and protect vision.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer post-excision anti-recurrence adjuncts for recurrent/high-risk pterygium that avoid mitomycin C/antimetabolite toxicities.
- Disease-modifying topical therapy for early/primary pterygium to halt progression and prevent astigmatism/visual-axis involvement.
- Steroid-sparing and/or sustained-release anti-inflammatory therapy to reduce steroid-induced ocular hypertension risk and high drop-burden regimens.

name: Adenoma | renal
description: Tiny, low grade benign epithelial tumor of the renal cortex, typically asymptomatic and incidentally found, but viewed as a precursor lesion to papillary renal cell carcinoma. It is enriched in older men and in chronically injured kidneys such as end stage renal disease, acquired cystic disease, and long term hemodialysis. Key unmet needs are noninvasive diagnosis and risk stratification because imaging can be nondiagnostic and progression risk is hard to predict, plus renal sparing, ultra low toxicity strategies to prevent progression or stabilize multifocal disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Renal-sparing chemoprevention to prevent papillary adenoma → papillary RCC progression in high-risk “injured-kidney” patients (e.g., ESRD/acquired cystic disease/hemodialysis).
- Systemic or kidney-targeted therapy for multifocal/bilateral renal adenomatosis to reduce total lesion burden and avoid repetitive invasive management.
- Ultra-low-toxicity medical cytoreduction/growth-arrest for indeterminate small papillary renal lesions to keep them below the ≤15 mm benign threshold and reduce unnecessary procedures.

name: Valve disease | tricuspid regurgitation
description: Tricuspid regurgitation is failure of the tricuspid valve to close, causing backflow into the right atrium and progressive right sided volume overload that is usually secondary in older adults, often driven by atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension, or other pressure and volume overload. It is frequently under recognized until patients present with systemic venous congestion and right heart failure symptoms such as fatigue, leg edema, and abdominal swelling that can progress to ascites and liver and kidney dysfunction. Care remains largely symptomatic with diuretics, but diuretic resistance is common and evidence for disease modifying medical therapy is limited, creating demand for earlier detection, remodeling targeted therapies, and catheter based valve interventions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Reverse-remodeling pharmacotherapy for functional severe TR that reduces RV dilation and TR severity (e.g., ↓RV end-systolic volume index, ↓vena contracta width)
- Cardiorenal-safe decongestion for severe TR with severe renal failure/venous congestion that improves renal outcomes beyond loop-diuretic–only care
- Etiology-targeted therapy for secondary TR driven by pulmonary disease/pulmonary hypertension that improves RV function and slows TR progression

name: Helicobacter pylori infection
description: Chronic Helicobacter pylori stomach infection, typically acquired in childhood and often asymptomatic until it damages the gastric lining causing gastritis or peptic ulcer disease, sometimes presenting with gastrointestinal bleeding and increasing long term malignancy risk. Treatment is limited by antibiotic resistance and high pill burden 14 day multi drug regimens, driving need for susceptibility guided therapy and simpler combinations such as potassium competitive acid blocker based regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Empiric regimens that maintain ≥90% eradication in high/unknown clarithromycin-resistance settings and in clarithromycin-resistant infections.
- Low pill-burden (BID or simpler) fixed-dose/blister-pack alternatives to 14-day optimized bismuth quadruple therapy to improve adherence.
- Better-tolerated eradication options with substantially lower adverse-event rates than 10–14-day bismuth quadruple therapy while preserving high cure rates.

name: Persistent Pupillary Membrane
description: Persistent pupillary membrane is a common congenital iris anomaly in infants where fetal vascular remnants persist as strands across the pupil and usually regress within the first year. In rare dense cases the membrane blocks the visual axis and can cause amblyopia, making early restoration of a functional pupillary opening the key clinical priority. Current options are limited to dilation plus amblyopia therapy, with laser mainly for older patients and surgery reserved for severe cases due to anesthesia and intraocular complication risks, creating demand for safer early interventions.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical pharmacotherapy to clear/lyse dense PPM and restore a functional pupillary aperture (≥~1.5 mm) in cases occluding the visual axis.
- Pediatric-safe sustained mydriasis/cycloplegia (low systemic exposure) to create space around the membrane without current mydriatic toxicity/age limits.
- Adjunct drug therapy to enable safer YAG/Nd:YAG membranotomy by reducing bleeding/inflammation/IOP spikes and avoiding intraocular surgery, especially in young children.
medlineUrl: No standalone MedlinePlus URL for Persistent Pupillary Membrane (PPM)

name: Darwin’s tubercle
description: Darwin’s tubercle is a common benign congenital cartilage prominence on the posterior helix of the ear, usually an incidental asymptomatic finding needing only reassurance. Treatment is typically unnecessary unless cosmetic concerns drive elective correction, where current management relies on surgical full thickness excision, creating an unmet need for a predictable low scar cosmetic option.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified

name: Torus Palatinus
description: Torus palatinus is a common benign midline bony overgrowth of the hard palate, usually asymptomatic and found incidentally. Unmet needs cluster in the minority with large lesions that complicate denture or appliance fit or whose thin overlying mucosa is repeatedly traumatized, causing ulceration and functional or quality of life issues. Management is typically observation and reassurance, with oral surgery reserved for interference with function, prosthodontic work, or recurrent injury.
keyUnmetNeeds: - No opportunities identified
medlineUrl: No dedicated MedlinePlus URL for Torus Palatinus

name: Elevated lipoprotein(a)
description: Elevated lipoprotein(a) is a largely inherited lipid abnormality that is often missed without dedicated testing and drives residual risk for heart attack, stroke, and aortic stenosis even when standard cholesterol is controlled. Care is mostly indirect risk management because current lipid drugs do not directly target lipoprotein(a) and the only clearly effective option is burdensome, limited-access apheresis about every two weeks. A major unmet need is scalable therapies with proven cardiovascular outcomes benefit and potential to slow valve disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Lp(a)-lowering drug that proves major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) reduction in secondary-prevention ASCVD patients with high Lp(a) (e.g., ≥70 mg/dL or ≥175–200 nmol/L).
- Lp(a)-targeted therapy that slows aortic valve calcification/stenosis and delays valve replacement (valve outcomes, not just lipid lowering).
- Potent pharmacologic alternative to dialysis-like lipoprotein apheresis that reduces/eliminates need for apheresis and expands access beyond narrow FH+CVD eligibility.

name: Astrovirus infection
description: Human astrovirus is a fecal oral enteric infection causing mostly mild, self limited gastroenteritis in children under 2, with 2 to 5 days of watery diarrhea and vomiting managed with rehydration. No human vaccine or targeted therapy exists, and the biggest unmet need is in immunocompromised patients where disease can persist with prolonged viral shedding and rarely spread beyond the gut, including to the central nervous system.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Pediatric-safe, short-course oral antiviral to shorten acute illness vs rehydration-only care
- Immunocompromised-focused viral-clearance therapy (e.g., FcRn entry-blocking) to stop persistent shedding and prevent systemic/CNS spread
- Vaccine or passive immunoprophylaxis (neutralizing antibodies) for prevention

name: BK virus infection
description: BK virus disease after kidney transplant is BK polyomavirus reactivation under immunosuppression, often silent but sometimes causing acute kidney injury, allograft dysfunction, and premature graft loss. Management relies on frequent viral load surveillance and reducing immunosuppression, since there is no reliably effective targeted antiviral therapy, forcing a high stakes tradeoff between controlling virus and triggering rejection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Immunosuppression-sparing BKPyV clearance (rapid ≥1 log10 drop/undetectable DNAemia) without increasing graft-rejection risk
- Prevent progression to, and/or achieve biopsy-proven resolution of, BKPyV-associated nephropathy (BKVAN) to avert graft loss
- Kidney-safe (non-nephrotoxic), practical outpatient regimen (e.g., q4-week) that reduces today’s high-frequency BK viral-load monitoring burden

name: Blastocystosis
description: Blastocystosis is a common intestinal protozoan carriage or infection that is often asymptomatic but can cause persistent, non specific gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain or distension, and nausea, with occasional urticaria and ongoing debate about true pathogenicity. In symptomatic cases treated after other causes are excluded, current antibiotics have highly variable and often unreliable stool eradication, frequently requiring multi dose 10 day courses. A key unmet need is a short, well tolerated regimen that predictably clears infection and relieves symptoms, particularly for children and immunocompromised patients.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Predictable symptom relief plus durable fecal eradication in persistent symptomatic blastocystosis despite metronidazole nonresponse/variable cure rates.
- Regimens with proven safety/efficacy for high‑risk groups (children, immunocompromised, pregnancy/lactation) where current options have restrictions or limited data.
- Ultra‑short, low pill‑burden oral courses to improve adherence versus multi‑day, multi‑dose regimens.

name: Norovirus infection
description: Norovirus causes rapid-onset, highly contagious acute gastroenteritis with vomiting and diarrhea that usually resolves in 1 to 3 days but can lead to dangerous dehydration in children and older adults and drive prolonged outbreaks in hospitals and long term care. With no specific treatment, no Food and Drug Administration approved antivirals, and no licensed vaccine, care is largely supportive, leaving major unmet needs for therapies that prevent or shorten severe, prolonged disease in immunocompromised patients and for broadly protective vaccines despite rapidly evolving strain diversity and short lived immunity.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral direct-acting antiviral that shortens vomiting/diarrhea duration (time-to-symptom-resolution endpoint) to reduce dehydration/IV-fluid hospitalization risk in young children and older adults.
- Viral-clearance therapy for chronic norovirus in immunocompromised/transplant patients, with demonstrable reductions in stool RT-PCR viral load and time to negativity.
- Broadly protective prophylaxis (vaccine or durable preventive) that overcomes strain diversity to prevent/limit prolonged outbreaks in long-term care and hospital settings.

name: Chlamydia pneumoniae infection
description: Chlamydia pneumoniae causes usually mild, droplet spread respiratory infection often starting in school aged children and young adults with slow onset sore throat or hoarseness progressing to a gradually worsening cough and fatigue that can persist for weeks, including 2 to 6 weeks in children. Standard antibiotics are used but eradication can be unreliable, with reports of persistent infection for months, leaving a need for more dependable clearance and faster symptom resolution.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Relapse-/persistence-proof regimens that eradicate viable *C. pneumoniae* and prevent recurrence after standard antibiotics.
- Therapies that shorten weeks–months of persistent cough/malaise despite appropriate antibiotic therapy.
- Safer first-line oral options for pediatrics/risk-sensitive patients where tetracyclines are avoided and fluoroquinolone toxicity is a concern.

name: Enterovirus infection
description: Non polio enterovirus infections are common in children and teens and usually cause a self limited febrile respiratory illness with cough, runny nose, rash and mouth blisters. Care is largely symptomatic because there is no disease specific antiviral. The key unmet need is in the small but high impact minority that develop acute flaccid myelitis with permanent paralysis or severe neonatal disseminated disease with viral sepsis, hepatitis and myocarditis, where management remains primarily supportive and outcomes can be catastrophic.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Antiviral/neutralizing antibody for neonatal (≤30 days) disseminated enterovirus/echovirus sepsis-/hepatitis-/myocarditis-/meningitis that reduces mortality and organ failure.
- CNS-penetrant antiviral or rapid-onset neutralizing biologic for EV‑D68/EV‑A71 neuroinvasive disease/AFM that improves limb-function recovery and prevents long-term neurologic sequelae.
- Convenient oral early outpatient antiviral for symptomatic pediatric non‑polio enterovirus infection that shortens symptoms/viral shedding and reduces hospitalization risk.

name: Exanthem subitum
description: Exanthem subitum, or roseola infantum, is a common human herpesvirus 6B and sometimes human herpesvirus 7 infection of infants and young children, peaking around 6 to 12 months, marked by abrupt high fever for 3 to 5 days followed by a brief rash as the fever breaks. With no specific treatment, care is supportive, and the main clinical gap is preventing fever driven complications such as febrile seizures and addressing severe central nervous system disease risk in immunocompromised patients where antiviral use lacks controlled trial evidence.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-start, pediatric-safe (ideally oral) anti‑HHV‑6/HHV‑7 therapy to reduce febrile-seizure incidence in immunocompetent infants/toddlers
- Safer, CNS-active HHV‑6 treatment for immunocompromised patients (e.g., transplant recipients) to prevent/treat encephalitis/limbic injury/multiorgan failure
- Transplant-focused HHV‑6 prophylaxis that is safe/effective enough to justify routine prevention

name: Haemophilus influenzae infection
description: Haemophilus influenzae disease includes respiratory infections such as pneumonia and adult bronchitis, with fever, cough, dyspnea and chest pain and higher invasive risk in adults 65+. In chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, non typeable strains can persist in the airway as biofilm, driving recurrent exacerbations. Treatment is pressured by beta lactam resistance from penicillin binding protein 3 variants that can blunt amoxicillin even with clavulanate, plus safety and tolerability constraints in older comorbid patients including Clostridioides difficile diarrhea and macrolide QT prolongation. This creates demand for more resistance robust oral options, airway delivered antibiofilm approaches, and preventive vaccines.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Oral regimens that maintain CAP cure/rapid clinical stability in older/comorbid (e.g., COPD) patients despite ftsI/PBP3 (BLNAR/rPBP3) β-lactam resistance that can undermine β‑lactam/β‑lactamase‑inhibitor therapy
- Airway-delivered anti-biofilm/anti-persistence therapies for chronic NTHi colonization in COPD/bronchiectasis to reduce recurrent infections/exacerbations and repeat antibiotic use
- Shorter-course, better-tolerated oral options that reduce macrolide QT/torsades risk and β‑lactam/β‑lactamase‑inhibitor GI/C. difficile diarrhea burden in older polypharmacy patients

name: Human bocavirus infection
description: Human bocavirus is a pediatric respiratory virus mainly affecting infants and toddlers aged 6 months to 2 years, typically causing fever, cough, rhinorrhea and wheeze and sometimes bronchiolitis or pneumonia. Clinical management is complicated by frequent co-infections and prolonged viral shedding that blurs attribution and drives misdiagnosis and unnecessary antibiotic use. With no targeted antiviral or effective vaccine, care is supportive, leaving unmet need for antivirals, prevention for high-risk children, and therapies that clear persistent infection.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Virus-targeted antiviral for hospitalized pediatric HBoV LRTI that reduces length-of-stay and symptom duration vs supportive care
- Preventive immunization (vaccine or long-acting passive immunotherapy) for high-risk children with pre-existing medical conditions to prevent severe/fatal disease
- Viral-eradication therapy achieving PCR-confirmed clearance for persistent/prolonged HBoV infection with extended shedding/viremia

name: Basal cell carcinoma
description: Basal cell carcinoma is a slow growing, locally aggressive skin cancer driven largely by ultraviolet damage, usually presenting in older fair skinned adults as a pearly bump or a bleeding nonhealing sore on sun exposed areas. It rarely metastasizes, but unchecked tumors can invade deeply and cause disfiguring tissue destruction. Surgery is often curative, yet advanced unresectable disease still needs durable, well tolerated control. Hedgehog pathway inhibitors can work but chronic muscle spasms and weight loss limit long term use, while cemiplimab adds ongoing intravenous dosing, and some non surgical options lack microscopic confirmation of complete clearance.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Better-tolerated Hedgehog inhibitor therapy enabling months–years of continuous control for laBCC/mBCC (reduce class-toxicity–driven interruptions/discontinuations).
