- Higher-ORR, more durable systemic options for post-HHI (HHI-resistant/intolerant) advanced BCC, ideally with more convenient dosing than IV q3w PD-1 monotherapy.
- Non-surgical topical/field or lesion-directed drug therapies achieving reliable histologic clearance beyond superficial-only BCC and lowering failure/recurrence vs current topicals.

name: Human metapneumovirus infection
description: Human metapneumovirus is a seasonal winter to spring respiratory virus that usually causes cold like symptoms but can progress to bronchitis or pneumonia in infants, older adults, and immunocompromised patients. With no approved vaccine or specific antiviral and care largely supportive, the major unmet need is rapid outpatient antivirals and safe preventive options for high risk groups.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-start (outpatient) antiviral to prevent progression to bronchiolitis/pneumonia and reduce hospitalization in high-risk groups (young children, older adults, immunosuppressed).
- Safe/effective prophylactic vaccine for infants/seronegative children (± maternal immunization) that prevents severe pediatric LRTI without VAED.
- Potent antiviral and/or passive immunotherapy to reduce LRTI mortality in immunocompromised patients (e.g., transplant/cancer).

name: Pediculosis capitis
description: Pediculosis capitis is a common childhood scalp infestation, typically in ages 3 to 11, with nits near the neckline and behind the ears and symptoms that can lag for weeks before itching, irritability, and sleep loss emerge. While it does not transmit disease and causes little medical morbidity, it triggers outsized family and school anxiety and can lead to excoriations with secondary bacterial infection. Treatment is operationally difficult because many products are not reliably egg killing, driving repeat dosing and meticulous combing, and growing pyrethroid resistance increases failure rates, creating demand for safe, simple, truly ovicidal options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Single-application, truly ovicidal topical pediculicide eliminating routine retreatment and prolonged nit removal/combing
- Non-pyrethroid therapy effective in pyrethroid/permethrin-resistant head lice
- Pediatric-first safety upgrade (non-flammable, low-irritant/low-toxicity-with-repetition) suitable for younger children and reducing misuse/overuse risks

name: Pneumococcal infection
description: Pneumococcal disease is infection with Streptococcus pneumoniae ranging from otitis media and sinusitis to invasive pneumonia, bacteremia, and meningitis, with highest risk in young children and adults 65+. Despite vaccines, >100 serotypes drive serotype replacement, invasive disease remains severe with ~10% mortality, and antibiotic resistance is common with >40% of invasive isolates non susceptible to at least one antibiotic class, sustaining demand for broader, serotype independent prevention and better treatments.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Serotype-independent (or ultra-high-valency) vaccine/long-acting mAb prophylaxis to prevent invasive disease from non-vaccine serotypes driving serotype replacement.
- Once-daily oral or long-acting injectable anti-pneumococcal therapy to replace high-frequency outpatient regimens (e.g., amoxicillin 1 g TID) and remain effective where macrolide resistance limits use.
- Adjunctive host-directed/anti-virulence therapies for hospitalized invasive pneumococcal disease to reduce mortality and long-term sequelae beyond antibiotics alone.

name: Rhinovirus infection
description: Rhinovirus infection is the leading cause of the common cold, typically causing runny nose, nasal congestion, cough, sneezing, and sore throat that peak within 2 to 4 days and usually resolve within about a week. Care is largely supportive because there is no specific antiviral therapy and no vaccine, in part due to many distinct virus types. While often self limited, rhinoviruses disproportionately drive serious morbidity by triggering asthma attacks and exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, underscoring the need for broadly protective prevention and therapies that reduce exacerbations in high risk patients.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute direct-acting rhinovirus antiviral (intranasal/oral) to shorten time-to-symptom resolution and reduce symptom severity vs OTC-only care
- Cross-serotype prophylaxis (polyvalent vaccine or long-acting antibody) for high-risk allergic-asthma/COPD patients to prevent RV infection and reduce RV-triggered exacerbations/hospitalizations
- Post-exposure prophylaxis/ultra-early intervention to reduce secondary transmission despite pre-symptomatic spread

name: Ureaplasma urealyticum infection
description: Ureaplasma urealyticum genital infection is often asymptomatic, making colonization vs disease hard to distinguish, but can cause urethritis and is linked in pregnancy to chorioamnionitis, premature rupture of membranes, and preterm delivery; management relies on doxycycline or azithromycin, yet pregnancy contraindications and rising tetracycline and macrolide resistance limit options, underscoring a need for better diagnostics and safer, more durable therapies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Microbiologic-cure therapy for symptomatic/high-load *U. urealyticum* urethritis that remains active vs tetM tetracycline-resistant and 23S rRNA macrolide-resistant strains
- Pregnancy-safe treatments for azithromycin-resistant *U. urealyticum* cervical/genital infection (where tetracyclines/quinolones are contraindicated)
- One-visit/ultra-short-course “resistance-sparing” regimens that improve adherence vs doxycycline BID ×7d and reduce resistance selection vs single-dose azithromycin

name: Aging
description: Aging is a progressive loss of intrinsic capacity and functional ability, often manifesting as frailty and sarcopenia with slow gait and weakness that raise fall and hip fracture risk. Care is complicated by multimorbidity and polypharmacy, while treatment still relies largely on exercise and nutrition rather than approved drugs that reliably restore mobility or resilience. The unmet need is disease modifying approaches that can measurably improve function using endpoints like gait speed and the short physical performance battery, with growing interest in targeting senescence and chronic inflammation biology.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Post-hip/femur fracture (60–85) frailty/sarcopenia drugs that deliver measurable 90‑day functional recovery (SPPB, 4‑m walk, 6MWT, grip strength).
- Pharmacologic therapy for mild–moderate frailty (CFS 4–6) that improves objective mobility/strength and fall-related confidence beyond exercise/nutrition-only care.
- Senescence/inflammaging-targeted treatments

name: Tinnitus
description: Tinnitus is a chronic phantom sound perception, often linked to hearing loss, that can significantly impair sleep, concentration, and mood. Care today is largely coping focused using sound therapy devices such as hearing aids and cognitive behavioral therapy, plus medications for anxiety or sleep rather than the sound itself. With no cure or tinnitus specific drug, the main unmet need is therapies that directly and durably reduce the perceived sound and earlier interventions that prevent acute symptoms from becoming chronic.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drug that reduces tinnitus sound/symptoms (not just distress) with clinically meaningful change (e.g., THI −11 and/or TFI −9 at 12 weeks)
- Short-course therapy for new-onset tinnitus (<3 months, ideally <28 days) to prevent chronification
- Tinnitus-driven insomnia/anxiety pharmacotherapy with cleaner tolerability, improving sleep/mood endpoints (e.g., PSQI/GAD-7)

name: Medullary cystic kidney disease | type 1
description: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease due to MUC1 causes slowly progressive tubulointerstitial fibrosis and chronic kidney disease, often first detected in the late teens or early 20s with bland urinalysis and few cysts. Patients may develop hypertension and hyperuricemia with occasional gout as function declines, eventually requiring dialysis or kidney transplant. Management is supportive because there are no specific therapies, creating a major unmet need for disease modifying treatments that prevent or reverse fibrosis by targeting the toxic MUC1 frameshift protein.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying small molecules that clear intracellular MUC1fs deposits to slow progression/delay kidney failure in genetically confirmed ADTKD‑MUC1.
- Kidney-targeted RNAi/siRNA silencing of MUC1fs to reduce the toxic protein earlier in the secretory pathway.
- Anti-fibrotic/tubule-protective therapies that reduce tubular injury and interstitial fibrosis to slow eGFR decline and delay renal replacement therapy.

name: Macular telangiectasia
description: Macular telangiectasia type 2 is a bilateral, slowly progressive midlife macular disease linked to neurodegeneration and Müller cell dysfunction that causes distorted central vision, reading difficulty, and paracentral scotomas, with central vision loss typically unfolding over 10 to 20 years. Care is largely symptomatic, with intravitreal anti vascular endothelial growth factor injections for proliferative neovascular disease and a newly approved option, Encelto, delivered via a single surgical procedure. The key gaps are durable disease modification that preserves real world visual function and reduces procedure burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Clinically meaningful visual-function gains (e.g., improved/maintained reading speed and microperimetry retinal sensitivity), not just slowed OCT ellipsoid-zone area loss.
- Non-surgical, safer disease-modifying therapy that avoids intravitreal implant/procedure risks and reduces serious ocular adverse events.
- Proven options for neovascular/proliferative MacTel that reduce frequent anti-VEGF injection burden while preserving/improving visual acuity.

name: Insomnia disorder
description: Chronic insomnia disorder is persistent difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep despite adequate opportunity, occurring at least 3 nights per week for at least 3 months, and causing meaningful daytime impairment. It is common, especially in women and older adults, and current sleep hygiene, cognitive behavioral therapy, and hypnotics often fall short because many sedative hypnotics are intended for short-term use and can impair next-day function, increase fall risk in older adults, and rarely trigger dangerous complex sleep behaviors, leaving a need for safer, more durable treatments that preserve daytime performance.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Daytime-function–first insomnia therapy that improves daytime sleepiness/mood/alertness-cognition while avoiding next-day driving/psychomotor impairment
- Older-/fall-risk–optimized option that eliminates complex sleep behaviors and minimizes hypnotic-related falls/injuries
- Durable chronic-use pharmacotherapy usable beyond short-term (4–5 weeks) framing and not dependent on a full-night (≥7–8h) sleep opportunity

name: Glutaric acidemia | type 2
description: Glutaric acidemia type II (multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency) is an inherited failure of fat and protein energy metabolism that can cause life threatening metabolic acidosis. Late onset cases often present in adolescence with chronic muscle weakness and exercise intolerance punctuated by crises triggered by fasting or infection with vomiting, nonketotic hypoglycemia, and liver dysfunction. Management is largely supportive with restrictive diet, strict fasting avoidance, and riboflavin, carnitine, and coenzyme Q10, yet decompensations still require rapid intravenous dextrose and severe neonatal disease can be fatal, leaving a premium on reliable at home rescue and true disease modifying restoration of enzyme function.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying restoration of ETF/ETFDH function for severe neonatal and riboflavin-nonresponsive ETFA/ETFB/ETFDH-mutant patients.
- At-home rapid “sick-day” pharmacologic rescue to prevent catabolic-stress metabolic decompensation without hospital IV dextrose.
- Therapies that improve chronic myopathy/exercise intolerance while reducing restrictive diet/fasting constraints and multi-dose supplement burden (carnitine/CoQ10).

name: Dup15q syndrome
description: 15q11-q13 duplication syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder marked by infant hypotonia, feeding difficulty, and early developmental delay that often progresses to moderate to severe intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, and epilepsy. Seizures can become complex and medically refractory, sometimes causing falls, developmental regression, and rare sleep related sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. Care is largely supportive with no disease specific therapy, leaving major unmet needs for durable seizure control and treatments that meaningfully improve adaptive function such as communication and daily living skills.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable control of early-onset, medication-resistant epilepsy (esp. idic(15) Dup15q) to prevent progression (e.g., to LGS/complex patterns), falls/developmental regression, and sleep-associated SUDEP risk
- Neurodevelopment-targeted therapy that improves adaptive function (communication, daily living skills, motor) beyond symptomatic care (e.g., Vineland-3 domains)
- Chronic anti-seizure therapy that maintains seizure control without worsening aggression/irritability, language/memory, or insomnia

name: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder
description: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is a severe premenstrual mood disorder marked by late luteal irritability, depression or anxiety that rapidly resolves after menses, often impairing work, home life, and relationships. Current mainstays include selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and a drospirenone ethinyl estradiol oral contraceptive, but only about half respond and many discontinue due to side effects such as sexual dysfunction and fatigue. This leaves demand for non-contraceptive, mechanism-based, cycle-timed options targeting abnormal brain sensitivity to normal hormonal and neuroactive-steroid fluctuations.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- SSRI-alternative for PMDD patients who are nonresponders or intolerant, with comparable symptom response but fewer AEs/discontinuations.
- Non-contraceptive (non-estrogenic) option improving PMDD mood/function without drospirenone/EE restrictions and tolerability/discontinuation burdens.
- Convenient mechanism-targeted luteal-phase therapy for core affective symptoms that also improves physical symptoms (vs current neurosteroid/progesterone-pathway signals with injection burden and limited physical-symptom benefit).

name: Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder
description: Pediatric disorder with chronic irritability and frequent severe temper outbursts (often ages 6–10) that disrupt home, school, and peers; major unmet need is a DMDD specific, approvable therapy since care relies on off label stimulants, antidepressants needing suicidality monitoring, and antipsychotics with high side effect burden and polypharmacy risk.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- DMDD-targeted, FDA-approvable pharmacotherapy that reduces ≥3/week severe outbursts and near-daily irritability in children ≥6 with functional gains across home/school/peers
- Antipsychotic-sparing option for severe irritability/outbursts that avoids pediatric weight gain and sedation
- Simpler, low-monitoring regimen that reduces need for polypharmacy/psychotherapy-heavy approaches and minimizes SSRI suicidality monitoring burden

name: Social anxiety disorder
description: Social anxiety disorder is a common anxiety disorder, often beginning in the teens, marked by intense fear of being judged in social or performance situations that drives avoidance and major impairment. Care relies on psychotherapy and antidepressants, but many patients face slow onset of benefit and incomplete durable control, with roughly one third to one half not achieving sustained remission.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid, as-needed (≤1 hour) symptom control for performance/public-speaking SAD addressing cognitive/emotional symptoms (not just peripheral signs).
- Higher-probability remission for SSRI partial responders/nonresponders without requiring months-long, high-touch CBT add-on care.
- Better-tolerated pharmacotherapy for adolescents/young adults (<30) with lower AE-driven discontinuation and reduced suicidality-monitoring burden.

name: Acquired angioedema
description: Acquired angioedema due to complement 1 inhibitor deficiency is a rare, bradykinin driven swelling disorder of older adults without a family history, causing recurrent non itchy facial or tongue swelling, abdominal attacks, and occasional life threatening laryngeal edema. Standard allergy medications like antihistamines and steroids are usually ineffective, and there is no licensed therapy beyond identifying and treating an underlying autoimmune or lymphoproliferative driver when present. Patients need faster self administered rescue for airway attacks, safer durable prophylaxis, and more etiology directed disease control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Ultra-rapid, fully home-use on-demand control of high-risk laryngeal/airway attacks to avoid ED airway interventions and markedly shorten treated attack duration
- Safer long-term prophylaxis achieving attack-free control without thrombotic/hepatic liabilities of danazol/tranexamic acid
- Etiology-directed therapy for B-cell/autoantibody–driven AAE (e.g., MGUS/NHL/anti–C1-INH) to induce durable remission and reduce need for rescue meds

name: X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency
description: X linked severe combined immunodeficiency is a rare inherited IL2RG driven failure of lymphocyte development where boys may appear healthy at birth but soon face life threatening bacterial viral and fungal infections with thrush diarrhea and failure to thrive unless immunity is restored. Newborn screening increasingly finds asymptomatic infants, but outcomes still hinge on reaching transplant or gene therapy before uncontrolled infection, especially viral. Today’s hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is lifesaving yet often leaves incomplete antibody recovery requiring long term immunoglobulin and relies on genotoxic conditioning with serious late effects, creating demand for safer targeted conditioning and more durable immune reconstitution.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Consistent B‑cell/antibody reconstitution enabling immunoglobulin (IVIG/gamma‑globulin) independence
- Non‑genotoxic conditioning/niche‑opening that still achieves durable engraftment (incl. B‑cell function) without late toxicities
- Rapid infection‑bridging therapies (esp. for viral infection) to restore transplant eligibility and improve outcomes in infants with active infection at HSCT

name: X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism
description: X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism is an ultra-rare inherited movement disorder largely limited to men of Filipino descent, typically starting in early adulthood with parkinsonism followed by spreading dystonia that can impair speech and swallowing and lead to aspiration-related death. Care is mainly symptomatic using oral drugs, botulinum toxin, and neuromodulation, but benefit is limited and swallowing safety can constrain treatment. Key unmet needs are disease-modifying approaches that address the underlying TAF1 splicing defect and safer control of bulbar dystonia and dysphagia.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- TAF1 splice-defect correction to reverse the SVA-in-TAF1 transcription/splicing defect (e.g., reduce TAF1-32i and restore full-length TAF1).
- Swallowing-safe therapy to control bulbar (orolingual/pharyngeal) dystonia–related dysphagia and reduce aspiration pneumonia/early death risk.
- Truly effective, well-tolerated oral symptomatic therapy that outperforms marginal current oral options and avoids anticholinergic/benzodiazepine cognitive/sedation burdens.

name: Thyroid dyshormonogenesis
description: Thyroid dyshormonogenesis is a form of congenital hypothyroidism where the thyroid gland is present but cannot make enough hormone, often detected on newborn screening while babies may initially look well. The stakes are high because delayed treatment can cause preventable neurodevelopmental harm. Levothyroxine replacement is effective but execution is fragile in infants since dosing requires crushed tablets and absorption is easily disrupted by common feeds and supplements. Even with biochemical control, some patients develop lifelong goiter and nodules, creating ongoing surveillance and thyroid cancer management uncertainty.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Tighter early-life thyroid-hormone control to normalize T4 within 1–2 weeks and TSH by 4 weeks while avoiding overtreatment, to prevent residual neurodevelopmental and hearing deficits.
- Feeding-compatible, low-variability infant thyroid-hormone replacement that avoids crushed-tablet prep and absorption interference from soy/iron/calcium.
- Adjunctive/etiology-targeted therapies in genetic goitrous dyshormonogenesis (e.g., TPO/TG defects) to prevent goiter and high lifetime thyroid nodule (± cancer) risk despite levothyroxine.

name: Tic disorder | chronic motor or vocal
description: Childhood-onset tic disorder with motor or vocal tics persisting over a year, often urge-driven and fluctuating, worsened by stress or fatigue and frequently comorbid with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder or obsessive-compulsive disorder. Care is limited by scarce access to Comprehensive Behavioral Intervention for Tics and by antipsychotics that rarely fully suppress tics and can cause weight gain and sedation, creating demand for better tolerated, durable control and scalable behavioral options such as telehealth.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Weight‑neutral, non‑sedating tic pharmacotherapy for pediatric patients to avoid antipsychotic metabolic/somnolence burdens and intensive safety monitoring
- Higher‑efficacy, durable tic control for severe/impairing chronic tics (including patients failing CBIT/current drugs), targeting near‑remission
- Scalable, broadly accessible treatment delivering CBIT‑like benefit without weekly in‑office visits (telehealth/home usable despite limited trained providers)

name: Cataract | Morgagni
description: Morgagnian cataract is the hypermature stage of cataract where the lens cortex liquefies and the dense nucleus sinks, often leaving patients near blind with glare and sometimes acute painful red eye from lens induced secondary glaucoma. Care depends on cataract extraction, but advanced lenses make surgery higher risk and outcomes less predictable. Key unmet needs are safer medical bridging to control intraocular pressure and inflammation while awaiting surgery, and simpler long acting perioperative drug delivery to reduce complex multi drop regimens and noncompliance.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-surgical cataract-clearing pharmacotherapy (e.g., eye drops that reverse lens opacity) to prevent progression to hypermature/Morgagnian cataract.
- Rapid, safer bridge-to-extraction drug regimen for lens-induced/phacolytic glaucoma that stabilizes IOP with less reliance on multi-drug topical + systemic agents.
- Long-acting peri-/post-op anti-infective + anti-inflammatory delivery to replace weeks of postoperative self-administered eye-drop regimens.

name: ACTH-independent macronodular adrenal hyperplasia
description: Rare midlife-onset disorder where both adrenal glands develop macronodules that autonomously overproduce cortisol, often found incidentally or as subclinical hypercortisolism, progressing to Cushing syndrome morbidity. Treatment is a tradeoff between chronic steroidogenesis or receptor-targeted medical therapy that can be limited by side effects and loss of response, and surgery where bilateral adrenalectomy reliably controls cortisol but leaves lifelong adrenal insufficiency. Major unmet need is durable, physiologic cortisol control without permanent adrenal failure, with emerging precision approaches based on aberrant hormone receptors and ARMC5-driven disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Aberrant-receptor precision therapy for receptor-positive PBMAH (ligand suppression or receptor antagonism) to control cortisol and avoid bilateral adrenalectomy/lifelong steroid replacement
- Durable non-surgical cortisol control for ACS/subclinical PBMAH that restores physiologic circadian rhythm (normalize UFC + late-night salivary cortisol) without escape/tolerability limits of current receptor-directed attempts
- ARMC5-stratified disease modification (esp. ARMC5-variant carriers) to reduce long-term relapse/need for contralateral adrenalectomy after unilateral adrenalectomy

name: Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase deficiency
description: Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase deficiency is an inherited neurotransmitter disorder where DDC variants impair dopamine and serotonin production, with severe infant-onset feeding problems, hypotonia, oculogyric crises, developmental delay, movement disorder, and autonomic instability. Current disease-modifying gene therapy requires stereotactic neurosurgery with infusion into the putamen and is indicated from 18 months, leaving major unmet needs for earlier, lower-burden central nervous system delivery and more complete control of persistent autonomic and serotonergic symptoms.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Disease-modifying therapy usable in very young infants (≤16–18 months)/pre–skull maturity to prevent early severe neurodevelopmental loss
- Non-neurosurgical (lower-burden) CNS delivery that avoids stereotactic brain surgery and reduces procedure-related serious risks
- Adjunct/next-gen therapies that eliminate persistent symptoms (e.g., autonomic/mood symptoms, oculogyric crises) and achieve higher functional outcomes (standing/walking) beyond partial motor milestone gains

name: Periampullary cancer
description: Rare periampullary malignancy near the ampulla of Vater often presenting with obstructive jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale stools, weight loss, and abdominal or back pain. Even after potentially curative resection, 30 to 50 percent recur and adjuvant therapy remains poorly defined and hard to deliver after Whipple recovery. Key needs are more effective, tolerable perioperative systemic options and biomarker guided treatments for subsets such as human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 amplified disease about 13 percent and microsatellite instability high or mismatch repair deficient tumors about 2 to 6 percent.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Perioperative systemic therapy that reduces the ~40–50% post‑R0 recurrence risk (DFS/OS) and is deliverable despite low adjuvant chemo initiation/completion after Whipple.
- HER2‑targeted therapy for the ~13% ERBB2/HER2+ subgroup to improve ORR vs chemotherapy in metastatic disease.
- Checkpoint immunotherapy for MSI‑H/dMMR tumors (~2–6%) to achieve durable responses (ORR/DoR).

name: Obesity | sarcopenic
description: Sarcopenic obesity is the coexistence of excess fat mass and low muscle mass and function, common in older adults and linked to mobility loss, disability, frailty, falls, and higher metabolic risk. Treatment is hampered by non-uniform definitions and by the weight loss tradeoff where modern incretin-based obesity drugs can reduce fat-free mass, worsening weakness. The priority is muscle-sparing fat loss with meaningful functional gains measured by endpoints such as grip strength and walking speed.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Muscle-sparing fat-loss drugs for older adults with sarcopenic obesity that deliver ~10–15% weight/fat loss without DXA lean-mass decline and with improved gait speed/grip strength.
- Function-first therapies that improve frailty/disability (e.g., modified PPT, 400‑m walk gait speed, 6‑minute walk) rather than body composition alone in high-risk obese seniors.
- Geriatric-tolerable, lower-burden pharmacotherapy that reduces reliance on intensive diet/exercise programs while avoiding tolerability issues of current obesity drugs (e.g., GI side effects, fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption).

name: Obesity
description: Obesity is a chronic disease of excess body fat, defined in adults as body mass index 30 or higher, that drives major cardiometabolic and mechanical complications including type 2 diabetes, heart disease, sleep apnea, and osteoarthritis. Today’s leading medicines can produce meaningful weight loss but are limited by gastrointestinal side effects and treatment discontinuation, substantial weight regain after stopping therapy, and loss of lean mass. A key frontier is approaches that make weight loss more durable and tolerable while preferentially reducing fat and preserving muscle.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable weight-loss maintenance without rebound after stopping/pausing GLP-1 therapy
- Lean-mass–sparing weight loss (preserve skeletal muscle/strength while reducing fat)
- High-efficacy obesity drugs with markedly better tolerability (lower GI AEs/discontinuations) and simpler administration than weekly injectables (e.g., oral/less titration)

name: Allergic rhinitis
description: Allergic rhinitis is an allergen triggered immunoglobulin E mediated inflammatory disease causing sneezing, runny or blocked nose and itchy watery eyes, with nasal obstruction often the most burdensome symptom due to sleep disruption and daytime somnolence. Current sprays and antihistamines relieve symptoms but do not modify the underlying disease and are limited by side effects and adherence, while disease modifying immunotherapy typically requires years of treatment and supervised administration, leaving a need for more durable, convenient control of congestion and broader symptom burden.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid-onset relief of nasal congestion in moderate–severe patients inadequately controlled on INCS/antihistamines, with improvement on congestion endpoints (e.g., TNSS congestion, PNIF) within ≤30 minutes and sleep/function benefit.
- Longer-acting, as‑needed-compatible regimens that improve real-world adherence/satisfaction while reducing limiting AEs (sedation/performance impairment; bitter taste/epistaxis/somnolence).
- Short-course, safer, lower-burden allergen immunotherapy that delivers durable benefit without ≥3 years of therapy and without SCIT supervision/30‑minute post-dose observation requirements.

name: African trypanosomiasis
description: Human African trypanosomiasis is a tsetse transmitted parasitic infection in rural sub Saharan Africa that is often diagnosed late as subtle early symptoms progress to fatal central nervous system disease with sleep disturbance and neuropsychiatric decline. Care is constrained by hard to scale diagnosis and staging that can require lumbar puncture and by treatments needing supervised fed dosing or intravenous infusions, with toxicity concerns in some forms. The key unmet need is a safe stage agnostic child friendly single visit oral cure that can be delivered at primary care level without cerebrospinal fluid staging.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Ultra-simple oral cure (ideally single-dose) effective in severe stage-2 g-HAT (CSF WBC ≥100/µL) to avoid NECT and fexinidazole fed/DOT constraints
- Safer, easier (preferably oral) regimen for acute T. b. rhodesiense HAT (both stages) to replace suramin/melarsoprol reliance
- Age/weight-appropriate oral therapies for children <6 years or <20 kg, reducing dependence on lumbar-puncture CSF staging

name: Aortic dissection
description: Aortic dissection is an immediately life threatening tear in the aorta that splits the vessel wall, typically causing sudden severe tearing chest or back pain and rapid early mortality. Care is time critical blood pressure and heart rate control with intravenous beta blockers and, for ascending dissections, emergency surgery, but survivors often face chronic false lumen degeneration with aneurysm risk, lifelong imaging, and repeat endovascular or surgical interventions. Durable therapies that prevent extension, malperfusion, and long term aortic remodeling remain a major unmet need.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Acute disease-modifying pharmacotherapy to prevent dissection expansion/rupture beyond BP/HR “anti-impulse” control.
- Targeted adjunct drug therapy for acute Type A dissection patients with malperfusion syndrome to prevent end-organ failure and improve perioperative outcomes.
- Post-acute/chronic therapy for Type B dissection survivors with patent false lumen to drive durable false-lumen thrombosis/positive remodeling and reduce aortic growth/reintervention.

name: Amusia
description: Amusia is a brain based disorder of music perception or production marked by impaired fine grained pitch perception, often lifelong in congenital cases and sometimes following stroke. Patients struggle to recognize familiar tunes without lyrics or detect out of tune singing, and some also have difficulty interpreting speech intonation and emotional prosody. There are no established effective treatments, with care limited to training based approaches that show early but task specific gains, leaving a need for scalable central nervous system active or neuroplasticity driven interventions with durable real world benefit.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- CNS-active therapy to improve fine-grained pitch-error detection (e.g., sub-semitone deviation detection) in congenital amusia
- Therapy to improve subtle speech intonation/emotional-prosody processing deficits in the congenital amusia subset
- Neuroprotective/neurorestorative therapy for acquired post-stroke amusia targeting the right-hemisphere music network (e.g., superior temporal gyrus) to reduce persistent amusia/severity

name: Mucopolysaccharidosis | type III
description: Mucopolysaccharidosis type III (Sanfilippo syndrome) is a childhood onset lysosomal storage disorder in which failure to break down heparan sulfate drives progressive central nervous system dysfunction. Children are often typical at birth, then develop early speech and developmental delay with worsening hyperactivity, aggression, and sleep disruption, followed by relentless neurocognitive decline, loss of function, and premature death. Care is largely supportive because no disease modifying therapy exists, and many emerging approaches still require invasive delivery to the brain, creating a premium on early, brain penetrant treatments that safely slow or halt progression.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Early-start CNS disease modification in children (~age 1–4) to preserve neurodevelopment and prevent/slow plateau→regression
- Non-sedating, metabolically safer control of hyperactivity/aggression and severe sleep disruption vs antipsychotic-based symptom management
- BBB-penetrant systemic CNS therapies that avoid invasive intracerebroventricular delivery and/or frequent infusions

name: Multiple sclerosis | secondary progressive
description: Secondary progressive multiple sclerosis is the phase after relapsing remitting disease when disability becomes continuously present and slowly worsens due to neurodegeneration, with growing problems in mobility and balance, fatigue, cognition, and bladder or bowel function. Current disease modifying therapies largely target inflammatory relapses and have limited impact once progression is relapse independent, leaving a major unmet need for treatments that protect nerves, repair myelin, and restore function, including for non active progressive disease.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Neuroprotective/anti-PIRA therapies that slow relapse-independent disability progression in non-active SPMS.
- Remyelinating/restorative or symptomatic agents that deliver meaningful ambulation improvement (e.g., T25FW/MSWS-12), not just slowed decline.
- High-efficacy DMTs with lower long-term immunosuppression and simpler use (avoid genotyping/titration, infusion reactions/monitoring, boxed-warning risks).

name: Tinea cruris
description: Tinea cruris is a superficial fungal infection of the groin causing an itchy, scaly rash that spreads from the groin crease to the upper thigh and typically spares the scrotum and penis. Most cases clear in 1 to 3 weeks with topical antifungals, but rising terbinafine resistant Trichophyton indotineae and steroid misuse can worsen or prolong disease, creating demand for short course, high adherence, steroid sparing regimens.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- New topical/oral antifungals that reliably cure terbinafine‑resistant *Trichophyton indotineae* tinea cruris (including cases with azole resistance/relapse).
- Short‑course, high‑adherence regimens (once‑daily, ≤2 weeks) that still achieve durable “complete cure” (symptom resolution + mycologic negativity).
- Steroid‑sparing antifungal approaches that control inflammation/pruritus without driving inappropriate topical corticosteroid use.

name: Herpes zoster
description: Shingles (herpes zoster) is reactivation of lifelong latent varicella zoster virus in nerve cells, increasingly common after age 50, causing prodromal localized pain or itching followed by a unilateral dermatomal vesicular rash that typically heals in 2 to 4 weeks. The key unmet need is preventing and better treating postherpetic neuralgia, chronic pain persisting more than 90 days that affects about 10% to 18% of patients, given the narrow 72 hour antiviral treatment window, limited evidence for later starts, and tolerability limiting neuropathic pain drugs such as gabapentin. Prevention remains imperfect in immunocompromised patients.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Higher-efficacy shingles prevention for immunocompromised adults (e.g., autologous HCT recipients) where current Shingrix/RZV effectiveness can be ~64–68%.
- Oral acute-shingles antivirals with proven benefit when started >72 hours after rash onset (late presenters).
- Better-tolerated post-herpetic neuralgia pain control for older adults with materially lower CNS adverse effects than gabapentin.

name: Human immunodeficiency virus infection
description: HIV is a chronic viral infection that destroys CD4 T lymphocytes and progressively weakens immunity, often remaining clinically silent during latency. Antiretroviral therapy suppresses viral load and prevents progression but does not cure because latent reservoirs persist and can drive rebound if treatment stops. Key unmet needs include durable therapy free remission or functional cure approaches, more forgiving long acting maintenance options, and effective salvage therapies for heavily treatment experienced patients with multidrug resistant virus where full suppression may be difficult.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Durable ART-free remission via reservoir elimination/control (extend time-to-viral-rebound after ART interruption)
- Ultra-long-acting, high-forgiveness maintenance regimens to reduce daily pill burden/visits and mitigate rebound/resistance risk from missed doses
- Novel-mechanism salvage options for heavily treatment-experienced/multidrug-resistant HIV with limited fully active agents and cumulative toxicity constraints

name: Cushing's syndrome
description: Rare endocrine disorder of chronic cortisol excess, typically in adults 30 to 50 and more often women, causing characteristic weight gain and skin changes plus muscle weakness and high cardiometabolic and infection risk. It is frequently missed because symptoms mimic common conditions, and even after biochemical control many patients have persistent complications and long lasting quality of life impairment. Current medical options can be burdensome and require intensive monitoring, leaving a need for earlier diagnosis and safer, more durable disease modifying control that improves long term outcomes.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Safer long‑term cortisol lowering with reduced monitoring burden (avoid adrenal insufficiency/QT–ECG/electrolyte or liver-toxicity monitoring seen with current agents)
- Metabolic‑comorbidity–optimized therapy for patients with T2D/IGT ± uncontrolled HTN without hypokalemia or major hyperglycemia tradeoffs
- Post‑remission symptom/QoL and cognition restoration beyond biochemical remission

name: Cushing syndrome | ectopic
description: Ectopic Cushing syndrome is life threatening hypercortisolism caused by an adrenocorticotropic hormone secreting tumor outside the pituitary, often in the lung, that may be malignant and metastatic before it is recognized. Patients can present abruptly with severe low potassium, hypertension, muscle weakness, and weight loss rather than classic cushingoid features. Care is constrained by the need for rapid, titratable cortisol control, which is often only achievable with intensive care unit based intravenous therapy, and by oral options that can worsen electrolyte and fluid issues or are hard to monitor. Better outpatient ready rescue and tumor localization remain key needs.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Rapid “rescue” cortisol control outside the ICU (avoiding etomidate-style ICU-only infusion with q4–8h cortisol titration)
- Mineralocorticoid-sparing cortisol suppression that avoids DOC buildup to reduce hypokalemia/edema/hypertension in patients with severe electrolyte/BP derangements
- GR modulation with objective, titratable monitoring and lower hypokalemia burden vs mifepristone (where cortisol is not a reliable biomarker)

name: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis | type 3
description: CLN3 disease is an inherited neurodegenerative disorder with onset around ages 4 to 8, marked by retinal degeneration leading to blindness by late childhood or adolescence plus progressive cognitive decline, movement and speech impairment, and seizures. Care is largely symptomatic with no approved disease modifying therapy, creating a premium on interventions that preserve vision early and slow central nervous system degeneration.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Vision-preserving therapy to delay progression to complete blindness after childhood-onset cone‑rod dystrophy.
- Disease-modifying CNS therapy to slow multi-domain neurodegeneration and preserve ambulation/independence.
- Better-tolerated therapeutics to reduce seizures and psychiatric/behavioral symptoms beyond current symptomatic meds.

name: Meningioma
description: Meningioma is a usually slow growing tumor of the meninges, often found incidentally in older, disproportionately female patients. When symptomatic it causes mass effect such as headaches, seizures, and focal neurologic deficits. Management is largely observation, surgery, and radiotherapy, leaving a major unmet need in recurrent or higher grade disease where systemic therapy remains experimental and outcomes after surgery and radiation failure are poor. Peritumoral brain edema can drive morbidity, and steroids have uncertain benefit with meaningful toxicity, creating demand for steroid sparing control.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Systemic disease control for surgery/RT‑refractory recurrent meningioma that exceeds historical PFS‑6 benchmarks (esp. WHO grade II/III ≥26% PFS‑6).
- Biomarker-/genomics-selected targeted therapy for defined subgroups (e.g., SMO/AKT/NF2/CDK alterations) rather than empiric salvage.
- Steroid-sparing anti–peritumoral-edema therapies to improve symptoms/QoL while reducing corticosteroid toxicity (with steroid use reduction as an endpoint).

name: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome
description: Advanced HIV disease (AIDS) is profound immune suppression, typically CD4 below about 200 cells/mm3, leading to opportunistic infections such as tuberculosis, Pneumocystis pneumonia and cryptococcal meningitis, plus wasting. Even after starting antiretroviral therapy, late presenters have high early mortality driven by tuberculosis, severe bacterial infections and cryptococcal disease. Key unmet needs include faster diagnosis and linkage, simpler regimens amid drug interactions like rifampin, and safer easier to deliver treatments for cryptococcosis that avoid amphotericin toxicity and intensive monitoring.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Simplified single-product “bridge” anti-infective strategy at ART initiation for advanced HIV (CD4 <100–200) to reduce early post-ART mortality from TB/cryptococcus/severe bacterial infections.
- All-oral cryptococcal meningitis induction regimen (no amphotericin) that maintains efficacy while eliminating nephrotoxicity/electrolyte/anaemia monitoring burden.
- Once-daily fixed-dose ART compatible with rifampicin-based TB therapy, avoiding twice-daily dolutegravir add-on dosing and complex ARV–TB drug–drug interaction management.

name: Mucopolysaccharidosis | type IVA
description: Morquio A syndrome is an ultra-rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease caused by GALNS deficiency, leading to keratan sulfate accumulation primarily in cartilage and progressive skeletal dysplasia. Children are typically normal at birth then develop short stature, joint hypermobility, and a waddling gait with frequent falls while cognition is usually preserved. Care includes weekly multi-hour intravenous elosulfase alfa infusions that carry hypersensitivity risk, yet enzyme replacement does not adequately reach or reverse cartilage and bone disease, leaving major unmet need for more effective skeletal targeting and less burdensome, better tolerated treatment.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Cartilage/bone‑penetrant GALNS therapy that meaningfully improves skeletal deformities and growth outcomes (especially with early childhood treatment)
- Less disruptive alternative to weekly 3.5–4.5h IV elosulfase alfa infusions (e.g., longer‑acting and/or self‑administered) while preserving functional gains
- Improved tolerability with lower hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis and respiratory complication risk, reducing premedication/monitoring burden

name: Mucopolysaccharidosis | type I-H
description: Hurler syndrome (severe mucopolysaccharidosis type I) is an infant onset lysosomal storage disorder caused by IDUA deficiency and glycosaminoglycan accumulation, leading to rapid multisystem decline with progressive cardiorespiratory, skeletal, and neurocognitive disease and death often by age 10 if untreated. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is standard but limited by complications and incomplete benefit, especially for skeletal and joint disease, corneal clouding, and cardiac involvement. Enzyme replacement requires weekly intravenous infusions, carries anaphylaxis risk, and provides little central nervous system benefit due to the blood brain barrier, leaving a premium on durable brain directed disease modifying delivery.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Non-HSCT neurocognitive protection via BBB-penetrant or intrathecal CNS enzyme delivery (IV ERT doesn’t treat CNS disease)
- Durable prevention/major reduction of progressive dysostosis multiplex and mobility loss that persists despite HSCT
- Safer, lower-burden chronic systemic therapy to avoid HSCT morbidity/mortality and weekly long IV infusions with anaphylaxis risk

name: Maternally inherited diabetes and deafness
description: Maternally inherited diabetes and deafness is a mitochondrial disorder, most often from the m.3243A>G MT-TL1 variant, where progressive high tone hearing loss typically precedes non obese adult onset diabetes driven by insulin deficiency, often progressing to insulin dependence and complicated by retinal and kidney disease. Care is largely extrapolated from general diabetes practice with limited disease specific trial evidence and mitochondrial safety constraints such as avoiding metformin due to lactic acidosis risk, leaving a premium on mitochondria safe glycemic control and strategies that preserve hearing and prevent multisystem decline.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Otoprotective disease modification to prevent/slow progressive high‑frequency hearing loss and delay need for bilateral hearing aids/cochlear implantation.
- Beta‑cell–preserving, mitochondria‑safe glycemic control in lean m.3243A>G patients to delay rapid progression to insulin dependence while avoiding metformin.
- Mitochondrial disease–modifying therapy beyond glucose lowering that improves fatigue and functional performance (and broader multisystem involvement).

name: Mucopolysaccharidosis | type VI
description: Mucopolysaccharidosis type VI (Maroteaux Lamy syndrome) is a progressive childhood onset lysosomal storage disease causing skeletal deformities and contractures, short stature, airway disease with sleep apnea, cardiac valve disease, hepatosplenomegaly, and corneal clouding with vision loss while cognition is typically preserved. Enzyme replacement therapy requires weekly 4+ hour intravenous infusions and carries anaphylaxis risk, yet has limited impact in hard to reach compartments such as cornea, cartilage and bone, and heart valves, leaving a premium on safer, more durable disease modifying approaches including gene therapy and oral glycosaminoglycan lowering strategies.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- ARSB-restoring therapies with penetration into poorly vascularized cartilage/bone and cardiac valves to improve joint ROM/growth and reverse valve stenosis/hypertrophy beyond IV galsulfase.
- Cornea-targeted treatments that prevent/reverse corneal clouding and improve visual function (e.g., densitometry/BCVA), reducing reliance on corneal transplantation.
- Less burdensome and safer alternatives to weekly ≥4-hour IV ERT that reduce infusion reactions and anaphylaxis risk (ideally less frequent or non-IV).

name: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and thrombosis syndrome
description: Immune mediated reaction to unfractionated or low molecular weight heparin where antibodies to platelet factor 4 and heparin trigger thrombocytopenia but a dangerous hypercoagulable state, often after perioperative prophylaxis, causing deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism. Management hinges on stopping heparin and starting a non heparin anticoagulant, yet care is constrained by intravenous regimens, monitoring and renal or hepatic dose complexity, while severe autoimmune, heparin independent cases still lack evidence based immunomodulatory options.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Regulator-approved fixed-dose oral non-heparin anticoagulant for acute HITTS enabling monitoring-free outpatient treatment in clinically stable patients
- Acute HITTS anticoagulant with predictable PK/PD across severe renal and hepatic impairment (ICU/dialysis/liver dysfunction) without continuous IV infusion or complex dose adjustments
- Targeted immunomodulator that rapidly blocks heparin-independent anti-PF4 platelet activation for autoimmune/spontaneous/refractory HITTS to reduce thrombosis/bleeding management tradeoffs

name: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
description: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is a common childhood-onset neurodevelopmental condition marked by persistent inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that impairs school or work performance and relationships. Care often relies on stimulant medications, but many are Schedule II controlled substances with misuse and diversion risk and can cause appetite suppression, weight loss, slowed pediatric growth, and insomnia. Achieving reliable all-day symptom control without sleep disruption or rebound effects remains a key unmet need, especially for long-term pediatric treatment.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Fast-onset, non–Schedule II ADHD option for patients at diversion/substance-misuse risk
- Pediatric long-term therapy that is growth/appetite/weight neutral
- Once-daily treatment with true late-afternoon/early-evening symptom control without insomnia-driving afternoon redosing

name: Multiple sclerosis | relapsing remitting
description: Relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis is an immune mediated central nervous system disease in which the immune system attacks myelin, causing episodic neurologic symptoms in young adults such as vision changes, sensory loss, imbalance, fatigue, and cognitive slowing. Current anti inflammatory disease modifying therapies reduce relapses but many patients still accumulate disability between attacks through relapse independent progression, while fatigue and cognition remain poorly controlled. High efficacy immunotherapies can bring serious infection risks and monitoring burden. The major unmet need is safe, durable neuroprotection and remyelination that preserves function and prevents long term degeneration.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Remyelination/neuroprotection to slow disability progression independent of relapses (PIRA) and promote recovery from demyelinating injury.
- Therapies with clinically meaningful improvements in fatigue and cognitive processing speed (e.g., MFIS and SDMT).
- High-efficacy relapse/lesion control with better safety and less monitoring/REMS burden than current high-efficacy DMTs (e.g., lower PML/infection/hypogammaglobulinemia risk).

name: Austism spectrum disoder | level 1
description: Autism spectrum disorder Level 1 is an early onset neurodevelopmental condition marked by social communication difficulties, restricted interests and rigid routines despite functional language. Without supports, impairments are noticeable and daily life is often limited by poor cognitive flexibility such as difficulty switching activities. Care is dominated by multi setting behavioral and educational services because no medication treats core symptoms, and drugs used for associated behaviors can add meaningful burdens such as weight gain and sedation, leaving a clear need for scalable, well tolerated treatments that improve core functioning.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- Drug that improves core social-communication impairment (±RRBs) in ASD Level 1, demonstrated on standardized endpoints (e.g., SRS-2, Vineland).
- Weight-neutral, low-sedation pharmacotherapy for ASD-associated irritability/aggression/ADHD-target symptoms vs current antipsychotics.
- Pharmacologic adjuncts that reduce reliance on highly intensive early-intervention schedules and have evidence/approval for children <6 years.

name: Menorrhagia
description: Menorrhagia (heavy menstrual bleeding) is menstrual bleeding heavy enough to disrupt daily functioning, often with frequent pad or tampon changes, prolonged periods and large clots, and can cause iron deficiency anemia with fatigue or shortness of breath. Causes are heterogeneous including fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis, ovulatory dysfunction and bleeding disorders, and treatment ranges from medications to ablation or fertility ending hysterectomy, leaving unmet need for consistent diagnosis and durable, well tolerated, cause directed bleeding control and standardized care pathways.
keyUnmetNeeds:
- More convenient nonhormonal, fertility-preserving therapy (trying-to-conceive patients) with tranexamic-acid–like bleeding control but reduced in-menses multi-dose burden
- Durable medical therapy for fibroid-associated HMB (esp. fibroids >3 cm) without 24-month bone-loss–driven treatment limits
- Safer nonhormonal bleeding-control option for patients with thrombotic risk and/or GI-risk comorbidities where tranexamic acid/NSAIDs are contraindicated or poorly tolerated
